        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
             ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery(query)) {
            display(result);
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("   error: " + ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

    // search for an article by its name: the name is the value of a parameter
    private static void searchWithParameter(String name) {
        IO.println("[" + name + "]");
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD);
             PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                     "select id, name, price from articles where name = ?")) {
            statement.setString(1, name);
            try (ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery()) {
                display(result);
            }
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("   error: " + ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

    // display of the result of a select
    private static void display(ResultSet result) throws SQLException {
        int nbRows = 0;
        while (result.next()) {
            IO.println("   " + result.getInt(1) + " " + result.getString(2) + " "
                    + result.getBigDecimal(3));
            nbRows++;
        }
        IO.println("   " + nbRows + " row(s)");
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc05
1 - query built by concatenation
[bike] -> select id, name, price from articles where name = 'bike'
   1 bike 500.00
   1 row(s)
[diver's oxygen tanks] -> select id, name, price from articles where name = 'diver's oxygen tanks'
   error: You have an error in your SQL syntax; check the manual that corresponds to your MySQL server version for the right syntax to use near 's oxygen tanks'' at line 1
[x' or '1'='1] -> select id, name, price from articles where name = 'x' or '1'='1'
   1 bike 500.00
   2 pump 10.00
   3 bow 600.00
   4 arrows - set of 6 100.00
   5 diving suit 300.00
   6 diver's oxygen tanks 120.00
   6 row(s)

2 - parameterized query
[bike]
   1 bike 500.00
   1 row(s)
[diver's oxygen tanks]
   6 diver's oxygen tanks 120.00
   1 row(s)
[x' or '1'='1]
   0 row(s)
  • line 20: three names that a user might type: a regular name, a name containing an apostrophe, and malicious text;
  • line 29: the first search method inserts the name into the query text (line 30), executed by a standard [Statement]:
    • row 3 of the results: with a regular name, everything works fine;
    • line 6: the apostrophe in the name prematurely terminates the SQL string; the query is invalid (line 7). An article whose name contains an apostrophe cannot be found;
    • line 8: the user entered text containing apostrophes placed in such a way as to produce a valid query, but for which the condition [name = 'x' or '1'='1'] is true for all rows: the query returns the entire table (line 15). If the query were verifying a username and password, the same process would allow the user to log in without knowing the password. With a driver that accepts multiple SQL commands in a single query, the user could even add a command of their choice after a semicolon, such as a [delete]. Connector/J rejects this by default (setting [allowMultiQueries=false]), which limits the scope of the injection without eliminating it;
  • Line 42: The second method uses a parameterized query (lines 45–47). The parameter value is never interpreted as "SQL"; it is simply data, regardless of its content. The name with an apostrophe is found (line 22 of the results), and the malicious text is simply the name of an article that does not exist (line 25).

One could “neutralize” the apostrophes by doubling them, but the rules depend on DBMS, and it’s easy to overlook a case. The rule is simple: values provided by the user (or any external source) must never be concatenated with the text of a SQL request; we always use a PreparedStatement and parameters. The interactive program [Jdbc01.java] does not follow this rule by its very nature: it executes the SQL commands typed by the user. It is an administrator tool, not an example to follow.

docs.title: 10.6.1. General Information
docs.text:
A transaction is a sequence of SQL commands executed “atomically”:

  • either all operations succeed;
  • or one of them fails, in which case all preceding operations are rolled back.

Ultimately, either all operations in a transaction are successfully applied, or none are. The classic example is a bank transfer: the debit from one account and the credit to another must both be completed or neither at all. When the application itself controls the transaction, it commits it with a [COMMIT] command or rolls it back with a [ROLLBACK] command.

In our previous examples, we did not use a transaction. And yet there were transactions, because in a DBMS, a SQL command is always executed within a transaction. If the application does not start an explicit transaction itself, the DBMS uses an implicit transaction. There are then two cases:

  • each SQL command is part of a transaction, opened by the DBMS before the command and committed afterward. This is referred to as autocommit mode. It behaves as if the application were creating a transaction for each SQL command;
  • DBMS is not in autocommit mode: it begins an implicit transaction with the first SQL command issued outside a transaction and allows the application to complete it. All subsequent SQL commands are part of this implicit transaction, which can end due to various events (connection closure, start of a new transaction, etc.), according to rules specific to DBMS. This mode should be avoided.

JDBC enforces the first case: a JDBC connection is in autocommit mode when it is opened, regardless of the setting for DBMS (MySQL, with the InnoDB storage engine used by default, is also in autocommit mode).

The SQL commands from different users execute simultaneously, within transactions that run in parallel. Operations performed by one transaction may affect those performed by another. There are four levels of isolation between transactions from different users:

  • Read Uncommitted;
  • Read Committed;
  • Repeatable Read;
  • Serializable.

Read Uncommitted

This isolation level is also known as “Dirty Read.” Here is an example of what can happen in this mode:

  • A user named U1 starts a transaction on table T;
  • a user named U2 starts a transaction on the same table T;
  • user U1 modifies rows in table T but has not yet committed the changes;
  • user U2 “sees” these changes and makes decisions based on what they see;
  • User U1 rolls back their transaction using [ROLLBACK].

In step 4, user U2 made a decision based on data that later turned out to be incorrect.

Read Committed

This isolation level avoids the previous pitfall: in step 4, user U2 does not “see” the changes made by user U1 to table T. They will only see them after U1 has committed their transaction with a [COMMIT]. In this mode, however, the following situation may occur:

  • a user U1 starts a transaction on table T;
  • a user U2 starts a transaction on the same table T;
  • user U2 executes a [select] to calculate the average of column C for rows in T that meet a certain condition;
  • user U1 modifies ([update]) certain values in column C of T and commits the changes ([commit]);
  • User U2 repeats the same [select] as in step 3. They discover that the average of column C has changed due to the modifications made by U1.

User U2 now sees only the changes committed by U1, but while still within the same transaction, two identical operations yield different results. This situation is called a “non-repeatable read.” It is problematic for anyone who wants a consistent view of table T.

Repeatable Read

In this isolation level, a user is guaranteed to obtain the same results from database reads as long as they remain within the same transaction. They work on a “snapshot” of the data that does not reflect changes made by other transactions, even if those changes have been committed. They will only see those changes once they have completed their own transaction.

This isolation level is not yet perfect in theory: another transaction may add ([insert]) rows that satisfy the condition in step 3, which would change the result of a subsequent read. These rows are called “phantom reads.” This is the default isolation level for MySQL (InnoDB), which also prevents phantom reads for simple reads.

Serializable

In this isolation mode, transactions are completely isolated from one another: the result of two transactions executed simultaneously is the same as if they had been executed one after the other. To achieve this, the DBMS locks the data being read and causes transactions that attempt to modify it to wait (or fail). This level reduces parallelism and, consequently, performance.

The four isolation levels are not available in all DBMS instances. The default isolation level is generally Read Committed (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle) or Repeatable Read (MySQL). The desired isolation level can be explicitly specified by the application.

docs.title: 10.6.2. Transaction Management (API)
docs.text:
With JDBC, transactions are managed by the connection. There is no “transaction” object: a connection has at most one active transaction, and all SQL commands executed on that connection are part of it. The relevant methods of the [Connection] interface are as follows:

MethodRole[setAutoCommit][setAutoCommit(false)] exits autocommit mode: the subsequent SQL commands are part of a transaction, which begins with the first of them and ends with [commit] or [rollback]. A new transaction then begins with the next command. [setAutoCommit(true)] returns to autocommit mode, committing the current transaction.[commit]commits the transaction: the results of the SQL commands issued within the transaction become final and visible to other transactions.[rollback]Rolls back the transaction: the results of the SQL commands issued in the transaction are undone.[setSavepoint]Sets a savepoint (a [Savepoint] object) in the current transaction.[rollback(Savepoint)]rolls back the SQL commands executed since the savepoint, without rolling back those that preceded it: the transaction continues.[setTransactionIsolation]sets the transaction isolation level for the connection. It must be called before the start of a transaction.

The isolation level is one of the constants of the [Connection] interface:

ValueMeaning[TRANSACTION_READ_UNCOMMITTED]The transaction can read data written by another transaction that it has not yet committed. Should be avoided.[TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED]The transaction cannot read data written by another transaction that it has not yet committed. However, data read twice in succession within the transaction may change, because another transaction may have modified it in the meantime; another transaction may also have added rows (ghost rows).[TRANSACTION_REPEATABLE_READ]The data read by the transaction does not change until the transaction is complete. In theory, this does not prevent another transaction from adding rows.[TRANSACTION_SERIALIZABLE]Everything behaves as if the transaction were running alone. This reduces performance because transactions no longer run in parallel.

A connection that has exited autocommit mode must be closed after the transaction has been committed or rolled back. If it is closed while a transaction is in progress, the result depends on the driver (MySQL Connector/J rolls it back): you must always explicitly commit a transaction.

docs.title: 10.6.3. The sample program
docs.text:
The program [Jdbc06.java] demonstrates the effect of a transaction:

package jdbc;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Savepoint;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.List;

// transactions
public class Jdbc06 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String USER = "root";
    private static final String PASSWORD = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        IO.println("JDBC URL of the database: [" + URL + "]");

        // two articles with the same name: the UNQ_NAME uniqueness constraint will reject the second one
        List<Article> articles = List.of(new Article(0, "article", new BigDecimal("100"), 10, 1),
                new Article(0, "article", new BigDecimal("200"), 20, 2));

        try {
            // 1 - insertion without an explicit transaction
            IO.println("\nInsertion without a transaction...");
            executeUpdate("delete from articles");
            try {
                insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articles);
            } catch (SQLException ex) {
                IO.println("Database access error (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
            }
            displayArticles();

            // 2 - the same thing in a transaction
            IO.println("\nInsertion in a transaction...");
            executeUpdate("delete from articles");
            insertArticlesInTransaction(articles);
            displayArticles();

            // 3 - a transaction with a savepoint
            IO.println("\nInsertion in a transaction with a savepoint...");
            executeUpdate("delete from articles");
            insertArticlesWithSavepoint(articles);
            displayArticles();
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("Database access error (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

    // insertion of a list of articles without an explicit transaction (autocommit mode)
    private static void insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(List<Article> articles) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD);
             PreparedStatement statement = createInsertStatement(connection)) {
            for (Article article : articles) {
                insertArticle(statement, article);
            }
        }
    }

    // insertion of a list of articles in a transaction
    private static void insertArticlesInTransaction(List<Article> articles) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD)) {
            // start of the transaction: the autocommit mode is left
            connection.setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED);
            connection.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (PreparedStatement statement = createInsertStatement(connection)) {
                for (Article article : articles) {
                    insertArticle(statement, article);
                }
                // everything went well: the transaction is committed
                connection.commit();
                IO.println("transaction committed...");
            } catch (SQLException ex) {
                // an insertion failed: the transaction is rolled back
                connection.rollback();
                IO.println("transaction rolled back (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
            }
        }
    }

    // insertion in a transaction: the failure of an insertion only cancels what follows
    // the last savepoint
    private static void insertArticlesWithSavepoint(List<Article> articles) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD)) {
            connection.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (PreparedStatement statement = createInsertStatement(connection)) {
                for (Article article : articles) {
                    // a savepoint before each insertion
                    Savepoint beforeInsertion = connection.setSavepoint();
                    try {
                        insertArticle(statement, article);
                    } catch (SQLException ex) {
                        // only the failed insertion is undone
                        connection.rollback(beforeInsertion);
                        IO.println("insertion of [" + article.name() + ", " + article.price() + "] cancelled ("
                                + ex.getMessage() + ")");
                    }
                }
                connection.commit();
                IO.println("transaction committed...");
            } catch (SQLException ex) {
                connection.rollback();
                IO.println("transaction rolled back (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
            }
        }
    }

    // the parameterized statement inserting an article
    private static PreparedStatement createInsertStatement(Connection connection) throws SQLException {
        return connection.prepareStatement(
                "insert into articles(name, price, currentstock, minimumstock) values(?, ?, ?, ?)");
    }

    // insertion of an article with the parameterized statement
    private static void insertArticle(PreparedStatement statement, Article article) throws SQLException {
        statement.setString(1, article.name());
        statement.setBigDecimal(2, article.price());
        statement.setInt(3, article.currentStock());
        statement.setInt(4, article.minimumStock());
        statement.executeUpdate();
        IO.println("article [" + article.name() + ", " + article.price() + "] inserted");
    }

    // execution of an update statement
    private static void executeUpdate(String query) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement()) {
            IO.println("There were " + statement.executeUpdate(query) + " row(s) modified");
        }
    }

    // display of the content of the table
    private static void displayArticles() throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
             ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery(
                     "select id, name, price, currentstock, minimumstock from articles")) {
            IO.println("Content of the [articles] table:");
            while (result.next()) {
                IO.println("  " + result.getInt(1) + " " + result.getString(2) + " "
                        + result.getBigDecimal(3) + " " + result.getInt(4) + " " + result.getInt(5));
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc06
JDBC URL of the database: [jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles]

Insertion without a transaction...
There were 6 row(s) modified
article [article, 100] inserted
Database access error (Duplicate entry 'article' for key 'articles.UNQ_NAME')
Content of the [articles] table:
  7 article 100.00 10 1

Insertion in a transaction...
There were 1 row(s) modified
article [article, 100] inserted
transaction rolled back (Duplicate entry 'article' for key 'articles.UNQ_NAME')
Content of the [articles] table:

Insertion in a transaction with a savepoint...
There were 0 row(s) modified
article [article, 100] inserted
insertion of [article, 200] cancelled (Duplicate entry 'article' for key 'articles.UNQ_NAME')
transaction committed...
Content of the [articles] table:
  11 article 100.00 10 1
  • Lines 24–25: a list of two items with the same name, [article]. The uniqueness constraint [UNQ_NAME] on table [articles] prevents both from existing in the database at the same time: inserting the second one will trigger a [SQLException]. To demonstrate the effect of a transaction, the two items will be inserted in three ways:
    • first, outside of any explicit transaction. Since the connection is in autocommit mode, each insertion is performed in its own transaction. The first item will be inserted, but the second will not;
    • next, within a transaction encompassing both inserts. Because the second insert will fail, the first will be rolled back: ultimately, neither insert will be performed;
    • finally, within a transaction with a savepoint before each insertion: the failure of the second insertion will roll back only itself, and the transaction will be committed with the first;
  • lines 28–36: the table is cleared, then both items are inserted without an explicit transaction. Since we know the second insertion will throw an exception, it is caught by a [try] / [catch]; finally, the table is displayed;
  • lines 38–42: We repeat the same sequence, but with a transaction. This time, the exception is handled in the [insertArticlesInTransaction] method;
  • lines 44–48: the same applies to savepoints;
  • line 55: the insertion method without a transaction. It uses two methods: [createInsertStatement] (line 113), which creates the parameterized insertion command, and [insertArticle] (line 119), which assigns values to the parameters and executes the command;
  • line 65: the method for inserting within a transaction:
    • line 68: the isolation level [TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED], set before the transaction begins;
    • line 69: the connection exits autocommit mode; the transaction will begin with the first insert;
    • lines 71–73: the inserts;
    • line 75: everything went well: the transaction is committed, and the inserts are permanently added to the database;
    • lines 77–80: an insert failed: the transaction is rolled back;
  • line 87: the insertion method using savepoints:
    • line 93: a savepoint is set before each insertion;
    • line 98: if the insertion fails, we roll back to the savepoint: only the failed insertion is rolled back, and the loop continues;
    • Line 103: The transaction is committed, with the inserts successful.

In the results:

  • row 5: displayed by command [delete]: there were six rows in the table;
  • row 7: the exception caused by the second insertion. The message indicates that the constraint [UNQ_NAME] on table [articles] was not met;
  • row 9: the table is not empty: the first record was inserted;
  • row 12: displayed by command [delete]: there was one row in the table;
  • Line 13: The first insertion was successful… within the transaction;
  • line 14: the message displayed when the transaction fails;
  • line 15: the table is empty: the transaction’s [rollback] rolled back the first insertion;
  • lines 19–21: thanks to the savepoints, the second insertion was rolled back and the transaction committed;
  • line 23: the table contains the first item. Its [id] value is 11, not 8: each insertion attempt—even if rolled back or rejected—consumed a value from the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column, and MySQL does not reuse these values.

With MySQL, the failure of a SQL command cancels only that command, and the transaction can continue: the savepoint is therefore not essential here. This is not the case for all DBMS commands: with PostgreSQL, even the slightest error renders the transaction unusable until it is rolled back or until a rollback point is reached. The code with rollback points works with both.

docs.title: 10.7. Queries that return a single value
docs.text:
Some queries return only one value, such as [select count(*) from articles]: a row from a single column. JDBC does not have a specific method for these: you execute the query using [executeQuery] and read the first column of the first row of the result. The program [Jdbc07.java] implements a method for this and demonstrates a few ways to use it:

package jdbc;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.RoundingMode;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;

// queries that return a single value
public class Jdbc07 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String USER = "root";
    private static final String PASSWORD = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            // the single values returned by selects, in the type chosen by the driver
            Object averagePrice = singleValue("select avg(price) from articles");
            IO.println("Average price of the articles = " + averagePrice + " (type " + type(averagePrice) + ")");
            Object nbArticles = singleValue("select count(id) from articles");
            IO.println("Number of articles = " + nbArticles + " (type " + type(nbArticles) + ")");
            Object name = singleValue(
                    "select name from articles where price = (select max(price) from articles)");
            IO.println("Most expensive article = " + name + " (type " + type(name) + ")");
            Object missing = singleValue("select name from articles where price > 10000");
            IO.println("Article of more than 10000 euros: " + missing);
            Object empty = singleValue("select max(price) from articles where price > 10000");
            IO.println("Maximum price beyond 10000 euros: " + empty);

            // the same values in the requested type: the driver does the conversion
            BigDecimal average = singleValue("select avg(price) from articles", BigDecimal.class);
            Integer number = singleValue("select count(id) from articles", Integer.class);
            IO.println("Rounded average = " + average.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)
                    + ", number = " + number);
            // a direct cast fails: count returns a Long and not an Integer
            int n = (int) nbArticles;
            IO.println("n = " + n);
        } catch (SQLException | ClassCastException ex) {
            IO.println(ex.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + ex.getMessage());
        }
    }

    // execution of a select that returns a single value: first column of the first row
    // the result is null if the select returns no row or if the value is SQL NULL
    private static Object singleValue(String query) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
             ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery(query)) {
            return result.next() ? result.getObject(1) : null;
        }
    }

    // the same thing, the value being converted by the driver into the requested type
    private static <T> T singleValue(String query, Class<T> type) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
             ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery(query)) {
            return result.next() ? result.getObject(1, type) : null;
        }
    }

    // the simple name of the class of an object
    private static String type(Object object) {
        return object == null ? "null" : object.getClass().getSimpleName();
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc07
Average price of the articles = 271.666667 (type BigDecimal)
Number of articles = 6 (type Long)
Most expensive article = bow (type String)
Article of more than 10000 euros: null
Maximum price beyond 10000 euros: null
Rounded average = 271.67, number = 6
ClassCastException : class java.lang.Long cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer (java.lang.Long and java.lang.Integer are in module java.base of loader 'bootstrap')
  • Line 48: The method [singleValue] executes the query and returns the first column of the first row via [getObject(1)], or [null] if the query returns no rows (line 52);
  • line 21: the average price of the items. The Java type of the result depends on the SQL type of the value: the average of a [DECIMAL] column is a [BigDecimal], in this case with six decimal places (line 2 of the results);
  • line 23: the number of items. MySQL returns an integer of type [BIGINT], which becomes a [Long] in Java (line 3);
  • lines 25–26: the name of the most expensive item, a string. The query contains a subquery, enclosed in parentheses;
  • line 28: if the query returns no rows, the method returns [null] (line 5);
  • line 30: if the query returns a row whose value is SQL [NULL] (the maximum of an empty set), [getObject] also returns [null] (line 6). Our method therefore does not distinguish between the two cases—no row or a value of [NULL]; if the distinction matters, one must test the result of [next] oneself;
  • line 57: a second, generic version of the method (Chapter 4) receives the desired type in the form of a [Class<T>] object and returns a value of that type. [getObject(1, type)] (line 61) instructs the driver to convert the value to that type;
  • lines 34–35: the driver itself converts the value to the requested type: the average to [BigDecimal], and the number of items ([BIGINT]) to [Integer]. [setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)] rounds the average to two decimal places (line 7);
  • Line 39: A direct conversion fails because the object is a [Long]: The [(int)] conversion of a [Object] requires a [Integer], which is then "unboxed," and a [Long] is not a [Integer]. A [ClassCastException] is initiated (line 8). This code would work with a DBMS whose [count] returns an integer of type [INT], but fails with MySQL: This is an example of the peculiarities of DBMS that JDBC does not hide. Reading using [getInt], [getLong], or [getObject(i, type)], which leaves the conversion to the driver, is safer;
  • line 41: a multiple [catch] clause (Java 7) catches both types of exceptions.

docs.title: 10.8. JDBC is blocking: virtual threads
docs.text:
Chapter 9 showed that I/O operations must not block an application thread in applications serving many users (servers, web services): while a SQL command is executing on the server, the thread that issued it waits. However, JDBC is a blocking API: [getConnection], [executeQuery], [next], [commit]… do not yield control until DBMS has responded. There is no asynchronous version of JDBC: a project for an asynchronous API (ADBA) was abandoned in 2019, and the reactive API, R2DBC—which exists outside of JDK—did not replace JDBC.

Since Java 21, the Java platform’s solution has been the virtual thread (Chapter 8): a lightweight thread, managed by JVM, of which thousands can be created. When a virtual thread is waiting for a response from the network, the JVM sets it aside and frees up the system thread that was executing it, allowing that thread to execute another virtual thread. The code remains sequential and blocking—simple to write and read—but the wait no longer incurs any overhead. Recent JDBC drivers, including Connector/J 9, are written to work with virtual threads, and since Java 24 (JEP 491), a virtual thread waiting in a [synchronized] block no longer monopolizes the system thread.

One limitation remains: the number of connections. A thousand virtual threads querying the database do not have a thousand connections; they share the connections in the pool and wait for a connection to become available. The program [Jdbc08.java] demonstrates this, using a pool HikariCP of four connections:

package jdbc;

import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariConfig;
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.SQLTimeoutException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import javax.sql.DataSource;

// JDBC is blocking: concurrent queries executed by virtual threads
public class Jdbc08 {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        // the data source: a pool of at most 4 connections to the [dbarticles] database
        HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles");
        config.setUsername("root");
        config.setPassword("");
        config.setMaximumPoolSize(4);

        try (HikariDataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource(config)) {
            // 1 - an update statement, in a transaction
            try (Connection connection = dataSource.getConnection()) {
                connection.setAutoCommit(false);
                try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                        "update articles set price = price * 1.1 where price < ?")) {
                    statement.setInt(1, 200);
                    int nbRows = statement.executeUpdate();
                    connection.commit();
                    IO.println(nbRows + " price(s) increased by 10 %");
                }
            }

            // 2 - six concurrent queries, each one in its virtual thread
            long start = System.nanoTime();
            List<Future<Article>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
            try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
                for (int id = 1; id <= 6; id++) {
                    int articleId = id;
                    tasks.add(executor.submit(() -> getArticleSlowly(dataSource, articleId)));
                }
            } // closing the executor waits for the end of the six tasks
            for (Future<Article> task : tasks) {
                IO.println(task.get());
            }
            IO.println("6 one-second queries executed in %.1f s with %d connections"
                    .formatted((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e9, config.getMaximumPoolSize()));

            // 3 - a single value
            try (Connection connection = dataSource.getConnection();
                 Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
                 ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery("select sum(price * currentstock) from articles")) {
                result.next();
                IO.println("Stock value: " + result.getBigDecimal(1) + " euros");
            }

            // 4 - a query blocked by another transaction, abandoned after one second
            // the [blocking] transaction modifies article no. 1 and does not end:
            // the row remains locked
            try (Connection blocking = dataSource.getConnection()) {
                blocking.setAutoCommit(false);
                try (Statement statement = blocking.createStatement()) {
                    statement.executeUpdate("update articles set currentstock = currentstock - 1 where id = 1");
                }
                // another connection wants to modify the same row: it must wait for the end of [blocking]
                long chrono = System.nanoTime();
                try (Connection connection = dataSource.getConnection();
                     Statement statement = connection.createStatement()) {
                    statement.setQueryTimeout(1);
                    statement.executeUpdate("update articles set price = price * 2 where id = 1");
                } catch (SQLTimeoutException ex) {
                    IO.println(ex.getClass().getSimpleName() + " after "
                            + Math.round((System.nanoTime() - chrono) / 1e9) + " s: " + ex.getMessage());
                }
                // the [blocking] transaction was not committed: it is rolled back
                blocking.rollback();
            }
        } catch (SQLException | ExecutionException ex) {
            IO.println("Database access error (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

    // an article read by a query that lasts one second (the MySQL sleep function simulates a slow query)
    private static Article getArticleSlowly(DataSource dataSource, int id) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = dataSource.getConnection();
             PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement("select id, name, price, currentstock, "
                     + "minimumstock, sleep(1) from articles where id = ?")) {
            statement.setInt(1, id);
            try (ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery()) {
                result.next();
                return new Article(result.getInt(1), result.getString(2), result.getBigDecimal(3),
                        result.getInt(4), result.getInt(5));
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc08
3 price(s) increased by 10 %
Article[id=1, name=bike, price=500.00, currentStock=10, minimumStock=5]
Article[id=2, name=pump, price=11.00, currentStock=10, minimumStock=2]
Article[id=3, name=bow, price=600.00, currentStock=4, minimumStock=1]
Article[id=4, name=arrows - set of 6, price=110.00, currentStock=12, minimumStock=20]
Article[id=5, name=diving suit, price=300.00, currentStock=8, minimumStock=2]
Article[id=6, name=diver's oxygen tanks, price=132.00, currentStock=10, minimumStock=5]
6 one-second queries executed in 2.4 s with 4 connections
Stock value: 12550.00 euros
MySQLTimeoutException after 1 s: Statement cancelled due to timeout or client request
  • lines 24–28: configuration of a pool with a maximum of four connections;
  • line 30: the data source [HikariDataSource], closed at the end of the program by the try-with-resources statement;
  • lines 32–41: an update statement within a transaction, using a connection obtained from the pool. The implicit [close] on line 41 returns the connection to the pool. The results show that the three prices below 200 euros were increased by 10% (line 2 of the results);
  • line 93: the [getArticleSlowly] method reads an article in a query that takes one second: the MySQL and [sleep(1)] functions (lines 95–96) wait one second before returning 0. This simulates a slow query;
  • lines 44–56: six article reads, executed simultaneously:
    • line 46: [Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor] (Java 21, Chapter 8) creates an executor that launches each task in a new virtual thread. The executor is closed at the end of the try-with-resources block (line 51), and its method *[close]* (Java 19) waits for all tasks to complete;
    • line 49: Each task is a lambda that returns a [Article]: a *[Callable<Article>]*, whose *[call]* method can throw checked exceptions, in this case the *[SQLException] from *[getArticleSlowly]*. [submit] returns a [Future<Article>]. The lambda uses the copy [articleId]* of the loop variable (line 48), because a lambda can only use local variables that are not modified;
    • lines 52–54: the items are displayed in the order of the tasks. [Future.get] returns the result of the task; if the task threw an exception, [get] launches a [ExecutionException] that encapsulates it (intercepted on line 87). [get] can also throw a [InterruptedException], which [main] declares (line 22);
    • Lines 55–56: Total duration. Six one-second queries executed one after the other would take six seconds; executed simultaneously using six connections, they would take one second. With four connections, it takes about two seconds (line 9 of the results): four virtual threads obtain a connection and execute their requests at the same time, while the other two wait in [getConnection] for a connection to be returned to the pool, then execute theirs. The remaining time is spent opening connections from the pool. A thread that waits too long for a connection (30 seconds by default, setting [connectionTimeout] in HikariCP) receives a [SQLTransientConnectionException];
  • lines 59–64: a single value, the stock value;
  • lines 69–86: Abandoning a query that is taking too long:
    • lines 69–73: a first connection exits autocommit mode and modifies item #1 without completing its transaction. The DBMS has locked the modified row until the end of the transaction;
    • lines 76–79: a second connection attempts to modify the same row. It must wait for the first transaction to complete… which it will not do. [setQueryTimeout(1)] (line 78) limits the command’s execution time to one second: after one second, Connector/J instructs the server to abort the request (command MySQL [KILL QUERY]), and [executeUpdate] triggers a [SQLTimeoutException], in this case from the driver’s [MySQLTimeoutException] class (line 11 of the results). Without this timeout, the query would have waited for the lock timeout of MySQL—50 seconds by default—and then failed;
    • line 85: the [blocking] transaction is never committed; it is rolled back. The connection is then returned to the pool.

Virtual threads offer no benefit to a small console program that performs one task at a time: they do not make a request any faster. But they allow a server application—such as the Spring Boot web services in Chapter 13 (where the [spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true] property is sufficient)—to serve many users at once using ordinary JDBC code. The size of the connection pool then becomes the true control for parallelism with respect to the database.

docs.title: 10.9. Batch Execution
docs.text:
Each execution of a SQL command involves a round trip between the application and the server. When multiple SQL commands need to be executed, they can be sent to DBMS in a single exchange, in the form of a batch. JDBC has supported this since version 2.0:

  • for a [Statement], [addBatch(sql)] adds a SQL command to the batch;
  • for a [PreparedStatement], [addBatch()] adds the current parameter values to the batch: the batch contains the same SQL command executed with different values;
  • [executeBatch] executes the batch and returns an array of integers: the number of rows modified by each command in the batch. If a command fails, it launches a [BatchUpdateException], whose method [getUpdateCounts] returns the results of the executed commands.

The program [Jdbc09.java] uses the following batches:

package jdbc;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.Arrays;

// batch execution: several SQL statements sent to the DBMS in a single exchange
public class Jdbc09 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String USER = "root";
    private static final String PASSWORD = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD)) {
            IO.println("The driver can execute batches: "
                    + connection.getMetaData().supportsBatchUpdates());

            // 1 - a batch of three different update statements
            try (Statement statement = connection.createStatement()) {
                statement.addBatch("insert into articles(name, price, currentstock, minimumstock) "
                        + "values('canoe', 800, 5, 1)");
                statement.addBatch("update articles set currentstock = currentstock + 10 "
                        + "where currentstock < minimumstock");
                statement.addBatch("delete from articles where name = 'pump'");
                int[] nbRows = statement.executeBatch();
                IO.println("Rows modified by each statement: " + Arrays.toString(nbRows)
                        + ", total: " + Arrays.stream(nbRows).sum());
            }

            // 2 - 1000 insertions by a batch of the same parameterized statement, without then with batch rewriting
            insertBatch(URL, 1000);
            insertBatch(URL + "?rewriteBatchedStatements=true", 1000);
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("Database access error (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }

        // 3 - two selects sent in a single exchange: one statement, two successive results
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL + "?allowMultiQueries=true",
                USER, PASSWORD);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement()) {
            statement.execute("select name, currentstock from articles where currentstock < minimumstock + 5;"
                    + "select count(*), sum(price * currentstock) from articles");
            IO.println("Articles to watch:");
            try (ResultSet result = statement.getResultSet()) {
                while (result.next()) {
                    IO.println("  " + result.getString(1) + " : " + result.getInt(2));
                }
            }
            // moving to the next result
            statement.getMoreResults();
            try (ResultSet result = statement.getResultSet()) {
                result.next();
                IO.println(result.getLong(1) + " articles, stock value: " + result.getBigDecimal(2)
                        + " euros");
            }
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("Database access error (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

    // insertion of n articles by a batch, in a transaction, then deletion of these articles
    private static void insertBatch(String url, int n) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, USER, PASSWORD)) {
            connection.setAutoCommit(false);
            long start = System.nanoTime();
            try (PreparedStatement statement = connection.prepareStatement(
                    "insert into articles(name, price, currentstock, minimumstock) values(?, ?, ?, ?)")) {
                for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
                    statement.setString(1, "batch-" + i);
                    statement.setBigDecimal(2, BigDecimal.TEN);
                    statement.setInt(3, i);
                    statement.setInt(4, 0);
                    // the values of the parameters are added to the batch
                    statement.addBatch();
                }
                int[] nbRows = statement.executeBatch();
                connection.commit();
                long duration = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
                IO.println("%d insertions (%s) in %d ms: %s...".formatted(nbRows.length,
                        url.replaceFirst(".*/", ""), duration, Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOf(nbRows, 3))));
            }
            // the table is put back into its previous state
            try (Statement statement = connection.createStatement()) {
                statement.executeUpdate("delete from articles where name like 'batch-%'");
                connection.commit();
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc09
The driver can execute batches: true
Rows modified by each statement: [1, 1, 1], total: 3
1000 insertions (dbarticles) in 2341 ms: [1, 1, 1]...
1000 insertions (dbarticles?rewriteBatchedStatements=true) in 207 ms: [-2, -2, -2]...
Articles to watch:
  bow : 4
  arrows - set of 6 : 22
  canoe : 5
6 articles, stock value: 17200.00 euros
  • lines 21–22: The [supportsBatchUpdates] method in the connection metadata indicates whether the driver can execute batches;
  • Lines 25–34: A batch of three different update commands, added to the batch of a [Statement] by [addBatch]:
    • line 31: the three commands are executed. [executeBatch] returns the number of rows modified by each: one insertion ([canoe]), one update (the stock of arrows, which is below the minimum stock), and one deletion ([pump]);
    • Lines 32–33: [Arrays.toString] displays the array, [Arrays.stream] converts it into a stream of integers ([IntStream]), and [sum] calculates the sum (line 3 of the results);
  • lines 37–38: the method [insertBatch] is called twice, with two different URL instances;
  • line 68: the [insertBatch] method inserts [n] items with a batch:
    • line 70: the insertions are performed in a single transaction, which is also much faster than committing each one individually;
    • Lines 74–81: For each item, the parameters are assigned their values, then [addBatch()] adds these values to the batch;
    • lines 82–83: the batch is executed, then the transaction is committed;
    • lines 84–86: the number of inserts, the duration, and the first three elements of the array returned by [executeBatch] are displayed;
    • lines 89–92: The inserted items are deleted to restore the table to its previous state;
  • Line 4 of the results: With the simple URL, the MySQL driver sends the 1,000 inserts one after another: batch processing adds almost no benefit. Each element in the array is 1;
  • Line 5 of the results: With the [rewriteBatchedStatements=true] parameter of the URL driver, Connector/J rewrites the batch into several [insert into articles(…) values (…), (…), (…)…] commands, each of which inserts numerous rows. Execution is ten times faster. The array elements are then set to -2, the value of the constant [Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO]: the command succeeded, but the driver does not know how many rows each batch element modified. This is an important setting to be aware of: without it, batches are of little use with MySQL;
  • lines 43–64: two [select] commands sent in a single exchange:
    • lines 44–45: the connection is opened with the parameter [allowMultiQueries=true], which allows multiple SQL commands separated by semicolons in a single request. As we have seen, this is disabled by default to limit the scope of SQL injections;
    • lines 47–48: both commands are executed by [execute], which accepts any command;
    • line 50: [getResultSet] returns the result of the first command;
    • line 56: [getMoreResults] moves to the next result (it closes the current result and returns [true] if the next result is a [ResultSet]);
    • line 57: the result of the second query: a row with two columns.

Batches are useful for large-scale inserts and updates (such as data imports). Hibernate (Chapter 11) also supports them.

docs.title: 10.10. Offline mode: CachedRowSet
docs.text:
The offline mode of JDBC is based on the [javax.sql.rowset.CachedRowSet] interface, derived from [ResultSet]: A [CachedRowSet] is a query result copied into memory, which can be traversed in both directions and modified offline, after which the changes are sent back to the database. The program [Jdbc10.java] demonstrates this:

package jdbc;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import javax.sql.rowset.CachedRowSet;
import javax.sql.rowset.RowSetFactory;
import javax.sql.rowset.RowSetProvider;

// disconnected mode: an in-memory copy of the rows, modified offline then sent back to the database
public class Jdbc10 {

    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles";
    private static final String USER = "root";
    private static final String PASSWORD = "";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try {
            // the RowSet factory of the Java platform
            RowSetFactory factory = RowSetProvider.newFactory();
            try (CachedRowSet articles = factory.createCachedRowSet()) {
                // the connection parameters and the query
                articles.setUrl(URL);
                articles.setUsername(USER);
                articles.setPassword(PASSWORD);
                articles.setCommand("select id, name, price, currentstock, minimumstock from articles");
                // the table to update and its primary key (column no. 1)
                articles.setTableName("articles");
                articles.setKeyColumns(new int[]{1});
                // connection, copy of the rows into memory, disconnection
                articles.execute();
                IO.println(articles.size() + " rows copied into memory");

                // offline work: restocking of the out-of-stock articles
                while (articles.next()) {
                    int currentStock = articles.getInt("currentstock");
                    int minimumStock = articles.getInt("minimumstock");
                    if (currentStock < minimumStock) {
                        articles.updateInt("currentstock", minimumStock + 10);
                        articles.updateRow();
                        IO.println("[" + articles.getString("name") + "] : stock " + currentStock + " -> "
                                + articles.getInt("currentstock"));
                    }
                }
                // adding a row: id 0 asks MySQL to generate one
                articles.moveToInsertRow();
                articles.updateInt("id", 0);
                articles.updateString("name", "canoe");
                articles.updateBigDecimal("price", new BigDecimal("800"));
                articles.updateInt("currentstock", 5);
                articles.updateInt("minimumstock", 1);
                articles.insertRow();
                articles.moveToCurrentRow();
                // deletion of the 2nd row
                articles.absolute(2);
                IO.println("deletion of [" + articles.getString("name") + "]");
                articles.deleteRow();

                // the database has not been modified yet
                displayArticles("Database before acceptChanges:");
                // connection, sending of the modifications in a transaction, disconnection
                try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD)) {
                    connection.setAutoCommit(false);
                    articles.acceptChanges(connection);
                }
            }
            displayArticles("Database after acceptChanges:");
        } catch (SQLException ex) {
            IO.println("Database access error (" + ex.getMessage() + ")");
        }
    }

    // display of the content of the table, read in connected mode
    private static void displayArticles(String title) throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(URL, USER, PASSWORD);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
             ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery(
                     "select id, name, price, currentstock, minimumstock from articles")) {
            IO.println(title);
            while (result.next()) {
                IO.println("  " + result.getInt(1) + " " + result.getString(2) + " "
                        + result.getBigDecimal(3) + " " + result.getInt(4) + " " + result.getInt(5));
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=jdbc.Jdbc10
6 rows copied into memory
[arrows - set of 6] : stock 12 -> 30
deletion of [pump]
Database before acceptChanges:
  1 bike 500.00 10 5
  2 pump 10.00 10 2
  3 bow 600.00 4 1
  4 arrows - set of 6 100.00 12 20
  5 diving suit 300.00 8 2
  6 diver's oxygen tanks 120.00 10 5
Database after acceptChanges:
  1 bike 500.00 10 5
  3 bow 600.00 4 1
  4 arrows - set of 6 100.00 30 20
  5 diving suit 300.00 8 2
  6 diver's oxygen tanks 120.00 10 5
  7 canoe 800.00 5 1
  • Lines 23–24: [RowSetProvider.newFactory] (Java 7) returns a factory ([RowSetFactory]) from the various types of RowSet derived from JDK, of which [createCachedRowSet] creates a [CachedRowSet]. A [CachedRowSet] is a resource closed by the try-with-resources statement;
  • lines 26–29: the [CachedRowSet] receives the connection parameters and the query that will populate it;
  • lines 31–32: to be able to commit the changes to the database, it must know the modified table and its primary key—in this case, column 1—[id];
  • line 34: [execute] opens a connection, executes the query, copies all rows of the result into memory, and closes the connection. The rest of the work is done offline;
  • Lines 38–47: A [CachedRowSet] is a [ResultSet]: it is iterated over using [next], and the columns are read using [getXxx]. The [updateXxx] methods modify a column in the current row, and [updateRow] saves the change… to the in-memory copy. The arrow stock, which is below the minimum stock level, is increased to 30 (row 3 of the results);
  • lines 49–56: adding a row. [moveToInsertRow] places the cursor on a special row, the “insertion row,” whose columns are specified by [updateXxx]; [insertRow] adds it to [CachedRowSet], and [moveToCurrentRow] returns the cursor to its previous position. [CachedRowSet] requires a value for all [NOT NULL] columns, including [id]: a value of 0, inserted into a [AUTO_INCREMENT] column, instructs MySQL to generate one;
  • lines 58–60: [absolute(2)] places the cursor on the second line, which is enabled by [CachedRowSet]—a column that can be traversed in any direction—and [deleteRow] deletes it;
  • line 63: the database has not yet been modified (lines 5–11 of the results);
  • Lines 65–68: [acceptChanges] commits the changes to the database: a [update], a [insert], and a [delete], all executed within a transaction that is committed at the end. For each modified row, the implementation of JDK verifies that the database row has not been modified by someone else since it was read (an “optimistic” check); otherwise, it launches a [SyncProviderException]. The parameter-less version of [acceptChanges] opens the connection itself, but leaves it in autocommit mode and then calls [commit], which Connector/J refuses; therefore, it is passed a connection that has exited autocommit mode;
  • line 70: the database has been modified (lines 12–18 of the results).

[CachedRowSet] has the advantage of being a standard API derived from JDK, but its limitations are evident: it manipulates rows and column numbers, not business objects; the modifications are made by an implementation whose SQL we do not fully understand. This is why it is rarely used today: working with in-memory objects and subsequently saving the changes is the domain of ORM frameworks such as Hibernate (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 10.11. Sample Application—Version 6
docs.text:
We’ll revisit the [Tax] sample application. The latest version, version 5, was covered in Chapter 6. It was a three-tier application whose [dao] layer retrieved its data from a text file, a JSON file, or from its own code, and whose layers were integrated by Spring’s dependency injection container. We’re writing a new layer, [dao], that retrieves its data from a database, MySQL:

We reuse the modules from version 5 as-is, via Maven dependencies, and write only what is new: the [dao] layer and the program that integrates the layers.

docs.title: 10.11.1. The database
docs.text:
The tax brackets are stored in the [brackets] table within the MySQL and [dbtaxes] databases, created by the [sql/dbtaxes.sql] script:

-- creation of the database [dbtaxes] of the application [Tax] (version 6)
-- execution: mysql -uroot < dbtaxes.sql

-- the script is written in UTF-8
SET NAMES utf8mb4;

-- the database is recreated on each execution of the script
DROP DATABASE IF EXISTS dbtaxes;
CREATE DATABASE dbtaxes CHARACTER SET utf8mb4 COLLATE utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci;
USE dbtaxes;

-- the table of the tax brackets (2004 scale on 2003 income)
CREATE TABLE brackets (
    id      INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
    limits  DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
    coeffr  DECIMAL(6,3) NOT NULL,
    coeffn  DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO brackets (limits, coeffr, coeffn) VALUES
    (4962, 0, 0),
    (8382, 0.068, 291.09),
    (14753, 0.191, 1322.92),
    (23888, 0.283, 2668.39),
    (38868, 0.374, 4846.98),
    (47932, 0.426, 6883.66),
    (0, 0.481, 9505.54);

-- a user specific to the application, who only has rights on the database [dbtaxes]
CREATE USER IF NOT EXISTS 'admtaxes'@'localhost' IDENTIFIED BY 'pwdtaxes';
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON dbtaxes.* TO 'admtaxes'@'localhost';
  • Lines 13–18: The table [brackets] has four columns: the primary key [id], generated by DBMS, followed by the three columns [limits], [coeffr], and [coeffn], which represent a tax bracket of type [DECIMAL]: these are amounts and coefficients that must be exact. They will be read in Java as [BigDecimal], the field type of the [TaxBracket] record;
  • lines 19–26: the seven brackets of the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, used since the beginning of the course (this is an exercise: the schedule is not up to date). The brackets are listed in ascending order of their thresholds, and the [id] column reflects this order;
  • lines 29–30: creation of a user MySQL [admtaxes], with password [pwdtaxes], who is granted full permissions ([GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES]) on all objects in the database [dbtaxes] ([dbtaxes.*]), and only on those objects. The application will run as this user rather than as the administrator [root]: if the administrator’s password were to be compromised, only the database [dbtaxes] would be at risk. [IF NOT EXISTS] allows the script to be run multiple times.

The script is executed by the administrator:

> mysql -uroot < dbtaxes.sql

then we verify that the user [admtaxes] has access to the brackets (the [-p] option alone prompts for the password, which is not displayed as it is typed):

> mysql -uadmtaxes -p -t dbtaxes -e "select * from brackets"
Enter password: 
+----+----------+--------+---------+
| id | limits   | coeffr | coeffn  |
+----+----------+--------+---------+
|  1 |  4962.00 |  0.000 |    0.00 |
|  2 |  8382.00 |  0.068 |  291.09 |
|  3 | 14753.00 |  0.191 | 1322.92 |
|  4 | 23888.00 |  0.283 | 2668.39 |
|  5 | 38868.00 |  0.374 | 4846.98 |
|  6 | 47932.00 |  0.426 | 6883.66 |
|  7 |     0.00 |  0.481 | 9505.54 |
+----+----------+--------+---------+

docs.title: 10.11.2. The TaxV6 project
docs.text:
Version 6 is a Maven project consisting of two modules, located in the [10-jdbc/TaxV6] folder, which uses three modules from version 5:

java-oct-2026/
  06-architectures/TaxV5/               version 5, reused
    pom.xml                             parent project tax-v5
    tax-dao/                            entities, interface ITaxDao, implementations of version 5
    tax-business/                       layer [business]
    tax-ui/                             layer [ui] (class Dialog) and program of version 5
  10-jdbc/
    sql/
      dbtaxes.sql                       creation script of the database
    TaxV6/
      pom.xml                           parent project tax-v6
      tax-dao-mysql/                    the new layer [dao]
        pom.xml
        src/main/java/tax/dao/
          MySqlTax.java
        src/test/java/tax/dao/
          MySqlTaxTests.java            JUnit tests of the new layer [dao]
      tax-ui-mysql/                     integration of the layers
        pom.xml
        tax.properties
        tax-base.properties
        tax-password.properties
        tax-server.properties
        tax-query.properties
        tax-postgresql.properties
        src/main/java/tax/ui/mysql/
          Main.java

The Version 5 modules are not part of the [TaxV6] project: they are dependencies, such as the JDBC driver or Spring. For Maven to find them, you must first install them in the local Maven repository (the [.m2/repository] folder in the user’s home directory), where Maven stores all the libraries it downloads. This is what the [mvn install] command does, which is entered once and for all in the version 5 folder:

> cd 06-architectures/TaxV5
> mvn install

It compiles the three modules, runs their tests, creates their archives [tax-dao-5.0.jar], [tax-business-5.0.jar], and [tax-ui-5.0.jar], and copies them, along with the [pom.xml] from the parent project, to the local repository under the identifiers [examples.tax:tax-dao:5.0], [examples.tax:tax-business:5.0], and [examples.tax:tax-ui:5.0]. Any Maven project on the machine can then use them just like any library from Maven Central.

This demonstrates the value of a layered architecture. The [business] and [ui] layers only recognize the [ITaxDao] interface, defined in the [tax-dao] module of version 5; the new layer [dao] implements this interface in a new module. No lines of code in version 5 are modified, and its source files are not even recompiled.

The [pom.xml] from the parent project is as follows:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- parent project of the [Tax] application, version 6: the [dao] layer reads a database -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
    <artifactId>tax-v6</artifactId>
    <version>6.0</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>

    <!-- the two new modules; those of version 5 are dependencies -->
    <modules>
        <module>tax-dao-mysql</module>
        <module>tax-ui-mysql</module>
    </modules>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <!-- the versions of the libraries, common to all the modules -->
    <dependencyManagement>
        <dependencies>
            <!-- the modules of version 5, installed in the local Maven repository by [mvn install] -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
                <artifactId>tax-dao</artifactId>
                <version>5.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
                <artifactId>tax-business</artifactId>
                <version>5.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
                <artifactId>tax-ui</artifactId>
                <version>5.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <!-- the new [dao] module -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
                <artifactId>tax-dao-mysql</artifactId>
                <version>6.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
                <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
                <version>9.7.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
                <version>7.0.9</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
                <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
                <version>6.0.3</version>
            </dependency>
        </dependencies>
    </dependencyManagement>

    <build>
        <pluginManagement>
            <plugins>
                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                    <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                    <version>3.15.0</version>
                    <configuration>
                        <parameters>true</parameters>
                        <compilerArgs>
                            <arg>-Xlint:all</arg>
                        </compilerArgs>
                    </configuration>
                </plugin>
                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
                    <version>3.5.6</version>
                </plugin>
                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                    <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                    <version>3.5.1</version>
                </plugin>
            </plugins>
        </pluginManagement>
    </build>
</project>
  • lines 8–11: the parent project, package [pom]: it does not produce an archive; it groups modules and provides them with a common configuration;
  • lines 14–17: the project’s two modules;
  • lines 25–65: the section [dependencyManagement] specifies the versions of the modules’ dependencies, which are then declared without versions:
    • lines 28–42: the three modules from version 5, installed in the local repository by [mvn install];
    • lines 44–48: the new module [dao], on which the module [ui] depends;
    • lines 49–63: the JDBC driver for MySQL, Spring, and JUnit;
  • lines 67–93: the common configuration for the compilation, testing, and execution plugins.

docs.title: 10.11.3. The [dao] layer
docs.text:
The [pom.xml] file in the [tax-dao-mysql] module is as follows:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <!-- the parent project provides the common versions and configuration -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
        <artifactId>tax-v6</artifactId>
        <version>6.0</version>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>tax-dao-mysql</artifactId>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- the entities and the ITaxDao interface of version 5 -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-dao</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- the MySQL JDBC driver: the code only uses it at runtime -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
            <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
            <scope>runtime</scope>
        </dependency>
        <!-- for the tests: the [business] layer of version 5 and JUnit -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-business</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
            <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
            <scope>test</scope>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

</project>
  • lines 8–12: the parent project;
  • lines 18–21: the [tax-dao] module from version 5, which contains the entities ([TaxBracket], [TaxException]) and the [ITaxDao] interface;
  • lines 23–27: the JDBC driver for MySQL, with the scope ([scope]) [runtime]: it is not used at compile time, but it is present at runtime and during testing. This provides a guarantee: if the code mistakenly used a class from the driver, it would not compile. The layer [dao] depends only on JDBC;
  • lines 29–38: for testing only (scope [test]), the [business] layer from version 5 and JUnit.

The class [MySqlTax] implements the interface [ITaxDao]:

package tax.dao;

import tax.entities.TaxException;
import tax.entities.TaxBracket;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

// a [dao] layer that reads the tax brackets from a MySQL database
public class MySqlTax implements ITaxDao {

    // error codes specific to this implementation
    public static final int ACCESS = 101, DATA = 102;

    // the default query: the brackets must be returned in ascending order of the limits
    public static final String DEFAULT_QUERY = "select limits, coeffr, coeffn from brackets order by id";

    // tax brackets
    private final List<TaxBracket> taxBrackets;

    // constructor with the default query
    public MySqlTax(String url, String user, String password) {
        this(url, user, password, DEFAULT_QUERY);
    }

    // constructor: the brackets are read once and for all
    public MySqlTax(String url, String user, String password, String query) {
        List<TaxBracket> brackets = new ArrayList<>();
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
             ResultSet result = statement.executeQuery(query)) {
            // one bracket per row of the result: limit, coeffR, coeffN
            while (result.next()) {
                brackets.add(readBracket(result));
            }
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            // database access error: it is wrapped in a TaxException
            throw new TaxException("Error accessing the tax brackets database", e, ACCESS);
        }
        // an empty table is also an error
        if (brackets.isEmpty()) {
            throw new TaxException("The database contains no tax bracket", DATA);
        }
        // an unmodifiable copy of the list is returned
        taxBrackets = List.copyOf(brackets);
    }

    @Override
    public List<TaxBracket> getTaxBrackets() {
        return taxBrackets;
    }

    // the bracket of the current row: three numeric columns, without a NULL value
    private static TaxBracket readBracket(ResultSet result) {
        try {
            BigDecimal limit = result.getBigDecimal(1);
            BigDecimal coeffR = result.getBigDecimal(2);
            BigDecimal coeffN = result.getBigDecimal(3);
            if (limit == null || coeffR == null || coeffN == null) {
                throw new TaxException("A tax bracket of the database has a NULL value", DATA);
            }
            return new TaxBracket(limit, coeffR, coeffN);
        } catch (SQLException e) {
            // a missing or non-numeric column
            throw new TaxException("The tax brackets of the database are incorrect", e, DATA);
        }
    }
}
  • line 1: the class is in the [tax.dao] package, like the other implementations of [ITaxDao], although it is in a different archive;
  • line 15: the class [MySqlTax] implements the [ITaxDao] interface from version 5: a method [getTaxBrackets] that returns the list of brackets (line 54);
  • line 18: error codes specific to this implementation, modeled after those of [FileTax] and [JsonTax]: 101 for a database access error, 102 for incorrect data;
  • Line 21: The query that returns the brackets. The clause [order by id] is important: the [business] layer expects the brackets in ascending order of their limits, and a [select] without [order by] returns the rows in an order that SQL does not guarantee;
  • lines 27–29: a constructor that uses the default query, calling the other constructor via [this(…)];
  • line 32: the constructor receives the connection parameters and the query. The brackets are read once and for all within the constructor: the [dao] layer is a singleton in the application, and the database is not queried again afterward. A connection opened by [DriverManager] is therefore sufficient; a connection pool would serve no purpose;
  • Lines 34–36: the connection, the query SQL, and the result, as in the previous examples;
  • lines 38–40: Each line of the result becomes a [TaxBracket] object, constructed by the [readBracket] method;
  • lines 41–44: a database access error is encapsulated in a [TaxException] with code [ACCESS], just as [FileTax] and [JsonTax] did with input/output errors. [TaxException] is an unhandled exception: the [ui] layer does not need to be aware of [SQLException], which are handled exceptions of JDBC;
  • lines 46–48: an empty table is a data error;
  • line 50: the list is made read-only by [List.copyOf] (Java 10);
  • lines 59–72: reading a bracket:
    • lines 61–63: [getBigDecimal(i)] reads column No. i as a [BigDecimal];
    • lines 64–66: a column with the value [NULL] yields a [BigDecimal] [null]: this is a data error;
    • lines 68–71: A query that returns fewer than three columns, or a non-numeric column, results in a [SQLException] in [getBigDecimal]: this is also a data error. The [TaxException] raised on line 65 is not a [SQLException]: it passes through the [catch] clause on line 68 without being intercepted, and then the one on line 41; the constructor’s try-with-resources block nevertheless closes the connection.

Note that the class name is the only place where MySQL appears: the code uses only the interfaces of [java.sql]. We’ll come back to this.

docs.title: 10.11.4. Tests for the [dao] layer
docs.text:
The tests for the [dao] layer are in the [src/test/java] folder of the module:

package tax.dao;

import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertInstanceOf;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertNotEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrowsExactly;

import tax.entities.TaxException;
import tax.entities.TaxBracket;
import tax.business.ITaxBusiness;
import tax.business.TaxBusiness;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.List;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.CsvSource;

// tests of the MySqlTax [dao] layer (the [dbtaxes] database must exist)
class MySqlTaxTests {

    // the test database
    private static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbtaxes";
    private static final String USER = "admtaxes";
    private static final String PASSWORD = "pwdtaxes";

    // the brackets read from the database are those of the "hardwired" version
    @Test
    void sameBrackets() {
        List<TaxBracket> reference = new HardwiredTax().getTaxBrackets();
        List<TaxBracket> brackets = new MySqlTax(URL, USER, PASSWORD).getTaxBrackets();
        // equals also compares the scale of the BigDecimals: 4962.00 (database) is not equal to 4962 (hardwired)
        assertNotEquals(reference, brackets);
        // compareTo only compares the values
        assertEquals(reference.size(), brackets.size());
        for (int i = 0; i < reference.size(); i++) {
            assertEquals(0, reference.get(i).limit().compareTo(brackets.get(i).limit()));
            assertEquals(0, reference.get(i).coeffR().compareTo(brackets.get(i).coeffR()));
            assertEquals(0, reference.get(i).coeffN().compareTo(brackets.get(i).coeffN()));
        }
    }

    // the [business] layer of version 5 with the new [dao] layer
    @ParameterizedTest
    @CsvSource({
        "true, 2, 60000, 4282",
        "true, 3, 60000, 2959",
        "false, 0, 60000, 11519"
    })
    void calculateTax(boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary, int tax) {
        ITaxBusiness business = new TaxBusiness(new MySqlTax(URL, USER, PASSWORD));
        assertEquals(tax, business.calculateTax(married, nbChildren, salary));
    }

    // missing database (or forbidden to the user)
    @Test
    void missingDatabase() {
        TaxException e = assertThrowsExactly(TaxException.class,
                () -> new MySqlTax(URL.replace("dbtaxes", "dbtaxesunknown"), USER, PASSWORD));
        assertEquals(MySqlTax.ACCESS, e.getCode());
        assertInstanceOf(SQLException.class, e.getCause());
    }

    // wrong password
    @Test
    void incorrectPassword() {
        TaxException e = assertThrowsExactly(TaxException.class,
                () -> new MySqlTax(URL, USER, "x"));
        assertEquals(MySqlTax.ACCESS, e.getCode());
    }

    // unreachable server
    @Test
    void unreachableServer() {
        TaxException e = assertThrowsExactly(TaxException.class,
                () -> new MySqlTax(URL.replace("3306", "3399"), USER, PASSWORD));
        assertEquals(MySqlTax.ACCESS, e.getCode());
    }

    // query that returns only two columns
    @Test
    void incorrectQuery() {
        TaxException e = assertThrowsExactly(TaxException.class,
                () -> new MySqlTax(URL, USER, PASSWORD, "select limits, coeffr from brackets"));
        assertEquals(MySqlTax.DATA, e.getCode());
    }

    // query that returns no row
    @Test
    void noBracket() {
        TaxException e = assertThrowsExactly(TaxException.class,
                () -> new MySqlTax(URL, USER, PASSWORD,
                        "select limits, coeffr, coeffn from brackets where id < 0"));
        assertEquals(MySqlTax.DATA, e.getCode());
    }

    // query in which a column is NULL
