    @Test
    void nullValue() {
        TaxException e = assertThrowsExactly(TaxException.class,
                () -> new MySqlTax(URL, USER, PASSWORD,
                        "select limits, coeffr, null from brackets"));
        assertEquals(MySqlTax.DATA, e.getCode());
    }
}
  • Lines 22–24: The tests use the database [dbtaxes], which must have been created by the script [dbtaxes.sql]. These are therefore no longer unit tests in the strict sense—which would test a class in isolation—but rather integration tests: they verify the operation of the [dao] layer with DBMS. For these tests, we often use an in-memory H2 database, created at the start of the tests, or a DBMS instance launched in a Docker container by the Testcontainers library; here, we’ll simply use the machine’s MySQL database;
  • Lines 28–40: The records read from the database are those from the “hard-coded” version [HardwiredTax]… but not in the sense of [equals] (line 32)! The [equals] method for a record compares its fields with their [equals] method, and the [BigDecimal] method compares the value and the scale (the number of decimal places): the [BigDecimal] values read from the database have two decimal places ([4962.00]), as does the [DECIMAL(10,2)] column, whereas those for [HardwiredTax] have none ([4962]). [compareTo], on the other hand, compares only the values (lines 35–39). This is a classic pitfall of [BigDecimal] (Chapter 3);
  • lines 43–52: the [business] layer in version 5 calculates the expected taxes using the new [dao] layer. [@CsvSource] provides the parameters for the three test runs;
  • lines 55–61: a nonexistent database triggers a [TaxException] with code [ACCESS], which encapsulates the original [SQLException] ([assertInstanceOf] accepts a derived class);
  • lines 64–69: the same applies to an incorrect password;
  • lines 72–77: an unreachable server (no server is listening on port 3399) also causes an access error;
  • methods [incorrectQuery] (line 81), [noBracket] (line 89), and [nullValue] (line 98): A query that returns only two columns, returns no rows, or has a column with the value [NULL] triggers a [TaxException] error with code [DATA].

The tests are run using [mvn test] in the module folder (or [mvn install] in the [TaxV6] folder, which also runs the tests). Maven displays only the summary; the IDE script and the JUnit launcher in console mode display the following tree (the summary following the tree is abbreviated):

╷
└─ JUnit Jupiter ✔
   └─ MySqlTaxTests ✔
      ├─ missingDatabase() ✔
      ├─ incorrectQuery() ✔
      ├─ incorrectPassword() ✔
      ├─ noBracket() ✔
      ├─ nullValue() ✔
      ├─ calculateTax(boolean, int, int, int) ✔
      │  ├─ [1] married=true, nbChildren=2, salary=60000, tax=4282 ✔
      │  ├─ [2] married=true, nbChildren=3, salary=60000, tax=2959 ✔
      │  └─ [3] married=false, nbChildren=0, salary=60000, tax=11519 ✔
      ├─ unreachableServer() ✔
      └─ sameBrackets() ✔
...
[        10 tests successful      ]
[         0 tests failed          ]

docs.title: 10.11.5. Integrating the Layers
docs.text:
The [tax-ui-mysql] module contains the program that integrates the layers. Its [pom.xml] file is as follows:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <!-- the parent project provides the common versions and configuration -->
    <parent>
        <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
        <artifactId>tax-v6</artifactId>
        <version>6.0</version>
    </parent>

    <artifactId>tax-ui-mysql</artifactId>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- the new [dao] layer (and, transitively, the MySQL JDBC driver) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-dao-mysql</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- the [business] and [ui] layers of version 5, unchanged -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-business</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-ui</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- the Spring dependency injection container -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- mvn exec:java executes the main class -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>tax.ui.mysql.Main</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
  • Lines 18–21: the new layer [dao]. By transitivity, the JDBC driver for MySQL—a scope dependency of [runtime] in this module—is part of the application’s libraries;
  • Lines 23–30: the [business] and [ui] layers of version 5. The [tax-ui] module contains the main program for version 5, but we only use its public class [Dialog];
  • lines 32–35: Spring’s dependency injection container, as in version 5;
  • lines 41–47: the class executed by [mvn exec:java].

The configuration file [tax.properties] is as follows:

# configuration of the [Tax] application, version 6: the [dao] layer reads a database
dao.implementation=MySqlTax
dao.url=jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbtaxes
dao.user=admtaxes
dao.password=pwdtaxes
dao.query=select limits, coeffr, coeffn from brackets order by id
  • line 2: the implementation of the [dao] layer;
  • Lines 3–5: the URL, JDBC from the [dbtaxes] database, and the user IDs [admtaxes];
  • line 6: the query that returns the brackets. Including it in the configuration allows you to use a different database—even one with tables or columns that have different names—without modifying the code.

The class [Main] is the one for version 5, with the exception of the record in layer [dao]:

package tax.ui.mysql;

import tax.dao.HardwiredTax;
import tax.dao.ITaxDao;
import tax.dao.MySqlTax;
import tax.entities.TaxException;
import tax.business.ITaxBusiness;
import tax.business.TaxBusiness;
import tax.ui.Dialog;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.Reader;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Properties;
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext;

// the [Tax] application, version 6: the [dao] layer reads the tax brackets from a database
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // the configuration file: tax.properties by default, or the one passed as an argument
        String configFile = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "tax.properties";

        // integration of the layers
        ITaxBusiness business;
        try {
            // reading the configuration, in the current folder
            Properties config = new Properties();
            try (Reader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of(configFile))) {
                config.load(reader);
            }
            String implementation = config.getProperty("dao.implementation", "MySqlTax");
            String url = config.getProperty("dao.url");
            if (url == null) {
                throw new TaxException("The [dao.url] parameter is missing from the configuration");
            }
            String user = config.getProperty("dao.user", "");
            String password = config.getProperty("dao.password", "");
            String query = config.getProperty("dao.query", MySqlTax.DEFAULT_QUERY);

            // the Spring container: the layers are registered in it
            GenericApplicationContext context = new GenericApplicationContext();
            // the [dao] layer: the implementation is chosen by the configuration
            context.registerBean(ITaxDao.class, () -> switch (implementation) {
                case "MySqlTax" -> new MySqlTax(url, user, password, query);
                case "HardwiredTax" -> new HardwiredTax();
                default -> throw new TaxException(
                        "Unknown implementation [" + implementation + "] of the [dao] layer");
            });
            // the [business] layer of version 5: the container will pass the [dao] layer to its constructor
            context.registerBean(TaxBusiness.class);

            // starting the container: it creates the [dao] layer, then the [business] layer
            context.refresh();
            business = context.getBean(ITaxBusiness.class);
        } catch (IOException | RuntimeException e) {
            // display of the error and end of the program
            Dialog.displayError(e);
            System.exit(1);
            return;
        }

        // the dialog with the user: the [ui] layer of version 5
        Dialog.run(business);
    }
}
  • Line 1: The class is in a package specific to version 6, [tax.ui.mysql], to avoid confusion with the [tax.ui.Main] class from version 5, which is also present in the classpath;
  • Line 22: the configuration file, [tax.properties] by default, or the one passed as an argument;
  • lines 28–31: reading the properties file from the current directory;
  • lines 32–39: the parameters for the [dao] layer. The absence of URL is an error; the request has a default value;
  • lines 44–49: the [dao] layer is registered in the Spring container under the [ITaxDao] interface, with a [Supplier] that creates it according to the configuration: a [MySqlTax] (line 45) or, for comparison, the “hard-coded” version from version 5 (line 46). The [FileTax] and [JsonTax] implementations of version 5 could be added in the same way: they are in the classpath;
  • line 51: the [business] layer of version 5;
  • line 54: when the container starts up, it creates the [dao] layer, and thus reads the database, followed by the [business] layer;
  • lines 56–61: a configuration or database access error is displayed by the [displayError] method from version 5, and the program terminates;
  • line 64: the Version 5 dialog box, unchanged.

To run the application, first install the Version 6 modules in the local repository (the [dao] layer must be available for the [tax-ui-mysql] module), then run the program from the [tax-ui-mysql] folder, which contains the configuration files:

> cd 10-jdbc/TaxV6
> mvn install
> cd tax-ui-mysql
> mvn -q exec:java

Running with the [tax.properties] file:

> mvn -q exec:java
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 3 60000
Tax=2959 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: n 0 60000
Tax=11519 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

The course reference values are as follows: 4,282 euros for a couple with two children, 2,959 euros for a couple with three children, and 11,519 euros for a single person without children, with an annual salary of 60,000 euros.

With the file [tax-base.properties], where URL refers to a base file [dbtaxesunknown]:

> mvn -q exec:java -Dexec.args="tax-base.properties"
Oct 03, 2026 7:08:56 PM org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext refresh
WARNING: Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
----------------------------------------
tax.entities.TaxException: Error accessing the tax brackets database
----------------------------------------
java.sql.SQLSyntaxErrorException: Access denied for user 'admtaxes'@'localhost' to database 'dbtaxesunknown'
----------------------------------------
  • lines 2–3: a Spring logging message written to the error output: the container reports that the creation of the [dao] layer failed. This was already the case in version 5;
  • lines 6–10: the exception chain displayed by [Dialog.displayError]: the Spring container wrapped the [TaxException] exception thrown by the [dao] layer—which itself wraps the driver’s [SQLException] exception—into a [BeanCreationException] exception. The user [admtaxes] has permissions only on the database [dbtaxes]: MySQL denies access to any other database, whether it exists or not (line 10).

With the file [tax-password.properties], which has an incorrect password:

> mvn -q exec:java -Dexec.args="tax-password.properties"
Oct 03, 2026 7:09:00 PM org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext refresh
WARNING: Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
----------------------------------------
tax.entities.TaxException: Error accessing the tax brackets database
----------------------------------------
java.sql.SQLException: Access denied for user 'admtaxes'@'localhost' (using password: YES)
----------------------------------------

With the file [tax-server.properties], where URL specifies port 3399, on which no server is listening (this is what would happen if the MySQL server were stopped):

> mvn -q exec:java -Dexec.args="tax-server.properties"
Oct 03, 2026 7:09:02 PM org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext refresh
WARNING: Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
----------------------------------------
tax.entities.TaxException: Error accessing the tax brackets database
----------------------------------------
com.mysql.cj.jdbc.exceptions.CommunicationsException: Communications link failure

The last packet sent successfully to the server was 0 milliseconds ago. The driver has not received any packets from the server.
----------------------------------------
com.mysql.cj.exceptions.CJCommunicationsException: Communications link failure

The last packet sent successfully to the server was 0 milliseconds ago. The driver has not received any packets from the server.
----------------------------------------
java.net.ConnectException: Connection refused (connect failed)
----------------------------------------

The exception chain here shows that the driver exception itself encapsulates other exceptions, all the way down to the network exception [ConnectException]: the connection was refused.

With the file [tax-query.properties], whose request asks only for the columns [limits] and [coeffr]:

> mvn -q exec:java -Dexec.args="tax-query.properties"
Oct 03, 2026 7:09:05 PM org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext refresh
WARNING: Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanCreationException: Error creating bean with name 'tax.dao.ITaxDao': Instantiation of supplied bean failed
----------------------------------------
tax.entities.TaxException: The tax brackets of the database are incorrect
----------------------------------------
java.sql.SQLException: Column Index out of range, 3 > 2. 
----------------------------------------

In all cases, the [dao] layer encapsulated the original exception in a [TaxException], which is displayed by the [Dialog.displayError] method in version 5, and the program terminates.

docs.title: 10.11.6. Change the database
docs.text:
The [dao] [MySqlTax] layer uses only the interfaces of JDBC: despite its name, it is not specific to MySQL (a name like [JdbcTax] would be more appropriate). To use a PostgreSQL database (or SQL Server, or Oracle), all you would need to do is:

  • create the bracket table in a PostgreSQL database—for example, a table named [data] with columns [data1], [data2], and [data3], to highlight the benefit of placing the query in the configuration;
  • to add to [pom.xml] in the [tax-ui-mysql] module the dependency of the JDBC driver on PostgreSQL, [org.postgresql:postgresql] (or [com.microsoft.sqlserver:mssql-jdbc], [com.oracle.database.jdbc:ojdbc11]), with scope [runtime];
  • to write a configuration file similar to [tax.properties], such as the file [tax-postgresql.properties] from the module:
# the same application with a PostgreSQL database (driver org.postgresql:postgresql to be added to pom.xml)
dao.implementation=MySqlTax
dao.url=jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/dbtaxes
dao.user=admtaxes
dao.password=pwdtaxes
dao.query=select data1, data2, data3 from data order by id

Only MySQL is installed on the machine used to write this course: we did not implement this configuration. The layers [business] and [ui], the class [MySqlTax], and the program [Main] do not need to be modified: only the configuration and the driver in the classpath change. Note that the request from [MySqlTax] has no parameters and uses only standard SQL: this is what allows it to be executed by any DBMS. A more feature-rich [dao] layer (searches, updates) would quickly encounter the specific characteristics of each SQL as seen above: that’s where a ORM like Hibernate takes over.

docs.title: 10.12. Conclusion
docs.text:
This chapter has covered database access using JDBC:

  • JDBC is a set of interfaces ([Connection], [Statement], [PreparedStatement], [ResultSet], [DataSource]…), from the [java.sql] and [javax.sql] packages, implemented by a driver specific to each DBMS (MySQL Connector/J for MySQL), which [DriverManager] selects based on the URL and JDBC from the database;
  • a connection is opened as late as possible and closed as early as possible, using a **try-with-resources statement; a connection pool such as HikariCP, via the [DataSource] interface, makes this practice cost-effective;
  • [executeQuery] executes a [select] and returns a [ResultSet], which is traversed line by line using [next], reading the columns, numbered starting from 1, using the [getXxx] methods; [executeUpdate] executes a [insert], [update], or [delete] and returns the number of modified lines;
  • Errors are [SQLException], checked exceptions, which return an error code specific to the DBMS and a standardized SQLSTATE code;
  • external values are always passed via the parameters of a [PreparedStatement] and are never concatenated with the query text, which protects against SQL injection;
  • The transactions ([setAutoCommit(false)], [commit], [rollback], savepoints) make a sequence of SQL commands atomic;
  • JDBC is blocking: Java 21 virtual threads allow serving many users with standard JDBC code, within the limits of the pool size; batches ([addBatch], [executeBatch]) reduce the number of exchanges with the server;
  • offline mode ([CachedRowSet]) exists, but working with in-memory objects is currently the domain of ORM.

Version 6 of the [Tax] application demonstrated that, thanks to the layered architecture, switching from a file to a database requires only writing a new [dao] layer and modifying the configuration. The next chapter will create a seventh version of this layer using Hibernate, which generates the SQL commands itself.

To learn more:

  • Oracle’s JDBC tutorial: JDBC Database Access (written for Java 8, but API has hardly changed since then);
  • the MySQL Connector/J documentation: MySQL Connector/J Developer Guide;
  • the documentation for HikariCP: HikariCP;
  • the SQL injection, explained by OWASP: SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet.

docs.title: 15.1. The MySQL DBMS with Laragon
docs.text: Chapters 10 and 11 of this document use the MySQL 8 DBMS. The easiest way to install it on Windows is to install Laragon, a portable development environment that includes MySQL, the graphical client HeidiSQL, a configured terminal, Apache, and PHP. The author also uses it for his PHP courses.

docs.title: 15.1.1. Installation
docs.text:
Laragon can be downloaded from https://laragon.org. The installation process is standard; you can keep the suggested installation folder ([C:\laragon]). Laragon provides MySQL 8 (the exact version depends on the Laragon version), with a [root] administrator account that has no password and a server listening on port 3306 on the local machine. This is the configuration assumed by the examples in the document, where the JDBC URLs are in the form:

jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/dbarticles

with the username [root] and an empty password. If MySQL was installed differently, with a password for [root], you must update the examples accordingly ([.properties] files or constants at the top of the programs).

For a system without Laragon, you can also install MySQL Community Server from https://dev.mysql.com/downloads/mysql/, or its open-source derivative, MariaDB. However, the examples have only been tested with MySQL 8: the scripts in Chapter 10 use a collation specific to MySQL 8 ([utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci]), and with MariaDB, it would need to be adapted, as would the JDBC driver (MariaDB provides its own).

docs.title: 15.1.2. Starting and Stopping MySQL
docs.text:
The Laragon main window includes a “Start All” button that starts the servers (Apache and MySQL) and a “Stop” button that stops them. MySQL is not a Windows service that runs at system startup: it only runs when started from Laragon, which prevents it from consuming resources when not in use. The Laragon menu (right-click in the window) also allows you to start only MySQL and to select its version.

When MySQL is not running, the programs in Chapters 10 and 11 fail with an exception from the JDBC driver indicating that no connection could be established ([CommunicationsException]: “Communications link failure”): this is the first thing to check in case of an error.

docs.title: 15.1.3. The command-line client
docs.text:
The Terminal button in Laragon opens a terminal where Laragon commands are available, including the command-line client MySQL ([mysql]). To connect to the server, use:

> mysql -u root

then enter SQL commands ending with a semicolon ([show databases;], [use dbarticles;], [select * from articles;]) and [exit] to exit. The client can also run a script SQL, which is what Chapter 10 does to create its databases:

> cd java-oct-2026\10-jdbc\sql
> mysql -u root < dbarticles.sql
> mysql -u root < dbtaxes.sql

The scripts completely recreate their database each time they are run: you can rerun them to restore the data to its initial state after testing.

docs.title: 15.1.4. The HeidiSQL graphical client
docs.text:
The Laragon Database button launches the graphical client HeidiSQL. Upon first launch, HeidiSQL offers a connection session that is already configured for the Laragon server MySQL (host [127.0.0.1], user [root], blank password, port 3306); simply open it. You will see:

  • on the left, the tree view of the server’s databases and their tables;
  • on the right, tabs showing a table’s structure, its data (which can be edited directly), and a field for entering SQL queries (the “Query” tab), which are executed by [F9].

To create a database using a script from Chapter 10, open the script (via the “File” menu, using the command to load an SQL file) in a query tab, then execute it ([F9]). You can also create a database, a user, and user permissions using the menus in HeidiSQL (right-click on the connection / “Create New” / "Database"; "Tools" menu / "User Manager"), but the SQL scripts have the advantage of being reproducible and able to be rerun.

IDEs can also connect to a database: IntelliJ IDEA via its “Database” window, VS Code via an extension such as “SQLTools” or “MySQL.”

docs.title: 15.1.5. The Databases in This Document
docs.text:
Chapters 10 and 11 use the following databases, all located on the local MySQL server:

DatabaseChapterCreation[dbarticles]10Script [10-jdbc/sql/dbarticles.sql]: Table [articles] from the JDBC examples[dbtaxes]10script [10-jdbc/sql/dbtaxes.sql]: the [brackets] table from version 6 of the [Tax] application and the [admtaxes] user[hbfirst], [hbarticles], [hbshop], [hbclients], [hbconcurrency]11created by the programs themselves (option [createDatabaseIfNotExist=true] of the JDBC URL; tables created by Hibernate or by versioned scripts)[hbtaxes]11Created and populated by the [CreateDatabase] program in version 7 of the [Tax] application

Once testing is complete, a database can be deleted using the command SQL [drop database name;], in the [mysql] client, or in HeidiSQL.

docs.title: 9. Asynchronous Programming
docs.text:
The previous chapter introduced threads: we can execute multiple pieces of code “at the same time,” synchronize them, and assign tasks to a thread pool via an executor ([ExecutorService]). This chapter addresses a related but distinct issue: how to write a program that waits a lot (for the disk, the network, or a database) without tying up threads during these waits.

Java does not have language keywords for this (other languages, such as C# or JavaScript, have the keywords [async] and [await]). It offers two solutions, which complement each other and are both presented in this chapter:

  • the [CompletableFuture<T>] class (Java 8, since enhanced) represents an ongoing operation whose subsequent steps are composed using callback methods: “when the result is ready, do this, then that” ([thenApply], [thenCompose], [thenCombine], [allOf]…). No thread waits: it is the completion of the operation that triggers the next step;
  • virtual threads ( Java 21), on the other hand, allow you to write blocking, sequential code that reads from top to bottom: when a virtual thread waits for input/output, the JVM detaches it from the system thread that was executing it (its “carrier thread”) and frees that thread for another virtual thread. This makes it possible to have hundreds of thousands of virtual threads for just a few system threads. This is Java’s modern solution to the problem that other languages solve with [async] / [await].

These tools are everywhere today: the following chapters will explore them to access databases, write TCP servers that serve each client via a virtual thread, web clients using [java.net.http.HttpClient], and web services using Spring Boot.

All the examples in this chapter are compact source files ([Async01.java], [Async02.java]…) that are run using [java AsyncNN.java] in the [09-async] folder. Many of them measure execution times using [System.nanoTime()]: the milliseconds displayed vary from one run to another and from one machine to another (the examples were run on a dual-processor machine). It’s the orders of magnitude that matter: 1 second or 10 seconds, 300 ms or 0 ms.

docs.title: 9.1.1. Operations that wait
docs.text:
A program performs two types of work:

  • computational tasks, which occupy the processor: sorting a list, calculating a tax, analyzing a text;
  • input/output (I/O), which essentially consists of waiting for a peripheral device: reading a file from disk, sending a request to a web server and waiting for its response, executing a SQL query on a database server.

The orders of magnitude are very different. A processor executes a few billion instructions per second. A read operation on a disk (SSD) takes on the order of one-tenth of a millisecond; a round trip over a local network takes a fraction of a millisecond; a round trip to a server located on the other side of the country takes a few tens of milliseconds; and a somewhat complex SQL request can sometimes take several seconds. During these waits, the processor could have executed millions of instructions.

When a program reads a line over a network connection using a blocking method, the thread performing this read is blocked: it does nothing, but it still exists. A “classic” Java thread—now referred to as a “platform thread”—is an operating system thread: it occupies memory (its stack, on the order of a megabyte), it is recognized by the system, and, most importantly, it is no longer available to do anything else. This isn’t a problem in a small console program that does one thing at a time. It becomes much more of an issue in two situations:

  • in a server: each client served by a blocked thread ties up that thread. If the server’s thread pool has N threads and all N threads are performing a blocking operation, there are no threads left available for a new client. A modern server handles thousands of simultaneous requests: this is possible because its waiting operations do not tie up system threads;
  • in a graphical user interface: a single thread—the UI thread (Swing’s “Event Dispatch Thread,” the “JavaFX Application Thread”)—handles clicks and redraws windows. If it is blocked by a download, the window freezes.

Asynchrony involves initiating the I/O operation, freeing up the system thread while it is in progress (the hardware and operating system do not need it to transfer data), and then resuming work once the operation is complete, possibly on another system thread:

  • In [1], the platform thread T1 initiates the I/O and remains blocked until it finishes;
  • in [2], the virtual thread V1 initiates the I/O; JVM detaches it from its parent thread P1, which can then immediately execute other virtual threads. When the I/O completes, JVM reattaches V1 to a free carrier thread, P2 (which could also be P1), and V1 continues its execution immediately after the blocking instruction, as if nothing had happened.

The program [Async01.java] measures the difference over 100 operations, each of which waits for one second (the wait simulates I/O). It uses instructions that we will explain later in this chapter ([Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor], [CompletableFuture]): here, we are primarily interested in the results.

// why asynchrony: 100 operations that each wait one second
// (a wait simulates an I/O: disk read, network request, SQL query…)
import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory;

final int nbOperations = 100;
long start;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    IO.println(nbOperations + " operations of one second, "
            + Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors() + " processors");

    // 1 - one platform thread per operation, each thread is blocked during the wait
    start = System.nanoTime();
    List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++) {
        threads.add(Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> waitFor(1000)));
    }
    display("1 - one platform thread per operation", jvmThreads());
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
    display("    end", -1);

    // 2 - the operations are given to a pool of 10 threads, but they block it
    start = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)) {
        for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++) {
            pool.submit(() -> waitFor(1000));
        }
        display("2 - pool of 10 threads, blocking waits", jvmThreads());
    } // close() waits for the end of all the operations
    display("    end", -1);

    // 3 - one virtual thread per operation: it releases its carrier thread during the wait
    start = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++) {
            executor.submit(() -> waitFor(1000));
        }
        display("3 - one virtual thread per operation", jvmThreads());
    }
    display("    end", -1);

    // 4 - asynchronous waits: no thread waits, a timer completes each operation
    start = System.nanoTime();
    var operations = new CompletableFuture<?>[nbOperations];
    for (int i = 0; i < nbOperations; i++) {
        operations[i] = new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, 1000, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    }
    display("4 - asynchronous waits (CompletableFuture)", jvmThreads());
    CompletableFuture.allOf(operations).join();
    display("    end", -1);
}

// a blocking wait of [ms] milliseconds
void waitFor(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// number of platform threads of the JVM, half a second after the operations are started
int jvmThreads() {
    long elapsed = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
    if (elapsed < 500) {
        waitFor(500 - elapsed);
    }
    return ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().getThreadCount();
}

// display of the elapsed time and, if provided (>= 0), of the number of threads
void display(String message, int nbThreads) {
    String threadsInfo = nbThreads < 0 ? "" : String.format(", %3d threads in the JVM", nbThreads);
    long elapsed = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
    IO.println(String.format("%-44s : %5d ms%s", message, elapsed, threadsInfo));
}

Results:

> java Async01.java
100 operations of one second, 2 processors
1 - one platform thread per operation        :   534 ms, 106 threads in the JVM
    end                                      :  1061 ms
2 - pool of 10 threads, blocking waits       :   501 ms,  16 threads in the JVM
    end                                      : 10021 ms
3 - one virtual thread per operation         :   501 ms,  10 threads in the JVM
    end                                      :  1091 ms
4 - asynchronous waits (CompletableFuture)   :   500 ms,  11 threads in the JVM
    end                                      :  1003 ms

Comments:

  • Lines 12–22: the simplest solution—one platform thread per operation. [Thread.ofPlatform().start(task)] (Java 21) creates and starts a thread, just like [new Thread(task).start()]. Each thread executes [Thread.sleep(1000)]: it is blocked for one second. The 100 waits occur simultaneously, and the entire process takes exactly one second (line 4 of the results), but at the cost of 100 additional system threads: JVM has 106 of them (line 3). With 10,000 operations, 10,000 system threads would be required;
  • Lines 24–32: The operations are assigned to a pool of 10 threads ([Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10)]), a reasonable size for computations. But here, these threads aren’t computing—they’re idle. The operations wait for a free thread, in batches of 10, and the whole process takes… ten seconds (line 6). This is known as “thread pool starvation,” the most common flaw in servers that mix thread pools with blocking I/O. The method [close()] of an executor (Java 19), called upon exit from [try], rejects new tasks and waits for the ones that have been submitted to finish;
  • Lines 34–42: One virtual thread per operation. [Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()] (Java 21) returns an executor that creates a new virtual thread for each submitted task. The task code is the same as in Step 1: a blocking [Thread.sleep(1000)]. However, a blocked virtual thread does not tie up a system thread: the JVM detaches it from its carrier thread. The 100 waits last a total of one second (line 8), and the JVM counts only 10 system threads (line 7): its service threads, and the two carrier threads—one per processor—that executed the 100 virtual threads. The virtual threads are not included in this count: they are objects of JVM, not system threads;
  • lines 44–52: the same wait with no threads waiting. [new CompletableFuture<Void>()] creates a “pending” operation, and [completeOnTimeout(value, timeout, unit)] (Java 9) requests that it be completed with the specified value once the timeout expires. A single timer from JVM manages the 100 timeouts. [CompletableFuture.allOf(...)] returns an operation that completes when all others have finished, and [join()] waits for it to finish. The entire process lasts one second (line 10), with only one additional thread compared to step 3—the timer thread (line 9);
  • lines 55–62: [Thread.sleep] can throw the checked exception [InterruptedException] if the thread is interrupted while sleeping (we’ll discuss this further in the section on cancellation); the [waitFor] method intercepts it so that the lambdas on lines 16, 28, and 38 do not have to handle it;
  • Lines 64–71: [ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean().getThreadCount()] returns the number of live platform threads for JVM. The class [ManagementFactory] belongs to the module [java.management]: a compact source file automatically imports only the module [java.base], hence the import on line 3.

Let’s remember the lesson: to wait, you must not block any system threads. Asynchrony doesn’t make I/O faster; it allows you to handle a large number of I/O operations simultaneously using few system threads, while keeping the threads the application needs available. Java offers two approaches for this: creating [CompletableFuture] (Step 4), or writing ordinary blocking code executed by virtual threads (Step 3).

docs.title: 9.1.2. Several Successive Models
docs.text:
Java has offered several ways to write code that waits without blocking. The older ones are still found in existing code, so it’s useful to recognize them.

PatternIntroductionPrinciple[Future] and RuntimesJava 5 (2004)[ExecutorService.submit] assigns a task to a thread pool and returns a [Future<T>], which represents the upcoming result. But the only way to obtain this result is to wait, blocking, with [get()].Callback methods of NIO.2Java 7 (2011)Asynchronous channels ([AsynchronousSocketChannel], [AsynchronousFileChannel]) initiate an operation and receive a callback object ([CompletionHandler]) whose method [completed] or [failed] is called by a thread from a pool once the operation is complete.[CompletableFuture]Java 8 (2014)a [Future] that you can terminate yourself and whose sequence is composed of callback methods ([thenApply], [thenCompose], [exceptionally]…); reactive streams [java.util.concurrent.Flow] (Java 9) are an extension of this for sequences of values. Reactive libraries (Project Reactor, used by Spring WebFlux, RxJava) are based on the same concepts.virtual threadsJava 21 (2023)of ordinary blocking code, executed by virtual threads: JVM frees the system thread during waits. This is the recommended model today for new applications.structured concurrencyPreview of Java 21 through Java 25[StructuredTaskScope] organizes a group of subtasks executed by virtual threads as a single block of code, with shared error handling and cancellation (see the end of the chapter).

Callback methods have a drawback: the code is fragmented. What naturally reads as “connect, then read, then display” becomes a method that initiates the connection, a callback method that initiates the read operation, and another callback method that displays the result; variables must be shared among these methods, exceptions are caught at different locations, and a simple loop (“read as long as there is data”) becomes a callback method that recursively calls itself. [CompletableFuture] makes this fragmentation more readable by chaining the steps together; virtual threads make it disappear: asynchronous code takes the form of synchronous code, because it is synchronous code.

The program [Async02.java] implements the same client, TCP, using two extreme approaches: first, using the callback methods of NIO.2, and then using blocking code executed by a virtual thread. It also contains a small server, run by a thread, that responds to two clients (network programming will be covered in detail in Chapter 12; for now, it suffices to know that a client connects to the server and reads the message the server sends it).

// the same TCP client written with callback methods (NIO.2, Java 7), then with a virtual thread (Java 21)
final int port = 27500;
final InetAddress local = InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress();
final ByteBuffer buffer = ByteBuffer.allocate(1024);
final CountDownLatch end = new CountDownLatch(1);

void main() throws IOException, InterruptedException {
    // a minimal server, executed by a thread: it serves two clients then stops
    var listener = new ServerSocket(port, 10, local);
    Thread server = Thread.ofPlatform().name("server").start(() -> {
        try (listener) {
            for (int i = 1; i <= 2; i++) {
                try (Socket service = listener.accept()) {
                    // the server takes its time to answer
                    Thread.sleep(500);
                    byte[] message = ("Hello client no. " + i).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
                    service.getOutputStream().write(message);
                }
            }
        } catch (IOException | InterruptedException e) {
            display("server: " + e);
        }
    });
    display("start of the program");

    // 1 - the "callback methods" style: AsynchronousSocketChannel and CompletionHandler
    var client = AsynchronousSocketChannel.open();
    // we start the connection, giving the object to call back when it is done
    client.connect(new InetSocketAddress(local, port), client, new Connected());
    display("callbacks: connection started, the program continues");
    // the main thread has nothing left to do: it waits for the signal of the last callback method
    end.await();

    // 2 - the blocking style, executed by a virtual thread: the code reads from top to bottom
    Thread virtual = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
        try (var client2 = new Socket(local, port)) {
            display("virtual thread: connected, read started");
            byte[] bytes = new byte[1024];
            int nbBytes = client2.getInputStream().read(bytes);
            String message = new String(bytes, 0, nbBytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
            display("virtual thread: received [" + message + "]");
        } catch (IOException e) {
            display("virtual thread: " + e);
        }
    });
    virtual.join();
    server.join();
}

// callback method no. 1: the connection is made (or has failed)
class Connected implements CompletionHandler<Void, AsynchronousSocketChannel> {
    @Override
    public void completed(Void nothing, AsynchronousSocketChannel channel) {
        display("callbacks: connected, read started");
        // we start reading the server's answer with another callback object
        channel.read(buffer, channel, new Received());
    }

    @Override
    public void failed(Throwable e, AsynchronousSocketChannel channel) {
        display("callbacks: connection failed: " + e);
        end.countDown();
    }
}

// callback method no. 2: data has arrived
class Received implements CompletionHandler<Integer, AsynchronousSocketChannel> {
    @Override
    public void completed(Integer nbBytes, AsynchronousSocketChannel channel) {
        display("callbacks: received [" + new String(buffer.array(), 0, nbBytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) + "]");
        try {
            channel.close();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            display("callbacks: " + e);
        }
        // we notify the main thread
        end.countDown();
    }

    @Override
    public void failed(Throwable e, AsynchronousSocketChannel channel) {
        display("callbacks: read failed: " + e);
        end.countDown();
    }
}

// display prefixed by the thread executing it
// (name of a platform thread, description of a virtual thread)
void display(String message) {
    Thread thread = Thread.currentThread();
    IO.println("[" + (thread.isVirtual() ? thread.toString() : thread.getName()) + "] " + message);
}

Results:

> java Async02.java
[main] start of the program
[main] callbacks: connection started, the program continues
[InnocuousThread-4] callbacks: connected, read started
[InnocuousThread-2] callbacks: received [Hello client no. 1]
[VirtualThread[#28]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1] virtual thread: connected, read started
[VirtualThread[#28]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2] virtual thread: received [Hello client no. 2]

Comments:

  • Lines 8–23: the server. It listens on port 27500 of the local machine ([InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress()], i.e., 127.0.0.1), accepts two connections one after the other, and sends each client a welcome message after half a second. It is executed by a platform thread named [server]. The form [try (listener)] (Java 9) will close the [ServerSocket] declared on line 9 at the end of the block;
  • lines 26–32: the client writes using callback methods:
    • line 27: a *[AsynchronousSocketChannel]* is a TCP channel whose operations are asynchronous;
    • line 29: [connect] initiates the connection and immediately returns control (line 3 of the results). Its last two parameters are an arbitrary object that the callback method will receive (here, the channel itself) and the callback object, of type [Connected];
    • line 32: the main thread has nothing left to do. To ensure the program does not terminate before the exchange is complete, it waits for a signal from the last callback method: a [CountDownLatch] initialized to 1 (line 5), whose method [await] blocks the thread that calls it until another thread calls its method [countDown];
  • lines 50–64: The connection’s callback object implements the [CompletionHandler<V, A>] interface, where [V] is the result type of the operation ([Void] for a connection) and [A] is the type of the passed-in object. Its method [completed] is called if the operation succeeds, and its method [failed] is called if it fails. Once connected, reading is initiated with [read] by specifying a second callback object of type [Received] (line 56);
  • lines 66–85: the read callback object receives the number of bytes read, displays the message, closes the channel, and releases the main thread. The classes [Connected] and [Received] are internal classes of the implicit class of the compact file: they have access to its fields [buffer] and [end] and to its method [display];
  • the results show that the callback methods are executed by threads other than the main thread (threads from the JVM pool dedicated to asynchronous channels, named [InnocuousThread-N]);
  • lines 34–46: the same client, written using a standard [Socket] and blocking operations ([new Socket(...)] connects, [read] waits for data), executed by a virtual thread created by [Thread.ofVirtual().start(task)] (Java 21). The code reads from top to bottom like synchronous code; the variables are ordinary local variables; errors are handled by a single [try / catch]; there are no callback methods or signals to manage;
  • lines 87–92: Each display is prefixed with the thread that executes it. For a virtual thread, [toString()] returns a description in the form [VirtualThread[#28]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]: the virtual thread number, its state, and its current host thread. Lines 6 and 7 of the results show the same virtual thread No. 28, carried first by [worker-1] and then by [worker-2]: while waiting for the server’s response, it was detached from its first carrier and then reattached to another.

It is not necessary to retain the [CompletionHandler] interface. If you must use a API that only offers this model, convert it to [CompletableFuture] (we’ll do this in [Async17.java]), or use its blocking version on a virtual thread.

docs.title: 9.2. Upcoming tasks: Future and CompletableFuture
docs.text:
A [Future<T>] (interface of the [java.util.concurrent] package, Java 5) is an object that represents the result—of type [T]—of an ongoing or completed operation. We encountered it in the previous chapter: this is what the [submit] method of an executor returns. You can query it (has it finished? was it successful?), cancel it ([cancel]), and wait for its result ([get]), but nothing else: the only way to use the result is to block a thread until it is available.

The [CompletableFuture<T>] class (Java 8) implements [Future<T>] and adds two essential capabilities:

  • you can terminate it yourself, with a result ([complete]) or an exception ([completeExceptionally]);
  • you can attach a follow-up operation to it—a function that will be executed when the result is available ([thenApply], [thenAccept], [thenCompose]…), which produces a new [CompletableFuture]. In this way, chains of operations are constructed without any threads having to wait. These methods are declared by the [CompletionStage<T>] interface, which [CompletableFuture] also implements.

A [CompletableFuture] is not a thread. It may represent a process executed by a thread of an executor (as is the case with those created by [supplyAsync]), but many are not executed by any thread: the one in step 4 of [Async01.java] is simply “completed” by a timer after one second, and the one returned by [HttpClient.sendAsync] is completed when the server’s response arrives. It is a promise of a result.

The program [Async03.java] demonstrates the main ways to create, query, and wait for a [CompletableFuture]:

// CompletableFuture: creation, waiting, state, result, continuation
void main() throws InterruptedException {
    // 1 - supplyAsync gives a processing to an executor and returns a CompletableFuture<T>
    CompletableFuture<Long> f1 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> {
        // a computation of a few tenths of a second
        long sum = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= 200_000_000; i++) {
            sum += i % 7;
        }
        return sum;
    });
    IO.println("f1 started, state: " + f1.state());
    // join() waits for the end of the processing, blocking the current thread, and returns its result
    long result = f1.join();
    IO.println("f1 finished, state: " + f1.state() + ", result: " + result);

    // 2 - a CompletableFuture completed by a timer after 300 ms, without occupying a thread
    CompletableFuture<Void> f2 = new CompletableFuture<Void>()
            .completeOnTimeout(null, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    IO.println("f2 started, state: " + f2.state());
    f2.join();
    IO.println("f2 finished, state: " + f2.state());

    // 3 - CompletableFutures already completed, successfully or with a failure
    CompletableFuture<Integer> f3 = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(42);
    CompletableFuture<Integer> f4 = CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new IllegalStateException("failure"));
    IO.println("f3: state " + f3.state() + ", result " + f3.resultNow()
            + " ; f4: state " + f4.state() + ", exception " + f4.exceptionNow());

    // 4 - a processing that fails: join() throws a CompletionException that wraps its exception
    CompletableFuture<Integer> f5 = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> Integer.parseInt("abc"));
    try {
        f5.join();
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        IO.println("f5: state " + f5.state() + ", join() throws " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                + " containing " + e.getCause());
    }

    // 5 - get(), inherited from the Future interface, wraps the exception in an ExecutionException
    try {
        f5.get();
    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
        IO.println("f5: get() throws " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                + " containing " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
    }

    // 6 - a continuation: what to do when the CompletableFuture is completed
    CompletableFuture<Integer> f6 = f2.thenApply(nothing -> 2 * 21);
    CompletableFuture<Void> f7 = f6.thenAccept(value -> IO.println("f7: the continuation received " + value));
    f7.join();

    // 7 - isDone, isCompletedExceptionally, isCancelled
    IO.println("f1: isDone=" + f1.isDone() + ", f5: isDone=" + f5.isDone()
            + ", isCompletedExceptionally=" + f5.isCompletedExceptionally()
            + ", isCancelled=" + f5.isCancelled());
}

Results:

> java Async03.java
f1 started, state: RUNNING
f1 finished, state: SUCCESS, result: 599999998
f2 started, state: RUNNING
f2 finished, state: SUCCESS
f3: state SUCCESS, result 42 ; f4: state FAILED, exception java.lang.IllegalStateException: failure
f5: state FAILED, join() throws CompletionException containing java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "abc"
f5: get() throws ExecutionException containing NumberFormatException
f7: the continuation received 42
f1: isDone=true, f5: isDone=true, isCompletedExceptionally=true, isCancelled=false

Comments:

  • Lines 4–11: [CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(supplier)] passes a function with no parameters ([Supplier<T>]) to an executor and immediately returns a [CompletableFuture<T>] representing its execution. The function returns a [long], so we obtain a [CompletableFuture<Long>]. Without an explicit executor, the common pool for JVM and [ForkJoinPool.commonPool()] executes the function; we’ll see later how to choose the executor. For a processing operation with no result ([Runnable]), we use [runAsync], which returns a [CompletableFuture<Void>];
  • Line 12: The method [state()] (Java 19) returns the status of the operation: [RUNNING] (in progress), [SUCCESS] (completed successfully), [FAILED] (terminated due to an exception), or [CANCELLED] (canceled). These are the constants of the [Future.State] enumeration; the last three are final states: a completed operation no longer changes state;
  • line 14: [join()] waits for the operation to finish and returns its result. Like [Thread.join] in the previous chapter, this is a blocking wait: the current thread is suspended (the main thread in this case, which is not a problem for a small console program);
  • Lines 17–22: A [CompletableFuture] created as "in progress" by its creator and terminated by a timer after 300 ms ([completeOnTimeout], Java 9). No thread is occupied during this time: this is the asynchronous equivalent of [Thread.sleep(300)]. Its type is [CompletableFuture<Void>]: it does not return a result ([Void] is the class corresponding to [void]; its only value is [null]);
  • Lines 25–28: [completedFuture(42)] returns a previously completed [CompletableFuture] with a result of 42, and [failedFuture(exception)] (Java 9) returns a [CompletableFuture] that has already failed. They are used when a method needs to return a *[CompletableFuture] but already has the result (a cached value, for example) or already knows that it will fail. [resultNow()] and [exceptionNow()] (Java 19) return the result or exception of a completed operation without waiting (they throw a [IllegalStateException]* if the operation is not in the desired state);
  • lines 31–37: An operation whose function throws an exception ends in the [FAILED] state. The exception is stored in [CompletableFuture], and [join()] triggers a [CompletionException] (an unhandled exception) whose cause ([getCause()]) is the original exception, in this case a [NumberFormatException];
  • lines 40–45: [get()], the method inherited from the [Future] interface also waits in a blocking state, but wraps the exception in a [ExecutionException]—a checked exception—and can also throw a [InterruptedException], which is also checked: The call is therefore placed within a *[try / catch], which intercepts the first one, and the *[main] method declares the second one (line 2). [join()] is more convenient in code that manipulates [CompletableFuture]; [get()] is the only one available for a simple [Future], and there is a version with a delay, [get(timeout, unit)];
  • Lines 48–50: a continuation. [f2.thenApply(function)] returns a new [CompletableFuture], which will be completed with the result of the function applied to the result of [f2] once [f2] is completed. Here, the function ignores its parameter ([null]) and returns 42: this results in a [CompletableFuture<Integer>]. [thenAccept] attaches a function that consumes the result without producing one ([Consumer<T>]) and returns a [CompletableFuture<Void>]. If the original operation fails, the continuation is not executed and the failure propagates along the chain;
  • lines 53–55: the Boolean methods [isDone()] (completed, regardless of how), [isCompletedExceptionally()] (completed with an exception or aborted), and [isCancelled()] (aborted).

There are numerous methods in [CompletableFuture] (more than fifty). The following table lists the ones we will use:

MethodRole[supplyAsync(f)], [runAsync(r)]Execute a function (with or without a result) using an executor[completedFuture(v)], [failedFuture(e)]Create an operation that has already been completed, whether successfully or unsuccessfully[complete(v)], [completeExceptionally(e)]complete a task on your own[thenApply(f)]Transform the result: [T → U][thenAccept(c)], [thenRun(r)]Use the result, or perform an action after the operation[thenCompose(f)]Chain another asynchronous operation: [T → CompletableFuture<U>][thenCombine(other, f)]Combine the results of two operations performed in parallel[allOf(...)], [anyOf(...)]Wait for all operations to complete, or for the first one to finish[exceptionally(f)], [handle(f)], [whenComplete(c)]Handle or observe a failure[orTimeout(...)], [completeOnTimeout(...)]limit the duration of an operation[join()], [get()]Wait for the result by blocking the current thread

The methods [thenXxx], [handle], and [whenComplete] also exist in the [thenXxxAsync] version: we’ll discuss the difference in the section “Which thread executes the rest of the code?”

docs.title: 9.3.1. First approach: returning a CompletableFuture
docs.text:
In Java, an asynchronous method is simply a method that initiates an operation and immediately returns, without waiting, a [CompletableFuture] that represents it:

  • [CompletableFuture<Void>] if the operation returns no result;
  • [CompletableFuture<T>] if it returns a result of type [T].

The language does not impose any naming conventions. Java libraries often suffix these methods with [Async] ([sendAsync], [supplyAsync]), but this is not a rule: the return type is sufficient to identify them.

The program [Async04.java] makes coffee and counts sugar cubes:

// methods that return a CompletableFuture: the steps are composed with thenRun and thenCompose
final long start = System.nanoTime();

void main() {
    display("call of makeCoffee");
    CompletableFuture<Void> preparation = makeCoffee();
    display("makeCoffee has returned: the program continues");
    display("call of countSugars");
    CompletableFuture<Integer> counting = countSugars(3);
    display("countSugars has returned");
    // we combine the two operations, then wait for the result of the combination
    int nbSugars = preparation.thenCombine(counting, (nothing, count) -> count).join();
    display("coffee ready, with " + nbSugars + " sugar(s)");
}

// an operation that returns no result: it returns a CompletableFuture<Void>
CompletableFuture<Void> makeCoffee() {
    display("  coffee: the machine is heating up");
    // the method describes the sequence of steps, then returns immediately
    return delay(1000)
            .thenRun(() -> display("  coffee: the machine is pouring the coffee"))
            .thenCompose(nothing -> delay(500))
            .thenRun(() -> display("  coffee: done"));
}

// an operation that returns an integer: it returns a CompletableFuture<Integer>
CompletableFuture<Integer> countSugars(int count) {
    // a chain of steps that starts with an already completed CompletableFuture
    CompletableFuture<Void> steps = CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
    for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
        // a lambda can only use an effectively final local variable
        int number = i;
        steps = steps.thenCompose(nothing -> delay(200))
                .thenRun(() -> display("  sugar no. " + number));
    }
    // at the end of the chain, the result: the number of sugars
    return steps.thenApply(nothing -> count);
}

// the asynchronous equivalent of Thread.sleep: a CompletableFuture completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delay(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// display with the time elapsed since the start
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async04.java
    3 ms : call of makeCoffee
   12 ms :   coffee: the machine is heating up
   15 ms : makeCoffee has returned: the program continues
   16 ms : call of countSugars
   17 ms : countSugars has returned
  217 ms :   sugar no. 1
  417 ms :   sugar no. 2
  618 ms :   sugar no. 3
 1014 ms :   coffee: the machine is pouring the coffee
 1515 ms :   coffee: done
 1516 ms : coffee ready, with 3 sugar(s)

Comments:

  • Lines 40–43: The [delay] method is the asynchronous equivalent of [Thread.sleep]: it returns a [CompletableFuture<Void>] that will complete after the timeout, without occupying a thread. We will use it in many examples to simulate I/O;
  • Lines 17–24: an operation with no result. The method displays an initial message, then describes the sequence of steps and immediately returns the final [CompletableFuture]: this is why line 4 of the results appears right after line 3, rather than a second and a half later. The steps will be executed later, each one once the previous one is complete:
    • line 21: [thenRun(action)] performs an action when the previous operation is complete;
    • line 22: [thenCompose(function)] triggers another asynchronous operation: the function itself returns a [CompletableFuture] (in this case, a new 500-ms delay), and the [CompletableFuture] returned by [thenCompose] will not be completed until this second operation is finished. With [thenApply], we would have obtained a [CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Void>>], which would have completed as soon as the second delay began: [thenCompose] is to [thenApply] as [flatMap] is to [map] in the API stream;
  • Lines 27–38: An operation that returns an integer. A loop cannot “wait” on every iteration: it builds the sequence of steps, with each iteration adding a delay and a display to the existing sequence, starting from a pre-computed [CompletableFuture] (line 29). The entire string is constructed in a few microseconds and then unfolds as the delays occur. The variable [number] (line 32) is necessary because a lambda can only use a local variable that is effectively final, which [i] is not. Finally, [thenApply] converts the string into a [CompletableFuture<Integer>], the result of which is the number of sugars;
  • Lines 6–10: The main program calls both methods. It retrieves two [CompletableFuture] values and continues execution. The two operations then proceed “simultaneously”: the sugars are counted (lines 7–9 of the results) while the machine warms up;
  • line 12: [preparation.thenCombine(counting, function)] returns a completed [CompletableFuture] when both operations are finished, along with the result of the function applied to their two results: in this case, the number of sugar cubes is retained. [join()] waits for this result. The coffee is ready after 1.5 seconds—the duration of the longer of the two operations—and not after 2.1 seconds (1.5 + 3 × 0.2).

We can see the strengths and limitations of this approach. No thread waits: the steps are executed by the timer thread as the time intervals elapse. But the code no longer reads like a sequence of instructions: the [countSugars] loop doesn’t do what a loop usually does (it constructs a string instead of executing iterations), and a simple [if] or [try / catch] in the middle of the steps requires dedicated methods. That’s the price you pay when the language doesn’t offer keywords like [await].

docs.title: 9.3.2. Second approach: blocking code on virtual threads
docs.text:
Virtual threads allow you to write the same methods as ordinary, blocking methods. The program [Async05.java] makes the same cup of coffee:

// the same coffee with virtual threads: ordinary, blocking methods that read from top to bottom
final long start = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
    // an executor that creates a virtual thread for each task given to it
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        display("start of makeCoffee");
        Future<?> preparation = executor.submit(this::makeCoffee);
        display("makeCoffee is started: the program continues");
        display("start of countSugars");
        Future<Integer> counting = executor.submit(() -> countSugars(3));
        display("countSugars is started");
        // we now wait for the two results
        preparation.get();
        int nbSugars = counting.get();
        display("coffee ready, with " + nbSugars + " sugar(s)");
    }
}

// an ordinary method that returns no result
void makeCoffee() {
    display("  coffee: the machine is heating up");
    // a blocking wait: on a virtual thread, it releases the carrier thread
    sleep(1000);
    display("  coffee: the machine is pouring the coffee");
    sleep(500);
    display("  coffee: done");
}

// an ordinary method that returns an integer
int countSugars(int count) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= count; i++) {
        sleep(200);
        display("  sugar no. " + i);
    }
    return count;
}

// Thread.sleep without checked exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        // we restore the interrupt flag of the thread before throwing the exception
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("wait interrupted");
    }
}

// display with the time elapsed since the start
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async05.java
    3 ms : start of makeCoffee
   17 ms :   coffee: the machine is heating up
   18 ms : makeCoffee is started: the program continues
   18 ms : start of countSugars
   19 ms : countSugars is started
  221 ms :   sugar no. 1
  422 ms :   sugar no. 2
  623 ms :   sugar no. 3
 1020 ms :   coffee: the machine is pouring the coffee
 1521 ms :   coffee: done
 1522 ms : coffee ready, with 3 sugar(s)

Comments:

  • Lines 20–37: Both operations are regular methods: [makeCoffee] returns nothing ([void]), and [countSugars] returns a [int]. The calls are blocking [Thread.sleep] operations; the loop is a true loop. Nothing in these methods indicates that they will be executed concurrently: they could be called directly;
  • lines 39–48: the method [sleep] calls [Thread.sleep] and converts any [InterruptedException] (checked exception) into a [CancellationException] (unchecked exception), after resetting the thread’s interrupt flag: this is the rule when intercepting a [InterruptedException] without propagating it (we’ll return to this in the section on cancellation);
  • line 6: an executor that creates a virtual thread for each task. It is declared in a [try] with a resource: its [close()] method will wait for all tasks to complete;
  • Lines 8 and 11: [submit] delegates each method to a new virtual thread and returns a [Future]. The method reference [this::makeCoffee] is a [Runnable] (the method returns nothing), resulting in a [Future<?>]; the lambda [() -> countSugars(3)] is a [Callable<Integer>], resulting in a [Future<Integer>];
  • Lines 14–15: The main program waits for both results using [get()]. This is a blocking wait by the main thread, which has no consequence here;
  • the results are the same as with [Async04.java]: 1.5 seconds total, with the sugar counted while the machine warms up. During the waits, no system threads are blocked: the two virtual threads are detached from their carrier threads.

With virtual threads, asynchrony is no longer a matter of code writing but of execution: we write blocking code, and it is the executor’s choice (virtual threads rather than a platform thread pool) that determines whether the waits block system threads. This is why existing Java libraries (JDBC, files, sockets, [HttpClient.send]…), all written in a blocking manner, take advantage of virtual threads without modification.

docs.title: 9.3.3. What JVM Does
docs.text:
How can a virtual thread be interrupted in the middle of a loop, release its host thread, and then resume later at the same point, with the same local variable values, possibly on a different host thread? A virtual thread is a Java object ([java.lang.VirtualThread], a class derived from [Thread]) that has its own call stack. To execute it, JVM “mounts” it onto a carrier thread—a platform thread of a [ForkJoinPool] reserved for this purpose, which by default has as many threads as there are processors. When the virtual thread calls a blocking operation ([Thread.sleep], reading from a socket; [BlockingQueue.take], waiting for a lock…), the classes in JVM—rewritten for this purpose in Java 21—do not block the containing thread:

  • they register the operation with the system (a timer for a delay, the system’s I/O notification mechanism—[epoll] on Linux—for a socket);
  • they “unmount” the virtual thread: its call stack frames are copied to the heap as an object called a continuation, and the carrier thread is returned to [ForkJoinPool], which assigns it another virtual thread ready to execute;
  • when the operation completes, the virtual thread becomes ready again: it will be remounted onto the first available carrier thread, its stack frames will be recopied, and execution will resume immediately after the blocking call.

This is the principle behind callback methods (“call me back when the operation is complete”), but it is the JVM that breaks down the execution, saves the variables, and restores the context at the call stack level, without the source code showing any trace of it. Other languages entrust this task to the compiler, which transforms each [async] method into a “state machine”; Java entrusts it to the JVM, which allows it to handle all existing code in the same way.

There are two limitations to be aware of:

  • certain operations cannot detach the virtual thread; it therefore remains “pinned” to its host thread, which is blocked while waiting. This occurs during the execution of a native method, and during most file reads and writes (the system does not provide a notification for files that can be used by the JVM); for the latter, the [ForkJoinPool] compensates by temporarily creating an additional carrier thread. Up to Java 23, this was also the case for a virtual thread waiting inside a [synchronized] block; since Java 24, this is no longer the case;
  • a virtual thread does not speed up a computation: a virtual thread performing a computation occupies its host thread for the entire duration of the computation. Virtual threads are intended for programs that do a lot of waiting, not those that do a lot of computation (for the latter, thread pools and parallel streams from the previous chapter are available).

docs.title: 9.3.4. Which thread executes the next section?
docs.text:
The program [Async06.java] displays the thread that executes each piece of code:

// which thread executes the rest of a processing?
void main() throws InterruptedException {
    display("start of the program, parallelism of the common pool: " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism());

    // 1 - the continuation of an already completed CompletableFuture is executed immediately, by the caller
    CompletableFuture.completedFuture(42).thenAccept(value -> display("1 - thenAccept, result known"));

    // 2 - otherwise, it is executed by the thread that completes the CompletableFuture
    delay(100).thenRun(() -> display("2 - thenRun after a delay")).join();
    CompletableFuture<String> order = new CompletableFuture<>();
    order.thenAccept(text -> display("2 - thenAccept after complete(\"" + text + "\")"));
    Thread.ofPlatform().name("deliverer").start(() -> order.complete("delivered")).join();

    // 3 - the xxxAsync variants give the continuation to an executor
    delay(100).thenRunAsync(() -> display("3 - thenRunAsync, default executor")).join();
    ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofPlatform().name("pool-", 1).factory();
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, factory)) {
        delay(100).thenRunAsync(() -> display("3 - thenRunAsync, chosen executor"), pool).join();
        CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> display("3 - runAsync, chosen executor"), pool).join();
    }
    try (ExecutorService virtuals = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> display("3 - runAsync, virtual threads"), virtuals).join();
    }

    // 4 - a virtual thread may change carrier thread after each wait
    Thread a = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> work("A"));
    Thread b = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> work("B"));
    a.join();
    b.join();
    display("end of the program");
}

void work(String name) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
        display("  " + name + i + " : before the wait");
        sleep(100);
    }
}

// a CompletableFuture completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delay(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// Thread.sleep without checked exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("wait interrupted");
    }
}

// display prefixed by the thread executing it
// (name of a platform thread, description of a virtual thread)
void display(String message) {
    Thread thread = Thread.currentThread();
    IO.println("[" + (thread.isVirtual() ? thread.toString() : thread.getName()) + "] " + message);
}

Results:

> java Async06.java
[main] start of the program, parallelism of the common pool: 1
[main] 1 - thenAccept, result known
[ForkJoinPool.commonPool-delayScheduler] 2 - thenRun after a delay
[deliverer] 2 - thenAccept after complete("delivered")
[ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1] 3 - thenRunAsync, default executor
[pool-1] 3 - thenRunAsync, chosen executor
[pool-2] 3 - runAsync, chosen executor
[VirtualThread[#28]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1] 3 - runAsync, virtual threads
[VirtualThread[#31]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]   A1 : before the wait
[VirtualThread[#32]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2]   B1 : before the wait
[VirtualThread[#32]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2]   B2 : before the wait
[VirtualThread[#31]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]   A2 : before the wait
[VirtualThread[#31]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2]   A3 : before the wait
[VirtualThread[#32]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]   B3 : before the wait
[main] end of the program

Comments:

  • line 3: the shared pool ([ForkJoinPool.commonPool()]), the default executor for [CompletableFuture], has a parallelism equal to the number of processors minus one, which is 1 on our 2-processor machine (line 2 of the results);
  • Line 6: The continuation of a [CompletableFuture] that has already completed is executed immediately by the thread that attached it: thread [main] (line 3);
  • lines 9–12: if the operation is not complete, the continuation will be executed by the thread that will complete it: the timeout timer thread for [delay(100)] (line 4), the thread [deliverer], which calls [complete] for the order (line 5). Therefore, the thread that executes a non-asynchronous continuation is not chosen; this is irrelevant for a brief action, but a long or blocking continuation would immobilize that thread (the timer thread, for example, which handles all the timeouts for [CompletableFuture]);
  • lines 15–23: the [xxxAsync] variants ([thenRunAsync], [thenApplyAsync]…) delegate the continuation to an executor: without additional parameters, to the shared pool (line 6 of the results); with an executor as the last parameter, to that executor. This allows one to choose platform threads (lines 7–8: a pool of two threads whose names are determined by a thread factory, [ThreadFactory], constructed by [Thread.ofPlatform().name("pool-", 1).factory()]), or virtual threads (line 9). [supplyAsync] and [runAsync] also accept an executor;
  • Lines 26–38: Two virtual threads that display a message and then sleep, three times in a row. The results show that they do not remain attached to a single host thread: virtual thread No. 31 (A) starts at [worker-1] and ends at [worker-2], while No. 32 (B) does the opposite. While one is sleeping, its carrier thread is free for the other. Therefore, in a virtual thread, one must never assume that the code following a wait is executed by the same carrier thread as the code preceding it; but it is always the same virtual thread, and that is what matters to the program ([Thread.currentThread()] returns the virtual thread; its variables, [ThreadLocal], are preserved).

This method of performing multiple operations simultaneously without increasing the number of system threads is called concurrency. It differs from parallelism, which involves executing multiple calculations at the same time across multiple processors (as discussed in the previous chapter: thread pools, parallel streams). Asynchrony facilitates I/O concurrency; it does not make calculations faster.

The choice of executor is therefore important:

  • the shared pool is suitable for brief continuations and short computations; blocking operations should not be executed there, as this risks the starvation described in [Async01.java] (it has only one thread on our machine);
  • for a blocking operation (I/O, calls to JDBC or [Thread.sleep]), use a virtual thread executor: [CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(supplier, virtualExecutor)];
  • for a graphical user interface, we pass an executor that has the continuation executed by the UI thread, which allows the graphical components to be updated: with Swing, [thenAcceptAsync(action, SwingUtilities::invokeLater)] (the method reference [SwingUtilities::invokeLater] is a valid [Executor], since [Executor] is a functional interface whose sole method takes a [Runnable]); with JavaFX, [Platform::runLater].

docs.title: 9.3.5. The Main Program
docs.text:
In other languages, the main method of an asynchronous program must be declared in a specific way. In Java, there is no such requirement: the method [main] is executed by the platform thread [main], and it is up to that method to wait for the operations it has initiated—using [join()] or [get()]—to complete. This is the only place where a blocking wait on a [CompletableFuture] is normal. The [Async07.java] program performs an asynchronous countdown:

// the main program waits for the end of the asynchronous operations and sets the exit code
void main(String[] args) {
    // the number of seconds is passed as an argument
    if (args.length != 1 || !args[0].matches("\\d+")) {
        IO.println("syntax: java Async07.java nbSeconds");
        // the exit code of the program: 0 for a success, something else for an error
