        System.exit(1);
    }
    CompletableFuture<Void> countdown = countDown(Integer.parseInt(args[0]));
    IO.println("countdown started");
    // without this wait, main would end immediately and the program with it
    countdown.join();
    IO.println("finished");
}

// an asynchronous loop is written with recursion: each step starts the next one
CompletableFuture<Void> countDown(int nbSeconds) {
    if (nbSeconds == 0) {
        return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(null);
    }
    IO.println("still " + nbSeconds + " s");
    return delay(1000).thenCompose(nothing -> countDown(nbSeconds - 1));
}

// a CompletableFuture completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delay(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

Results, first with and then without an argument:

> java Async07.java 3
still 3 s
countdown started
still 2 s
still 1 s
finished

> java Async07.java
syntax: java Async07.java nbSeconds
> echo $?
1

Comments:

  • line 2: the [args] parameter of [main] receives the command-line arguments, which are placed after the filename: [java Async07.java 3];
  • Lines 4–8: If the argument is missing or is not a positive integer (regular expression [\d+]: one or more digits), the program terminates with [System.exit(1)]. The integer passed to [System.exit] is the program’s exit code (0 for success, any other value for an error), which can be checked by a script: [echo $?] on Linux (second result), [echo %ERRORLEVEL%] on Windows. A program whose [main] method terminates normally returns code 0;
  • lines 16–23: an asynchronous countdown. An asynchronous loop is naturally implemented using recursion: each step displays a message and then, using [thenCompose], introduces a one-second delay followed by the next step. There is no call stack: the recursive call is made via the continuation, one second later;
  • lines 9–12: the method [countDown] displays its first message and then returns control (lines 2–3 of the results); the main program waits for the operation to finish with [join()]. Without this wait, [main] would terminate immediately, and the program along with it: JVM stops when only daemon threads remain, and the timer and shared pool threads are daemons. The same applies to virtual threads, which are always daemons: a program must wait for the virtual threads it has launched to finish (using [join], [get], or the [close] method of their executor).

docs.title: 9.4.1. allOf and invokeAll
docs.text:
The coffee example demonstrated this: the moment an asynchronous operation is initiated and the moment it is awaited can be different. Writing [method().join()] initiates the operation and awaits it immediately; writing [var f = method();] and then, later, [f.join();] allows other operations to be launched in between. The program [Async08.java] compares the two approaches using operations that take one second:

// sequential execution and concurrent execution of one-second operations
long start = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    // 1 - in sequence: each operation is awaited before starting the next one
    int a = readTemperature("Angers").join();
    int b = readTemperature("Brest").join();
    int c = readTemperature("Colmar").join();
    IO.println("in sequence: " + a + ", " + b + ", " + c + " in " + elapsed() + " ms");

    // 2 - concurrently: we start the three operations, then we wait for them
    start = System.nanoTime();
    CompletableFuture<Integer> fa = readTemperature("Angers");
    CompletableFuture<Integer> fb = readTemperature("Brest");
    CompletableFuture<Integer> fc = readTemperature("Colmar");
    CompletableFuture.allOf(fa, fb, fc).join();
    IO.println("concurrently: " + fa.resultNow() + ", " + fb.resultNow() + ", " + fc.resultNow()
            + " in " + elapsed() + " ms");

    // 3 - allOf on a list of CompletableFutures, then the list of the results
    start = System.nanoTime();
    List<String> cities = List.of("Angers", "Brest", "Colmar", "Dijon", "Évry", "Foix");
    List<CompletableFuture<Integer>> readings = cities.stream().map(this::readTemperature).toList();
    List<Integer> temperatures = CompletableFuture.allOf(readings.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new))
            .thenApply(nothing -> readings.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList())
            .join();
    IO.println(cities.size() + " cities: " + temperatures + " in " + elapsed() + " ms");

    // 4 - the same thing with virtual threads and a blocking method
    start = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        List<Callable<Integer>> tasks = cities.stream()
                .map(city -> (Callable<Integer>) () -> readTemperatureBlocking(city))
                .toList();
        // invokeAll starts all the tasks and returns their Futures when they are all finished
        List<Integer> results = executor.invokeAll(tasks).stream().map(Future::resultNow).toList();
        IO.println(cities.size() + " cities (virtual threads): " + results + " in " + elapsed() + " ms");
    }
}

// simulates querying a remote service that answers in one second
CompletableFuture<Integer> readTemperature(String city) {
    // a "temperature" derived from the name of the city
    return delay(1000).thenApply(nothing -> 10 + city.length());
}

// the same operation, written in a blocking way
int readTemperatureBlocking(String city) throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    return 10 + city.length();
}

// a CompletableFuture completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delay(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// milliseconds elapsed since [start]
long elapsed() {
    return (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
}

Results:

> java Async08.java
in sequence: 16, 15, 16 in 3007 ms
concurrently: 16, 15, 16 in 1000 ms
6 cities: [16, 15, 16, 15, 14, 14] in 1006 ms
6 cities (virtual threads): [16, 15, 16, 15, 14, 14] in 1013 ms

Comments:

  • lines 41–45: the simulated operation: a one-second delay, followed by a “temperature” derived from the length of the city name;
  • lines 6–8: Each operation is started and then waited for before starting the next one. The three operations are performed one after the other: 3 seconds (line 2 of the results). This is the correct approach when one operation requires the result of the previous one (in which case, one would instead write a chain of [thenCompose]);
  • lines 13–15: The three operations are started without waiting for each other. They run simultaneously;
  • line 16: [CompletableFuture.allOf(...)] returns a [CompletableFuture<Void>], which completes once all the operations passed to it are finished. We wait for it with [join()]: 1 second instead of 3 (line 3);
  • lines 17–18: The three operations are complete, so [resultNow()] returns their results immediately;
  • lines 22–27: the case of a list of operations. [allOf] waits for an array ([CompletableFuture<?>...]): the [toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)] method in the list creates it. [allOf] does not return the results: they are collected in a continuation by calling [join()] on each operation, which does not block since they have all completed. The list of results is obtained in the order of the operations (not in the order in which they completed). The expression [cities.stream().map(this::readTemperature).toList()] calls the method for each city, thereby launching six operations simultaneously; all six together take one second (line 4);
  • lines 29–38: the same thing with a blocking method (lines 47–51) executed by virtual threads. The method [invokeAll] of an executor receives a collection of [Callable<T>], launches them all, and returns the list of their [Future<T>] when they are all complete: This is the blocking equivalent of *[allOf]. The type cast [(Callable<Integer>)] on line 33 tells the compiler the type of the lambda, which it cannot infer on its own in a [map]*. The six operations together take one second (line 5).

docs.title: 9.4.2. anyOf
docs.text:
[CompletableFuture.anyOf(...)] returns a [CompletableFuture<Object>] that terminates as soon as one of the operations passed to it is completed, with the result (or exception) of that operation. The program [Async09.java] uses it in two ways:

// anyOf: reacting to the first completed operation
long start = System.nanoTime();

void main() {
    // 1 - we query three mirror servers and keep the first answer
    List<CompletableFuture<String>> requests = List.of(
            query("mirror-paris", 800),
            query("mirror-lyon", 300),
            query("mirror-lille", 600));
    // anyOf returns a CompletableFuture<Object> that completes like the first completed operation
    Object first = CompletableFuture.anyOf(requests.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
    display("first answer: " + first);
    // the other requests continue: we wait for them here to see their answers
    CompletableFuture.allOf(requests.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
    display("all the answers: " + requests.stream().map(CompletableFuture::resultNow).toList());

    // 2 - a time-limited operation: we "race" it against a delay
    start = System.nanoTime();
    CompletableFuture<String> slow = query("slow-server", 2000);
    CompletableFuture<Object> race = CompletableFuture.anyOf(slow, delay(500));
    race.join();
    if (slow.isDone()) {
        display("answer obtained in time: " + slow.join());
    } else {
        display("the slow server did not answer within the 500 ms delay");
    }
}

// simulates a server that answers after [duration] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<String> query(String server, int duration) {
    return delay(duration).thenApply(nothing -> server + " (" + duration + " ms)");
}

// a CompletableFuture completed after [ms] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<Void> delay(long ms) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, ms, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// display with the time elapsed since [start]
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async09.java
  309 ms : first answer: mirror-lyon (300 ms)
  806 ms : all the answers: [mirror-paris (800 ms), mirror-lyon (300 ms), mirror-lille (600 ms)]
  500 ms : the slow server did not answer within the 500 ms delay

Comments:

  • lines 6–9: Three mirror servers are queried; they all hold the same information and respond at varying speeds. The three operations are stored in a list;
  • line 11: [anyOf] returns a [CompletableFuture<Object>], whose result is that of the first completed operation. Its type is [Object] because the operations passed to [anyOf] may have different result types: it would need to be cast to use it as a string. The first response arrives after 300 ms (line 2 of the results);
  • line 14: the other requests are not terminated by [anyOf]; they continue until they finish. Here, we wait for them to display all the responses (line 3);
  • lines 19–26: a common use of [anyOf]: limiting the duration of a wait by setting up a “race” between the operation and a timeout. If the operation is not finished when the race is over, the timeout has won: the operation took too long (line 4). [CompletableFuture] offers a more direct way to write this case, the [orTimeout] method, which is presented later.

docs.title: 9.4.3. Processing Results as They Come In
docs.text:
We often want to process the results of multiple operations as they complete, without waiting for the slowest one. With [CompletableFuture], this is straightforward: simply attach a continuation to each operation. For tasks submitted to an executor, the [ExecutorCompletionService] class (Java 5) returns the [Future] objects in the order in which the tasks complete. The program [Async10.java] processes five “files,” each of which takes between 100 and 900 ms to process, in both ways:

// processing the results in the order in which the operations finish
long start = System.nanoTime();
final int[] durations = {900, 300, 700, 100, 500};

void main() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
    // 1 - with CompletableFutures: one continuation per operation, executed as soon as it finishes
    List<CompletableFuture<Void>> displays = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < durations.length; i++) {
        displays.add(process("file" + i + ".txt", durations[i]).thenAccept(this::display));
    }
    CompletableFuture.allOf(displays.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
    display("1 - all the files have been processed");

    // 2 - with virtual threads: a CompletionService delivers the Futures in the order they finish
    start = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        CompletionService<String> service = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(executor);
        for (int i = 0; i < durations.length; i++) {
            String file = "file" + i + ".txt";
            int duration = durations[i];
            service.submit(() -> processBlocking(file, duration));
        }
        // take() waits (blocking) for the next finished task
        for (int i = 0; i < durations.length; i++) {
            display(service.take().get());
        }
    }
    display("2 - all the files have been processed");
}

// simulates the processing of a file that lasts [duration] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<String> process(String file, int duration) {
    return new CompletableFuture<String>()
            .completeOnTimeout(file + " processed in " + duration + " ms", duration, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// the same processing, written in a blocking way
String processBlocking(String file, int duration) throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.sleep(duration);
    return file + " processed in " + duration + " ms";
}

// display with the time elapsed since [start]
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async10.java
  107 ms : file3.txt processed in 100 ms
  318 ms : file1.txt processed in 300 ms
  508 ms : file4.txt processed in 500 ms
  707 ms : file2.txt processed in 700 ms
  906 ms : file0.txt processed in 900 ms
  907 ms : 1 - all the files have been processed
  115 ms : file3.txt processed in 100 ms
  314 ms : file1.txt processed in 300 ms
  514 ms : file4.txt processed in 500 ms
  714 ms : file2.txt processed in 700 ms
  914 ms : file0.txt processed in 900 ms
  915 ms : 2 - all the files have been processed

Comments:

  • Lines 7–11: Each processing task receives its own continuation, [thenAccept(this::display)], which is executed as soon as it finishes: file 3 (100 ms) is displayed first, file 0 (900 ms) last (lines 2–6 of the results). The method [process] (lines 31–35) returns a completed [CompletableFuture<String>] after the specified duration with the desired message ([completeOnTimeout] directly receives the result value). The list of continuations is used to wait for all displays to finish with [allOf];
  • lines 16–27: a [CompletionService<T>] wraps an executor (in this case, a virtual thread executor). Its method [submit] launches a task; its method [take()] waits, blocking, for the next completed task and returns its [Future], whose result is immediately returned by [get()]. The loop in lines 24–26 therefore processes the files in the order in which they are completed (lines 8–12);
  • in both cases, the entire process takes 900 ms—the duration of the longest processing step—and each result is displayed as soon as possible.

docs.title: 9.5.1. Propagation, exceptionally, handle, whenComplete
docs.text:
An exception thrown by an asynchronous operation is not thrown back to the code that initiated the operation: it is stored in [CompletableFuture], which transitions to the [FAILED] state. It then propagates along the continuation chain until it reaches a method that handles it, or until it reaches [join()], which rethrows it wrapped in a [CompletionException]. The program [Async11.java] examines the various cases:

// exceptions in asynchronous code
void main() {
    // 1 - join() throws a CompletionException that wraps the exception of the operation
    try {
        int value = readValue("twelve").join();
        IO.println("value = " + value);
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        IO.println("1 - join() throws " + name(e) + ", with cause " + name(e.getCause())
                + " : " + e.getCause().getMessage());
    }

    // 2 - exceptionally provides a replacement value in case of failure
    int value = readValue("thirteen").exceptionally(e -> -1).join();
    IO.println("2 - exceptionally: replacement value " + value);

    // 3 - handle receives the result or the exception; whenComplete observes them without changing anything
    for (String text : List.of("14", "fifteen")) {
        String outcome = readValue(text)
                .whenComplete((v, e) -> IO.println("3 - whenComplete saw: " + (e == null ? v : name(e))))
                .handle((v, e) -> e == null ? "value " + v : "failure, " + name(cause(e)))
                .join();
        IO.println("3 - handle returned: " + outcome);
    }

    // 4 - a method that returns a CompletableFuture can also throw an exception right at the call
    try {
        readValue(" ");
        IO.println("4 - the call threw nothing");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        IO.println("4 - it is the call itself that throws " + name(e) + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }

    // 5 - allOf with several failing operations
    List<CompletableFuture<Integer>> readings = Stream.of("1", "two", "3", "four")
            .map(this::readValue)
            .toList();
    try {
        CompletableFuture.allOf(readings.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        // join() rethrows only one of the exceptions…
        IO.println("5 - allOf fails with " + name(e.getCause()) + " : " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        // … but each operation has kept its exception or its result
        for (CompletableFuture<Integer> reading : readings) {
            switch (reading.state()) {
                case SUCCESS -> IO.println("      success, result = " + reading.resultNow());
                case FAILED -> IO.println("      failure, " + name(reading.exceptionNow())
                        + " : " + reading.exceptionNow().getMessage());
                default -> IO.println("      unexpected state: " + reading.state());
            }
        }
    }
}

// an asynchronous operation that fails if the string is not an integer
CompletableFuture<Integer> readValue(String text) {
    // immediate check of the parameter, before starting the operation
    if (text == null || text.isBlank()) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("the text must not be empty");
    }
    // the reading takes a little time
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>()
            .completeOnTimeout(null, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .thenApply(nothing -> Integer.parseInt(text));
}

// continuations often receive a CompletionException: we go back to its cause
Throwable cause(Throwable e) {
    return e instanceof CompletionException && e.getCause() != null ? e.getCause() : e;
}

// the simple name of the class of an exception
String name(Throwable e) {
    return e.getClass().getSimpleName();
}

Results:

> java Async11.java
1 - join() throws CompletionException, with cause NumberFormatException : For input string: "twelve"
2 - exceptionally: replacement value -1
3 - whenComplete saw: 14
3 - handle returned: value 14
3 - whenComplete saw: CompletionException
3 - handle returned: failure, NumberFormatException
4 - it is the call itself that throws IllegalArgumentException : the text must not be empty
5 - allOf fails with NumberFormatException : For input string: "two"
      success, result = 1
      failure, NumberFormatException : For input string: "two"
      success, result = 3
      failure, NumberFormatException : For input string: "four"

Comments:

  • Lines 54–64: the method being tested. It first checks its parameter and launches a [IllegalArgumentException] if the string is [null] or empty. Otherwise, it returns an operation that waits 100 ms and then converts the entire string, which throws a [NumberFormatException] if the string is not a number;
  • lines 4–10: the standard case. The exception thrown by [Integer.parseInt] in the continuation of line 63 is caught by [CompletableFuture]; [join()] rethrows the exception wrapped in a [CompletionException], from which [getCause()] returns the original exception (line 2 of the results);
  • line 13: [exceptionally(function)] returns a [CompletableFuture] that has the same result as the operation if it succeeds, and otherwise the result of the function applied to the exception: this is the [catch] from the world of [CompletableFuture]. Here, a failure is replaced with the value -1 (line 3);
  • lines 17–23: two other methods, applied to a successful operation and then to a failed operation:
    • [whenComplete(action)] receives the result and the exception (one of the two is [null]) and does not change anything: the [CompletableFuture] it returns has the same result or the same exception as the operation. It is used for observation (logging, freeing a resource): this is the [finally] of the [CompletableFuture] world;
    • [handle(function)] also receives the result and the exception, and returns a new value in both cases: it transforms both a success and a failure into a result;
    • Lines 6 and 7 of the results reveal a pitfall: the exception received by the continuations is not [NumberFormatException] but a [CompletionException] that wraps it, because the failure occurred in a previous step of the chain (the continuation on line 63). The method [cause] (lines 66–69) traces back to the original exception: we’ll get into the habit of writing it out;
  • lines 26–31: an important difference from the [async] methods in other languages: a method that returns a [CompletableFuture] is an ordinary method, which can throw an exception as soon as it is called, before creating any [CompletableFuture]. This is the case here for an empty string (line 8 of the results). The calling code must therefore expect both types of errors, or the method must return an operation that has already failed ([return CompletableFuture.failedFuture(new IllegalArgumentException(...));]), which is often preferable;
  • lines 34–38: We wait with [allOf] for four operations, two of which fail. The [CompletableFuture] from [allOf] fails in turn, but with only one of the exceptions (line 9 of the results);
  • lines 43–50: Each operation has retained its result or exception. We examine their status using a [switch]; [exceptionNow()] returns the original exception, without a wrapper. The failure of [allOf] does not prevent the other operations from succeeding (lines 10 and 12).

With virtual threads, the issue does not arise in the same way: the code executed by a virtual thread is ordinary code, where exceptions propagate as usual and are intercepted by [try / catch]. Only the boundary between two threads requires special attention: an exception from a task submitted to an executor is stored in its [Future], and [get()] rethrows it wrapped in a [ExecutionException].

docs.title: 9.5.2. Forgotten Operations
docs.text:
What happens to the exception from an operation that no one is waiting for? The program [Async12.java] demonstrates this:

// an operation started then forgotten: its exception is lost
void main() {
    // the handler of the exceptions that no code has caught in a thread
    Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((thread, e) ->
            IO.println("uncaught exception in [" + thread.getName() + "] : " + e.getMessage()));

    // 1 - an awaited CompletableFuture: its exception is caught
    try {
        save("a").join();
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        IO.println("1 - awaited CompletableFuture: exception caught: " + e.getCause().getMessage());
    }

    // 2 - a forgotten CompletableFuture: its exception stays in the object, nobody will see it
    save("b");
    IO.println("2 - forgotten CompletableFuture: the call has returned");

    // 3 - a task submitted to an executor and forgotten: its exception stays in the Future
    ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
    executor.submit(() -> saveBlocking("c"));
    IO.println("3 - forgotten Future: the task is started");

    // 4 - a thread: the uncaught exception ends the thread and reaches the handler
    Thread.ofVirtual().name("recorder").start(() -> saveBlocking("d"));
    IO.println("4 - virtual thread started");

    // 5 - start without waiting, but handling the failure
    save("e").exceptionally(e -> {
        IO.println("5 - failure reported by exceptionally: " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        return null;
    });

    // the program continues its work…
    for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {
        sleep(100);
        IO.println("the program is working (" + i + ")");
    }
    executor.close();
    IO.println("normal end of the program");
}

// an asynchronous operation that fails after 200 ms
CompletableFuture<Void> save(String data) {
    return new CompletableFuture<Void>()
            .completeOnTimeout(null, 200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
            .thenRun(() -> {
                throw new IllegalStateException("failed to save [" + data + "]");
            });
}

// the same operation, written in a blocking way
void saveBlocking(String data) {
    sleep(200);
    throw new IllegalStateException("failed to save [" + data + "]");
}

// Thread.sleep without checked exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("wait interrupted");
    }
}

Results:

> java Async12.java
1 - awaited CompletableFuture: exception caught: failed to save [a]
2 - forgotten CompletableFuture: the call has returned
3 - forgotten Future: the task is started
4 - virtual thread started
the program is working (1)
5 - failure reported by exceptionally: failed to save [e]
uncaught exception in [recorder] : failed to save [d]
the program is working (2)
the program is working (3)
the program is working (4)
normal end of the program

Comments:

  • lines 4–5: [Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler] sets up the handler that is called when an exception is not caught by any code in a thread, just before the end of that thread. Without it, JVM displays the exception’s stack trace in the error output;
  • lines 8–12: The operation is expected, and its exception is intercepted normally;
  • lines 14–16: the operation is launched and then forgotten. Its exception is stored in [CompletableFuture], which no one will ever consult: it is lost, without so much as a message;
  • lines 18–21: The same applies to a task submitted by [submit] to an executor: its exception is stored in the returned [Future], which is ignored;
  • line 24: a thread launched directly has no [Future]: the exception it fails to handle terminates the thread and reaches the uncaught exception handler (line 8 of the results). The program, however, continues;
  • lines 28–31: the correct way to start an operation without waiting for it: attach a continuation [exceptionally] (or [whenComplete]) to it that handles failure, in this case by printing a message (line 7);
  • Lines 33–39 show that, in all cases, the program continues running until its normal termination. This differs from some languages, where an uncaught exception can terminate the program; in Java, it goes unnoticed, which isn’t any better: a record error that no one sees means lost data.

The rule is therefore: an operation that has been initiated must be completed ([join], [get], [allOf], or the [close] method of an executor, which waits for its tasks), or receive a continuation that handles its failure. Code analysis tools (SpotBugs, IntelliJ IDEA's inspections) may also flag the ignored result of a method that returns a [Future].

docs.title: 9.6.1. Future.cancel and thread termination
docs.text:
A long-running operation must be able to be canceled: the user clicked on [Cancel], a server client disconnected, the application shut down, or a timeout occurred. Java uses a cooperative mechanism for this—thread interruption:

  • a thread’s [interrupt()] method sets its interrupt flag; it does not stop the thread (the [Thread.stop] method, which forced a stop, has been deprecated since Java 20: it calls [UnsupportedOperationException]);
  • if the thread is blocked in an interruptible wait ([Thread.sleep], [Object.wait], [Thread.join], [BlockingQueue.take], [Future.get]…), the wait is immediately interrupted and triggers a [InterruptedException], clearing the flag;
  • a thread that performs calculations checks its own indicator regularly using [Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()] and terminates gracefully if it is set;
  • the [cancel(true)] method of a [Future] returned by an executor transitions the task to the [CANCELLED] state and interrupts the thread executing it ([cancel(false)] simply prevents the task from starting if it has not yet done so). After cancellation, [get()] launches a [CancellationException].

The mechanism is cooperative: no one forcibly stops an operation; the operation stops itself at a point where it can do so cleanly. This is why a method that intercepts a [InterruptedException] must not ignore it: it must either propagate it, terminate itself, or at the very least reset the flag with [Thread.currentThread().interrupt()] so that the calling code knows that an interruption has been requested (this is what our method [sleep] does).

The program [Async13.java] cancels a simulated download in several ways:

// cancelling an operation: Future.cancel(true) and thread interruption
long start = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        // 1 - we do not wait for the result more than 1.2 seconds, then we cancel the operation
        Future<?> download1 = executor.submit(() -> download(10));
        try {
            download1.get(1200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            // cancel(true) interrupts the thread executing the task
            download1.cancel(true);
            display("1 - " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", state: " + download1.state());
        }

        // 2 - a computation that checks itself, regularly, whether it has been interrupted
        start = System.nanoTime();
        Future<Long> computation = executor.submit(this::compute);
        Thread.sleep(300);
        computation.cancel(true);
        try {
            display("2 - result: " + computation.get());
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            display("2 - get() throws " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ", state: " + computation.state());
        }
        Thread.sleep(100);

        // 3 - the cancellation is requested by the program after 700 ms
        start = System.nanoTime();
        Future<?> download3 = executor.submit(() -> download(10));
        Thread.sleep(700);
        display("3 - the program requests the cancellation");
        download3.cancel(true);
        display("3 - isCancelled=" + download3.isCancelled());
        Thread.sleep(100);

        // 4 - cancel() on a CompletableFuture does not interrupt the operation it represents
        start = System.nanoTime();
        CompletableFuture<Void> download4 = CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> download(3), executor);
        Thread.sleep(400);
        download4.cancel(true);
        display("4 - CompletableFuture cancelled: isCancelled=" + download4.isCancelled()
                + ", but the operation continues");
    } // close() waits for the end of all the tasks
}

// simulates the download of [nbBlocks] blocks of data (one block every 300 ms)
void download(int nbBlocks) {
    try {
        for (int i = 1; i <= nbBlocks; i++) {
            // a blocking wait is interrupted as soon as the thread is interrupted
            Thread.sleep(300);
            display("  block " + i + "/" + nbBlocks + " received");
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        display("  download interrupted");
    }
}

// a long computation that checks the interrupt flag of its thread every 1,000,000 rounds
long compute() {
    long sum = 0;
    for (long i = 0; i < 100_000_000_000L; i++) {
        if (i % 1_000_000 == 0 && Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
            display("  computation interrupted at round " + i);
            return -1;
        }
        sum += i % 7;
    }
    return sum;
}

// display with the time elapsed since [start]
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async13.java
  318 ms :   block 1/10 received
  638 ms :   block 2/10 received
  939 ms :   block 3/10 received
 1212 ms :   download interrupted
 1214 ms : 1 - TimeoutException, state: CANCELLED
  301 ms : 2 - get() throws CancellationException, state: CANCELLED
  303 ms :   computation interrupted at round 131000000
  302 ms :   block 1/10 received
  603 ms :   block 2/10 received
  701 ms : 3 - the program requests the cancellation
  702 ms :   download interrupted
  702 ms : 3 - isCancelled=true
  309 ms :   block 1/3 received
  404 ms : 4 - CompletableFuture cancelled: isCancelled=true, but the operation continues
  609 ms :   block 2/3 received
  910 ms :   block 3/3 received

Comments:

  • Lines 47–58: The simulated download receives a block every 300 ms. It is executed by a virtual thread and uses a blocking wait, [Thread.sleep], which terminates as soon as the thread is interrupted: [InterruptedException] exits the loop, and the download stops by signaling this. It requires no special parameters to be cancelable: the waits for [java.util.concurrent] react in the same way to the interruption, as do, in a virtual thread, the blocking I/O operations on sockets (the socket is then closed, and the operation initiates a [SocketException]);
  • Lines 6–14: [get(1200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)] waits for the result for at most 1.2 seconds, then launches a [TimeoutException]. The wait is abandoned but not the operation: it is explicitly canceled with [cancel(true)], which interrupts the download’s virtual thread. The thread has received three blocks and stops at 1,200 ms (lines 2–6 of the results);
  • lines 16–26: a cancelable calculation (not a wait). The [compute] method (lines 60–71) checks its thread’s interrupt flag every million cycles and stops if it is set. The program aborts it after 300 ms: [get()] immediately launches a [CancellationException] (line 7), and the calculation stops on its own shortly thereafter (line 8);
  • lines 28–35: The program requests cancellation after 700 ms. It takes effect immediately: the wait for the third block is interrupted (lines 11–13);
  • Lines 37–43: A pitfall to be aware of. The method *[cancel] of a *[CompletableFuture] terminates the latter in the state *[CANCELLED], but does not interrupt anything: a [CompletableFuture] does not know which thread, if any, is working for it (its [mayInterruptIfRunning] parameter is ignored). The download continues until completion (lines 16–17); only its result will be ignored. For a [CompletableFuture] to be able to stop the operation it represents, that operation must monitor the state of the [CompletableFuture] ([isCancelled()]), or the [Future]* or the task’s thread must be retained to interrupt it;
  • Line 44: The executor’s [close()] method waits for all tasks to complete, including the one in step 4.

docs.title: 9.6.2. Multiple processes, multiple outcomes
docs.text:
The program [Async14.java] launches five processes lasting 1 to 5 seconds: process No. 3 throws an exception, and process No. 4 is canceled. It processes each task as soon as it finishes, regardless of how it ended, and always knows which task it is:

// five processings of 1 to 5 seconds executed by virtual threads:
// no. 3 throws an exception, no. 4 is cancelled
long start;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    start = System.nanoTime();
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();
         ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()) {
        // the CompletionService will deliver each task as soon as it is finished
        CompletionService<ProcessingResult> service = new ExecutorCompletionService<>(executor);
        List<Future<ProcessingResult>> tasks = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
            int number = i;
            tasks.add(service.submit(() -> sleep(number, number + 1)));
        }
        // we cancel processing no. 4 after 2.5 seconds
        scheduler.schedule(() -> tasks.get(4).cancel(true), 2500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        display("the " + tasks.size() + " processings are started");

        // we use each processing as soon as it is finished, whatever the way it finished
        for (int i = 0; i < tasks.size(); i++) {
            Future<ProcessingResult> task = service.take();
            int number = tasks.indexOf(task);
            String outcome = switch (task.state()) {
                case SUCCESS -> String.format("finished: scheduled duration %d s, actual duration %.1f s",
                        task.resultNow().duration(), task.resultNow().actualDuration());
                case FAILED -> "encountered the following error: " + task.exceptionNow().getMessage();
                case CANCELLED -> "cancelled";
                case RUNNING -> "still running?";
            };
            display("processing " + number + " " + outcome);
        }
    }
}

// the processing: sleeping [duration] seconds, in one-second slices
ProcessingResult sleep(int number, int duration) throws InterruptedException {
    long processingStart = System.nanoTime();
    // exception for processing no. 3
    if (number == 3) {
        throw new IllegalStateException("test....");
    }
    for (int i = 1; i <= duration; i++) {
        Thread.sleep(1000);
    }
    // the result returned to the caller
    return new ProcessingResult(duration, (System.nanoTime() - processingStart) / 1e9);
}

// the result of a processing
record ProcessingResult(int duration, double actualDuration) {
}

// display with the time elapsed since the start, in seconds
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%4.1f s : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e9, message));
}

Results:

> java Async14.java
 0.0 s : the 5 processings are started
 0.0 s : processing 3 encountered the following error: test....
 1.0 s : processing 0 finished: scheduled duration 1 s, actual duration 1.0 s
 2.0 s : processing 1 finished: scheduled duration 2 s, actual duration 2.0 s
 2.5 s : processing 4 cancelled
 3.0 s : processing 2 finished: scheduled duration 3 s, actual duration 3.0 s

Comments:

  • Lines 36–48: the process. No. 3 throws an exception; the others “sleep” for [duration] seconds in one-second increments, with an interruptible [Thread.sleep], and return a result—a [record]—that contains the programmed duration and the actual duration. The method declares [InterruptedException]: it is called by a [Callable], whose method [call] can throw checked exceptions;
  • lines 7–8: two executors declared within the same [try]: the virtual thread executor, and a [ScheduledExecutorService], an executor capable of executing a task after a delay (we’ll revisit this in the section on time);
  • lines 10–15: the five processes are submitted to the [CompletionService] already encountered in [Async10.java], and their [Future] instances are stored in a list;
  • line 17: [ScheduledExecutorService] will cancel process No. 4 after 2.5 seconds, even though it still has 2.5 seconds left to run;
  • lines 21–32: [take()] delivers each process as soon as it is completed, regardless of how it ended: a canceled [Future] is also delivered. We do not call [get()], which would throw an exception, but instead examine the state of [Future] using a [switch] expression that covers the four constants of [Future.State] (the compiler verifies that none are missing). The processing number is determined by the position of its [Future] in the list ([indexOf]);
  • the results show that No. 3 fails immediately, that Nos. 0, 1, and 2 terminate after 1, 2, and 3 seconds, respectively, and that No. 4 is canceled at 2.5 seconds.

docs.title: 9.6.3. Limiting the Duration of a Wait
docs.text:
The program [Async15.java] provides tools for limiting the duration of a wait: the methods [orTimeout] and [completeOnTimeout] from [CompletableFuture] (Java 9), and the method [get] with a delay from [Future]. It also shows how to combine two stop causes.

// limiting the duration of a wait: orTimeout, completeOnTimeout, get(timeout)
long start = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        // 1 - orTimeout: we do not wait more than one second
        CompletableFuture<String> slow = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(
                () -> queryBlocking("slow-server", 3000), executor);
        try {
            display("1 - answer: " + slow.orTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).join());
        } catch (CompletionException e) {
            display("1 - " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName() + ", state: " + slow.state());
        }
        // the operation itself continues: we let it finish
        Thread.sleep(2200);

        // 2 - completeOnTimeout: beyond one second, we settle for a default answer
        start = System.nanoTime();
        String answer = query("slow-server", 3000)
                .completeOnTimeout("default answer", 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
                .join();
        display("2 - " + answer);

        // 3 - to really stop the operation, we interrupt the thread executing it
        start = System.nanoTime();
        Future<String> slow3 = executor.submit(() -> queryBlocking("slow-server", 3000));
        try {
            display("3 - answer: " + slow3.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS));
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            slow3.cancel(true);
            display("3 - one-second timeout exceeded, operation cancelled, state: " + slow3.state());
        }
    }

    // 4 - two causes of stopping: the timeout specific to each processing and a general stop
    start = System.nanoTime();
    CompletableFuture<Void> generalStop = new CompletableFuture<>();
    CompletableFuture<Void> all = CompletableFuture.allOf(
            processWithTimeout("fast", 500, 1000, generalStop),
            processWithTimeout("slow", 3000, 1000, generalStop),
            processWithTimeout("medium", 1500, 2000, generalStop));
    // the caller requests the general stop after 1,200 ms
    Thread.sleep(1200);
    display("4 - general stop requested");
    generalStop.complete(null);
    all.join();
}

// a processing limited to [timeout] milliseconds, which can also be stopped by the caller
CompletableFuture<Void> processWithTimeout(String name, int duration, int timeout, CompletableFuture<Void> stop) {
    CompletableFuture<String> answer = query(name, duration).orTimeout(timeout, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    // the general stop cancels the wait for the answer
    stop.thenRun(() -> answer.cancel(false));
    // we examine the way the wait ended
    return answer.handle((text, e) -> switch (e) {
        case null -> text;
        case TimeoutException _ -> name + " : timeout of " + timeout + " ms exceeded";
        case CancellationException _ -> name + " : stopped at the caller's request";
        default -> name + " : " + e;
    }).thenAccept(message -> display("4 - " + message));
}

// simulates a server that answers after [duration] milliseconds
CompletableFuture<String> query(String server, int duration) {
    return new CompletableFuture<String>()
            .completeOnTimeout(server + " answered in " + duration + " ms", duration, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
}

// the same operation, written in a blocking way
String queryBlocking(String server, int duration) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(duration);
        display("  " + server + " has finished its work");
        return server + " answered in " + duration + " ms";
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        display("  " + server + " was interrupted");
        throw new CancellationException("operation interrupted");
    }
}

// display with the time elapsed since [start]
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async15.java
 1028 ms : 1 - TimeoutException, state: FAILED
 3025 ms :   slow-server has finished its work
 1001 ms : 2 - default answer
 1003 ms :   slow-server was interrupted
 1004 ms : 3 - one-second timeout exceeded, operation cancelled, state: CANCELLED
  501 ms : 4 - fast answered in 500 ms
 1005 ms : 4 - slow : timeout of 1000 ms exceeded
 1206 ms : 4 - general stop requested
 1207 ms : 4 - medium : stopped at the caller's request

Comments:

  • lines 7–8: the slow operation is a blocking method (lines 69–79), executed by a virtual thread using [supplyAsync] with an executor;
  • Line 10: [orTimeout(timeout, unit)] terminates [CompletableFuture] with a [TimeoutException] if it is not completed within the time limit. This is the direct write of the “run” with [anyOf] from the [Async09.java] program. [orTimeout] does not create a new [CompletableFuture]: it modifies the one to which it applies (and returns it); which is why the state of [slow] is [FAILED] (line 2 of the results);
  • Lines 14–15: [orTimeout] aborts the wait, not the operation: the virtual thread continues to run and completes its work at 3 seconds (line 3), to no avail. This is the same issue seen earlier with [cancel]: a [CompletableFuture] cannot interrupt the operation it represents;
  • lines 17–22: [completeOnTimeout(value, timeout, unit)] terminates [CompletableFuture] with a default value if it is not completed within the time limit: after one second, a “default answer” is returned (line 4);
  • lines 24–32: To truly stop the operation, it is submitted to the executor; we wait for its [Future] for at most one second, then cancel it with [cancel(true)], which interrupts its thread: the operation stops after 1 second (lines 5–6). This is the preferred solution when the operation is blocking and interruptible;
  • lines 49–61: a process may be stopped for several reasons; here, its own timeout and a general stop request from the caller:
    • line 51: the process’s own timeout is set with [orTimeout];
    • line 53: the general termination is itself a [CompletableFuture<Void>], which the caller will terminate; a continuation is attached to it that cancels the wait for the response;
    • lines 55–60: Regardless of the cause, the wait ends in failure; [handle] checks for an exception using a [switch] on the types (Java 21): [case null] for success, [case TimeoutException _] for timeout, [case CancellationException _] for general termination. The character [_] (Java 22) is an anonymous variable: the type is tested without needing to name the object;
  • lines 36–46: three processes and a general shutdown requested at 1,200 ms upon completion of [CompletableFuture] and [generalStop]. Process [fast] completes normally; process [slow] exceeds its one-second time limit; process [medium], which was allotted two seconds, is terminated by the general shutdown (lines 7–10).

docs.title: 9.7. Reporting Progress
docs.text:
A long-running operation often needs to report its progress (a progress bar, a percentage). The simplest approach is to pass it a callback function that receives progress reports: a [Consumer<T>], the functional interface from Chapter 7 whose sole method, [accept(T)], takes a value. The operation calls [accept] at each step; it is unaware of how the progress reports will be displayed.

In a graphical user interface, the reports—generated by the thread executing the operation—cannot directly update the graphical components: [Consumer] must delegate the update to the UI thread ([SwingUtilities.invokeLater(() -> bar.setValue(percentage))] with Swing, [Platform.runLater] with JavaFX). In a console program, it can display the output directly. The program [Async16.java] simulates a file copy that the user can cancel by typing [Enter]:

// reporting the progress of an operation with a Consumer; the user can cancel it
void main() throws InterruptedException {
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        IO.println("Copy in progress, press [Enter] to cancel it");
        // the copy is executed by a virtual thread; the display method displays its reports
        Future<Integer> copy = executor.submit(() -> copy(8, this::display));
        // another virtual thread waits for the user to press [Enter] to cancel the copy
        Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
            // readln returns null if the standard input is closed: we cancel nothing
            if (IO.readln() != null) {
                copy.cancel(true);
            }
        });
        try {
            IO.println("Copy finished: " + copy.get() + " files copied");
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            IO.println("Copy cancelled by the user");
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            IO.println("Copy failed: " + e.getCause());
        }
    }
}

// the operation does not know how its progress is displayed: it only reports it
int copy(int nbFiles, Consumer<Progress> progress) throws InterruptedException {
    for (int i = 1; i <= nbFiles; i++) {
        // the copy of a file
        Thread.sleep(300);
        // the progress report (the caller may not want it: progress is then null)
        if (progress != null) {
            progress.accept(new Progress(100 * i / nbFiles, "file" + i + ".dat"));
        }
    }
    return nbFiles;
}

// a progress report
record Progress(int percentage, String file) {
}

// display of the progress reports in the console: a bar of 20 characters
void display(Progress progress) {
    int nbHashes = progress.percentage() / 5;
    String bar = "#".repeat(nbHashes) + ".".repeat(20 - nbHashes);
    IO.println(String.format("[%s] %3d %% %s", bar, progress.percentage(), progress.file()));
}

Results without cancellation:

> java Async16.java
Copy in progress, press [Enter] to cancel it
[##..................]  12 % file1.dat
[#####...............]  25 % file2.dat
[#######.............]  37 % file3.dat
[##########..........]  50 % file4.dat
[############........]  62 % file5.dat
[###############.....]  75 % file6.dat
[#################...]  87 % file7.dat
[####################] 100 % file8.dat
Copy finished: 8 files copied

Results when the user enters [Enter] during the copy operation, after about one and a half seconds:

> java Async16.java
Copy in progress, press [Enter] to cancel it
[##..................]  12 % file1.dat
[#####...............]  25 % file2.dat
[#######.............]  37 % file3.dat
[##########..........]  50 % file4.dat
[############........]  62 % file5.dat
Copy cancelled by the user

Comments:

  • Lines 24–35: The operation receives a [Consumer<Progress>]. After each file, it reports its progress using a [Progress] object (a [record] that includes the percentage and the file name). A caller who does not want reports passes [null], hence the check on line 30;
  • lines 41–46: displaying a report: a 20-character bar constructed using [String.repeat] (Java 11). The method reference [this::display] (line 6) is the [Consumer<Progress>] passed to the operation;
  • line 6: the copy is performed by a virtual thread;
  • lines 8–13: another virtual thread waits for the user to type [Enter] ([IO.readln()] is a blocking read, which is why this thread: it is this thread that is blocked, not the program), then cancels the copy with [cancel(true)], which interrupts the [Thread.sleep] on line 28. The program does not wait for it: it is a daemon thread, abandoned at the end of the program if the user has not entered anything;
  • lines 14–20: the program waits for the copy to finish. A cancellation results in a [CancellationException], while a copy failure results in a [ExecutionException].

docs.title: 9.8.1. Files
docs.text:
I/O is the very reason for asynchronous processing. Java provides two families of classes for files:

  • the “classic,” blocking classes: [Files] ([readAllLines], [readString], [lines], [writeString], [newBufferedReader], [newBufferedWriter]…), [BufferedReader], [BufferedWriter]. These are now executed on a virtual thread when you do not want to block an important thread;
  • the [AsynchronousFileChannel] class (Java 7), whose operations return a [Future] or call a [CompletionHandler]. It is rarely used: on Linux, it actually performs blocking reads on a thread pool internal to JVM, and its interface is cumbersome.

The program [Async17.java] displays both families by reading the tax bracket file from the main program, [TaxData.txt], located in the program’s directory:

4962:0:0
8382:0.068:291.09
14753:0.191:1322.92
23888:0.283:2668.39
38868:0.374:4846.98
47932:0.426:6883.66
0:0.481:9505.54

Each line contains the bracket threshold, the coefficient [coeffR] and the coefficient [coeffN], separated by the character [:] and written with a decimal point (the tax scale is the 2004 scale for 2003 income, retained as-is for this exercise). The program runs in the [09-async] folder and searches for its files in the current folder.

// file input / output: AsynchronousFileChannel, then blocking I/O on a virtual thread
final Path data = Path.of("TaxData.txt");
final Path report = Path.of("report-17.txt");

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    // 1 - AsynchronousFileChannel (Java 7): an asynchronous read, returned as a CompletableFuture
    String content = readAsynchronously(data).join();
    IO.println("1 - AsynchronousFileChannel: " + content.lines().count() + " lines");

    // 2 to 7 - ordinary blocking I/O, executed by a virtual thread
    Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
        try {
            processFiles();
        } catch (IOException e) {
            IO.println("error: " + e);
        }
    }).join();
}

// reads a whole (small) file with an AsynchronousFileChannel
CompletableFuture<String> readAsynchronously(Path file) {
    CompletableFuture<String> result = new CompletableFuture<>();
    try {
        AsynchronousFileChannel channel = AsynchronousFileChannel.open(file, StandardOpenOption.READ);
        ByteBuffer buffer = ByteBuffer.allocate((int) channel.size());
        // the read is started; the callback object will complete the CompletableFuture
        channel.read(buffer, 0, buffer, new CompletionHandler<Integer, ByteBuffer>() {
            @Override
            public void completed(Integer nbBytes, ByteBuffer read) {
                result.complete(new String(read.array(), 0, nbBytes, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            }

            @Override
            public void failed(Throwable e, ByteBuffer read) {
                result.completeExceptionally(e);
            }
        });
        // the channel will be closed when the read is finished, whatever its outcome
        result.whenComplete((text, e) -> close(channel));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        result.completeExceptionally(e);
    }
    return result;
}

void processFiles() throws IOException {
    // 2 - reading the whole file in a single operation
    List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(data);
    IO.println("2 - Files.readAllLines: " + lines.size() + " lines");

    // 3 - reading line by line with a BufferedReader
    List<TaxBracket> brackets = new ArrayList<>();
    try (BufferedReader reader = Files.newBufferedReader(data)) {
        String line;
        // readLine returns null at the end of the file
        while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
            brackets.add(TaxBracket.parse(line));
        }
    }
    IO.println("3 - BufferedReader.readLine: " + brackets.size() + " brackets, 2nd: " + brackets.get(1));

    // 4 - Files.lines returns a Stream of lines, read on demand
    try (Stream<String> stream = Files.lines(data)) {
        IO.println("4 - Files.lines: " + stream.count() + " lines");
    }

    // 5 - writing with a BufferedWriter
    try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(report)) {
        writer.write("Brackets of the tax scale (exercise: 2004 tax scale on 2003 income)");
        writer.newLine();
        for (int i = 0; i < brackets.size(); i++) {
            TaxBracket bracket = brackets.get(i);
            String limit = bracket.limit().signum() == 0 ? "beyond"
                    : String.format("up to %,d €", bracket.limit().intValue());
            writer.write(String.format("bracket %d : %-18s rate %.1f %%",
                    i + 1, limit, bracket.coeffR().multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(100))));
            writer.newLine();
        }
    }

    // 6 - reading the whole file as a string
    String text = Files.readString(report);
    IO.print("5 and 6 - content of [" + report + "] :\n" + text);

    // 7 - appending at the end of the file then deleting it
    Files.writeString(report, "end of the report\n", StandardOpenOption.APPEND);
    IO.println("7 - last line: " + Files.readAllLines(report).getLast());
    Files.delete(report);
}

// closes a channel without checked exception
void close(Channel channel) {
    try {
        channel.close();
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("error while closing: " + e);
    }
}

// a tax bracket; the file uses the decimal point, which BigDecimal understands
record TaxBracket(BigDecimal limit, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
    static TaxBracket parse(String line) {
        String[] fields = line.split(":");
        return new TaxBracket(new BigDecimal(fields[0]), new BigDecimal(fields[1]),
                new BigDecimal(fields[2]));
    }
}

Results:

> java Async17.java
1 - AsynchronousFileChannel: 7 lines
2 - Files.readAllLines: 7 lines
3 - BufferedReader.readLine: 7 brackets, 2nd: TaxBracket[limit=8382, coeffR=0.068, coeffN=291.09]
4 - Files.lines: 7 lines
5 and 6 - content of [report-17.txt] :
Brackets of the tax scale (exercise: 2004 tax scale on 2003 income)
bracket 1 : up to 4,962 €      rate 0.0 %
bracket 2 : up to 8,382 €      rate 6.8 %
bracket 3 : up to 14,753 €     rate 19.1 %
bracket 4 : up to 23,888 €     rate 28.3 %
bracket 5 : up to 38,868 €     rate 37.4 %
bracket 6 : up to 47,932 €     rate 42.6 %
bracket 7 : beyond             rate 48.1 %
7 - last line: end of the report

Comments:

  • Lines 20–44: Reading with a [AsynchronousFileChannel], presented in the form of a [CompletableFuture<String>]. This is the general technique for converting a API with callback methods into a [CompletableFuture]: we create a “work-in-progress” [CompletableFuture] (line 22), return it immediately (line 43), and the callback methods complete it, returning either the result ([complete], line 30) or the exception ([completeExceptionally], line 35). The callback object is an anonymous class that implements [CompletionHandler<Integer, ByteBuffer>]: the result of a read operation is the number of bytes read, and the object passed here is the buffer itself. A single read operation is sufficient for a small file; a large file would require successive read operations, which the callback methods would need to chain together;
  • line 39: [whenComplete] closes the channel when the read operation is complete, whether it was successful or not;
  • Lines 11–17: The other operations are ordinary blocking I/O operations, grouped within the [processFiles] method and executed by a virtual thread. The lambda of a [Runnable] cannot throw a checked exception: the [IOException] is intercepted within the lambda;
  • line 48: [Files.readAllLines] reads the entire file and returns a list of its lines (using UTF-8 by default, like all methods of [Files]);
  • lines 52–59: line-by-line reading using a [BufferedReader]; [readLine()] returns [null] at the end of the file. Each line is converted to [TaxBracket] by the record’s [parse] method (lines 100–107); the numbers are [BigDecimal], whose constructor expects a decimal point regardless of the machine’s language. The representation of a record produced by its [toString] method appears on line 4 of the results;
  • lines 63–65: [Files.lines] returns a [Stream<String>] consisting of lines read on demand: unlike [readAllLines], it does not load the entire file into memory. This is the preferred method for large files. The stream keeps the file open: it must be closed, hence the [try] with a resource;
  • Lines 68–79: Writing with a [BufferedWriter], which is closed (and thus flushed to disk) upon exit from the [try]. The [%,d] format inserts the thousands separator for the machine’s language (a thin non-breaking space in French);
  • Lines 82–88: [Files.readString] (Java 11) re-reads the written file; [Files.writeString], using the [StandardOpenOption.APPEND] option, adds a line to it; [getLast()] (Java 21) returns the last element of the list, then the file is deleted.

Recall the limitation mentioned above: file reads and writes pin the virtual thread to its carrier thread during the operation, and JVM compensates by adding a carrier thread. For local files, this is rarely noticeable; for network operations, virtual threads actually release their carriers during waits.

docs.title: 9.8.2. Network: HttpClient
docs.text:
The Java client HTTP, [java.net.http.HttpClient] (Java 11), offers both approaches: [send], which is blocking and returns the response, and [sendAsync], which immediately returns a [CompletableFuture] containing the response. Chapter 12 will examine this in detail; the program [Async18.java] simply compares the two methods by querying a small local server, HTTP, which takes one second to return the “temperature” of a city:

// HttpClient: asynchronous (sendAsync) or blocking (send) HTTP requests to a small local server
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;

final int port = 27510;
final List<String> cities = List.of("Angers", "Brest", "Colmar", "Dijon", "Évry", "Foix");
long start;

void main() throws IOException, InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
    // an HTTP server that takes one second to give the "temperature" of a city
    HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port), 0);
    server.createContext("/temperature", exchange -> {
        // the request has the form /temperature?city=xxx
        String parameter = exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery().substring("city=".length());
        String city = URLDecoder.decode(parameter, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        sleep(1000);
        byte[] response = (city + " : " + (10 + city.length()) + " °C").getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, response.length);
        try (OutputStream stream = exchange.getResponseBody()) {
            stream.write(response);
        }
    });
    // each received request is handled by a virtual thread
    server.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
    server.start();

    try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).build()) {
        // a first request, so that the JVM loads the client classes before the measurements
        client.send(request("Paris"), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.discarding());

        // 1 - sendAsync immediately returns a CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>
        start = System.nanoTime();
        List<CompletableFuture<String>> responses = cities.stream()
                .map(city -> client.sendAsync(request(city), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
                        .thenApply(HttpResponse::body))
                .toList();
        CompletableFuture.allOf(responses.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
        display("1 - sendAsync: " + responses.stream().map(CompletableFuture::resultNow).toList());

        // 2 - send is blocking: we call it from virtual threads
        start = System.nanoTime();
        try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            List<Future<String>> responses2 = new ArrayList<>();
            for (String city : cities) {
                responses2.add(executor.submit(
                        () -> client.send(request(city), HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body()));
            }
            List<String> texts = new ArrayList<>();
            for (Future<String> response : responses2) {
                texts.add(response.get());
            }
            display("2 - send on virtual threads: " + texts);
        }
    } finally {
        server.stop(0);
    }
}

// the GET request that asks for the temperature of a city
HttpRequest request(String city) {
    String parameter = URLEncoder.encode(city, StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    URI address = URI.create("http://localhost:" + port + "/temperature?city=" + parameter);
    return HttpRequest.newBuilder(address).build();
}

// Thread.sleep without checked exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("wait interrupted");
    }
}

// display with the time elapsed since [start]
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async18.java
 1033 ms : 1 - sendAsync: [Angers : 16 °C, Brest : 15 °C, Colmar : 16 °C, Dijon : 15 °C, Évry : 14 °C, Foix : 14 °C]
 1023 ms : 2 - send on virtual threads: [Angers : 16 °C, Brest : 15 °C, Colmar : 16 °C, Dijon : 15 °C, Évry : 14 °C, Foix : 14 °C]

Comments:

  • lines 12–27: the server. The JVM file contains a small HTTP server, the [HttpServer] class from the [jdk.httpserver] module, imported on line 2 (a compact file automatically imports only the [java.base] module; the client classes, from the [java.net.http] module, are imported on lines 3–5). [createContext] associates a handler with the [/temperature] path—a lambda that receives the HTTP exchange: it decodes the [city] parameter from the requested address, waits one second, and then sends the response. Line 26 has each request processed by a virtual thread: a server configured this way can serve thousands of waiting clients;
  • Lines 29–31: The client is created by a constructor ([newBuilder]) that sets the protocol version here. Since Java 21, it implements [AutoCloseable] and declares itself in a [try] with a resource. An initial request is used to “warm up” the JVM: the first time a client is used, it loads numerous classes, which would skew the subsequent measurement by a few hundred milliseconds;
  • lines 33–40: [sendAsync(request, handler)] sends the request and immediately returns a [CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>>]; the body handler [BodyHandlers.ofString()] indicates that the response body must be read as a string. [thenApply(HttpResponse::body)] retains only the body. The six requests are sent simultaneously, and their responses arrive together after one second (line 2 of the results). While waiting, no thread waits for the response: the client monitors its connections using a “selector” thread;
  • Lines 42–55: [send] is blocking; it is being called from six virtual threads. The result is the same: one second for all six requests (line 3), and no system threads are blocked;
  • lines 61–66: the request GET. [URLEncoder.encode] encodes characters that cannot appear as-is in an address (the [É] from Évry), and the server decodes them using [URLDecoder.decode] (line 17).

docs.title: 9.9. Asynchronous Value Streams
docs.text:
An asynchronous operation returns a result after a certain amount of time. A stream ([Stream]) or an iterator returns a sequence of values, produced on demand. Sometimes it is necessary to combine the two: a sequence of values where each one requires a wait before being produced. This is the case for lines in a large file, the rows in the result of a query SQL, messages arriving over a network connection, sensor readings… Other languages have a dedicated type for this; Java offers two models:

  • the “pull” model: the consumer requests the next value and waits for it to be available. With virtual threads, this is simply a [Iterator] or a [Stream] where the production of each value blocks, read by a virtual thread;
  • the “push” model: the producer sends values to its subscribers as they are produced, and the subscribers control the throughput. This is the reactive stream model, standardized by the [java.util.concurrent.Flow] interfaces (Java 9).

docs.title: 9.9.1. The pull model: a Stream read by a virtual thread
docs.text:
The program [Async19.java] produces measurements—one every 200 ms—in the form of a [Stream<Measurement>]:

// a sequence of values produced with waits: a "blocking" Stream read by a virtual thread
long start;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    // all the work is done by a virtual thread: its waits block no carrier thread
    Thread.ofVirtual().start(this::consume).join();
}

void consume() {
    start = System.nanoTime();
    // 1 - each value is processed as soon as it is produced
    try (Stream<Measurement> measurements = readMeasurements("sensor-1", 4)) {
        measurements.forEach(measurement -> display("1 - received " + measurement));
    }

    // 2 - we can leave the loop before the end: the producer does not produce the following values
    start = System.nanoTime();
    try (Stream<Measurement> measurements = readMeasurements("sensor-2", 100)) {
        Iterator<Measurement> iterator = measurements.iterator();
        while (iterator.hasNext()) {
            Measurement measurement = iterator.next();
            display("2 - received " + measurement);
            if (measurement.value() >= 22) {
                break;
            }
        }
    }

    // 3 - cancellation: another thread interrupts the thread reading the stream
    start = System.nanoTime();
    Thread reader = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> {
        try (Stream<Measurement> measurements = readMeasurements("sensor-3", 100)) {
            measurements.forEach(measurement -> display("3 - received " + measurement));
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            display("3 - reading cancelled");
        }
    });
    waitForEnd(reader, 700);

    // 4 - all the operations of the Stream API apply to the stream
    start = System.nanoTime();
    String high;
    try (Stream<Measurement> measurements = readMeasurements("sensor-4", 6)) {
        high = measurements
                .filter(measurement -> measurement.value() > 21)
                .map(measurement -> NumberFormat.getInstance().format(measurement.value()))
                .collect(Collectors.joining(" ; ", "[", "]"));
    }
    display("4 - measurements above 21: " + high);
}

// a producer: one measurement every 200 ms, produced only when the consumer asks for it
Stream<Measurement> readMeasurements(String sensor, int count) {
    return IntStream.rangeClosed(1, count)
            .mapToObj(i -> {
                // waiting for the next measurement
                sleep(200);
                return new Measurement(sensor, i, 19.5 + i * 0.75);
            })
            // executed by close(): at the normal end, after a break or on cancellation
            .onClose(() -> IO.println("          " + sensor + " : end of production"));
}

// waits [timeout] ms for the end of a thread, then interrupts it and waits for its end
void waitForEnd(Thread thread, long timeout) {
    try {
        thread.join(timeout);
        thread.interrupt();
        thread.join();
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// Thread.sleep without checked exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("wait interrupted");
    }
}

// display with the time elapsed since [start]
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

// a measurement
record Measurement(String sensor, int number, double value) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return sensor + " no. " + number + " : " + NumberFormat.getInstance().format(value) + " °C";
    }
}

Results:

> java Async19.java
  249 ms : 1 - received sensor-1 no. 1 : 20.25 °C
  455 ms : 1 - received sensor-1 no. 2 : 21 °C
  656 ms : 1 - received sensor-1 no. 3 : 21.75 °C
  857 ms : 1 - received sensor-1 no. 4 : 22.5 °C
          sensor-1 : end of production
  200 ms : 2 - received sensor-2 no. 1 : 20.25 °C
  401 ms : 2 - received sensor-2 no. 2 : 21 °C
  603 ms : 2 - received sensor-2 no. 3 : 21.75 °C
  804 ms : 2 - received sensor-2 no. 4 : 22.5 °C
          sensor-2 : end of production
  201 ms : 3 - received sensor-3 no. 1 : 20.25 °C
  402 ms : 3 - received sensor-3 no. 2 : 21 °C
  602 ms : 3 - received sensor-3 no. 3 : 21.75 °C
          sensor-3 : end of production
  702 ms : 3 - reading cancelled
          sensor-4 : end of production
 1206 ms : 4 - measurements above 21: [21.75 ; 22.5 ; 23.25 ; 24]

Comments:

  • Lines 52–62: the producer. It returns a [Stream<Measurement>] constructed from the integers 1 through [count]; the [mapToObj] function waits 200 ms and then returns a measurement. Since a stream is lazy, this function is called only when the consumer requests the next value, and each measurement is processed before the next one is produced. [onClose] records an action executed when the stream is closed, regardless of the reason: this is the producer’s [finally];
  • line 6: all the work is done by a virtual thread: the 200 ms wait for each measurement does not block any system threads;
  • Lines 11–14: Each measurement is processed as soon as it is produced: one every 200 ms (lines 2–5 of the results). The stream is declared in a [try] with a resource: closing it triggers the [onClose] action (line 6);
  • lines 16–27: To exit the loop before it ends, the stream is traversed using its iterator. After the [break], the producer does not produce the remaining 96 measurements, and the stream is closed upon exiting the [try] (line 11). The methods [takeWhile] (Java 9) or [limit] also allow you to stop a stream;
  • lines 29–38: cancellation. The stream is read by another virtual thread, which the [waitForEnd] method (lines 64–73) interrupts after 700 ms. The wait for the fourth measurement is interrupted: the [sleep] method invokes a [CancellationException], which traverses the stream; the [try] with a resource closes the stream (line 15 of the results), then the [catch] reports the cancellation (line 16);
  • lines 40–49: everything the API Stream can do is applied to the stream: filtering, transformation, collection. The result is only available at the end of the stream, after 6 × 200 ms;
  • lines 90–96: the [toString] method of the [Measurement] record is redefined for a more compact display; [NumberFormat.getInstance()] formats the real number according to the machine’s language, without unnecessary decimal places ([21], [21.75]).

The same pattern applies to a [BufferedReader] (its lines are read on demand, and its method [lines()] returns a [Stream<String>]), to a [ResultSet], JDBC, or to a socket’s incoming stream: on a virtual thread, a blocking stream is an asynchronous stream.

docs.title: 9.9.2. The push model: Flow and SubmissionPublisher
docs.text:
The [java.util.concurrent.Flow] interface (Java 9) groups together four internal interfaces that standardize reactive streams:

  • [Flow.Publisher<T>], the publisher, produces values; its method [subscribe] adds a subscriber to it;
  • [Flow.Subscriber<T>], the subscriber, receives values via its method [onNext], the end of the stream via [onComplete], an error via [onError], and at the beginning, the object [Flow.Subscription], which links it to the publisher via [onSubscribe];
  • [Flow.Subscription], the subscription: [request(n)] requests additional values from [n], and [cancel()] terminates the subscription. The publisher never sends more values than the subscriber has requested: this is “backpressure,” which prevents a fast publisher from overwhelming a slow subscriber;
  • [Flow.Processor<T, R>] is both a subscriber and a publisher (a transformation node).

Java provides an implementation of the publisher, [SubmissionPublisher<T>], which delivers values to each subscriber via an executor and a buffer specific to that subscriber. Reactive libraries (Project Reactor, RxJava) implement these same interfaces and add dozens of operators to them. The program [Async20.java] publishes six metrics to two subscribers: a fast display that unsubscribes when the temperature exceeds 22 °C, and a slow archive:

// the "push" model: java.util.concurrent.Flow and SubmissionPublisher (Java 9)
final long start = System.nanoTime();

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    Subscriber screen = new Subscriber("screen", 0, 22);
    Subscriber archive = new Subscriber("archive", 500, Double.MAX_VALUE);
    // the publisher gives the delivery of the values to an executor and keeps a buffer of 2 values per subscriber
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        var publisher = new SubmissionPublisher<Measurement>(executor, 2);
        publisher.subscribe(screen);
        publisher.subscribe(archive);
        for (int i = 1; i <= 6; i++) {
            sleep(200);
            // submit waits if there is no room left in a subscriber's buffer; it returns the estimated lag
            int lag = publisher.submit(new Measurement("sensor-1", i, 19.5 + i * 0.75));
            display("publisher: measurement no. " + i + " published, estimated lag: " + lag);
        }
        // close() signals the end of the stream to the subscribers: their onComplete method will be called
        display("publisher: end of publication");
        publisher.close();
        // we wait for the archive to have processed everything
        archive.end.await();
    }
}

// a subscriber that processes each measurement in [duration] ms and unsubscribes beyond [threshold]
class Subscriber implements Flow.Subscriber<Measurement> {
    private final String name;
    private final long duration;
    private final double threshold;
    private Flow.Subscription subscription;
    final CountDownLatch end = new CountDownLatch(1);

    Subscriber(String name, long duration, double threshold) {
        this.name = name;
        this.duration = duration;
        this.threshold = threshold;
    }

    @Override
    public void onSubscribe(Flow.Subscription subscription) {
        this.subscription = subscription;
        // the subscriber requests the values one by one: it is the one that controls the rate
        subscription.request(1);
    }

    @Override
