    public void onNext(Measurement measurement) {
        display("  " + name + " : received " + measurement);
        sleep(duration);
        if (measurement.value() >= threshold) {
            display("  " + name + " : threshold reached, unsubscribing");
            subscription.cancel();
        } else {
            subscription.request(1);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void onError(Throwable e) {
        display("  " + name + " : error " + e);
        end.countDown();
    }

    @Override
    public void onComplete() {
        display("  " + name + " : end of the stream");
        end.countDown();
    }
}

// Thread.sleep without checked exception: an interruption becomes a CancellationException
void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        throw new CancellationException("wait interrupted");
    }
}

// display with the time elapsed since the start
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

// a measurement
record Measurement(String sensor, int number, double value) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return sensor + " no. " + number + " : " + NumberFormat.getInstance().format(value) + " °C";
    }
}

Results:

> java Async20.java
  221 ms : publisher: measurement no. 1 published, estimated lag: 1
  269 ms :   archive : received sensor-1 no. 1 : 20.25 °C
  274 ms :   screen : received sensor-1 no. 1 : 20.25 °C
  466 ms : publisher: measurement no. 2 published, estimated lag: 2
  466 ms :   screen : received sensor-1 no. 2 : 21 °C
  667 ms :   screen : received sensor-1 no. 3 : 21.75 °C
  667 ms : publisher: measurement no. 3 published, estimated lag: 3
  770 ms :   archive : received sensor-1 no. 2 : 21 °C
  867 ms : publisher: measurement no. 4 published, estimated lag: 3
  868 ms :   screen : received sensor-1 no. 4 : 22.5 °C
  868 ms :   screen : threshold reached, unsubscribing
 1271 ms :   archive : received sensor-1 no. 3 : 21.75 °C
 1271 ms : publisher: measurement no. 5 published, estimated lag: 3
 1771 ms :   archive : received sensor-1 no. 4 : 22.5 °C
 1772 ms : publisher: measurement no. 6 published, estimated lag: 3
 1772 ms : publisher: end of publication
 2274 ms :   archive : received sensor-1 no. 5 : 23.25 °C
 2775 ms :   archive : received sensor-1 no. 6 : 24 °C
 3276 ms :   archive : end of the stream

Comments:

  • lines 26–70: the subscriber, which processes each measurement in [duration] milliseconds and unsubscribes when the measurement reaches [threshold]:
    • lines 40–45: [onSubscribe] receives the subscription and requests an initial value;
    • lines 47–57: [onNext] processes a value and then either requests another one ([request(1)]) or terminates the subscription ([cancel()]). By requesting values one at a time, the subscriber controls the data rate themselves;
    • lines 59–69: [onError] and [onComplete] signal the end of the stream, either due to an error or normally. [CountDownLatch] allows the main program to wait for this end;
  • line 9: The publisher delivers the values to each subscriber via a task of the specified executor—in this case, virtual threads (without an executor, it would use the shared pool, where waiting for the archive would block one of its few threads)—and maintains a buffer of up to 2 values for each subscriber;
  • lines 12–17: the publisher publishes a measurement every 200 ms using [submit], which returns an estimate of the delay: the largest number of values published but not yet consumed by a subscriber. When a subscriber’s buffer is full, [submit] waits for a slot to become available: measurement #5, ready at around 1,070 ms, is not published until 1,271 ms (line 14 of the results), when the archive has processed measurement #3. This is backpressure: the publisher is slowed down to the pace of the slowest subscriber. ([SubmissionPublisher] also offers [offer], which allows a value to be discarded instead of waiting);
  • the results show that the screen, which is fast, processes each measurement as soon as it is published and unsubscribes at measurement No. 4 (22.5 °C, lines 11–12), while the archive, which takes 500 ms per measurement, falls behind and receives all six measurements;
  • lines 18–22: [close()] signals the end of the stream: each subscriber still subscribed will receive [onComplete] after processing the values in its buffer (line 20). The program waits for the end of the archive with the message [CountDownLatch].

The push model is suitable for sources that produce data at their own pace (sensors, events, messages) and for reactive processing chains; the pull model, which is simpler to write and read, is suitable for reading from a source on demand. With virtual threads, the pull model is usually sufficient.

docs.title: 9.10. Cache, switch back to the correct thread, and finish the operation yourself
9.10.1. A cache for asynchronous operations
docs.text:
A [CompletableFuture] is an object: each call to a method that returns one allocates at least one object on the heap, which the garbage collector must reclaim. This is negligible for I/O that lasts milliseconds, and current garbage collectors in JVM handle short-lived objects very efficiently: Java does not have a “lightweight” variant of [CompletableFuture] (other languages do have one, for asynchronous methods called millions of times that most often already have their result).

For an asynchronous method that often already has the result, best practice is to cache the [CompletableFuture] objects themselves: a value that is already known is returned by a [CompletableFuture] that has already completed, without a new allocation, and multiple concurrent requests for the same value share the same ongoing operation. The [Async21.java] program applies this to an exchange rate service:

// a cache of CompletableFutures: an asynchronous operation that, most of the time, already has the result
void main() {
    var service = new RateService();
    // 1 - successive readings: only the first reading of a currency queries the server
    for (String code : List.of("EUR", "USD", "EUR", "EUR", "USD", "GBP", "EUR")) {
        long readingStart = System.nanoTime();
        BigDecimal rate = service.readRate(code).join();
        IO.println(String.format("%s : %6s read in %3d ms", code, NumberFormat.getInstance().format(rate),
                (System.nanoTime() - readingStart) / 1_000_000));
    }
    IO.println("1 - server accesses: " + service.nbServerAccesses() + ", readings: " + service.nbReadings());

    // 2 - three simultaneous readings of the same currency: they share the same operation
    List<CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> readings = List.of(
            service.readRate("CHF"), service.readRate("CHF"), service.readRate("CHF"));
    IO.println("2 - same object: " + (readings.get(0) == readings.get(2))
            + ", rate: " + NumberFormat.getInstance().format(readings.get(0).join())
            + ", server accesses: " + service.nbServerAccesses() + ", readings: " + service.nbReadings());

    // 3 - a failed operation is not kept in the cache
    try {
        service.readRate("XYZ").join();
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        IO.println("3 - " + e.getCause().getMessage() + ", cached currencies: " + service.cachedCurrencies());
    }
}

class RateService {
    // the cache contains the CompletableFutures themselves, completed or in progress
    private final Map<String, CompletableFuture<BigDecimal>> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final AtomicInteger nbServerAccesses = new AtomicInteger();
    private final AtomicInteger nbReadings = new AtomicInteger();

    CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> readRate(String code) {
        nbReadings.incrementAndGet();
        // if the currency is in the cache, we return the existing CompletableFuture: no object is created
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(code, this::readRateFromServer);
    }

    private CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> readRateFromServer(String code) {
        nbServerAccesses.incrementAndGet();
        // simulates querying a remote server (300 ms)
        CompletableFuture<BigDecimal> reading = new CompletableFuture<Void>()
                .completeOnTimeout(null, 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
                .thenApply(nothing -> switch (code) {
                    case "EUR" -> BigDecimal.ONE;
                    case "USD" -> new BigDecimal("1.17");
                    case "GBP" -> new BigDecimal("0.87");
                    case "CHF" -> new BigDecimal("0.94");
                    default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown currency: " + code);
                });
        // in case of failure, we remove the operation from the cache so that a later reading is retried
        return reading.whenComplete((rate, e) -> {
            if (e != null) {
                cache.remove(code);
            }
        });
    }

    int nbServerAccesses() {
        return nbServerAccesses.get();
    }

    int nbReadings() {
        return nbReadings.get();
    }

    Set<String> cachedCurrencies() {
        return new TreeSet<>(cache.keySet());
    }
}

Results:

> java Async21.java
EUR :      1 read in 363 ms
USD :   1.17 read in 300 ms
EUR :      1 read in   0 ms
EUR :      1 read in   0 ms
USD :   1.17 read in   0 ms
GBP :   0.87 read in 300 ms
EUR :      1 read in   0 ms
1 - server accesses: 3, readings: 7
2 - same object: true, rate: 0.94, server accesses: 4, readings: 10
3 - unknown currency: XYZ, cached currencies: [CHF, EUR, GBP, USD]

Comments:

  • line 30: The cache associates each currency code with the [CompletableFuture] for its exchange rate, whether completed or still in progress. This is a [ConcurrentHashMap] (Chapter 8), because it can be used by multiple threads at the same time (the main thread, the timer thread that completes the reads);
  • Lines 34–38: [computeIfAbsent(key, function)] returns the value associated with the key if it exists; otherwise, it calls the function, stores its result in the dictionary, and returns it. For a [ConcurrentHashMap], this operation is atomic: two threads that simultaneously request a currency that is not present trigger only a single access to the server;
  • lines 40–58: the simulated server query (300 ms). The continuation [thenApply] contains a [switch] expression on a string, whose branch [default] throws an exception for an unknown currency;
  • lines 52–57: in case of failure, the operation is removed from the cache so that a subsequent request for the same currency will query the server again instead of indefinitely returning the same failure. It is the [CompletableFuture] returned by [whenComplete] that is stored in the cache: it does not complete until after the action has been executed, which guarantees the caller that the cache is up to date when they receive the result;
  • lines 5–11: For the caller, nothing changes: it waits for the result with [join()]. The results show the three server accesses (300 ms each; slightly longer for the first one, during which JVM loads the necessary classes) and the four immediate responses from the cache;
  • lines 13–18: Three simultaneous requests for the Swiss franc exchange rate retrieve the same object and result in only one server access (line 10 of the results);
  • lines 20–25: the unknown currency resulted in a failure and is no longer in the cache (line 11).

docs.title: 9.10.2. Return to the GUI thread
docs.text:
The program [Async06.java] demonstrated that a continuation is executed, depending on the case, either by the thread that completes the operation or by a thread of the selected executor. In a graphical application (Swing, JavaFX), this matters: a graphical component can only be manipulated by the UI thread. Java has no mechanism that automatically returns the rest of the code to this thread; it is up to the program to request this, either by passing the correct executor to the continuation or by using the tools of the graphics library:

  • with Swing, *[SwingUtilities.invokeLater(action)] causes the action to be executed by the interface thread; the method reference [SwingUtilities::invokeLater] can serve as an executor for a continuation: [download.thenAcceptAsync(page -> textArea.setText(page), SwingUtilities::invokeLater)]******. The [SwingWorker] class also provides a method, [doInBackground], which is executed by a background thread, and methods [process] and [done]*, which are executed by the interface’s thread;
  • along with JavaFX, [Platform.runLater(action)] serves the same purpose, and the classes [Task] and [Service] of [javafx.concurrent] encapsulate a background process along with its progress.

In all cases, the rule is the same: the UI thread must never wait ([join()], [get()], blocking I/O), otherwise the window freezes. The long-running task is executed by another thread (a virtual thread, for example), and only the final update of the components is handled by the interface thread.

docs.title: 9.10.3. Terminating a CompletableFuture Manually
docs.text:
Sometimes you may need to use a API that signals its events via listeners (Chapter 7), while the rest of the code is written using [CompletableFuture]. We saw the technique with [Async17.java]: create a “pending” [CompletableFuture] using its constructor, return it immediately, and terminate it yourself when needed:

  • [complete(value)] completes it successfully;
  • [completeExceptionally(exception)] fails to complete it;
  • [cancel(false)] cancels it.

These three methods have no effect if [CompletableFuture] has already been completed ([complete] and [completeExceptionally] then produce [false]): the first one to complete it wins, which naturally resolves contention situations (such as a result and a timeout arriving at the same time). The program [Async22.java] waits for a thermometer—which notifies its listeners with each measurement—to reach a certain temperature:

// a CompletableFuture completed "by hand": turning a listener-based API into an asynchronous operation
final long start = System.nanoTime();

void main() {
    var thermometer = new Thermometer();
    thermometer.start();

    // 1 - we wait for the first measure greater than or equal to 21 °C
    double measure = waitForTemperature(thermometer, 21).join();
    display("1 - temperature reached: " + format(measure) + " °C");

    // 2 - the same wait, limited to one second
    try {
        measure = waitForTemperature(thermometer, 30).orTimeout(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).join();
        display("2 - temperature reached: " + format(measure) + " °C");
    } catch (CompletionException e) {
        display("2 - 30 °C not reached in one second: " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
    thermometer.stop();
}

// turns the thermometer's notifications into a CompletableFuture
CompletableFuture<Double> waitForTemperature(Thermometer thermometer, double threshold) {
    // a CompletableFuture that we will complete ourselves
    CompletableFuture<Double> result = new CompletableFuture<>();
    // the listener completes the CompletableFuture when the threshold is reached
    DoubleConsumer listener = temperature -> {
        if (temperature >= threshold) {
            result.complete(temperature);
        }
    };
    thermometer.addListener(listener);
    // whatever the way it ends (threshold, timeout, cancellation), we remove the listener
    result.whenComplete((temperature, e) -> thermometer.removeListener(listener));
    // the CompletableFuture is returned immediately; it will be completed later
    return result;
}

// a thermometer that notifies its listeners every 200 ms (an "old-style" API)
class Thermometer {
    private final List<DoubleConsumer> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    private final ScheduledExecutorService timer = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();
    private double temperature = 19;

    void addListener(DoubleConsumer listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
    }

    void removeListener(DoubleConsumer listener) {
        listeners.remove(listener);
    }

    void start() {
        timer.scheduleAtFixedRate(() -> {
            temperature += 0.5;
            IO.println("          measure: " + format(temperature) + " °C");
            listeners.forEach(listener -> listener.accept(temperature));
        }, 200, 200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
    }

    void stop() {
        timer.shutdown();
    }
}

// a real number in the local format, without useless decimals
String format(double value) {
    return NumberFormat.getInstance().format(value);
}

// display with the time elapsed since the start
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async22.java
          measure: 19.5 °C
          measure: 20 °C
          measure: 20.5 °C
          measure: 21 °C
  807 ms : 1 - temperature reached: 21 °C
          measure: 21.5 °C
          measure: 22 °C
          measure: 22.5 °C
          measure: 23 °C
          measure: 23.5 °C
 1809 ms : 2 - 30 °C not reached in one second: TimeoutException

Comments:

  • Lines 39–64: The thermometer, an “old-school” class: a [ScheduledExecutorService] increases the temperature by 0.5 °C every 200 ms and transmits it to its listeners, of type [DoubleConsumer] (a [Consumer] specialized for the [double] type). The list of listeners is a [CopyOnWriteArrayList], a list that can be modified by one thread (adding or removing a listener) while another thread iterates through it;
  • lines 22–37: the method that converts notifications into a [CompletableFuture]. It creates a temporary [CompletableFuture<Double>], registers a listener with the thermometer, and immediately returns the [CompletableFuture], which is not yet complete;
  • lines 27–31: With each measurement, the listener checks the threshold. When it is reached, it terminates the [CompletableFuture] with the temperature as the result. Subsequent measurements continue to call [complete], to no effect, until the listener is removed;
  • line 34: Regardless of how [CompletableFuture] ends (threshold reached, timeout, cancellation by the caller), [whenComplete] removes the listener. Without this, a listener whose threshold is never reached would remain registered indefinitely;
  • Lines 8–18: For the caller, waiting for a temperature is an asynchronous operation like any other: the caller waits for it with [join()] and sets a time limit on it with [orTimeout]. Since [orTimeout] terminates [CompletableFuture] itself (and not a copy), the action [whenComplete] on line 34 is executed, and the listener is removed.

A note of caution: the continuations attached to [CompletableFuture] are executed by the thread that calls [complete]—in this case, the thermometer thread—in the middle of notifying its listeners. If these continuations are lengthy, they should be written using the [xxxAsync] variants and an executor, or [CompletableFuture] should be terminated with [completeAsync(() -> value, executor)] (Java 9), which causes the executor to call [complete].

docs.title: 9.11.1. Virtual threads and semaphores
docs.text:
[allOf] and one virtual thread per operation launch all operations simultaneously. This is not always desirable: to download 10,000 web pages, you don’t want to open 10,000 simultaneous connections to the same server. With platform threads, concurrency was limited by the size of the thread pool. With virtual threads, threads are not pooled (they are so inexpensive that one is created per task): access to the scarce resource is limited using a [Semaphore] (Chapter 8), whose permissions represent the number of concurrent operations allowed. The program [Async23.java] downloads nine pages, no more than three at a time:

// processing a collection with a limited number of simultaneous operations: virtual threads and Semaphore
final AtomicInteger inProgress = new AtomicInteger();

long start;

void main() {
    start = System.nanoTime();
    List<String> pages = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 9).mapToObj(i -> "page" + i + ".html").toList();
    // at most 3 downloads at the same time: a semaphore with 3 permits
    var permits = new Semaphore(3);
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        // one virtual thread per page: they are cheap, we can create as many as there are pages
        for (String page : pages) {
            executor.submit(() -> {
                // the thread waits for a permit (without blocking a carrier thread)
                permits.acquire();
                try {
                    download(page);
                } finally {
                    permits.release();
                }
                return null;
            });
        }
    } // close() waits for the end of all the downloads
    display("the " + pages.size() + " pages are downloaded");
}

void download(String page) throws InterruptedException {
    // counter shared by the simultaneous operations: we modify it atomically
    int n = inProgress.incrementAndGet();
    display("start of " + page + " (" + n + " in progress)");
    // the simulated download of a page
    Thread.sleep(1000);
    inProgress.decrementAndGet();
    display("end of " + page);
}

// display with the time elapsed since the start and the thread executing the display
void display(String message) {
    Thread thread = Thread.currentThread();
    String name = thread.isVirtual() ? "virtual #" + thread.threadId() : thread.getName();
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms [%-11s] : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, name, message));
}

Results:

> java Async23.java
   13 ms [virtual #25] : start of page2.html (2 in progress)
   13 ms [virtual #27] : start of page3.html (3 in progress)
   13 ms [virtual #23] : start of page1.html (1 in progress)
 1026 ms [virtual #25] : end of page2.html
 1026 ms [virtual #27] : end of page3.html
 1026 ms [virtual #23] : end of page1.html
 1026 ms [virtual #28] : start of page4.html (1 in progress)
 1027 ms [virtual #29] : start of page5.html (2 in progress)
 1027 ms [virtual #30] : start of page6.html (3 in progress)
 2027 ms [virtual #29] : end of page5.html
 2027 ms [virtual #30] : end of page6.html
 2028 ms [virtual #31] : start of page7.html (1 in progress)
 2028 ms [virtual #32] : start of page8.html (2 in progress)
 2027 ms [virtual #28] : end of page4.html
 2028 ms [virtual #33] : start of page9.html (3 in progress)
 3028 ms [virtual #31] : end of page7.html
 3028 ms [virtual #32] : end of page8.html
 3029 ms [virtual #33] : end of page9.html
 3030 ms [main       ] : the 9 pages are downloaded

Comments:

  • line 10: a semaphore with 3 permissions;
  • lines 13–24: one virtual thread per page. The task is a lambda that ends with [return null;]: this is therefore a [Callable], whose method can throw checked exceptions, which avoids having to handle the [InterruptedException], [acquire], and [Thread.sleep] here;
  • Lines 16–21: Each thread waits for a permit ([acquire]), downloads its page, and then returns the permit ([release]) in a [finally], so that it is returned even if the download fails. A virtual thread waiting for authorization is detached from its host thread, just as during an I/O operation;
  • Lines 29–37: The counter [inProgress], shared by the threads, is an atomically modified version of [AtomicInteger];
  • The results show three waves of three pages: as soon as one page is finished, another begins, and the number of downloads in progress never exceeds 3. The entire process takes 3 seconds instead of 9. When two threads write at nearly the same time, the order of the lines may vary from one execution to another, and a displayed time may even be slightly earlier than that of the previous line;
  • each page has its own virtual thread (nos. 23 through 33; the numbers are shared by all threads in JVM, including the carrier threads, hence the gaps), but these nine virtual threads were executed by the machine’s only two carrier threads.

docs.title: 9.11.2. Producers / Consumers: BlockingQueue
docs.text:
The previous chapter introduced the producer/consumer model: producers place items into a queue, and consumers remove them. The [BlockingQueue<E>] interface is the tool for this: [put] places an item in the queue and waits—if the queue is bounded and full—for a spot to become available; [take] removes an element and waits—if the queue is empty—for one to arrive; [offer] and [poll] attempt the same thing without waiting (or with a delay). These waits are blocking; when executed by virtual threads, they do not block any system threads, and the blocking queue becomes the communication tool between asynchronous operations.

The program [Async24.java] has commands—generated every 50 ms—processed by two consumers, each of which takes 400 ms to process a command:

// producer / consumers with a blocking queue, executed by virtual threads
// the value that signals to the consumers that there will be no more orders
static final int END = -1;
// a bounded queue: it holds at most 2 orders waiting to be processed
final BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);
long start;

void main() {
    start = System.nanoTime();
    // the producer and two consumers work at the same time
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        executor.submit(() -> produce(8));
        executor.submit(() -> consume("C1"));
        executor.submit(() -> consume("C2"));
    }
    display("all the orders have been processed");
}

// the producer: one order every 50 ms
Void produce(int nbOrders) throws InterruptedException {
    for (int i = 1; i <= nbOrders; i++) {
        Thread.sleep(50);
        // offer puts the order immediately if there is room in the queue
        if (queue.offer(i)) {
            display("P  : order " + i + " queued");
        } else {
            // queue full: put waits for a place to become free
            display("P  : queue full, order " + i + " waits");
            queue.put(i);
            display("P  : order " + i + " queued");
        }
    }
    // nothing more will be produced: we put the end marker
    queue.put(END);
    display("P  : end of production");
    return null;
}

// a consumer: processing an order takes 400 ms
Void consume(String name) throws InterruptedException {
    while (true) {
        // take waits until there is an order in the queue
        int order = queue.take();
        if (order == END) {
            // we put the end marker back in the queue for the other consumer
            queue.put(END);
            break;
        }
        display(name + " : processing of order " + order);
        Thread.sleep(400);
    }
    display(name + " : no more orders");
    return null;
}

// display with the time elapsed since the start
void display(String message) {
    IO.println(String.format("%5d ms : %s", (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, message));
}

Results:

> java Async24.java
   58 ms : P  : order 1 queued
   62 ms : C1 : processing of order 1
  118 ms : C2 : processing of order 2
  119 ms : P  : order 2 queued
  169 ms : P  : order 3 queued
  220 ms : P  : order 4 queued
  271 ms : P  : queue full, order 5 waits
  469 ms : P  : order 5 queued
  469 ms : C1 : processing of order 3
  519 ms : C2 : processing of order 4
  519 ms : P  : order 6 queued
  570 ms : P  : queue full, order 7 waits
  870 ms : C1 : processing of order 5
  870 ms : P  : order 7 queued
  920 ms : C2 : processing of order 6
  920 ms : P  : order 8 queued
 1270 ms : C1 : processing of order 7
 1271 ms : P  : end of production
 1320 ms : C2 : processing of order 8
 1672 ms : C1 : no more orders
 1721 ms : C2 : no more orders
 1721 ms : all the orders have been processed

Comments:

  • line 5: a [ArrayBlockingQueue] with capacity 2: it contains at most 2 pending commands;
  • Lines 11–15: The producer and the two consumers are executed by three virtual threads; the program waits for all three to finish using the executor’s [close()] method. The methods [produce] and [consume] return [Void] and end with [return null;]: the lambdas on lines 12–14 are therefore [Callable], and the methods can declare [InterruptedException];
  • Lines 19–37: The producer attempts to submit each order using [offer]. If the queue is full, it signals this and waits for space using [put]: the producer is throttled to the consumers’ pace (lines 8–9 of the results). This is the benefit of a bounded queue: a producer that is too fast cannot fill up memory;
  • line 34: production is complete; the producer places a specific value, the end marker [END] (line 3), which the consumers will recognize. A blocking queue, in fact, has no way of signaling that it is “closed”;
  • Lines 39–54: Each consumer retrieves orders with [take]. An order is delivered to only one consumer: orders are distributed between C1 and C2 based on their availability. The consumer that receives the end token places it back in the queue for the other consumer, then stops;
  • as in the previous example, two lines displayed at nearly the same time may appear out of order.

docs.title: 9.12. Time: ScheduledExecutorService and Clock
docs.text:
Two tools complement those related to time:

  • a [ScheduledExecutorService] (Java 5) is an executor capable of running a task after a delay ([schedule]) or periodically ([scheduleAtFixedRate], at fixed intervals measured from the start of one execution to the next; [scheduleWithFixedDelay], with a fixed delay between the end of one execution and the start of the next). A periodic task is never executed twice at the same time: if an execution takes longer than the period, the next one is delayed. A single-threaded executor is obtained with [Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()];
  • the abstract class [java.time.Clock] (Java 8) represents the clock: it provides the current time and time zone. [Clock.systemDefaultZone()] is the system clock in the machine’s time zone. All [now()] methods of API, [java.time] ([LocalDateTime.now(clock)], [Instant.now(clock)]…) accept a clock. A class that depends on the time receives a [Clock] instead of calling [LocalDateTime.now()]: it can then be tested with a controlled clock.

The program [Async25.java] uses both:

// time: ScheduledExecutorService and Clock
void main() throws InterruptedException {
    // 1 - an action every 500 ms, stopped after 2.2 seconds
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    AtomicInteger nbTicks = new AtomicInteger();
    try (ScheduledExecutorService scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()) {
        // scheduleAtFixedRate: first tick in 500 ms, then one tick every 500 ms
        ScheduledFuture<?> ticks = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate(
                () -> IO.println(String.format("%6d ms : tick no. %d",
                        (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, nbTicks.incrementAndGet())),
                500, 500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        // schedule: a single action, in 2.2 seconds, that stops the ticks
        ScheduledFuture<?> stop = scheduler.schedule(
                () -> ticks.cancel(false), 2200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
        stop.get();
        IO.println(String.format("%6d ms : timer stopped after %d ticks",
                (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000, nbTicks.get()));
    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
        IO.println("error: " + e.getCause());
    }

    // 2 - Clock: a class that depends on the time receives its clock instead of calling LocalDateTime.now()
    Clock morning = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-10-03T09:30:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    Clock evening = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-10-03T19:45:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
    IO.println(new Reception(morning).greet("Pierre"));
    IO.println(new Reception(evening).greet("Pierre"));
    IO.println(new Reception(Clock.systemDefaultZone()).greet("Pierre") + " (system clock)");
}

// a class that depends on the current time
record Reception(Clock clock) {
    String greet(String name) {
        LocalDateTime now = LocalDateTime.now(clock);
        String greeting = now.getHour() < 18 ? "Hello" : "Good evening";
        String date = now.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm"));
        return "[" + date + "] " + greeting + " " + name;
    }
}

Results:

> java Async25.java
   504 ms : tick no. 1
  1003 ms : tick no. 2
  1503 ms : tick no. 3
  2003 ms : tick no. 4
  2204 ms : timer stopped after 4 ticks
[03/10/2026 09:30] Hello Pierre
[03/10/2026 19:45] Good evening Pierre
[03/10/2026 19:18] Good evening Pierre (system clock)

Comments:

  • Lines 8–11: [scheduleAtFixedRate(task, initialDelay, period, unit)] runs the task for the first time after 500 ms, and then every 500 ms. It returns a [ScheduledFuture] and a [Future], which, among other things, allows future executions to be canceled. The top counter is a [AtomicInteger]: a lambda cannot modify a local variable;
  • Lines 13–15: [schedule(task, delay, unit)] executes a single task after 2.2 seconds: it cancels the tops. [stop.get()] waits for this task to finish. The beeps occurred at 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2 seconds, and the timer stops at 2.2 seconds, after 4 beeps;
  • lines 30–38: the record [Reception] says “Hello” or “Good evening” depending on the time. It receives its clock from its constructor instead of calling [LocalDateTime.now()]: this is an injected dependency, just as the [dao] layer is injected into the [business] layer in Chapter 6;
  • Lines 23–27: [Clock.fixed(instant, zone)] returns a stopped clock that always shows the same time; this allows us to verify the behavior of [Reception] in the morning and evening without having to wait until evening. The last line uses the system clock (so the result depends on the execution time). For more sophisticated tests, you can write your own class derived from [Clock], which you can advance as desired. The [InstantSource] interface (Java 17), which returns only the current time, is an even lighter dependency when the time zone is irrelevant.

To measure a duration, do not use the clock (which can be adjusted during the measurement, for example, by synchronizing the system time) but use [System.nanoTime()], as shown in the examples in this chapter.

docs.title: 9.13. Structured Concurrency (Overview)
docs.text:
In the previous examples, the operations launched by a program run independently of it: if one fails, the others continue; if the code that launched them is interrupted, they continue as well; and nothing forces that code to wait for them to finish. Structured concurrency proposes treating a group of subtasks as a single block: they are launched within a scope, the scope waits for them to complete, and if one fails, the others are canceled. The [StructuredTaskScope] class implements this idea using virtual threads. It has been available since Java 21 but is still in “preview” status in Java 25: its API may still change, and a program that uses it must be compiled and run with the [--enable-preview] option. It is therefore not included in the course exercises; the following code (file [preview/StructuredConcurrency.txt], to be copied into a file named [StructuredConcurrency.java] to test it) gives an idea of how it works:

// structured concurrency: preview API in Java 25
// execution: java --enable-preview StructuredConcurrency.java
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Joiner;
import java.util.concurrent.StructuredTaskScope.Subtask;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    // 1 - two subtasks that must both succeed
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {
        Subtask<Integer> angers = scope.fork(() -> readTemperature("Angers", 1000));
        Subtask<Integer> brest = scope.fork(() -> readTemperature("Brest", 500));
        // join waits for the end of the subtasks; if one fails, the other is cancelled
        // and join throws an exception
        scope.join();
        IO.println("Angers: " + angers.get() + ", Brest: " + brest.get());
    }
    // 2 - the first answer is enough: the other subtasks are cancelled
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open(Joiner.<Integer>anySuccessfulResultOrThrow())) {
        scope.fork(() -> readTemperature("mirror-paris", 800));
        scope.fork(() -> readTemperature("mirror-lyon", 300));
        IO.println("first answer: " + scope.join());
    }
}

int readTemperature(String city, long duration) throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.sleep(duration);
    return 10 + city.length();
}

Results:

> java --enable-preview StructuredConcurrency.java
Angers: 16, Brest: 15
first answer: 21

Comments:

  • line 8: [StructuredTaskScope.open()] opens a scope, declared in a [try] with a resource; closing it ensures that no subtasks survive it;
  • Lines 9–10: [fork] launches a subtask in a new virtual thread and returns a [Subtask];
  • line 13: [join()] waits for all subtasks to finish. With the default policy, if a subtask fails, the others are canceled (aborted) and [join()] throws an exception;
  • line 14: the results of the subtasks, all of which have completed;
  • Lines 17–21: Another policy, provided by [Joiner]: the first successful subtask returns the result of [join()], and the others are canceled. This is the structured equivalent of [anyOf], but the losing requests are actually terminated.

docs.title: 9.14. Application: Tax Calculation with Virtual Threads
docs.text:
The program [Async26.java] brings together several tools from this chapter related to the tax calculation of the main thread. It reads the tax brackets from the file [TaxData.txt], which has already been used, and reads a list of taxpayers from the file [taxpayers.txt]:

y 2 60000
y 3 60000
n 0 60000
n 2 25000
y 5 120000
x 1 20000
y 1 -5

(each line contains: married [y/n], number of children, annual salary), calculates each person’s tax, and writes the results to the file [results.txt]. Both reads are performed concurrently by virtual threads, and the entire process is limited to 10 seconds.

// application: the tax calculation, with input / output executed by virtual threads
// - the brackets are read in [TaxData.txt], the taxpayers in [taxpayers.txt]
// - the results are written in [results.txt]
// a correct taxpayer line: married (y/n), number of children, annual salary
static final Pattern TAXPAYER = Pattern.compile("([yn])\\s+(\\d+)\\s+(\\d+)");

void main() {
    Path results = Path.of("results.txt");
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        // the two input files are read at the same time, by two virtual threads
        Future<List<TaxBracket>> bracketsReading = executor.submit(
                () -> loadBrackets(Path.of("TaxData.txt")));
        Future<List<String>> taxpayersReading = executor.submit(
                () -> Files.readAllLines(Path.of("taxpayers.txt")));
        // the calculation waits for the two readings, then writes the results
        Future<Integer> processing = executor.submit(
                () -> calculateTaxes(bracketsReading.get(), taxpayersReading.get(), results));
        try {
            // the whole processing is limited to 10 seconds
            int nbResults = processing.get(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
            IO.println(nbResults + " lines written in [" + results + "] :");
            IO.print(Files.readString(results));
        } catch (TimeoutException e) {
            processing.cancel(true);
            IO.println("processing abandoned: timeout exceeded");
        }
    } catch (ExecutionException e) {
        // the error of a reading is wrapped twice: by the reading and by the calculation that waited for it
        Throwable cause = e.getCause();
        while (cause instanceof ExecutionException) {
            cause = cause.getCause();
        }
        IO.println("error: " + cause.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + cause.getMessage());
    } catch (IOException | InterruptedException e) {
        IO.println("error: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

// reads the tax brackets (limit:coeffR:coeffN, decimal point)
List<TaxBracket> loadBrackets(Path file) throws IOException {
    try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(file)) {
        return lines.filter(line -> !line.isBlank()).map(TaxBracket::parse).toList();
    }
}

// calculates the tax of each taxpayer and writes the results
int calculateTaxes(List<TaxBracket> brackets, List<String> taxpayers, Path output) throws IOException {
    try (BufferedWriter writer = Files.newBufferedWriter(output)) {
        for (String line : taxpayers) {
            Matcher fields = TAXPAYER.matcher(line.trim());
            String result = fields.matches()
                    ? "tax = " + calculateTax(brackets, fields.group(1).equals("y"),
                            Integer.parseInt(fields.group(2)), Integer.parseInt(fields.group(3))) + " €"
                    : "incorrect line";
            writer.write(String.format("%-12s : %s", line, result));
            writer.newLine();
        }
    }
    return taxpayers.size();
}

// the tax calculation (2004 tax scale on 2003 income, kept for the exercise)
int calculateTax(List<TaxBracket> brackets, boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary) {
    BigDecimal shares = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbChildren).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
            .add(BigDecimal.valueOf(married ? 2 : 1));
    if (nbChildren >= 3) {
        shares = shares.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
    }
    BigDecimal income = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salary));
    BigDecimal quotient = income.divide(shares, MathContext.DECIMAL64);
    // the first bracket whose limit exceeds the family quotient, otherwise the last one
    TaxBracket bracket = brackets.stream()
            .filter(t -> quotient.compareTo(t.limit()) <= 0)
            .findFirst()
            .orElse(brackets.getLast());
    return bracket.coeffR().multiply(income).subtract(bracket.coeffN().multiply(shares)).intValue();
}

// a tax bracket
record TaxBracket(BigDecimal limit, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
    static TaxBracket parse(String line) {
        String[] fields = line.split(":");
        return new TaxBracket(new BigDecimal(fields[0]), new BigDecimal(fields[1]),
                new BigDecimal(fields[2]));
    }
}

Results:

> java Async26.java
7 lines written in [results.txt] :
y 2 60000    : tax = 4282 €
y 3 60000    : tax = 2959 €
n 0 60000    : tax = 11519 €
n 2 25000    : tax = 792 €
y 5 120000   : tax = 11109 €
x 1 20000    : incorrect line
y 1 -5       : incorrect line

The same program, run in a folder where the file [TaxData.txt] is missing:

> java Async26.java
error: NoSuchFileException : TaxData.txt

Comments:

  • lines 11–14: The two input files are read simultaneously by two virtual threads using standard blocking read methods ([Files.lines], [Files.readAllLines]);
  • lines 16–17: The calculation is a third task, which begins by waiting for the two reads to complete using [get()]. These waits block a virtual thread, which incurs no cost;
  • lines 18–26: The main program waits for the result for up to 10 seconds. After that, it aborts the process (which terminates its virtual thread) and reports the error;
  • lines 27–36: Errors are handled in a single location within the main program. A read error (missing file, incorrect number) is stored in the [Future] associated with the read operation; the [get()] from the calculation rethrows it into a [ExecutionException], which in turn becomes the calculation’s exception, rethrown by the main program’s [get] into a second [ExecutionException]. The loop in lines 30–32 traces back to the original cause (second result). This is the drawback of dependent tasks; structured concurrency, as described in the previous paragraph, will eliminate this issue;
  • lines 39–44: reading the brackets, using a [Stream] that skips empty lines;
  • lines 46–60: processing taxpayers. Each line is validated by the regular expression in line 5: a [y] or an [n], followed by two positive integers separated by spaces ([\s+]). The parentheses define three groups, which [group(1)], [group(2)], and [group(3)] return once [matches()] has verified that the entire line matches the expression. An incorrect line ([x] instead of [y/n], negative salary) is flagged as such;
  • Lines 62–77: tax calculation, in [BigDecimal]. Dividing the income by the number of shares may not be exact: this is done with a precision of 16 significant digits ([MathContext.DECIMAL64]). The first tax bracket whose threshold is greater than or equal to the family quotient is determined by a stream; [orElse(brackets.getLast())] returns the last bracket if none match. [intValue()] rounds the tax down to the nearest euro;
  • the results provide the control values for the red thread: €4,282 for a married couple with 2 children and a salary of €60,000, €2,959 with 3 children, and €11,519 for a single person without children.

The calculation itself is synchronous: it performs no I/O and takes a few microseconds. It would be pointless—and even harmful—to offload it to another thread. Only tasks that involve waiting are made asynchronous.

docs.title: 9.15. The Golden Rules
docs.text:
Let’s summarize the rules of asynchronous programming in Java:

  • to wait, do not block a system thread: a wait (I/O, timeout, or other operation) is performed either in a virtual thread or by attaching a continuation to a [CompletableFuture];
  • for new code, prefer virtual threads: write blocking, sequential, and readable code (loops, [try / catch], ordinary local variables), executed by [Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()]; one virtual thread per task, never use a pool of virtual threads;
  • Use [CompletableFuture] to compose operations, or to use a API that returns [CompletableFuture] ([HttpClient.sendAsync], reactive libraries); We then choose the continuation executor ([xxxAsync(..., executor)]) and never execute a blocking operation in the shared pool;
  • no [join()] or [get()] in a continuation or in a GUI thread: these waits block the thread executing them. They belong in the main program or in a virtual thread;
  • Virtual threads are used for waits, not computations: for computations, use a platform-specific thread pool sized according to the number of processors, or parallel streams;
  • limit access to scarce resources using a [Semaphore], not by the size of a thread pool;
  • Cancellation is cooperative: a task is canceled via [Future.cancel(true)], which interrupts its thread; an interrupted task terminates gracefully; a [InterruptedException] is never masked (it is either propagated or the interrupt flag is reset). And remember that [CompletableFuture.cancel] does not interrupt anything;
  • limit wait times: [orTimeout], [completeOnTimeout], [get(timeout, unit)]; and terminate the operation itself if the wait is abandoned;
  • start first, then wait: to run multiple independent operations simultaneously, start them all and then wait for them ([allOf], [invokeAll], the executor’s [close] method);
  • A launched operation must be waited on or monitored: a forgotten operation hides its exceptions ([exceptionally], [whenComplete] to handle them); by tracing back a [CompletionException] or a [ExecutionException], we seek the root cause.

The following table summarizes the equivalences between the world of platform threads and blocking waits (previous chapter), that of [CompletableFuture], and that of virtual threads:

Platform threads, blocking waitsCompletableFutureVirtual threads[Thread.sleep(1000)] (blocks the thread)[new CompletableFuture<Void>().completeOnTimeout(null, 1, SECONDS)][Thread.sleep(1000)] (releases the carrier)[thread.start()] followed by [thread.join()][supplyAsync(...)] followed by [join()] or a continuation[executor.submit(...)] followed by [get()]Wait for multiple threads ([join] in a loop)[allOf(...)], [anyOf(...)][invokeAll(...)], [ExecutorCompletionService], [close()]Recall methods ([CompletionHandler])[thenApply], [thenCompose], [thenCombine]The code following the blocking call[try / catch] around [get()] ([ExecutionException])[exceptionally], [handle], [whenComplete][try / catch] (standard)[thread.interrupt()][cancel(...)] (does not interrupt anything)[future.cancel(true)] (interrupts the thread)[future.get(timeout, unit)][orTimeout(...)], [completeOnTimeout(...)][future.get(timeout, unit)]fixed-size thread poolcontinuation executor [xxxAsync][Semaphore][BlockingQueue] (blocks the thread)[Flow], [SubmissionPublisher][BlockingQueue] (releases the carrier)[ScheduledExecutorService][completeOnTimeout], [delayedExecutor][Thread.sleep] in a loop

The following chapters will apply these rules: database access using JDBC (Chapter 10) and Hibernate (Chapter 11), whose API operations are blocking and work naturally with virtual threads, the TCP server, which serves each client via a virtual thread, and the [HttpClient] client (Chapter 12); Spring Boot web services, where the Tomcat server can process each request via a virtual thread; and their clients (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 4.1.1. Overview
docs.text:
We will now explore object-oriented programming through examples. An object is an entity that contains data defining its state (referred to as fields, attributes, etc.) and functions (referred to as methods). An object is created based on a template called a class. For example, a class named [C1] declares two fields, [Type1 p1;] and [Type2 p2;], and two methods, [Type3 m3(...) { ... }] and [Type4 m4(...) { ... }], all enclosed within the curly braces of the declaration [public class C1 { ... }].

From the class [C1], you can create many objects such as [o1], [o2], … All of them will have the fields [p1], [p2], … and the methods [m3], [m4], … However, they will have different values for their [pi] fields, thus each having its own unique state. If [o1] is an object of type [C1], [o1.p1] refers to the [p1] field of [o1], and [o1.m3(...)] refers to the call to the [m3] method of [o1].

Let’s consider an initial object model: the class [Person].

docs.title: 4.1.2. A program consisting of multiple files
docs.text:
In the examples from the previous chapter, a program fit into a single source file. From now on, a program can consist of multiple source files: one class per file, plus the main program. In Java, a public class must be placed in a file that bears its name: the public class [Person] is in the file [Person.java]. We store the files for a single program in a folder—in this case, the [Persons] folder within the [04-classes] folder:

Persons/
  Person.java       the Person class
  Main.java         the main program

Starting with Java 22, the source code launcher—which we already used in the previous chapter—can run a program consisting of multiple files: the command [java Main.java], entered in the [Persons] folder, compiles the file [Main.java] in memory, then, on demand, the other files in the folder that it needs—in this case, [Person.java]—and runs the program. No compiled files are written to disk. You can also explicitly compile the files using the [javac] compiler, which writes a [.class] file (intermediate code, or “bytecode”) per class, and then run the program with the command [java], specifying where to find the compiled classes (option [-cp], the “classpath”):

> javac -d classes *.java
> ls classes
Main.class
Person.class
> java -cp classes Main
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

The multi-file launcher is sufficient for the programs in this chapter, which use only the classes from JDK. When a program requires external libraries, we will use a Maven project, as introduced in Chapter 2: Maven downloads the libraries, compiles the project, and runs it. The files in this chapter can be opened as-is in IntelliJ, IDEA, or VS Code.

docs.title: 4.1.3. Definition of the Person Class
docs.text:
The definition of the [Person] class in the source file [Person.java] will be as follows:

public class Person {
    // attributes (fields)
    private String firstName = "";
    private String lastName = "";
    private int age;

    // method
    public void initialize(String p, String n, int age) {
        this.firstName = p;
        this.lastName = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // method
    public void identify() {
        IO.println("[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • Line 1: The class is public ([public]): it can be used by all other classes. It does not belong to any package—or, more precisely, it belongs to the unnamed package; packages are discussed at the end of the chapter;
  • Lines 3–5: The three fields of the class. Both strings are initialized with the empty string: otherwise, they would be set to [null] when the object is created (an uninitialized object field is set to [null], a numeric field to 0, and a Boolean field to [false]);
  • lines 8–12: a method that sets the object’s state;
  • lines 15–17: a method that displays the object’s state. [IO] is the Java 25 console I/O class we used in the previous chapter.

Here we have the definition of a class—that is, a data type. When we create variables of this type, we call them objects or class instances. A class is therefore a template from which objects are constructed. By convention, a class name begins with a capital letter ([Person]), while a field or method name begins with a lowercase letter ([firstName], [initialize]).

The members of a class can be data (fields) or methods (functions). These members can be accompanied by one of the following keywords:

KeywordAccess[private]A private member is accessible only by the class’s internal methods(none)If no keyword is specified, the member is accessible by any method in a class from the same package. This is the default access, known as “package access”[protected]A protected member is accessible by methods of classes in the same package and by methods of derived classes (see the concept of inheritance below)[public]A public member is accessible by any method, whether or not it is defined within the class

In general, a class’s data is declared private, while its methods are declared public. This means that the user of an object (the programmer):

  • will not have direct access to the object’s private data;
  • can call the object’s public methods, including those that provide access to its private data.

The order in which the members [private], [protected], and [public] are declared is arbitrary. Note that the default access is not private: a field declared without a keyword is visible to all classes in the package. Therefore, you must remember to write [private].

docs.title: 4.1.4. The initialize method
docs.text:
What is the role of the method [initialize]? Because [lastName], [firstName], and [age] are private members of the [Person] class, a statement such as [p1.firstName = "Jean";], written in the main program, is invalid. The compiler rejects it:

> java Main.java
Main.java:4: error: firstName has private access in Person
    p1.firstName = "Jean";
      ^
1 error
error: compilation failed

The compiler message is in English: JDK has no French translation for its messages. It specifies the file and line number of the error, then marks it with a circumflex accent. We need to initialize an object of type [Person] via a public method. This is the role of the [initialize] method. We will write [p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);]. This syntax is valid because [initialize] is publicly accessible.

docs.title: 4.1.5. The new operator
docs.text:
However, something is still missing. The declaration [Person p1;] declares [p1] as a reference to an object of type [Person]. This object does not yet exist, and therefore [p1] is not initialized. When we then write [p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], we call the method [initialize] of the object referenced by [p1]. However, this object does not exist, and the compiler reports the error: the local variable [p1] has not been assigned a value.

> java Main.java
Main.java:4: error: variable p1 might not have been initialized
    p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    ^
1 error
error: compilation failed

If we write [Person p1 = null;] followed by [p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], we explicitly indicate with the keyword [null] that the variable [p1] does not yet reference any object. The compiler accepts the program, but at runtime, the method call triggers a [NullPointerException] exception:

> java Main.java
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "Person.initialize(String, String, int)" because "<local1>" is null
    at Main.main(Main.java:4)

Starting with Java 14, the exception message specifies which operation failed; [<local1>] refers to the local variable [p1], whose name was not preserved by the in-memory compilation. For [p1] to reference an object, you must write [Person p1 = new Person();].

This creates an object of type [Person] that has not yet been initialized: its fields have their default values—in this case, the empty string for [lastName] and [firstName], and 0 for [age]. Now that [p1] references an object, the initialization statement for this object, [p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);], is valid.

docs.title: 4.1.6. The this keyword
docs.text:
Let’s look at the code for the [initialize] method:

    public void initialize(String p, String n, int age) {
        this.firstName = p;
        this.lastName = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

The statement [this.firstName = p;] means that the field [firstName] of the current object ([this]) is assigned the value [p]. The keyword [this] refers to the current object: the one on which the method is executed. How do we know this? Let’s look at how the object referenced by [p1] is initialized in the calling program: [p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);]. It is the method [initialize] of the object [p1] that is called. When, within this method, the object [this] is referenced, it actually refers to the object [p1].

When a method of an object references a field [a] of that object, the notation [this.a] is implied: the method [initialize] could have written [firstName = p;] and [lastName = n;]. You must use [this] explicitly when there is a conflict of identifiers. This is the case with the statement [this.age = age;] (line 11), where [age] refers to both a field of the current object and the parameter [age] received by the method. In the method, the name [age] alone refers to the parameter; the field must be referred to as [this.age].

docs.title: 4.1.7. A Test Program
docs.text:
Here is a short test program. It is written in the source file [Main.java]:

// the main program
void main() {
    // a Person object
    Person p1 = new Person();
    p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    p1.identify();
}
  • Line 2: The method [main] is the program’s entry point. As in the previous chapter, it is written without an enclosing class: the file [Main.java] is a compact source file (see the following paragraph);
  • line 4: creation of a [Person] object referenced by [p1]. Since the [Person] class belongs to the same package (the unnamed package), it is recognized without an import statement;
  • Line 5: Initialization of the object;
  • line 6: display of its status.

Results:

> java Main.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.8. Compact source files
docs.text:
For a short example, a folder containing multiple files is unnecessarily large. As in the previous chapter, we will therefore write a compact source file (Java 25): a file that contains the method [void main()], possibly other methods and fields, and the classes the program needs. We run it with the source code launcher: [java Classes01.java].

It is important to understand how the compiler processes such a file. It wraps it in an implicit class, which bears the file’s name ([Classes01]): the file’s methods and fields become members of this class, and the classes declared in the file become nested classes of this implicit class. The explicit compilation of the file demonstrates this:

> javac -d classes Classes01.java
> ls classes
Classes01$Person.class
Classes01.class

The full name of the class [Person] in the file [Classes01.java] is therefore [Classes01$Person]. This has two consequences that we will encounter in the examples:

  • a class and the classes it contains share their private members: the [main] method in a compact file has access to the private fields of the classes in that file. To ensure that a private field is inaccessible from outside its class, you must, as in the [Persons] folder, place the class in its own file;
  • A regular nested class is an internal class: its objects are bound to an object of the enclosing class. This is not apparent as long as the objects are created by methods in the file, but a static method (see the section on class members) cannot create them. We then declare the nested class [static]. Records and interfaces, discussed later, are always static.

Finally, a compact file automatically imports all public classes from the [java.base] module: [List], [ArrayList], [BigDecimal], [Objects]… can be used there without the [import] clause. This is not the case for a regular file such as [Person.java], as we will see.

docs.title: 4.1.9. Another initialize method: overloading
docs.text:
Let’s continue to consider the class [Person] and add a second method to it: [initialize]. The program [Classes01.java] is as follows:

// overloading of the initialize method
void main() {
    Person p1 = new Person();
    p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    p1.identify();
    Person p2 = new Person();
    p2.initialize(p1);
    p2.identify();
}

// the Person class is declared after the main method
class Person {
    // attributes
    private String firstName = "";
    private String lastName = "";
    private int age;

    // initialization from three values
    public void initialize(String p, String n, int age) {
        firstName = p;
        lastName = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // initialization from another person
    public void initialize(Person p) {
        firstName = p.firstName;
        lastName = p.lastName;
        age = p.age;
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void identify() {
        IO.println("[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • lines 2–9: the main program;
  • line 12: the class [Person] is declared after the method [main]. It is not public: in a compact file, this is unnecessary;
  • lines 19–23: the [initialize] method from the previous paragraph;
  • lines 26–30: a second method, [initialize].

We now have two methods named [initialize]: this is valid as long as they accept different parameters (in number or type). The method [initialize] is said to be overloaded. The compiler chooses which method to call based on the actual parameters: [p1.initialize("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] (line 4) calls the first one, and [p2.initialize(p1)] (line 7) calls the second one. The return type alone is not sufficient to distinguish between two methods: two methods with the same name and the same parameters that differ only in their return type would be rejected.

The parameter of the second method is a reference ([p]) to a person. The fields of the person ([p]) are then assigned to the current object ([this]). Note that the method [initialize] has direct access to the fields of the object [p] even though they are private (lines 27–29). This is always true: a method of a class [C] has access to the private members of all objects of the same class [C].

Results:

> java Classes01.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.1.10. Constructors of the Person class
docs.text:
A constructor is a method that bears the name of the class and is called when the object is created. It is generally used to initialize the object. It is a method that can accept parameters but does not return a value. Its declaration is not preceded by any type (not even [void]).

If a class [C] has a constructor that accepts n parameters, the declaration and initialization of an object of this class can be done in the form [C object = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);], or in two steps: [C object;], followed later by [object = new C(arg1, arg2, ... argn);].

When a class [C] has one or more constructors, one of these constructors must be used to create an object of that class. If a class [C] has no constructors, it has a default constructor with no parameters that does nothing. The object’s fields then retain their initial values. This is what happened in the previous programs, where we had written [new Person()].

The program [Classes02.java] returns three constructors for class [Person]:

// constructors of the Person class
void main() {
    Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    p1.identify();
    Person p2 = new Person(p1);
    p2.identify();
    Person p3 = new Person();
    p3.identify();
}

class Person {
    // attributes
    private String firstName;
    private String lastName;
    private int age;

    // main constructor
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // copy constructor: it calls the main constructor
    public Person(Person p) {
        this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age);
    }

    // parameterless constructor: it also calls the main constructor
    public Person() {
        this("?", "?", 0);
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void identify() {
        IO.println("[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • lines 18–22: the “main” constructor initializes the three fields. Since its parameters have the same names as the fields, the fields are distinguished using [this];
  • lines 25–27: the copy constructor. The statement [this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age);] calls the constructor of the same class, which accepts three parameters: [String], [String], and [int]. This is referred to as chained constructors. As a result, the initialization code is written only once;
  • lines 30–32: the parameterless constructor, which is also chained to the main constructor. Since the class has declared constructors, it no longer has a default constructor: if you want to be able to write [new Person()], you must declare it;
  • lines 13–15: the fields are no longer initialized at the time of their declaration; all constructors, either directly or through chaining, assign a value to them.

The call [this(...)] to another constructor can only be made within a constructor. Up to Java 24, it had to be the first statement; since Java 25, statements that do not use the object being constructed (to verify or prepare parameters, for example) may precede it. We could also have constructors call a method such as [initialize]; however, chaining is preferable: the initialization code is in a single location, and a constructor should not call a method that a derived class might override—we’ll see why.

Results:

> java Classes02.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[?, ?, 0]

docs.title: 4.1.11. Object References
docs.text:
We use the [Person] class from the previous program, omitting its parameterless constructor but including the [initialize(String, String, int)] method from the beginning of the chapter. The test program becomes the following [Classes03.java]:

// object references
void main() {
    // p1
    Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    IO.print("p1="); p1.identify();
    // p2 references the same object as p1
    Person p2 = p1;
    IO.print("p2="); p2.identify();
    // p3 references an object that is a copy of the object referenced by p1
    Person p3 = new Person(p1);
    IO.print("p3="); p3.identify();
    // we change the state of the object referenced by p1
    p1.initialize("Micheline", "Benoît", 67);
    IO.print("p1="); p1.identify();
    // since p2 = p1, the object referenced by p2 has changed state
    IO.print("p2="); p2.identify();
    // p3 does not reference the same object as p1: the object referenced by p3 has not changed
    IO.print("p3="); p3.identify();
    // are p1 and p2 the same reference? and p1 and p3?
    IO.println("p1 == p2 : " + (p1 == p2) + ", p1 == p3 : " + (p1 == p3));
}

class Person {
    // attributes
    private String firstName;
    private String lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructors
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public Person(Person p) {
        this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age);
    }

    // initialization
    public void initialize(String p, String n, int age) {
        firstName = p;
        lastName = n;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void identify() {
        IO.println("[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}

The [IO.print] method (lines 5, 8, …) writes its parameter without wrapping to the next line. Results:

> java Classes03.java
p1=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p2=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p2=[Micheline, Benoît, 67]
p3=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
p1 == p2 : true, p1 == p3 : false

When the variable [p1] is declared via [Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);] (line 4), [p1] references the object [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] but is not the object itself. In C, this would be referred to as a pointer—that is, the address of the created object. If we then write [p1 = null;], it is not the object [Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)] that is modified; rather, it is the reference [p1] that changes its value. The object will be “lost” if it is not referenced by any other variable: the memory it occupies will later be reclaimed by the Java virtual machine’s garbage collector.

When we write [Person p2 = p1;] (line 7), we initialize the reference [p2]: it “points” to the same object (it refers to the same object) as the reference [p1]. Thus, if the object “pointed to” (or referenced) by [p1] is modified, the object referenced by [p2] is also modified (lines 5–6 of the results).

When [Person p3 = new Person(p1);] is written (line 10), a new object, [Person], is created. This new object will be referenced by [p3]. If you modify the object referenced by [p1], you do not modify the one referenced by [p3] (line 7 of the results).

Finally, on line 20, the operator [==], applied to two object references, indicates whether they refer to the same object: [p1] and [p2] refer to the same object, while [p1] and [p3] refer to two different objects, although they have the same content (line 8 of the results). We will see later how to compare the contents of two objects using the [equals] method.

docs.title: 4.1.12. Passing Object Reference Parameters
docs.text:
In the previous chapter, we saw that Java passes method parameters by value: the method receives a copy of the actual parameter’s value. Let’s see what this means when the parameter is an object reference. To do this, we’ll use the [StringBuilder] class from JDK. A [String] object cannot be modified: an operation such as [s.toUpperCase()] returns a new [String] object. A [StringBuilder] object, on the other hand, is a mutable string: its [append] method adds characters to the string without creating a new object.

The program [Classes04.java] is as follows:

// passing parameters of object reference type
void main() {
    StringBuilder sb0 = new StringBuilder("test0"), sb1 = new StringBuilder("test1");
    IO.println("In calling function before call: sb0=" + sb0 + ", sb1=" + sb1);
    StringBuilder sb2 = changeStringBuilder(sb0, sb1);
    IO.println("In calling function after call: sb0=" + sb0 + ", sb1=" + sb1 + ", sb2=" + sb2);
}

// the called function
StringBuilder changeStringBuilder(StringBuilder sbf0, StringBuilder sbf1) {
    IO.println("Start of called function: sbf0=" + sbf0 + ", sbf1=" + sbf1);
    // we modify the object referenced by sbf0
    sbf0.append("*****");
    // sbf1 now references a new object
    sbf1 = new StringBuilder("test1*****");
    // a new object is returned to the caller
    StringBuilder sbf2 = new StringBuilder("test2*****");
    IO.println("End of called function: sbf0=" + sbf0 + ", sbf1=" + sbf1 + ", sbf2=" + sbf2);
    return sbf2;
}
  • line 3: two references, [sb0] and [sb1], to objects of type [StringBuilder];
  • line 5: these are passed to the method [changeStringBuilder], whose result—a third reference—is assigned to [sb2];
  • lines 10–20: a method in the compact file, which has the formal parameters [sbf0] and [sbf1]. When the method starts, [sbf0] and [sb0] are two distinct references that point to the same object: the reference [sb0] was copied into [sbf0] (references are passed by value). The same applies to [sbf1] and [sb1].

Results:

> java Classes04.java
In calling function before call: sb0=test0, sb1=test1
Start of called function: sbf0=test0, sbf1=test1
End of called function: sbf0=test0*****, sbf1=test1*****, sbf2=test2*****
In calling function after call: sb0=test0*****, sb1=test1, sb2=test2*****

Explanations:

  • [sb0] and [sbf0] are two distinct references to the same object. This object was modified via [sbf0] (line 13). This modification is visible via [sb0] (line 5 of the results);
  • [sb1] and [sbf1] are two distinct references to the same object. [sbf1] is assigned a new value in the method and now points to a new object (line 15). This does not change the value of [sb1], which continues to point to the original, unmodified object;
  • a Java method cannot, therefore, change the value of a caller’s variable. To pass a new object back to the caller, it returns it as a result (lines 17 and 19). When there are multiple results, they are grouped into an object, such as a record (see below).

Keep in mind that a method can modify the object referenced by a parameter, but not the caller’s variable that contains the reference. Unlike other languages such as C#, Java does not support passing parameters by reference.

docs.title: 4.1.13. Temporary Objects
docs.text:
In an expression, you can explicitly call an object’s constructor: the object is created, but there is no variable to access it later (to modify it, for example). This temporary object is created for the purpose of evaluating the expression and is then discarded. The memory space it occupied will later be automatically reclaimed by the garbage collector, whose role is to reclaim memory space occupied by objects that are no longer referenced by the program’s data.

Consider the following program, [Classes05.java], where the constructors of the [Person] class display a message:

// temporary objects
void main() {
    new Person(new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30)).identify();
}

class Person {
    // attributes
    private String firstName;
    private String lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructors
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        IO.println("Constructor Person(String, String, int)");
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public Person(Person p) {
        IO.println("Constructor Person(Person)");
        firstName = p.firstName;
        lastName = p.lastName;
        age = p.age;
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void identify() {
        IO.println("[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • Line 3: The object [Person("Jean", *"Dupont", 30)]* is constructed and then passed to the copy constructor, which constructs a second object, whose method [identify] is called. Neither of the two objects is referenced by a variable.

Results:

> java Classes05.java
Constructor Person(String, String, int)
Constructor Person(Person)
[Jean, Dupont, 30]

The results show the successive creation of the two temporary objects.

docs.title: 4.1.14. Accessors and Mutators
docs.text:
We add the necessary methods to the [Person] class to read or modify the state of the fields in the [Classes06.java] objects:

// methods for reading (getters) and writing (setters) private attributes
void main() {
    Person p = new Person("Jean", "Michelin", 34);
    IO.println("p=(" + p.getFirstName() + "," + p.getLastName() + "," + p.getAge() + ")");
    p.setAge(56);
    IO.println("p=(" + p.getFirstName() + "," + p.getLastName() + "," + p.getAge() + ")");
}

class Person {
    // attributes
    private String firstName;
    private String lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructor
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // getters
    public String getFirstName() {
        return firstName;
    }

    public String getLastName() {
        return lastName;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    // setters
    public void setFirstName(String firstName) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
    }

    public void setLastName(String lastName) {
        this.lastName = lastName;
    }

    public void setAge(int age) {
        this.age = age;
    }
}
  • lines 23–33: the read methods, called getters;
  • Lines 36–46: Writing methods, called "setters."

Results:

> java Classes06.java
p=(Jean,Michelin,34)
p=(Jean,Michelin,56)

The names of these methods follow a convention established since the early days of Java, namely “JavaBeans”: the getter for the field [age] is named [getAge], and its setter is named [setAge]; the getter for a boolean field named [active] is instead called [isActive]. Many libraries (such as Jackson for JSON and Hibernate for databases, which we’ll use later) rely on this convention to retrieve an object’s data. Unlike other languages such as C#, Java does not have “properties”: accessing an object’s state always involves methods, or—for immutable objects—records, which we’ll cover later. Development environments can generate getters and setters from fields (in IntelliJ and IDEA, under the “Code / Generate…” menu).

docs.title: 4.1.15. Setters that validate received values
docs.text:
The advantage of modifiers over public fields is the ability to control the values assigned to the fields: a modifier can verify the validity of the received value and throw an exception if it is invalid. Consider the program [Classes07.java]:

// setters that check the validity of the values received
void main() {
    Person p = new Person("Jean", "Michelin", 34);
    IO.println("p=(" + p.getFirstName() + "," + p.getLastName() + "," + p.getAge() + ")");
    p.setAge(56);
    IO.println("p=(" + p.getFirstName() + "," + p.getLastName() + "," + p.getAge() + ")");
    try {
        p.setAge(-4);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
    // parameterless constructor then calls to the setters
    Person p2 = new Person();
    p2.setAge(7);
    p2.setFirstName("Arthur");
    p2.setLastName("Martin");
    IO.println("p2=(" + p2.getFirstName() + "," + p2.getLastName() + "," + p2.getAge() + ")");
    try {
        Person p3 = new Person();
        p3.setFirstName("Paul");
        p3.setLastName(" ");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
}

class Person {
    // attributes
    private String firstName = "";
    private String lastName = "";
    private int age;

    // constructors
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        // we go through the setters to benefit from their checks
        setFirstName(firstName);
        setLastName(lastName);
        setAge(age);
    }

    public Person() {
    }

    // getters
    public String getFirstName() {
