        return firstName;
    }

    public String getLastName() {
        return lastName;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    // setters: they are declared final because the constructor calls them
    public final void setFirstName(String firstName) {
        // valid first name?
        if (firstName == null || firstName.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("first name (" + firstName + ") invalid");
        }
        this.firstName = firstName;
    }

    public final void setLastName(String lastName) {
        // valid last name?
        if (lastName == null || lastName.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("last name (" + lastName + ") invalid");
        }
        this.lastName = lastName;
    }

    public final void setAge(int age) {
        // valid age?
        if (age < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("age (" + age + ") invalid");
        }
        this.age = age;
    }
}

The three modifiers validate the received value (lines 60–62, 68–70, 76–78).

  • Lines 60–62: The method [isBlank] (Java 11) returns [true] if the string is empty or consists solely of spaces. The [firstName == null] test is performed first: if [firstName] is equal to [null], the operator [||] does not evaluate its second operand, which would cause a [NullPointerException] exception. The exception thrown is of type [IllegalArgumentException], the exception provided by Java to signal an invalid parameter. This is an uncaught exception: the method does not need to declare it with [throws];
  • lines 34–39: the constructor initializes the object using accessors rather than fields. This allows it to take advantage of the validations performed by the accessors, which are written in only one place;
  • lines 58, 66, 74: the modifiers are declared as [final]. We will see with inheritance that a derived class can override the methods of its parent class; the keyword [final] prevents this. Without it, a derived class could redefine [setAge], and the constructor of [Person] would call this new version even before the derived class’s constructor has been executed. The compiler, with the [-Xlint:all] option, flags this risk (warning [this-escape]) for a public class written in its own file;
  • lines 41–42: a parameterless constructor, which leaves the fields at their initial values.

Results:

> java Classes07.java
p=(Jean,Michelin,34)
p=(Jean,Michelin,56)
age (-4) invalid
p2=(Arthur,Martin,7)
last name ( ) invalid

Line 4 of the results shows that the call to [p.setAge(-4)] (line 8) was rejected by the modifier. Lines 13–16: An instance is created using the parameterless constructor and then initialized by its setters. Lines 19–21: The name containing a space is rejected (line 6 of the results).

Unlike other languages, Java does not have an object initializer—a syntax that would allow multiple fields to be set within the [new] expression itself: instead, as shown here, we chain the constructor and setter calls, or we write a constructor that takes all the values. We’ll look at two other solutions: “fluid” modifiers and records.

docs.title: 4.1.16. Final fields and required parameters
docs.text:
A field declared as [final] must be assigned a value exactly once—either at declaration or within each constructor—and cannot be modified thereafter. The compiler enforces this rule. Combined with the absence of modifiers, this allows for the creation of read-only data. The program [Classes08.java] demonstrates several cases:

// final fields, read-only, mandatory parameters
void main() {
    Person p = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30, "Angers");
    IO.println(p.getIdentity());
    // the first name is read / write
    p.setFirstName("Jacques");
    // the age can only be modified inside the class
    p.growOlder();
    IO.println(p.getIdentity());
    // the following lines are rejected by the compiler
    // p.setLastName("Durand"); // there is no setter for the last name
    // p.setAge(40);         // there is no setter for the age
    // p.city = "Paris";     // the city field is final

    // a mandatory parameter
    Contact c = new Contact("jean.dupont@example.com");
    IO.println("Contact: " + c.getEmail() + ", " + c.getPhone());
    try {
        Contact c2 = new Contact(null);
        IO.println("Contact: " + c2.getEmail());
    } catch (NullPointerException ex) {
        IO.println("Error: " + ex.getMessage());
    }
}

class Person {
    // fields
    private String firstName;
    // final fields: they receive their value once and for all in the constructor
    private final String lastName;
    private final String city;
    private int age;

    // constructor
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age, String city) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
        this.city = city;
    }

    // first name read / write
    public String getFirstName() {
        return firstName;
    }

    public void setFirstName(String firstName) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
    }

    // last name, age and city read-only
    public String getLastName() {
        return lastName;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    public String getCity() {
        return city;
    }

    // a computed value
    public String getIdentity() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + ", " + city + "]";
    }

    // the age is only modified by the methods of the class
    public void growOlder() {
        age++;
    }
}

class Contact {
    // the email is mandatory, the phone optional
    private final String email;
    private final String phone;

    // constructor with both values
    public Contact(String email, String phone) {
        this.email = Objects.requireNonNull(email, "the email is mandatory");
        this.phone = phone;
    }

    // constructor without the phone: default value
    public Contact(String email) {
        this(email, "unknown");
    }

    public String getEmail() {
        return email;
    }

    public String getPhone() {
        return phone;
    }
}
  • lines 28 and 43–49: the first name is both read-only and writable; it has a getter and a setter;
  • lines 30–31: the last name and city are [final] fields. The constructor assigns a value to them (lines 37 and 39), which cannot be changed afterward;
  • line 32 and lines 56–58: The age is readable by everyone but does not have a public setter; it can only be modified by the class’s methods, such as [growOlder] (lines 70–72);
  • lines 65–67: the method [getIdentity] returns a value calculated from the fields. To the user of the class, it is indistinguishable from an accessor;
  • lines 11–13: three statements that the compiler rejects, for the reasons given in the comments. For the third one, the compiler’s message is: [cannot assign a value to final variable city];
  • Lines 75–98: The [Contact] class has one required field—email—and one optional field—phone. The required field is enforced by the constructor: a [Contact] object cannot be created without an email address. The [Objects.requireNonNull(value, message)] method (line 82) returns its first parameter if it is not [null] and throws a [NullPointerException] exception with the specified message otherwise: An email address of the form [null] is rejected (lines 18–23);
  • lines 87–89: the optional nature of the phone number is expressed through a second constructor, which provides a default value. Java does not have optional parameters: we overload the constructor.

Note that in a compact file, the method [main] has access to the private fields of the file’s classes: this is why the comments on lines 11–13 do not rely on the private nature of the fields, but rather on the absence of a modifier and on the keyword [final].

Results:

> java Classes08.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30, Angers]
[Jacques, Dupont, 31, Angers]
Contact: jean.dupont@example.com, unknown
Error: the email is mandatory

docs.title: 4.1.17. Fluid modifiers
docs.text:
When an object has many optional fields, the number of constructors increases and modifier calls become longer. A common technique is to have each modifier return the current object ([this]): the calls can then be chained together; these are referred to as “fluid” methods. The program [Classes09.java] illustrates this:

// "fluent" setters: they return the current object
void main() {
    Person p = new Person().setFirstName("  jean ").setLastName("Dupont").setAge(30);
    IO.println(p.getIdentity());
    try {
        p.setLastName("");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
    try {
        p.setAge(-4);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
    IO.println(p.getIdentity());
}

class Person {
    // fields
    private String firstName = "";
    private String lastName = "";
    private int age;

    // fluent setters: each one returns the current object (this)
    public Person setFirstName(String firstName) {
        this.firstName = check(firstName, "first name");
        return this;
    }

    public Person setLastName(String lastName) {
        this.lastName = check(lastName, "last name");
        return this;
    }

    public Person setAge(int age) {
        if (age < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("age (" + age + ") invalid");
        }
        this.age = age;
        return this;
    }

    // identity
    public String getIdentity() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]";
    }

    // checking a mandatory string: it is returned without its leading and trailing spaces
    private static String check(String value, String label) {
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(label + " (" + value + ") invalid");
        }
        return value.strip();
    }
}
  • lines 25–28: the modifier [setFirstName] checks the received value, assigns it to the field, and returns the current object. Its return type is therefore [Person];
  • line 3: the calls are chained: [new Person()] returns a person, on which [setFirstName] is called, which returns the same person, on which [setLastName] is called, and so on. The syntax resembles an object initializer;
  • Lines 49–54: The checks for the first name and last name, which are identical, are factored into the private method [check]. It is declared as [static] because it does not use any fields of the object (static members are discussed in the following paragraph). The method [strip] (Java 11) removes the leading and trailing spaces from the string.

Results:

> java Classes09.java
[jean, Dupont, 30]
last name () invalid
age (-4) invalid
[jean, Dupont, 30]

The first name “jean,” provided with spaces on either side (line 3), was stored without them (line 2 of the results). Fluid modifiers do not follow the JavaBeans convention, according to which a modifier returns nothing ([void]): some libraries do not recognize them. To construct complex objects, the “Builder” design pattern is also used: an auxiliary class, equipped with fluid methods, collects the values and then constructs the final object, which can then be immutable.

docs.title: 4.1.18. Class Methods and Attributes
docs.text:
Suppose we want to count the number of [Person] objects created in an application. We could manage a counter ourselves, but we risk overlooking temporary objects that are created here and there. It seems safer to include an instruction in the constructors of the [Person] class that increments a counter. This counter cannot be an ordinary field, since each object has its own fields: it is a field of the class itself and not that of a particular instance of that class. It is declared using the keyword [static]: [private static long nbPersons;].

To refer to it, we write [Person.nbPersons] to indicate that it is a field of the [Person] class itself. Here, we have created a private field that cannot be accessed directly from outside the class. We therefore create a public accessor to provide access to the class field [nbPersons]. To retrieve the value of [nbPersons], this accessor does not require a specific [Person] object; therefore, we also declare it as *[static]. From the outside, it will be called using the syntax [Person.getNbPersons()]. Here is an example of [Classes10.java]*:

// class members (static)
void main() {
    Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    Person p2 = new Person(p1);
    new Person(p1);
    IO.println("Number of persons created: " + Person.getNbPersons());
    // a class method
    Person p3 = Person.unknown();
    p3.identify();
    IO.println("Number of persons created: " + Person.getNbPersons());
}

// static nested class: see the explanations
static class Person {
    // class attribute
    private static long nbPersons;

    // class getter
    public static long getNbPersons() {
        return nbPersons;
    }

    // class method
    public static Person unknown() {
        return new Person("?", "?", 0);
    }

    // instance attributes
    private String firstName;
    private String lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructors
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
        nbPersons++;
    }

    public Person(Person p) {
        this(p.firstName, p.lastName, p.age);
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void identify() {
        IO.println("[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • line 16: the class field. Like any numeric field, it is initialized to 0;
  • lines 19–21: the class accessor;
  • lines 24–26: a class method. It is called using the class name: [Person.unknown()] (line 8). A class method has no current object: the keyword [this] has no meaning there, and it can only directly use the class members [static]. A static method that creates and returns an object of its class, such as this one, is called a static factory;
  • line 38: the primary constructor increments the counter. The copy constructor, which is chained to the primary constructor, therefore increments it as well;
  • Line 14: The class [Person] is declared as [static]. As explained in the section on compact files: a class declared in a compact file is a nested class of the implicit class. Without the [static] keyword, it is an internal class, where each object is bound to an object of the enclosing class; the static method [unknown], which has no current object, would be unable to create one, and the compiler would report the error [non-static variable this cannot be referenced from a static context]. A class written in its own file does not have this problem.

Results:

> java Classes10.java
Number of persons created: 3
[?, ?, 0]
Number of persons created: 4

The program correctly counted the temporary object created on line 5. We have been using class members from the beginning: [IO.println], [Integer.parseInt], [Math.sqrt] are [static] methods, and [Math.PI] is a [static] field. The class [Math] contains only static members: it is declared as [final], and its sole constructor is private, which prevents the creation of instances. This is the Java way of writing a utility class.

docs.title: 4.1.19. An array of people
docs.text:
An object is a piece of data like any other, and as such, multiple objects can be grouped together in an array [Classes11.java]:

// an array of persons
void main() {
    Person[] friends = new Person[3];
    friends[0] = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    friends[1] = new Person("Sylvie", "Vartan", 52);
    friends[2] = new Person("Neil", "Armstrong", 66);
    // display
    for (Person friend : friends) {
        friend.identify();
    }
}

class Person {
    // attributes
    private String firstName;
    private String lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructor
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // identity of the person
    public void identify() {
        IO.println("[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]");
    }
}
  • Line 3: creates an array of 3 elements of type [Person]. These 3 elements are initialized here with the value [null], meaning they do not reference any objects. Technically speaking, we refer to this as an “array of objects,” even though it is actually just an array of object references. The creation of the array—which is itself an object (as indicated by [new])—does not create any objects of the same type as its elements; this must be done subsequently;
  • lines 4–6: creation of the 3 objects of type [Person];
  • lines 8–10: display the contents of the array [friends].

Results:

> java Classes11.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Sylvie, Vartan, 52]
[Neil, Armstrong, 66]

docs.title: 4.1.20. Type inference and array initialization
docs.text:
The program [Classes12.java] features two constructs that simplify the creation of objects and arrays:

// type inference with var and array initialization
void main() {
    // the type of the variable is deduced from the expression that initializes it
    var p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    var p2 = new Person();
    p2.setFirstName("Arthur");
    p2.setLastName("Martin");
    p2.setAge(7);
    // an array created and initialized by a list of values between braces
    Person[] friends = {
        p1,
        p2,
        new Person("Sylvie", "Vartan", 52),
        new Person("Neil", "Armstrong", 66),
    };
    for (var friend : friends) {
        IO.println(friend.getIdentity());
    }
    // an anonymous array passed as a parameter
    display(new Person[] { new Person("Pauline", "Leduc", 12), p1 });
}

// a method that receives an array of persons
void display(Person[] persons) {
    for (Person p : persons) {
        IO.println("Display: " + p.getIdentity());
    }
}

class Person {
    // fields
    private String firstName = "";
    private String lastName = "";
    private int age;

    // constructors
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public Person() {
    }

    // setters
    public void setFirstName(String firstName) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
    }

    public void setLastName(String lastName) {
        this.lastName = lastName;
    }

    public void setAge(int age) {
        this.age = age;
    }

    // identity
    public String getIdentity() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]";
    }
}
  • Line 4: With the keyword [var] (Java 10), the type of the local variable is inferred from the expression that initializes it, in this case [Person]. The variable is nonetheless typed: [p1] is of type [Person] and can only reference a single person. [var] can only be used for local variables initialized at declaration, not for fields or parameters;
  • lines 10–15: an array created and populated with a list of values enclosed in curly braces and separated by commas. The size of the array is the number of values. A trailing comma (line 14) is allowed: it makes it easier to add an element. This syntax is only allowed in the array declaration;
  • line 16: [var] within a loop [for];
  • line 20: outside of an array declaration, an initialized array is created by specifying its type: [new Person[] { ... }]. This is called an anonymous array: it is not referenced by any variable in the [main] method;
  • Lines 24–28: A method in the compact file that receives an array of people.

Results:

> java Classes12.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Arthur, Martin, 7]
[Sylvie, Vartan, 52]
[Neil, Armstrong, 66]
Display: [Pauline, Leduc, 12]
Display: [Jean, Dupont, 30]

docs.title: 4.2.1. Overview
docs.text:
Here we introduce the concept of inheritance. The purpose of inheritance is to “customize” an existing class so that it meets our needs. Suppose we want to create a class [Teacher]: a teacher is a specific type of person. They have attributes that other people do not have: the subject they teach, for example. But they also have the attributes common to all people: first name, last name, and age. A teacher is therefore a full member of the class [Person] but has additional attributes. Rather than creating a class [Teacher] from scratch, we prefer to build upon the existing class [Person] and adapt it to the specific characteristics of teachers. This is made possible by the concept of inheritance.

To indicate that the class [Teacher] inherits from the class [Person], we write [public class Teacher extends Person].

[Person] is called the parent class (or base class, or superclass), and [Teacher] is called the derived class (or child class, or subclass). A [Teacher] object has all the properties of a [Person] object: it has the same fields and methods. These fields and methods from the parent class are not repeated in the definition of the child class; we simply specify the fields and methods added by the child class. A Java class can inherit from only one parent class.

The examples in this paragraph are two multi-file programs, located in the [Inheritance1] and [Inheritance2] folders. In the [Inheritance1] folder, the [Person] class is defined as follows: [Person.java]:

public class Person {
    // class field: the number of persons created
    private static long nbPersons;

    // instance fields
    private String firstName;
    private String lastName;
    private int age;

    // constructor
    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        setFirstName(firstName);
        setLastName(lastName);
        setAge(age);
        nbPersons++;
        IO.println("Constructor Person(String, String, int)");
    }

    // number of persons created
    public static long getNbPersons() {
        return nbPersons;
    }

    // getters
    public String getFirstName() {
        return firstName;
    }

    public String getLastName() {
        return lastName;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    // setters
    public final void setFirstName(String firstName) {
        this.firstName = check(firstName, "first name");
    }

    public final void setLastName(String lastName) {
        this.lastName = check(lastName, "last name");
    }

    public final void setAge(int age) {
        if (age < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("age (" + age + ") invalid");
        }
        this.age = age;
    }

    // identity of the person
    public String getIdentity() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]";
    }

    // checking a mandatory string
    private static String check(String value, String label) {
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(label + " (" + value + ") invalid");
        }
        return value;
    }
}
  • line 3: the person counter from the previous paragraph;
  • lines 11–17: the constructor initializes the object via its modifiers, increments the counter, and displays a progress message;
  • lines 38–51: three modifiers that validate their values. The validations for the first name and last name, which are identical, are factored into the private class method [check] (lines 59–64). The modifiers are declared as [final] because the constructor calls them (see the program [Classes07.java]);
  • lines 54–56: the [identify] method from the previous examples has been replaced by the [getIdentity] method, which returns the person’s identity instead of displaying it.

We create a class named [Teacher] that inherits from the [Person] class: [Teacher.java]:

public class Teacher extends Person {
    // field specific to the Teacher class
    private int section;

    // constructor
    public Teacher(String firstName, String lastName, int age, int section) {
        // construction of the Person part of the object
        super(firstName, lastName, age);
        // we store the section
        this.section = section;
        // tracing
        IO.println("Constructor Teacher(String, String, int, int)");
    }

    // getter and setter of the section
    public int getSection() {
        return section;
    }

    public void setSection(int section) {
        this.section = section;
    }
}

The [Teacher] class adds to the fields and methods of the [Person] class:

  • line 1: the class [Teacher] derives from the class [Person];
  • line 3: a field [section], which is the number of the section to which the teacher belongs within the teaching staff (roughly one section per subject);
  • lines 6–13: a constructor used to initialize all of a teacher’s fields;
  • lines 16–22: the getter and setter for the [section] field.

docs.title: 4.2.2. Creating a Teacher Object
docs.text:
A child class does not inherit constructors from its parent class. It must define its own constructors. The constructor for the [Teacher] class is as follows:

    public Teacher(String firstName, String lastName, int age, int section) {
        // construction of the Person part of the object
        super(firstName, lastName, age);
        // we store the section
        this.section = section;
        // tracing
        IO.println("Constructor Teacher(String, String, int, int)");
    }

The constructor receives four parameters ([firstName], [lastName], [age], [section]) and passes three ([firstName], [lastName], [age]) to its parent class—in this case, the class [Person]—using the statement [super(firstName, lastName, age);] (line 3). We know that this class has a constructor, [Person(String, String, int)], which will be used to create a person with the passed parameters. Once the construction of the [Person] part is complete, the construction of the [Teacher] object continues by executing the rest of the constructor (lines 5–7).

In summary, the constructor of a derived class:

  • passes to its parent class, via [super(...)], the parameters that the parent class needs to construct itself;
  • uses the other parameters to initialize its own fields.

We could have chosen to initialize the fields [firstName], [lastName], and [age] directly in the constructor of class [Teacher], using statements like [this.firstName = firstName;]. This is impossible for two reasons. First, the private fields [firstName], [lastName], and [age] are accessible only to methods of the [Person] class. All other objects, including objects of derived classes as in this case, must access them through public (or protected) members. This would have been different if the class [Person] had declared these fields as protected (*[protected]*): it would then have allowed derived classes to access them directly. Furthermore, the [Person] part of the object must in any case be constructed by a constructor of the [Person] class: in the absence of a call to [super(...)], the compiler inserts a call to [super()]—the parameterless constructor of the parent class. However, the class [Person] does not have one. If the [super(firstName, lastName, age);] statement is removed, the compiler reports the following error:

> java Main.java
.../Inheritance1/Teacher.java:6: error: constructor Person in class Person cannot be applied to given types;
    public Teacher(String firstName, String lastName, int age, int section) {
                                                                            ^
  required: String,String,int
  found:    no arguments
  reason: actual and formal argument lists differ in length
1 error
error: compilation failed

Using the parent class’s constructor is therefore the correct solution and the standard approach: when constructing a child object, first call the parent object’s constructor, then complete the initializations specific to the child object ([section] in our example). As with [this(...)], only statements that do not use the object being constructed may precede the call to [super(...)] (since Java 25; previously, [super(...)] had to be the first statement).

docs.title: 4.2.3. Inherited Methods
docs.text:
The class [Teacher] does not define a method named [getIdentity]. The expression [e.getIdentity()], where [e] is a teacher, therefore refers to the method [getIdentity] inherited from the class [Person]: it is public and, by inheritance, becomes a public method of the [Teacher] class. The test program [Main.java] in the [Inheritance1] folder is as follows:

void main() {
    // a teacher
    Teacher e = new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
    // the getIdentity method inherited from the Person class
    IO.println(e.getIdentity());
    // the getSection method specific to the Teacher class
    IO.println("section=" + e.getSection());
    // a person
    Person p = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    // the display method receives a Person or an object of a derived class
    display(e);
    display(p);
    // the toString method inherited from the Object class
    IO.println(e.toString());
    IO.println(p.toString());
    IO.println("Number of persons created: " + Person.getNbPersons());
}

// displays the identity of p
void display(Person p) {
    IO.println(p.getIdentity());
}
  • line 3: creates a teacher;
  • line 5: displays the teacher’s identity, obtained via the [getIdentity] method inherited from the [Person] class;
  • line 7: the [getSection] method, specific to the [Teacher] class;
  • lines 11–12: call to the [display] method (lines 20–22) with a teacher and then a person. We’ll come back to this in the next paragraph;
  • lines 14–15: call to the [toString] method for both objects. We’ll also come back to this.

Results:

> java Main.java
Constructor Person(String, String, int)
Constructor Teacher(String, String, int, int)
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
section=61
Constructor Person(String, String, int)
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Teacher@70325e14
Person@37ceb1df
Number of persons created: 2

We can see that:

  • an object [Person] (line 2 of the results) was constructed before the object [Teacher] (line 3);
  • [e.getIdentity()] provided the identity of the teacher’s [Person] part, without its section (line 4);
  • the person counter also counts the teacher (line 11): a teacher is a person.

To obtain a teacher’s complete identity, the class [Teacher] must define its own method [getIdentity]. This is what the folder [Inheritance2] does.

docs.title: 4.2.4. Polymorphism
docs.text:
Consider a class hierarchy: C0 ← C1 ← C2 ← … ← Cn, where Ci ← Cj indicates that class Cj is derived from class Ci. This implies that class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Let Oi be objects of type Ci. It is valid to write [Oi = Oj] with j > i. Indeed, by inheritance, class Cj has all the characteristics of class Ci plus additional ones. Therefore, an object Oj of type Cj contains an object of type Ci. The operation [Oi = Oj] causes the variable Oi, of type Ci, to reference the object Oj: only the members defined in class Ci can be accessed through it.

The fact that a variable Oi of class Ci can actually reference not only an object of class Ci but any object derived from class Ci is called polymorphism: the ability of a variable to reference different types of objects.

Let’s take an example and consider the method [display] from the previous program:

void display(Person p) {
    IO.println(p.getIdentity());
}

We can pass it either a [Person] or a [Teacher]: In the latter case, the formal parameter [p], which is of type [Person], receives a value of type [Teacher]. Since the type [Teacher] is derived from the type [Person], this is valid. The [p.getIdentity()] statement here executed the [getIdentity] method of the [Person] class, the only one that exists in the program: for the teacher (line 7 of the results), we only get the identity of its “Person” part. Let’s see what happens when the class [Teacher] has its own method [getIdentity].

docs.title: 4.2.5. Method Overriding and Dynamic Linking
docs.text:
In the [Inheritance2] folder, the [Person] class is the same as the one in the [Inheritance1] folder with one addition:

    // identity of the person: method overridden in the Teacher class
    public String getIdentity() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]";
    }

    // overriding the toString method of the Object class
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return getIdentity();
    }
  • lines 6–10: a redefinition of the method [toString], discussed in the following paragraph.

In the [Teacher] class, the [getIdentity] method is redefined as follows:

// a final class: it cannot be derived from
public final class Teacher extends Person {
    // field specific to the Teacher class
    private int section;

    // constructor
    public Teacher(String firstName, String lastName, int age, int section) {
        super(firstName, lastName, age);
        this.section = section;
        IO.println("Constructor Teacher(String, String, int, int)");
    }

    // getter and setter of the section
    public int getSection() {
        return section;
    }

    public void setSection(int section) {
        this.section = section;
    }

    // the getIdentity method overrides the one of the parent class
    @Override
    public String getIdentity() {
        return "Teacher[" + super.getIdentity() + "," + section + "]";
    }
}
  • Lines 23–26: The method [getIdentity] overrides the method in the parent class; it has the same name, the same parameters, and the same return type. It relies on the method [getIdentity] from its parent class, referred to as [super.getIdentity()], to retrieve the “Person” portion, then supplements it with the section specific to the class [Teacher];
  • Line 23: The annotation [@Override] tells the compiler that the method intends to override a method of the parent class. It is not mandatory, but it is strongly recommended: if the method did not override anything (due to a typo in the name or different parameters), the compiler would report the error instead of silently creating a new method;
  • Line 2: The class is final ([final]), which we’ll explain in more detail later.

Consider a teacher object [E]. This object contains a [Person] object within it:

The method [getIdentity] is defined in both the class [Teacher] and its parent class [Person]. In Java, all instance methods that are neither private nor final can be overridden, and the choice of which method is executed by [p.getIdentity()] is made at runtime, based on the actual type of the object referenced by [p], rather than at compile time based on the declared type of the variable. This is known as dynamic binding. To execute [o.m()], the virtual machine searches for a method named [m] in the following order:

  • in the class of the [o] object;
  • in its parent class, if it has one;
  • in the parent class of its parent class, if it exists;
  • and so on.

Inheritance therefore allows you to redefine methods in the child class that have the same signature as those in the parent class. This is what enables you to adapt the child class to its own needs. The program [Main.java] in the folder [Inheritance2] is as follows:

void main() {
    // a teacher
    Teacher e = new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
    display(e);
    // a person
    Person p = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    display(p);
    // seen as a Person, the teacher remains a teacher
    Person pe = e;
    IO.println(pe.getIdentity());
    IO.println(((Person) e).getIdentity());
    // IO.println(Object) displays the result of the toString method of the object
    IO.println(e);
    IO.println(p);
    // an array of persons of different types
    Person[] persons = { p, e };
    for (Person person : persons) {
        IO.println(person.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + person);
    }
}

// displays the identity of p
void display(Person p) {
    IO.println(p.getIdentity());
}

Results:

> java Main.java
Constructor Person(String, String, int)
Constructor Teacher(String, String, int, int)
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
Constructor Person(String, String, int)
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
Person : [Jean, Dupont, 30]
Teacher : Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]

This time, on line 4 of the results, the [display] method correctly displayed the teacher’s full name. Lines 9–11 of the program show that, whether viewed through a variable of type [Person] or converted to [Person] by the operator [(Person)], the teacher remains a teacher: it is still the method [getIdentity] of the class [Teacher] that is executed (lines 7–8 of the results). The conversion changes the type of the reference, not that of the object. Unlike other languages such as C#, where a method can only be overridden if it is declared virtual, Java methods are “virtual” by default; there is no such thing as overriding an instance method.

docs.title: 4.2.6. The Object class and the toString method
docs.text:
The [java.lang.Object] class is the “parent” class of all Java classes. Thus, when you write [public class Person], you are implicitly writing [public class Person extends Object].

The [Object] class defines several methods that all objects inherit:

  • [String toString()]: returns a textual representation of the object. By default, this is the object’s class name, followed by the character [@] and a hash code written in hexadecimal;
  • [boolean equals(Object o)]: indicates whether the object is “equal” to the object [o]. By default, it is equal only to itself: the method compares references, like the operator [==];
  • [int hashCode()]: returns a hash code for the object, used by dictionaries and sets (see the next chapter). The methods [equals] and [hashCode] are discussed later;
  • [Class<?> getClass()]: returns the description of the object’s actual class. The method [getSimpleName] in this description returns the class name, while [getName] returns its full name.

It is the method [toString] of the class [Object] that was used by the calls [e.toString()] and [p.toString()] in the folder [Inheritance1]: [Teacher@70325e14] and [Person@37ceb1df] (lines 9–10 of the results; the numbers vary from one execution to another). Although we did not redefine the method [toString] in the classes [Person] and [Teacher], the method [toString] in the class [Object] was able to display the actual class name of the object.

In the [Inheritance2] folder, the [Person] class redefines the [toString] method (see above). Let’s return to the program [Main.java] in the folder [Inheritance2]:

    // IO.println(Object) displays the result of the toString method of the object
    IO.println(e);
    IO.println(p);
    // an array of persons of different types
    Person[] persons = { p, e };
    for (Person person : persons) {
        IO.println(person.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + person);
    }

Line 2: The [IO.println(Object)] method accepts a parameter of type [Object]; therefore, since [Object] is the superclass of all classes, any object—in this case, a [Teacher]—can be passed. It prints the result of the object’s [toString] method to the console. Since the binding is dynamic, the [toString] method of the actual object is used—in this case, the one inherited from the [Person] class. This returns [getIdentity()], a redefined method: For the teacher [e], the method [getIdentity] from the class [Teacher] is therefore executed, as shown in line 9 of the results. It is therefore unnecessary to redefine [toString] in the class [Teacher].

The same mechanism applies to the concatenation of a string and an object: in [" : " + person] (line 7), the object [person] is converted to a string by its method [toString]. The loop in lines 6–8 iterates over an array of references [Person] that actually point to objects of different types: [getClass().getSimpleName()] returns the actual class name of each object (lines 11–12 of the results).

docs.title: 4.2.7. Final classes and sealed classes
docs.text:
The class [Teacher] in the package [Inheritance2] is declared as [public final class Teacher extends Person]. The keyword [final] prevents classes from being derived from the class [Teacher]: the declaration [class TeacherResearcher extends Teacher] would be rejected by the compiler. A class is marked as final when it is not intended to be derived from. We have seen that the keyword also applies to methods: a [final] method cannot be overridden by derived classes without prohibiting derivation from that class. For example, the class [String], derived from JDK, is final.

Between a class open to all derivations and a final class, Java 17 has added an intermediate option: the sealed class ([sealed]), which provides an exhaustive list of its direct derived classes. The program [Classes13.java] illustrates this:

// final classes and sealed classes (Java 17)
void main() {
    Person[] persons = {
        new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 61),
        new Student("Paul", "Martin", "computer science"),
        new Adjunct("Marc", "Petit"),
        new Consultant("Lise", "Morel", "Airbus"),
    };
    for (Person p : persons) {
        IO.println(p.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + p.getIdentity());
    }
    // the permitted direct subclasses of the sealed class Person
    IO.println("Person is sealed: " + Person.class.isSealed());
    for (Class<?> c : Person.class.getPermittedSubclasses()) {
        IO.println("permitted subclass: " + c.getSimpleName());
    }
}

// a sealed class: only the classes listed after permits can derive from it
abstract sealed class Person permits Teacher, Student, Adjunct {
    private final String firstName;
    private final String lastName;

    protected Person(String firstName, String lastName) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
    }

    public String getIdentity() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + "]";
    }
}

// a class derived from a sealed class must be final, sealed or non-sealed
final class Teacher extends Person {
    private final int section;

    public Teacher(String firstName, String lastName, int section) {
        super(firstName, lastName);
        this.section = section;
    }

    @Override
    public String getIdentity() {
        return super.getIdentity() + ", section " + section;
    }
}

final class Student extends Person {
    private final String major;

    public Student(String firstName, String lastName, String major) {
        super(firstName, lastName);
        this.major = major;
    }

    @Override
    public String getIdentity() {
        return super.getIdentity() + ", major " + major;
    }
}

// non-sealed: the hierarchy is open again from this class
non-sealed class Adjunct extends Person {
    public Adjunct(String firstName, String lastName) {
        super(firstName, lastName);
    }
}

// a class derived from Adjunct: allowed, since Adjunct is not sealed
class Consultant extends Adjunct {
    private final String company;

    public Consultant(String firstName, String lastName, String company) {
        super(firstName, lastName);
        this.company = company;
    }

    @Override
    public String getIdentity() {
        return super.getIdentity() + ", company " + company;
    }
}

// rejected by the compiler: Artist is not listed in the permits clause of Person
// final class Artist extends Person { ... }
  • Line 20: The abstract class (see below: you cannot create objects of this class, only of its derived classes) [Person] is sealed. Only the classes [Teacher], [Student], and [Adjunct], listed after the keyword [permits], can be derived from it. When derived classes are declared in the same file, as here, the [permits] clause may be omitted: the authorized classes are then those in the file that are directly derived from it. In a larger program, the authorized classes must belong to the same package as the sealed class (or to the same module if the sealed class belongs to a named module);
  • line 24: the constructor is protected ([protected]): it is intended only for derived classes;
  • Lines 35 and 49: A class derived from a sealed class must specify how it itself can be derived. The classes [Teacher] and [Student] are final;
  • line 64: the class [Adjunct] is declared as [non-sealed]: this reopens the hierarchy, allowing any class to derive from it. A third option is to declare it as [sealed] itself, with its own list of permitted classes;
  • lines 71–83: The class [Consultant] derives from [Adjunct], which is allowed;
  • lines 85–86: a class [Artist] derived from [Person] would be rejected;
  • Lines 13–16: The description of a class ([Person.class]) indicates whether it is sealed ([isSealed]) and lists its authorized direct derived classes ([getPermittedSubclasses]).

Results:

> java Classes13.java
Teacher : [Lucile, Dumas], section 61
Student : [Paul, Martin], major computer science
Adjunct : [Marc, Petit]
Consultant : [Lise, Morel], company Airbus
Person is sealed: true
permitted subclass: Teacher
permitted subclass: Student
permitted subclass: Adjunct

If you uncomment the class [Artist] (by providing it with a constructor), the compiler reports:

> java Classes13.java
Classes13.java:86: error: class is not allowed to extend sealed class: Classes13.Person (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause)
final class Artist extends Person { Artist() { super("a", "b"); } }
      ^
1 error
error: compilation failed

What is the purpose of a sealed class? It allows the author of a class hierarchy to maintain control over it: the author knows that any [Person] is a [Teacher], a [Student], or a [Adjunct]. The compiler knows this as well and uses it in pattern filtering, which is discussed at the end of the chapter: a [switch] that handles all three cases is complete. The mechanism also applies to interfaces ([sealed interface]), which are discussed later.

docs.title: 4.3. No operator overloading: equals, compareTo…
docs.text:
Some languages, such as C# or C++, allow you to redefine the meaning of operators ([+], [==], [<]…) for a class. Java does not allow this: operators always have the meaning assigned to them by the language. The only exception is the [+] operator applied to a string, which performs concatenation and uses the [toString] method of the concatenated object to do so. Instead of operators, we write methods that follow well-established conventions:

OperationJava MethodExampleContent equality ([==] compares references)[boolean equals(Object o)], inherited from [Object][s1.equals(s2)]Comparison ([<], [>]…)[int compareTo(T other)] from the [Comparable<T>] interface: negative, null, or positive result[s1.compareTo(s2) < 0]arithmetic operationsexplicitly named methods[a.add(b)], [a.multiply(b)] for [BigDecimal]Addition to a collection ([+=])[add][list.add(p)]

docs.title: 4.3.1. An example
docs.text:
The folder [Lists] contains a class [ListOfPersons], a list of people, whose methods act as the operators [+] and [+=]. The classes [Person] and [Teacher] in this folder are simplified versions of those in the [Inheritance2] folder: the fields are [final] and have no modifiers; there are no longer any tracking messages or counters. The people are organized into a generic list [List<Person>] (generic classes are discussed later in this chapter; lists are covered in the next chapter). Rather than having the class [ListOfPersons] inherit from a list class derived from JDK, we place the list in a private field of the class. This is referred to as using composition rather than inheritance: the class [ListOfPersons] thus exposes only the operations it has chosen. From the interface [List<Person>], we use only the following elements:

  • the method [l.add(p)], which adds the person [p] to the list [l], and the [l.addAll(l2)] method, which adds all elements from the [l2] list to it;
  • the method [l.size()], which returns the number of elements in the list [l];
  • the methods [l.get(i)] and [l.set(i, p)], which read and modify element number i of the list [l].

The definition of class [ListOfPersons] is as follows: [ListOfPersons.java]:

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.StringJoiner;

public class ListOfPersons {
    // the persons of the list
    private final List<Person> persons = new ArrayList<>();

    // number of persons in the list
    public int size() {
        return persons.size();
    }

    // the equivalent of a + operator: returns a new list containing the persons
    // of the current list and the person p
    public ListOfPersons plus(Person p) {
        ListOfPersons result = new ListOfPersons();
        result.persons.addAll(persons);
        result.persons.add(p);
        return result;
    }

    // the equivalent of a += operator: adds p to the current list, which is returned
    public ListOfPersons add(Person p) {
        persons.add(p);
        return this;
    }

    // the equivalent of an indexer: reading and writing element no. i
    public Person get(int i) {
        return persons.get(i);
    }

    public void set(int i, Person p) {
        persons.set(i, p);
    }

    // position of the person with the given last name, -1 if it does not exist
    public int indexOf(String lastName) {
        for (int i = 0; i < persons.size(); i++) {
            if (persons.get(i).getLastName().equals(lastName)) {
                return i;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }

    // toString: returns (person1,person2,...)
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(",", "(", ")");
        for (Person p : persons) {
            joiner.add(p.toString());
        }
        return joiner.toString();
    }
}
  • lines 1–3: Unlike the compact file [Main.java], a regular file does not automatically import the classes from the [java.base] module: it must import the ones it uses (except for those from the [java.lang] package, such as [String], which are always known). The [import] clauses are provided with the packages;
  • line 7: the list of people. The keyword [final] indicates that the field will always refer to the same list; the list itself may change in content. [new ArrayList<>()] creates an empty list; the “diamond” operator [<>] allows the compiler to infer the type of the elements, [Person], from the field type;
  • lines 10–12: the number of people;
  • lines 16–21: the method [plus] acts as a [+] operator for the operation [l.plus(p)], where [l] is of type [ListOfPersons] and [p] is of type [Person] or a derivative thereof. It creates a new list (line 17), copies the people from the current list into it (line 18), and then adds the person [p] (line 19). As with the [+] operator for numbers or strings, the operands are not modified. Since the list [result] is of the same class, the method has access to its private field [result.persons]. The returned list is of type [ListOfPersons], which allows for chained calls as in [l.plus(p1).plus(p2)];
  • lines 24–27: the method [add] acts as a [+=] operator: it modifies the current list by adding the person [p] to it and returns that same list, which also allows for chained calls;
  • Lines 49–56: We redefine the [toString] method to display a list of people in the form (person1, person2, ...), where personi is itself the result of the person’s [toString] method. A [StringJoiner] object (line 51) constructs a string from successive elements ([add], line 53), separating them with the specified separator (in this case, a comma) and enclosing them with a prefix and a suffix (in this case, parentheses).

Note that the class [ListOfPersons] has no constructor. It therefore uses the default constructor, which takes no parameters and does nothing other than initialize the field [persons] with the value specified in its declaration. Lines 29–46 are discussed in the following section.

The test program [Main.java] begins as follows:

void main() {
    // --- methods instead of operators
    String s1 = "jean";
    String s2 = new StringBuilder("je").append("an").toString();
    IO.println("s1 == s2 : " + (s1 == s2) + ", s1.equals(s2) : " + s1.equals(s2));
    IO.println("s1.compareTo(\"paul\") : " + s1.compareTo("paul"));
    BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("0.10"), b = new BigDecimal("0.20");
    IO.println("a + b = " + a.add(b) + ", a < b : " + (a.compareTo(b) < 0));

    // --- the plus method
    // a list of persons
    ListOfPersons l = new ListOfPersons();
    // adding persons
    l = l.plus(new Person("jean", "martin", 10)).plus(new Person("pauline", "leduc", 12));
    // display
    IO.println("l=" + l);
    // l.plus(p) returns a new list: l is not modified
    ListOfPersons l2 = l.plus(new Person("louis", "durand", 8));
    IO.println("l=" + l);
    IO.println("l2=" + l2);

    // --- the add method
    ListOfPersons l3 = l;
    // add modifies the list referenced by l, without creating a new list
    l.add(new Teacher("camille", "germain", 27, 60));
    IO.println("l=" + l);
    // l and l3 still reference the same object
    IO.println("l3 == l : " + (l3 == l));
  • Lines 3–5: two strings with the same content but distinct: the string [s2] is constructed at runtime. The operator [==] compares the references, while the method [equals] compares the contents. To compare two strings, you must always use [equals];
  • line 6: the method [compareTo] returns a negative number because “jean” comes before “paul” in the character code order;
  • Lines 7–8: The class [BigDecimal] (exact decimal numbers, which we will use for the amounts) replaces the operators [+] and [<] with the methods [add] and [compareTo];
  • line 12: creation of an empty list of people [l];
  • line 14: Add two people using the [plus] method;
  • line 18: [l.plus(p)] creates a new list, [l2]; the list [l] remains unchanged;
  • line 25: adds a teacher using the [add] method;
  • lines 16–20: concatenating a string and an object uses the [toString] method, which is redefined from the [ListOfPersons] class.

Results (beginning):

> java Main.java
s1 == s2 : false, s1.equals(s2) : true
s1.compareTo("paul") : -6
a + b = 0.30, a < b : true
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12])
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12])
l2=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12],[louis, durand, 8])
l=([jean, martin, 10],[pauline, leduc, 12],Teacher[[camille, germain, 27],60])
l3 == l : true

Why are there two methods, when [l = l.plus(p)] produces the same output as [l.add(p)]? The [plus] method creates a new list, copies all the people from [l] into it, and then [l] references this new list, while the old one is discarded by the garbage collector. The method [add] adds the person to the existing list without copying them. Line 23 stores a second reference, [l3], to the list [l]; after the call to [l.add(...)], both references still point to the same object (line 9 of the results), which proves that the list was not recreated. For a large list, or within a loop, the difference in performance is significant. The choice between the two styles is evident in JDK: the immutable objects [String] and [BigDecimal] return new objects; lists and [StringBuilder] are modified.

docs.title: 4.4. No indexers: get and set methods
docs.text:
Here, we continue to use the [ListOfPersons] class. If [l] is a [ListOfPersons] object, we want to be able to refer to the person at index i in the [l] list for both reading and writing. Some languages allow you to define an “indexer” for this purpose, which enables the [l[i]] notation to be used on an object. Java does not allow this: the [[i]] notation is reserved for arrays. By convention, we write methods [get(int i)] and [set(int i, value)], just as the JDK lists do:

    // the equivalent of an indexer: reading and writing element no. i
    public Person get(int i) {
        return persons.get(i);
    }

    public void set(int i, Person p) {
        persons.set(i, p);
    }

    // position of the person with the given last name, -1 if it does not exist
    public int indexOf(String lastName) {
        for (int i = 0; i < persons.size(); i++) {
            if (persons.get(i).getLastName().equals(lastName)) {
                return i;
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }
  • lines 2–4: the method [get] returns person No. i from the private list [persons];
  • lines 6–8: the [set] method assigns person [p] to it;
  • lines 11–18: We also want to be able to obtain the position in the list of the person with a given name, or -1 if that person is not in the list. The name [indexOf] is that of the equivalent method for lists and strings, JDK. The names are compared using [equals] (line 13).

The test program continues as follows:

    // --- the get, set and indexOf methods instead of indexers
    // changing element no. 1
    l.set(1, new Person("franck", "gallon", 5));
    // displaying element no. 1
    IO.println("l.get(1)=" + l.get(1));
    // displaying the list l
    IO.println("l=" + l);
    // searching for persons by their last name
    String[] lastNames = { "martin", "germain", "xx" };
    for (String lastName : lastNames) {
        int index = l.indexOf(lastName);
        if (index != -1) {
            IO.println("Person(" + lastName + ")=" + l.get(index));
        } else {
            IO.println("Person(" + lastName + ") does not exist");
        }
    }
  • line 3: call to the [set] method;
  • line 5: call to method [get];
  • line 11: call to method [indexOf];
  • line 13: call to method [get].

Results (end):

...
l.get(1)=[franck, gallon, 5]
l=([jean, martin, 10],[franck, gallon, 5],Teacher[[camille, germain, 27],60])
Person(martin)=[jean, martin, 10]
Person(germain)=Teacher[[camille, germain, 27],60]
Person(xx) does not exist

docs.title: 4.5. No Structures: Primitive Types and Records
4.5.1. Value and Reference
docs.text:
Other languages, such as C or C#, offer structures in addition to classes: types whose variables directly contain the data, rather than a reference to an object. Java does not have them. It distinguishes between two families of types:

  • the eight primitive types ([byte], [short], [int], [long], [float], [double], [char], [boolean]): a variable of a primitive type contains the value itself;
  • reference types: classes (including [String]), interfaces, arrays, records, etc. A variable of a reference type contains a reference to an object, such as [null].

The program [Classes14.java] illustrates the difference:

// primitive types and reference types: copy of value, copy of reference
void main() {
    // two variables of primitive type
    int age1 = 10;
    int age2 = age1;
    IO.println("age1=" + age1 + ", age2=" + age2);
    // age2 is modified
    age2 = 30;
    // checking age1 and age2
    IO.println("age1=" + age1 + ", age2=" + age2);

    // an object op1
    CPerson op1 = new CPerson();
    op1.name = "paul";
    op1.age = 10;
    IO.println("op1=CPerson(" + op1.name + "," + op1.age + ")");
    // an object op2
    CPerson op2 = op1;
    IO.println("op2=CPerson(" + op2.name + "," + op2.age + ")");
    // op2 is modified
    op2.name = "nicole";
    op2.age = 30;
    // checking op1 and op2
    IO.println("op1=CPerson(" + op1.name + "," + op1.age + ")");
    IO.println("op2=CPerson(" + op2.name + "," + op2.age + ")");

    // an explicit copy of the object
    CPerson op3 = new CPerson();
    op3.name = op1.name;
    op3.age = op1.age;
    op3.age = 50;
    IO.println("op1=CPerson(" + op1.name + "," + op1.age + ")");
    IO.println("op3=CPerson(" + op3.name + "," + op3.age + ")");
}

// CPerson class
class CPerson {
    String name = "";
    int age;
}
  • Lines 37–40: a class with two fields accessible from the package: [name], [age]. The non-private fields—which are generally discouraged—make the example easier to read here.

Results:

> java Classes14.java
age1=10, age2=10
age1=10, age2=30
op1=CPerson(paul,10)
op2=CPerson(paul,10)
op1=CPerson(nicole,30)
op2=CPerson(nicole,30)
op1=CPerson(nicole,30)
op3=CPerson(nicole,50)

The declaration [int age1 = 10;] (line 4) reserves a memory location that contains the integer 10: the value of [age1] is the integer itself. In the case of the class, the object ([name], [age]) is created explicitly using the operator [new] (line 13). The object is placed in a memory area managed by the garbage collector, the heap, and the value of [op1] is the address (the reference) of this object.

When [int age2 = age1;] is written in the program (line 5), the value of [age1]—the integer 10—is copied into [age2]: this is a value copy. Modifying [age2] does not modify [age1] (line 3 of the results). Now consider the instruction [CPerson op2 = op1;] (line 18). The value of [op1] is copied to [op2], but since this value is the object’s address, the object itself is not duplicated: [op1] and [op2] refer to the same object. If the object pointed to by [op2] is modified, the object pointed to by [op1] is also modified since they are the same (lines 6–7 of the results). To obtain a second object, you must create it and copy the fields from the first one into it (lines 28–30): modifying the copy does not modify the original (lines 8–9 of the results).

From these explanations, we can conclude that:

  • the value of a variable of a primitive type is the data itself;
  • the value of a reference-type variable is the address of the object it points to;
  • assignment and parameter passing always copy the value of the variable: the data itself for a primitive type, the reference for an object.

Each primitive type corresponds to a so-called “wrapper” class in the [java.lang] package: [Integer] for [int], [Double] for [double], [Boolean] for [boolean], and so on. The compiler automatically converts a primitive value to a wrapper object and vice versa (“autoboxing” and “unboxing”): we’ll need this with generics, which only accept reference types. A variable [Integer] can be equal to [null], but a variable [int] never can.

To represent a small composite piece of data (a point, a color, a date, an amount) that is treated as a value, Java uses immutable classes: their objects cannot be modified after they are created. Sharing a reference to an immutable object is safe: no one can modify it, and the object then behaves like a value. Two tools round out this system: the *[equals]* method, which compares two objects based on their content, and records, which declare an immutable class in a single line. This is the subject of the following two paragraphs.

docs.title: 4.5.2. Equality of Two Objects: equals and hashCode
docs.text:
As we have seen, the [==] operator applied to two references indicates whether they refer to the same object, and the [equals] method, inherited from [Object], does the same. For two distinct objects with the same content to be considered equal, a class must redefine the method [equals], and, necessarily along with it, the method [hashCode]. The program [Classes15.java] demonstrates this:

// equality of two objects: equals and hashCode
void main() {
    Person p1 = new Person("paul", 10);
    Person p2 = new Person("paul", 10);
    Person p3 = new Person("nicole", 30);
    // == compares the references, equals compares the values
    IO.println("p1 == p2 : " + (p1 == p2) + ", p1.equals(p2) : " + p1.equals(p2)
            + ", p1.equals(p3) : " + p1.equals(p3));
    // two equal objects have the same hash code
    IO.println("p1.hashCode() == p2.hashCode() : " + (p1.hashCode() == p2.hashCode()));
    // a set (Set) does not contain two equal objects
    Set<Person> persons = new HashSet<>();
    persons.add(p1);
    persons.add(p2);
    persons.add(p3);
    IO.println("size of the set: " + persons.size());
    IO.println("the set contains (paul,10): " + persons.contains(new Person("paul", 10)));
}

class Person {
    // fields
    private final String name;
    private final int age;

    // constructor
    public Person(String name, int age) {
        this.name = name;
        this.age = age;
    }

    // two persons are equal if they have the same name and age
    @Override
    public boolean equals(Object o) {
        // same object?
        if (this == o) {
            return true;
        }
        // is o a Person (and not null)?
        if (!(o instanceof Person other)) {
            return false;
        }
        // comparison of the fields
        return age == other.age && Objects.equals(name, other.name);
    }

    // hash code consistent with equals
    @Override
    public int hashCode() {
        return Objects.hash(name, age);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Person(" + name + "," + age + ")";
    }
}
  • lines 32–44: The method [equals] overrides that of the class [Object]. Its parameter is of type [Object]: a person can be compared to any object. The method follows a standard pattern:
    • lines 35–37: an object is equal to itself;
    • lines 39–41: the expression [o instanceof Person other] (Java 16) is true if [o] refers to an object of type [Person] (or a derived class), and false otherwise, in particular if [o] is equal to [null]. When it is true, the variable [other], of type [Person], refers to the object [o]: its fields can be used. This “type pattern” is explained in detail at the end of the chapter;
    • line 43: the fields are compared. The method [Objects.equals(a, b)] compares two objects with [equals] by handling the case where one of them is [null];
  • lines 47–50: The method [hashCode] returns an integer calculated from the same fields, in this case by the method [Objects.hash]. The rule is mandatory: two objects that are equal in the sense of [equals] must have the same hash code. The dictionaries and sets in JDK (next chapter) sort objects based on this code and would no longer function if the rule were not followed;
  • lines 12–17: A [HashSet] set never contains two equal objects: adding [p2], which is equal to [p1], has no effect, and the search for a new person ([paul, 10]) is successful.

Results:

> java Classes15.java
p1 == p2 : false, p1.equals(p2) : true, p1.equals(p3) : false
p1.hashCode() == p2.hashCode() : true
size of the set: 2
the set contains (paul,10): true

Typing [equals] and [hashCode] by hand is tedious and prone to errors; development environments can generate them. Records, on the other hand, provide them automatically.

docs.title: 4.5.3. Immutable Objects
docs.text:
The program [Classes16.java] demonstrates two ways to define immutable data:

// immutable objects: an immutable class and a record
void main() {
    Point a = new Point(1, 2);
    // a.x = 5;   // rejected: the x field is final
    Point b = a.move(3, 4);
    IO.println("a=" + a + ", b=" + b);

    // a record: constructor, accessors, toString, equals and hashCode are generated
    Color red = new Color(255, 0, 0);
    Color red2 = new Color(255, 0, 0);
    IO.println("red=" + red + ", r=" + red.r());
    IO.println("red.equals(red2) : " + red.equals(red2) + ", red == red2 : " + (red == red2));
    // a modified copy, created by hand-written methods
    Color pink = red.withG(128).withB(128);
    IO.println("red=" + red + ", pink=" + pink);
}

// an immutable class: final, private and final fields, no setter
final class Point {
    private final int x;
    private final int y;

    public Point(int x, int y) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }

    public int getX() {
        return x;
    }

    public int getY() {
        return y;
    }

    // we do not modify the point: we return a new one
    public Point move(int dx, int dy) {
        return new Point(x + dx, y + dy);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "(" + x + "," + y + ")";
    }
}

// a record: an immutable class declared in one line... or almost
record Color(int r, int g, int b) {
    // methods that return a modified copy of the record
    public Color withG(int g) {
        return new Color(r, g, b);
    }

    public Color withB(int b) {
        return new Color(r, g, b);
    }
}
  • lines 19–45: a manually written immutable class. It is final, so that no derived class can add mutable state to it; its fields are private and [final]; it has no modifiers. To “move” a point, the method [move] returns a new point (lines 37–39);
  • Line 48: a record (Java 16). The header [record Color(int r, int g, int b)] declares a final class with three private fields—[final], known as the record components—a three-parameter constructor, and three accessors: [r()], [g()], [b()], and methods [toString], [equals], and [hashCode], all of which use the components;
  • Lines 50–56: You can add methods to a record. Since a record is immutable, it cannot be modified: instead, a copy is created in which one component has been changed. These methods are called “withers” (from the English “with”); other languages provide an expression for this purpose, [with], which does not exist in Java 25;
  • line 11: An accessor for a component is named after the component, without the prefix [get];
  • line 12: two records of the same components are equal in the sense of [equals], even though they are distinct;
  • line 14: the “wither” methods are chained together.

Results:

> java Classes16.java
a=(1,2), b=(4,6)
red=Color[r=255, g=0, b=0], r=255
red.equals(red2) : true, red == red2 : false
red=Color[r=255, g=0, b=0], pink=Color[r=255, g=128, b=128]

The generated [toString] displays the record name and its components (line 3 of the results). Note here that a record is the most concise way to declare a small, immutable piece of data: this is the type we will use for the tax bracket tiers in this chapter’s example application. Records are discussed in detail later.

docs.title: 4.6.1. A First Example
docs.text:
An interface is a set of method declarations that forms a contract. A class that chooses to implement an interface commits to providing an implementation of all the abstract methods defined in the interface. The compiler verifies this implementation.

For example, here is the (simplified) definition of the [java.util.Iterator<E>] interface of JDK, which allows you to iterate over the elements of a collection: [public interface Iterator<E> { boolean hasNext(); E next(); }]. The methods of the interface are defined only by their signatures, followed by a semicolon: they have no code and are implicitly public and abstract. It is the classes that implement the interface that provide code for its methods. A class named [C] declares that it implements the interface using the keyword [implements]: [public class C implements Iterator<String>], and it must then define the two public methods [public boolean hasNext() { ... }] and [public String next() { ... }].

A common convention (though not universal—JDK does not follow it) is to start an interface name with the letter I. The following examples make up the [Statistics] folder. Consider the following interface, [IStats.java]:

public interface IStats {
    // average of a series of values
    double average();

    // standard deviation of the series
    double standardDeviation();
}

The [IStats] interface contains:

  • a method [average]: to calculate the mean of a series of values;
  • a method [standardDeviation]: to calculate the standard deviation.

Note that it is not specified anywhere which set of values is being referred to. It could be the average grades of a class, the monthly average sales of a particular product, the average temperature in a given location… This is the principle behind interfaces: we assume the existence of methods in the object but not that of specific data. The methods do not have the prefix [get]: they are calculations rather than field accesses, and this choice will allow a record to implement the interface.

A first class implementing the [IStats] interface could be a class used to store the grades of students in a class for a given subject. A student is characterized by the following [Student] record, [Student.java]:

// a student
public record Student(String firstName, String lastName) {
}

The student is identified by their first and last name. The record shown in the previous paragraph does this in a single line. A grade is represented by the following record, [Grade], which follows [Grade.java]:

// the grade of a student
public record Grade(Student student, double value) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[" + student.firstName() + "," + student.lastName() + "," + value + "]";
    }
}

The grade is defined by the student being graded and the grade itself. The record redefines the method [toString] generated by the compiler to display a grade in the form [firstName,lastName,value].

The grades of all students in a given subject are grouped in the following class [ArrayOfGrades]: [ArrayOfGrades.java]:

import java.util.Arrays;

public class ArrayOfGrades implements IStats {
    // fields
    private final String subject;
    private final Grade[] grades;
    private final double average;
    private final double standardDeviation;

    // constructor
    public ArrayOfGrades(String subject, Grade[] grades) {
        // storing the data
        this.subject = subject;
        this.grades = grades;
        // computing the average of the grades
        double sum = 0;
        for (Grade grade : grades) {
            sum += grade.value();
        }
        average = grades.length != 0 ? sum / grades.length : -1;
        // computing the standard deviation
        double squares = 0;
        for (Grade grade : grades) {
            squares += Math.pow(grade.value() - average, 2);
        }
        standardDeviation = grades.length != 0 ? Math.sqrt(squares / grades.length) : -1;
    }

    // getters
    public String getSubject() {
        return subject;
    }

    public Grade[] getGrades() {
        return grades;
    }

    // implementation of the methods of the IStats interface
    @Override
    public double average() {
        return average;
    }

    @Override
    public double standardDeviation() {
        return standardDeviation;
    }

    // toString
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "subject=" + subject + ", grades=" + Arrays.toString(grades);
    }
}
  • Line 3: The class [ArrayOfGrades] implements the interface [IStats]. It must therefore implement the methods [average] and [standardDeviation]. These are implemented on lines 39–47. The annotation [@Override] is also used for implementing an interface method;
  • lines 5–8: four fields [final]: the subject for which the object stores grades, the grade array, the average, and the standard deviation of the grades;
  • lines 11–27: the constructor. Here, we assume that the grades passed to the constructor will not change afterward. Therefore, we use the constructor to immediately calculate the mean and standard deviation of these grades and store them. A field such as [final], like [average], can be assigned a value in the constructor (line 20); it cannot be assigned a value afterward. The expressions [condition ? value1 : value2] set the mean and standard deviation of an empty array to -1. [Math.pow(x, 2)] calculates x², and [Math.sqrt] calculates the square root;
  • lines 50–53: the method [toString] uses the static method [Arrays.toString], which returns the elements of an array in square brackets, separated by commas, each converted to a string by its method [toString], in this case, the one for record [Grade].

In the previous class, grades were stored in an array. It was not possible to add a new grade after the [ArrayOfGrades] object was created. We now propose a second implementation of the [IStats] interface, called [ListOfGrades], where this time the notes are stored in a [List<Grade>] list, with the ability to add notes after the initial creation of the [ListOfGrades] object: [ListOfGrades.java]:

import java.util.List;

public class ListOfGrades implements IStats {
    // fields
    private final String subject;
    private final List<Grade> grades;
    // stored average and standard deviation (null: not yet computed)
    private Double average;
    private Double standardDeviation;

    // constructor
    public ListOfGrades(String subject, List<Grade> grades) {
        this.subject = subject;
        this.grades = grades;
    }

    // getters
    public String getSubject() {
        return subject;
    }

    public List<Grade> getGrades() {
        return grades;
    }

    // adding a grade
    public void add(Grade grade) {
        grades.add(grade);
        // the average and the standard deviation will have to be recomputed
        average = null;
        standardDeviation = null;
    }

    // average of the grades: computed on the first request
    @Override
    public double average() {
        if (average == null) {
            average = computeAverage();
        }
        return average;
    }

    // standard deviation of the grades: computed on the first request
    @Override
    public double standardDeviation() {
        if (standardDeviation == null) {
            standardDeviation = computeStandardDeviation();
        }
        return standardDeviation;
    }

    private double computeAverage() {
        if (grades.isEmpty()) {
            return -1;
        }
        double sum = 0;
        for (Grade grade : grades) {
            sum += grade.value();
        }
        return sum / grades.size();
    }

    private double computeStandardDeviation() {
        if (grades.isEmpty()) {
            return -1;
        }
        double m = average();
        double squares = 0;
        for (Grade grade : grades) {
            squares += Math.pow(grade.value() - m, 2);
        }
        return Math.sqrt(squares / grades.size());
    }

    // toString
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "subject=" + subject + ", grades=" + grades;
    }
}
  • line 3: the class [ListOfGrades] implements the interface [IStats];
  • line 6: Notes are now stored in a list rather than an array;
  • lines 27–32: You can now add a grade to those already stored. The mean and standard deviation are no longer calculated in the constructor but on demand, within the interface methods themselves: [average] (lines 35–41) and [standardDeviation] (lines 44–50). Once calculated, these values are stored so they are not recalculated with every request: they are said to be cached. Adding a score invalidates the cache;
  • lines 8–9: the cache. The type [Double] is the wrapper class for the primitive type [double]: unlike a [double] variable, a [Double] variable can have the value [null], which here means “not yet calculated.” Uninitialized fields are set to [null] when the object is constructed;
  • lines 38 and 40: the compiler automatically converts the [double] returned by [computeAverage] into the object [Double] (“autoboxing”), and the object [Double] into [double] for the method’s return value (“unboxing”).

A test program might look like the following [Main.java]:

void main() {
    // a few students and their English grades
    Student[] students = {
        new Student("Paul", "Martin"), new Student("Maxime", "Germain"), new Student("Berthine", "Samin")
    };
    Grade[] grades = { new Grade(students[0], 14), new Grade(students[1], 16), new Grade(students[2], 18) };
    // which are stored in an ArrayOfGrades object
    ArrayOfGrades english = new ArrayOfGrades("english", grades);
    // display of average and standard deviation
    displayStats(english);
    // the same grades in a ListOfGrades object
    ListOfGrades french = new ListOfGrades("french", new ArrayList<>(List.of(grades)));
