    displayStats(french);
    // we add a grade
    french.add(new Grade(new Student("Jérôme", "Jaric"), 10));
    displayStats(french);
    // a variable can have an interface as its type
    IStats stats = english;
    IO.println("English average: " + stats.average());
    stats = french;
    IO.println("French average: " + stats.average());
}

// display of the average and standard deviation of an object implementing IStats
void displayStats(IStats values) {
    IO.println(values + ", Average=" + values.average() + ", Standard deviation=" + values.standardDeviation());
}
  • lines 3–5: creation of an array of students;
  • line 6: creation of an array of grades;
  • line 8: a [ArrayOfGrades] object whose mean and standard deviation are displayed on line 10;
  • line 12: an object [ListOfGrades], whose mean and standard deviation are displayed on line 13. [List.of(grades)] returns a read-only list of the array’s elements; the constructor of the [ArrayList] class turns it into a modifiable list to which notes can be added;
  • line 15: a new note is added, followed by a refresh of the display;
  • Lines 25–27: The method [displayStats] takes a *[IStats] type as a parameter, which is an interface type. This means that the actual parameter can be any object that implements the *[IStats] interface. When using a data object of an interface type, only the methods of the interface that are implemented by the data object are used. The rest are ignored. This property is similar to the polymorphism discussed for classes. If a set of classes Ci that are not related to one another through inheritance (and therefore cannot use inheritance-based polymorphism) share a set of methods with the same signature, it may be useful to group these methods into an interface I that all the relevant classes would implement. Instances of these classes Ci can then be used as actual parameters for methods that accept a formal parameter of type I—that is, methods that use only the methods of the Ci objects defined in the interface I, and not the specific fields and methods of the various Ci classes;
  • lines 18–21: A variable can be of the type of an interface. It can then refer to any object of a class that implements the interface. The compiler allows access only to the methods of the interface (and to those of the class [Object], such as [toString]).

Results:

> java Main.java
subject=english, grades=[[Paul,Martin,14.0], [Maxime,Germain,16.0], [Berthine,Samin,18.0]], Average=16.0, Standard deviation=1.632993161855452
subject=french, grades=[[Paul,Martin,14.0], [Maxime,Germain,16.0], [Berthine,Samin,18.0]], Average=16.0, Standard deviation=1.632993161855452
subject=french, grades=[[Paul,Martin,14.0], [Maxime,Germain,16.0], [Berthine,Samin,18.0], [Jérôme,Jaric,10.0]], Average=14.5, Standard deviation=2.958039891549808
English average: 16.0
French average: 14.5

Concatenating a number ([double]) with a string uses the [Double.toString] method, which always writes the number with a decimal point and at least one decimal place (16.0), regardless of the workstation’s language settings. For a French-style display, use [String.format("%.2f", x)], as in the following example.

Finally, note that interfaces can be implemented multiple times; that is, one can write [public class DerivedClass extends BaseClass implements I1, I2, ..., In], where the Ij are interfaces: a class inherits from only one class but can implement as many interfaces as it wishes. An interface can itself extend one or more other interfaces: [interface I3 extends I1, I2].

docs.title: 4.6.2. Default, static, and private interface methods
docs.text:
Since Java 8, an interface can provide a default implementation for some of its methods, declared with the keyword [default]. A class that implements the interface can then use this implementation or provide its own. This makes it possible, in particular, to add a method to an already published interface without requiring all classes that implement it to be modified: this is how the collections in the JDK have been expanded over successive versions. An interface can also contain static methods (Java 8) and private methods (Java 9). The program [Classes17.java] provides an example:

// default (Java 8), static (Java 8) and private (Java 9) interface methods
void main() {
    IShape[] shapes = { new Square(2), new Circle(1), IShape.unitSquare() };
    for (IShape shape : shapes) {
        IO.println(shape.description());
    }
    // the default method is inherited by the Square class
    Square square = new Square(3);
    IO.println(square.description());
}

interface IShape {
    // abstract method: to be implemented
    double area();

    // method with a default implementation
    default String description() {
        return getClass().getSimpleName() + " with area " + format(area());
    }

    // static method: it is called with the name of the interface
    static IShape unitSquare() {
        return new Square(1);
    }

    // private method: usable only by the methods of the interface
    private String format(double value) {
        return String.format("%.2f", value);
    }
}

// Square uses the default implementation of description
// (static class because the interface creates squares: see Classes10)
static class Square implements IShape {
    private final double side;

    public Square(double side) {
        this.side = side;
    }

    @Override
    public double area() {
        return side * side;
    }
}

// Circle provides its own implementation of description
class Circle implements IShape {
    private final double radius;

    public Circle(double radius) {
        this.radius = radius;
    }

    @Override
    public double area() {
        return Math.PI * radius * radius;
    }

    @Override
    public String description() {
        return String.format("Circle with radius %s and area %.2f", radius, area());
    }
}
  • lines 12–30: the [IShape] interface:
    • line 14: an abstract method [area], to be implemented;
    • lines 17–19: a method [description] with a default implementation. This method can use the other methods of the interface ([area], [format]) and those of [Object] ([getClass]);
    • lines 22–24: a static method, which is called using the interface name: [IShape.unitSquare()] (line 3). This is a static factory method;
    • lines 27–29: a private method, accessible only to the methods of the interface. [String.format("%.2f", value)] formats the number to two decimal places, following the conventions of the system’s locale—in this case, the French decimal comma;
  • lines 34–45: the class [Square] implements only [area]; it uses the method [description] by default. It is declared as [static] because the static method [unitSquare] of the interface creates squares (see [Classes10.java]);
  • lines 48–64: The class [Circle] provides its own method, [description]. The format [%s] inserts the radius converted to a string by [Double.toString] (“1.0”), and the format [%.2f] inserts the area with two decimal places;
  • Line 9: The default method is inherited by the [Square] class just like any other method: it can be called on a variable of type [Square].

Results:

> java Classes17.java
Square with area 4,00
Circle with radius 1.0 and area 3,14
Square with area 1,00
Square with area 9,00

A class can implement two interfaces, each of which provides a default method with the same signature: the compiler then requires the class to redefine the method, even if it means calling one of the two versions via [I1.super.method()]. Unlike an abstract class, an interface has no state: it cannot declare instance fields, only constants ([static final], implicitly).

docs.title: 4.7. Abstract classes
docs.text:
An abstract class is a class that cannot be instantiated. You must create derived classes, which can be instantiated. You can use abstract classes to refactor the code of a class hierarchy. Let's examine the following example, which forms the folder [Users] [User.java]:

public abstract class User {
    // fields
    private final String login;
    private final String password;
    private final String role;

    // constructor
    @SuppressWarnings("this-escape")
    protected User(String login, String password) throws UnknownUserException {
        // we store the information
        this.login = login;
        this.password = password;
        // we identify the user
        String role = identify();
        // identified?
        if (role == null) {
            throw new UnknownUserException("[" + login + "," + password + "]");
        }
        this.role = role;
    }

    // toString
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "User[" + login + "," + password + "," + role + "]";
    }

    // identification: returns the role of the user or null if they are not recognized
    protected abstract String identify();
}
  • line 1: the class is declared abstract using the keyword [abstract];
  • Lines 9–20: the constructor for the class [User]. This class stores information about a web application’s user. The application has various types of users authenticated by a username and password (lines 3–4). These two pieces of information are verified against a directory (LDAP) for some users, against a database for others, and so on. The constructor is [protected]: it is intended for the constructors of derived classes;
  • lines 11–12: the authentication information is stored;
  • line 14: they are verified by a method [identify]. Because the identification method is not known at this level, it is declared abstract (line 29) with the keyword [abstract]. An abstract method has no body: derived classes will provide one. A class that has an abstract method must itself be declared abstract. The method [identify] returns a string specifying the user’s role (basically, what they are authorized to do), or [null] if the user is not recognized;
  • lines 16–18: if the user is not recognized, an exception is thrown. The [UnknownUserException] exception is a checked exception (see below): the constructor must declare it using the [throws UnknownUserException] clause (line 9);
  • lines 23–26: the method [toString], which identifies an instance of the class.

Here, we assume that the developer wants to control the creation of instances of the class [User] and its derived classes, perhaps because they want to ensure that an exception of a certain type is thrown if the user is not recognized. Derived classes can rely on this constructor. To do so, they must provide the [identify] method. Note that the constructor here calls a method overridden by the derived classes even though those classes have not yet executed their own constructors: the [identify] method must therefore not use any fields of the derived class, as they have not yet been initialized. This is a practice that should be used with caution, and the compiler flags it when compiling with the [-Xlint:all] option, which enables all warnings (here without the annotation on line 8, hence the line number 13 in the message):

> javac -Xlint:all -d classes *.java
User.java:13: warning: [this-escape] possible 'this' escape before subclass is fully initialized
        String role = identify();
                              ^
1 warning

The warning [this-escape] (Java 21) indicates that the object being constructed ([this]) “escapes” the constructor before being fully initialized. In this case, this is intentional and harmless, since the [identify] methods of the derived classes do not use any fields. After verifying this, the warning is suppressed—for this constructor only—using the annotation [@SuppressWarnings("this-escape")] (line 8). The source code launcher ([java Main.java]) does not enable these warnings: it is a good idea to compile your programs regularly with [javac -Xlint:all], which is what we have done for all the programs in this course.

The [UnknownUserException] class is as follows:

public class UnknownUserException extends Exception {
    // version number of the class (see the explanations)
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    public UnknownUserException(String message) {
        super(message);
    }
}
  • Line 1: It derives from the class [Exception]. It is therefore a checked exception: the compiler verifies that any method that can throw it declares it using a [throws] clause, and that any code that calls such a method either catches it or declares it in turn. An exception derived from [RuntimeException], such as [IllegalArgumentException], is not a checked exception;
  • line 3: Exceptions are “serializable” objects (convertible to a sequence of bytes); the compiler, with the [-Xlint:all] option, requires that a serializable class declare a version number [serialVersionUID]. We simply use the value 1;
  • Lines 5–7: It has only a single constructor that takes an error message as a parameter. This is passed to the parent class, which has the same constructor.

We now derive the child class [Administrator] from the class [User]:

public class Administrator extends User {
    // constructor
    public Administrator(String login, String password) throws UnknownUserException {
        super(login, password);
    }

    // identification
    @Override
    protected String identify() {
        // LDAP identification
        // ...
        return "admin";
    }
}
  • lines 3–5: The constructor simply passes the parameters it receives to its parent class. It also declares the exception that the parent constructor may throw;
  • lines 8–13: the [identify] method of the [Administrator] class. We assume that an administrator is identified by a directory LDAP. This method implements the abstract method [identify] of its parent class. It retains the access level [protected] of the method it overrides (an overridden method can expand access, but not restrict it).

The classes [Observer] and [Unknown] also derive from the class [User]. They differ from class [Administrator] only in their method [identify]. The method in class [Observer] assumes that an observer is identified by a database and returns the “observer” role:

    // identification
    @Override
    protected String identify() {
        // identification through a database
        // ...
        return "observer";
    }

The method for class [Unknown] returns the reference [null] to indicate that the user was not recognized:

    // identification
    @Override
    protected String identify() {
        // user not known
        // ...
        return null;
    }

Ultimately, the objects [Administrator], [Observer], and [Unknown] are initialized by the same constructor—that of the parent class [User]. This constructor uses the [identify] method provided by these classes. A test program for [Main.java] might look like this:

void main() {
    try {
        IO.println(new Observer("observer", "pwd1"));
        IO.println(new Administrator("admin", "pwd2"));
        IO.println(new Unknown("xx", "yy"));
    } catch (UnknownUserException e) {
        IO.println("Unknown user: " + e.getMessage());
    }
    // User u = new User("x", "y");   // rejected: the User class is abstract
}

Note that in lines 3 and 4, the method [User.toString()] is used by the method *[println]. On line 5, the constructor throws a [UnknownUserException] exception, which is caught on line 6: the object is not created, and nothing is displayed by [println]. The three object creations are placed within a [try] block, because the compiler requires that the checked exception be caught. Line 9, if uncommented, is rejected by the compiler ([User is abstract; cannot be instantiated]*): you cannot create an object of an abstract class.

Results:

> java Main.java
User[observer,pwd1,observer]
User[admin,pwd2,admin]
Unknown user: [xx,yy]

An abstract class is similar to an interface: both declare methods that other classes must implement. However, an abstract class can have fields, constructors, and code common to its derived classes; conversely, a class can derive from only one abstract class, whereas it can implement multiple interfaces. The two are often combined: an interface defines the contract, and an abstract class that implements it factors out the code common to multiple implementations. This is what the example application in this chapter will do.

docs.title: 4.8.1. Generic Classes and Methods
docs.text:
Suppose we want to write a class [IntPair] that stores two integers and can swap them: two fields, [int first] and [int second], and a method, [swap()], that swaps their values using a temporary variable, [int temp]. If we then wanted a pair of strings, followed by a pair of people, we would write two more classes, [StringPair] and [PersonPair], identical to the previous one except for the type: [String] or [Person] instead of [int].

Generic classes, interfaces, and methods address the need for code that differs only in the type of certain data. They were introduced with Java 5 (2004): prior to that, the type [Object] was used, which accepted anything, at the cost of explicit type conversions and errors detected only at runtime. Note that Java does not support passing parameters by reference: a method cannot swap the values of two variables from the caller, but it can swap two elements of an object, a pair, or an array.

The program [Classes18.java] features a generic class, a generic method, and a second generic class:

// generic classes and methods
void main() {
    // --- a generic class Pair<T>
    // Integer
    Pair<Integer> pi = new Pair<>(1, 2);
    pi.swap();
    IO.println("pi=" + pi);
    // String
    Pair<String> ps = new Pair<>("s1", "s2");
    ps.swap();
    IO.println("ps=" + ps);
    // Person
    Person p1 = new Person("jean", "clu", 20), p2 = new Person("pauline", "dard", 55);
    Pair<Person> pp = new Pair<>(p1, p2);
    pp.swap();
    IO.println("pp=" + pp);
    // the first element is of type Person: no conversion
    Person first = pp.getFirst();
    IO.println("first element: " + first);

    // --- a generic method Generic2.swap<T>
    Integer[] integers = { 1, 2, 3 };
    Generic2.<Integer>swap(integers, 0, 2);
    IO.println("integers=" + Arrays.toString(integers));
    // the compiler deduces T from the type of the actual parameters
    Person[] persons = { p1, p2 };
    Generic2.swap(persons, 0, 1);
    IO.println("persons=" + Arrays.toString(persons));

    // --- a generic class with a state: a stack of elements of type T
    MyStack<Person> stack = new MyStack<>();
    stack.push(p1);
    stack.push(p2);
    IO.println("The stack contains " + stack.size() + " persons");
    Person top = stack.pop();
    IO.println("Popped person: " + top + ", " + stack.size() + " left");
    // stack.push("x");   // rejected: the stack only accepts Person objects
}

// a generic class: a pair of two elements of type T
class Pair<T> {
    private T first;
    private T second;

    public Pair(T first, T second) {
        this.first = first;
        this.second = second;
    }

    public T getFirst() {
        return first;
    }

    public T getSecond() {
        return second;
    }

    // the two elements are swapped
    public void swap() {
        T temp = first;
        first = second;
        second = temp;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "(" + first + "," + second + ")";
    }
}

// a non-generic class with a generic method
class Generic2 {
    // swaps elements no. i and j of an array of elements of type T
    public static <T> void swap(T[] array, int i, int j) {
        T temp = array[i];
        array[i] = array[j];
        array[j] = temp;
    }
}

// a stack of elements of type T
class MyStack<T> {
    // the elements of the stack
    private final List<T> elements = new ArrayList<>();

    // number of elements
    public int size() {
        return elements.size();
    }

    // adding an element at the top of the stack
    public void push(T element) {
        elements.add(element);
    }

    // removing the element at the top of the stack
    public T pop() {
        if (elements.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("empty stack");
        }
        return elements.removeLast();
    }
}

// a person
record Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]";
    }
}
  • lines 41–69: The class [Pair] is parameterized by a type denoted as *[T], enclosed in angle brackets after the class name. You can name it whatever you like; by convention, it is an uppercase letter ([T] for type, [E] for element, [K] and [V] for key and value). This type, [T], is then used in the class just like any other type: for the two fields, the constructor parameters, the results of the accessors, and the temporary variable [temp]* (line 60). The class [Pair] is said to be a generic class;
  • Line 5: When using a generic class parameterized by the types T1, T2, …, these types must be specified. Here, [Pair<Integer>] is a pair of [Integer] objects. A generic parameter can only be a reference type: we write [Pair<Integer>], not [Pair<int>]. The integers 1 and 2 are automatically converted to [Integer] objects (“autoboxing”). On the right, the “diamond” operator [new Pair<>(...)] allows the compiler to infer the type [Integer] from that of the variable. Lines 9 and 14: the same applies to the types [String] and [Person];
  • Line 18: The method [getFirst] of a [Pair<Person>] returns an object of type [Person], without conversion;
  • lines 72–79: the class [Generic2] is not generic, but its static method [swap] is: the parameter of type [<T>] is declared before the return type (line 74). The method swaps elements i and j of an array of elements of type [T];
  • line 23: the method [swap] is called, specifying the type *[T] between ***[<>]. In fact, the compiler is able to infer [T] from the type of the actual parameters. Therefore, the notation in line 27 is valid, and this is the one used in practice;
  • lines 82–103: a generic class with a state: a stack of elements of type [T]. Elements are pushed onto the top of the stack and popped from the top. The elements are stored in a generic list of type [List<T>] (line 84), which is itself parameterized by the [T] type of the stack. The method [removeLast] (Java 21) retrieves and returns the last element of the list. An empty stack throws a [IllegalStateException] exception, the exception defined by Java for an operation requested from an object that is not in the expected state;
  • line 31: a stack of people. The compiler guarantees that it will contain only people: the statement on line 37 would be rejected. The method [pop] returns an object of type [Person], without conversion;
  • lines 106–111: The person is a record for which the method [toString] has been redefined.

Results:

> java Classes18.java
pi=(2,1)
ps=(s2,s1)
pp=([pauline, dard, 55],[jean, clu, 20])
first element: [pauline, dard, 55]
integers=[3, 2, 1]
persons=[[pauline, dard, 55], [jean, clu, 20]]
The stack contains 2 persons
Popped person: [pauline, dard, 55], 1 left

docs.title: 4.8.2. Generic parameter bounds
docs.text:
In the [Pair<T>] class, the compiler knows nothing about the [T] type: it allows only the methods of the [Object] class to be called on objects of type [T]. To be able to use other methods, we constrain the generic parameter with the keyword [extends]:

ConstraintMeaning[<T extends BaseClass>]T must be the specified class or a derived class[<T extends Interface>]T must implement the specified interface (written as [extends], not [implements])[<T extends BaseClass & I1 & I2>]Multiple parameters: at most one class, listed first, followed by interfaces[<T extends Comparable<T>>]A bound that uses T itself: T must be comparable to T

There is no constraint requiring that T be a reference type (it always is) or that it have a parameterless constructor: you cannot write [new T()] in a generic class (see type erasure below). The program [Classes19.java] uses a constraint:

// the bounds of generic parameters
void main() {
    // --- T is always an object type: int is replaced by Integer
    Pair<Integer> pi = new Pair<>(1, 2);
    // Pair<int> pe = new Pair<>(1, 2);   // error: int is a primitive type
    IO.println("pi=" + pi);

    // --- the bound T extends IValue
    // ordering pairs of objects of type RandomValue
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
        Pair<RandomValue> pair = new Pair<>(new RandomValue(), new RandomValue());
        IO.print("Before --> " + pair);
        Generic4.order(pair);
        IO.println("   After --> " + pair);
    }
    // ordering a pair of objects of type StringValue
    Pair<StringValue> strings = new Pair<>(new StringValue("xxxxxxxxxxxxxx"), new StringValue("xx"));
    IO.println("Before --> " + strings);
    Generic4.order(strings);
    IO.println("After --> " + strings);
    // Generic4.order(pi);   // error: Integer does not implement IValue
}

// a pair of two elements of type T
class Pair<T> {
    private T first;
    private T second;

    public Pair(T first, T second) {
        this.first = first;
        this.second = second;
    }

    public T getFirst() {
        return first;
    }

    public T getSecond() {
        return second;
    }

    public void swap() {
        T temp = first;
        first = second;
        second = temp;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "(" + first + "," + second + ")";
    }
}

// the type T must implement IValue
class Generic4 {
    public static <T extends IValue> void order(Pair<T> pair) {
        // if the 1st element is greater than the 2nd, the elements are swapped
        if (pair.getFirst().value() > pair.getSecond().value()) {
            pair.swap();
        }
    }
}

// an object having an integer value
interface IValue {
    int value();
}

// an object having a random value
class RandomValue implements IValue {
    // random number generator shared by all instances
    // (initialized with a fixed seed so that the results are reproducible)
    private static final Random generator = new Random(2026);
    // value of the object
    private final int value = generator.nextInt(100);

    @Override
    public int value() {
        return value;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return String.valueOf(value);
    }
}

// an object whose value is the length of a string
class StringValue implements IValue {
    private final String s;

    public StringValue(String s) {
        this.s = s;
    }

    @Override
    public int value() {
        return s.length();
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return s;
    }
}
  • line 5: if you uncomment this line, the compiler reports an error because the type *[int]* is a primitive type;
  • Lines 55–62: The generic method [order] requires that the type [T] implement the interface [IValue] (lines 65–67). This interface has a method named [value], used on line 58, which returns the value of the object of type [T]. Without the bound, the compiler would reject the call to [pair.getFirst().value()]: any [T] type does not have a [value] method. The two elements of the pair are swapped only if the value of the first is greater than that of the second: the method [order] sorts the two elements in ascending order by value;
  • lines 70–86: The class [RandomValue] implements the interface [IValue]. The value of an instance is a random number between 0 and 99 (line 75), provided by a random number generator in the [Random] class shared by all instances (line 73). This generator is initialized with a fixed “seed”: it therefore always produces the same sequence of numbers, making the results reproducible. If reproducibility is not required, the generator created by [new Random()] is used; for security purposes, the class [SecureRandom] is used instead;
  • lines 89–105: The class [StringValue] also implements the interface [IValue]: the value of an instance is the length of the character string passed to the constructor;
  • lines 10–15: Pairs of objects of type [RandomValue] are ordered;
  • lines 17–20: a pair of objects of type [StringValue] is ordered;
  • line 21: if this line is uncommented, the compiler reports that the type [Integer] does not satisfy the bound.

Results:

> java Classes19.java
pi=(1,2)
Before --> (99,50)   After --> (50,99)
Before --> (97,30)   After --> (30,97)
Before --> (49,38)   After --> (38,49)
Before --> (73,36)   After --> (36,73)
Before --> (34,78)   After --> (34,78)
Before --> (xxxxxxxxxxxxxx,xx)
After --> (xx,xxxxxxxxxxxxxx)

Here are the errors obtained when running the program after lines 5 and 21 have been uncommented:

> java Classes19.java
Classes19.java:5: error: unexpected type
    Pair<int> pe = new Pair<>(1, 2);   // error: int is a primitive type
         ^
  required: reference
  found:    int
Classes19.java:21: error: method order in class Classes19.Generic4 cannot be applied to given types;
    Generic4.order(pi);   // error: Integer does not implement IValue
            ^
  required: Classes19.Pair<T>
  found:    Classes19.Pair<Integer>
  reason: inference variable T has incompatible bounds
    equality constraints: Integer
    upper bounds: IValue
  where T is a type-variable:
    T extends IValue declared in method <T>order(Classes19.Pair<T>)
2 errors
error: compilation failed

The second message is typical of errors involving generics: the compiler attempted to infer the type [T]; the pair constraint requires [T] = [Integer] (“equality constraints”), the bound constraint requires that [T] implements [IValue] (“upper bounds”); the two constraints are incompatible.

docs.title: 4.8.3. Generic Interfaces: Comparable<T> and Comparator<T>
docs.text:
To illustrate the concept of a generic interface, we will sort an array of people according to different criteria. The method that allows us to sort an array is the static method [sort] of the class [java.util.Arrays]. It is overloaded; we will use two variants:

  • [Arrays.sort(Object[] array)] sorts the array according to the natural order of its elements: these elements must implement the [Comparable<T>] interface, whose sole method, [int compareTo(T other)], compares the current object to the [other] object;
  • [Arrays.sort(T[] array, Comparator<? super T> comparator)] sorts the array according to the order defined by a comparator object, which implements the [Comparator<T>] interface, whose [int compare(T x, T y)] method compares two objects (the type [? super T] is explained in the following paragraph).

The methods [compareTo] and [compare] follow the same rule: they return a positive number if x > y, 0 if x == y, and a negative number if x < y. It is up to the developer to define the meaning of the operators <, ==, and >. For example, if [p1] and [p2] are two [Person] objects, we can say that p1 > p2 if the name of [p1] comes after the name of [p2] in alphabetical order. This will result in an ascending sort based on the people’s names. If we want to sort by age, we’ll say that p1 > p2 if the age of [p1] is greater than the age of [p2]. To sort in descending order, simply reverse the signs of the results.

We know enough to sort a table of people. The program [Classes20.java] is as follows:

// the generic interfaces Comparable<T> and Comparator<T>: sorting an array of persons
void main() {
    Person[] persons = {
        new Person("claude", "pollon", 25),
        new Person("valentine", "germain", 35),
        new Person("paul", "germain", 32),
    };
    // display
    display("Array to sort", persons);
    // sort according to the natural order of persons (Comparable): the age
    Arrays.sort(persons);
    display("Array after sorting by age", persons);
    // sort according to last and first names (Comparator)
    Arrays.sort(persons, new CompareNames());
    display("Array after sorting by last and first names", persons);
    // sort by descending age, with an anonymous class
    Arrays.sort(persons, new Comparator<Person>() {
        @Override
        public int compare(Person p1, Person p2) {
            return Integer.compare(p2.getAge(), p1.getAge());
        }
    });
    display("Array after sorting by descending age", persons);
}

// display of an array of persons
void display(String text, Person[] persons) {
    IO.println(text + "-".repeat(50 - text.length()));
    for (Person p : persons) {
        IO.println(p);
    }
}

// a person, comparable to another person
class Person implements Comparable<Person> {
    private final String firstName;
    private final String lastName;
    private final int age;

    public Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public String getFirstName() {
        return firstName;
    }

    public String getLastName() {
        return lastName;
    }

    public int getAge() {
        return age;
    }

    // the natural order of persons: the order of ages
    @Override
    public int compareTo(Person other) {
        return Integer.compare(age, other.age);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]";
    }
}

// comparison of the last and first names of two persons
class CompareNames implements Comparator<Person> {
    // comparison of strings according to the rules of the French language
    private final Collator collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRENCH);

    @Override
    public int compare(Person p1, Person p2) {
        // we compare the last names
        int i = collator.compare(p1.getLastName(), p2.getLastName());
        if (i != 0) {
            return i;
        }
        // equal last names: we compare the first names
        return collator.compare(p1.getFirstName(), p2.getFirstName());
    }
}
  • lines 3–7: the array of people;
  • lines 35–68: the class [Person] implements the generic interface [Comparable<Person>]: its objects are comparable to other people. Its method [compareTo] (lines 59–62) defines the natural order of people, in this case by age. The static method [Integer.compare(a, b)] returns a negative, zero, or positive number depending on whether [a] is less than, equal to, or greater than [b]: this is exactly what the method [compareTo] expects;
  • line 11: sorting in natural order;
  • line 14: sorts the array of people by last name and first name. The second parameter of the [sort] method is an instance of the [CompareNames] class, which implements the generic interface [Comparator<Person>];
  • lines 71–85: the class [CompareNames]. Its method [compare] implements the method [int compare(T x, T y)] of the interface [Comparator<T>], where [T] = [Person]. Strings are not compared using their [compareTo] method, which follows the order of character codes (uppercase letters before lowercase, accented letters after “z”), but rather by a [Collator] object (line 73) that applies the sorting rules for the French language;
  • lines 17–22: sorting by age in descending order. The comparator this time is an instance of an anonymous class: the expression [new Comparator<Person>() { ... }] declares an unnamed class that implements the [Comparator<Person>] interface and immediately creates an instance of that class. The body of the class (lines 18–21) provides the method [compare]. An anonymous class avoids having to declare a class that is used only once;
  • line 28: the [repeat] method (Java 11) pads a string: the title line is padded with dashes up to 50 characters.

Results:

> java Classes20.java
Array to sort-------------------------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[paul, germain, 32]
Array after sorting by age------------------------
[claude, pollon, 25]
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]
Array after sorting by last and first names-------
[paul, germain, 32]
[valentine, germain, 35]
[claude, pollon, 25]
Array after sorting by descending age-------------
[valentine, germain, 35]
[paul, germain, 32]
[claude, pollon, 25]

We have now encountered three types of classes declared inside another: static nested classes ([static class]), inner classes (without [static], which are associated with an object of the enclosing class), and anonymous classes. In Chapter 7, we’ll see that for an interface with only one abstract method, such as [Comparator], we can use an even shorter alternative than an anonymous class: a lambda, [Arrays.sort(persons, (p1, p2) -> Integer.compare(p2.getAge(), p1.getAge()));], or a method reference, [Arrays.sort(persons, Comparator.comparing(Person::getLastName));].

docs.title: 4.8.4. Wildcards and Type Erasure
docs.text:
A [List<Integer>] is not a [List<Number>], even though [Integer] derives from [Number]: if it were, we could add a [Double] to a list of integers via a variable of type [List<Number>]. A method that accepts a [List<Number>] therefore rejects a [List<Integer>]. To write methods that accept lists of elements of related types, Java uses wildcards:

TypeMeaningUsage[List<? extends Number>]a list of elements of an unknown type derived from [Number]You can read [Number] from it, but you cannot add elements to it[List<? super Integer>]A list of items of an unknown type from which [Integer] is derived ([Integer], [Number], [Object])[Integer] can be added to this list[List<?>]a list of items of an unknown typeYou can read [Object]

The program [Classes21.java] illustrates wildcards and a special feature of Java generics: type erasure:

// wildcards, bounds and type erasure
void main() {
    List<Integer> integers = List.of(1, 2, 3);
    List<Double> reals = List.of(1.5, 2.25);
    // ? extends Number: a list of elements of a type derived from Number
    IO.println("Sum of integers: " + sum(integers));
    IO.println("Sum of reals: " + sum(reals));
    // ? super Integer: a list that can receive Integers
    List<Number> numbers = new ArrayList<>();
    addIntegers(numbers, 3);
    numbers.add(2.5);
    IO.println("numbers=" + numbers + ", sum=" + sum(numbers));
    // a recursive bound: T must be comparable to itself
    IO.println("max : " + max(List.of("paul", "jean", "valentine")) + ", " + max(integers));
    // type erasure: at runtime, a list is a list
    List<String> l1 = new ArrayList<>();
    List<Integer> l2 = new ArrayList<>();
    IO.println("same class: " + (l1.getClass() == l2.getClass()) + " (" + l1.getClass().getName() + ")");
}

// sum of the elements of a list of numbers
double sum(List<? extends Number> values) {
    double sum = 0;
    for (Number value : values) {
        sum += value.doubleValue();
    }
    // values.add(1);   // rejected: the exact type of the elements is unknown
    return sum;
}

// adding the integers 1, 2, ..., n to a list able to receive Integers
void addIntegers(List<? super Integer> list, int n) {
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        list.add(i);
    }
}

// the largest element of a non-empty list
<T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(List<T> elements) {
    T max = elements.getFirst();
    for (T element : elements) {
        if (element.compareTo(max) > 0) {
            max = element;
        }
    }
    return max;
}
  • Lines 22–29: The [sum] method accepts a list of elements of any type derived from [Number]: [Integer], [Double], [BigDecimal]… It treats the elements as [Number] and uses their [doubleValue] method. Java does not support generic arithmetic: you cannot write [a + b] for two objects of type [T], hence the need to use [double]. Adding an element to the list (line 27) is rejected: the compiler does not know whether it is a list of [Integer] or [Double];
  • lines 6–7: the same method concatenates a list of [Integer] with a list of [Double]. [List.of(...)] creates a read-only list;
  • lines 32–36: the [addIntegers] method accepts any list capable of holding [Integer] entries, in this case a [List<Number>] (line 10). We follow the rule “producer: [extends], consumer: [super]”: a list whose elements are read is written using [extends], and a list that is filled is written using [super];
  • Lines 39–47: The generic method *[max] returns the largest element in a list. The [T extends Comparable<? super T>] bound requires that the elements be comparable to one another; it applies to strings as well as integers (line 14). The [getFirst]* method (Java 21) returns the first element of the list;
  • lines 16–18: At runtime, a ***[List<String>] and a ***[List<Integer>] are two objects of the same class, *[ArrayList]*. The compiler checks the generic types and then erases them: the compiled code only recognizes [ArrayList] and [Object], and conversions are inserted where necessary. This “type erasure,” adopted in 2004 to ensure that generic code remains compatible with existing code, explains several limitations: you cannot write [new T()] or [new T[10]], nor can you test [o instanceof List<String>], nor can you use a primitive type as a generic parameter.

Results:

> java Classes21.java
Sum of integers: 6.0
Sum of reals: 3.75
numbers=[1, 2, 3, 2.5], sum=8.5
max : valentine, 3
same class: true (java.util.ArrayList)

Unlike other languages such as C#, where interfaces can declare abstract static members to implement generic computations, Java does not allow requiring a type like [T] to have a static method: static methods of an interface are called using the interface’s name and are not inherited by the classes that implement it.

docs.title: 4.9. Packages
docs.text:
To write a line on the screen, we use the [IO.println(...)] statement. If we look at the definition of the [IO] class in the JDK documentation, we find that it is part of the [java.lang] package. This means that its full name is [java.lang.IO] and that we could write [java.lang.IO.println(...)]. The classes in the [java.lang] package ([String], [Object], [Math], [Integer]…) are always referred to by their simple names. For the others, a [import] clause is used, placed at the beginning of the file:

  • [import java.util.List;] imports the class [List] from the package [java.util];
  • [import java.util.*;] imports all public classes from the [java.util] package on demand;
  • [import module java.base;] (Java 25) imports all public classes from the packages exported by the [java.base] module (see below). This is what a compact file does implicitly;
  • [import static java.lang.Math.sqrt;] imports a static member of a class, which can then be used without specifying the class name: [sqrt(2)].

When the compiler encounters a class’s short name, it looks for it in the current package and among the imported classes. A [import] clause adds nothing to the program: it merely avoids having to write out the full names.

When you create a class, you place it in a package. The purpose of packages is to avoid name conflicts between classes, for example, when they are distributed. Consider two companies, E1 and E2, distributing classes packaged in the archives [e1.jar] and [e2.jar], respectively. Suppose a customer C purchases these two sets of classes, in which both companies have defined a class named [Person]. If company E1 creates its classes in a package named [e1] and company E2 creates its classes in a package named [e2], the two classes [Person] will then be named [e1.Person] and [e2.Person]. The client can import one of them and refer to the other by its full name. The package resolves this ambiguity. By convention, package names are in lowercase and begin with the reverse domain name of the organization that publishes them ([com.mysql.cj.jdbc], [org.hibernate]…); for our examples, we will use short names.

To place a class in a package, you write the declaration [package name;] at the top of its file. Unlike other languages, Java requires a one-to-one correspondence between packages and directories: the source files for the [e1] package are stored in a folder named [e1], and those for the [tax.dao] package are stored in a folder named [tax/dao], starting from the root of the source directory. The [Namespaces] folder illustrates these concepts:

Namespaces/
  Main.java             the main program (unnamed package)
  e1/
    Person.java         the class e1.Person
  e2/
    Person.java         the class e2.Person

The first class, [Person] [e1/Person.java]:

// the classes of this file belong to the e1 package
package e1;

public class Person {
    private final String firstName;
    private final String lastName;

    public Person(String firstName, String lastName) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "e1.Person[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + "]";
    }
}

The second: [e2/Person.java]:

// the classes of this file belong to the e2 package
package e2;

public class Person {
    private final String name;

    public Person(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "e2.Person[" + name + "]";
    }
}

Both classes are public: a class without the keyword [public] is accessible only to classes in its own package. The main program [Main.java] is as follows:

// importing a class from a package
import e1.Person;
// static import of a static member of a class
import static java.lang.Math.sqrt;

void main() {
    // Person designates e1.Person, which was imported
    Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont");
    // the full name of a class removes any ambiguity
    e2.Person p2 = new e2.Person("Durand");
    IO.println(p1 + " " + p2);
    // full name and package of a class
    IO.println(Person.class.getName() + ", " + e2.Person.class.getName());
    IO.println("package of the Person class: " + Person.class.getPackageName());
    // the module that contains a class
    IO.println("e1.Person is in a named module: " + Person.class.getModule().isNamed());
    IO.println(String.class.getName() + " is in the module " + String.class.getModule().getName());
    // StringBuilder is known thanks to the automatic import of the java.base module
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("abc");
    IO.println(sb.append("def"));
    // sqrt is known thanks to the static import
    IO.println("sqrt(2)=" + sqrt(2));
}
  • line 2: import of the class [e1.Person];
  • line 4: static import of the method [sqrt] from the class [Math];
  • Line 8: [Person] refers to the class [e1.Person], which was imported;
  • Line 10: The full name of the class [e2.Person] removes any ambiguity. Java does not support type aliases: you cannot give a class a different name;
  • Lines 13–14: The method [getName] in the class description returns its full name, prefixed by its package; [getPackageName] returns the package name;
  • lines 16–17: the method [getModule] returns the module containing the class (see below);
  • lines 19–20: the class [java.lang.StringBuilder] is recognized without an import;
  • line 22: use of static import.

The source code launcher automatically finds classes in subfolders: the command [java Main.java], entered in the [Namespaces] folder, compiles the files [e1/Person.java] and [e2/Person.java] on demand. Results:

> java Main.java
e1.Person[Jean, Dupont] e2.Person[Durand]
e1.Person, e2.Person
package of the Person class: e1
e1.Person is in a named module: false
java.lang.String is in the module java.base
abcdef
sqrt(2)=1.4142135623730951

If we replace the import on line 2 with the two on-demand imports [import e1.*;] and [import e2.*;], the name [Person] becomes ambiguous and the compiler rejects it:

> java Main.java
Main.java:9: error: reference to Person is ambiguous
    Person p1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont");
    ^
  both class e2.Person in e2 and class e1.Person in e1 match
...

docs.title: 4.9.1. Modules
docs.text: Starting with Java 9, packages are themselves grouped into modules (“Java Platform Module System,” JPMS). JDK is divided into modules: [java.base] contains the core packages ([java.lang], [java.util], [java.math], [java.io]…), [java.sql] provides database access, [java.net.http] is the client, HTTP, etc. A module declares, in a file named [module-info.java] located at the root of its source code, its name, the modules it requires ([requires java.sql;]), and the packages it makes available to other modules ([exports tax.business;]): An unexported package is invisible from the outside, even for its public classes. The classes in an application that does not declare a module—such as ours—belong to the unnamed module (line 5 of the results), which has access to all modules. This is the case for most applications, and for all those in this course: modules are primarily of interest to library authors and to the JDK module itself.

docs.title: 4.10. Records
docs.text:
Many classes serve only to carry data: a person, a grade, a tax bracket… For these, we always write the same code: private fields and [final], a constructor that copies its parameters into the fields, accessors, a [toString] method that displays the fields, and the [equals] and [hashCode] methods. Java 16 introduced records: the compiler generates this code from a single-line declaration. We encountered them in the section on immutable objects; the program [Classes22.java] demonstrates them more fully:

// records (Java 16)
void main() {
    Person r1 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    Person r2 = new Person("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    // toString generated by the compiler
    IO.println(r1);
    // the accessors have the name of the components
    IO.println("first name=" + r1.firstName() + ", identity=" + r1.identity());
    // equality by value: r1 and r2 are two different but equal objects
    IO.println("r1.equals(r2) : " + r1.equals(r2) + ", r1 == r2 : " + (r1 == r2));
    // the components are read-only
    // r1.age = 31;   // rejected: the age field is final
    // a modified copy, with a "wither" method
    Person r3 = r1.withAge(31);
    IO.println(r3);
    IO.println("r1.equals(r3) : " + r1.equals(r3));
    // deconstruction into variables with a record pattern (Java 21)
    if (r1 instanceof Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age)) {
        IO.println("first name=" + firstName + ", last name=" + lastName + ", age=" + age);
    }

    // the same thing with a class
    PersonC c1 = new PersonC("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    PersonC c2 = new PersonC("Jean", "Dupont", 30);
    IO.println(c1);
    IO.println("c1.equals(c2) : " + c1.equals(c2));

    // two records that implement the same interface
    Teacher e = new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61);
    IO.println(e);
    IO.println(e.identity());
    // equality takes the type into account: a Person is not equal to a Teacher
    Person pe = new Person("Lucile", "Dumas", 56);
    IO.println("pe.equals(e) : " + pe.equals(e));
    // the common type: the HasIdentity interface
    HasIdentity[] identities = { pe, e };
    for (HasIdentity i : identities) {
        IO.println(i.identity());
    }
}

// an interface implemented by the records
interface HasIdentity {
    String identity();
}

// a record: firstName, lastName, age are its components
record Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) implements HasIdentity {
    // methods can be added
    @Override
    public String identity() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]";
    }

    // a "wither" method: a copy in which one component has changed
    public Person withAge(int age) {
        return new Person(firstName, lastName, age);
    }
}

// a record cannot derive from another record
record Teacher(String firstName, String lastName, int age, int section) implements HasIdentity {
    @Override
    public String identity() {
        return "Teacher[[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]," + section + "]";
    }
}

// an equivalent class... or almost
final class PersonC {
    private final String firstName;
    private final String lastName;
    private final int age;

    public PersonC(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
        this.firstName = firstName;
        this.lastName = lastName;
        this.age = age;
    }

    public String firstName() {
        return firstName;
    }

    public String lastName() {
        return lastName;
    }

    public int age() {
        return age;
    }
}
  • lines 48–59: the record [Person]. The declaration [record Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age)] generates:
    • three private fields—[final], [firstName], [lastName], and [age]—which are the components of the record;
    • a three-parameter constructor, known as the canonical constructor;
    • three public accessors: [firstName()], [lastName()], and [age()] (line 8);
    • a method [toString] that displays the type name and its components (line 6);
    • the methods [equals] and [hashCode], which compare the values of the components rather than the references;
  • lines 51–53 and 56–58: a record, like a class, can have additional methods and implement interfaces (line 48);
  • line 10: [r1] and [r2] are two distinct objects ([==] is the same as [false]) but they are equal to [equals] because their components have the same values. For an ordinary class, [equals] compares references (line 26);
  • line 14: since a record is immutable, it cannot be modified (line 12): the “wither” method [withAge] creates a copy of [r1] whose age has changed;
  • lines 18–20: a record pattern (Java 21): if [r1] is a [Person], its components are extracted into the variables [firstName], [lastName], and [age]. This is referred to as record decomposition. We will encounter these patterns again when filtering by pattern;
  • lines 62–67: a record is implicitly final and implicitly derives from the class [java.lang.Record]; it cannot derive from another class or record, nor can it be derived from. To give the records [Person] and [Teacher] a common type, we have them implement the same interface, in this case [HasIdentity] (lines 43–45). The record [Teacher] therefore contains the person’s components;
  • line 34: record equality takes into account the actual type of the objects: a [Person] is never equal to a [Teacher], even if their common components are equal;
  • lines 36–39: the common interface allows both records to be handled polymorphically;
  • lines 70–92: a class that resembles the [Person] record… except that the fields, constructor, and accessors had to be written, and equality by value and [toString] are not provided.

Results:

> java Classes22.java
Person[firstName=Jean, lastName=Dupont, age=30]
first name=Jean, identity=[Jean, Dupont, 30]
r1.equals(r2) : true, r1 == r2 : false
Person[firstName=Jean, lastName=Dupont, age=31]
r1.equals(r3) : false
first name=Jean, last name=Dupont, age=30
Classes22$PersonC@206a70ef
c1.equals(c2) : false
Teacher[firstName=Lucile, lastName=Dumas, age=56, section=61]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]
pe.equals(e) : false
[Lucile, Dumas, 56]
Teacher[[Lucile, Dumas, 56],61]

Note that the method [toString] of the class [PersonC] is the same as that of the class [Object] (line 8 of the results) and that the equality of the two objects [PersonC] is false (line 9).

Let’s summarize the differences between a class and a record:

ClassRecordEquality between [equals]same object (unless redefined)same component values, same type[toString]class name and hash coderecord name and componentsfields, constructor, accessorsto be writtengenerated by the declarationstatuseditable or notimmutable (fields [final]), no other instance fieldsmodified copyto be writtento be written (using "wither" methods)inheritancefrom a class, from multiple interfacesfrom no classes, from multiple interfaces; a record is always final

A record is used for data defined by its value (a person retrieved from a database, a message exchanged over a network, a tax bracket), and a class is used for an object with an identity and behavior (a computing service, a connection, a mutable list). Note: A record is “superficially” immutable: if a component references a mutable object—such as a list—the contents of that list remain mutable. In such cases, immutable lists are used ([List.copyOf]).

docs.title: 4.11. Record constructors
docs.text:
The canonical constructor for a record simply copies its parameters into the fields. However, you may want to validate or normalize these parameters. Java provides the compact constructor for this purpose, as well as the ability to add other constructors. The program [Classes23.java] illustrates this:

// record constructors: compact constructor, other constructors
void main() {
    Person p = new Person("  Jean ", "Dupont", 30);
    IO.println(p.identity());
    // a record is immutable: growOlder returns a new person
    Person p2 = p.growOlder();
    IO.println(p.identity() + " -> " + p2.identity());
    // another constructor
    Person unknown = new Person("Martin");
    IO.println(unknown.identity());
    // the checks of the compact constructor
    try {
        new Person("Paul", " ", 20);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
    try {
        new Person("Paul", "Martin", -4);
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException ex) {
        IO.println(ex.getMessage());
    }
    // a record with a method and a static factory
    Point pt = new Point(3, 4);
    IO.println("pt=" + pt + ", distance to the origin: " + pt.distance() + ", origin=" + Point.origin());
}

record Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
    // compact constructor: it checks and normalizes the parameters,
    // the fields are then initialized automatically
    Person {
        firstName = check(firstName, "first name");
        lastName = check(lastName, "last name");
        if (age < 0) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("age (" + age + ") invalid");
        }
    }

    // any other constructor must call the canonical constructor
    Person(String lastName) {
        this("?", lastName, 0);
    }

    // a method that returns a new person
    public Person growOlder() {
        return new Person(firstName, lastName, age + 1);
    }

    public String identity() {
        return "[" + firstName + ", " + lastName + ", " + age + "]";
    }

    // a static checking method
    private static String check(String value, String label) {
        if (value == null || value.isBlank()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException(label + " (" + value + ") invalid");
        }
        return value.strip();
    }
}

record Point(double x, double y) {
    // a static field is allowed, not an instance field
    private static final Point ORIGIN = new Point(0, 0);

    public static Point origin() {
        return ORIGIN;
    }

    public double distance() {
        return Math.sqrt(x * x + y * y);
    }
}
  • Lines 30–36: the compact constructor. It is written without a parameter list; its parameters are implicitly those of the canonical constructor ([firstName], [lastName], [age]). Its code executes first; then the fields are automatically initialized with the values—which may have been modified—of the parameters. Here, the first name and last name are validated and stripped of their leading and trailing spaces (lines 31–32), and a negative age is rejected (lines 33–35). In a compact constructor, you cannot assign values to fields ([this.firstName = ...] is rejected): you modify the parameters;
  • lines 39–41: a record may have other constructors, but these must call the canonical constructor with [this(...)]: any creation of [Person] thus goes through the compact constructor’s validations;
  • lines 44–46: a record is immutable; aging it means creating a new instance;
  • lines 53–58: a static private validation method;
  • lines 61–72: A record can have static fields (line 63) and static methods (lines 65–67), such as the static factory [origin], but no instance fields in addition to its components.

Results:

> java Classes23.java
[Jean, Dupont, 30]
[Jean, Dupont, 30] -> [Jean, Dupont, 31]
[?, Martin, 0]
last name ( ) invalid
age (-4) invalid
pt=Point[x=3.0, y=4.0], distance to the origin: 5.0, origin=Point[x=0.0, y=0.0]

The first name, provided surrounded by spaces (line 3), was stored without them (line 2 of the results). The compact constructor is the idiomatic way to ensure that a record is always valid: there is no way to create a [Person] without using it.

docs.title: 4.12. No extension methods: static utility methods
docs.text:
How do you add a method to a class that cannot be modified, such as the [String] class derived from JDK? Some languages, such as C# or Kotlin, offer “extension methods”: static methods that are used like instance methods of the extended type. Java does not have them. Instead, we write static methods, grouped together in a utility class, and call them using the name of their class, passing the object as a parameter. The JDK program is full of them: [Arrays], [Collections], [Objects], [Math]… The program [Classes24.java] illustrates this:

// no extension methods in Java: static utility methods
import static java.lang.Character.toUpperCase;

void main() {
    Person p = new Person("jean", "dupont", 30);
    // the utility methods are called with the name of their class
    IO.println(Tools.initials(p));
    IO.println(Tools.firstUpper("jean"));
    IO.println(Tools.fullName(p) + " is an adult: " + Tools.isAdult(p));
    IO.println("\"it is sunny\" has " + Tools.nbWords("it is sunny") + " words");
    // a static method of the record itself
    Person unknown = Person.unknown();
    IO.println(Tools.fullName(unknown) + " is an adult: " + Tools.isAdult(unknown));
}

// a person
record Person(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
    // static factory: an unknown person
    static Person unknown() {
        return new Person("?", "?", 0);
    }
}

// a utility class: final, private constructor, static methods
final class Tools {
    private Tools() {
    }

    static String initials(Person p) {
        return toUpperCase(p.firstName().charAt(0)) + "." + toUpperCase(p.lastName().charAt(0)) + ".";
    }

    static String firstUpper(String s) {
        return s.isEmpty() ? s : toUpperCase(s.charAt(0)) + s.substring(1);
    }

    static boolean isAdult(Person p) {
        return p.age() >= 18;
    }

    static String fullName(Person p) {
        return firstUpper(p.firstName()) + " " + p.lastName().toUpperCase();
    }

    static int nbWords(String s) {
        return s.isBlank() ? 0 : s.strip().split("\\s+").length;
    }
}
  • lines 25–48: the utility class [Tools]. It is final, and its sole constructor is private (lines 26–27): it cannot be derived from or instantiated. All of its methods are static;
  • lines 29–31: the method [initials] takes the person as a parameter. Like a utility class written in another file, it uses only the public members of the [Person] record—in this case, its accessors (in a compact file, however, it would have access to private fields); [charAt(0)] returns the first character of a string;
  • line 2: The static import of the method [Character.toUpperCase], which capitalizes a character, allows it to be called without its class name (lines 30 and 34);
  • lines 45–47: the method [nbWords] splits the string using the method [split], whose parameter is a regular expression: ["\\s+"] matches a sequence of one or more whitespace characters;
  • lines 7–10: Utility methods are called using the class name: [Tools.initials(p)], not [p.initials()];
  • lines 19–21: when the type can be modified, its methods are naturally placed there: the static factory [unknown] is a method of the record [Person] (line 12).

Results:

> java Classes24.java
J.D.
Jean
Jean DUPONT is an adult: true
"it is sunny" has 3 words
? ? is an adult: false

With a static import ([import static tools.Tools.*;] if the class were in a package named [tools]), one could write [initials(p)] without the class name. For a utility method to be usable, its class must be accessible and, if it is in another package, imported.

docs.title: 4.13. Pattern matching on objects
docs.text:
The [switch] statement and pattern matching are not limited to simple values (numbers, strings); they also apply to objects. You can test an object’s type, deconstruct a record, add a condition, and retrieve the object converted to the correct type—all in a single expression. The program [Classes25.java] uses a sealed interface and three records that implement it:

// pattern matching on objects
void main() {
    Object[] objects = {
        new Individual("Jean", "Dupont", 30),
        new Individual("Lise", "Morel", 12),
        new Teacher("Lucile", "Dumas", 56, 61),
        new Teacher("Marc", "Petit", 44, 27),
        new Student("Paul", "Martin", 19, "computer science"),
        "a string",
        42,
        null,
    };

    // 1 - the type pattern: instanceof Type variable (Java 16)
    for (Object o : objects) {
        if (o instanceof Person p) {
            // here p is a Person
            IO.println(p.firstName() + " is of type " + p.getClass().getSimpleName());
        }
    }

    // 2 - the type pattern followed by a condition
    for (Object o : objects) {
        if (o instanceof Person p && p.age() >= 18) {
            IO.println(p.firstName() + " is an adult");
        }
    }

    // 3 - the switch on the type of the object, with guards and record patterns (Java 21)
    for (Object o : objects) {
        IO.println(describe(o));
    }

    // 4 - an exhaustive switch on a sealed interface
    for (Object o : objects) {
        if (o instanceof Person p) {
            IO.println(p.firstName() + " : " + category(p));
        }
    }
}

String describe(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case Teacher e when e.section() == 27 -> e.firstName() + " teaches computer science";
        case Teacher e -> e.firstName() + " teaches in section " + e.section();
        case Student(var firstName, _, _, var major) -> firstName + " studies " + major;
        case Person p when p.age() < 18 -> p.firstName() + " is a minor";
        case Person p -> p.firstName() + " is " + p.age() + " years old";
        case String s -> "a string of " + s.length() + " characters";
        case Integer n when n > 0 -> "the positive integer " + n;
        case null -> "the null reference";
        default -> "an unknown object";
    };
}

// no default: the compiler knows that the three cases cover all persons
String category(Person p) {
    return switch (p) {
        case Individual _ -> "individual";
        case Teacher _ -> "teacher";
        case Student _ -> "student";
    };
}

// a sealed interface and the three records that implement it
sealed interface Person permits Individual, Teacher, Student {
    String firstName();
    String lastName();
    int age();
}

record Individual(String firstName, String lastName, int age) implements Person {
}

record Teacher(String firstName, String lastName, int age, int section) implements Person {
}

record Student(String firstName, String lastName, int age, String major) implements Person {
}
  • Lines 66–79: A sealed interface [Person], implemented by three records: [Individual], [Teacher], and [Student]. The interface declares the methods [firstName], [lastName], and [age]: the records automatically implement them through their accessors, since they have components with the same names. Since a record is final, it can implement a sealed interface without further specification;
  • lines 3–12: an array of objects of various types, including an integer (automatically converted to *[Integer]) and the reference *[null];
  • line 16: the pattern of type [o instanceof Person p] (Java 16) is true if [o] references an object of type [Person]; in this case, the variable [p], of type [Person], references this object. This avoids the sequence used in Java prior to version 16: testing the type with [instanceof], then converting with [(Person) o]. The pattern is false if [o] is equal to [null];
  • line 24: the pattern variable [p] can be used in the rest of the condition, after [&&]: Java does not have property patterns; field values are tested using a condition;
  • lines 42–54: the expression [switch] on an object (Java 21) tries the patterns in order and returns the value associated with the first one that matches:
    • line 44: a teacher from section 27. The clause [when] adds a condition, called a guard, to the type pattern;
    • line 45: any other teacher. The order is important: if placed before the previous one, this pattern would have made it inaccessible, which the compiler would have reported as an error;
    • line 46: a record pattern: it extracts the components of the record [Student] in the order they are declared; [var] lets the compiler infer their type, and the character [_] (Java 22) ignores a component;
    • lines 47–48: a minor, followed by any other person;
    • line 50: a positive integer;
    • line 51: the case [null]. Without it, a [switch] on a null reference throws a [NullPointerException] exception;
    • line 52: the case [default] handles everything else. Without it, the compiler would report that the expression [switch] does not cover all cases: a [switch] on an object must be exhaustive;
  • lines 57–63: a [switch] on a [Person], without [default]. However, it is exhaustive: since the interface is sealed, the compiler knows that a person is either a [Individual], a [Teacher], or a [Student]. The pattern [Individual _] tests the type without declaring a variable.

Results:

> java Classes25.java
Jean is of type Individual
Lise is of type Individual
Lucile is of type Teacher
Marc is of type Teacher
Paul is of type Student
Jean is an adult
Lucile is an adult
Marc is an adult
Paul is an adult
Jean is 30 years old
Lise is a minor
Lucile teaches in section 61
Marc teaches computer science
Paul studies computer science
a string of 8 characters
the positive integer 42
the null reference
Jean : individual
Lise : individual
Lucile : teacher
Marc : teacher
Paul : student

If the case [Student] is removed from the method [category], the compiler reports an error:

> java Classes25.java
Classes25.java:58: error: the switch expression does not cover all possible input values
    return switch (p) {
           ^
1 error
error: compilation failed

This is the great advantage of combining sealed types with pattern filtering: if a fourth record is added to the hierarchy, the compiler identifies all the [switch] records that need to be filled in. Note also that the type pattern corresponds to the types that implement the interface: the type pattern loop (lines 15–20) has selected the three types of people. Pattern filtering is a useful alternative to cascading [if (o instanceof ...)] statements; however, it should not replace polymorphism: when behavior depends on the object’s type and the class hierarchy is well-defined, a method redefined in each class often remains the object-oriented solution. Pattern-based filtering is well-suited for data hierarchies (records) on which one wishes to write processing logic external to that data.

docs.title: 4.14. Handling the null value
docs.text:
Any reference-type variable can have the value [null], and using a null reference causes the [NullPointerException] exception, the most common runtime error in Java. Unlike other languages such as C# or Kotlin, the Java compiler does not distinguish between types that can be [null] and those that cannot. However, the JDK and libraries provide several tools to mitigate this risk:

  • the [Optional<T>] class (Java 8), the return type of a method that may return nothing;
  • the methods of the [Objects] class: [requireNonNull] to reject [null] at the entry point of a method or constructor, and [requireNonNullElse] to provide a default value;
  • annotations that document intent and are verified by certain analysis tools. The most recent ones, proposed by a group of vendors (Google, JetBrains, Spring…), are those from the JSpecify library: [@Nullable] on a type that can be [null], and [@NullMarked] on a class or package to indicate that other types cannot be. Spring Framework 7, which we will be using, employs them. They require a library, so we will not use them in this chapter.

The program [Classes26.java] demonstrates the first two:

// handling the null value: Optional, Objects.requireNonNull...
void main() {
    Person jean = new Person("Jean", "Dupont");
    jean.setMiddleName("Marie");
    Person[] persons = { jean, new Person("Paul", "Martin") };
    for (Person p : persons) {
        // a default value when the reference is null
        String middle = Objects.requireNonNullElse(p.getMiddleName(), "(none)");
        // an explicit test
        String length = p.getMiddleName() == null ? "null" : String.valueOf(p.getMiddleName().length());
        IO.println(p.getFirstName() + " : middle name=" + middle + ", length=" + length);
    }

    // a method that may find nothing: it returns an Optional<Person>
    Optional<Person> found = find(persons, "Durand");
    IO.println("Durand found: " + found.isPresent());
    IO.println(found.map(Person::getFirstName).orElse("Durand: person not found"));
    // we test the presence of a value before using it
    found = find(persons, "Martin");
    if (found.isPresent()) {
        IO.println("Martin : " + found.get().getFirstName());
    }
    // ifPresent: the action is only performed if a value is present
    find(persons, "Dupont").ifPresent(p -> p.setMiddleName("Louise"));
    find(persons, "Durand").ifPresent(p -> p.setMiddleName("Louise"));
    IO.println(jean.getMiddleName());
    // orElseThrow: we assert that the value is present, otherwise an exception is thrown
    Person martin = find(persons, "Martin").orElseThrow();
    IO.println(martin.getFirstName());

    // Objects.requireNonNull: a mandatory parameter
    try {
        new Person(null, "Morel");
    } catch (NullPointerException ex) {
        IO.println("Error: " + ex.getMessage());
    }
    // the NullPointerException exception and its detailed message (Java 14)
    try {
        Person lise = new Person("Lise", "Morel");
        IO.println(lise.getMiddleName().length());
    } catch (NullPointerException ex) {
        IO.println("Error: " + ex.getMessage());
    }
}

// searching for a person by last name
Optional<Person> find(Person[] persons, String lastName) {
    for (Person p : persons) {
        if (p.getLastName().equals(lastName)) {
            return Optional.of(p);
        }
    }
    return Optional.empty();
}

class Person {
    // mandatory fields: they must never be null
    private final String firstName;
    private final String lastName;
    // optional field: null means "no middle name"
    private String middleName;

    public Person(String firstName, String lastName) {
        this.firstName = Objects.requireNonNull(firstName, "the first name is mandatory");
        this.lastName = Objects.requireNonNull(lastName, "the last name is mandatory");
    }

    public String getFirstName() {
        return firstName;
    }

    public String getLastName() {
        return lastName;
    }

    public String getMiddleName() {
        return middleName;
    }

    public void setMiddleName(String middleName) {
        this.middleName = middleName;
    }
}
  • lines 56–83: The [Person] class has two required fields, initialized by the constructor, and one optional field, [middleName]: [null] means “no middle name.” The constructor rejects a first name or last name of [null] using [Objects.requireNonNull] (lines 64–65): the error is detected when the object is created rather than much later, when the field is used;
  • line 8: [Objects.requireNonNullElse(value, defaultValue)] (Java 9) returns [value] if it is not equal to [null]; otherwise, it returns [defaultValue];
  • line 10: An explicit check is often the simplest approach;
  • lines 47–54: The method [find] returns the person being searched for wrapped in a [Optional] object, or an empty [Optional]: its return type, [Optional<Person>], warns the caller that the result may be missing, and requires the caller to handle this case to retrieve the person. [Optional.of(p)] creates a [Optional] containing [p], [Optional.empty()], and an empty [Optional];
  • line 16: [isPresent] indicates whether [Optional] contains a value;
  • line 17: [map(Person::getFirstName)] converts any person present into their first name; [orElse(value)] returns the present value or, if none, the specified value. The notation [Person::getFirstName] is a method reference, which we will examine in Chapter 7; here, it refers to “the person’s [getFirstName] method”;
  • lines 20–22: [get] returns the present value; it is called only after verifying its presence;
  • lines 24–25: [ifPresent] executes the specified action only if a value is present. The action is a lambda (Chapter 7): [p -> p.setMiddleName("Louise")] reads “for person p, set their middle name.” Dupont exists and is assigned a new middle name; Durand does not exist, and the statement does nothing;
  • Line 28: [orElseThrow] returns the value if it is present, or throws a [NoSuchElementException] exception if [Optional] is empty. This is used when you are certain the value is present;
  • lines 32–36: A person without a first name is rejected by the constructor;
  • lines 38–43: Using a null reference throws the [NullPointerException] exception. Since Java 14, its message specifically identifies the null expression.

Results:

> java Classes26.java
Jean : middle name=Marie, length=5
Paul : middle name=(none), length=null
Durand found: false
Durand: person not found
Martin : Paul
Louise
Paul
Error: the first name is mandatory
Error: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because the return value of "Classes26$Person.getMiddleName()" is null

[Optional] is intended for method return values; it is not used for fields or parameters. In this course, we document whether a value is optional, verify required parameters using [Objects.requireNonNull], and prefer objects that are always complete (constructed with all their required values) over objects that are populated incrementally.

docs.title: 4.15. Example Application - V2
docs.text:
We’ll revisit the tax calculation already covered in the previous chapter (version 1) and now implement it using classes and interfaces. Let’s review the problem. We aim to write a program to calculate a taxpayer’s tax. We’ll consider the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only their salary to report (the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income, used as-is: this is an exercise):

  • we calculate the employee’s number of shares: shares = nbChildren / 2 + 1 if they are unmarried, nbChildren / 2 + 2 if he is married, where nbChildren is the number of his children;
  • if he has at least three children, he receives an additional half-share;
  • his taxable income R is calculated as R = 0.72 × S, where S is his annual salary;
  • his family quotient is calculated as QF = R / shares;
  • his tax I is calculated using the following table:
thresholdcoeffRcoeffN49620083820.068291.0914,7530.1911,322.9223,8880.2832,668.3938,8680.3744,846.9847,9320.4266,883.6600.4819,505.54

Each row has three fields. To calculate tax I, find the first row where QF ≤ the limit. For example, if QF = 5,000, the row (8,382; 0.068; 291.09) will be found. Tax I is then equal to 0.068 × R - 291.09 × shares. If QF is such that the condition QF ≤ limit is never satisfied, then the coefficients of the last row are used, resulting in tax I = 0.481 × R - 9,505.54 × shares.

The application generates the file [TaxV2]. The calculation classes are organized into a package named [tax]:

TaxV2/
