  Main.java                 the program that dialogues with the user
  tax/
    TaxBracket.java         a bracket of the tax scale
    ITax.java               the tax calculation interface
    AbstractTax.java        an abstract class implementing ITax
    HardwiredTax.java       a derived class, with hard-coded data

First, we define a type capable of encapsulating a row from the previous array [TaxBracket.java]:

package tax;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

// a bracket of the tax scale
public record TaxBracket(BigDecimal limit, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
}

We use a record:

  • because a bracket is a small piece of data without an identity, defined solely by its value, and there is no reason for it to be modified once created: a record is immutable;
  • because the compiler generates the constructor, the accessors, [toString], and the equality operator from a single line.

The components are of type [BigDecimal] (package [java.math], hence the import on line 3). The types [float] and [double] represent numbers in binary: a decimal number such as 0.068 has no exact representation in them, and calculations accumulate small rounding errors. The [BigDecimal] class represents decimal numbers exactly: this is the type to use for amounts. Its drawback is the lack of operators: we write [a.add(b)], [a.multiply(b)], [a.compareTo(b)].

Next, we define an interface [ITax] capable of calculating the tax [ITax.java]:

package tax;

public interface ITax {
    // tax calculation of a taxpayer
    int calculate(boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary);
}
  • Line 5: The method for calculating the tax based on three pieces of data: the taxpayer’s marital status, the number of children, and annual salary. It rounds the tax down to the nearest euro.

Next, we define an abstract class that implements this interface [AbstractTax.java]:

package tax;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.MathContext;
import java.util.List;

public abstract class AbstractTax implements ITax {
    // the tax brackets needed for the calculation come from an external source
    // that only the derived classes know
    protected abstract List<TaxBracket> getTaxBrackets();

    // tax calculation
    @Override
    public int calculate(boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary) {
        // calculation of the number of shares
        BigDecimal shares = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbChildren).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
                .add(BigDecimal.valueOf(married ? 2 : 1));
        if (nbChildren >= 3) {
            shares = shares.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
        }
        // calculation of the taxable income and of the family quotient
        BigDecimal income = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salary));
        BigDecimal quotient = income.divide(shares, MathContext.DECIMAL128);
        // searching for the tax bracket: the last one is used if no limit fits
        List<TaxBracket> brackets = getTaxBrackets();
        TaxBracket bracket = brackets.getLast();
        for (int i = 0; i < brackets.size() - 1; i++) {
            if (quotient.compareTo(brackets.get(i).limit()) <= 0) {
                bracket = brackets.get(i);
                break;
            }
        }
        // tax calculation
        return income.multiply(bracket.coeffR()).subtract(shares.multiply(bracket.coeffN())).intValue();
    }
}
  • Line 1: The class belongs to the [tax] package; its file is therefore in the [tax] folder;
  • Line 7: The class [AbstractTax] implements the interface [ITax];
  • Line 10: The scale data, provided by a protected abstract method. The [AbstractTax] class does not know where this data comes from (written in the code, read from a file, a database, etc.). It leaves this up to the derived classes. This is why it is declared abstract, which prevents it from being instantiated. The abstract method requires derived classes to provide the brackets; the compiler verifies this;
  • lines 13–35: the implementation of the [calculate] method of the [ITax] interface. Derived classes will not need to rewrite this method. The [AbstractTax] class thus serves as a factorization class for the derived classes: it contains what is common to all of them;
  • lines 16–17: the number of shares. [BigDecimal.valueOf(n)] converts an integer to [BigDecimal]; division by [BigDecimal.TWO] is exact (3 / 2 = 1.5), unlike integer division by [nbChildren / 2] (3 / 2 = 1). The expression [married ? 2 : 1] equals 2 for a married taxpayer, 1 otherwise;
  • lines 18–20: the additional half-share. A [BigDecimal] is immutable: [add] returns a new object, which must be assigned to the variable;
  • lines 22–23: taxable income and the family quotient. Decimal constants are created from strings ([new BigDecimal("0.72")]) to ensure they are exact. Dividing a [BigDecimal] can result in an infinite number of decimal places (1 / 3): we specify the desired precision, in this case [MathContext.DECIMAL128] (34 significant digits);
  • lines 25–32: searching for the bracket. By default, this is the last bracket ([brackets.getLast()], line 26). The loop iterates through all brackets except the last one and stops ([break]) at the first bracket whose limit is greater than or equal to the family quotient, as tested by [compareTo(...) <= 0];
  • line 34: the tax calculation. The method [intValue] truncates the result to its integer part.

A class that implements the [ITax] interface can be created by deriving it from the [AbstractTax] class. This is what we are now doing with [HardwiredTax.java]:

package tax;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class HardwiredTax extends AbstractTax {
    // tax calculation data (2004 tax scale on 2003 income), "hardwired"
    private static final double[] LIMITS = { 4962, 8382, 14753, 23888, 38868, 47932, 0 };
    private static final double[] COEFF_R = { 0, 0.068, 0.191, 0.283, 0.374, 0.426, 0.481 };
    private static final double[] COEFF_N = { 0, 291.09, 1322.92, 2668.39, 4846.98, 6883.66, 9505.54 };

    // the tax brackets
    private final List<TaxBracket> taxBrackets;

    // constructor
    public HardwiredTax() {
        // creating and filling the list of tax brackets
        List<TaxBracket> brackets = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < LIMITS.length; i++) {
            brackets.add(new TaxBracket(BigDecimal.valueOf(LIMITS[i]),
                    BigDecimal.valueOf(COEFF_R[i]), BigDecimal.valueOf(COEFF_N[i])));
        }
        // the stored list is not modifiable
        taxBrackets = List.copyOf(brackets);
    }

    // implementation of the abstract method of the parent class
    @Override
    protected List<TaxBracket> getTaxBrackets() {
        return taxBrackets;
    }
}
  • Lines 9–11: The class [HardwiredTax] hardcodes the data needed to calculate the tax. These are class fields ([static]) [final]: they are shared by all instances and cannot be replaced by other arrays. By convention, the names of the constants ([static final]) are written in uppercase;
  • lines 17–26: the constructor uses this data to build the list of tax brackets. [BigDecimal.valueOf(double)] (lines 21–22) converts a [double] to a [BigDecimal] via its shortest decimal representation: [BigDecimal.valueOf(0.068)] is exactly 0.068. Do not use the constructor [new BigDecimal(0.068)], which reproduces all the decimal places of the approximated binary value (0.068000000000000004884981308350688…);
  • line 25: [List.copyOf] returns a read-only copy of the list: no class will be able to modify the scale;
  • lines 29–32: the parent class’s abstract method is implemented: it returns the list of brackets.

The next chapter will add other classes derived from [AbstractTax], which will read the brackets from a text file or from JSON: they will only need to provide the [getTaxBrackets] method.

A test program could be the following [Main.java]:

// interactive tax calculation program
// the user types three pieces of data on the keyboard: married nbChildren salary
// the program then displays the tax to pay
import tax.HardwiredTax;
import tax.ITax;

static final String SYNTAX = """
        syntax: Married NbChildren Salary
        Married: y for married, n for not married
        NbChildren: number of children
        Salary: annual salary in euros""";

void main() {
    // creation of an ITax object
    ITax tax = new HardwiredTax();

    // input loop
    while (true) {
        // we ask for the tax calculation parameters
        String parameters = IO.readln("Tax calculation parameters in the format: "
                + "Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: ");
        // end of standard input or empty line: we stop
        if (parameters == null || parameters.isBlank()) {
            break;
        }
        // checking the number of fields of the typed line
        String[] fields = parameters.strip().split("\\s+");
        if (fields.length != 3) {
            IO.println(SYNTAX);
            continue;
        }
        // checking the validity of the parameters
        // married
        String married = fields[0].toLowerCase();
        if (!married.equals("y") && !married.equals("n")) {
            IO.println(SYNTAX + "\nIncorrect married argument: type y or n");
            continue;
        }
        // nbChildren
        int nbChildren = positiveInteger(fields[1]);
        if (nbChildren < 0) {
            IO.println(SYNTAX + "\nIncorrect NbChildren argument: type a positive or zero integer");
            continue;
        }
        // salary
        int salary = positiveInteger(fields[2]);
        if (salary < 0) {
            IO.println(SYNTAX + "\nIncorrect salary argument: type a positive or zero integer");
            continue;
        }
        // the parameters are correct: we calculate the tax
        IO.println("Tax=" + tax.calculate(married.equals("y"), nbChildren, salary) + " euros");
    }
}

// returns the positive or zero integer represented by the string, -1 if the string does not represent one
int positiveInteger(String input) {
    try {
        int value = Integer.parseInt(input);
        return value >= 0 ? value : -1;
    } catch (NumberFormatException ex) {
        return -1;
    }
}

The program above allows the user to perform repeated tax calculation simulations.

  • Lines 4–5: The main program is in the unnamed package; it imports the two types it needs from the [tax] package. These types must be public;
  • Lines 7–11: The help message is a constant of the implicit class, written as a text block (Java 15) delimited by three quotation marks: the string can span multiple lines, and the common indentation of the lines is removed. Since the closing quotation mark is placed at the end of the last line, the string does not end with a line break;
  • line 15: creation of a [tax] object that implements the [ITax] interface. This object is obtained by instantiating a type [HardwiredTax], a type that implements the interface [ITax]. Note that the variable [tax] was not assigned the type [HardwiredTax] but rather the type [ITax]. By writing this, we indicate that we are only interested in the [calculate] method of the [tax] object and not in the rest. To use data from a file, simply change this single line;
  • lines 18–53: the loop for tax calculation simulations;
  • lines 20–21: the three parameters required for the [calculate] method are requested in a single line entered via the keyboard. [IO.readln(message)] displays the message and then reads a line; it returns [null] if standard input is closed: the check on line 23 then terminates the program, just as an empty line would;
  • line 27: the [split] method splits the line—with leading and trailing spaces removed—into words separated by one or more space characters (regular expression ["\\s+"]);
  • Lines 40 and 46: The method [positiveInteger] (lines 57–64) verifies that the last two fields are positive integers or zero. [Integer.parseInt] throws a [NumberFormatException] exception if the string does not represent an integer: the method catches it and returns -1, which indicates an error;
  • line 52: call to the [calculate] method of the [tax] object implementing the [ITax] interface.

Here is an example of the program’s execution, launched from the [TaxV2] folder:

The tax amounts are calculated correctly: 4,282 euros for a married taxpayer with two children and an annual salary of 60,000 euros (line 26), and 2,959 euros with three children (line 28). An unmarried taxpayer with no children pays 11,519 euros for the same salary (line 30).

Compared to Version 1, the calculation is now encapsulated in classes behind an interface: the dialog program only recognizes the [ITax] interface. Subsequent versions will take advantage of this separation: Version 3 (next chapter) will change the data source by deriving new classes from [AbstractTax], and then the application will be organized into layers (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 5. Commonly Used Java Classes
docs.text:
Here we present a few frequently used classes from the Java platform: strings, arrays, collections, files, and regular expressions. We also include the API Stream (Java 8), which is currently the most common way to search, sort, group, or transform elements in a Java collection. Before that, we’ll show you how to find information about the thousands of available classes. This resource is indispensable for any Java developer, even experienced ones.

With the exception of two (the JSON example and the sample application at the end), the examples in this chapter are compact source files executed by the source code launcher: [java File.java]. They are located in the [05-classes-java] folder of the course code and run in an English locale. Note that a compact source file automatically imports all public classes from the [java.base] module: [java.util], [java.io], [java.nio.file], [java.util.regex], [java.util.stream], [java.time]… This is why the programs below do not contain any [import] statements.

docs.title: 5.1. Seeking Help with Java Classes
docs.text: The Java Standard Library (the API Java SE) includes more than 4,000 public classes. No one knows them all: Java developers constantly consult their documentation. This documentation is available online, free of charge, and published for each version of Java.

docs.title: 5.1.1. Online Documentation
docs.text:
The starting point is Oracle’s website at docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25. There you’ll find:

  • the Java 25 reference: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/. It describes, module by module and package by package, all Java classes and interfaces: their constructors, fields, and methods;
  • a search box at the top of each page of the reference, where you can type the name of a class or method ([StringBuilder], [Matcher.find]…): the list of results populates as you type;
  • the Java language specification (JLS) and topic-specific guides (JDK tools, security, regular expressions…);
  • a “New Features” page that describes what’s new in each version. The new features themselves are described by JEP (JDK Enhancement Proposals), available on openjdk.org/jeps: For example, JEP 512 describes the compact source files used in this chapter.

A class page, such as java.lang.String, provides:

  • the class’s module and package;
  • its declaration, its parent classes, and the interfaces it implements;
  • a general description, often lengthy and detailed, with examples;
  • a summary list of its fields, constructors, and methods, followed by details for each: parameters, return value, possible exceptions, and the Java version in which it was introduced (under the “Since” heading).

The documentation is in English. A search on a search engine using the class’s full name and version (“java.lang.StringBuilder 25”) usually leads directly to the correct page.

docs.title: 5.1.2. Javadoc and the editor’s help
docs.text:
This documentation is generated by the [javadoc] tool from the JDK tool based on the documentation comments written in the source code of the classes. Such a comment begins with [/**] and is placed immediately before a class, field, or method. For example, here is the tax calculation method from the sample application in this chapter, documented as follows:

    /**
     * Calculates the tax of a taxpayer.
     *
     * @param married    true if the taxpayer is married
     * @param nbChildren number of children
     * @param salary     annual salary in euros
     * @return the amount of the tax, in euros
     */
    int calculate(boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary);

The comment begins with a summary sentence; the [@param] tags describe the parameters, and [@return] describes the returned value ([@throws] would describe an exception). You can document your own code in this way; the command [javadoc] (or [mvn javadoc:javadoc] in a Maven project) generates HTML pages similar to those in Java. Starting with Java 23, documentation comments can also be written in Markdown, with lines beginning with [///].

The code editor (IntelliJ IDEA, Visual Studio Code with the Extension Pack for Java) leverages these comments and provides immediate assistance without leaving the code:

  • autocompletion: after typing [aString.], the editor displays a list of the object’s methods, along with their parameters and return types;
  • Quick documentation: Hovering over a class or method name (or pressing Ctrl+Q in IntelliJ IDEA) displays its Javadoc;
  • Parameter help: When you type the opening parenthesis of a call (or press Ctrl+P in IntelliJ IDEA), the editor displays the different method overloads and the role of each parameter;
  • Go to Definition (Ctrl+B in IntelliJ, IDEA, F12 in VS Code): displays the source code for the class or method. JDK comes with the source code for its entire library (file [lib/src.zip]): This allows you to read the code for [ArrayList] or [HashMap], written by top Java experts, which is very educational.

Finally, the [jshell] tool from JDK lets you test a method without writing a program: you enter an expression, and it displays its value. Thus, ["abc".repeat(3)] displays ["abcabcabc"]. The command [/help] from [jshell] lists its options.

docs.title: 5.2.1. The String class
docs.text:
The [String] type ([java.lang] package) represents character strings. It offers numerous methods. Here are a few of them:

Methodrole[int length()]number of characters in the string[char charAt(int index)]Character No. [index]; the first character is No. 0[boolean startsWith(String prefix)]returns [true] if the string begins with [prefix][boolean endsWith(String suffix)]returns [true] if the string ends with [suffix][boolean contains(CharSequence s)]returns [true] if the string contains [s][boolean equals(Object other)]returns [true] if the string has the same content as [other]; [equalsIgnoreCase] is case-insensitive[int indexOf(String str)]the first occurrence of [str] in the string, or -1. Another overload starts the search at position [fromIndex][int indexOf(int ch)]same for the character [ch][int lastIndexOf(int ch)]same as [indexOf] but returns the last position instead of the first[static String join(CharSequence delimiter, CharSequence... elements)]Class method: concatenates the elements, separating them with [delimiter][String replace(char oldChar, char newChar)]returns a copy of the string where the character [oldChar] has been replaced by [newChar]; an overload replaces one string with another[String[] split(String regex)]the string is treated as a sequence of fields separated by a separator described by the regular expression [regex]; the result is an array of these fields[String substring(int beginIndex, int endIndex)]substring consisting of the characters from position [beginIndex] (inclusive) to position [endIndex] (exclusive)[String toLowerCase()], [String toUpperCase()]converts the string to lowercase, uppercase[String strip()]removes leading and trailing spaces from the string (Java 11; [stripLeading], [stripTrailing]: on one side only)[String repeat(int count)]repeats the string [count] times (Java 11)[boolean isEmpty()], [boolean isBlank()]returns [true] if the string is empty, or if it contains only spaces (Java 11)[Stream<String> lines()]returns the lines of the string as a stream (Java 11; see API Stream below)[String formatted(Object... args)]returns the string, used as a template, in which the placeholders [%s], [%d]… have been replaced by the arguments (Java 15)

It is important to note that a string of type [String] is immutable; it cannot be modified after it is created. When a method returns a string, that string is different from the string on which the method was applied. Thus, [s1.strip()] returns the string [s2], and [s1] and [s2] are two different strings: [s1] has not changed.

Unlike in other languages, a Java string is not an array: you do not write [c[i]] but [c.charAt(i)], and the number of characters is obtained using the [c.length()] method (with parentheses, whereas the length of an array is the [array.length] field, without parentheses).

The program [Strings01.java] is as follows:

// a few methods of the String class
void main() {
    String aString = "the bird flies above the clouds";
    display("aString=" + aString);
    display("aString.length()=" + aString.length());
    display("aString.charAt(10)=" + aString.charAt(10));
    display("aString.indexOf(\"flies\")=" + aString.indexOf("flies"));
    display("aString.indexOf(\"x\")=" + aString.indexOf("x"));
    display("aString.lastIndexOf('a')=" + aString.lastIndexOf('a'));
    display("aString.lastIndexOf('x')=" + aString.lastIndexOf('x'));
    display("aString.substring(4, 11)=" + aString.substring(4, 11));
    display("aString.toUpperCase()=" + aString.toUpperCase());
    display("aString.toLowerCase()=" + aString.toLowerCase());
    display("aString.replace('a', 'A')=" + aString.replace('a', 'A'));
    // no insert method: two substrings are glued back together
    display("insertion of \"never \" at position 9=" + aString.substring(0, 9) + "never "
            + aString.substring(9));
    // splitting the string into words (separator: a sequence of spaces)
    String[] fields = aString.split("\\s+");
    for (int i = 0; i < fields.length; i++) {
        display("fields[" + i + "]=[" + fields[i] + "]");
    }
    display("String.join(\":\", fields)=" + String.join(":", fields));
    display("\"  abc  \".strip()=[" + "  abc  ".strip() + "]");
    // the original string has not been modified
    display("aString=" + aString);
}

// a display method
void display(String msg) {
    IO.println(msg);
}

Results:

> java Strings01.java
aString=the bird flies above the clouds
aString.length()=31
aString.charAt(10)=l
aString.indexOf("flies")=9
aString.indexOf("x")=-1
aString.lastIndexOf('a')=15
aString.lastIndexOf('x')=-1
aString.substring(4, 11)=bird fl
aString.toUpperCase()=THE BIRD FLIES ABOVE THE CLOUDS
aString.toLowerCase()=the bird flies above the clouds
aString.replace('a', 'A')=the bird flies Above the clouds
insertion of "never " at position 9=the bird never flies above the clouds
fields[0]=[the]
fields[1]=[bird]
fields[2]=[flies]
fields[3]=[above]
fields[4]=[the]
fields[5]=[clouds]
String.join(":", fields)=the:bird:flies:above:the:clouds
"  abc  ".strip()=[abc]
aString=the bird flies above the clouds

Comments:

  • line 6: character #10, i.e., the 11th character in the string;
  • Lines 8, 10: An unsuccessful search returns -1;
  • Line 11: The two parameters of [substring] are the positions of the first kept character and the first non-kept character: this yields the 7 characters at positions 4 through 10. This is the general Java convention for specifying an index range (start included, end excluded): it appears in many methods;
  • Lines 16–17: The [String] class does not have an insertion method: we concatenate the beginning of the string, the inserted text, and the end of the string. We’ll see that the [StringBuilder] class has a [insert] method;
  • Line 19: [split] splits the string into fields. Its parameter is not a single character but a regular expression, which we’ll examine at the end of the chapter: ["\\s+"] denotes a sequence of one or more whitespace characters (space, tab, line break, etc.). The character [\] must be doubled in a Java string, hence the notation [\\s];
  • line 23: the static method [join] performs the inverse of [split];
  • line 24: [strip] (Java 11) removes leading and trailing spaces. There is also the older method [trim], which recognizes only the spaces in the code for ASCII; [strip] recognizes all Unicode spaces and should be preferred;
  • line 26: all of the previous methods returned new strings: [aString] remained unchanged (line 22 of the results);
  • Lines 30–32: a method from the compact source file, called by the method [main] as in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 5.2.2. The split and join methods
docs.text:
The program [Strings02.java] performs a more detailed split of a string into fields:

// split and join
void main() {
    String line = "one:two::three:";
    // splitting with the ':' separator
    String[] fields = line.split(":");
    for (int i = 0; i < fields.length; i++) {
        IO.println("fields[" + i + "]=[" + fields[i] + "]");
    }
    // the reverse operation does not give back the initial string: the final empty field has disappeared
    IO.println("join=[" + String.join(":", fields) + "]");

    // with a negative limit, split keeps the trailing empty fields
    fields = line.split(":", -1);
    IO.println("split(\":\", -1) : " + fields.length + " fields, join=[" + String.join(":", fields) + "]");

    // the separator is a regular expression: ":+" designates a sequence of ':'
    fields = line.split(":+");
    IO.println("split(\":+\") : " + fields.length + " fields [" + String.join("|", fields) + "]");

    // several separators and removal of the spaces around the fields
    String person = " dupont , jean ;  45 ";
    fields = person.strip().split("\\s*[,;]\\s*");
    IO.println("split(\"\\\\s*[,;]\\\\s*\") : " + fields.length + " fields ["
            + String.join("|", fields) + "]");

    // removal of spaces and empty fields, field by field
    String list = "  red ,, green ,  , blue ";
    List<String> colors = new ArrayList<>();
    for (String field : list.split(",")) {
        String color = field.strip();
        if (!color.isEmpty()) {
            colors.add(color);
        }
    }
    IO.println("strip + isEmpty : " + colors.size() + " fields [" + String.join("|", colors) + "]");

    // a separator that contains special characters of regular expressions
    String text = "apple | pear | apricot";
    fields = text.split(Pattern.quote(" | "));
    IO.println("Pattern.quote : [" + String.join(", ", fields) + "]");

    // join only accepts strings: the integers must first be converted
    int[] numbers = {1, 2, 3, 4};
    String[] texts = new String[numbers.length];
    for (int i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
        texts[i] = String.valueOf(numbers[i]);
    }
    IO.println("join on integers: " + String.join(" + ", texts));
}

Results:

> java Strings02.java
fields[0]=[one]
fields[1]=[two]
fields[2]=[]
fields[3]=[three]
join=[one:two::three]
split(":", -1) : 5 fields, join=[one:two::three:]
split(":+") : 3 fields [one|two|three]
split("\\s*[,;]\\s*") : 3 fields [dupont|jean|45]
strip + isEmpty : 3 fields [red|green|blue]
Pattern.quote : [apple, pear, apricot]
join on integers: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4

Comments:

  • Line 5: The fields are separated by the character [:]. Two consecutive [:] characters delimit an empty field (line 4 of the results). But be careful: [split] removes empty fields from the end. The final [:] in the string delimits a fifth, empty field that has been removed: only 4 fields are obtained, and [join] does not reconstruct the original string (line 6 of the results). This is a common pitfall;
  • line 13: the second parameter of [split] is a limit. A negative limit instructs the program to keep all fields, including the empty fields at the end: we do indeed get 5 fields, and [join] reconstructs the original string;
  • line 17: Since the separator is a regular expression, we can define complex separators: [":+"] matches one or more consecutive [:] characters. The two consecutive [:]s form a single separator, and the empty field disappears;
  • Line 22: The pattern [\\s*[,;]\\s*] matches a comma or semicolon, preceded and followed by any number of spaces: the spaces surrounding the separators are removed along with them. Those at the beginning and end of the string are removed beforehand by [strip]. This produces the three “cleaned up” fields in a single statement;
  • lines 27–35: To remove both the spaces around the fields and the empty fields, you can also process the fields one by one: the field consisting of two spaces between two commas becomes empty after [strip] and is not retained. The list [ArrayList] used here to store the retained fields will be discussed a little later. We will also see that the API stream allows this processing to be written in a single instruction;
  • line 39: the [" | "] separator contains the character [|], which has a special meaning in a regular expression (“or”). The [Pattern.quote] method converts any string into a regular expression that literally matches it. We’ll use it whenever a separator contains one of the characters [\ ^ $ . | ? * + ( ) [ ] { }];
  • Lines 43–48: [join] accepts only strings (more precisely, [CharSequence] objects, an interface implemented by [String] and [StringBuilder]): an array of integers must first be converted to an array of strings. We will see that with the API Stream, [Arrays.stream(numbers).mapToObj(String::valueOf).collect(Collectors.joining(" + "))] does the same thing in a single instruction.

docs.title: 5.2.3. Searching for and Comparing Strings
docs.text:
String comparison is more subtle than it seems: should uppercase and lowercase letters be distinguished? How should “éclair” be compared to “essay”? And most importantly, in Java, what does the [==] operator compare? The program [Strings03.java] demonstrates the search and comparison methods:

// searching and comparing strings
void main() {
    String title = "Learning the Java language, version 25";

    // contains, startsWith, endsWith: exact comparison
    IO.println("contains(\"language\") : " + title.contains("language"));
    IO.println("contains(\"LANGUAGE\") : " + title.contains("LANGUAGE"));
    IO.println("startsWith(\"Learning\") : " + title.startsWith("Learning"));
    IO.println("endsWith(\"25\") : " + title.endsWith("25"));

    // ignoring case: we compare the strings converted to lowercase
    String searched = "LANGUAGE";
    IO.println("toLowerCase().contains(searched.toLowerCase()) : "
            + title.toLowerCase().contains(searched.toLowerCase()));
    // regionMatches(ignoreCase, start, other, start in other, length)
    IO.println("regionMatches(true, 0, \"learning\", 0, 8) : "
            + title.regionMatches(true, 0, "learning", 0, 8));

    // equality: equals compares the contents, == compares the references
    String answer = "YES";
    String yes = new StringBuilder("ye").append('s').toString();
    IO.println("yes.equals(\"yes\") : " + yes.equals("yes"));
    IO.println("yes == \"yes\" : " + (yes == "yes"));
    IO.println("answer.equals(\"yes\") : " + answer.equals("yes"));
    IO.println("answer.equalsIgnoreCase(\"yes\") : " + answer.equalsIgnoreCase("yes"));

    // alphabetical order: according to the character codes or according to the language
    String a = "éclair", b = "essay";
    IO.println("\"" + a + "\".compareTo(\"" + b + "\") : " + a.compareTo(b));
    Collator collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    IO.println("collator.compare(\"" + a + "\", \"" + b + "\") : " + collator.compare(a, b));

    // empty or blank strings
    String empty = "";
    String blank = "   ";
    String missing = null;
    IO.println("\"\".isEmpty() : " + empty.isEmpty());
    IO.println("\"   \".isEmpty() : " + blank.isEmpty());
    IO.println("\"   \".isBlank() : " + blank.isBlank());
    IO.println("missing == null || missing.isBlank() : " + (missing == null || missing.isBlank()));

    // alignment and repetition
    IO.println("[" + String.format("%8s", "abc") + "] [" + String.format("%-8s", "abc") + "] ["
            + "-".repeat(8) + "]");
}

Results:

> java Strings03.java
contains("language") : true
contains("LANGUAGE") : false
startsWith("Learning") : true
endsWith("25") : true
toLowerCase().contains(searched.toLowerCase()) : true
regionMatches(true, 0, "learning", 0, 8) : true
yes.equals("yes") : true
yes == "yes" : false
answer.equals("yes") : false
answer.equalsIgnoreCase("yes") : true
"éclair".compareTo("essay") : 132
collator.compare("éclair", "essay") : -1
"".isEmpty() : true
"   ".isEmpty() : false
"   ".isBlank() : true
missing == null || missing.isBlank() : true
[     abc] [abc     ] [--------]

Comments:

  • lines 6–9: [contains], [startsWith], and [endsWith] perform an exact, character-by-character comparison: “LANGUAGE” is not found;
  • lines 12–14: These methods do not have a case-insensitive variant. The simplest way to perform a case-insensitive search is to convert both strings to lowercase;
  • lines 16–17: The [regionMatches] method compares a portion of one string to a portion of another string. Its first parameter specifies whether to ignore case; the subsequent parameters are the starting position in the string, the other string, the starting position in the other string, and the number of characters to compare;
  • lines 20–25: the most important part of this program. A variable of type [String] contains a reference to a string object (Chapter 4). The operator [] compares the references: it returns [true] if the two variables refer to the same object, and not to two objects with the same content. The variable [yes] (line 21) refers to a string “yes” constructed at runtime: this is a different object from the program’s literal string “yes,” and [yes == "yes"] evaluates to [false] (line 9 of the results), even though the two strings have the same content. To compare contents, we always use the method [equals], or [equalsIgnoreCase] to ignore case, which is the correct way to test a “yes” response entered from the keyboard in uppercase or lowercase. The comparison using [] “works” sometimes, when both strings are program literals, of which Java stores only a single instance: this is what makes the error difficult to detect;
  • lines 28–31: The method [compareTo] returns a negative, zero, or positive integer depending on whether the string precedes, equals, or follows the parameter string. It compares the character codes: “éclair” comes after “essay” because the code for the character é (233) is greater than that for the character e (101); here, it returns the difference between the two codes, 132. To sort words according to the rules of a language, use a [java.text.Collator] object: in French, the character “é” is grouped with “e,” and “éclair” comes before “essay” (line 13 of the results). We’ll use the order defined by a [Collator] to sort words intended for a user, and [compareTo] to compare technical identifiers (file names, keys, etc.);
  • lines 34–40: [isEmpty] checks for an empty string, while [isBlank] (Java 11) checks for an empty string or one containing only spaces. A variable of type [String] can also be [null] (no string): calling a method on [null] throws a [NullPointerException] exception. Therefore, we first test for [missing == null]; thanks to the short-circuit behavior of the [||] operator, [missing.isBlank()] is not evaluated when [missing] is [null];
  • Lines 43–44: [String.format("%8s", ...)] pads a string with spaces up to a length of 8 characters, either on the left or on the right, using the format [%-8s]; [repeat] repeats a string.

docs.title: 5.2.4. Formats and Text Blocks
docs.text:
So far, we have built the strings to be displayed using concatenation with the [+] operator. To align values in columns, set the number of decimal places for a number, or display a date, use the [String.format] method, or the [formatted] instance method (Java 15), which does the same thing. The first parameter is a format: a string in which [%[-][width][.precision]conversion] specifiers indicate where and how to insert the following parameters. The [Strings04.java] program provides examples of this, as well as the Java 15 text blocks:

// formats, text blocks
void main() {
    String name = "dupont";
    int age = 45;
    double salary = 2345.678;
    double rate = 0.0525;
    LocalDateTime date = LocalDateTime.of(2026, 10, 3, 14, 5, 9);

    // simple concatenation
    IO.println(name + " is " + age + " years old");
    // %[-]width: width > 0 aligns right, the - sign aligns left
    IO.println(String.format("[%10s] [%-10s] [%5d]", name, name, age));
    IO.println(String.format("[%12.2f] [%-12.1f] [%,.2f]", salary, salary, salary));
    IO.println(String.format("[%05d] [%X] [%,d] [%e]", age, age, 1234567, salary));
    // the formatted instance method (Java 15): same result
    IO.println("%s is %s".formatted(name, age >= 18 ? "an adult" : "a minor"));

    // currency and percentage: the NumberFormat class
    NumberFormat currency = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    NumberFormat percentage = NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(Locale.FRANCE);
    percentage.setMinimumFractionDigits(2);
    IO.println("[" + currency.format(salary) + "] [" + percentage.format(rate) + "]");

    // dates: the DateTimeFormatter class
    IO.println("[" + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy")) + "] ["
            + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss")) + "] ["
            + date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy")) + "]");

    // an aligned table
    String[] products = {"apple", "pear", "apricot"};
    double[] prices = {2.5, 3.15, 12};
    for (int i = 0; i < products.length; i++) {
        IO.println("%-10s|%8.2f €".formatted(products[i], prices[i]));
    }

    // the \ character must be doubled in a string
    String path = "C:\\data\\courses\\infos.txt";
    IO.println(path);

    // text block (Java 15): delimited by """, on several lines
    String json = """
        {
          "name": "dupont",
          "path": "C:\\data"
        }
        """;
    IO.print(json);
    // a text block with %s and %d placeholders filled by formatted
    String json2 = """
        { "name": "%s", "age": %d }""".formatted(name, age);
    IO.println(json2);
}

Results:

> java Strings04.java
dupont is 45 years old
[    dupont] [dupont    ] [   45]
[     2345.68] [2345.7      ] [2,345.68]
[00045] [2D] [1,234,567] [2.345678e+03]
dupont is an adult
[2 345,68 €] [5,25 %]
[03/10/2026] [14:05:09] [Saturday 3 October 2026]
apple     |    2.50 €
pear      |    3.15 €
apricot   |   12.00 €
C:\data\courses\infos.txt
{
  "name": "dupont",
  "path": "C:\data"
}
{ "name": "dupont", "age": 45 }

Comments:

  • line 12: a width aligns the value to the right within a 10-character field; when preceded by the [-] symbol, it aligns it to the left;
  • Lines 12–14: The most common conversions:
specifierMeaningexample[%s]string; any object is converted using its [toString] methoddupont[%d], [%5d]integer, possibly 5 characters long45[%05d]integer with at least 5 digits, padded with zeros00045[%X]hexadecimal integer ([%x]: in lowercase)2D[%.2f], [%12.2f]real number with 2 decimal places, possibly 12 characters long2345.68[%,.2f], [%,d]same as above, with a thousands separator2,345.68[%e]real number in scientific notation2.345678e+03[%n]system line break [%%]the % character%
  • Numbers are formatted according to the current language, in this case English: decimal point, comma as a thousands separator. In the French formats of lines 19–22, the thousands separator is a space: a thin non-breaking space (character U+202F), which looks like a regular space but prevents a line break in the middle of a number; Similarly, a non-breaking space (U+00A0) precedes the € symbol and the % symbol. This will be taken into account when comparing these texts to strings written with regular spaces;
  • line 16: ["...".formatted(...)] is equivalent to [String.format("...", ...)]. A conditional expression can provide a parameter;
  • lines 19–22: Monetary amounts and percentages are formatted using [java.text.NumberFormat] objects, which are derived for a given language and country ([Locale.FRANCE]). The percentage format multiplies the value by 100;
  • lines 25–27: Dates from the [java.time] API (Java 8) are formatted using a [DateTimeFormatter] object constructed from a template: [dd] day, [MM] month, [yyyy] year, [HH] hour, [mm] minutes, [ss] seconds, [EEEE] day of the week spelled out, [MMMM] month spelled out. Be careful with case: [MM] is the month, [mm] is the minutes. The names of the days and months are those used in everyday language;
  • lines 30–34: the column widths allow data to be displayed in columns;
  • Line 37: In a string, the character [\] introduces an escape sequence ([\n], [\t], [\"]…); to obtain the character [\] itself, you must double it. Java does not have “raw” strings where [\] would be a regular character, which makes writing Windows paths and regular expressions a bit cumbersome;
  • Lines 41–46: A text block (Java 15) is delimited by three quotation marks; the text begins on the line following the opening quotation marks. It can span multiple lines and contain unescaped quotation marks. The indentation common to all lines (that of the least-indented line, counting from the closing quotation marks) is removed: the text JSON is displayed without the code margin. Escape sequences remain active here: [\] must still be doubled (line 44). Since the closing quotation marks are on their own line, the text ends with a line break: hence the use of [IO.print] on line 47 ([IO.println] would add a blank line after the closing curly brace);
  • lines 49–50: Java does not support string interpolation—that is, expressions written directly within the text, such as [${name}] in other languages (a proposal, “String Templates,” was tested as a preview in Java 21 and 22, then removed). With a block of text, placeholders such as [%s], [%d]… are used, filled in by [formatted]. Placing the closing quotation marks at the end of the text prevents a final line break.

There is also the class [java.text.MessageFormat], whose formats refer to parameters by their numbers: [MessageFormat.format("{0} is {1} years old", name, age)]. It is used for messages translated into multiple languages, where the order of parameters may vary from one language to another.

docs.title: 5.2.5. The StringBuilder class
docs.text:
We mentioned that the methods of the [String] class that are applied to a [s1] string return another [s2] string. The [java.lang.StringBuilder] class allows you to modify a string without creating a new string for each operation. This improves performance when constructing a string through many successive additions, by avoiding the proliferation of strings with very short lifespans.

The class supports various constructors:

constructorrole[StringBuilder()]creates an empty object with an initial capacity of 16 characters[StringBuilder(String str)]construct and initialize with [str]; the initial capacity is the length of [str] plus 16[StringBuilder(int capacity)]constructing an empty object with an initial capacity of [capacity] characters

A [StringBuilder] object stores its characters in an array whose size—its capacity—is automatically adjusted as the text grows. The program [Strings05.java] illustrates this concept of capacity:

// size and capacity of a StringBuilder
void main() {
    StringBuilder str = new StringBuilder("test");
    IO.println("size=" + str.length() + ", capacity=" + str.capacity());
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        str.append("test");
        IO.println("size=" + str.length() + ", capacity=" + str.capacity());
    }
    // a StringBuilder with an initial capacity of 10
    StringBuilder str2 = new StringBuilder(10).append("test");
    IO.println("size=" + str2.length() + ", capacity=" + str2.capacity());
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
        str2.append("test");
        IO.println("size=" + str2.length() + ", capacity=" + str2.capacity());
    }
}

Results:

> java Strings05.java
size=4, capacity=20
size=8, capacity=20
size=12, capacity=20
size=16, capacity=20
size=20, capacity=20
size=24, capacity=42
size=28, capacity=42
size=32, capacity=42
size=36, capacity=42
size=40, capacity=42
size=44, capacity=86
size=4, capacity=10
size=8, capacity=10
size=12, capacity=22
size=16, capacity=22
size=20, capacity=22
size=24, capacity=46
size=28, capacity=46
size=32, capacity=46
size=36, capacity=46
size=40, capacity=46
size=44, capacity=46

Comments:

  • line 3: creation of a [StringBuilder] object containing “test”: its initial capacity is 4 + 16 = 20 characters;
  • line 4: [length] is the current number of characters; [capacity] is the number of characters the object can hold before it needs to expand its array;
  • line 6: [append] appends a string to the end of the text;
  • line 10: creation of an empty [StringBuilder] object with an initial capacity of 10, to which “test” is immediately added. The method [append] returns the object itself: it can be called directly on the result of the constructor.

The results show that when the capacity is insufficient, it is slightly more than doubled: the new capacity is the old one multiplied by 2, plus 2 (20, 42, 86 for the first object; 10, 22, 46 for the second). Each resize allocates a new array and copies the characters into it. If the approximate size of the text is known in advance, setting it at construction time avoids these successive resizes.

Here are some of the class’s methods:

methodrole[StringBuilder append(String str)]Add [str] to the end of the text. Overridden to accept the types [int], [double], [char], [boolean], [Object]…[StringBuilder insert(int offset, String str)]Inserts [str] at the position of [offset]; overwritten as [append][StringBuilder delete(int start, int end)]deletes characters from positions [start] (inclusive) to [end] (exclusive); [deleteCharAt] deletes one character[StringBuilder replace(int start, int end, String str)]replaces the characters at positions [start] (inclusive) through [end] (exclusive) with [str][StringBuilder reverse()]reverses the order of the characters[void setCharAt(int index, char ch)]replaces character No. [index] with [ch][int indexOf(String str)]position of [str] in the text, or -1[String toString()]converts the text into a string [String]

The program [Strings06.java] uses them:

// the StringBuilder methods return the StringBuilder object itself: they can be chained
void main() {
    StringBuilder str3 = new StringBuilder("test");
    IO.println(str3.append("abCD").insert(2, "xyZT").delete(0, 2).replace(0, 2, "XY"));
    // reverse reverses the order of the characters
    IO.println(new StringBuilder("éclair").reverse());

    // building a string piece by piece
    StringBuilder lines = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
        lines.append("line ").append(i).append('\n');
    }
    // String.join to add elements separated by a comma
    lines.append(String.join(", ", "a", "b", "c")).append('\n');
    // a formatted string
    int total = 42;
    lines.append("total=%6.1f".formatted((double) total));
    // the final string
    String result = lines.toString();
    IO.println(result);
    IO.println(result.length() + " characters");

    // StringJoiner: separator, prefix and suffix
    StringJoiner joiner = new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]");
    for (String color : new String[]{"red", "green", "blue"}) {
        joiner.add(color);
    }
    IO.println(joiner);
}

Results:

> java Strings06.java
XYZTstabCD
rialcé
line 1
line 2
line 3
a, b, c
total=  42.0
41 characters
[red, green, blue]

Comments:

  • Line 4: The modification methods return the [StringBuilder] object itself, which allows them to be chained together. Let’s follow the steps: “test” becomes “testabCD " ([append]), then “texyZTstabCD” ([insert] in position 2), then “xyZTstabCD " ([delete] for characters 0 and 1), and finally "XYZTstabCD" ([replace] for characters 0 and 1, with "XY"). Note that, unlike the [replace] method of [String], the method of [StringBuilder] does not search for text: it replaces a range of positions. [IO.println] displays the object by calling its method [toString];
  • line 6: [reverse] reverses the text. Since [String] does not have a [reverse] method, this is the standard way to reverse a string;
  • lines 9–12: constructing a multi-line text through successive additions—this is the typical use of [StringBuilder]. The additions are chained together on a single line of code;
  • line 14: [StringBuilder] has no equivalent to [join]: the result of [String.join] is appended;
  • line 17: a formatted string is added. The conversion [%f] requires a real number: passing the integer [total] would throw a [IllegalFormatConversionException] exception at runtime, hence the conversion [(double) total];
  • line 19: the final text is obtained as a string [String];
  • lines 24–28: the class [java.util.StringJoiner] constructs a string consisting of elements separated by a separator, with an optional prefix and suffix. [String.join] performs the same function, without a prefix or suffix.

For a few concatenations, the [+] operator is sufficient: the compiler optimizes them. [StringBuilder] is necessary when the number of additions is large or unknown, typically within a loop: the [s = s + ...] concatenation in a loop with n iterations creates n strings and copies the entire previously constructed string in each iteration. In older code, you’ll find the [StringBuffer] class, which has the same methods as [StringBuilder] but makes them usable simultaneously by multiple threads, at the cost of some performance overhead: today, [StringBuilder] is preferred over it.

docs.title: 5.2.6. Parsing a string without copying it
docs.text:
Each call to [substring] creates a new string in memory. In performance-critical code (such as parsing large files or network requests), you may want to avoid these creations. Java does not have a “view of a string segment” type built into the language, but several methods operate on a portion of a string without copying it. The program [Strings07.java] compares the two ways of parsing a line in the format “last name:first name:age”:

// parsing a string without creating substrings
void main() {
    String line = "dupont:jean:45";

    // with substring: each field is a new string allocated in memory
    int p1 = line.indexOf(':');
    int p2 = line.lastIndexOf(':');
    String lastName = line.substring(0, p1);
    int age = Integer.parseInt(line.substring(p2 + 1));
    IO.println("substring : last name=" + lastName + ", age=" + age);

    // parseInt on part of the string (Java 9): no intermediate string
    age = Integer.parseInt(line, p2 + 1, line.length(), 10);
    // regionMatches compares part of the string to another string, without copying
    boolean du = line.regionMatches(0, "du", 0, 2);
    IO.println("parseInt(line, start, end, radix) : age=" + age + ", the last name starts with \"du\": " + du);

    // a view on part of the string: CharBuffer.wrap does not copy the characters
    CharSequence lastNameView = CharBuffer.wrap(line, 0, p1);
    IO.println("view: last name=" + lastNameView + ", length of the view=" + lastNameView.length()
            + ", lastNameView.charAt(0)=" + lastNameView.charAt(0));

    // indexOf with a search range (Java 21): the ':' searched between p1+1 and the end
    IO.println("indexOf(':', p1 + 1, line.length())=" + line.indexOf(':', p1 + 1, line.length()));

    // a string is only created if it is really needed
    String firstName = line.substring(p1 + 1, p2);
    IO.println("first name=" + firstName);
}

Results:

> java Strings07.java
substring : last name=dupont, age=45
parseInt(line, start, end, radix) : age=45, the last name starts with "du": true
view: last name=dupont, length of the view=6, lastNameView.charAt(0)=d
indexOf(':', p1 + 1, line.length())=11
first name=jean

Comments:

  • lines 8–9: Each call to [substring] creates a new string, even if, as with the age, it is only used for a moment;
  • line 13: an overloaded version of [Integer.parseInt] (Java 9) parses the characters between two positions in the string, relative to the specified base (here 10), without creating a substring;
  • line 15: [regionMatches], which we’ve already encountered, compares a portion of the string to another string without copying it;
  • line 19: [CharBuffer.wrap] (package [java.nio]) returns a view of the characters from 0 to [p1] - 1 in the string: an object that does not contain a copy of the characters, but provides a way to access them. It implements the [CharSequence] interface, just like [String] and [StringBuilder]: many Java methods accept a [CharSequence] ([String.join], [contains], [append], and regular expressions, for example);
  • line 24: an overloaded version of [indexOf] (Java 21) limits the search to a range of positions;
  • line 27: a string is created only if it is actually needed.

These techniques are optimization tools: for an ordinary program, [substring] works perfectly well. Since Java 9, the virtual machine has also been storing strings that contain only characters from the Latin-1 character set (as is the case with French text) at one byte per character instead of two (“compact strings”), which cuts the memory they occupy in half. We’ll only try to avoid copies in code that has been measured to be critical for performance.

docs.title: 5.3.1. The Arrays Class
docs.text:
Java arrays are objects, but they have no useful methods: aside from the [length] field, all operations on arrays are static methods of the utility class [java.util.Arrays]. These methods allow you to sort an array, search for an element in it, copy it, fill it, and so on… Almost all of them are overloaded: there is a version for each primitive type ([int[]], [double[]], [char[]]…) and a version for arrays of objects.

methodrole[static int binarySearch(int[] a, int key)]Returns the position of [key] in [a], which must be sorted; a negative number if [key] is missing[static int[] copyOf(int[] original, int newLength)]returns a new array of [newLength] elements containing the first elements of [original], padded with zeros if necessary ([false] for Booleans, [null] for references)[static int[] copyOfRange(int[] original, int from, int to)]returns a new array consisting of the elements from [from] (inclusive) to [to] (exclusive)[static boolean equals(int[] a, int[] a2)]Returns [true] if both arrays have the same elements in the same order[static void fill(int[] a, int val)]assigns [val] to all elements of [a]; an override fills only a range of indices[static void sort(int[] a)]sorts [a] according to the natural order of its elements; an overload sorts only a range of indices; for an array of objects, an overload receives a [Comparator] that defines the order (Chapter 4)[static String toString(int[] a)]returns the elements of the array as a string [[e1, e2, ...]]; [deepToString] does the same for an array of arrays[static <T> List<T> asList(T... a)]returns a list that is a view of the array of objects [a][static IntStream stream(int[] array)]returns a stream of the array’s elements (see the API Stream section below)

In addition, there is the [System.arraycopy(source, sourceStart, destination, destinationStart, count)] method, which copies elements from one array into another existing array.

The program [Arrays01.java] illustrates the use of certain methods of the [Arrays] class:

// the Arrays class: enlarging, sorting, searching
void main() {
    // reading the elements of an array typed on the keyboard
    double[] elements = input();
    // display of the unsorted array
    display("Unsorted array", elements);
    // linear search in the unsorted array
    search(elements, SearchType.LINEAR);
    // sorting the array
    Arrays.sort(elements);
    // display of the sorted array
    display("Sorted array", elements);
    // binary search in the sorted array
    search(elements, SearchType.BINARY);
}

// input of the values of the array: returns the created array
double[] input() {
    // at the start, the array is empty
    double[] elements = {};
    // input loop for the elements of the array
    while (true) {
        String answer = read("Element (real) " + elements.length + " of the array (nothing to finish): ");
        // end of input if empty string
        if (answer.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
        // checking the input
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(answer);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Incorrect input, try again");
            continue;
        }
        // one more element: the array is enlarged by one cell
        elements = Arrays.copyOf(elements, elements.length + 1);
        // and the new element is stored in it
        elements[elements.length - 1] = element;
    }
    return elements;
}

// display of the elements of an array
void display(String text, double[] elements) {
    IO.println(text + "-".repeat(50 - text.length()));
    for (double element : elements) {
        IO.println(element);
    }
}

// searching the array for elements typed on the keyboard
void search(double[] elements, SearchType type) {
    while (true) {
        String answer = read("Element searched for (nothing to stop): ");
        // finished?
        if (answer.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
        // checking
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(answer);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Error, try again...");
            continue;
        }
        // we search for the element in the array
        int i = type == SearchType.BINARY
                ? Arrays.binarySearch(elements, element)     // sorted array
                : indexOf(elements, element);                 // any array
        // display of the answer
        IO.println(i >= 0 ? "Found at position " + i : "Not in the array (" + i + ")");
    }
}

// linear search: the Arrays class has no indexOf method
int indexOf(double[] elements, double element) {
    for (int i = 0; i < elements.length; i++) {
        if (elements[i] == element) {
            return i;
        }
    }
    return -1;
}

// reading a line on the keyboard, without the surrounding spaces; "" at end of stream
String read(String prompt) {
    String line = IO.readln(prompt);
    return line == null ? "" : line.strip();
}

// search type
enum SearchType { LINEAR, BINARY }

Comments:

  • Lines 18–42: The [input] method enters array elements typed from the keyboard. Since the number of elements is unknown in advance, the program starts with an empty array (line 20) and expands it by one element for each new entry (line 37). The size of a Java array is fixed at creation: [Arrays.copyOf] actually creates a new array, one element larger, and copies the elements from the old one into it. A more efficient algorithm would allocate space in groups of N elements. An array is not designed to be expanded: this scenario is better handled with a list [ArrayList], as we will see shortly;
  • line 39: the last element of an array has the index [length - 1];
  • lines 30–35: the conversion of the entered string to a real number by [Double.parseDouble], which throws an exception [NumberFormatException] if the string is not a number. [Double.parseDouble] is not dependent on the system’s language: it always expects a decimal point and rejects the input “3,6” (line 5 of the results);
  • lines 53–75: The method [search] searches the array for the characters typed on the keyboard. For an unsorted array, a linear search is performed (line 71), which examines the elements one by one. The class [Arrays] does not have a method named [indexOf]: we write it (lines 78–85). For a sorted array, we perform a binary search using [Arrays.binarySearch] (line 70), which halves the search range at each step: it finds an element among one million in about twenty comparisons;
  • line 10: we sort the array. Here we use a variant of [sort] that has only one parameter: the array to be sorted. The ordering relation used to compare the array elements is then the implicit one for those elements: in this case, the natural order of numbers;
  • Lines 45–50: Displaying an array. [IO.println] displays a [double] with a decimal point, regardless of the machine’s language, and always with at least one decimal place: -7 is displayed as -7.0;
  • lines 88–91: [IO.readln] (Java 25) displays a prompt, then reads a line typed on the keyboard; it returns [null] if standard input is exhausted, for example when it comes from a file;
  • line 94: an enumeration, declared in the compact source file just like methods.

Results:

> java Arrays01.java
Element (real) 0 of the array (nothing to finish): 3.6
Element (real) 1 of the array (nothing to finish): 7.4
Element (real) 2 of the array (nothing to finish): -1.5
Element (real) 3 of the array (nothing to finish): 3,6
Incorrect input, try again
Element (real) 3 of the array (nothing to finish): -7
Element (real) 4 of the array (nothing to finish): 
Unsorted array------------------------------------
3.6
7.4
-1.5
-7.0
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 7.4
Found at position 1
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 0
Not in the array (-1)
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 
Sorted array--------------------------------------
-7.0
-1.5
3.6
7.4
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 7.4
Found at position 3
Element searched for (nothing to stop): 0
Not in the array (-3)
Element searched for (nothing to stop):

When the searched-for element is missing, the method [indexOf] returns -1 and [binarySearch] returns a negative number (line 27): this is [-(p + 1)], where p is the position where the element should be inserted to keep the array sorted. Here, -3 = -(2 + 1): the number 0 should be inserted at position 2, between -1.5 and 3.6. Note: [binarySearch] on an unsorted array returns a meaningless result.

docs.title: 5.3.2. Other methods of the Arrays class
docs.text:
The program [Arrays02.java] demonstrates other methods of the [Arrays] class:

// other methods of the Arrays class
void main() {
    int[] numbers = {40, 10, 30, 20, 50};
    display("numbers", Arrays.toString(numbers));

    // sort on part of the array: the elements at indices 1 to 3 (4 excluded)
    Arrays.sort(numbers, 1, 4);
    display("after sort(numbers, 1, 4)", Arrays.toString(numbers));

    // copy of 3 elements into another array
    int[] copy = new int[5];
    System.arraycopy(numbers, 0, copy, 0, 3);
    display("arraycopy", Arrays.toString(copy));
    // copyOf, copyOfRange: the copy is a new array, shortened or padded with 0s
    display("copyOf(numbers, 7)", Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOf(numbers, 7)));
    display("copyOfRange(numbers, 1, 3)", Arrays.toString(Arrays.copyOfRange(numbers, 1, 3)));

    // fill: fills the array, or part of the array, with a value
    Arrays.fill(copy, 7);
    display("after fill(copy, 7)", Arrays.toString(copy));
    Arrays.fill(copy, 1, 3, 0);
    display("after fill(copy, 1, 3, 0)", Arrays.toString(copy));

    // equality of two arrays: == compares the references, Arrays.equals the contents
    int[] other = {7, 0, 0, 7, 7};
    IO.println("copy == other : " + (copy == other) + ", Arrays.equals(copy, other) : "
            + Arrays.equals(copy, other));

    // an array of objects seen as a list: indexOf, lastIndexOf, reverse
    String[] colors = {"red", "green", "blue", "green"};
    List<String> view = Arrays.asList(colors);
    IO.println("indexOf(green)=" + view.indexOf("green") + ", lastIndexOf(green)=" + view.lastIndexOf("green")
            + ", indexOf(black)=" + view.indexOf("black"));
    // the list is a view on the array: reversing the list reverses the array
    Collections.reverse(view);
    display("after reverse", Arrays.toString(colors));

    // sorting an array of strings: order of the character codes
    String[] words = {"essay", "Zoé", "éclair", "apricot"};
    Arrays.sort(words);
    display("sorted words", Arrays.toString(words));
    // sorting according to the rules of the French language
    Arrays.sort(words, Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE));
    display("sorted words (Collator)", Arrays.toString(words));

    // a two-dimensional array is an array of arrays
    int[][] matrix = new int[2][3];
    matrix[1][2] = 5;
    IO.println("matrix.length=" + matrix.length + ", matrix[0].length=" + matrix[0].length
            + ", deepToString=" + Arrays.deepToString(matrix));
}

// display of a text and an array on one line
void display(String text, String array) {
    IO.println("%-28s: %s".formatted(text, array));
}

Results:

> java Arrays02.java
numbers                     : [40, 10, 30, 20, 50]
after sort(numbers, 1, 4)   : [40, 10, 20, 30, 50]
arraycopy                   : [40, 10, 20, 0, 0]
copyOf(numbers, 7)          : [40, 10, 20, 30, 50, 0, 0]
copyOfRange(numbers, 1, 3)  : [10, 20]
after fill(copy, 7)         : [7, 7, 7, 7, 7]
after fill(copy, 1, 3, 0)   : [7, 0, 0, 7, 7]
copy == other : false, Arrays.equals(copy, other) : true
indexOf(green)=1, lastIndexOf(green)=3, indexOf(black)=-1
after reverse               : [green, blue, green, red]
sorted words                : [Zoé, apricot, essay, éclair]
sorted words (Collator)     : [apricot, éclair, essay, Zoé]
matrix.length=2, matrix[0].length=3, deepToString=[[0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 5]]

Comments:

  • Line 4: [Arrays.toString] displays a table on a single line. Displaying an array directly with [IO.println(numbers)] would result in text similar to [[I@1b6d3586]]: the type ([[I]], array of integers) and an object identifier, without its elements;
  • line 7: only elements with indices 1 through 3 are sorted, with the second index excluded: 10, 30, 20 become 10, 20, 30;
  • line 12: copies the first 3 elements of [numbers] to the beginning of [copy], while the other elements retain their initial value of 0;
  • lines 15–16: [copyOf] and [copyOfRange] create a new array. An array longer than the original is padded with zeros;
  • lines 19–22: [fill] fills the array, then resets the elements at indices 1 and 2 (excluding 3) to 0;
  • lines 25–27: As with strings, the operator [==] compares the references of two arrays, not their contents: [Arrays.equals] must be used;
  • line 31: [Arrays.asList] returns a [List] (presented in the following section), which is a view of an array of objects: it does not copy the array but provides access to it using list methods. This yields [indexOf] and [lastIndexOf] (line 32);
  • line 35: the method [Collections.reverse] reverses the order of the elements in a list. Since the list is a view of the array, it is the array itself that is reversed (line 11 of the results). The class [Arrays] does not have a reversal method; this process applies only to arrays of objects, not to arrays of primitive types such as [int[]];
  • line 40: an array of strings is sorted according to the order of the [compareTo] method described above, that is, by character codes: uppercase letters (codes 65 through 90) come before lowercase letters (97 through 122), which come before accented letters (é: 233). “Zoé” is the first word and “éclair” is the last;
  • line 43: to sort according to French rules, we pass an object of type [Collator]—which compares strings—to [sort];
  • Lines 47–50: Java does not have two-dimensional rectangular arrays: [new int[2][3]] creates an array of 2 elements, each of which is an array of 3 integers. [matrix.length] is the number of rows, and [matrix[0].length] is the number of elements in row 0. [Arrays.deepToString] displays an array of arrays.

The API Stream, which we will discuss later, offers other ways to search, sort, or transform the elements of an array, for example, [Arrays.stream(numbers).sum()].

docs.title: 5.4. Collections
docs.text:
In addition to arrays, Java provides various classes for storing collections of elements. These form the Collections Framework in the [java.util] package, which was introduced in Java 1.2 and made generic in Java 5. It is organized around interfaces, which describe what a collection does, and classes that implement them, each in its own way:

interfaceroleMain Implementations[List<E>]an ordered sequence of elements, accessible by their position[ArrayList], [LinkedList][Set<E>]a set: no duplicates[HashSet], [LinkedHashSet], [TreeSet][Map<K,V>]a dictionary: (key, value) pairs, where the keys are unique[HashMap], [LinkedHashMap], [TreeMap][Deque<E>]a double-ended queue, usable as a queue or a stack[ArrayDeque], [LinkedList][Queue<E>]a queue[ArrayDeque], [PriorityQueue]

The interfaces [List], [Set], and [Queue] are derived from the interface [Collection<E>] ([size], [isEmpty], [contains], [add], [remove], [clear]…), which itself derives from [Iterable<E>], the interface for objects that can be iterated over using a loop [for]. Best practice is to declare variables and parameters using the interface type and to use the class name only at creation time: [List<String> cities = new ArrayList<>();]. This allows you to change the implementation without modifying the rest of the code.

A Java collection contains only objects. Java generics do not support primitive types: you do not write [List<int>] but rather [List<Integer>], where [Integer] is the wrapper class for the type [int] (similarly, [Double] for [double], [Boolean] for [boolean]…). The compiler automatically converts a [int] to [Integer] during an assignment (“autoboxing”) and a [Integer] into a [int] during a read (“unboxing”). This conversion incurs a cost in terms of memory and time: a list of one million integers contains one million [Integer] objects. For large volumes of numbers, it is preferable to use a [int[]] array or the primitive streams ([IntStream]) introduced with the API Stream.

The [java.util] package also contains the Java 1.0 collections: [Vector] (a list), [Hashtable] (a dictionary), and [Stack] (a stack). These are now obsolete: since they are synchronized on every operation, they are slower than their replacements [ArrayList], [HashMap], and [ArrayDeque]. They should no longer be used in new code. Similarly, avoid “raw types”—that is, generic collections used without type parameters ([List list = new ArrayList();])—as was done before Java 5: the compiler can no longer verify the type of the added elements and issues a warning for each use.

docs.title: 5.4.1. The List interface and the ArrayList class
docs.text:
The class [java.util.ArrayList<E>] implements a list of objects of type [E] whose size varies during program execution. It stores its elements in an internal array that it automatically resizes, just like [StringBuilder]. Element i of a [l] list is retrieved by [l.get(i)] and modified by [l.set(i, value)].

Here are some of the methods of the [List<E>] interface:

methodrole[int size()]number of items in the list[boolean add(E e)]Adds [e] to the end of the list[void add(int index, E element)]Insert [element] at position [index] in the list[boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c)]adds the items from [c] to the end of the list[E get(int index)], [E set(int index, E element)]reads and replaces element No. [index][E getFirst()], [E getLast()]the first and last elements (Java 21)[void clear()]deletes all elements from the list[boolean contains(Object o)]returns [true] if [o] is in the list, [false] otherwise[int indexOf(Object o)]returns the position of [o] in the list, or -1 if [o] is not found; [lastIndexOf] returns the last position[boolean remove(Object o)]deletes the first occurrence of [o]; returns [true] if the operation succeeds, [false] otherwise[E remove(int index)]deletes element No. [index] and returns[List<E> subList(int from, int to)]returns a view of the elements from [from] (inclusive) to [to] (exclusive)[void sort(Comparator<? super E> c)]sorts the list according to the order defined by [c]; [sort(null)] uses the natural order of the elements[<T> T[] toArray(IntFunction<T[]> generator)]returns the list elements as an array (Java 11)[static <E> List<E> of(E... elements)]creates an immutable list containing the given elements (Java 9)

The utility class [java.util.Collections] complements these methods, just as [Arrays] does for arrays: [sort], [binarySearch], [reverse], [shuffle], [max], [min]…

Let’s revisit the example we covered earlier using an array and now process it using an object of type [ArrayList<Double>]. Since a list is similar to an array, the code changes very little. This is the program [Collections01.java]:

// the ArrayList class: the Arrays01.java program rewritten with a list
void main() {
    // reading the elements of a list typed on the keyboard
    List<Double> elements = input();
    // number of elements
    IO.println("The list has " + elements.size() + " elements");
    // display of the unsorted list
    display("Unsorted list", elements);
    // linear search in the unsorted list
    search(elements, SearchType.LINEAR);
    // sorting the list according to the natural order of its elements
    Collections.sort(elements);
    // display of the sorted list
    display("Sorted list", elements);
    // binary search in the sorted list
    search(elements, SearchType.BINARY);
}

// input of the values of the list: returns the created list
List<Double> input() {
    // at the start, the list is empty
    List<Double> elements = new ArrayList<>();
    // input loop for the elements of the list
    while (true) {
        String answer = read("Element (real) " + elements.size() + " of the list (nothing to finish): ");
        // end of input if empty string
        if (answer.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
        // checking the input
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(answer);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Incorrect input, try again");
            continue;
        }
        // one more element in the list: it grows by itself
        elements.add(element);
    }
    return elements;
}

// generic method to display the elements of any collection
<T> void display(String text, Iterable<T> elements) {
    IO.println(text + "-".repeat(50 - text.length()));
    for (T element : elements) {
        IO.println(element);
    }
}

// searching the list for elements typed on the keyboard
void search(List<Double> elements, SearchType type) {
    while (true) {
        String answer = read("Element searched for (nothing to stop): ");
        // finished?
        if (answer.isEmpty()) {
            break;
        }
        // checking
        double element;
        try {
            element = Double.parseDouble(answer);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            IO.println("Error, try again...");
            continue;
        }
        // we search for the element in the list
        int i = type == SearchType.BINARY
                ? Collections.binarySearch(elements, element)    // sorted list
                : elements.indexOf(element);                      // any list
        // display of the answer
        IO.println(i >= 0 ? "Found at position " + i : "Not in the list (" + i + ")");
    }
}

// reading a line on the keyboard, without the surrounding spaces; "" at end of stream
String read(String prompt) {
    String line = IO.readln(prompt);
    return line == null ? "" : line.strip();
}

// search type
enum SearchType { LINEAR, BINARY }

Comments:

  • line 22: the list is created empty. The diamond operator [<>] (Java 7) avoids repeating the element type: the compiler infers it from the variable’s type;
  • line 39: there is no longer any need to handle list expansion; the list expands automatically. The value [element], of type [double], is automatically converted to a [Double] object;
  • line 6: the number of elements in the list. Unlike [StringBuilder], [ArrayList] does not allow you to determine its capacity; the [ensureCapacity] method only allows you to set it in advance;
  • lines 12, 70, 71: sorting and binary search are performed using the static methods [Collections.sort] and [Collections.binarySearch]; linear search using the [indexOf] method on the list, which the arrays did not have;
  • Lines 45–50: The generic method [display] accepts two parameters:
    • the first is the text to be written;
    • the second is an object that implements the generic interface [java.lang.Iterable<T>], whose only abstract method is [Iterator<T> iterator()].

The loop [for (T element : elements)] is valid for any [elements] object that implements the [Iterable<T>] interface, as well as for arrays. All collections implement [Iterable]; arrays, however, do not implement it, and the [display] method is not suitable for an array: this is why we did not use it in [Arrays01.java]. We will revisit this interface with the API Stream.
