For common operations, the utility class [Files] eliminates the need to handle streams: a single method opens the file, reads or writes it in its entirety, and then closes it. It also allows you to create, copy, move, and delete files and folders. The [Path] interface handles paths.

Methodrole[Files.readString(path)]returns the file’s contents as a string (Java 11)[Files.readAllLines(path)]returns the lines of the file in a list [List<String>][Files.lines(path)]Returns the lines of the file as a stream ([Stream<String>]) that is read on demand and must be closed after use[Files.writeString(path, text, options...)]creates (or overwrites) the file and writes [text] (Java 11) to it; with the [StandardOpenOption.APPEND] option, appends the text to the end of the file[Files.write(path, lines, options...)]writes a collection of lines, each followed by a newline[Files.readAllBytes(path)], [Files.write(path, bytes)]reads and writes the file as a byte array[Files.exists(path)], [Files.size(path)], [Files.delete(path)], [Files.copy(source, target)], [Files.move(source, target)]checks if a file exists, returns its size, deletes it, copies it, moves it[Files.createDirectories(path)]creates the folder and its parent folders if they do not exist[Files.list(folder)], [Files.walk(folder)]the elements of the folder and its entire tree structure, in the form of a stream [Stream<Path>][path.resolve(other)]builds a path by appending [other] to [path], using the system separator[path.getFileName()], [path.getParent()], [path.toAbsolutePath()]the file name, its folder, and its full path

The program [Files03.java] uses them:

// the Path and Files classes
void main() throws IOException {
    // resolve builds a path with the system separator (\ on Windows, / on Linux)
    Path folder = Path.of("data");
    Path path = folder.resolve("cities.txt");
    String name = path.getFileName().toString();
    IO.println("path=" + path + ", name=" + name + ", folder=" + path.getParent()
            + ", without extension=" + name.substring(0, name.lastIndexOf('.')));

    // createDirectories creates the folder (and its parents) if it does not exist
    Files.createDirectories(folder);

    // writeString: creates (or overwrites) a file with the given text, in UTF-8
    Files.writeString(path, "Angers\nNantes\n");
    // write with the APPEND option: adds lines at the end of the file
    Files.write(path, List.of("Paris", "Lyon"), StandardOpenOption.APPEND);
    // readAllLines: all the lines in a list
    List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(path);
    IO.println("readAllLines : " + lines.size() + " lines " + lines);
    // readString: the whole file in a string
    IO.println("readString : " + Files.readString(path).length() + " characters");
    // lines: a stream of lines read on demand, to be closed after use
    try (Stream<String> stream = Files.lines(path)) {
        stream.filter(l -> l.startsWith("N") || l.startsWith("L"))
                .forEach(city -> IO.println("lines + filter : " + city));
    }

    // the encoding: UTF-8 by default; another one can be imposed
    String text = "café";
    Files.writeString(folder.resolve("utf8.txt"), text);
    Files.writeString(folder.resolve("utf8bom.txt"), "\uFEFF" + text);
    Files.writeString(folder.resolve("latin1.txt"), text, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1);
    HexFormat hex = HexFormat.of().withUpperCase();
    for (String file : List.of("utf8.txt", "utf8bom.txt", "latin1.txt")) {
        byte[] bytes = Files.readAllBytes(folder.resolve(file));
        IO.println("%-12s: %2d bytes: %s".formatted(file, bytes.length, hex.formatHex(bytes)));
    }
    // a Latin-1 file read back in UTF-8: readString rejects invalid bytes
    Path latin1 = folder.resolve("latin1.txt");
    try {
        IO.println(Files.readString(latin1));
    } catch (MalformedInputException e) {
        IO.println("latin1.txt read as UTF-8: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
    // new String(bytes, UTF_8) replaces each invalid byte with the � character
    IO.println("latin1.txt decoded as UTF-8: "
            + new String(Files.readAllBytes(latin1), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    IO.println("latin1.txt read as Latin-1: " + Files.readString(latin1, StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1));
    // the BOM is not removed when reading: it is one more character
    IO.println("utf8bom.txt : " + Files.readString(folder.resolve("utf8bom.txt")).length() + " characters");

    // exists, list
    IO.println("exists(cities.txt)=" + Files.exists(path) + ", exists(xx.txt)="
            + Files.exists(folder.resolve("xx.txt")));
    try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(folder)) {
        for (Path file : files.sorted().toList()) {
            IO.println("  %-12s %3d bytes".formatted(file.getFileName(), Files.size(file)));
        }
    }

    // cleanup: a folder must be empty to be deleted; its content is deleted first
    try (Stream<Path> tree = Files.walk(folder)) {
        for (Path p : tree.sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).toList()) {
            Files.delete(p);
        }
    }
    IO.println("after deletion: exists(data)=" + Files.exists(folder));
}

Results:

> java Files03.java
path=data/cities.txt, name=cities.txt, folder=data, without extension=cities
readAllLines : 4 lines [Angers, Nantes, Paris, Lyon]
readString : 25 characters
lines + filter : Nantes
lines + filter : Lyon
utf8.txt    :  5 bytes: 636166C3A9
utf8bom.txt :  8 bytes: EFBBBF636166C3A9
latin1.txt  :  4 bytes: 636166E9
latin1.txt read as UTF-8: MalformedInputException : Input length = 1
latin1.txt decoded as UTF-8: caf�
latin1.txt read as Latin-1: café
utf8bom.txt : 5 characters
exists(cities.txt)=true, exists(xx.txt)=false
  cities.txt    25 bytes
  latin1.txt     4 bytes
  utf8.txt       5 bytes
  utf8bom.txt    8 bytes
after deletion: exists(data)=false

Comments:

  • Line 2: The methods in [Files] throw [IOException]. To keep this demo program lightweight, the [main] method declares them using the [throws IOException] clause instead of intercepting them: an error would terminate the program and display the exception;
  • Lines 4–8: [resolve] uses the system’s path separator. The course runs were performed on Linux: the resulting path is [data/cities.txt]; on Windows, it would be [data\cities.txt]. Building paths using [resolve] (or [Path.of("data", "cities.txt")]) rather than concatenating strings makes the code portable. Since [Path] does not have a method that returns a file extension, it is separated from the name using [lastIndexOf];
  • Line 11: Creating the folder [data] does not cause an error if it already exists;
  • Lines 14–21: writing, adding, and reading, each in a single statement;
  • Lines 23–26: [Files.lines] returns a stream: the lines are read one by one as the program processes them. You can apply the API stream to it, and thus process a file several gigabytes in size without loading it into memory, which is what [readAllLines] would do. The stream keeps the file open: it must be closed, hence the [try] instruction with resources ([Stream] implements [AutoCloseable]);
  • lines 29–37: the same text “café” is written using three encodings, then the bytes in the files are displayed in hexadecimal using the [HexFormat] class (Java 17):
    • In UTF-8, Java’s default encoding, accented characters take up 2 bytes (é = C3 A9) and the others 1 byte: 5 bytes for 4 characters;
    • in UTF-8 with BOM (Byte Order Mark), the file begins with the 3 bytes EF BB BF, which signal to software that the file is encoded in UTF-8. Java never writes BOM on its own: it is obtained by writing the character U+FEFF at the beginning of the text, denoted as ["\uFEFF"];
    • in Latin-1 (ISO-8859-1), the traditional encoding for Western European texts, each character occupies one byte (é = E9);
  • Lines 39–44: Reading a file using an encoding different from the one used to write it alters accented characters: the byte E9 at the end of the file is invalid in UTF-8. [Files.readString] and [Files.readAllLines] reject such a file by throwing a [MalformedInputException] exception (derived from [IOException]);
  • Lines 46–47: The conversion of a byte array to a string by the [new String(bytes, encoding)] constructor is less strict: each invalid byte is replaced by the character �. A [InputStreamReader] behaves the same way; in contrast, the [BufferedReader] returned by [Files.newBufferedReader] is strict, like [Files.readString], and also throws a [MalformedInputException];
  • line 48: when read with the correct encoding, the file is correct;
  • line 50: Upon reading, Java does not recognize the BOM: it is read as an invisible character at the beginning of the text, which has 5 characters instead of 4. If you need to read UTF-8 files generated with a BOM (by certain Windows software), you must remove this character yourself. Today, the rule is simple: write and read text files in UTF-8, without BOM;
  • lines 53–59: the files in the folder. [Files.list] returns a stream that must be closed, just like the one for [Files.lines], and does not guarantee the order of the names: [sorted] sorts them;
  • lines 62–67: deleting the folder. [Files.delete] refuses to delete a non-empty folder: we traverse the entire directory tree using [Files.walk], and sort the paths in reverse order ([Comparator.reverseOrder()]) to delete a folder’s contents before the folder itself.

The methods of [Files] block the thread that calls them until the operation is complete. In Chapter 9, which covers asynchronous programming, we’ll see how to avoid blocking a program during a long I/O operation.

docs.title: 5.7.1. The DataOutputStream and DataInputStream classes
docs.text:
The classes [java.io.DataOutputStream] and [java.io.DataInputStream] are used to write to and read from binary files. In such a file, data is not written as text but in its internal form: a [int] always occupies 4 bytes, regardless of its value. These are byte streams: they are derived from the classes [OutputStream] and [InputStream], whereas text streams are derived from [Writer] and [Reader].

Consider the following application:

// syntax: java Files04.java text binary logs
// we read a text file (text) and store its content in a binary file (binary)
// the text file has lines of the form name : age which are written as (String, int)
// (logs) is a text file of logs

The text file [persons1.txt] has the following content:

paul : 10
helene : 15

jacques : 11
sylvain : 12
xx : -1

xx: yy : zz
xx : yy

The program [Files04.java] is as follows:

// syntax: java Files04.java text binary logs
// we read a text file (text) and store its content in a binary file (binary)
// the text file has lines of the form name : age which are written as (String, int)
// (logs) is a text file of logs
void main(String[] args) {
    // 3 arguments are needed
    if (args.length != 3) {
        IO.println("syntax: java Files04.java text binary logs");
        System.exit(1);
    }
    // opening the three files; they will be closed at the end of the try, in reverse order
    try (BufferedReader input = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of(args[0]));
         DataOutputStream output = new DataOutputStream(
                 new BufferedOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(Path.of(args[1]))));
         PrintWriter logs = new PrintWriter(Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of(args[2])))) {
        // processing the text file
        String line;
        int lineNumber = 0, nbPersons = 0;
        while ((line = input.readLine()) != null) {
            // one more line
            lineNumber++;
            // empty line? it is ignored
            if (line.isBlank()) {
                continue;
            }
            // a name : age line
            String[] fields = line.strip().split("\\s*:\\s*");
            // we need 2 fields
            if (fields.length != 2) {
                logs.println("Line no. [" + lineNumber + "] of the file [" + args[0]
                        + "] has an incorrect number of fields");
                continue;
            }
            // the 1st field must not be empty
            boolean error = false;
            String name = fields[0];
            if (name.isEmpty()) {
                logs.println("Line no. [" + lineNumber + "] of the file [" + args[0] + "] has an empty name");
                error = true;
            }
            // the second field must be an integer >= 0
            int age = integer(fields[1]);
            if (age < 0) {
                logs.println("Line no. [" + lineNumber + "] of the file [" + args[0] + "] has an incorrect age ["
                        + fields[1] + "]");
                error = true;
            }
            // if no error, the data is written to the binary file
            if (!error) {
                output.writeUTF(name);
                output.writeInt(age);
                nbPersons++;
            }
        }
        IO.println(lineNumber + " lines read, " + nbPersons + " persons written to [" + args[1]
                + "], errors in [" + args[2] + "]");
    } catch (NoSuchFileException e) {
        IO.println("The file [" + e.getFile() + "] does not exist");
        System.exit(2);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("The following error occurred: " + e);
        System.exit(3);
    }
}

// a positive or zero integer, -1 if the string is not one
int integer(String field) {
    try {
        return Integer.parseInt(field);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        return -1;
    }
}

Let’s take a closer look at the operations related to class [DataOutputStream]:

  • Lines 13–14: The [DataOutputStream] object is built around another byte stream, following the principle of nested streams (the “decorator” design pattern):
    • [Files.newOutputStream(Path.of(args[1]))] writes a byte stream to the file, which is created or flushed if it already exists;
    • [BufferedOutputStream] adds a buffer to it, so as not to access the disk with every write;
    • [DataOutputStream] adds methods for writing basic data types;
  • Lines 50–51: the write operations. The [DataOutputStream] class has one method per simple data type: [writeInt], [writeDouble], [writeLong], [writeBoolean], [writeUTF] for a string…;
  • Lines 12–15: The three streams are opened in a single [try] statement with resources, with their declarations separated by semicolons. They will be closed at the end of the [try] block, in the reverse order in which they were opened. Closing the outer stream ([DataOutputStream]) closes the streams it contains. The log file is written via a [PrintWriter], to make use of the [println] method;
  • line 27: the separator is the character [:], surrounded by any spaces, which are removed along with it;
  • Lines 42–47: The age must be a positive integer or zero. Java does not have a method that converts a string to an integer without throwing an exception in case of an error: the method [integer] (lines 67–73) catches the exception [NumberFormatException] and returns -1, which is an invalid value for an age;
  • lines 9, 59, 62: [System.exit(n)] terminates the program with exit code n, which a script can check (0: success; this is the exit code of a program whose [main] method terminates normally).

The program’s three arguments are passed after the source file name in the [java] command. The results are as follows:

> java Files04.java persons1.txt persons1.bin logs.txt
9 lines read, 4 persons written to [persons1.bin], errors in [logs.txt]

The log file [logs.txt] has the following content:

> cat logs.txt
Line no. [6] of the file [persons1.txt] has an incorrect age [-1]
Line no. [8] of the file [persons1.txt] has an incorrect number of fields
Line no. [9] of the file [persons1.txt] has an incorrect age [yy]

The contents of the binary file [persons1.bin] can be displayed in hexadecimal using the Linux command [od] (on Windows, the command PowerShell [Format-Hex] produces a similar display):

> od -A d -t x1z persons1.bin
0000000 00 04 70 61 75 6c 00 00 00 0a 00 06 68 65 6c 65  >..paul......hele<
0000016 6e 65 00 00 00 0f 00 07 6a 61 63 71 75 65 73 00  >ne......jacques.<
0000032 00 00 0b 00 07 73 79 6c 76 61 69 6e 00 00 00 0c  >.....sylvain....<
0000048

This shows how [DataOutputStream] writes the data:

  • a string is written by [writeUTF], preceded by its length in bytes, on 2 bytes: 00 04, followed by the 4 bytes of “paul” (70 61 75 6c). The characters are encoded using a variant of UTF-8;
  • an integer [int] is written over 4 bytes, with the most significant byte first (known as “big-endian” order, used in network protocols): 10 is written as 00 00 00 0a. This format is the same on all machines: a file written by [DataOutputStream] on Windows can be read on Linux;
  • the data is written consecutively, without any separators or line breaks: the file is 48 bytes long (line 5: with the [-A d] option, [od] displays the positions in decimal).

To read this file, you must therefore know the exact order and type of the written data. For each method [writeXX] of [DataOutputStream], the class [DataInputStream] has a corresponding method [readXX]: [readUTF], [readInt], [readDouble]… However, it cannot indicate how many bytes remain to be read: a file read by [DataInputStream] must begin with the number of records it contains, or be read until the [EOFException] exception occurs, which signals the end of the stream. However, an exception must remain exceptional, and the end of a file is not.

docs.title: 5.7.2. The RandomAccessFile class
docs.text:
The [java.io.RandomAccessFile] class reads from and writes to a file using direct access: you can position the read/write head at any location in the file before reading or writing. It has the same read and write methods as [DataInputStream] and [DataOutputStream] (it implements the same interfaces, [DataInput] and [DataOutput]), and additionally:

methodrole[RandomAccessFile(String name, String mode)]opens the file for reading ([mode] "r") or for reading and writing ("rw")[long length()]the file size, in bytes[long getFilePointer()]the current position in the file[void seek(long pos)]moves to position [pos] in the file

The program [Files05.java] performs the reverse operation of the previous program: it reads the binary file to create a text file. If the resulting text file contains the correct data from the original file, we will know that the text → binary → text conversion was successful.

// syntax: java Files05.java binary text
// we read a binary file (binary) and store its content in a text file (text)
// the binary file contains (String, int) pairs
// the text file will have lines of the form name:age
void main(String[] args) {
    // 2 arguments are needed
    if (args.length != 2) {
        IO.println("syntax: java Files05.java binary text");
        System.exit(1);
    }
    // opening the binary file for reading ("r") and the text file for writing
    try (RandomAccessFile input = new RandomAccessFile(args[0], "r");
         PrintWriter output = new PrintWriter(Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of(args[1])))) {
        // processing the binary file, as long as we are not at the end of the file
        int nbPersons = 0;
        while (input.getFilePointer() < input.length()) {
            // reading name, then age: in the order in which they were written
            String name = input.readUTF();
            int age = input.readInt();
            // writing to the text file
            output.println(name + ":" + age);
            nbPersons++;
        }
        IO.println(nbPersons + " persons read from [" + args[0] + "] and written to [" + args[1] + "]");
        // direct access: back to the start of the file and re-reading of the first person
        input.seek(0);
        IO.println("first person: " + input.readUTF() + ", " + input.readInt() + " years old");
    } catch (EOFException e) {
        // the file ends in the middle of a record
        IO.println("The file [" + args[0] + "] is truncated");
        System.exit(2);
    } catch (FileNotFoundException e) {
        // RandomAccessFile reports a missing file with a FileNotFoundException
        IO.println(e.getMessage());
        System.exit(3);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("The following error occurred: " + e);
        System.exit(4);
    }
}

Let’s take a closer look at the operations involving the [RandomAccessFile] class:

  • line 12: the [RandomAccessFile] object is opened in read-only mode (“r” mode);
  • lines 18–19: the read operations, [readUTF] and [readInt]. They must be called in the order of the writes;
  • line 16: reading continues until the current position in the file reaches the end of the file;
  • lines 26–27: direct access: [seek] resets the position to the beginning of the file, and the first record is read again. If all records were the same size, we could read the nth record directly by moving to position n × size: this is the principle behind direct-access files, the precursors to databases;
  • line 28: the exception [EOFException] now signals a true anomaly: a file that ends in the middle of a record;
  • line 32: [RandomAccessFile], a subclass of [java.io], signals a missing file via a [FileNotFoundException], whose message—provided by the system—contains the file name.

Let’s run the program on the [persons1.bin] file generated earlier:

> java Files05.java persons1.bin persons2.txt
4 persons read from [persons1.bin] and written to [persons2.txt]
first person: paul, 10 years old

The contents of [persons2.txt] are as follows:

> cat persons2.txt
paul:10
helene:15
jacques:11
sylvain:12

We find the 4 valid people from the file [persons1.txt]. With a file [truncated.bin] consisting of the first 33 bytes of [persons1.bin], reading Jacques’s age fails:

> java Files05.java truncated.bin truncated.txt
The file [truncated.bin] is truncated

And with a nonexistent file:

> java Files05.java xx.bin xx.txt
xx.bin (No such file or directory)

Java also has a mechanism for binary serialization of objects: the classes *[ObjectOutputStream] and [ObjectInputStream] write and read entire objects, provided that their class implements the *[java.io.Serializable] interface. This mechanism is now deprecated: deserializing data from an untrusted source has enabled numerous attacks, as deserialization can execute code chosen by the attacker. A text-based format such as JSON is preferred instead. However, the [Serializable] interface is still found in many classes, particularly exceptions, which inherit it from the [Throwable] class: which is why the compiler, when using the [-Xlint:all] option, requires that they declare a [serialVersionUID] field, as we will see in the sample application.

docs.title: 5.7.3. JSON Serialization with Jackson
docs.text:
Writing to and reading from a binary file one data point at a time is tedious, and even the slightest discrepancy between writing and reading produces incorrect results. It is generally preferable to serialize objects: automatically converting them into a sequence of characters, then deserializing them to reconstruct them.

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text-based, human-readable, and universal format: it is the exchange format for web services (Chapter 13) and many configuration files. An object is written within curly braces as pairs of "property": value, or as an array enclosed in square brackets.

The Java standard library cannot read or write JSON. An external library is used; the most common one is Jackson, which Spring Boot uses by default. Version 3 (2025) has changed packages: [tools.jackson.*] instead of [com.fasterxml.jackson.*] for version 2, which is still commonly encountered; its annotations remain in the [com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation] package. An external library is obtained using Maven (Chapter 2): the program is therefore a Maven project, [Files06], with the following directory structure:

05-classes-java/
  Files06/
    pom.xml
    src/main/java/json/
      Files06.java

The file [pom.xml] declares the dependency on Jackson:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>examples.classes</groupId>
    <artifactId>files06</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Jackson 3: JSON serialization -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>tools.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>3.1.5</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.15.0</version>
                <configuration>
                    <parameters>true</parameters>
                    <compilerArgs>
                        <arg>-Xlint:all</arg>
                    </compilerArgs>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
            <!-- mvn exec:java runs the main class -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.5.1</version>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>json.Files06</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>

Comments:

  • lines 7–9: the project details;
  • lines 11–14: the Java version and the encoding of the source files;
  • lines 16–23: the dependency on the [jackson-databind] library. Maven downloads it from the central repository (Maven Central), along with the libraries on which it itself depends ([jackson-core] and [jackson-annotations]);
  • lines 27–37: the compiler, configured as in all projects in the course: warnings enabled ([-Xlint:all]) and parameter names preserved in the compiled code;
  • lines 39–46: the plugin [exec-maven-plugin], which executes the main class using the command [mvn exec:java].

The central object in Jackson is [JsonMapper], which has two main methods:

methodrole[String writeValueAsString(Object value)]returns the text JSON representing the object [value][<T> T readValue(String content, Class<T> valueType)]reconstructs an object of type [T] from the text JSON [content]; throws a [JacksonException] if the text is incorrect. An overload receives a [TypeReference] instead of a [Class]

The program [Files06.java] uses them:

package json;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonProperty;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import tools.jackson.core.JacksonException;
import tools.jackson.core.json.JsonWriteFeature;
import tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference;
import tools.jackson.databind.MapperFeature;
import tools.jackson.databind.SerializationFeature;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

// JSON serialization with Jackson 3
public class Files06 {

    // a person: a record, whose components become the JSON properties
    record Person(String name, int age, List<String> hobbies) {
    }

    // an article: the @JsonProperty annotation sets the name of the JSON property
    record Article(@JsonProperty("reference") String code, BigDecimal price) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        List<Person> persons = List.of(
                new Person("paul", 10, List.of("football")),
                new Person("hélène", 15, List.of("piano", "tennis")),
                new Person("jacques", 11, List.of()));

        // 1 - a JsonMapper with the default configuration: a single line
        JsonMapper mapper = JsonMapper.builder().build();
        String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(persons.get(1));
        IO.println("[default] " + json);
        // non-ASCII characters can be escaped
        JsonMapper ascii = JsonMapper.builder().enable(JsonWriteFeature.ESCAPE_NON_ASCII).build();
        IO.println("[ESCAPE_NON_ASCII] " + ascii.writeValueAsString(persons.get(1)));

        // 2 - an option: indentation
        JsonMapper indented = JsonMapper.builder().enable(SerializationFeature.INDENT_OUTPUT).build();
        json = indented.writeValueAsString(persons);
        // writing to a text file
        Path file = Path.of("persons.json");
        Files.writeString(file, json);
        IO.println("[persons.json]");
        IO.println(Files.readString(file));

        // 3 - deserialization: from JSON text to objects
        String text = Files.readString(file);
        // TypeReference passes the full type List<Person> to Jackson
        List<Person> readBack = mapper.readValue(text, new TypeReference<List<Person>>() {
        });
        IO.println("[read back] " + readBack.size() + " persons");
        for (Person p : readBack) {
            IO.println("  " + p.name() + ", " + p.age() + " years old, hobbies: " + p.hobbies());
        }

        // 4 - a property name set by an annotation
        String jsonArticle = mapper.writeValueAsString(new Article("A12", new BigDecimal("12.5")));
        IO.println("[@JsonProperty] " + jsonArticle);
        // reading can ignore the case of the property names
        JsonMapper caseMapper = JsonMapper.builder()
                .enable(MapperFeature.ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES)
                .build();
        Article article = caseMapper.readValue("""
                { "REFERENCE": "B7", "Price": 3 }""", Article.class);
        IO.println("[ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES] " + article);

        // 5 - an incorrect JSON document causes a JacksonException
        try {
            mapper.readValue("""
                    { "name": "x", "age": "twelve" }""", Person.class);
        } catch (JacksonException e) {
            IO.println("[error] " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getOriginalMessage());
            IO.println("[error] line " + e.getLocation().getLineNr() + ", column "
                    + e.getLocation().getColumnNr() + ", path: " + e.getPathReference());
        }
    }
}

It is run in the project folder using the command [mvn compile exec:java], or from IDE. We do not reproduce the Maven messages, but only the program’s output:

> mvn compile exec:java
[default] {"name":"hélène","age":15,"hobbies":["piano","tennis"]}
[ESCAPE_NON_ASCII] {"name":"h\u00E9l\u00E8ne","age":15,"hobbies":["piano","tennis"]}
[persons.json]
[ {
  "name" : "paul",
  "age" : 10,
  "hobbies" : [ "football" ]
}, {
  "name" : "hélène",
  "age" : 15,
  "hobbies" : [ "piano", "tennis" ]
}, {
  "name" : "jacques",
  "age" : 11,
  "hobbies" : [ ]
} ]
[read back] 3 persons
  paul, 10 years old, hobbies: [football]
  hélène, 15 years old, hobbies: [piano, tennis]
  jacques, 11 years old, hobbies: []
[@JsonProperty] {"reference":"A12","price":12.5}
[ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES] Article[code=B7, price=3]
[error] InvalidFormatException : Cannot deserialize value of type `int` from String "twelve": not a valid `int` value
[error] line 1, column 23, path: json.Files06$Person["age"]

Comments:

  • line 1: In a Maven project, classes are organized into packages: the class [Files06] from the package [json] is located in the file [src/main/java/json/Files06.java];
  • Lines 3–14: Unlike a compact source file, a regular class must import the classes it uses, including those from the standard library;
  • lines 20–21: the [Person] record to be serialized, declared in the [Files06] class. Jackson 3 can serialize a record: each component becomes a JSON property with the same name;
  • lines 24–25: the annotation [@JsonProperty] sets the name of a component’s JSON property to [reference] instead of [code];
  • line 27: the method [main] is a static method of a class. It declares the exception [IOException], which can be thrown by methods of [Files];
  • lines 34–36: A [JsonMapper] is created by an object builder: [JsonMapper.builder()] returns an object to which the desired options are specified, and then [build] creates the [JsonMapper]. With the default options, the text is written on a single line, and accented characters are written as-is (line 2 of the results);
  • Lines 38–39: The [ESCAPE_NON_ASCII] option instructs the system to write non-ASCII characters as escape sequences: [é] becomes [\u00E9]. The text remains correct, but it is difficult to read; this is useful when the text JSON must pass through a system that only recognizes ASCII;
  • lines 42–43: The option [INDENT_OUTPUT] produces indented text spread across multiple lines. A list is serialized into an array JSON;
  • lines 45–48: the text JSON is written to a text file and then read back to be displayed: this is how binary serialization is replaced today;
  • lines 53–54: deserialization reconstructs the list. Jackson creates the objects [Person] by calling the record’s constructor, whose parameters are associated with the JSON properties of the same name. For a list, you must specify the type of its elements to Jackson. However, the expression [List<Person>.class] does not exist: Java generics are erased at compile time (“type erasure”), and at runtime there is only a [List] class, without any type parameters. The trick with [TypeReference] is to create an anonymous class ([new TypeReference<List<Person>>() { }]***) derived from [TypeReference<List<Person>>]***: the parent type of a class is preserved in the compiled code, and Jackson can read it. For an array, which is simpler, we write [Person[].class];
  • lines 61–62: serialization of a [Article]: the property [reference] has the name specified by the annotation. A [BigDecimal] is written as a number JSON;
  • lines 64–69: With the [ACCEPT_CASE_INSENSITIVE_PROPERTIES] option, Jackson ignores case in property names during parsing: [REFERENCE] and [Price] are accepted;
  • lines 72–79: An invalid JSON document—in this case, a string where a number is expected—triggers an exception derived from [JacksonException], in this case [InvalidFormatException]. In Jackson 3, these exceptions are unchecked (they are derived from [RuntimeException]), whereas in Jackson 2 they were derived from [IOException]. [getOriginalMessage] returns the message without the location information, which [getLocation] and [getPathReference] provide separately: row 1, column 23, property [age] of record [Person].

A [JsonMapper] is costly to create, but once created, it is reusable and can be shared among multiple threads: a program typically creates only one, stored in a constant. We will use JSON in the following example application and throughout the course.

docs.title: 5.8. Regular Expressions
docs.text:
The [java.util.regex] package supports the use of regular expressions. These allow you to validate the format of a string. For example, you can verify that a string representing a date is indeed in the dd/mm/yy format. To do this, you use a pattern and compare the string to that pattern. In this example, d, m, and y must be digits. The pattern for a valid date format is therefore [\d\d/\d\d/\d\d], where the symbol [\d] represents a digit. The symbols that can be used in a pattern are as follows:

characterdescription[\]marks the following character as a special character or literal. For example, [n] corresponds to the character n, [ ] corresponds to a newline character, [\] corresponds to \, and [\(] corresponds to ([^]corresponds to the beginning of the string[$]corresponds to the end of the string[*]matches the preceding element zero or more times. Thus, [zo*] matches z or zoo[+]matches the preceding element one or more times. Thus, [zo+] matches "zoo," but not "z"[?]matches the preceding element zero or one time. For example, [a?ve?] matches "ve" in "lever"[.]matches any single character, except for a newline character[(pattern)]searches for the pattern and stores the match (a group). The matching substring can be extracted from the result using the [group] method. To find matches with characters in parentheses, use [\(] or [\)][x|y]matches either x or y. For example, [z|foot] matches z or foot; [(z|f)oo] matches zoo or foo[{n}]n is a non-negative integer. Corresponds exactly n times to the previous element. For example, [o{2}] does not correspond to o in Bob, but to the first two o’s in fooooot[{n,}]matches the previous element at least n times. For example, [o{2,}] does not match the 'o' in "Bob," but matches all the 'o's in "fooooot." [o{1,}] is equivalent to [o+], and [o{0,}] is equivalent to [o*][{n,m}]matches the previous element at least n times and at most m times. For example, [o{1,3}] matches the first three “o”s in “foooooot”; [o{0,1}] is equivalent to [o?][[xyz]]character set: matches one of the specified characters. For example, [[abc]] matches the letter “a” in “plain”[[^xyz]]negative character set: matches any character not listed. For example, [[^abc]] matches "p" in "plain"[[a-z]]Character range: matches any character in the specified range, in this case a lowercase unaccented letter[[^m-z]]negative character range: matches any character not between 'm' and 'z'[ ]matches a word boundary, that is, the position between a word character and a non-word character. For example, [er ] matches "er" in "lever," but not "er" in "verb"[\B]corresponds to a position that is not a word boundary. [en*t\B] corresponds to “ent” in “mentor”[\d]matches a digit; is equivalent to [[0-9]][\D]corresponds to a character that is not a digit[ ], [ ], [ ], [ ]correspond to the characters page break, new line, carriage return, and tab, respectively[\s]corresponds to any whitespace: space, tab, page break, line break… Equivalent to [[ \x0B ]][\S]matches any character that is not a whitespace character[\w]matches any word character: by default in Java, this is an unaccented letter, a digit, or an underscore; equivalent to [[a-zA-Z_0-9]]. With the [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS] option (see below), it also recognizes accented letters[\W]matches any character that is not a word character[ um]num is a positive integer: refers to group number num. For example, [(.)\1] corresponds to two consecutive identical characters[\xnn], [\unnnn]corresponds to the hexadecimal character nn (2 digits) or nnnn (4 digits). For example, [\x41] corresponds to A

An element in a pattern can appear once or multiple times. Let’s look at a few examples using the symbol [\d], which represents a single digit:

patternMeaning[\d]one digit[\d?]0 or 1 digit[\d*]0 or more digits[\d+]1 or more digits[\d{2}]2 digits[\d{3,}]At least 3 digits[\d{5,7}]between 5 and 7 digits

Now let’s imagine a model capable of describing the expected format for a string:

target stringpatterna date in dd/mm/yy format[\d{2}/\d{2}/\d{2}]a time in the hh:mm:ss format[\d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2}]an unsigned integer[\d+]a sequence of spaces, which may be empty[\s*]an unsigned integer that may be preceded or followed by spaces[\s*\d+\s*]an integer that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces[\s*[+-]?\s*\d+\s*]an unsigned real number that may be preceded or followed by spaces[\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]a real number that may be signed and preceded or followed by spaces[\s*[+-]?\s*\d+(\.\d*)?\s*]a string containing the word "just"[ just ]

Note that within square brackets, the character [|] has no specific meaning: the [[+|-]] pattern, which is sometimes used for the sign, also accepts the character | before a number. Similarly, the decimal point must be escaped, [\.]: an unescaped period matches any character.

You can specify where to search for the pattern in the string:

patternmeaning[^pattern]the pattern starts the string[pattern$]The pattern ends the string[^pattern$]The pattern starts and ends the string[pattern]The pattern is searched for anywhere in the string, starting from the beginning of the string search stringpatterna string ending with an exclamation point[!$]a string ending with a period[\.$]a string beginning with the sequence //[^//]a string consisting of a single word, possibly preceded or followed by spaces[^\s*\w+\s*$]a string consisting of exactly two words, possibly preceded or followed by spaces[^\s*\w+\s+\w+\s*$]a string containing the word "secret"[ secret ]

Sub sets of a pattern can be “extracted.” Thus, not only can we verify that a string matches a particular pattern, but we can also extract from that string the elements corresponding to the pattern’s sub sets that have been enclosed in parentheses. For example, if we parse a string containing a date in the format dd/mm/yy and also want to extract the elements dd, mm, and yy from that date, we would use the pattern [(\d\d)/(\d\d)/(\d\d)].

In Java code, a pattern is written as a regular string: each character [\] in the pattern must be duplicated. The pattern [\d+] is written as ["\d+"], and the pattern [\], which represents the \ character, is written as ["\\"]. Text blocks do not change this: [\] is also an escape character here. The editor makes it easier to read: IntelliJ IDEA recognizes the strings passed to [Pattern.compile], highlights them as regular expressions, and allows you to test them.

docs.title: 5.8.1. Check whether a string matches a given pattern
docs.text:
A pattern is first compiled into a [java.util.regex.Pattern] object, which then provides [Matcher] objects responsible for searching within a given string:

methodrole[static Pattern compile(String regex)]compiles the [regex] pattern; throws a [PatternSyntaxException] exception if the pattern is invalid[static Pattern compile(String regex, int flags)]same as above, with options (see below)[Matcher matcher(CharSequence input)]returns a [Matcher] object that looks up the pattern in [input][boolean find()] (class [Matcher])searches for the next occurrence of the pattern in the string; returns [true] if one is found[boolean matches()] (class [Matcher])returns [true] if the entire string matches the pattern[static boolean matches(String regex, CharSequence input)]compiles the pattern and checks whether the entire string matches it

The program [Regex01.java] is as follows:

// checking that a string matches a pattern
void main() {
    String pattern1 = "^\\s*\\d+\\s*$";
    Pattern regex1 = Pattern.compile(pattern1);
    // comparing samples to the pattern
    for (String sample : List.of("  123  ", "  123a  ", "4567")) {
        if (regex1.matcher(sample).find()) {
            IO.println("[" + sample + "] matches the pattern [" + pattern1 + "]");
        } else {
            IO.println("[" + sample + "] does not match the pattern [" + pattern1 + "]");
        }
    }
    // find searches for the pattern in the string; matches requires the whole string to match
    Pattern number = Pattern.compile("\\d+");
    IO.println("find(\"abc 123\") : " + number.matcher("abc 123").find()
            + ", matches(\"abc 123\") : " + number.matcher("abc 123").matches());
    // the static method Pattern.matches and the matches method of String: the whole string
    IO.println("Pattern.matches(date, \"18/05/97\") : "
            + Pattern.matches("\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{2}", "18/05/97"));
    IO.println("\"5/1/01\".matches(date) : " + "5/1/01".matches("\\d{2}/\\d{2}/\\d{2}"));
}

Results:

> java Regex01.java
[  123  ] matches the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[  123a  ] does not match the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
[4567] matches the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$]
find("abc 123") : true, matches("abc 123") : false
Pattern.matches(date, "18/05/97") : true
"5/1/01".matches(date) : false

Comments:

  • line 3: the pattern for an unsigned integer, possibly surrounded by spaces, which occupies the entire string (anchors [^] and [$]). The [\] entries are duplicated;
  • line 4: the pattern compilation;
  • line 7: [find] searches for the pattern in the string. The string “123a,” surrounded by spaces, does not match the pattern: the character “a” cannot be a digit or a space. Without the anchors [^] and [$], the string would match, since it contains a number;
  • lines 14–16: the difference between [find], which searches for the pattern within the string, and [matches], which requires that the entire string match the pattern, as if it were bounded by [^] and [$];
  • Lines 18–20: The static method [Pattern.matches] and the method [matches] of the class [String] also test the entire string. They compile the pattern on every call: while useful for a standalone test, they should be avoided in a loop. The method [split] of [String], which we’ve already encountered, likewise compiles its pattern on every call, except for separators consisting of a single ordinary character, which it processes without a regular expression.

docs.title: 5.8.2. Finding all occurrences of a pattern in a string
docs.text:
The [find] method of a [Matcher] object can be called multiple times: each call searches for the next occurrence of the pattern. After a successful call, the [Matcher] object provides information about the occurrence found:

  • [group()]: the text of the occurrence, i.e., an element matching the pattern;
  • [start()]: the position where the element was found in the searched string; [end()]: the position following the element.

The program [Regex02.java] is as follows:

// finding all the occurrences of a pattern in a string
void main() {
    String pattern2 = "\\d+";
    Pattern regex2 = Pattern.compile(pattern2);
    String sample3 = "  123  456  789 ";
    IO.println("Pattern=[" + pattern2 + "], sample=[" + sample3 + "]");
    // find advances from occurrence to occurrence
    Matcher matcher = regex2.matcher(sample3);
    int nbOccurrences = 0;
    while (matcher.find()) {
        nbOccurrences++;
        IO.println("[" + matcher.group() + "] found at position " + matcher.start());
    }
    IO.println("There are " + nbOccurrences + " occurrences of the pattern in the sample");
    // results (Java 9): the stream of occurrences, to which the Stream API applies
    int sum = regex2.matcher(sample3).results().mapToInt(m -> Integer.parseInt(m.group())).sum();
    IO.println("sum of the numbers found: " + sum);
    long vowels = Pattern.compile("[aeiouy]").matcher("antidisestablishmentarianism").results().count();
    IO.println("number of vowels of \"antidisestablishmentarianism\": " + vowels);
}

Results:

> java Regex02.java
Pattern=[\d+], sample=[  123  456  789 ]
[123] found at position 2
[456] found at position 7
[789] found at position 12
There are 3 occurrences of the pattern in the sample
sum of the numbers found: 1368
number of vowels of "antidisestablishmentarianism": 11

Comments:

  • Line 3: The pattern being searched for is a sequence of digits;
  • line 5: the string in which this pattern is searched for;
  • lines 8–13: Each call to [find] finds the next occurrence; the loop stops when there are no more. Each occurrence and its position are displayed;
  • line 16: the [results] method (Java 9) returns the stream of occurrences as [MatchResult] objects (which have the methods [group], [start], [end]): the API Stream is applied to it. Here, the sum of the found numbers is calculated;
  • line 18: the number of occurrences of the pattern [[aeiouy]], which denotes a vowel, is the number of elements in the stream.

docs.title: 5.8.3. Retrieving Parts of a Pattern
docs.text:
As mentioned, the parts of a pattern enclosed in parentheses are stored: these are the groups. The program [Regex03.java] uses them:

// retrieving parts of a pattern: groups
void main() {
    String pattern3 = "(\\d\\d):(\\d\\d):(\\d\\d)";
    Pattern regex3 = Pattern.compile(pattern3);
    String sample4 = "It is 18:05:49";
    // find searches for the first occurrence of the pattern
    Matcher result = regex3.matcher(sample4);
    if (result.find()) {
        IO.println("The sample [" + sample4 + "] matches the pattern [" + pattern3 + "]");
        // we display the parenthesized groups; group 0 is the whole occurrence
        for (int i = 0; i <= result.groupCount(); i++) {
            IO.println("groups[" + i + "]=[" + result.group(i) + "] found at position "
                    + result.start(i));
        }
    } else {
        IO.println("The sample [" + sample4 + "] does not match the pattern [" + pattern3 + "]");
    }

    // named groups: (?<name>...)
    Pattern regexDate = Pattern.compile("(?<day>\\d{1,2})/(?<month>\\d{1,2})/(?<year>\\d{4})");
    String text = "Appointment on 3/10/2026, then on 15/11/2026.";
    DateTimeFormatter format = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEEE d MMMM yyyy");
    Matcher m = regexDate.matcher(text);
    while (m.find()) {
        // a group is designated by its name rather than by its number
        int day = Integer.parseInt(m.group("day"));
        int month = Integer.parseInt(m.group("month"));
        int year = Integer.parseInt(m.group("year"));
        LocalDate date = LocalDate.of(year, month, day);
        IO.println("[" + m.group() + "] : day=" + day + ", month=" + month + ", year=" + year + " -> "
                + date.format(format));
    }

    // replaceAll: the groups can be reused in the replacement string
    String reversed = regexDate.matcher(text).replaceAll("${year}-${month}-${day}");
    IO.println("replaceAll(string) : " + reversed);
    // replaceAll with a function (Java 9): the replacement is computed for each occurrence
    String iso = regexDate.matcher(text).replaceAll(r -> LocalDate.of(Integer.parseInt(r.group(3)),
            Integer.parseInt(r.group(2)), Integer.parseInt(r.group(1))).toString());
    IO.println("replaceAll(function) : " + iso);
}

Results:

> java Regex03.java
The sample [It is 18:05:49] matches the pattern [(\d\d):(\d\d):(\d\d)]
groups[0]=[18:05:49] found at position 6
groups[1]=[18] found at position 6
groups[2]=[05] found at position 9
groups[3]=[49] found at position 12
[3/10/2026] : day=3, month=10, year=2026 -> Saturday 3 October 2026
[15/11/2026] : day=15, month=11, year=2026 -> Sunday 15 November 2026
replaceAll(string) : Appointment on 2026-10-3, then on 2026-11-15.
replaceAll(function) : Appointment on 2026-10-03, then on 2026-11-15.

Comments:

  • lines 7–8: the string [sample4] is compared to the pattern [regex3]; [find] searches for the first occurrence of the pattern. After a successful call, we use two new methods from [Matcher]:
    • [groupCount] (line 11): the number of parenthesis groups in the pattern;
    • [group(i)] (line 12): the text captured by group #i; [group(0)], or [group()], is the entire occurrence of the pattern. [start(i)] is the position of this text in the parsed string. The loop therefore runs from 0 to [groupCount], inclusive;
  • line 20: a group can be named using the syntax [(?<name>...)]. Here, the pattern recognizes a date in the format d/m/yyyy, with a one- or two-digit day and month;
  • lines 26–28: A named group is referred to by its name rather than its number: the code is more readable and does not depend on the order of the parentheses;
  • lines 29–31: The class [LocalDate] (Java 8) represents a date without a time. It is displayed using the pattern [EEEE d MMMM yyyy]: the day of the week appears in English, the language of the machine;
  • line 35: the [replaceAll] method replaces each occurrence of the pattern with a string in which [${name}] (or [$1], [$2]… for numbered groups) denotes the value of a group. Dates are thus rewritten in year-month-day format;
  • lines 38–39: an overloaded version of [replaceAll] (Java 9) takes a function that calculates the replacement text from each occurrence, of type [MatchResult]. Here, the date is constructed and replaced with its standardized notation ISO 8601, which is returned by the [toString] method of [LocalDate]: days and months always have two digits.

docs.title: 5.8.4. A Learning Program
docs.text:
Finding the regular expression that verifies whether a string matches a certain pattern can sometimes be a real challenge. The program [Regex04.java] allows you to practice. It takes a pattern and a string as input and indicates whether the string matches the pattern or not.

// a program for learning regular expressions
void main() {
    while (true) {
        // we ask for the pattern
        String pattern = read("Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ");
        // finished?
        if (pattern.isBlank()) {
            break;
        }
        // we compile the regular expression; an incorrect pattern causes an exception
        Pattern regex;
        try {
            regex = Pattern.compile(pattern);
        } catch (PatternSyntaxException e) {
            IO.println("Error: " + e.getDescription() + " (position " + e.getIndex() + ")");
            continue;
        }
        // we ask for the samples to compare to the pattern
        while (true) {
            String input = read("Type the string to compare to the pattern [" + pattern
                    + "] or nothing to stop: ");
            // finished?
            if (input.isBlank()) {
                break;
            }
            try {
                // we do the comparison, with a limit of one second
                Matcher m = regex.matcher(new TimeLimitedString(input, Duration.ofSeconds(1)));
                boolean found = false;
                while (m.find()) {
                    found = true;
                    // we display the element matching the pattern
                    IO.println("I found the match [" + m.group() + "] at position ["
                            + m.start() + "]");
                    // and its sub-elements (groups 1, 2, ...)
                    for (int j = 1; j <= m.groupCount(); j++) {
                        IO.println("    sub-element [" + m.group(j) + "] at position ["
                                + m.start(j) + "]");
                    }
                }
                if (!found) {
                    IO.println("I did not find any matches");
                }
            } catch (TimeoutExceededException e) {
                IO.println("The search was abandoned: it lasted more than one second");
            }
        }
    }
}

// reading a line on the keyboard; "" at end of stream
String read(String prompt) {
    String line = IO.readln(prompt);
    return line == null ? "" : line;
}

// a string that refuses to be read beyond a deadline
record TimeLimitedString(CharSequence text, long deadline) implements CharSequence {

    TimeLimitedString(CharSequence text, Duration delay) {
        this(text, System.nanoTime() + delay.toNanos());
    }

    @Override
    public char charAt(int index) {
        // the regular expression engine reads the string character by character
        if (System.nanoTime() > deadline) {
            throw new TimeoutExceededException();
        }
        return text.charAt(index);
    }

    @Override
    public int length() {
        return text.length();
    }

    @Override
    public CharSequence subSequence(int start, int end) {
        return new TimeLimitedString(text.subSequence(start, end), deadline);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return text.toString();
    }
}

// the exception thrown when the deadline is exceeded (static: usable in the record)
static class TimeoutExceededException extends RuntimeException {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
}

Comments:

  • line 13: compilation of the pattern entered via the keyboard. An incorrect pattern triggers an exception [PatternSyntaxException], for which [getDescription] returns the error description and [getIndex] returns its position in the pattern (line 15). Its full message, returned by [getMessage], spans several lines and shows the pattern with a marker below the error;
  • line 28: the search is not performed directly on the typed string, but on an object [TimeLimitedString] (lines 58–87), which limits the search duration to one second: if the search takes longer, a [TimeoutExceededException] exception is thrown and then caught on line 44. We’ll see later why this is useful and how it works;
  • lines 36–39: for each match, groups #1 and subsequent groups are displayed, if any;
  • lines 52–55: Unlike previous programs, spaces are not removed from the entered line; they may be part of the pattern or the string to be tested.

Here is an example of the output:

> java Regex04.java
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: \d+
Type the string to compare to the pattern [\d+] or nothing to stop: 123 456 789
I found the match [123] at position [0]
I found the match [456] at position [4]
I found the match [789] at position [8]
Type the string to compare to the pattern [\d+] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: (\d{2}):(\d\d)
Type the string to compare to the pattern [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] or nothing to stop: 14:15 abcd 17:18 xyzt
I found the match [14:15] at position [0]
    sub-element [14] at position [0]
    sub-element [15] at position [3]
I found the match [17:18] at position [11]
    sub-element [17] at position [11]
    sub-element [18] at position [14]
Type the string to compare to the pattern [(\d{2}):(\d\d)] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^\s*\d+\s*$
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$] or nothing to stop:    1456
I found the match [   1456] at position [0]
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^\s*\d+\s*$] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^\s*(\d+)\s*$
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop: 1456
I found the match [1456] at position [0]
    sub-element [1456] at position [0]
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop: abcd 1456
I did not find any matches
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^(a+)+$
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^(a+)+$] or nothing to stop: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
I did not find any matches
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^(a+)+$] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: ^(a+)+\1$
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^(a+)+\1$] or nothing to stop: aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!
The search was abandoned: it lasted more than one second
Type the string to compare to the pattern [^(a+)+\1$] or nothing to stop: 
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop: (\d+
Error: Unclosed group (position 4)
Type the pattern to test or nothing to stop:

The patterns [^\s*\d+\s*$] and [^\s*(\d+)\s*$] demonstrate the benefits of using groups: the first recognizes the string “1456” preceded by three spaces, including the spaces; the second also extracts the number without the spaces. The [^(a+)+$] and [^(a+)+\1$] patterns are discussed below.

docs.title: 5.8.5. The split method
docs.text:
We have already encountered the [split] method of the [String] class, whose separator is a regular expression. The [Pattern] class has the same method, which uses the precompiled pattern:

methodrole[String[] split(CharSequence input)]The string [input] is split into fields, which are separated by a separator corresponding to the pattern[Stream<String> splitAsStream(CharSequence input)]same as above, but the fields are returned as a stream

Suppose, for example, that a text file contains lines of the form field1, field2, ..., fieldn. The fields are separated by a comma, but this comma may be preceded or followed by spaces. The pattern [\s*,\s*] describes this separator exactly, as shown by the program [Regex05.java]:

// split: the separator is defined by a pattern
void main() {
    String line = "abc  , def  ,ghi ,   jkl";
    // a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces
    Pattern separator = Pattern.compile("\\s*,\\s*");
    String[] fields = separator.split(line);
    for (int i = 0; i < fields.length; i++) {
        IO.println("fields[" + i + "]=[" + fields[i] + "]");
    }
    // several possible separators: ; or | or a sequence of spaces
    String[] words = "one;two|three   four".split("[;|]|\\s+");
    IO.println("words=" + Arrays.toString(words));
    // splitAsStream: the fields as a stream
    IO.println("splitAsStream : " + separator.splitAsStream(line).map(String::toUpperCase).toList());
}

Results:

> java Regex05.java
fields[0]=[abc]
fields[1]=[def]
fields[2]=[ghi]
fields[3]=[jkl]
words=[one, two, three, four]
splitAsStream : [ABC, DEF, GHI, JKL]

Comments:

  • line 5: the separator: a comma preceded and followed by any number of spaces. The spaces are removed along with the separator. Once compiled, the pattern can split as many lines as desired without being recompiled: this is the method for splitting all the lines in a file;
  • line 11: a separator that can take several forms: a semicolon or a vertical bar ([[;|]]), or ([|]) a sequence of spaces ([\s+]);
  • line 14: [splitAsStream] returns the fields as a stream, to which the operation [map] is applied here.

docs.title: 5.8.6. Precompiled patterns, options, and searches that take too long
docs.text:
Unlike other platforms, Java does not have a mechanism that generates the code for a regular expression search at program compile time: a pattern is always parsed at runtime by [Pattern.compile]. This compilation comes at a cost; therefore, best practice is to compile each known pattern once and for all in advance and store the [Pattern] object in a constant, as the program [Regex06.java] does. A [Pattern] object is immutable and can be used simultaneously by multiple threads; a [Matcher] object, which stores the state of a search, cannot.

// patterns compiled once and for all, options, protection against searches that take too long

// a time hh:mm:ss with named groups
static final Pattern TIME = Pattern.compile("(?<h>\\d\\d):(?<m>\\d\\d):(?<s>\\d\\d)");
// yes, whatever the case
static final Pattern YES = Pattern.compile("^\\s*yes\\s*$", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);
// a pathological pattern: a repeated group followed by a back reference to this group
static final Pattern CATASTROPHIC = Pattern.compile("^(a+)+\\1$");

void main() {
    // 1 - patterns compiled only once, stored in constants
    IO.println("TIME.matcher(\"It is 18:05:49\").find() : " + TIME.matcher("It is 18:05:49").find());
    Matcher m = TIME.matcher("departure at 07:45:00");
    if (m.find()) {
        IO.println("hours=" + m.group("h") + ", minutes=" + m.group("m") + ", seconds=" + m.group("s"));
    }

    // 2 - the options: here CASE_INSENSITIVE, set when the pattern is compiled
    for (String answer : List.of("yes", "YES", "Yes", "no", "yesss")) {
        IO.print(answer + "=" + YES.matcher(answer).matches() + " ");
    }
    IO.println();
    // MULTILINE: ^ and $ match each start and end of line; \w only recognizes [a-zA-Z0-9_]
    String text = "price: 10\nentrée: 3\ntotal: 30";
    display(Pattern.compile("^(\\w+): (\\d+)$", Pattern.MULTILINE), text);
    // UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS: \w also recognizes accented letters
    display(Pattern.compile("^(\\w+): (\\d+)$", Pattern.MULTILINE | Pattern.UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS), text);
    // the options can also be written in the pattern: (?i) for CASE_INSENSITIVE, (?m) for MULTILINE
    IO.println("(?i)yes on \"YES\" : " + "YES".matches("(?i)yes"));

    // 3 - a pattern with catastrophic backtracking, without then with a time limit
    for (int n : new int[]{10, 15, 20}) {
        String input = "a".repeat(n) + "!";
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        boolean found = CATASTROPHIC.matcher(input).find();
        IO.println(n + " a : " + found + " in " + (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 + " ms");
    }
    String input = "a".repeat(30) + "!";
    try {
        IO.println(CATASTROPHIC.matcher(new TimeLimitedString(input, Duration.ofMillis(100))).find());
    } catch (TimeoutExceededException e) {
        IO.println("30 a : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : search abandoned after 100 ms");
    }
    // the Java engine recognizes the pattern (a+)+ without back reference and answers immediately
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    boolean found = Pattern.compile("^(a+)+$").matcher(input).find();
    IO.println("^(a+)+$ on 30 a : " + found + ", answer in less than one second: "
            + ((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 < 1000));
}

// display of the name=value pairs found in a text
void display(Pattern pattern, String text) {
    Matcher line = pattern.matcher(text);
    while (line.find()) {
        IO.print("[" + line.group(1) + "=" + line.group(2) + "] ");
    }
    IO.println();
}

// a string that refuses to be read beyond a deadline
record TimeLimitedString(CharSequence text, long deadline) implements CharSequence {

    TimeLimitedString(CharSequence text, Duration delay) {
        this(text, System.nanoTime() + delay.toNanos());
    }

    @Override
    public char charAt(int index) {
        if (System.nanoTime() > deadline) {
            throw new TimeoutExceededException();
        }
        return text.charAt(index);
    }

    @Override
    public int length() {
        return text.length();
    }

    @Override
    public CharSequence subSequence(int start, int end) {
        return new TimeLimitedString(text.subSequence(start, end), deadline);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return text.toString();
    }
}

// the exception thrown when the deadline is exceeded
static class TimeoutExceededException extends RuntimeException {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
}

Results:

> java Regex06.java
TIME.matcher("It is 18:05:49").find() : true
hours=07, minutes=45, seconds=00
yes=true YES=true Yes=true no=false yesss=false 
[price=10] [total=30] 
[price=10] [entrée=3] [total=30] 
(?i)yes on "YES" : true
10 a : false in 0 ms
15 a : false in 2 ms
20 a : false in 39 ms
30 a : TimeoutExceededException : search abandoned after 100 ms
^(a+)+$ on 30 a : false, answer in less than one second: true

Comments:

  • lines 4–8: The program’s patterns are compiled once and stored in [static final] constants (Chapter 4), written in uppercase as is customary. In a compact source file, these constants are fields of the implicit class that contains the file’s methods;
  • lines 12–16: The constants are used in the same way as the [Pattern] objects in the previous programs;
  • line 6: the second parameter of [compile] is a combination of options. [CASE_INSENSITIVE] is case-insensitive: “YES” and “Yes” match the pattern (line 4 of the results);
  • Lines 23–27: The options are combined with the operator [|]. [MULTILINE] matches [^] and [$] at the beginning and end of each line in the string, rather than just at the beginning and end of the string itself. However, with the default options, [\w] recognizes only unaccented letters: the line “entrée: 3” is not recognized (line 5 of the results). The option [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS] (Java 7) assigns the correct Unicode meanings to [\w], [\d], [\s], and [\b]: accented letters are treated as word characters (line 6 of the results). This option should be used for all French text. Other useful options include: [DOTALL] ([.] also handles line breaks), [COMMENTS] (spaces in the pattern are ignored, allowing it to be written across multiple lines, with comments), [UNICODE_CASE] (along with [CASE_INSENSITIVE], this also ignores the case of accented letters: É and é);
  • line 29: options can also be written at the beginning of the pattern: [(?i)] for [CASE_INSENSITIVE], [(?m)] for [MULTILINE], [(?U)] for [UNICODE_CHARACTER_CLASS]…

The rest of the program addresses a security issue. Some patterns are pathological: when applied to certain strings, they force the regular expression engine to try an enormous number of ways to match the string to the pattern before reaching a conclusion. The Java engine uses a process called “backtracking”: when an attempt fails, it returns to the last choice made and tries another one. The pattern [^(a+)+\1$] on line 8 is an example of this: When applied to a sequence of “a”s ending with another character, it tries every possible way to distribute the “a”s among the repetitions of the group and its backreference [\1] before concluding that the match has failed, and the number of possibilities multiplies with each additional “a.” This is known as a catastrophic backtracking. When applied to user-entered strings, such a pattern constitutes a security vulnerability (known as ReDoS, “regular expression denial of service”): just a few requests are enough to bring a server to a standstill.

  • Lines 32–37: The search duration is measured for 10, 15, and 20 a. It increases very rapidly (lines 8–10 of the results; durations vary from one execution and one machine to another). Since the duration roughly doubles with each additional a, the search would take several minutes with 30 a;
  • lines 38–43: The [Pattern] class has no timeout option. A standard technique is used: the search is performed in an object of type [TimeLimitedString] (lines 61–89), which implements the [CharSequence] interface accepted by [matcher]. The regular expression engine reads the string character by character using the [charAt] method: this method checks the time and throws a [TimeoutExceededException] exception (lines 92–95) if the deadline—stored when the object was created—has been exceeded. The search is abandoned after 100 ms;
  • lines 61–65: The [TimeLimitedString] record has two components: the text and the deadline, expressed as the value of the [System.nanoTime] clock, which must not be exceeded. The additional constructor calculates this deadline based on a timeout, an object [java.time.Duration];
  • line 92: The exception [TimeoutExceededException] is derived from [RuntimeException]: it is an unchecked exception that [charAt] can throw without declaring it. It is declared as [static] so that it can be created in the record, which is itself implicitly static. The field [serialVersionUID] prevents a compiler warning, since an exception is serializable;
  • lines 45–48: The Java runtime can recognize and efficiently handle simple cases of nested repetitions: the pattern [^(a+)+$], which is catastrophic with other runtimes, responds immediately here. It is the backward reference [\1] that prevents this optimization in the pattern on line 8.

It is important to note that you should be wary of patterns containing nested repetitions ([(a+)+], [(\w+\s?)*]…) and limit the duration of searches as soon as the pattern or string being searched for comes from outside the program. Java’s possessive quantifiers ([a++], [a*+]), which prevent backtracking within the element they repeat, also allow you to write safe patterns, provided you fully understand their meaning.

docs.title: 5.9. Example Application - V3
docs.text: We’ll revisit the application discussed in Chapter 3 (Version 1) and Chapter 4 (Version 2). Remember that this is an exercise: the tax scale used is the 2004 version (2003 income), which has remained unchanged since the original course.

docs.title: 5.9.1. Data in a File
docs.text:
In Version 2, the tax calculation was performed in the abstract class [AbstractTax], which we are reusing here in the project’s [tax] package, with two minor differences: the tax brackets are now provided in the form of a table ([TaxBracket[]]) rather than a list, and the division is performed with 16 significant digits instead of 34, which is more than sufficient:

package tax;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.math.MathContext;

public abstract class AbstractTax implements ITax {

    // the tax brackets needed for the calculation come from an external source
    // that only the derived classes know
    protected abstract TaxBracket[] getTaxBrackets();

    // tax calculation
    @Override
    public int calculate(boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary) {
        // calculation of the number of shares
        BigDecimal shares = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbChildren).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
                .add(married ? BigDecimal.TWO : BigDecimal.ONE);
        if (nbChildren >= 3) {
            shares = shares.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
        }
        // calculation of the taxable income and of the family quotient
        BigDecimal income = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salary));
        BigDecimal quotient = income.divide(shares, MathContext.DECIMAL64);
        // searching for the tax bracket: the last one is used if no limit fits
        TaxBracket[] brackets = getTaxBrackets();
        TaxBracket bracket = brackets[brackets.length - 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < brackets.length - 1; i++) {
            if (quotient.compareTo(brackets[i].limit()) <= 0) {
                bracket = brackets[i];
                break;
            }
        }
        // tax calculation
        return income.multiply(bracket.coeffR()).subtract(shares.multiply(bracket.coeffN())).intValue();
    }
}

The [calculate] method uses the tax brackets returned by the abstract method [getTaxBrackets] (line 10). The [AbstractTax] class does not know where these brackets come from: it is up to the derived classes to provide them. In version 2, the derived class [HardwiredTax] hard-coded them into its code. The calculations are performed using exact decimal numbers [java.math.BigDecimal] (Chapter 3): [BigDecimal.TWO] (Java 19) is the constant 2; the division of the revenue by the number of shares is performed with 16 significant digits ([MathContext.DECIMAL64]); and [intValue] returns the integer part of the result. A bracket is represented, as in version 2, by the record [TaxBracket]:

package tax;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

// a bracket of the tax scale
public record TaxBracket(BigDecimal limit, BigDecimal coeffR, BigDecimal coeffN) {
}

and the calculation is described by the [ITax] interface, documented here by a Javadoc comment:

package tax;

/**
 * The tax calculation.
 */
public interface ITax {

    /**
     * Calculates the tax of a taxpayer.
     *
     * @param married    true if the taxpayer is married
     * @param nbChildren number of children
     * @param salary     annual salary in euros
     * @return the amount of the tax, in euros
     */
    int calculate(boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary);
}

The new version stores the data in a file, which allows you to change the rate schedule without recompiling the program. We write two new classes derived from [AbstractTax]:

  • [FileTax] reads the brackets from a text file [TaxData.txt];
  • [JsonTax] reads them from a file named JSON [TaxData.json].

The text file [TaxData.txt] contains one segment per line, in the format limit:coeffR:coeffN:

4962:0:0
8382:0.068:291.09
14753:0.191:1322.92
23888:0.283:2668.39
38868:0.374:4846.98
47932:0.426:6883.66
0:0.481:9505.54

Numbers in the file are written with a decimal point. A data file must not depend on the language of the machine reading it: a file written with decimal commas and interpreted according to French rules ([NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.FRANCE)]) would be rejected or, worse, misinterpreted on an English-language machine. The [new BigDecimal(String)] generator, like [Double.parseDouble], always expects a decimal point, regardless of the machine’s language. This is also the convention for JSON and most data formats.

The file [TaxData.json] contains the same data, in the form of a JSON array of objects:

[
  { "limit": 4962, "coeffR": 0, "coeffN": 0 },
  { "limit": 8382, "coeffR": 0.068, "coeffN": 291.09 },
  { "limit": 14753, "coeffR": 0.191, "coeffN": 1322.92 },
  { "limit": 23888, "coeffR": 0.283, "coeffN": 2668.39 },
  { "limit": 38868, "coeffR": 0.374, "coeffN": 4846.98 },
  { "limit": 47932, "coeffR": 0.426, "coeffN": 6883.66 },
  { "limit": 0, "coeffR": 0.481, "coeffN": 9505.54 }
]

docs.title: 5.9.2. Errors
docs.text:
Processing these files may fail due to a missing file, a malformed line, an incorrect number, etc. We create a special exception class to report these errors, [TaxException]. It will also be used for other data sources (the JSON file here, and databases later). It carries an error code:

package tax;

import java.io.Serial;

// the exception thrown by the classes that read the tax brackets
// it derives from RuntimeException: it is an unchecked exception
public class TaxException extends RuntimeException {

    // version of the class for serialization (an exception is serializable)
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    // the error code (a combination of ErrorCode values)
    private final int code;

    public TaxException(String message, int code) {
        super(message);
        this.code = code;
    }

    public TaxException(String message, Throwable cause, int code) {
        super(message, cause);
        this.code = code;
    }

    public int getCode() {
        return code;
    }
}

Comments:

  • Line 7: The [TaxException] class derives from the [RuntimeException] class: this is an unchecked exception (Chapter 4). The compiler will not require the code that creates a [FileTax] or [JsonTax] object to catch this exception; that code will catch it where it is able to handle it;
  • Lines 10–11: Every exception is serializable by inheriting from the [Throwable] class. A serializable class should declare a version number [serialVersionUID], which is used to verify that a serialized object is deserialized by the same version of the class; otherwise, the compiler, when using the [-Xlint:all] option, issues a warning. The [@Serial] annotation (Java 14) indicates that the field is part of the serialization mechanism;
  • line 14: the error code, set when the exception is created;
  • lines 16–24: two constructors. The first takes an error message and a code; the second also takes the exception that caused the error (the cause), which will be accessible via the [getCause] method. It is this form of exception, with an integer code, that subsequent versions of the application will use.

The possible error codes are described by an enumeration:

package tax;

import java.util.EnumSet;

// the error codes: powers of 2, which can be combined
public enum ErrorCode {
    ACCESS(1),      // the file cannot be read
    LINE(2),        // a line does not have three fields
    FIELD1(4),      // field 1 (limit) is incorrect
    FIELD2(8),      // field 2 (coeffR) is incorrect
    FIELD3(16),     // field 3 (coeffN) is incorrect
    JSON(32);       // the JSON document is incorrect

    // the integer value of the code
    private final int value;

    ErrorCode(int value) {
        this.value = value;
    }

    public int getValue() {
        return value;
    }

    // the codes present in a combination of codes
    public static EnumSet<ErrorCode> decode(int code) {
        EnumSet<ErrorCode> codes = EnumSet.noneOf(ErrorCode.class);
        for (ErrorCode c : values()) {
            if ((code & c.value) != 0) {
                codes.add(c);
            }
        }
        return codes;
    }
}

Comments:

  • Lines 7–12: Possible error codes:
    • [ACCESS]: error accessing the data file;
    • [LINE]: row missing the three expected fields, or file containing no time periods;
    • [FIELD1], [FIELD2], [FIELD3]: Field 1, 2, or 3 in a row is incorrect;
    • [JSON]: The document JSON is incorrect;
  • Lines 15–23: A Java enum is a class; it can have fields, a (private) constructor, and methods. Each constant is constructed with its integer value, enclosed in parentheses;
