  • lines 29–31: the main thread iterates over the list. The iteration over a [CopyOnWriteArrayList] is performed on a snapshot of the internal array: it never throws [ConcurrentModificationException], even if other threads modify the list during the iteration;
  • lines 33–34: the dictionary is copied into a sorted dictionary [TreeMap] to display the numbers in order; the method [forEach] receives each key/value pair;
  • line 35: the sum of the values, calculated by a stream;
  • line 38: the method [computeIfAbsent(key, function)] returns the value associated with the key, after calculating it using the function and adding it if the key did not exist. As with [merge], the check and the addition form a single atomic operation: a [containsKey] check followed by a [put] would not be safe, since another thread could add the key in between.

Results:

> java Threads23.java
thread T1 finished its 100,000 draws
thread T0 finished its 100,000 draws
thread T2 finished its 100,000 draws
thread T3 finished its 100,000 draws
digit 0 : 40,244 draws
digit 1 : 40,093 draws
digit 2 : 39,719 draws
digit 3 : 40,052 draws
digit 4 : 39,911 draws
digit 5 : 39,687 draws
digit 6 : 39,959 draws
digit 7 : 39,814 draws
digit 8 : 40,235 draws
digit 9 : 40,286 draws
total: 400,000 draws (expected: 400,000)
computeIfAbsent(10, …) = 0, number of keys: 11

The total number of draws is correct: no updates were lost. The reports appear in the order in which the threads completed their work, which varies from one execution to another.

docs.title: 8.9.2. Producer and consumers: BlockingQueue
docs.text:
The problem of readers and writers is a variation on the classic producer-consumer problem: some threads produce data that other threads consume. The [BlockingQueue<E>] interface solves this without any explicit synchronization tools:

  • [put(element)] adds an element to the queue. If the queue has a limited capacity and is full, the producer is blocked until a spot becomes available;
  • [take()] removes the element at the head of the queue. If the queue is empty, the consumer is blocked until an element arrives;
  • [offer(element, timeout, unit)] and [poll(timeout, unit)] do the same, with a maximum wait time; [offer(element)] and [poll()], which have no timeout, never block: they return [false] or [null] in case of failure.

The queue is unaware that production has ended. A classic technique involves placing a special value—known in the English-speaking world as a “poison pill”—into the queue at the end of production: the consumer that retrieves it knows it must stop. Another technique is to interrupt the consumers, since [take] is interruptible. The program [Threads24.java] is as follows:

// producer / consumers with a BlockingQueue

// the value that signals the end of production ("poison pill")
static final int END = -1;

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    // a queue of at most 3 elements
    BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(3);
    final int nbConsumers = 2;

    // the producer puts 8 numbers then signals that it has finished
    var producer = new Thread(() -> {
        try {
            for (int i = 1; i <= 8; i++) {
                // blocking if the queue is full
                queue.put(i);
                IO.println(time() + " : P put " + i
                        + " (waiting elements: " + queue.size() + ")");
                Thread.sleep(100);
            }
            // one end marker per consumer
            for (int i = 0; i < nbConsumers; i++) {
                queue.put(END);
            }
            IO.println(time() + " : P has finished");
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }, "P");

    // two consumers take the numbers until the end marker
    var consumers = new Thread[nbConsumers];
    for (int i = 0; i < consumers.length; i++) {
        consumers[i] = new Thread(() -> {
            String name = Thread.currentThread().getName();
            try {
                while (true) {
                    // blocking if the queue is empty
                    int number = queue.take();
                    if (number == END) {
                        break;
                    }
                    IO.println(time() + " : " + name + " took " + number);
                    // processing of the number
                    Thread.sleep(600);
                }
                IO.println(time() + " : " + name + " has finished");
            } catch (InterruptedException e) {
                Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            }
        }, "C" + (i + 1));
    }

    // start of all the threads and waiting for them
    producer.start();
    for (Thread consumer : consumers) {
        consumer.start();
    }
    producer.join();
    for (Thread consumer : consumers) {
        consumer.join();
    }
}

// the current time, to the millisecond
static String time() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 4: the value that marks the end of production. It is a constant, declared outside any class: it is a static field of the implicit class;
  • line 8: a queue with at most 3 elements. [ArrayBlockingQueue] stores the elements in a fixed-size array; [LinkedBlockingQueue] has unlimited capacity by default;
  • lines 12–29: The producer places the numbers 1 through 8 into the queue, one every tenth of a second, followed by an end marker for each consumer (lines 22–24);
  • lines 34–51: Two consumers retrieve the numbers and spend 0.6 seconds processing each one. They consume them more slowly than the producer generates them;
  • line 39: blocking removal. Each number is removed by only one of the two consumers;
  • lines 40–42: a consumer that retrieves the end token exits its loop. Each consumer retrieves one, hence one token is deposited per consumer;
  • the producer and the consumers are lambdas that contain the instruction [try], because [put], [take], and [sleep] can invoke [InterruptedException].

Results:

> java Threads24.java
19:16:25.299 : P put 1 (waiting elements: 0)
19:16:25.304 : C2 took 1
19:16:25.427 : P put 2 (waiting elements: 1)
19:16:25.428 : C1 took 2
19:16:25.531 : P put 3 (waiting elements: 1)
19:16:25.631 : P put 4 (waiting elements: 2)
19:16:25.732 : P put 5 (waiting elements: 3)
19:16:25.927 : C2 took 3
19:16:25.927 : P put 6 (waiting elements: 3)
19:16:26.028 : C1 took 4
19:16:26.029 : P put 7 (waiting elements: 3)
19:16:26.528 : C2 took 5
19:16:26.528 : P put 8 (waiting elements: 3)
19:16:26.652 : C1 took 6
19:16:27.128 : P has finished
19:16:27.129 : C2 took 7
19:16:27.253 : C1 took 8
19:16:27.736 : C2 has finished
19:16:27.854 : C1 has finished

We see the producer quickly adding the first numbers, then, as soon as the queue contains 3 elements, only adding a number when a consumer removes one: it is blocked by [put] when the queue is full. The consumers share the numbers among themselves and stop when they remove the end marker. This rhythm is reproducible; the assignment of each number to C1 or C2 is not. The producer displays “P has finished” only after both of its end markers have been placed, that is, after C2 has removed the number 7 and freed up a slot.

We’ll revisit blocking queues in the next chapter, when discussing data transfer between asynchronous processes. With virtual threads, a consumer blocked on [take] does not occupy any system threads.

docs.title: 8.10.1. The Principle
docs.text:
Until now, to manage threads, we have created them and then launched them via [start()]. Creating a platform thread is a relatively costly operation: in particular, the system must allocate a stack to it, and each thread occupies memory as long as it exists. We’ll see in Chapter 10 that connection pools exist: open connections are kept in reserve and lent to threads that request them, since opening a connection is costly. A similar system exists for threads: the thread pool.

Java represents a thread pool using the [java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService] interface (an “executor”): threads are no longer created; instead, tasks are assigned to the executor, which has its threads execute them. A thread that has completed a task is not destroyed; it moves on to the next task. The [ThreadPoolExecutor] class, the most common implementation, works as follows:

  • it has a fixed number of threads (“core pool size”): as long as this number has not been reached, each new task triggers the creation of a new thread;
  • beyond that, tasks are placed in a queue (a [BlockingQueue]) from which the threads retrieve them;
  • if the queue is full, the pool creates additional threads, up to a maximum number (“maximum pool size”). These additional threads are destroyed if they remain inactive for longer than a certain amount of time;
  • if the maximum is reached and the queue is full, the task is rejected: by default, the method that submitted it throws the [RejectedExecutionException] exception.

The thread pool offers two advantages: it saves time spent creating threads (a few threads can handle hundreds of requests), and by limiting the number of threads, it prevents the application from becoming overwhelmed by too many requests.

An executor terminates via its [shutdown] method (it no longer accepts new tasks, and its threads stop once the tasks already submitted are completed), possibly followed by [awaitTermination] (which waits for the tasks to finish), or by [shutdownNow] (which interrupts the tasks in progress). Starting with Java 19, [ExecutorService] extends the [AutoCloseable] interface: its [close] method calls [shutdown] and then waits for all tasks to finish. You can therefore declare an executor in a [try] statement with a resource: upon exiting the block, all assigned tasks are completed. The [Threads25.java] program is as follows:

// a thread pool: ThreadPoolExecutor

void main() {
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");
    // 3 permanent threads, at most 5 threads, a waiting queue of 2 jobs
    try (var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(3, 5, 60, TimeUnit.SECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2))) {
        // we give 8 jobs of 3 s to the pool
        for (int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
            var data = new Data(i, LocalTime.now(), 3);
            try {
                pool.execute(() -> sleep(data, pool));
            } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) {
                IO.println(time() + " : job no. " + i + " was rejected by the pool");
            }
        }
        IO.println(time() + " : thread Main gave the jobs to the pool and waits for their end");
        // the end of the try block closes the pool: close() waits for the end of the submitted jobs
    }
    IO.println(time() + " : end of thread Main");
}

// the job executed by a thread of the pool
static void sleep(Data data, ThreadPoolExecutor pool) {
    // state of the pool
    IO.println("%s : job no. %d starts in thread %s (threads: %d, active: %d, queued: %d)"
            .formatted(time(), data.number(), Thread.currentThread().getName(),
                    pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size()));
    // sleep for [duration] seconds
    try {
        Thread.sleep(data.duration() * 1000L);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
    double duration = Duration.between(data.start(), LocalTime.now()).toMillis() / 1000.0;
    IO.println("%s : job no. %d ends: scheduled for %d s, it lasted %.2f s since its request"
            .formatted(time(), data.number(), data.duration(), duration));
}

// the information passed to each job
record Data(int number, LocalTime start, int duration) {
}

// the current time, to the hundredth of a second
static String time() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 6: the pool has 3 permanent threads, with a maximum of 5 threads; any additional thread that has been inactive for 60 seconds is destroyed; the task queue is a [ArrayBlockingQueue] with 2 slots. The pool is created in a [try] statement with a resource;
  • Lines 8–15: The pool is assigned 8 jobs, each lasting 3 seconds. The [execute(Runnable)] method assigns a task to the pool without waiting;
  • line 9: each job receives a [Data] object; this is a [record] (line 40), which is also defined outside of any class;
  • Lines 12–14: A job rejected by the pool triggers the [RejectedExecutionException] exception;
  • line 18: exiting the [try] block closes the pool and waits for the assigned jobs to finish;
  • lines 23–37: the job executed by a thread in the pool. The thread names ([pool-1-thread-1]…) are provided by the pool;
  • line 27: the pool’s status: the number of its threads ([getPoolSize]), the number of threads currently executing a job ([getActiveCount]), and the number of jobs waiting in the queue ([getQueue().size()]);
  • line 45: times are displayed to the hundredth of a second ([SS]).

Results:

> java Threads25.java
19:16:31.71 : job no. 7 was rejected by the pool
19:16:31.72 : thread Main gave the jobs to the pool and waits for their end
19:16:31.62 : job no. 1 starts in thread pool-1-thread-2 (threads: 2, active: 2, queued: 0)
19:16:31.72 : job no. 2 starts in thread pool-1-thread-3 (threads: 5, active: 5, queued: 2)
19:16:31.72 : job no. 6 starts in thread pool-1-thread-5 (threads: 5, active: 5, queued: 2)
19:16:31.71 : job no. 5 starts in thread pool-1-thread-4 (threads: 5, active: 5, queued: 2)
19:16:31.62 : job no. 0 starts in thread pool-1-thread-1 (threads: 2, active: 2, queued: 0)
19:16:34.81 : job no. 2 ends: scheduled for 3 s, it lasted 3.10 s since its request
19:16:34.81 : job no. 3 starts in thread pool-1-thread-3 (threads: 5, active: 5, queued: 1)
19:16:34.82 : job no. 5 ends: scheduled for 3 s, it lasted 3.10 s since its request
19:16:34.82 : job no. 4 starts in thread pool-1-thread-4 (threads: 5, active: 5, queued: 0)
19:16:34.82 : job no. 6 ends: scheduled for 3 s, it lasted 3.10 s since its request
19:16:34.82 : job no. 0 ends: scheduled for 3 s, it lasted 3.21 s since its request
19:16:34.82 : job no. 1 ends: scheduled for 3 s, it lasted 3.20 s since its request
19:16:37.82 : job no. 4 ends: scheduled for 3 s, it lasted 6.10 s since its request
19:16:37.81 : job no. 3 ends: scheduled for 3 s, it lasted 6.10 s since its request
19:16:37.82 : end of thread Main
  • Jobs 0, 1, and 2 were assigned to the three permanent threads created for this purpose;
  • jobs 3 and 4 were placed in the queue, which is now full;
  • Jobs 5 and 6 triggered the creation of two additional threads ([pool-1-thread-4] and [pool-1-thread-5]): they started immediately, before jobs 3 and 4, which were waiting in the queue. This is the rule for [ThreadPoolExecutor]: the queue first, then the additional threads—which often comes as a surprise;
  • Job 7 was rejected: 5 threads busy, queue full;
  • Jobs 3 and 4 had to wait for a thread to become available after the first jobs finished: they reused threads 3 and 4. In total, they took a little over 6 seconds from the time of their request: 3 seconds of waiting and 3 seconds of processing;
  • The values displayed by each job when it starts (number of threads, queue) depend on the exact moment it obtained the processor: they vary from one execution to the next. However, the outcome of each job (immediate execution, waiting in the queue, or rejection) is reproducible.

You rarely build a *[ThreadPoolExecutor] yourself: the *[Executors] class provides construction methods for common cases:

MethodExecutor returned[newFixedThreadPool(n)]a pool of n permanent threads, with a queue of unlimited capacity[newCachedThreadPool()]a pool without permanent threads, which creates as many threads as necessary and destroys those that remain inactive for 60 seconds[newSingleThreadExecutor()]a single thread that executes tasks one after another, in the order they were submitted[newScheduledThreadPool(n)]A pool capable of executing tasks after a delay or periodically ([ScheduledExecutorService] interface)[newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()](Java 21) an executor without a pool, which creates a new virtual thread for each task

The last executor deserves a note: virtual threads are not placed in a pool. They are so inexpensive that a new one is created for each task; to limit resource usage, a semaphore is used, as in the program [Threads15.java].

docs.title: 8.10.2. Tasks with results: Callable and Future
docs.text:
The [execute] method passes a [Runnable] to the pool, which does not return a result. The [submit(task)] method also accepts a [Callable<V>], a functional interface whose [V call() throws Exception] method returns a result of type V and can throw checked exceptions. It returns a [Future<V>] object that allows you to track the task:

Future<V> MethodRole[V get()], [V get(long timeout, TimeUnit unit)]waits for the task to complete (for at most the duration of [timeout]) and returns its result. If the task throws an exception, [get] throws a [ExecutionException] that wraps it (method [getCause])[boolean isDone()]indicates whether the task has completed (normally, due to an exception or cancellation)[Future.State state()](Java 19) the task’s status: [RUNNING], [SUCCESS], [FAILED], or [CANCELLED][V resultNow()], [Throwable exceptionNow()](Java 19) the result or exception of a task that has already completed, without waiting[boolean cancel(boolean mayInterruptIfRunning)]cancels the task; if it has started and [mayInterruptIfRunning] is equal to [true], the thread executing it is interrupted

The executor’s [invokeAll(collection of Callable)] method submits all tasks in a collection, waits for them all to complete, and returns the list of their [Future] values, in the order of the collection. The [invokeAny] method returns the result of the first successfully completed task and cancels the others. The [Threads26.java] program is as follows:

// ExecutorService: submitting tasks and getting their result with Future

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    IO.println("Main thread: " + Thread.currentThread());

    // 1 - a pool of 2 threads, closed automatically at the end of the try block
    try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)) {
        // three tasks that each return a result of type Integer
        var futures = new ArrayList<Future<Integer>>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            int number = i;
            futures.add(pool.submit(() -> {
                IO.println(time() + " : task " + number + " runs in thread "
                        + Thread.currentThread().getName());
                // work: a Callable can throw checked exceptions
                Thread.sleep(500L * (number + 1));
                // the result of the task
                return number * 10;
            }));
        }
        // the results: get() waits for the end of the task
        for (int i = 0; i < futures.size(); i++) {
            Future<Integer> future = futures.get(i);
            try {
                IO.println("task " + i + " : result " + future.get() + ", state " + future.state());
            } catch (ExecutionException e) {
                IO.println("task " + i + " failed: " + e.getCause());
            }
        }

        // a task that throws an exception
        Future<Integer> failing = pool.submit(() -> fail());
        try {
            failing.get();
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            // the exception of the task is wrapped in an ExecutionException
            IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " containing " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName()
                    + " : " + e.getCause().getMessage());
        }
        IO.println("failing task: state " + failing.state());
    }

    // 2 - one virtual thread per task; invokeAll submits a collection of tasks and waits for their end
    try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        List<Callable<String>> jobs = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
            int number = i;
            jobs.add(() -> {
                Thread.sleep(300);
                return "job " + number + " executed by " + Thread.currentThread();
            });
        }
        for (Future<String> future : executor.invokeAll(jobs)) {
            // the task is finished: resultNow() returns its result without waiting
            IO.println(future.resultNow());
        }
    }
}

// the work of the failing task
static int fail() {
    throw new IllegalStateException("test....");
}

// the current time, to the millisecond
static String time() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • line 7: a pool of 2 threads, created by [Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2)] and closed at the end of the [try] block;
  • lines 12–19: Each task is a lambda that displays the thread executing it, sleeps for 0.5, 1, or 1.5 seconds, and then returns an integer result. Since the lambda returns a value, the compiler interprets it as a [Callable<Integer>], and [submit] yields a [Future<Integer>]. The [sleep] on line 16 does not need to be enclosed in a [try]: the method [call] of [Callable] declares [throws Exception];
  • line 25: [future.get()] waits for the task to finish and returns its result; [future.state()] returns its status;
  • line 32: a task that executes the [fail] method (lines 61–63), which throws an exception;
  • lines 34–38: the exception thrown in the task is not lost: it is stored in the [Future] object, then rethrown in the thread requesting the result, wrapped in a [ExecutionException] whose [getCause] method throws the original exception;
  • lines 44–57: an executor that creates one virtual thread per task. The method [invokeAll] (line 53) assigns the three jobs from the list [jobs] to it and waits for them to finish. Once the tasks are complete, [resultNow] (line 55) returns their results immediately.

Results:

> java Threads26.java
Main thread: Thread[#3,main,5,main]
19:16:39.815 : task 0 runs in thread pool-1-thread-1
19:16:39.816 : task 1 runs in thread pool-1-thread-2
19:16:40.333 : task 2 runs in thread pool-1-thread-1
task 0 : result 0, state SUCCESS
task 1 : result 10, state SUCCESS
task 2 : result 20, state SUCCESS
ExecutionException containing IllegalStateException : test....
failing task: state FAILED
job 0 executed by VirtualThread[#25]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1
job 1 executed by VirtualThread[#27]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2
job 2 executed by VirtualThread[#30]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1
  • the tasks run in the pool’s threads ([pool-1-thread-1] and [pool-1-thread-2]);
  • Task 2 did not start until Task 0 had finished, in the thread that Task 0 had freed up: the pool has only 2 threads, and Task 2 waited in the queue. This issue is reproducible;
  • the results are retrieved after the tasks have finished, and their status is [SUCCESS];
  • the exception from the task that failed was caught by the main thread, and the task’s status is [FAILED];
  • the three jobs in the second part were executed by three different virtual threads, mounted on the carrier threads [ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1] and [ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2].

Blocking a thread in [get] to wait for a result is simple, but you cannot chain processing operations to the completion of a task without waiting. The [CompletableFuture] class, presented in the next chapter, allows this. Finally, note that Java 25 offers, as a preview, structured concurrency ([StructuredTaskScope]), which treats a group of subtasks as a single unit of work (if one fails, the others are aborted); since it is not yet final, it is not used in this course.

docs.title: 8.11.1. Parallel streams
docs.text:
Let’s return to the first use of threads: utilizing all processors for a time-consuming computation. Streams from the API Stream (Chapter 5) can be executed in parallel: simply call [parallel()] on a stream, or [parallelStream()] instead of [stream()] on a collection. The stream then divides the data into chunks, has the chunks processed by multiple threads, and then combines the partial results. The threads used are those from the shared pool ([ForkJoinPool.commonPool()]), joined by the thread executing the stream. By default, the shared pool has as many threads as there are processors, minus one: the calling thread performs the count.

These streams are only suitable if the processing of each element is independent of the others: the processing order is undefined, and if the processing updates shared data, it must be protected. The program [Threads27.java] is as follows:

// parallel streams: parallelStream and IntStream.parallel

void main() {
    // 1 - counting the prime numbers below N
    final int N = 5_000_000;
    // sequential version: a for loop
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    int nbSequential = 0;
    for (int i = 2; i < N; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            nbSequential++;
        }
    }
    IO.println("sequential for       : %,d prime numbers in %d ms"
            .formatted(nbSequential, since(start)));

    // sequential version: a stream
    start = System.nanoTime();
    long nbStream = IntStream.range(2, N).filter(i -> isPrime(i)).count();
    IO.println("sequential stream    : %,d prime numbers in %d ms".formatted(nbStream, since(start)));

    // parallel version: the same stream, made parallel
    start = System.nanoTime();
    long nbParallel = IntStream.range(2, N).parallel().filter(i -> isPrime(i)).count();
    IO.println("parallel stream      : %,d prime numbers in %d ms".formatted(nbParallel, since(start)));

    // the threads that worked and the number of prime numbers found by each one
    var threads = new ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer>();
    IntStream.range(2, N).parallel()
            .filter(i -> isPrime(i))
            .forEach(i -> threads.merge(Thread.currentThread().getName(), 1, Integer::sum));
    new TreeMap<>(threads).forEach((name, nb) ->
            IO.println("  thread %-30s : %,d prime numbers found".formatted(name, nb)));

    // 2 - processing a collection in parallel
    List<String> files = List.of("a.txt", "b.txt", "c.txt", "d.txt", "e.txt");
    files.parallelStream().forEach(file -> {
        IO.println(time() + " : processing of " + file + " in thread "
                + Thread.currentThread().getName());
        // simulated processing
        sleep(500);
    });
    IO.println("parallel forEach finished");
    IO.println("Parallelism of the common pool: " + ForkJoinPool.getCommonPoolParallelism());
}

// primality test (deliberately simple)
static boolean isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

// the number of milliseconds elapsed since [start] (in nanoseconds)
static long since(long start) {
    return (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// the current time, to the millisecond
static String time() {
    return LocalTime.now().format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm:ss.SSS"));
}

Comments:

  • Lines 7–15: Prime numbers less than 5,000,000 are counted using a standard [for] loop. The function [isPrime] (lines 48–58) tests divisors up to the square root of the number: this is a time-consuming process, and the iterations are independent;
  • lines 18–20: the same calculation using a sequential workflow: [IntStream.range(2, N)] generates integers from 2 to N–1, [filter] keeps only the prime numbers, and [count] counts them;
  • lines 23–25: the same stream, made parallel by [parallel()]. Nothing else needs to be changed: each thread counts the prime numbers in its segments, and the stream adds up the partial counts. No data is shared between threads;
  • lines 28–33: To determine which threads have completed their work, the parallel stream counts, for each thread, the prime numbers it has found and stores them in a shared [ConcurrentHashMap]. This is shared data, updated by an atomic operation ([merge]);
  • lines 36–42: The method ***[parallelStream()], which takes a list of filenames, returns a parallel stream; *[forEach] processes each file (the processing is simulated by a half-second pause). With a parallel stream, [forEach] does not preserve the order of the list; [forEachOrdered] would preserve it, at the cost of some parallelism;
  • Line 44: the number of threads in the shared pool.

Results:

> java Threads27.java
sequential for       : 348,513 prime numbers in 1419 ms
sequential stream    : 348,513 prime numbers in 1253 ms
parallel stream      : 348,513 prime numbers in 780 ms
  thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1 : 224,082 prime numbers found
  thread main                           : 124,431 prime numbers found
19:16:47.328 : processing of b.txt in thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
19:16:47.328 : processing of c.txt in thread main
19:16:47.838 : processing of a.txt in thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
19:16:47.838 : processing of e.txt in thread main
19:16:48.339 : processing of d.txt in thread ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1
parallel forEach finished
Parallelism of the common pool: 1
  • All three versions find the same number of prime numbers;
  • two threads participated in the parallel processing: the thread [main] and the single thread from the shared pool ([ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1]): on this dual-processor machine, the shared pool has only one thread (line 13);
  • file processing occurs in pairs, half a second apart, and in an order that does not match the list;
  • the parallel stream was faster, but not twice as fast: the threads in our program were sharing the two processors with other very active programs at the time of the capture, and the measured times varied significantly from one run to the next. On a lightly loaded machine with n processors, a parallel stream like this one can be nearly n times faster than the sequential stream. Always measure before drawing conclusions: parallelization comes at a cost (work partitioning, synchronization, combining results) that is only worthwhile if processing each element requires a significant amount of computation.

docs.title: 8.11.2. Divide and conquer: ForkJoinPool and RecursiveTask
docs.text:
Parallel streams are based on the Fork/Join framework (Java 7), which can also be used directly. It is well-suited for “divide and conquer” algorithms: a task that is too large is broken down into subtasks, which are in turn broken down further, until the pieces are small enough to be processed directly; the results of the subtasks are then combined. A task is a class derived from [RecursiveTask<V>] (a task that returns a result of type V) or from [RecursiveAction] (no result), for which the method [compute] is overridden. In [compute], a subtask’s [fork()] method immediately submits it to the pool, and its [join()] method waits for its result.

The tasks are executed by a [ForkJoinPool], in which each thread has its own task queue. A thread that has nothing left to do “steals” tasks from another thread’s queue (“work stealing”): the load is thus distributed automatically. The threads carrying the virtual threads also form a [ForkJoinPool]: this is the one we saw in the textual representation of the virtual threads ([ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1]). The program [Threads28.java] counts prime numbers using a recursive task:

// divide and conquer: ForkJoinPool and RecursiveTask

void main() {
    final int N = 5_000_000;
    // the common pool, used by default by parallel streams
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    int nb = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new CountPrimes(2, N));
    IO.println("common pool       : %,d prime numbers in %d ms".formatted(nb, since(start)));

    // a pool of 4 threads, closed at the end of the try block
    try (var pool = new ForkJoinPool(4)) {
        CountPrimes.chunks.clear();
        start = System.nanoTime();
        nb = pool.invoke(new CountPrimes(2, N));
        IO.println("pool of 4 threads : %,d prime numbers in %d ms".formatted(nb, since(start)));
        IO.println("tasks stolen by one thread from another: " + pool.getStealCount());
    }
    // the distribution of the chunks among the threads of the last pool
    new TreeMap<>(CountPrimes.chunks).forEach((name, nbChunks) ->
            IO.println("  %-25s : %d chunks processed".formatted(name, nbChunks)));
}

// a task that counts the prime numbers of the interval [start, end[
static class CountPrimes extends RecursiveTask<Integer> {
    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
    // below this threshold, the chunk is processed directly
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 100_000;
    // the number of chunks processed by each thread
    static final Map<String, Integer> chunks = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    private final int start;
    private final int end;

    CountPrimes(int start, int end) {
        this.start = start;
        this.end = end;
    }

    @Override
    protected Integer compute() {
        // chunk small enough: we process it sequentially
        if (end - start <= THRESHOLD) {
            chunks.merge(Thread.currentThread().getName(), 1, Integer::sum);
            int nb = 0;
            for (int i = start; i < end; i++) {
                if (isPrime(i)) {
                    nb++;
                }
            }
            return nb;
        }
        // otherwise, we cut it in two
        int middle = (start + end) >>> 1;
        var left = new CountPrimes(start, middle);
        var right = new CountPrimes(middle, end);
        // the left half is given to the pool (another thread may "steal" it)
        left.fork();
        // the right half is processed by the current thread
        int nbRight = right.compute();
        // we wait for the result of the left half and combine the two results
        return left.join() + nbRight;
    }
}

// primality test (deliberately simple)
static boolean isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) {
        return false;
    }
    for (int d = 2; d * d <= n; d++) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

// the number of milliseconds elapsed since [start] (in nanoseconds)
static long since(long start) {
    return (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
}

Comments:

  • lines 24–64: The task [CountPrimes] counts prime numbers in the interval [start, end[. It is derived from [RecursiveTask<Integer>];
  • lines 25–26: Fork/Join tasks are serializable: the compiler option [-Xlint:all] therefore requires declaring the serialization version number [serialVersionUID], with the annotation [@Serial] (Java 14);
  • line 28: for fewer than 100,000 numbers, an interval is processed directly;
  • line 30: for each thread, the number of chunks it has processed;
  • lines 43–52: A sufficiently small chunk is processed sequentially;
  • lines 54–56: a chunk that is too large is split into two subtasks. The expression [(start + end) >>> 1] calculates the middle value using an unsigned right shift, which prevents an overflow if the sum exceeds the capacity of a [int];
  • line 58: the left half is assigned to the pool; another thread may “steal” it;
  • line 60: the right half is processed by the current thread via a direct call to [compute]. There is no need to assign both halves to the pool: the current thread would have nothing left to do but wait;
  • line 62: the thread waits for the result of the left half (which it will process itself if no one has “stolen” it) and combines the two results;
  • line 7: the task is first executed by the shared pool. The [invoke(task)] method submits the task and waits for its result;
  • lines 11–17: then by a pool of 4 threads, created in a [try] statement with a resource ([ForkJoinPool] is a [ExecutorService]). The [getStealCount] method returns the number of tasks stolen by one thread from another;
  • lines 19–20: the distribution of chunks among the threads in this pool.

Results:

> java Threads28.java
common pool       : 348,513 prime numbers in 1506 ms
pool of 4 threads : 348,513 prime numbers in 648 ms
tasks stolen by one thread from another: 6
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1   : 15 chunks processed
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-2   : 19 chunks processed
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3   : 12 chunks processed
  ForkJoinPool-1-worker-4   : 18 chunks processed
  • the shared pool was no faster than a sequential loop (compare with the previous program): on this machine, it has only one thread, and the main thread—which waits for the result in [invoke]—does not participate in the computation as it does in a parallel stream;
  • the 4-thread pool utilized both processors and was about twice as fast. Having more threads than processors offers no benefit for a pure computation, but doesn’t cost much here;
  • The 64 chunks (5,000,000 / 100,000, rounded up to the next power of 2 due to halving) were distributed roughly equally among the 4 threads, thanks to task stealing. This distribution varies from one run to the next.

Parallel streams are sufficient in most cases; a Fork/Join task is only written for a recursive algorithm that cannot be easily expressed as a stream (sorting, tree traversal, etc.).

docs.title: 8.12.1. The Principle
docs.text:
Consider a three-tier application:

Suppose the application is multi-user, such as a web application. Each user request is handled by a thread. The thread’s lifecycle is as follows:

  • the thread is created (virtual thread) or requested from a thread pool to fulfill a user’s request;
  • if this request requires data, the thread executes a method in the [ui] layer, which calls a method in the [business] layer, which in turn calls a method in the [dao] layer;
  • the thread returns the response to the user. It then either terminates or is returned to the thread pool.

During the second step, it may be useful for the thread to have its own data—that is, data not shared with other threads. This data could, for example, belong to the specific user the thread is serving and be used across the various [ui, business, dao] layers without being passed as a parameter to each method.

Java provides two tools for this purpose:

  • The [ThreadLocal<T>] class (Java 1.2): an object whose value—read by [get()] and written by [set(value)]—is different for each thread. The constructor [ThreadLocal.withInitial(supplier)] provides the initial value for each thread; the method [remove()] clears the value of the current thread. The derived class [InheritableThreadLocal<T>] passes the value held by the creating thread to the newly created thread;
  • the [ScopedValue<T>] class (final in Java 25): a value bound, for a delimited scope of the code, to a thread, and which cannot be modified within that scope.

docs.title: 8.12.2. The ThreadLocal class
docs.text:
The program [Threads29.java] compares a regular static field, a [ThreadLocal], and a [InheritableThreadLocal]:

// thread-local data: ThreadLocal and InheritableThreadLocal

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");
    // the main thread writes its own values
    Context.shared = 100;
    Context.perThread.set(100);
    Context.user.set("admin");
    Context.language.set("fr");

    // three threads write then read back the data
    var threads = new Thread[3];
    for (int i = 0; i < threads.length; i++) {
        int number = i;
        threads[i] = new Thread(() -> {
            // writing
            Context.shared = number;
            Context.perThread.set(number);
            // thread T2 does not set a user: it will have the initial value
            if (number != 2) {
                Context.user.set("user" + number);
            }
            // thread T1 changes the language inherited from the main thread
            if (number == 1) {
                Context.language.set("en");
            }
            // we let the other threads write in turn
            sleep(200);
            // reading back
            display();
        }, "T" + i);
        threads[i].start();
    }
    for (Thread thread : threads) {
        thread.join();
    }
    // reading back by the main thread
    display();
}

// displays the data seen by the current thread
static void display() {
    IO.println("%-4s : shared=%-3d perThread=%-3d user=%-20s language=%s".formatted(
            Thread.currentThread().getName(), Context.shared, Context.perThread.get(),
            Context.user.get(), Context.language.get()));
}

// the data of the program
static class Context {
    // a static (volatile) field: a single copy, shared by all the threads
    static volatile int shared;
    // one copy per thread; initial value null
    static final ThreadLocal<Integer> perThread = new ThreadLocal<>();
    // one copy per thread, initialized for each thread by the supplied factory
    static final ThreadLocal<String> user =
            ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> "anonymous (thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName() + ")");
    // one copy per thread, whose initial value is inherited from the creating thread
    static final InheritableThreadLocal<String> language = new InheritableThreadLocal<>();
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 51: a regular static field. There is only one instance of it, shared by all threads. It is [volatile], so that each thread sees the latest value written by the others;
  • line 53: a [ThreadLocal<Integer>] object. Each thread has its own value; as long as a thread hasn’t written to it, [get] returns [null];
  • lines 55–56: a [ThreadLocal<String>] object created by [ThreadLocal.withInitial(…)]. The lambda passed to this method is executed the first time a thread reads the value without having written it; it provides the initial value for that thread;
  • line 58: a [InheritableThreadLocal<String>] object: when a thread is created, its initial value is a copy of the value that the creating thread had at that time;
  • lines 6–9: the main thread writes its own values;
  • lines 17–26: Each thread writes its own values, except for thread T2, which does not set a user, and thread T1, which is the only one to change the language;
  • line 28: each thread waits for the others to write before reading the values again;
  • lines 42–46: the data viewed by the current thread is displayed.

Results:

> java Threads29.java
T1   : shared=2   perThread=1   user=user1                language=en
T0   : shared=2   perThread=0   user=user0                language=fr
T2   : shared=2   perThread=2   user=anonymous (thread T2) language=fr
Main : shared=2   perThread=100 user=admin                language=fr
  • the ordinary field [shared] has the same value for all threads: the last value written (in this execution, that of thread T2; another execution may yield a different value);
  • [perThread] has retained, in each thread, the value that thread wrote to it;
  • [user] has the value written by each thread; the thread T2, which had not written to it, obtained the initial value provided by the lambda of [withInitial];
  • [language] is equal to [fr] for the threads T0 and T2, which inherited it from the main thread without ever writing to it. The thread T1 changed it to [en] only for itself: the main thread and the other threads do not see this change.

A [ThreadLocal] requires some precautions. A thread’s value exists only as long as the thread itself: with a thread pool, the thread that handles one request will then handle other requests, and [remove] must be called at the end of each request; otherwise, the next request would find the data from the previous one (and the memory would never be freed). With virtual threads, you can create millions of threads, each with its own copy of the data: [InheritableThreadLocal] then copies its values into each of them. Finally, a value that can be modified by any method of the thread makes the code difficult to follow. The [ScopedValue] class avoids these issues.

docs.title: 8.12.3. The ScopedValue class
docs.text:
A [ScopedValue<T>] value is bound to a value for the execution of a piece of code, called its scope:

  • [ScopedValue.newInstance()] creates a bindable value, typically stored in a [static final] field;
  • [ScopedValue.where(sv, value).run(action)] executes the action (a [Runnable]) by binding [sv] to [value]. During the execution of the action—and all the methods it calls—in the current thread, [sv.get()] returns [value]. When the action ends, the link disappears: there is nothing to clean up;
  • [ScopedValue.where(sv, value).call(op)] does the same with an operation that returns a result;
  • Within the scope, the value cannot be modified; it can only be bound to another value for a nested scope;
  • [isBound()] indicates whether the value is bound in the current thread; [orElse(other)] returns the value, or, if it is not bound, [other]. Outside any scope, [get()] throws the [NoSuchElementException] exception.

The program [Threads30.java] is as follows:

// values bound to a scope: ScopedValue (Java 25)

// the user on whose behalf the code runs
static final ScopedValue<String> USER = ScopedValue.newInstance();

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    IO.println("Outside of any scope, is USER bound? " + USER.isBound());
    try {
        USER.get();
    } catch (NoSuchElementException e) {
        IO.println("get() out of scope: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName());
    }

    // 1 - two simultaneous processings, each one for its user
    Thread t1 = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> ScopedValue.where(USER, "alice").run(this::process));
    Thread t2 = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> ScopedValue.where(USER, "bob").run(this::process));
    t1.join();
    t2.join();

    // 2 - a scope can contain another one, which temporarily binds another value
    ScopedValue.where(USER, "admin").run(() -> {
        display("outer scope");
        ScopedValue.where(USER, "guest").run(() -> display("inner scope"));
        display("back in the outer scope");
        // a thread created in the scope does not inherit the binding
        Thread child = Thread.ofVirtual().start(
                () -> IO.println("child thread: bound? " + USER.isBound()));
        try {
            child.join();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    });

    // 3 - call: a bound processing that returns a result
    String message = ScopedValue.where(USER, "carole").call(() -> "hello " + USER.get());
    IO.println(message);
    // after the scope, the binding has disappeared
    IO.println("After the scopes: bound? " + USER.isBound()
            + ", orElse: " + USER.orElse("nobody"));
}

// the [business] layer calls the [dao] layer without passing it the user
void process() {
    display("[business] layer");
    dao();
}

// the [dao] layer finds the user in the current scope
void dao() {
    display("[dao] layer");
}

// displays the user bound in the current scope
static void display(String place) {
    IO.println(place + " : USER = " + USER.get());
}

Comments:

  • line 4: the bound value [USER], a static field of the implicit class;
  • lines 7–12: outside any scope, the value is unbound, and [get] throws an exception;
  • lines 15–16: two virtual threads execute the method [process], each within a scope where [USER] is bound to a different user;
  • lines 44–52: the method [process] (the [business] layer) calls the method [dao] (the [dao] layer) without passing the user to it: each retrieves it via [USER.get()] (line 56);
  • lines 21–33: a scope where [USER] equals [admin] contains a nested scope (line 23) where it equals [guest]. Upon exiting the nested scope, we find [admin];
  • lines 26–27: A thread created within the scope does not see the binding: unlike a *[InheritableThreadLocal]*, a *[ScopedValue] is not passed to threads created by *[Thread]. It is, however, passed to the subtasks of structured concurrency ([StructuredTaskScope], previewed in Java 25), which ensures that these subtasks complete before the scope ends;
  • line 36: [call] performs an operation within a scope and returns its result;
  • lines 39–40: after the scopes, the value is no longer bound.

Results:

> java Threads30.java
Outside of any scope, is USER bound? false
get() out of scope: NoSuchElementException
[business] layer : USER = alice
[dao] layer : USER = alice
[business] layer : USER = bob
[dao] layer : USER = bob
outer scope : USER = admin
inner scope : USER = guest
back in the outer scope : USER = admin
child thread: bound? false
hello carole
After the scopes: bound? false, orElse: nobody

The messages from the virtual threads in lines 4–7 may appear in a different order (bob before alice); the rest is reproducible. A [ScopedValue] is suitable for context data passed “downward,” from the caller to the called methods: authenticated user, transaction, regional settings, etc. When a called method needs to modify the data for subsequent processing, a [ThreadLocal] is required.

docs.title: 8.12.4. Application: A Transaction Shared Across Layers
docs.text:
Consider the following three-tier application, in which the [dao] layer manages an item table:

Suppose that the interface of the [dao] layer is initially as follows:

interface IDao {
    int insertArticle(Article article);

    List<Article> getAllArticles();

    void deleteAllArticles();
}

Later, the need arises to insert a list of items within a transaction, because the system must operate on an all-or-nothing basis: either all items are inserted, or none are. A method named [insertArticles(List<Article> articles)] can be added to the interface. Then, for another application, the need arises to delete a list of items, again within a transaction… To meet different business requirements, the [dao] layer will grow. We can take a different approach:

  • include only the basic operations (insert, update, delete, read an item) in the [dao] layer;
  • move operations that simultaneously update multiple items to the [business] layer. These operations use the basic operations from the [dao] layer.

The advantage of this solution is that the same [dao] layer can be used without modification with different [business] layers. It introduces a challenge in managing the transaction that groups the updates to be performed atomically:

  • the transaction must be started by the [business] layer before it calls the methods of the [dao] layer;
  • the methods in the [dao] layer must be aware of the transaction’s existence in order to participate in it;
  • The transaction must be completed (confirmed or canceled) by layer [business].

To ensure that the methods of the [dao] layer are aware of any ongoing transaction, the transaction could be added as a parameter to each method of the [dao] layer. This parameter would then appear in the signature of the interface’s methods, thereby binding the interface to a specific data source. Thread-local data provides a more elegant solution: the [business] layer places the transaction in the thread-local data, and that is where the [dao] layer retrieves it. The method signatures of the [dao] layer do not need to be changed. Multiple threads (multiple users) can work simultaneously: each has its own transaction.

Databases will be covered in Chapters 10 and 11. To keep the focus on threads, we are using an in-memory table and a simulated transaction here. The program [Threads31.java] combines all the layers into a single, compact source file. The entities are as follows:

// an article
record Article(int id, String name, double price, int currentStock, int minimumStock) {
}

// a simulated transaction: it records how to undo each update
static class Transaction {
    private static final AtomicInteger counter = new AtomicInteger();
    private final Deque<Runnable> undos = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int number = counter.incrementAndGet();

    int getNumber() {
        return number;
    }

    // records the operation that undoes an update
    void log(Runnable undo) {
        undos.push(undo);
    }

    // commits the transaction: the updates are kept
    void commit() {
        undos.clear();
    }

    // rolls back the transaction: the updates are undone, from the last to the first
    void rollback() {
        Runnable undo;
        while ((undo = undos.poll()) != null) {
            undo.run();
        }
    }
}

// the thread-local data shared by the layers
static class ThreadContext {
    // the current transaction of the thread (null if there is none)
    static final ThreadLocal<Transaction> transaction = new ThreadLocal<>();
}
  • line 68: an article is a [record] whose identifier [id] is set by the [dao] layer;
  • lines 72–98: a simulated transaction. Each update made within the transaction records the operation that allows it to be rolled back (method [log]); [commit] commits the transaction while ignoring these operations; [rollback] rolls it back by executing the rollback operations, from the last to the first. The operations are stored in a stack: the method [push] of a [Deque] adds to the top, while the method [poll] removes from the top (and returns [null] if the stack is empty). A real database operates in a similar way, using a transaction log;
  • line 75: each transaction is assigned a unique number. Since transactions can be created by multiple threads simultaneously, the counter is a [AtomicInteger], incremented atomically;
  • lines 101–104: the thread-local data shared by the layers: the thread’s current transaction, or [null] if there is none.

The [dao] layer is as follows:

// the [dao] layer: an in-memory table of articles with a uniqueness constraint on the name
interface IDao {
    int insertArticle(Article article);

    List<Article> getAllArticles();

    void deleteAllArticles();
}

static class Dao implements IDao {
    // the table, shared by all the threads, and its lock
    private final List<Article> table = new ArrayList<>();
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    private int nextId = 1;

    @Override
    public int insertArticle(Article article) {
        // is there a transaction in progress in the current thread?
        Transaction transaction = ThreadContext.transaction.get();
        synchronized (lock) {
            if (table.stream().anyMatch(a -> a.name().equals(article.name()))) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("an article named [" + article.name() + "] already exists");
            }
            Article inserted = new Article(nextId++, article.name(), article.price(),
                    article.currentStock(), article.minimumStock());
            table.add(inserted);
            // in a transaction, we record how to undo the insertion
            if (transaction != null) {
                transaction.log(() -> {
                    synchronized (lock) {
                        table.remove(inserted);
                    }
                });
            }
            String mode = transaction == null
                    ? "outside a transaction"
                    : "in transaction " + transaction.getNumber();
            IO.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] [dao] insertion of " + inserted.name()
                    + " (id " + inserted.id() + ") " + mode);
            return 1;
        }
    }

    @Override
    public List<Article> getAllArticles() {
        synchronized (lock) {
            return List.copyOf(table);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public void deleteAllArticles() {
        synchronized (lock) {
            table.clear();
        }
    }
}
  • line 117: the item table, shared by all threads. Access to it is protected by the lock on line 118;
  • line 124: the method [insertArticle] retrieves any transaction that the [business] layer has placed in the current thread’s local data;
  • lines 126–128: The table has a unique constraint on item names: inserting an item with a name that already exists throws an exception;
  • lines 129–131: The inserted item is a copy of the received item, with an identifier assigned by the [dao] layer. Since a [record] object is read-only, a new object is created;
  • lines 133–139: If there is a transaction, the [dao] layer participates by recording how to roll back the insertion. The rollback lambda captures the variable [inserted];
  • lines 140–144: a trace output shows the thread, the inserted item, and any transaction;
  • lines 150–154: The list of items returned is a read-only copy of the table ([List.copyOf]), so that the caller does not iterate over it while another thread is modifying it.

The [business] layer is as follows:

// the [business] layer
interface IBusiness {
    void insertArticlesInTransaction(List<Article> articles);

    void insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(List<Article> articles);

    List<Article> getAllArticles();

    void deleteAllArticles();
}

static class Business implements IBusiness {
    private final IDao dao;

    Business(IDao dao) {
        this.dao = dao;
    }

    // insertion of a list of articles: all or nothing
    @Override
    public void insertArticlesInTransaction(List<Article> articles) {
        // start of the transaction, stored in the thread-local data
        var transaction = new Transaction();
        ThreadContext.transaction.set(transaction);
        try {
            for (Article article : articles) {
                // the [dao] layer will find the transaction in the thread
                dao.insertArticle(article);
                // simulated processing, which gives other threads time to step in
                sleep(200);
            }
            transaction.commit();
            IO.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] [business] transaction "
                    + transaction.getNumber() + " committed");
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            transaction.rollback();
            IO.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] [business] transaction "
                    + transaction.getNumber() + " rolled back");
            // the exception is rethrown to the caller
            throw e;
        } finally {
            // the thread no longer has a transaction in progress
            ThreadContext.transaction.remove();
        }
    }

    // insertion of a list of articles without a transaction
    @Override
    public void insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(List<Article> articles) {
        for (Article article : articles) {
            dao.insertArticle(article);
        }
    }

    @Override
    public List<Article> getAllArticles() {
        return dao.getAllArticles();
    }

    @Override
    public void deleteAllArticles() {
        dao.deleteAllArticles();
    }
}
  • lines 176–180: The [dao] layer is injected by the constructor;
  • lines 186–187: the [insertArticlesInTransaction] method starts a transaction and saves it in the thread’s local data;
  • line 191: the insertion method of the [dao] layer is called for each item, without passing the transaction to it;
  • line 193: a pause simulates processing, in order to give another thread time to intervene during the transaction (third part of the test program);
  • line 195: if the program reaches this point, no exception has occurred: the transaction is committed;
  • lines 198–203: if an exception occurs, the transaction is rolled back and the exception is rethrown to the caller;
  • line 206: in all cases, the thread no longer has an active transaction: [remove()] removes the transaction ID from the thread. This is essential if the thread is reused (a pooled thread);
  • Lines 212–216: The same insertion, without a transaction.

The test program is as follows:

// thread-local data: the [business] layer puts the transaction there, the [dao] layer finds it there

void main() throws InterruptedException {
    // the layers of the application
    IDao dao = new Dao();
    IBusiness business = new Business(dao);
    Thread.currentThread().setName("Main");

    // two articles with the same name: the second violates the uniqueness constraint on the name
    List<Article> articles = List.of(new Article(0, "article", 100, 10, 1),
            new Article(0, "article", 100, 10, 1));

    // 1 - insertion outside a transaction
    IO.println("Inserting the articles outside a transaction...");
    execute(() -> business.insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articles));
    displayArticles(business);

    // 2 - insertion in a transaction
    business.deleteAllArticles();
    IO.println("Inserting the articles in a transaction...");
    execute(() -> business.insertArticlesInTransaction(articles));
    displayArticles(business);

    // 3 - two simultaneous threads: the transaction of thread A is not seen by thread B
    business.deleteAllArticles();
    IO.println("Two simultaneous threads...");
    List<Article> articlesA = List.of(new Article(0, "keyboard", 20, 5, 1), new Article(0, "mouse", 10, 5, 1),
            new Article(0, "keyboard", 20, 5, 1));
    List<Article> articlesB = List.of(new Article(0, "screen", 150, 2, 1));
    var threadA = new Thread(() -> execute(() -> business.insertArticlesInTransaction(articlesA)), "A");
    var threadB = new Thread(() -> execute(() -> business.insertArticlesOutOfTransaction(articlesB)), "B");
    threadA.start();
    Thread.sleep(100);
    threadB.start();
    threadA.join();
    threadB.join();
    displayArticles(business);
}

// executes an action, displaying the possible exception
static void execute(Runnable action) {
    try {
        action.run();
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        IO.println("[" + Thread.currentThread().getName() + "] " + e.getClass().getSimpleName()
                + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

// sleep for [ms] milliseconds
static void sleep(long ms) {
    try {
        Thread.sleep(ms);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

// displays the list of articles
static void displayArticles(IBusiness business) {
    IO.println("List of articles:");
    for (Article article : business.getAllArticles()) {
        IO.println("  " + article);
    }
}
  • Line 10: We create a list of two items with the same name. Attempting to insert the second item will be rejected. If the insertion is performed outside a transaction, the first item is inserted and remains in the list. If it is performed within a transaction, the first item is inserted and then removed when the transaction is rolled back;
  • Lines 13–16: Insert the list outside a transaction, then display the table;
  • Lines 18–22: Same procedure within a transaction;
  • lines 24–37: Two threads are working simultaneously. Thread A inserts three items within a transaction (the third violates the uniqueness constraint); meanwhile, Thread B inserts an item outside a transaction;
  • lines 41–48: the method [execute] executes an action and displays any exception, preceded by the thread name.

Results:

> java Threads31.java
Inserting the articles outside a transaction...
[Main] [dao] insertion of article (id 1) outside a transaction
[Main] IllegalStateException : an article named [article] already exists
List of articles:
  Article[id=1, name=article, price=100.0, currentStock=10, minimumStock=1]
Inserting the articles in a transaction...
[Main] [dao] insertion of article (id 2) in transaction 1
[Main] [business] transaction 1 rolled back
[Main] IllegalStateException : an article named [article] already exists
List of articles:
Two simultaneous threads...
[A] [dao] insertion of keyboard (id 3) in transaction 2
[B] [dao] insertion of screen (id 4) outside a transaction
[A] [dao] insertion of mouse (id 5) in transaction 2
[A] [business] transaction 2 rolled back
[A] IllegalStateException : an article named [keyboard] already exists
List of articles:
  Article[id=4, name=screen, price=150.0, currentStock=2, minimumStock=1]
  • The insert outside the transaction left the first record in the table (line 6). The method [toString] of a [record] displays the name and value of each of its components;
  • The insertion made within a transaction left no records in the table: the record with ID 2 was removed by the rollback;
  • In the third part, thread B inserted the screen while transaction 2 of thread A was in progress: it did so outside the transaction, since the transaction is a local variable of thread A. The rollback of transaction 2 removed the keyboard and mouse inserted by A, but not the screen inserted by B. This result is reproducible.

docs.title: 8.12.5. Conclusion
docs.text: The previous example demonstrated the value of thread-local data for transaction management. It should not be replicated exactly as shown, but it accurately describes how frameworks operate: Spring’s transaction management ([@Transactional] annotation) places the transaction and the database connection into [ThreadLocal], which the data access layers consult without their code having to manipulate the transaction; Hibernate can similarly associate the working session with the current thread. We’ll revisit these tools in Chapter 11. In new code, particularly when using virtual threads, a *[ScopedValue]* is the recommended way to pass this type of contextual information.

docs.title: 8.13. Further Reading
docs.text:
Thread synchronization is a challenging field. This chapter has introduced the main tools; to learn more:

  • the book by Brian Goetz et al., [Java Concurrency in Practice] (Addison-Wesley), which remains the definitive reference on the subject, even though it predates virtual threads;
  • the “Concurrency” section of Oracle’s Java tutorial: Lesson: Concurrency, which is outdated but still accurate for the basics;
  • the documentation for the [java.util.concurrent] package: Package java.util.concurrent, whose “Memory Consistency Properties” section summarizes the “happens-before” relationships;
  • the Java enhancement proposals (JEP) that introduced virtual threads and scoped values: JEP 444: Virtual Threads and JEP 506: Scoped Values.

In modern code, [Thread] objects are rarely manipulated directly. Instead, executors ([ExecutorService]), parallel streams for computations, and virtual threads for waiting processes are preferred. The following chapter introduces asynchronous programming using the [CompletableFuture] class, which allows you to chain processes to the completion of a long-running operation (network access, database, file) without blocking a thread. Nevertheless, the concepts covered in this chapter remain essential: all these tasks run in threads, and the data they share must be protected using the same tools ([synchronized], locks, atomic classes, concurrent collections).

docs.title: 7. Functional Interfaces, Lambdas, and Events
docs.text:
In many programs, we need to pass not data but behavior to a method: the sort criterion, the filtering condition, or the processing to be performed when something happens. Java addresses this need with a simple concept upon which this entire chapter is based: the functional interface—that is, an interface that declares only a single abstract method. An object that implements such an interface “carries” a function, which can be stored in a variable, passed as a parameter, returned as the result of a method, and executed at will.

Before Java 8 (2014), you had to write a class—often an anonymous class—for each behavior you wanted to express, which was verbose. Java 8 introduced lambda expressions and method references, which allow you to write this behavior in a single line. We’ve already used them without going into detail with the API Stream in Chapter 5: in [persons.stream().filter(p -> p.age() >= 18)], we pass a lambda—that is, an instance of a functional interface—to the [filter] method. This chapter explains what lies behind this syntax. It concludes with events, which Java handles using “listeners”: objects—often lambdas—that register with an emitter to be notified of what is happening there. Java graphical user interfaces (Swing, JavaFX) and web frameworks alike rely on this mechanism: a button click or the arrival of a request (HTTP) are signaled to registered listeners. This course does not cover graphical user interfaces; all examples are console programs.

The programs in this chapter are compact source files located in the [07-lambdas] folder. They are run using [java LambdasNN.java]. Note that a compact source file automatically imports the entire [java.base] module: the interfaces from the [java.util.function], [java.util], or [java.util.concurrent] packages can be used there without any [import] statements.

docs.title: 7.1.1. The concept of a functional interface
docs.text:
A functional interface is an interface that has exactly one abstract method. It may also have as many [default] and [static] methods as desired (see Chapter 4): these do not count. This single abstract method describes a model (also called a signature or a form) of a function: the types of its parameters and the type of its return value. A variable of the interface’s type can then refer to any object that provides a function of this form and execute it by calling the method.

The oldest example is the [java.lang.Runnable] interface, which has existed since Java 1.0 and represents a task to be executed (we’ll revisit it in connection with threads in Chapter 8). It consists of a single method: [void run();]. It describes a function:

  • with no parameters;
  • returning no result ([void]).

There are three ways to create an object of type [Runnable]:

  • write a class that implements the interface, either named or anonymous. This was the only way to do it before Java 8;
  • write a lambda expression: [Runnable task = () -> IO.println("task");];
  • write a method reference to an existing method that has the correct form: [Runnable task = Functions::display;].

In the last two cases, the compiler creates the object that implements the interface itself: the lambda or the referenced method becomes the body of the method [run]. The function is then executed by calling the interface method: [task.run()]. Unlike other languages, Java does not have a specific call syntax: the interface method is always called by its name ([run], [apply], [test]…).

docs.title: 7.1.2. Interfaces in the java.util.function package
docs.text:
Before Java 8, each library defined its own single-method interfaces ([Runnable], [Comparator], [ActionListener]…). Java 8 introduced the [java.util.function] package, which provides 43 generic functional interfaces covering virtually all requirements. The main ones are as follows:

InterfaceAbstract MethodFunctions Represented[Runnable] ([java.lang])[void run()]No parameters, no results[Supplier<T>][T get()]No parameters, one result: a “supplier”[Consumer<T>][void accept(T t)]one parameter, no result: a “consumer”[BiConsumer<T, U>][void accept(T t, U u)]two parameters, no results[Function<T, R>][R apply(T t)]one parameter, one result of type [R] (always the last type)[BiFunction<T, U, R>][R apply(T t, U u)]two parameters, one result[UnaryOperator<T>][T apply(T t)]one [Function<T, T>]: parameter and result of the same type[BinaryOperator<T>][T apply(T t1, T t2)]a [BiFunction<T, T, T>][Predicate<T>][boolean test(T t)]one parameter, one Boolean result: a “predicate”[BiPredicate<T, U>][boolean test(T t, U u)]two parameters, a Boolean result[Comparator<T>] ([java.util])[int compare(T o1, T o2)]two parameters of the same type, an integer result[Callable<V>] ([java.util.concurrent])[V call() throws Exception]Same as [Supplier<V>], but may throw a checked exception

Java generics apply only to object types: a [Function<Integer, Integer>] receives and returns [Integer], which requires automatic conversions (boxing and unboxing) between [int] and [Integer]. To avoid these, the package provides specialized versions for the primitive types [int], [long], and [double]: [IntBinaryOperator] ([int applyAsInt(int left, int right)]), [IntUnaryOperator], [IntPredicate], [IntSupplier], [IntConsumer], [IntFunction<R>] (with [int] as a parameter), [ToIntFunction<T>] (with [int] as the result), and their equivalents [Long…] and [Double…]. There is no predefined interface with three or more parameters; in that case, you must define your own (see the following paragraph).

The program [Lambdas01.java] uses these interfaces with method references:

// Java's predefined functional interfaces

void main() {
    // 1 - Runnable: no parameter, no result: void run()
    Runnable task = new Runnable() {
        @Override
        public void run() {
            Functions.display();
        }
    };
    // short form: a method reference
    task = Functions::display;
    // execution: we call the single abstract method of the interface
    task.run();

    // 2 - BiFunction<T, U, R>: two parameters, one result
    BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> operation = Functions::add;
    IO.println("operation.apply(2, 3)=" + operation.apply(2, 3));
    // Supplier<T>: no parameter, one result
    Supplier<String> greet = Functions::greet;
    IO.println("greet.get()=" + greet.get());
    // primitive version: IntBinaryOperator, int applyAsInt(int, int), without boxing
    IntBinaryOperator multiply = Functions::multiply;
    IO.println("multiply.applyAsInt(2, 3)=" + multiply.applyAsInt(2, 3));

    // 3 - Consumer<T>: one parameter, no result
    Consumer<String> write = IO::println;
    write.accept("Consumer<String> executed IO.println");

    // 4 - Predicate<T>: one parameter, a boolean result
    Predicate<Integer> isEven = Functions::isEven;
    IO.println("isEven.test(8)=" + isEven.test(8));
    List<Integer> numbers = new ArrayList<>(List.of(3, 8, 1, 6, 5, 4));
    // Collection's removeIf expects a Predicate
    boolean modified = numbers.removeIf(isEven);
    IO.println("even numbers removed: " + modified + ", remaining: " + numbers);

    // 5 - Comparator<T>: two T parameters, an int result
    List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("Paul", "Mélanie", "Jo", "Sébastien"));
    names.sort(Functions::compareLengths);
    IO.println("sorted by length: " + names);

    // 6 - a lambda is an object: the instance of a generated class that implements the interface
    IO.println("class: " + operation.getClass().getName());
    IO.println("interfaces: " + Arrays.toString(operation.getClass().getInterfaces()));
}

// the referenced methods, grouped in a class
// (the implicit class of a compact source file cannot be named)
class Functions {

    static void display() {
        IO.println("display() executed by Runnable.run()");
    }

    static int add(int n1, int n2) {
        return n1 + n2;
    }

    static int multiply(int n1, int n2) {
        return n1 * n2;
    }

    static String greet() {
        return "Hello";
    }

    static boolean isEven(int n) {
        return n % 2 == 0;
    }

    static int compareLengths(String s1, String s2) {
        return Integer.compare(s1.length(), s2.length());
    }
}

Results:

> java Lambdas01.java
display() executed by Runnable.run()
operation.apply(2, 3)=5
greet.get()=Hello
multiply.applyAsInt(2, 3)=6
Consumer<String> executed IO.println
isEven.test(8)=true
even numbers removed: true, remaining: [3, 1, 5]
sorted by length: [Jo, Paul, Mélanie, Sébastien]
class: Lambdas01$$Lambda/0x0000000020165a28
interfaces: [interface java.util.function.BiFunction]

Comments:

  • Lines 5–10: Creation of a [Runnable] object using an anonymous class—that is, a class without a name—declared and instantiated right where it is needed. It implements the [run] method, which calls the [display] method on line 52. This was the required syntax prior to Java 8;
  • line 12: the same thing using a method reference: [Functions::display] refers to the static method [display] of the class [Functions]. The compiler verifies that it has the form of the method [run] (no parameters, no return value) and creates the object [Runnable] that calls it. This is the standard syntax today;
  • line 14: the function is executed by calling the method of the interface. The method [display] on line 52 is executed (line 2 of the results);
  • Lines 48–50: The referenced methods are grouped into a class named [Functions]. We would have liked to write them directly in the file, next to [main], and name them [Lambdas01::add]. However, the implicit class that wraps a compact source file cannot be named in the code (the compiler returns [cannot find symbol]);
  • line 17: [BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer>] refers to a function with two parameters, [Integer], and returning a [Integer] (the last generic type). The method [add] on line 56, which works with [int], is suitable: the compiler adds the conversions between [int] and [Integer]. The function is called via its method [apply] (line 18);
  • line 20: [Supplier<String>] refers to a parameterless function that returns a string. It is called via its method [get];
  • line 23: the primitive version [IntBinaryOperator] operates directly on [int] values, without conversion. Its method is called [applyAsInt]. This is the preferred type for computationally intensive tasks;
  • Line 27: [Consumer<String>] refers to a function that takes one parameter, [String], and returns nothing. The static method [IO.println(Object)] is appropriate: a [String] is a [Object]. It is executed via its method [accept];
  • line 31: a predicate is a function that returns a Boolean; it is executed via its method [test] (line 32). The method [removeIf] of the interface [Collection] (line 35) expects a parameter of type [Predicate]: it removes from the collection all elements for which the predicate returns [true], and returns [true] if it has removed at least one element;
  • line 40: the method [sort] of the interface [List] accepts a [Comparator] that compares two elements (result can be negative, zero, or positive, like [compareTo]). Here, the names are sorted in ascending order by length. The method [compareLengths] (line 72) uses [Integer.compare], which compares two [int] objects without the risk of an overflow (which a simple subtraction does not guarantee);
  • Lines 44–45: A method reference, like a lambda, is an object. Its class, displayed on line 10 of the results, is a class generated at runtime by the virtual machine, whose name contains [$$Lambda] followed by an address that changes from one execution to the next. On line 11 of the results, we see that this class implements the [BiFunction] interface. A lambda is therefore not a new type of object: it is an instance of an ordinary class that implements a functional interface.

docs.title: 7.2. Defining Your Own Functional Interfaces
docs.text:
The predefined interfaces are often sufficient, but you can define your own. Simply write an interface with a single abstract method, for example:

  • [interface Operation { int calculate(int n1, int n2); }]

This interface represents a function that takes two integers and returns an integer. Compared to [IntBinaryOperator]*, the type *[Operation] has a name that describes its purpose, its method has a descriptive name ([calculate] rather than [applyAsInt]*), and its parameters have names ([n1], [n2]) that development tools display. It is preceded by the annotation [@FunctionalInterface]*: this is not required, but it instructs the compiler to verify that the interface is functional, and it documents the developer’s intent.
