  • objects are queried using Java (and the API stream), while tables are queried using SQL.

A ORM bridges the two worlds. We define the correspondence between classes and tables (the model, or “mapping”) once and for all; it then takes care of:

  • translating queries written in a language that refers to objects (HQL) or constructed by Java code (the API Criteria);
  • to create objects from the read lines (this is called materialization);
  • to store the read objects and detect those that have been modified, added, or deleted;
  • generate the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands that reflect these changes in the database;
  • and, if necessary, to create and update the database schema (tables, columns, indexes) based on the classes.

The architecture of an application that uses Hibernate with MySQL is as follows:

  • [1]: the application. Its [dao] layer no longer communicates directly with the JDBC driver but with Hibernate, through a [Session] object and HQL queries;
  • [2]: Hibernate, independent of DBMS: model, query translation, change tracking, schema generation;
  • [3]: the dialect specific to DBMS (here, [MySQLDialect]): it knows the SQL syntax of DBMS, its column types, and its functions. The dialects of the main DBMSs are part of Hibernate itself: nothing needs to be added to the project;
  • [4]: the JDBC driver for DBMS, the one from Chapter 10 (MySQL Connector/J): Hibernate does not replace JDBC; it uses it;
  • [5]: the DBMS.

docs.title: 11.1.2. Jakarta Persistence and Hibernate
docs.text:
Hibernate was created in 2001 by Gavin King in response to the cumbersomeness of the “entity beans” in the Java EE platform of the time. Its success was such that its concepts were incorporated into a standard, JPA (Java Persistence API), released in 2006 with Java EE 5. When Java EE was transferred to the Eclipse Foundation and renamed Jakarta EE, JPA became Jakarta Persistence, and its packages changed from [javax.persistence] to [jakarta.persistence] (version 3.0, 2020). The current version is Jakarta Persistence 3.2 (2024).

Jakarta Persistence is a specification: a set of interfaces ([EntityManagerFactory], [EntityManager]...), annotations ([@Entity], [@Id], [@Column]...), and a query language, JPQL. It is implemented by several products: Hibernate ORM (the most widely used, used in Spring Boot and Quarkus), EclipseLink (the reference implementation)... This course uses Hibernate ORM 7.4.5, which implements Jakarta Persistence 3.2.

Hibernate offers two ways to use it:

  • exclusively through the standard interfaces: in this case, the code depends only on [jakarta.persistence], and it would, in principle, be possible to switch implementations;
  • through its own, more feature-rich “native” API, whose interfaces extend those of the standard: a [SessionFactory] is a [EntityManagerFactory], and a [Session] is a [EntityManager].

We use Hibernate's own API, as recommended in its documentation: It provides all the standard methods ([persist], [find], [merge], [remove]...) as well as Hibernate’s extensions. The annotations, however, are always those defined by the standard. The following table shows the correspondences:

Jakarta PersistenceHibernateRole[EntityManagerFactory][SessionFactory]Hibernate configuration for a database: a heavy object, created once, shared by the entire application[EntityManager][Session]A database session: a lightweight, short-lived object[EntityTransaction][Transaction]a transactionJPQLHQLthe query language; HQL is a superset of JPQL[CriteriaBuilder][HibernateCriteriaBuilder]Query construction using Java code

docs.title: 11.1.3. Libraries
docs.text:
The libraries used in this chapter are as follows (they are summarized in the appendix on Maven dependencies):

Maven DependencyRole[org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core] 7.4.5.FinalHibernate itself; it includes the API from Jakarta Persistence 3.2 ([jakarta.persistence-api]) and its own dependencies (Byte Buddy for class generation, ANTLR for query analysis, JBoss Logging for logging, etc.)[com.mysql:mysql-connector-j] 9.7.0the JDBC driver for MySQL, the one from Chapter 10[ch.qos.logback:logback-classic] 1.5.38Logback, which will receive the Hibernate log

Hibernate writes its log (executed SQL commands, warnings, etc.) through JBoss Logging, a small library that simply forwards messages to the logging system it finds in the classpath: Log4j 2, or Logback (via SLF4J), or, failing that, the one from JDK or [java.util.logging]. Without configuration, the latter displays each message on two lines, in red in most consoles, which makes the program output difficult to read. We therefore add Logback to our projects and configure it using a [logback.xml] file.

docs.title: 11.1.4. Code First or Database First
docs.text:
The model (the mapping between classes and tables) can be built in two ways:

  • code-first: we write the Java classes, and Hibernate derives the database schema from them, which it can create on its own. This is the approach taken in this chapter;
  • database-first: the database already exists, and you generate the classes from its schema using Hibernate’s reverse-engineering tools (Hibernate Tools) or those of development environments (IntelliJ IDEA can generate entities from database tables). This is the approach for applications that need to work with an existing database. The generated code is similar to what we would write by hand.

docs.title: 11.2.1. The project
docs.text:
The examples in this chapter are modules of a multi-module Maven project (see Chapter 6), located in the [11-hibernate] folder:

11-hibernate/
  pom.xml                 the parent project
  tools/                  library: the compact SQL log
  articles/               library: the Article entity and the [hbarticles] database
  first/                  a first example
  model/                  the model: annotations, XML file, creation script
  crud/                   persist, find, merge, remove
  hql/                    HQL queries
  criteria/               Criteria API queries
  relations/              relationships between entities
  clients/                the evolution of the database schema
  async/                  Hibernate and virtual threads
  transactions/           transactions
  concurrency/            optimistic concurrency
  rawsql/                 native SQL
  bulkupdate/             bulk updates
  injection/              Hibernate and Spring
  TaxV7/                  the tax calculation application, version 7 (separate project)

The parent project sets the versions of the libraries and Maven extensions for all modules:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- the examples of chapter 11: Hibernate; one Maven module per example -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>examples.hibernate</groupId>
    <artifactId>hibernate</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>

    <!-- the modules, in the order of their dependencies -->
    <modules>
        <module>tools</module>
        <module>articles</module>
        <module>first</module>
        <module>model</module>
        <module>crud</module>
        <module>hql</module>
        <module>criteria</module>
        <module>relations</module>
        <module>clients</module>
        <module>async</module>
        <module>transactions</module>
        <module>concurrency</module>
        <module>rawsql</module>
        <module>bulkupdate</module>
        <module>injection</module>
    </modules>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <!-- the versions of the libraries, common to all the modules -->
    <dependencyManagement>
        <dependencies>
            <!-- the two common libraries of the chapter -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>examples.hibernate</groupId>
                <artifactId>tools</artifactId>
                <version>1.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>examples.hibernate</groupId>
                <artifactId>articles</artifactId>
                <version>1.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <!-- Hibernate ORM (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
                <artifactId>hibernate-core</artifactId>
                <version>7.4.5.Final</version>
            </dependency>
            <!-- the MySQL JDBC driver -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
                <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
                <version>9.7.0</version>
            </dependency>
            <!-- logging: Logback (through SLF4J) -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
                <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
                <version>1.5.38</version>
            </dependency>
            <!-- Spring Framework: dependency injection and transactions -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
                <version>7.0.9</version>
            </dependency>
            <dependency>
                <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
                <artifactId>spring-orm</artifactId>
                <version>7.0.9</version>
            </dependency>
            <!-- the HikariCP connection pool -->
            <dependency>
                <groupId>com.zaxxer</groupId>

    <build>
        <pluginManagement>
            <plugins>
                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                    <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                    <version>3.15.0</version>
                    <configuration>
                        <parameters>true</parameters>

                    </configuration>
                </plugin>

                    <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>

                </plugin>

                <plugin>
                    <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>

  • lines 38–87: the [dependencyManagement] section specifies the version of each library. A module that requires it references it without a version;
  • lines 108–116: the [exec-maven-plugin] extension will execute the class specified by the [exec.mainClass] property, which each module defines.

The first example is the module [first]. It is independent of the others:

        </dependency>
        <dependency>

            <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Logback: it receives the Hibernate log -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>

    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>

                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>

  • lines 8–12: the parent project;
  • line 18: the module’s main class;
  • lines 22–35: Hibernate, the JDBC driver for MySQL, and Logback, without a version number (it is provided by the parent project).

To run an example, build all the modules once and for all in the [11-hibernate] folder ([mvn install] installs the shared libraries in the local Maven repository), then navigate to the module’s folder:

> cd 11-hibernate
> mvn install
> cd first
> mvn compile exec:java

The database used is the [hbfirst] database on the local MySQL server, which is the Laragon server (see appendices). It does not need to exist yet: MySQL will create it.

docs.title: 11.2.2. The entity [Article]
docs.text:
A class whose objects are stored in a table is called an entity. Our first entity is a store item, as shown in table [articles] in Chapter 10:

package first;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

// an article of the shop: an ordinary Java class, plus a few annotations
@Entity
public class Article {

    // the primary key, generated by the DBMS
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;
    // the other columns of the table
    private String name;
    private BigDecimal price;
    private int currentStock;
    private int minimumStock;

    // the parameterless constructor required by Hibernate
    protected Article() {
    }

    // the constructor used by the program
    public Article(String name, BigDecimal price, int currentStock, int minimumStock) {
        this.name = name;
        this.price = price;
        this.currentStock = currentStock;
        this.minimumStock = minimumStock;
    }

    // display
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[%d, %s, %.2f, %d, %d]".formatted(id, name, price, currentStock, minimumStock);
    }
}
  • Line 10: The annotation [@Entity] (package [jakarta.persistence]) designates the class as an entity. It is almost a regular Java class, deriving from no Hibernate class: it is referred to as POJO (“Plain Old Java Object”);
  • lines 14–16: the primary key is designated by the [@Id] annotation. There is no naming convention: the annotation is required. [@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)] indicates that its values will be generated by DBMS (column [AUTO_INCREMENT] of MySQL). Its type is [Integer], not [int]: the value [null] means “not yet recorded in the database”;
  • lines 18–21: Each field in the class becomes a column with the same name. Since the annotation [@Id] is applied to a field, Hibernate accesses the fields directly (it reads and writes them via reflection, even if they are private): the class does not need accessors;
  • lines 24–25: Jakarta Persistence requires a parameterless constructor, which Hibernate uses to create objects read from the database. It can be protected ([protected]): the application code will not use it;
  • lines 28–33: the constructor used by the program. No identifier is provided; it will be generated by DBMS;
  • lines 36–39: a convenient display of the item. The [%.2f] format displays the price with two decimal places, in accordance with local conventions (a comma in France).

An entity cannot be a record (Chapter 4): Hibernate must be able to create the empty object, fill in its fields, and modify those fields when the application changes them—something that the immutability of a record prevents. Records remain very useful with Hibernate for query results that are not entities (projections), as we will see.

docs.title: 11.2.3. [SessionFactory] and [Session]
docs.text:
The program uses three Hibernate objects:

  • [SessionFactory] represents Hibernate configured for a database: the list of entities, the database, and the options. Its creation is resource-intensive (Hibernate analyzes the entities, connects to the server to determine its version, and prepares the SQL for common operations): only one is created per database and per application, at startup. It is thread-safe: all application threads can use it;
  • the [Session] represents a working session with the database. It obtains a connection when needed, stores the entities it has read or saved, and knows how to commit their changes to the database. It is a lightweight, short-lived object that is not thread-safe: one is opened for each unit of work and then closed;
  • [Transaction]: With Hibernate, all writes to the database occur within an explicit transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] (commit) or [rollback] (rollback).

[SessionFactory] and [Session] implement the [AutoCloseable] interface: they are created in a [try] statement with resources, which closes them at the end of the block.

docs.title: 11.2.4. The program
docs.text:
package first;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // the SessionFactory: Hibernate configured for the [hbfirst] database
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("first")
                // the entities
                .managedClass(Article.class)
                // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
                .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbfirst?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                // display of the SQL statements, formatted, without colors
                .showSql(true, true, false)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {

            // the tables are dropped then recreated from the entities
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);

            // adding three articles, in a transaction
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                IO.println("--- persist");
                session.persist(new Article("bike", BigDecimal.valueOf(500), 10, 5));
                session.persist(new Article("pump", BigDecimal.valueOf(10), 10, 2));
                session.persist(new Article("bow", BigDecimal.valueOf(600), 4, 1));
                IO.println("--- commit");
                transaction.commit();
            }

            // reading the table, with a new session
            IO.println("--- reading the articles");
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                List<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by name", Article.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (Article article : articles) {
                    IO.println(article);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
  • lines 14–22: creation of [SessionFactory]. There are several ways to configure Hibernate (we’ll discuss them later); we use the [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration] class from Hibernate 7, an enhanced version of the [PersistenceConfiguration] class introduced with Jakarta Persistence 3.2, which allows everything to be configured via code. Its parameter is the name of the persistence unit—a freely chosen name that appears in Hibernate messages. Each method returns the configuration itself, allowing calls to be chained together;
  • line 16: the list of entities;
  • lines 18–19: the URL and JDBC from the [hbfirst] database, in the same format as in Chapter 10, and the user ([root], with no password in Laragon). The parameter [createDatabaseIfNotExist=true] of URL is an option of the driver MySQL: it creates the database if it does not exist;
  • Line 21: [showSql(true, true, false)] instructs Hibernate to print each SQL command it executes to the console, formatted across multiple lines (second parameter), without colors (third parameter). Looking at the SQL sent to the server is the best way to understand what Hibernate does: we’ll do this in all the examples;
  • Line 22: [createEntityManagerFactory] constructs [SessionFactory] (the method name is that of the standard; the returned type is that of Hibernate);
  • Lines 25–26: The [SchemaManager] object from [SessionFactory] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) manages the entity tables: [drop(false)] deletes them if they exist, [create(false)] creates them (the [false] parameter specifies that the database itself should not be deleted or created). This is convenient for examples and tests; a real-world application manages its database differently, as we will see;
  • line 29: [openSession()] opens a session;
  • line 30: the start of a transaction;
  • lines 32–34: [persist] adds three new items to the session: they will be saved to the database. No value is specified for the identifier; it will be generated by DBMS;
  • line 36: [commit] commits the transaction. Prior to this, the session sends the SQL commands to the server, which are still necessary to save the changes it has stored: this is referred to as “flushing” the session to the database;
  • lines 42–44: a query written in HQL, Hibernate’s query language: the items in alphabetical order by name. It refers to the entity [Article] and its field [name], not to the table. The second parameter of [createSelectionQuery] is the result type: [getResultList] returns a [List<Article>].

The [src/main/resources/logback.xml] file in the module configures Logback. It displays Hibernate messages of level [INFO] or higher, one per line (level, log name, message):

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration: Hibernate information messages, on one line each -->
<configuration>
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>
    <root level="INFO">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>

Comments:

  • Lines 2–17: Hibernate informational messages: the name of the persistence unit, the Hibernate version, and database characteristics (URL, driver, selected dialect, server version, transaction isolation level, connection pool size). Hibernate queried the server to select the [MySQLDialect] dialect appropriate for its version;
  • line 4: a warning. Hibernate manages its own small connection pool, which is not intended for a production application. We’ll see, with Spring, how to provide it with the HikariCP pool from Chapter 10; for our examples, the built-in pool is sufficient;
  • Lines 18–28: Deleting and then creating the table [Article] based on the entity: the table name is the same as the entity’s name, the columns have the same names as the fields, and the column [id] is the primary key, with a generated value ([auto_increment]). The columns for primitive-type fields ([int]) are [not null]: a [int] cannot equal [null]. Those for reference-type fields ([String], [BigDecimal]) accept the value [NULL];
  • note the default types: [varchar(255)] for a string, and [decimal(38,2)] for a [BigDecimal] (38 digits, including 2 decimal places). These are rarely the ones you want: the following paragraph shows how to specify them;
  • Lines 29–51: The three configured [INSERT] commands were executed as soon as [persist] was called, before [commit]. This is a consequence of the key being generated by DBMS ([IDENTITY]): the session must know an entity’s identifier as soon as it takes over that entity, and to obtain it, it must execute the insert operation (the JDBC driver returns the generated key; see Chapter 10). With other generation methods, the insert operations are deferred until the session is synchronized. The parameter values ([?]) are not displayed: we will see how to make them appear;
  • lines 53–63: the query HQL [from Article order by name] was translated into a statement [SELECT ... ORDER BY]. Hibernate assigned the alias [a1_0] to the table and created a [Article] object for each row read (lines 64–66).

We haven't written any SQL commands or column read codes: that's the whole point of a ORM. We can also see that this doesn’t mean you don’t need to know SQL: to determine whether the generated SQL is correct and effective, you need to know how to read it.

docs.title: 11.3. The Model
docs.text:
Hibernate builds its model from entities in three steps:

  • First, it applies its default rules: anything that isn’t specified is assigned a reasonable value (this is known as “configuration by exception”);
  • it then supplements or corrects these values using the annotations placed on the entities;
  • finally, it applies the mapping files XML ([orm.xml]), which can fully describe a class without annotations or modify what its annotations specify.

docs.title: 11.3.1. Default Rules
docs.text:
We saw the basics of this in the first example:

  • an entity carries the annotation [@Entity] and has an identifier designated by [@Id]; both of these annotations are required;
  • the placement of the annotation [@Id] determines the access mode: when placed on a field, Hibernate reads and writes the fields directly; when placed on an accessor ([getId]), it uses the accessors ([getX]/[setX]). Access via fields is the most common: it allows the class to have whatever methods it wants;
  • any non-static field is stored in a column, unless it bears the annotation [@Transient] or the keyword [transient];
  • the table name is the entity name (the class’s simple name), and the column name is the field name. These names then undergo a naming strategy: Hibernate’s strategy keeps the names as-is, while another strategy—which we’ll try below—converts them to “snake case” ([currentStock] becomes [current_stock]). Spring Boot uses the latter by default;
  • a column of a primitive type ([int], [double], [boolean]) becomes [NOT NULL]; a column of a reference type ([Integer], [String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate]) accepts the value [NULL];
  • the SQL types are selected by the dialect. With MySQL: [integer] for [int], [bigint] for [long], [bit] for [boolean], [varchar(255)] for [String], [decimal(38,2)] for [BigDecimal], [date] for [LocalDate], [datetime(6)] (to the microsecond) for [LocalDateTime]. By default, an enumeration is recorded by its sequence number (see Chapter 3); the annotation [@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)] records it by its name, which is more reliable;
  • a field that refers to another entity, or to a collection of entities, defines a relationship (we will discuss this later).

docs.title: 11.3.2. The annotations and the mapping file XML
docs.text:
The module [model] defines two entities configured in two different ways. The first is configured using annotations:

package model;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import jakarta.persistence.Transient;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;

// an entity configured by annotations
@Entity
@Table(name = "products")
public class Product {

    // the primary key: @Id, whatever its name
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer code;

    // required string of 50 characters at most
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    private String name;

    // optional string (NULL column) of 200 characters at most
    @Column(length = 200)
    private String description;

    // name and SQL type of the column imposed
    @Column(name = "price_excl_tax", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal priceExclTax;

    // an optional date: an object can be null
    private LocalDate withdrawalDate;

    // a field without a column
    @Transient
    private boolean selected;

    protected Product() {
    }

    // a method is never saved: here Hibernate accesses the fields, not the methods
    public BigDecimal getPriceInclTax() {
        return priceExclTax.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.2"));
    }

    public boolean isSelected() {
        return selected;
    }
}
  • lines 3–9: Jakarta Persistence annotations;
  • line 15: [@Table] specifies the table name;
  • lines 19–21: the primary key, designated as [@Id] regardless of its name;
  • Lines 24–25: [@Column] specifies the column; [nullable = false] makes it mandatory ([NOT NULL]); [length = 50] sets its length ([varchar(50)]);
  • lines 28–29: an optional description of up to 200 characters; the column will accept the value [NULL];
  • lines 32–33: [@Column] also specifies the column name ([price_excl_tax]) and, for a decimal number, its precision (the total number of digits) and its scale (the number of digits after the decimal point): [decimal(10,2)];
  • line 36: an optional date. The type [LocalDate] (Chapter 5) represents a date without a time: it is associated with the types SQL and [date];
  • lines 39–40: [@Transient] excludes a field from the model: in this case, information useful to the user interface that does not belong in the database;
  • lines 46–48: a method, even if named like a getter, is not registered, since Hibernate accesses the fields directly. If accessed via getters, the annotation [@Transient] would need to be added to it.

The second entity has no annotations:

package model;

import java.time.LocalDateTime;

// a class without any annotation: its mapping is described by the [supplier.orm.xml] file
public class Supplier {

    private Integer number;
    private String companyName;
    private String phone;
    private LocalDateTime creationDate;

    protected Supplier() {
    }

    public Supplier(String companyName, String phone) {
        this.companyName = companyName;
        this.phone = phone;
    }
}

Its mapping to the table is described by a file named XML, located in the [src/main/resources/META-INF] folder of the module:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- the mapping of the [Supplier] class to its table, described in XML (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) -->
<entity-mappings xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm"
                 xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
                 xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm
                                     https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm/orm_3_2.xsd"
                 version="3.2">
    <entity class="model.Supplier" access="FIELD">
        <table name="suppliers">
            <!-- a unique index: two suppliers cannot have the same company name -->
            <index name="ix_suppliers_company_name" column-list="companyName" unique="true"/>
        </table>
        <attributes>
            <id name="number">
                <generated-value strategy="IDENTITY"/>
            </id>
            <basic name="companyName">
                <column nullable="false" length="60"/>
            </basic>
            <basic name="phone">
                <column name="tel" length="20"/>
            </basic>
            <!-- a default value computed by the DBMS: Hibernate never writes this column -->
            <basic name="creationDate">
                <column nullable="false" insertable="false" updatable="false"
                        column-definition="datetime(6) default current_timestamp(6)"/>
            </basic>
        </attributes>
    </entity>
</entity-mappings>
  • lines 3–7: the XML schema for Jakarta Persistence 3.2 mapping files;
  • line 8: the described class, with access via fields;
  • lines 9–12: the table, and a unique index on the company name: no two suppliers can have the same one. The equivalent annotation is [@Table(name = "suppliers", indexes = @Index(...))];
  • lines 14–16: the identifier, generated by DBMS;
  • lines 17–19: a required column of no more than 60 characters;
  • lines 20–22: the field [phone] is stored in the column [tel];
  • lines 24–27: the creation date has a default value, calculated by DBMS. The attribute [column-definition] provides the text SQL from the column definition, copied verbatim in the order [CREATE TABLE]; [insertable="false"] and [updatable="false"] indicate that Hibernate must never write to this column, which allows DBMS to use [current_timestamp(6)].

Everything that annotations do can be done in XML. Annotations have the advantage of placing the configuration next to the field, and this is the most common approach; the XML file, on the other hand, keeps the classes independent of Jakarta Persistence and consolidates the configuration in a single location. The two approaches can be combined: the XML file takes precedence in case of a conflict. Jakarta Persistence does not support configuring the model via Java code, as other frameworks (such as Entity Framework in C#) do.

The program displays the model built by Hibernate, followed by the SQL script that would create the tables:

package model;

import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.Attribute;
import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.EntityType;
import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.SingularAttribute;
import java.io.StringWriter;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // the table creation script will be written into this object
        StringWriter script = new StringWriter();
        // a SessionFactory that never connects to the server
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("model")
                // an annotated entity and a mapping described in XML
                .managedClass(Product.class)
                .mappingFile("META-INF/supplier.orm.xml")
                // no database: the DBMS and its version are given, for the SQL dialect
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_NAME, "MySQL")
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_MAJOR_VERSION, "8")
                .property(AvailableSettings.ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT, false)
                // the column names in "snake case": companyName -> company_name
                .property(AvailableSettings.PHYSICAL_NAMING_STRATEGY,
                        PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl.class.getName())
                // the table creation script, without executing it
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, "create")
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
                .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {

            // the model built by Hibernate: entities and attributes (Jakarta Persistence API)
            for (EntityType<?> entity : sessionFactory.getMetamodel().getEntities()) {
                IO.println("entity %s (%s)".formatted(entity.getName(), entity.getJavaType().getName()));
                for (Attribute<?, ?> attribute : entity.getAttributes()) {
                    boolean id = attribute instanceof SingularAttribute<?, ?> s && s.isId();
                    IO.println("  %-14s %s%s".formatted(attribute.getName(),
                            attribute.getJavaType().getSimpleName(), id ? " (identifier)" : ""));
                }
            }
        }
        // the table creation script, without the 4-space indentation of its lines
        IO.println("--- creation script");
        script.toString().strip().lines()
                .map(line -> line.startsWith("    ") ? line.substring(4) : line)
                .forEach(line -> IO.println(line.stripTrailing()));
    }
}
  • line 16: a [StringWriter] (package [java.io]), a write stream to a string in memory, will receive the SQL script;
  • lines 20–21: the annotated entity is declared by [managedClass], and the file XML by [mappingFile];
  • lines 23–25: The database [hbmodel] will never exist; this [SessionFactory] is used solely to examine the model. Therefore, there is no URL or JDBC. To select the SQL dialect without querying the server, Hibernate needs the name of the DBMS and its version; the [ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT] property ([hibernate.boot.allow_jdbc_metadata_access]) prevents it from connecting at startup. The names of the configuration properties are constants in the [AvailableSettings] interface;
  • lines 27–28: the “snake case” naming convention;
  • lines 30–33: Hibernate will write the table creation script (["create"]) to the [script] object without executing it; the commands are terminated by a semicolon and formatted across multiple lines;
  • line 37: the [getMetamodel] method (Jakarta Persistence) provides access to the model: its entities ([EntityType]) and, for each one, its attributes ([Attribute]);
  • Lines 38–43: For each entity, its name and class; for each attribute, its name, Java type, and whether it is the identifier. The pattern filtering in line 40 ([instanceof SingularAttribute<?, ?> s && s.isId()], Chapter 4) checks the attribute’s type and, if appropriate, uses it immediately;
  • lines 48–50: the script as displayed, without the four-space indentation that Hibernate adds to its lines.

Results:

> mvn compile exec:java
WARN  connection - HHH102003: No appropriate connection provider encountered; client must supply connections

  companyName    String

entity Product (model.Product)

  withdrawalDate LocalDate
--- creation script
create table products (
    code integer not null auto_increment,
    price_excl_tax decimal(10,2) not null,
    withdrawal_date date,
    name varchar(50) not null,
    description varchar(200),
    primary key (code)

create table suppliers (
    number integer not null auto_increment,
    creation_date datetime(6) default current_timestamp(6) not null,
    tel varchar(20),
    company_name varchar(60) not null,
    primary key (number)

alter table suppliers
   add constraint ix_suppliers_company_name unique (company_name);
  • line 2: The Hibernate warning confirms that it has no way to obtain a connection;
  • lines 3–13: the two entities and their attributes (the identifier first, then the others in alphabetical order). The field [selected] and the method [getPriceInclTax] do not appear in the model;
  • lines 15–21: the table [suppliers], described by the file XML. The naming strategy has changed [companyName] and [creationDate] to [company_name] and [creation_date]; the column [tel], whose name is fixed, remains unchanged. The definition of the column [creation_date] is that of the file XML, supplemented by [not null];
  • Lines 23–30: the table [products]. The types SQL come from annotations ([varchar(50)], [decimal(10,2)]) or from dialect choices for a Java type ([integer], [date]);
  • lines 32–33: the unique index, created under MySQL by a uniqueness constraint ([unique]).

docs.title: 11.3.3. Generated identifiers
docs.text:
The annotation [@GeneratedValue] indicates that the identifier value is generated. Its parameter [strategy] specifies how:

StrategyIdentifier Generation[IDENTITY]by DBMS, when inserting the row (column [AUTO_INCREMENT] of MySQL, [IDENTITY] of SQL Server, and PostgreSQL)[SEQUENCE]by a sequence from DBMS (PostgreSQL, Oracle), which Hibernate queries before insertion[TABLE]by a counter table managed by Hibernate[UUID]by Hibernate: a random universal identifier, such as [java.util.UUID][AUTO] (default)Hibernate chooses; with MySQL, which has no sequences, it simulates them using a table named [<table>_SEQ]

With MySQL, we still use [IDENTITY], which corresponds to the natural behavior of the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column. We’ve seen the result of this: the [INSERT] command is executed as soon as [persist] is called, and Hibernate cannot group multiple inserts into a batch (we’ll cover batches later). The [SEQUENCE] strategy, which allows you to know the ID before the insertion, is preferred for DBMS statements that use sequences.

docs.title: 11.3.4. Optional Values and [NULL] Columns
docs.text:
Whether a column is optional is therefore determined in Java by the field type (primitive or reference) and by the [nullable] attribute of [@Column]. This choice must be made carefully: the rule expresses both a constraint in the Java code (“this value may be missing”) and a constraint in the database. A few notes:

  • [@Column(nullable = false)] defines the [NOT NULL] constraint in the schema created by Hibernate, and Hibernate also uses it before sending a [INSERT] or [UPDATE] command: if the field is [null], it does not send the command and triggers a [PropertyValueException] (“not-null property references a null or transient value”). This Hibernate check is disabled by default when Jakarta Validation (below) is present: validation then falls back to its annotations, or, failing that, to DBMS, which rejects the command;
  • For more comprehensive validation performed by Java before any database access, we use Jakarta Validation (library [hibernate-validator]) and its annotations [@NotNull], [@Size(max = 30)], [@Positive].... When present in the classpath, Hibernate validates entities before saving them and takes these annotations into account when creating columns;
  • a field cannot be of type [Optional] (Chapter 4), which is not intended for this purpose; however, an accessor can return a [Optional] constructed from an optional field: [return Optional.ofNullable(description);].

docs.title: 11.4. The following examples: two common libraries
docs.text: The examples in the following paragraphs almost all use the [hbarticles] database and its [articles] table, populated with the six items from Chapter 10. Rather than repeating the Hibernate entity and configuration in each module, we place them in a library—the [articles] module—on which the other modules depend. We also replace the SQL log from [showSql]—which is too verbose for our examples—with a more compact log, placed in a second library, the [tools] module.

docs.title: 11.4.1. The compact SQL log
docs.text:
Rather than writing directly to the console ([showSql]), Hibernate can forward its activity to the logging system (in this case, Logback), with each message category written to a different logger:

LogLevelMessages[org.hibernate.SQL][DEBUG]SQL orders executed[org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind][TRACE]the value of each parameter in an order SQL[org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc][TRACE]including, among other things, the initiation, confirmation, and cancellation of transactions[org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch][TRACE]execution of order batches SQL[org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error][WARN]Errors reported by DBMS

A log only records messages of a level equal to or higher than its own. Therefore, you simply need to set the desired level for these logs in the [logback.xml] file to capture these messages. We process them through a layout class that makes them more compact:

package tools;

import ch.qos.logback.classic.Level;
import ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger;
import ch.qos.logback.classic.spi.ILoggingEvent;
import ch.qos.logback.core.LayoutBase;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

// a compact log of the SQL statements executed by Hibernate: a Logback layout
public class SqlLog extends LayoutBase<ILoggingEvent> {

    // the Hibernate loggers used
    public static final String SQL = "org.hibernate.SQL";
    public static final String PARAMETERS = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind";
    public static final String TRANSACTIONS = "org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc";
    public static final String ERRORS = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error";
    public static final String BATCHES = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch";

    // the maximum length of a clause written on a single line
    private static final int WIDTH = 100;

    // the execution of a batch of SQL statements: "Executing JDBC batch (3 / 3) - [...]"
    private static final Pattern BATCH = Pattern.compile("Executing JDBC batch \\((\\d+) / \\d+\\).*");

    // a parameter bound to an SQL statement: "binding parameter (1:VARCHAR) <- [bike]"
    private static final Pattern PARAMETER =
            Pattern.compile("binding parameter \\((\\d+):\\w+\\) <- \\[(.*)]");

    // layout of a message: the text to write is returned ("": nothing is written)
    @Override
    public String doLayout(ILoggingEvent event) {
        String message = event.getFormattedMessage();
        return switch (event.getLoggerName()) {
            case SQL -> sqlStatement(message);
            case PARAMETERS -> parameter(message);
            case TRANSACTIONS -> transaction(message);
            case ERRORS -> error(message);
            case BATCHES -> batch(message);
            default -> "";
        };
    }

    // the SQL statement formatted by Hibernate, made more compact: one line per clause (select, from...)
    private static String sqlStatement(String sql) {
        // the non-empty lines, without the trailing spaces
        List<String> lines = sql.lines().map(String::stripTrailing).filter(l -> !l.isBlank()).toList();
        // the clauses: a top-level line (the least indented) and the lines that follow it
        int indent = lines.stream().mapToInt(SqlLog::indent).min().orElse(0);
        List<List<String>> clauses = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String line : lines) {
            if (clauses.isEmpty() || indent(line) == indent) {
                clauses.add(new ArrayList<>());
            }
            clauses.getLast().add(line.substring(indent));
        }
        // each clause is written on one line, if it is not too long
        StringBuilder text = new StringBuilder();
        String start = "";
        for (List<String> clause : clauses) {
            String line = start + clause.stream().map(String::strip).collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
            if (line.equals("insert") || line.equals("delete")) {
                // [insert into ...], [delete from ...]: a single line
                start = line + " ";
                continue;
            }
            if (line.length() <= WIDTH) {
                text.append("    SQL> ").append(line).append('\n');
            } else {
                // clause too long: the Hibernate lines are kept
                for (int i = 0; i < clause.size(); i++) {
                    text.append("    SQL> ").append(i == 0 ? start : "").append(clause.get(i)).append('\n');
                }
            }
            start = "";
        }
        return text.toString();
    }

    // the number of spaces at the start of the line
    private static int indent(String line) {
        return line.length() - line.stripLeading().length();
    }

    // the value of a parameter of the SQL statement
    private static String parameter(String message) {
        Matcher m = PARAMETER.matcher(message);
        return m.matches() ? "    SQL> -- parameter " + m.group(1) + " = " + m.group(2) + "\n" : "";
    }

    // start, commit and rollback of the transactions (the other messages are ignored)
    private static String transaction(String message) {
        if (message.startsWith("HHH10003002")) {
            return "    SQL> -- start of transaction\n";
        }
        if (message.startsWith("HHH10003004")) {
            return "    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)\n";
        }
        if (message.startsWith("HHH10003006")) {
            return "    SQL> -- transaction rolled back (ROLLBACK)\n";
        }
        return "";
    }

    // the error reported by the DBMS (the line that gives its error codes is ignored)
    private static String error(String message) {
        return message.startsWith("HHH000247") ? "" : "    SQL> -- failure: " + message + "\n";
    }

    // the execution of a batch of SQL statements (the other messages are ignored)
    private static String batch(String message) {
        Matcher m = BATCH.matcher(message);
        return m.matches() ? "    SQL> -- execution of a batch of " + m.group(1) + " statement(s)\n" : "";
    }

    // executes an action without an SQL log
    public static void withoutLog(Runnable action) {
        List<Logger> loggers = Stream.of(SQL, PARAMETERS, TRANSACTIONS, ERRORS, BATCHES)
                .map(SqlLog::logger)
                .toList();
        // the current levels, restored at the end
        List<Level> levels = loggers.stream().map(Logger::getLevel).toList();
        loggers.forEach(l -> l.setLevel(Level.OFF));
        try {
            action.run();
        } finally {
            for (int i = 0; i < loggers.size(); i++) {
                loggers.get(i).setLevel(levels.get(i));
            }
        }
    }

    // the Logback logger with the given name
    private static Logger logger(String name) {
        return (Logger) LoggerFactory.getLogger(name);
    }
}
  • line 16: a Logback layout class derives from the [LayoutBase<ILoggingEvent>] class; its [doLayout] method (lines 36–47) receives each message (a [ILoggingEvent]) and returns the text to be written;
  • lines 19–23: the names of the Hibernate logs used;
  • lines 39–46: the processing depends on the log that sent the message ([switch] on a string, using the Java 14 “arrow” syntax);
  • lines 50–83: the order SQL, as formatted by Hibernate ([format_sql]), spread across multiple lines, with one column per line. We make it more compact. Non-empty lines are divided into clauses (lines 54–61): a clause begins with a top-level line ([select], [from], [where]...) and includes the indented lines that follow it. Each clause is then written on a single line, preceded by [SQL>], if it does not exceed 100 characters (lines 72–73); otherwise, its lines are retained (lines 76–78). The clauses [insert] and [delete] are combined with the following one (lines 67–71);
  • lines 91–94: The Hibernate message that provides a parameter’s value looks like [binding parameter (1:VARCHAR) <- [bike]]. The regular expression in lines 32–33 (Chapter 5) extracts the parameter number and its value;
  • lines 97–108: Among the many messages in the [org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc] log, only those indicating the start, commit, and rollback of a transaction are retained. Each Hibernate message begins with a code ([HHH10003002]...) that uniquely identifies it;
  • lines 111–113: an error in DBMS. Hibernate writes this as two messages: one containing the error codes (which we ignore) and the other containing the error text;
  • lines 116–119: execution of a batch of SQL commands, which we will encounter at the end of the chapter;
  • Lines 122–136: The [withoutLog] method executes an action without logging (SQL). It uses Logback’s API: each log ([Logger]) has a level that can be modified during execution. We set the five logs to level [OFF], execute the action, and then restore the original levels in a [finally] clause, so that they remain at those levels even if the action throws an exception;
  • lines 139–141: [LoggerFactory] is the class of SLF4J that returns a log; Since Logback is the current implementation of SLF4J, the returned object is a [ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger].

The [tools] module also contains the [logback.xml] file used in the examples. Placed at the root of the classpath ([src/main/resources]), it is found by Logback when the program starts:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration for the examples of the chapter -->
<configuration>

    <!-- the compact SQL log: layout by the [tools.SqlLog] class -->
    <appender name="SQL" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="ch.qos.logback.core.encoder.LayoutWrappingEncoder">
            <layout class="tools.SqlLog"/>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <!-- the other messages: level, short name of the logger, text -->
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger{0} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

    <!-- the SQL statements (DEBUG), their parameters, the transactions, the batches (TRACE) and the errors -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.SQL" level="DEBUG" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error" level="WARN" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>

    <!-- the built-in Hibernate connection pool is enough for our examples: its warning is silenced -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.connections.pooling" level="ERROR"/>

    <!-- dropping the tables of an empty database causes harmless errors: they are silenced -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.tool.schema" level="OFF"/>

    <!-- all the other loggers: warnings and errors only -->
    <root level="WARN">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
  • lines 6–10: An “appender” writes the messages, in this case to the console. It uses our formatting;
  • lines 13–17: a second “appender” for other messages: level, log short name, text;
  • lines 20–34: the Hibernate logs from the previous table, with their levels. Their messages go to the “appender” [SQL] and only to it ([additivity="false"]: they are not additionally forwarded to the root log);
  • line 37: the warning about Hibernate’s built-in connection pool is suppressed;
  • line 40: Hibernate deletes tables starting with their foreign keys; on an empty database, these deletions fail without consequence, but Hibernate logs this at length. These messages are suppressed;
  • lines 43–45: The other logs record only warnings and errors.

The [tools] module has only one dependency: Logback. A library does not typically impose its logging configuration on the applications that use it; we do so here to avoid repeating this file in every example.

docs.title: 11.4.2. The entity and the article database
docs.text:
The [Article] entity in the [articles] module uses the annotations from the previous paragraph. Here is the beginning of the code; the rest contains the two constructors for the entity from the first example, [getX]/[setX] getter and setter methods for each field (except [setId]: the identifier is managed by Hibernate) and the same method [toString]:

package articles;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import jakarta.persistence.UniqueConstraint;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

// an article of the shop, with the annotations that specify its table
@Entity
@Table(name = "articles",
        uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(name = "uk_articles_name", columnNames = "name"))
public class Article {

    // primary key, generated by the DBMS (AUTO_INCREMENT)
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    // name of the article: mandatory, at most 30 characters, unique (see @Table)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    private String name;

    // price: 10 digits of which 2 after the decimal point
    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal price;

    // current stock and minimum stock below which restocking is needed
    private int currentStock;
    private int minimumStock;

    // the parameterless constructor required by Hibernate (it can be protected)
    protected Article() {
    }
  • lines 14–15: the table is named [articles], as in Chapter 10. The parameter [uniqueConstraints] declares a uniqueness constraint, named [uk_articles_name], on the column [name]: two items cannot have the same name. Without an explicit name, Hibernate would generate an unreadable one ([UK3f8k...]), which would appear in error messages;
  • lines 24–25: a required name of no more than 30 characters;
  • lines 28–29: a price in [decimal(10,2)].

The [BaseArticles] class contains the Hibernate configuration for the [hbarticles] database:

package articles;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import tools.SqlLog;

// the [hbarticles] database: Hibernate configuration and database initialization
public final class BaseArticles {

    // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist (createDatabaseIfNotExist)
    public static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbarticles?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true";
    public static final String USER = "root";
    public static final String PASSWORD = "";

    // utility class: no instance
    private BaseArticles() {
    }

    // the Hibernate configuration: entities, database, formatting of the logged SQL
    public static HibernatePersistenceConfiguration configuration() {
        return new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("articles")
                .managedClass(Article.class)
                .jdbcUrl(URL)
                .jdbcCredentials(USER, PASSWORD)
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true);
    }

    // a SessionFactory for the [hbarticles] database, with the previous configuration
    public static SessionFactory createSessionFactory() {
        return configuration().createEntityManagerFactory();
    }

    // (re)creation of the [articles] table with its six articles, without an SQL log
    public static void initialize(SessionFactory sessionFactory) {
        SqlLog.withoutLog(() -> {
            // dropping then creating the tables of the entities
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);
            // the six articles, added in a transaction
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                session.persist(new Article("bike", BigDecimal.valueOf(500), 10, 5));
                session.persist(new Article("pump", BigDecimal.valueOf(10), 10, 2));
                session.persist(new Article("bow", BigDecimal.valueOf(600), 4, 1));
                session.persist(new Article("arrows - set of 6", BigDecimal.valueOf(100), 12, 20));
                session.persist(new Article("diving suit", BigDecimal.valueOf(300), 8, 2));
                session.persist(new Article("diver's oxygen tanks", BigDecimal.valueOf(120), 10, 5));
            });
        });
    }
}
  • lines 13–15: the database’s URL and the user, both public so that other modules can use them;
  • lines 22–28: the Hibernate configuration. It is returned by a public method, which will allow an instance to complete it before creating the [SessionFactory]. The [FORMAT_SQL] property ([hibernate.format_sql]) instructs Hibernate to format the SQL, which it then passes to the [org.hibernate.SQL] log: it is this formatted data that the [SqlLog] class then condenses;
  • lines 31–33: the [SessionFactory] from the [hbarticles] database;
  • lines 36–51: a method that recreates the table [articles] with its six items, without the log SQL: we do not want to see the SQL from this initialization in the example results;
  • line 42: [sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> ...)] opens a session, starts a transaction, executes the lambda (Chapter 7) by passing it the session, commits the transaction (or rolls it back if the lambda throws an exception), and closes the session. This is the shortest way to write a work unit; we’ll use it often, along with its variants [inSession] (a session without a transaction), [fromTransaction], and [fromSession] (which return the result of the lambda).

The [articles] module depends on the [tools] module, Hibernate, and the JDBC driver:

    <dependencies>
        <!-- the compact SQL log (and Logback) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.hibernate</groupId>
            <artifactId>tools</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Hibernate and the MySQL JDBC driver -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.hibernate.orm</groupId>
            <artifactId>hibernate-core</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.mysql</groupId>
            <artifactId>mysql-connector-j</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

The example modules therefore require only one dependency, that of the [articles] module; Maven adds its dependencies (these are called transitive dependencies). Here are the dependencies for the [crud] module:

    <dependencies>
        <!-- the [Article] entity and the [hbarticles] database (Hibernate, MySQL and the SQL log included) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.hibernate</groupId>
            <artifactId>articles</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

docs.title: 11.4.3. Other Ways to Configure Hibernate
docs.text:
We configure Hibernate programmatically using [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration]. There are other ways to do this, which can be found in applications and documentation:

  • a [META-INF/persistence.xml] file, the traditional approach used in Jakarta Persistence: it describes one or more persistence units (entity classes, connection properties, options), and the factory is created using [Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("articles")];
  • a [hibernate.properties] (or [hibernate.cfg.xml]) file, specific to Hibernate, read by the [org.hibernate.cfg.Configuration] class: [new Configuration().addAnnotatedClass(Article.class).buildSessionFactory()]. This is the approach used in older versions of Hibernate;
  • in a Spring Boot application, the properties [spring.datasource.*] and [spring.jpa.*] from the file [application.properties]: Spring Boot creates the factory itself.

The properties are the same everywhere ([hibernate.format_sql], [jakarta.persistence.jdbc.url]...): only the way they are specified changes.

docs.title: 11.5. Basic operations: add, read, update, delete
11.5.1. The [crud] program
docs.text:
The [crud] module demonstrates the four basic operations (CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete), as well as entity tracking via the session. To make this tracking visible, it uses a few internal Hibernate methods (its “SPI,” Service Provider Interface), intended for Hibernate extensions rather than applications: they are grouped in the utility methods at the end of the program.

package crud;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Objects;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.EntityEntry;
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.PersistenceContext;
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.SessionImplementor;
import org.hibernate.persister.entity.EntityPersister;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.createSessionFactory()) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
            BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                // 1 - search by the primary key
                IO.println("--- find(1)");
                Article bike = session.find(Article.class, 1);
                IO.println(bike);
                IO.println("--- find(1) a second time");
                Article bike2 = session.find(Article.class, 1);
                IO.println("same object: " + (bike == bike2));

                // 2 - adding an article
                IO.println("--- persist");
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                Article x = new Article("x", BigDecimal.valueOf(100), 10, 1);
                IO.println("before persist: state=" + state(session, x) + ", id=" + x.getId());
                session.persist(x);
                IO.println("after persist: state=" + state(session, x) + ", id=" + x.getId());
                transaction.commit();

                // 3 - modification: it is enough to modify the object
                IO.println("--- modification of the price");
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                x.setPrice(x.getPrice().multiply(new BigDecimal("1.1")));
                IO.println("session modified: %s, original price=%s, current price=%s"
                        .formatted(session.isDirty(), originalValue(session, x, "price"), x.getPrice()));
                IO.println("--- commit");
                transaction.commit();
                IO.println("after commit: session modified: " + session.isDirty());

                // 4 - deletion
                IO.println("--- remove");
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                session.remove(x);
                IO.println("before commit: state=" + state(session, x));
                transaction.commit();
                IO.println("after commit: state=" + state(session, x));

                // 5 - a detached object, modified then merged with the session
                IO.println("--- detach and merge");
                Article bow = session.find(Article.class, 3);
                session.detach(bow);
                IO.println("after detach: state=" + state(session, bow));
                bow.setPrice(BigDecimal.valueOf(550));
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                Article managedBow = session.merge(bow);
                IO.println("merge: same object=%s, state of the returned object=%s"
                        .formatted(bow == managedBow, state(session, managedBow)));
                transaction.commit();

                // 6 - the entities tracked by the session
                IO.println("--- the tracked entities");
                bike.setCurrentStock(bike.getCurrentStock() - 1);
                displayTrackedEntities(session);
            }
        }
    }

    // the state of an article with respect to the session (Hibernate internal API)
    private static String state(Session session, Article article) {
        EntityEntry entry = context(session).getEntry(article);
        if (entry != null) {
            // MANAGED, DELETED...
            return entry.getStatus().name();
        }
        // an object unknown to the session: never saved (without an identifier) or detached
        return article.getId() == null ? "TRANSIENT" : "DETACHED";
    }

    // the value of a property as it was read from the database (Hibernate internal API)
    private static Object originalValue(Session session, Object entity, String property) {
        return context(session).getEntry(entity).getLoadedValue(property);
    }

    // the entities of the persistence context of the session (Hibernate internal API)
    private static void displayTrackedEntities(Session session) {
        for (Map.Entry<Object, EntityEntry> pair : context(session).reentrantSafeEntityEntries()) {
            EntityEntry entry = pair.getValue();
            EntityPersister persister = entry.getPersister();
            IO.println("%s #%s %s".formatted(persister.getEntityName(), entry.getId(), entry.getStatus()));
            // current values of the properties, compared with the values read from the database
            String[] names = persister.getPropertyNames();
            Object[] current = persister.getValues(pair.getKey());
            Object[] originals = entry.getLoadedState();
            for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
                String modification = Objects.equals(current[i], originals[i]) ? ""
                        : " (modified, original value: " + originals[i] + ")";
                IO.println("    %s : %s%s".formatted(names[i], current[i], modification));
            }
        }
        IO.println("session modified: " + session.isDirty());
    }

    // the persistence context of the session (Hibernate internal API)
    private static PersistenceContext context(Session session) {
        return session.unwrap(SessionImplementor.class).getPersistenceContext();
    }
}

    currentStock : 9 (modified, original value: 10)
    minimumStock : 5
    name : bike

    minimumStock : 1
