Comments:

  • Line 25: [session.find(Article.class, 1)] searches for the primary key record 1. It returns [null] if the key does not exist. The generated SQL (lines 3–6 of the results) is a parameterized [SELECT], where the parameter is set to 1: the compact log now displays the parameter values;
  • line 28: the second call to [find(Article.class, 1)] does not send any SQL commands and returns the same object (line 9). The session stores the entities it has read or saved in its persistence context—also known as the first-level cache: before querying the database, [find] checks to see if the requested entity is already there. A session never contains two objects for the same row in the database;
  • Lines 34–37: adding an item. Before [persist], the object is [TRANSIENT] (“transient”): the session does not recognize it, and its identifier is [null] (line 12). [persist] brings it into the session, which immediately executes the command [INSERT] (lines 13–18) to obtain the generated key and places it in the field [id]. The item is then [MANAGED] (“managed” or “persistent”) and its identifier is 7 (line 19). The transaction is opened on line 33 and committed on line 38 (lines 11 and 20 of the results);
  • line 43: To modify a row in the database, simply modify the object. No [update] method is required: the session has retained a copy of the values read or saved (the original state) and compares the current values to those. This is known as “dirty checking”;
  • lines 44–45: [session.isDirty()] indicates whether the session contains changes that have not yet been committed to the database: this is the case (line 23). The method [originalValue] (lines 90–92) reads the original price value, 100, from the persistence context, whereas the current value is 110.0;
  • Line 47: [commit] synchronizes the session with the database (“flush”): the [UPDATE] command is executed (lines 25–32), and then the transaction is committed. After that, the session has no pending changes (line 34);
  • note that the [UPDATE] command writes all columns in the table, not just the one that has changed. This is Hibernate’s default behavior: a single SQL command, prepared once and for all, is used for all article updates. In contrast, the [@DynamicUpdate] annotation placed on the entity instructs it to generate a query limited to the modified columns each time;
  • Lines 53–56: deletion. [remove] changes the article’s state to [DELETED] (line 37); [commit] sends the command [DELETE] (lines 38–40). The object is then no longer recognized by the session: it becomes [DETACHED] (“detached,” line 42);
  • lines 60–63: the bow is read (lines 44–47), then detached from the session by [detach]: the session forgets it (line 48). Any change to its price is then ignored. A detached object is a common occurrence in an application: it is an object read by a session that is now closed—for example, during a previous HTTP query—and subsequently modified by the user;
  • line 65: [session.merge(bow)] merges the detached object with the session. The session reads the record from the database (lines 50–53), copies the state of the detached object into the entity it manages, and returns the latter: this is not the same object (line 54). The object passed to [merge] remains detached; the returned object is the one that must be used next. [commit] saves the new price (lines 55–62);
  • line 72: the bike’s inventory is updated, without saving;
  • lines 95–111: display of the persistence context. For each tracked entity ([EntityEntry]), its name, ID, and status are displayed, followed by the current value of each property and its original value if different. The [EntityPersister] object is the one in Hibernate that knows the mapping between an entity and its table: it provides the names of the properties and their values;
  • Lines 65–75 of the results: the session tracks the bike, whose inventory has changed from 10 to 9, and the bow. The change to the bike is not saved: the session is closed without synchronization. There is no [commit], and a session does not synchronize automatically upon closure.

docs.title: 11.5.2. The States of an Entity
docs.text:
An entity is, with respect to a session, in one of the following states (Jakarta Persistence refers to them as “new,” “managed,” “detached,” and “removed”):

StateMeaningTransient ([TRANSIENT])The object was created by [new] and has never been saved: it has no identifier and no session is aware of itManaged ([MANAGED])The object has been read or saved by the session, which is tracking it: changes to it will be reflected in the database during the next synchronizationDeleted ([DELETED])The object has been marked for deletion ([remove]): the next synchronization will send the command [DELETE]detached ([DETACHED])The object corresponds to a row in the database, but the session that read it is closed or has forgotten it ([detach], [clear]): its changes are ignored unless it is merged with a session ([merge])

The session synchronization (“flush”) sends the SQL commands to DBMS, which propagate the changes to the managed entities. This occurs:

  • during the [commit] phase of the transaction;
  • before executing a query whose result might depend on changes that have not yet been committed ([FlushMode.AUTO] mode, the default mode): the query thus sees the session data;
  • during an explicit call to [session.flush()]. The commands are then executed, but they will not be permanently committed until the transaction’s [commit].

Here’s an overview of the workflow with Hibernate: we open a session and a transaction, read entities, modify them as ordinary objects, add them ([persist]), and delete them ([remove]), then commit the transaction, which sends all necessary commands to the database in a single batch. The session acts as a “unit of work.” It is a lightweight object designed for a short lifespan: a unit of work, such as a HTTP query in a web application. You do not use the same session throughout the entire life of an application; otherwise, it would accumulate the tracked entities in its persistence context.

docs.title: 11.6.1. HQL and JPQL
docs.text:
To retrieve entities other than by their primary key, queries are written in a language similar to SQL, but one that refers to entities and attributes rather than tables and columns: HQL (Hibernate Query Language). Jakarta Persistence defines a similar language, JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language), of which HQL is a superset: a JPQL query is a valid HQL query. Hibernate translates the query into SQL, in the DBMS dialect, and DBMS executes it.

Some differences from SQL:

  • We use the entity name ([Article]), not the table name ([articles]), and the attribute names ([currentStock]), not the column names. Entity and attribute names are case-sensitive, just like in Java;
  • the clause [select] is optional in HQL: [from Article] returns entities [Article]. JPQL requires writing [select a from Article a];
  • relationships between entities are traversed using a dot ([p.category.name]), with Hibernate writing the joins itself, as we will see.

A query is created by the session’s [createSelectionQuery] method (Hibernate 6), which takes the text HQL and the result type as arguments, and returns a [SelectionQuery<T>] object. You can then set its parameters and execute it with [getResultList] (a list), [getSingleResult] (a single result; an exception if there are zero or multiple results), [getSingleResultOrNull] ([null] if there are none), or [getResultStream] (a stream). The Jakarta Persistence method [createQuery] also exists; it is used for both read queries and updates.

docs.title: 11.6.2. The program [hql]
docs.text:
The module [hql] provides several examples of queries:

package hql;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.query.SemanticException;

public class Main {

    // a projection: the name of an article and the value of its stock
    record StockValue(String name, BigDecimal value) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.createSessionFactory()) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
            BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                // 1 - filtering and sorting
                IO.println("--- the articles to restock, in alphabetical order");
                String hql = "from Article where currentStock < minimumStock order by name";
                List<Article> toOrder = session.createSelectionQuery(hql, Article.class).getResultList();
                toOrder.forEach(IO::println);

                // 2 - projection: only the useful columns are requested
                IO.println("--- value of the stock of each article");
                List<StockValue> values = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("""
                                select name, price * currentStock from Article
                                order by price * currentStock desc""", StockValue.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (StockValue v : values) {
                    IO.println("%s : %.2f euros".formatted(v.name(), v.value()));
                }

                // 3 - a single result; the value [minPrice] is passed by a named parameter
                IO.println("--- the first article over 200 euros");
                BigDecimal minPrice = BigDecimal.valueOf(200);
                Article article = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("""
                                select a from Article a
                                where a.price > :minPrice order by a.price""", Article.class)
                        .setParameter("minPrice", minPrice)
                        .setMaxResults(1)
                        .getSingleResultOrNull();
                IO.println(article == null ? "none" : article);

                // 4 - aggregates: the computation is done by the DBMS
                IO.println("--- aggregates");
                long nbArticles = session.createSelectionQuery("select count(*) from Article", Long.class)
                        .getSingleResult();
                BigDecimal stockValue = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("select sum(price * currentStock) from Article", BigDecimal.class)
                        .getSingleResult();
                IO.println("%d articles, value of the stock: %.2f euros".formatted(nbArticles, stockValue));

                // 5 - like and in; a Java list as the value of a parameter
                IO.println("--- like and in");
                List<String> names = List.of("bow", "pump", "racket");
                List<String> results = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("""
                                select name from Article
                                where name like 'b%' or name in :names""", String.class)
                        .setParameter("names", names)
                        .getResultList();
                IO.println(String.join(", ", results));

                // 6 - pagination: the third page of two articles, by ascending price
                IO.println("--- pagination");
                int pageSize = 2, pageNumber = 3;
                List<Article> page = session.createSelectionQuery("from Article order by price", Article.class)
                        .setFirstResult((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
                        .setMaxResults(pageSize)
                        .getResultList();
                IO.println("page %d : %s".formatted(pageNumber, page.stream()
                        .map(a -> "%s (%.2f euros)".formatted(a.getName(), a.getPrice()))
                        .collect(Collectors.joining(", "))));

                // 7 - an incorrect query is rejected as soon as it is created, before any execution
                IO.println("--- incorrect query");
                try {
                    session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where stock < minimumStock", Article.class);
                } catch (SemanticException e) {
                    IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
                }

                // 8 - a rule written in Java cannot be translated into SQL: in-memory filtering
                IO.println("--- in-memory filtering");
                try (Stream<Article> stream = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article", Article.class)
                        .getResultStream()) {
                    stream.filter(Rules::isOutOfStock).forEach(IO::println);
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // a business rule written in Java
    static final class Rules {

        private Rules() {
        }

        // an article is out of stock if its stock is below the minimum stock
        static boolean isOutOfStock(Article a) {
            return a.getCurrentStock() < a.getMinimumStock();
        }
    }
}

Results:

    SQL> order by a1_0.price

    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 200
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = 1
[5, diving suit, 300.00, 8, 2]
--- aggregates
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> select sum((a1_0.price*a1_0.currentStock))

6 articles, value of the stock: 12300.00 euros
--- like and in

    SQL> from articles a1_0

    SQL> limit ?, ?

    SQL> from articles a1_0

Comments:

  • Lines 26–27: The clause [where] compares two attributes of the entity; the [order by] clause sorts by name: they become the [WHERE] and [ORDER BY] clauses in the SQL sequence (lines 5–6). The query is executed by [getResultList];
  • lines 32–36: a projection. The query does not return entities, but rather two values per item: the name and the stock value. The generated SQL (line 9) requests only the necessary columns and performs the calculation itself. The result type is the [StockValue] record in lines 16–17: Hibernate creates one record per line, passing the values from the [select] clause to its constructor in order. These objects are not entities: the session does not track them. The query is written in a text block (Java 15, Chapter 3), which is more readable than a long string;
  • lines 44–50: a query written as in JPQL, with an alias ([a]). [:minPrice] is a named parameter, whose value is given by [setParameter]. It becomes a parameter of the order SQL (line 21): therefore, we do not need to worry about SQL injections, since the value is transmitted separately from the order text. This is the rule that Chapter 10 applied to prepared queries. [setMaxResults(1)] limits the result to one row: the clause [LIMIT] of MySQL (line 23). A literal value written in the query text (such as ['b%'] on line 68: line 36 of the results) is, on the other hand, copied into the order text SQL: values coming from outside the program must always be passed as parameters;
  • lines 55–59: the aggregates [count] and [sum] are calculated by DBMS (lines 28–31): only the result is transferred, not the rows. HQL also references [avg], [min], [max], the clauses [group by], and [having];
  • Lines 65–70: the operator [like] of SQL, and the operator [in], whose operand is a parameter that accepts a Java list: Hibernate expands it into as many SQL parameters as there are elements in the list (line 36). HQL supports numerous functions on strings ([upper], [length], [substring]...), dates, and numbers, which it translates into the DBMS dialect;
  • lines 76–79: pagination, to display a long list page by page. [setFirstResult] skips the entries from the previous pages, while [setMaxResults] keeps those from the requested page: the [LIMIT ?, ?] clause of MySQL (lines 45–47). Pagination only makes sense on a sorted list ([order by]). Lines 80–82 construct the page display using a stream and [Collectors.joining] (Chapter 5);
  • lines 86–90: a query that uses an attribute [stock] that does not exist. The error is detected as soon as the query is created, before any execution, because Hibernate parses the text HQL and compares it to the model: it throws a [SemanticException] (line 50; Hibernate messages are in English). A syntax error would result in a [SyntaxException];
  • lines 94–98: a query cannot use a Java method, such as [Rules.isOutOfStock] (lines 110–112): Hibernate does not know the code, and even if it did, it would not necessarily know how to write it as SQL. You can read all entities and filter them in memory using the API Stream: [getResultStream] returns a [Stream<Article>] (which must be closed after use, hence the [try] statement with resources). The result is correct (line 54), but the entire table was transferred (lines 52–53): with a large table, this should be avoided. It is better to include the condition in the query, as shown on line 26.

docs.title: 11.6.3. Named Queries and Compile-Time Validation
docs.text:
A query written in a string is only parsed at runtime. There are two ways to detect errors earlier:

  • named queries: the annotation ***[@NamedQuery(name = "Article.outOfStock", query = "from Article where currentStock < minimumStock")]***, placed on the entity, declares a query that Hibernate parses at startup, when creating the *[SessionFactory]*. It is then executed by its name: [session.createNamedSelectionQuery("Article.outOfStock", Article.class)];
  • the Hibernate annotation processor (“Hibernate Processor,” library [org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-processor]), declared in the compiler configuration ([annotationProcessorPaths] from [maven-compiler-plugin]). Executed by [javac] during compilation, it checks annotation requests and generates, for each entity, a “metamodel” class " class ([Article_] for [Article]), which we will encounter again with the API Criteria. We do not use it in this course.

docs.title: 11.7.1. Queries built using code
docs.text:
A HQL query is a string that can be constructed by concatenation: this is unreliable and hard to read as soon as the query depends on many optional criteria (a search form, for example). Jakarta Persistence offers another way to write queries: API Criteria, where the query is a tree of objects constructed through method calls. Hibernate translates this tree into SQL, just as it does with a HQL query (it also translates HQL into such a tree). The [criteria] module reuses several queries from the previous program:

package criteria;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.CriteriaQuery;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Expression;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Predicate;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Root;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.query.criteria.HibernateCriteriaBuilder;

public class Main {

    // a projection: the name of an article and the value of its stock
    record StockValue(String name, BigDecimal value) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.createSessionFactory()) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
            BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                // the factory of the query elements
                HibernateCriteriaBuilder cb = session.getCriteriaBuilder();

                // 1 - filtering and sorting
                IO.println("--- the articles to restock, in alphabetical order");
                CriteriaQuery<Article> query = cb.createQuery(Article.class);
                Root<Article> a = query.from(Article.class);
                query.select(a)
                        .where(cb.lt(a.<Integer>get("currentStock"), a.<Integer>get("minimumStock")))
                        .orderBy(cb.asc(a.get("name")));
                session.createSelectionQuery(query).getResultList().forEach(IO::println);

                // 2 - projection into a record
                IO.println("--- value of the stock of each article");
                CriteriaQuery<StockValue> projection = cb.createQuery(StockValue.class);
                Root<Article> p = projection.from(Article.class);
                Expression<BigDecimal> value = cb
                        .prod(p.<BigDecimal>get("price"), p.<Integer>get("currentStock"))
                        .as(BigDecimal.class);
                projection.select(cb.construct(StockValue.class, p.get("name"), value))
                        .orderBy(cb.desc(value));
                for (StockValue v : session.createSelectionQuery(projection).getResultList()) {
                    IO.println("%s : %.2f euros".formatted(v.name(), v.value()));
                }

                // 3 - a query built according to the provided criteria
                IO.println("--- search: maximum price 150 euros");
                search(session, BigDecimal.valueOf(150), null).forEach(IO::println);
                IO.println("--- search: maximum price 150 euros and name starting with [d]");
                search(session, BigDecimal.valueOf(150), "d").forEach(IO::println);

                // 4 - aggregates
                IO.println("--- aggregates");
                CriteriaQuery<Long> count = cb.createQuery(Long.class);
                count.select(cb.count(count.from(Article.class)));
                long nbArticles = session.createSelectionQuery(count).getSingleResult();
                CriteriaQuery<BigDecimal> sum = cb.createQuery(BigDecimal.class);
                Root<Article> s = sum.from(Article.class);
                sum.select(cb.sum(cb
                        .prod(s.<BigDecimal>get("price"), s.<Integer>get("currentStock"))
                        .as(BigDecimal.class)));
                BigDecimal stockValue = session.createSelectionQuery(sum).getSingleResult();
                IO.println("%d articles, value of the stock: %.2f euros".formatted(nbArticles, stockValue));
            }
        }
    }

    // the articles whose price does not exceed [maxPrice] and whose name starts with [nameStart],
    // each criterion being used only if it is not null
    static List<Article> search(Session session, BigDecimal maxPrice, String nameStart) {
        HibernateCriteriaBuilder cb = session.getCriteriaBuilder();
        CriteriaQuery<Article> query = cb.createQuery(Article.class);
        Root<Article> a = query.from(Article.class);
        // the conditions, added one by one
        List<Predicate> conditions = new ArrayList<>();
        if (maxPrice != null) {
            conditions.add(cb.le(a.get("price"), maxPrice));
        }
        if (nameStart != null) {
            conditions.add(cb.like(a.get("name"), nameStart + "%"));
        }
        query.select(a).where(conditions.toArray(Predicate[]::new)).orderBy(cb.asc(a.get("price")));
        return session.createSelectionQuery(query).getResultList();
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 28: the session returns a [HibernateCriteriaBuilder], the Hibernate-enhanced version of Jakarta Persistence’s [CriteriaBuilder]: this is the factory for all elements of a query (conditions, expressions, sorts);
  • Lines 32–36: The query from the first example, HQL. [createQuery(Article.class)] creates a query that returns articles; [from(Article.class)] declares the queried entity and returns its root ([Root<Article>]), which is the equivalent of the alias [a] for [from Article a]; [a.get("currentStock")] designates an attribute. The condition is constructed by [cb.lt(x, y)] (“less than,” [x < y]), and the sort by [cb.asc(...)]. The notation [a.<Integer>get(...)] provides the compiler with the attribute’s type, which the string ["currentStock"] does not allow it to determine;
  • line 37: the query is executed by the session as a HQL query. The generated SQL (lines 3–6) is the same as that of the HQL query;
  • Lines 41–47: a projection onto the record [StockValue]. [cb.prod(x, y)] is the product of two expressions; [as(BigDecimal.class)] specifies the result type; [cb.construct(StockValue.class, ...)] indicates that each row of the result must be passed to the record constructor;
  • Lines 76–90: This is where the API Criteria is most useful. The [search] method constructs a query based on the criteria provided to it: each condition is added to the list of conditions only if the corresponding criterion is not [null], and the [where] clause receives all the conditions from the list, combined by [and]. The first call (line 54) produces a query with one condition (line 21), while the second (line 56) produces a query with two conditions (line 30). Note that with the API criteria, Hibernate passes the values ([150], [d%]) as parameters in the order SQL;
  • lines 60–68: the aggregates [count] and [sum].

docs.title: 11.7.2. The static metamodel
docs.text:
The weakness of these queries is that attributes are designated by strings ([a.get("currentStock")]): a typo will not be detected until runtime, and the compiler ignores the attribute’s type. To address this, Jakarta Persistence provides a static metamodel: for each entity [Article], there is a class [Article_] that contains one field per attribute, describing its name and type. You then write ***[cb.lt(a.get(Article\_.currentStock), a.get(Article\_.minimumStock))]***, which the compiler fully validates. These classes are not written by hand: they are generated during compilation by the Hibernate annotation processor mentioned above. This is the recommended approach in a real-world project that uses API Criteria.

For a fixed query, HQL is more readable than the API Criteria; for a query that is constructed based on the circumstances, the API Criteria is safer. The two can be combined: Hibernate allows you to create a Criteria query from a HQL ([cb.createQuery(hql, Article.class)]) string and then supplement it with code.

docs.title: 11.8.1. The Store Model
docs.text:
The tables in a database are linked to one another. Hibernate represents these links as associations: fields that reference another entity or a collection of entities. The [relations] module uses a [hbshop] database that describes a small store with six entities. A category groups products together:

// a category groups several products (one-to-many relationship)
@Entity
@Table(name = "categories")
public class Category {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    private String name;

    // the products of the category: the inverse side of the relationship, described by Product.category
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "category", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    private List<Product> products = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Category() {
    }

    public Category(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    // adding a product: the two sides of the relationship are updated
    public void add(Product product) {
        products.add(product);
        product.setCategory(this);
    }

    public Integer getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public List<Product> getProducts() {
        return products;
    }
}

A product belongs to a category and has tags:

// a product belongs to a category and carries several tags
@Entity
@Table(name = "products")
public class Product {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal price;

    // many-to-one relationship: the foreign key [category_id] of the [products] table
    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "category_id", foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_products_category"))
    private Category category;

    // many-to-many relationship, stored in an association table
    @ManyToMany(cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    @JoinTable(name = "products_tags",
            joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "product_id"),
            inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "tag_id"),
            foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_products_tags_product"),
            inverseForeignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_products_tags_tag"))
    private Set<Tag> tags = new HashSet<>();

    protected Product() {
    }

    public Product(String name, BigDecimal price, Tag... tags) {
        this.name = name;
        this.price = price;
        // only the owning side of the relationship is filled in: it is the one Hibernate saves
        this.tags.addAll(List.of(tags));
    }

A tag is assigned to multiple products:

// a tag (promo, new...) is carried by several products
@Entity
@Table(name = "tags")
public class Tag {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 20)
    private String label;

    // the inverse side of the relationship described by Product.tags
    @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "tags")
    private Set<Product> products = new HashSet<>();

    protected Tag() {
    }

    public Tag(String label) {
        this.label = label;
    }

An order belongs to a customer and contains line items:

// an order of a client, made of lines
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class CustomerOrder {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    private LocalDate date;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "client_id")
    private Client client;

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    private List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>();

    protected CustomerOrder() {
    }

    public CustomerOrder(LocalDate date) {
        this.date = date;
    }

    // adding a line: the two sides of the relationship are updated
    public void add(OrderLine line) {
        lines.add(line);
        line.setOrder(this);
    }

The entities [Client] and [OrderLine] are built on the same model. A customer has an ID, a name, and a list of orders ([@OneToMany(mappedBy = "client", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)]), with a method [add(CustomerOrder)]; an order line has an ID, a quantity, and two many-to-one associations—one to its order and one to its product:

// an order line: a quantity of a product
@Entity
@Table(name = "order_lines")
public class OrderLine {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    private int quantity;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")
    private CustomerOrder order;

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "product_id")
    private Product product;

    protected OrderLine() {
    }

    public OrderLine(Product product, int quantity) {
        this.product = product;
        this.quantity = quantity;
    }

This example includes all three types of associations:

  • a many-to-one relationship ([@ManyToOne]): a product belongs to a category (Product, lines 17–19). In the database, this is represented by a foreign key, the column [category_id] in table [products], where [@JoinColumn] specifies the name and the constraint name ([fk_products_category]). [optional = false] enforces the relationship: the column will be [NOT NULL];
  • the inverse, one-to-many relationship ([@OneToMany]): a category contains multiple products (Category, lines 14–15). It does not create anything in the database: [mappedBy = "category"] indicates that it is described by the field [category] of the entity [Product]. [Product.category] is said to be the owner side of the relationship, and [Category.products] its inverse side: Hibernate saves the value of the owner side. However, both sides must be kept consistent in memory: this is the role of the [add] method (Category, lines 25–28), which adds the product to the list and sets its category;
  • a many-to-many relationship ([@ManyToMany]): a product has multiple labels, and a label is associated with multiple products. It is stored in an association table, [products_tags], whose name, the names of the two columns, and the names of the two foreign keys are provided by [@JoinTable] (Product, lines 22–28). The reverse side is [Tag.products] ([mappedBy = "tags"]). For a many-to-many relationship, a [Set] is preferred over a [List]: with a list, Hibernate deletes and re-inserts all rows in the association table every time the collection is modified;
  • [fetch = FetchType.LAZY] requires lazy loading of a product’s category: it will only be read if it is used. This is the default behavior for collections ([@OneToMany], [@ManyToMany]), but not for relationships to a single entity ([@ManyToOne]), which the standard loads immediately by default ([EAGER]): [fetch = FetchType.LAZY] is systematically added to them, as recommended by the Hibernate documentation;
  • [cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST] propagates the operation [persist]: persisting a category persists its products, and persisting a product persists its tags. The other values ([MERGE], [REMOVE], [ALL]...) propagate the other operations;
  • collections are initialized with an empty collection, and the field of a relationship to a single entity remains [null] until it has been populated. The methods [setCategory], [setClient], and [setOrder] are not public: only the [add] methods in the same package call them.

The [Shop] class configures Hibernate for the [hbshop] database and creates an initial dataset there:

package relations;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import tools.SqlLog;

// the [hbshop] database: Hibernate configuration and first data set
public final class Shop {

    private Shop() {
    }

    // a SessionFactory for the [hbshop] database and its six entities
    public static SessionFactory createSessionFactory() {
        return new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("shop")
                .managedClasses(Category.class, Product.class, Tag.class,
                        Client.class, CustomerOrder.class, OrderLine.class)
                .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbshop?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }

    // (re)creation of the tables and of a first data set, without an SQL log
    public static void initialize(SessionFactory sessionFactory) {
        SqlLog.withoutLog(() -> {
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                // two tags
                Tag promo = new Tag("promo");
                Tag novelty = new Tag("new");
                // three categories and their products: a graph of objects
                Category cycles = new Category("cycles");
                cycles.add(new Product("bike", BigDecimal.valueOf(500), promo));
                Product pump = new Product("pump", BigDecimal.valueOf(10));
                cycles.add(pump);
                Category archery = new Category("archery");
                Product bow = new Product("bow", BigDecimal.valueOf(600), novelty);
                archery.add(bow);
                archery.add(new Product("arrows - set of 6", BigDecimal.valueOf(100),
                        promo, novelty));
                Category diving = new Category("diving");
                // the persistence is propagated to the products and to the tags (cascade)
                session.persist(cycles);
                session.persist(archery);
                session.persist(diving);
                // a client and their order of two lines
                CustomerOrder order = new CustomerOrder(LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 28));
                order.add(new OrderLine(pump, 2));
                order.add(new OrderLine(bow, 1));
                Client martin = new Client("Martin");
                martin.add(order);
                session.persist(martin);
            });
        });
    }
}
  • lines 19–20: the six entities, declared by [managedClasses];
  • lines 34–46: an object graph: three categories, their products, and the products’ labels;
  • lines 48–50: it is sufficient to persist the categories: thanks to cascading, Hibernate traverses the associations and persists all the entities it reaches, in the correct order (the categories before the products that reference them), populating the foreign keys and the association table;
  • lines 52–57: a customer, their order, and its two line items, persisted in a single operation.

docs.title: 11.8.2. The program
docs.text:
package relations;

import jakarta.persistence.EntityGraph;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;

public class Main {

    // the results of the projection queries
    record ProductCategory(String product, String category) {
    }

    record OrderAmount(Integer id, String client, BigDecimal amount) {
    }

    record CategoryStatistics(String category, Long count, Double averagePrice) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = Shop.createSessionFactory()) {
            // 1 - creation of the tables and of a first data set, without a log
            Shop.initialize(sessionFactory);

            // 2 - a client, their order and its lines, added in one go
            IO.println("--- addition of a client, an order and its two lines");
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                Product bike = product(session, "bike");
                Product arrows = product(session, "arrows - set of 6");
                CustomerOrder order = new CustomerOrder(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1));
                order.add(new OrderLine(bike, 1));
                order.add(new OrderLine(arrows, 3));
                Client client = new Client("Dupont");
                client.add(order);
                session.persist(client);
                IO.println("client no. %d, order no. %d".formatted(client.getId(), order.getId()));
            });

            // 3 - lazy loading: the relationships are read on demand
            IO.println("--- lazy loading");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> {
                List<CustomerOrder> orders = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from CustomerOrder order by id", CustomerOrder.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (CustomerOrder order : orders) {
                    IO.println("order no. %d : client=%s, %d line(s)".formatted(order.getId(),
                            order.getClient().getName(), order.getLines().size()));
                }
            });

            // 4 - a relationship that is not loaded is no longer accessible once the session is closed
            IO.println("--- after the session is closed");
            CustomerOrder detachedOrder = sessionFactory.fromSession(s -> s.find(CustomerOrder.class, 1));
            try {
                IO.println(detachedOrder.getLines().size() + " line(s)");
            } catch (LazyInitializationException e) {
                IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
            }

            // 5 - join fetch: the orders, their client, their lines and their products in one query
            IO.println("--- join fetch");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> {
                List<CustomerOrder> orders = session.createSelectionQuery("""
                        from CustomerOrder c
                        join fetch c.client
                        join fetch c.lines l
                        join fetch l.product
                        order by c.id""", CustomerOrder.class).getResultList();
                for (CustomerOrder order : orders) {
                    IO.println("order no. %d of %s for %s".formatted(order.getId(), order.getDate(),
                            order.getClient().getName()));
                    for (OrderLine line : order.getLines()) {
                        Product product = line.getProduct();
                        IO.println("  %d x %s at %.2f euros"
                                .formatted(line.getQuantity(), product.getName(), product.getPrice()));
                    }
                }
            });

            // 6 - an entity graph: what must be loaded with the entity, described outside the query
            IO.println("--- entity graph");
            Category category = sessionFactory.fromSession(session -> {
                EntityGraph<Category> graph = session.createEntityGraph(Category.class);
                graph.addAttributeNode("products");
                return session.find(graph, 2);
            });
            // the session is closed, but the products have been loaded
            IO.println("%s : %s".formatted(category.getName(),
                    category.getProducts().stream().map(Product::getName).collect(Collectors.joining(", "))));

            // 7 - the many-to-many relationship in a query
            IO.println("--- the products on promotion");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session.createSelectionQuery("""
                            select p.name, p.category.name from Product p join p.tags e
                            where e.label = 'promo' order by p.name""", ProductCategory.class)
                    .getResultList()
                    .forEach(p -> IO.println("%s (%s)".formatted(p.product(), p.category()))));

            // 8 - a computation across the relationships, done by the DBMS
            IO.println("--- amount of the orders");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session.createSelectionQuery("""
                            select c.id, c.client.name, sum(l.quantity * l.product.price)
                            from CustomerOrder c join c.lines l
                            group by c.id, c.client.name order by c.id""", OrderAmount.class)
                    .getResultList()
                    .forEach(m -> IO.println("order no. %d (%s) : %.2f euros"
                            .formatted(m.id(), m.client(), m.amount()))));

            // 9 - a grouping: number of products and average price per category
            IO.println("--- products per category");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session.createSelectionQuery("""
                            select p.category.name, count(*), avg(p.price) from Product p
                            group by p.category.name order by p.category.name""", CategoryStatistics.class)
                    .getResultList()
                    .forEach(s -> IO.println("%s : %d product(s), average price %.2f euros".formatted(
                            s.category(), s.count(), s.averagePrice()))));
        }
    }

    // the product with the given name
    private static Product product(Session session, String name) {
        return session.createSelectionQuery("from Product where name = :name", Product.class)
                .setParameter("name", name)
                .getSingleResult();
    }
}
