Comments:

  • lines 15–22: the records that will receive the projection results;
  • lines 32–39: the output is read by the [product] method (lines 125–129); a customer, their order, and its two lines are persisted with a single call to [persist]. SQL (lines 12–28 of the results) shows the order of insertions: the customer, then the order, whose foreign key [client_id] receives the key generated for the customer (2), then the rows, whose foreign key [order_id] receives the key from the order;
  • Lines 46–52: lazy loading. The query reads only the orders (lines 32–34): the customer and the lines for each order are read only when the program uses them, via additional queries (lines 35–42 for the first order, 44–51 for the second). For the client, Hibernate has placed a proxy in the [client] field—an object of a subclass of [Client] generated by Hibernate (using Byte Buddy)—which contains only the identifier and loads the client upon the first call to a method ([getName()]). This is why an entity must not be a [final] class. For the rows, the list is a Hibernate collection, loaded upon its first use ([size()]);
  • lines 57–62: The command is read by a session that is immediately closed ([fromSession]). These rows were not loaded, and once the session is closed, they can no longer be loaded: accessing the collection triggers a [LazyInitializationException] (line 58), one of the most common exceptions in applications that use Hibernate. You must load what you need while the session is open;
  • Lines 67–72: preloading via a query. [join fetch] instructs Hibernate to load, along with the orders, their customers, their lines, and the product of each line: a single query with joins (lines 60–78). The display shows the two orders and their line items (lines 79–84). The join with the line items produces one SQL row per order line; Hibernate derives a single order for each identifier: the rendered list does indeed contain two orders;
  • lines 86–90: an “entity graph” (Jakarta Persistence) describes, independently of any query, the associations to be loaded with an entity: in this case, the products in the category. [session.find(graph, 2)] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) retrieves category 2 along with its products in a single query (lines 86–90 of the results). Once the session is closed, the products remain accessible (lines 92–93). To load an association later, while the session is open, we write [Hibernate.initialize(category.getProducts())];
  • lines 97–101: associations are used in queries: [join p.tags e] traverses the many-to-many relationship (two joins, with the association table and the label table, lines 95–96), and [p.category.name] is translated into an implicit join with the category table (line 97);
  • lines 105–111: a calculation across two relations—the total amount of each order—entirely performed by DBMS: joins, [sum] and [group by] (lines 103–109);
  • lines 115–120: a grouping. [group by p.category.name] groups products by category name; for each group, the number of products ([count]) and the average price ([avg], of type [Double]) are calculated by DBMS (lines 113–117). The category [diving], which has no products, does not appear: the join with the category table is an inner join ([join]).

docs.title: 11.8.3. The N+1 query problem
docs.text: The lazy loading in the example illustrates a problem that plagues any user of a ORM, known as the “N+1 queries” problem: one query to read the N orders, then one query per order to read its customer (and another for its lines). With a thousand orders, this results in a thousand and one round trips to the server, when a single one would have sufficed. The problem is all the more insidious because it’s invisible in the code: [order.getClient().getName()] doesn’t look like a query. The solutions are those shown in the example: [join fetch], an entity graph, or better yet, a projection that retrieves only the relevant data. Hibernate also offers batch loading ([@BatchSize(size = 20)] applied to a collection, or to the referenced entity class—in this case, [Client]), which, for example, retrieves the customers for twenty orders in a single query. The log SQL helps identify the problem: the same query being repeated numerous times.

docs.title: 11.9.1. The Problem
docs.text:
Until now, tables have been created by Hibernate after being deleted. This is impossible for a live application: its database contains data that must be preserved when the model evolves (a new column, a new table). It must be possible to migrate the database from one schema version to the next, in a safe and reproducible manner, both on the developer’s machine and on the production server. This is referred to as schema migration.

Hibernate does not support migrations: it can create a schema, validate it, and make limited updates to it. In the Java world, the standard practice is to handle migrations using versioned SQL scripts, applied by a dedicated tool—most often Flyway or Liquibase—and to have Hibernate verify that the resulting schema matches the entities.

docs.title: 11.9.2. Schema Management by Hibernate
docs.text:
The [hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto] property (or the [schemaToolingAction] method in the configuration, which the program below uses) specifies what Hibernate should do with the schema when creating the [SessionFactory]:

ValueConstant [Action]Effect[none][NONE]none (default value)[create-only][CREATE_ONLY]table creation[create][CREATE]Deleting and then creating tables[create-drop][CREATE_DROP]such as [create], and deletion of tables upon closing [SessionFactory]: for testing[drop][DROP]Delete tables[validate][VALIDATE]Verify that the tables and columns of the entities exist and have compatible types; throw an exception otherwise[update][UPDATE]Create any missing tables and columns

Jakarta Persistence defines a related property, [jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action], with the values [none], [create], [drop-and-create], and [drop]. The same actions are available programmatically, as we did with [SchemaManager] from [SessionFactory] ([create], [drop], [validate], [truncate]).

The value [update] is tempting: Hibernate compares the entities to the database schema and adds what’s missing. It has limitations that make it unsuitable for a production application:

  • it only adds: it never deletes a column or table that has become unnecessary, does not modify the type or length of an existing column, and cannot rename (renaming a field creates a new empty column, while the old one remains with its data);
  • it cannot transform data (fill a new required column, split a column into two);
  • what it does depends on the state of the database it encounters: it is impossible to know in advance which commands will be executed, or in what order, and no record of this is kept.

We therefore reserve [create], [create-drop], and [update] for development and testing, and we use [validate] (or [none]) in production, with the schema managed by scripts.

docs.title: 11.9.3. Versioned SQL scripts
docs.text:
The principle behind script-based migrations is simple:

  • each schema change is described by a SQL script, numbered: [V1__create_clients.sql], [V2__add_phone.sql]... Once a script has been applied to a database, it is never modified again: any correction is the subject of a new script;
  • the database contains a history table that lists the versions that have been applied to it;
  • When the application starts (or during deployment), a tool compares the available scripts with the history and applies, in order, those that have not yet been applied.

The scripts are part of the application’s source code: they are stored and managed along with the rest of the code (in a Git repository, for example). To understand how this works, the [clients] module implements a small versioned script executor, modeled after Flyway; we will then introduce Flyway itself.

docs.title: 11.9.4. The [clients] module
docs.text:
The [clients] module builds on the [hbclients] base. The entity is a client:

// a client
@Entity
@Table(name = "clients")
public class Client {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    private String name;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String email;

    @Column(length = 20)
    private String phone;

    protected Client() {
    }

    public Client(String name, String email, String phone) {
        this.name = name;
        this.email = email;
        this.phone = phone;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        String tel = phone == null ? "no phone" : phone;
        return "[%d, %s, %s, %s]".formatted(id, name, email, tel);
    }
}

In the first version of the application, the customer does not have a phone number: lines 16–17 do not yet exist. We will add them in the second version. The scripts are located in the module’s [src/main/resources/db/migration] folder, which will be copied to the classpath. The first script creates the table:

-- version 1: the clients table
create table clients (
    id integer not null auto_increment,
    name varchar(50) not null,
    email varchar(100) not null,
    primary key (id)
) engine=InnoDB;

The second adds the phone number column:

-- version 2: the (optional) phone of the clients
alter table clients
    add column phone varchar(20);

The [Migrations] class executes the scripts using JDBC (Chapter 10), independently of Hibernate:

package clients;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URISyntaxException;
import java.net.URL;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

// a small runner of versioned SQL scripts, modeled on Flyway: the scripts
// [db/migration/V<version>__<description>.sql] are applied only once, in the order of the versions,
// and the [migration_history] table of the database records those that have been
public class Migrations {

    // a migration script
    public record Script(int version, String description, Path path) {
        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return "V" + version + " (" + description + ")";
        }
    }

    // the name of a script: V1__create_clients.sql
    private static final Pattern NAME = Pattern.compile("V(\\d+)__(\\w+)\\.sql");

    // the history table
    private static final String CREATE_HISTORY = """
            create table if not exists migration_history (
                version integer not null primary key,
                description varchar(100) not null,
                applied_on datetime not null default current_timestamp
            ) engine=InnoDB""";

    // the database
    private final String url;
    private final String user;
    private final String password;

    public Migrations(String url, String user, String password) {
        this.url = url;
        this.user = user;
        this.password = password;
    }

    // the scripts of the [db/migration] folder of the classpath, in version order
    public List<Script> scripts() throws IOException, URISyntaxException {
        URL folder = Migrations.class.getResource("/db/migration");
        if (folder == null) {
            return List.of();
        }
        List<Script> scripts = new ArrayList<>();
        try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(Path.of(folder.toURI()))) {
            for (Path file : files.toList()) {
                Matcher m = NAME.matcher(file.getFileName().toString());
                if (m.matches()) {
                    int version = Integer.parseInt(m.group(1));
                    scripts.add(new Script(version, m.group(2).replace('_', ' '), file));
                }
            }
        }
        scripts.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Script::version));
        return scripts;
    }

    // the versions already applied to the database (the history table is created if needed)
    public Set<Integer> appliedVersions() throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password);
             Statement statement = connection.createStatement()) {
            statement.execute(CREATE_HISTORY);
            Set<Integer> versions = new TreeSet<>();
            try (ResultSet rows = statement.executeQuery("select version from migration_history")) {
                while (rows.next()) {
                    versions.add(rows.getInt(1));
                }
            }
            return versions;
        }
    }

    // the scripts that remain to be applied
    public List<Script> pending() throws SQLException, IOException, URISyntaxException {
        Set<Integer> applied = appliedVersions();
        return scripts().stream().filter(s -> !applied.contains(s.version())).toList();
    }

    // application of the pending scripts, up to version [target] included; the applied scripts are returned
    public List<Script> apply(int target) throws SQLException, IOException, URISyntaxException {
        List<Script> applied = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Script script : pending()) {
            if (script.version() > target) {
                break;
            }
            apply(script);
            applied.add(script);
        }
        return applied;
    }

    // application of a script and addition of its version to the history, in a transaction
    private void apply(Script script) throws SQLException, IOException {
        // the statements of the script, separated by semicolons, without the comment lines
        String text = Files.readString(script.path()).lines()
                .filter(line -> !line.strip().startsWith("--"))
                .reduce("", (a, b) -> a + "\n" + b);
        try (Connection connection = DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, password)) {
            connection.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
                 PreparedStatement history = connection.prepareStatement(
                         "insert into migration_history(version, description) values (?, ?)")) {
                for (String sql : text.split(";")) {
                    if (!sql.isBlank()) {
                        statement.execute(sql);
                    }
                }
                history.setInt(1, script.version());
                history.setString(2, script.description());
                history.executeUpdate();
                connection.commit();
            } catch (SQLException e) {
                // beware: with MySQL, a schema modification statement cannot be rolled back
                connection.rollback();
                throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}
  • Lines 29–34: A script is described by a record: its version, description, and path;
  • line 37: a script’s name follows the Flyway convention: [V], the version number, two underscores, and a description;
  • lines 40–45: the history table: one row per applied version, with its description and the date it was applied;
  • lines 59–76: the list of scripts. [getResource("/db/migration")] adds URL from the folder to the classpath, which is listed along with [Files.list] (Chapter 5). This code assumes that the folder is a real folder (which is the case when the program is run by Maven from the [target/classes] folder); Flyway can also read scripts from a [.jar] archive. The scripts are sorted by version number: alphabetical sorting would place [V10] before [V2];
  • lines 79–91: versions already applied, read from the history table, which is created as needed ([create table if not exists]);
  • lines 94–97: the scripts that remain to be applied;
  • lines 100–110: the application of pending scripts, up to a given version;
  • lines 113–138: the application of a script: its commands (separated by semicolons, with comment lines ignored), followed by the addition of its version to the history table, within a transaction. One caveat, noted in the comment on line 133: under MySQL, a schema modification command ([CREATE TABLE], [ALTER TABLE]) implicitly commits the current transaction and cannot be rolled back. If an error occurs in the middle of a script, the database may remain in an intermediate state. This is why it’s best to use short scripts, each containing only a single change.

The main program applies the migrations, then asks Hibernate to validate the schema:

package clients;

import jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import org.hibernate.tool.schema.Action;

public class Main {

    // the clients database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
    public static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbclients?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true";

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // the targeted version: the last one by default, or the one passed as an argument
        int target = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : Integer.MAX_VALUE;

        // the state of the migrations
        Migrations migrations = new Migrations(URL, "root", "");
        IO.println("applied versions: " + migrations.appliedVersions());
        IO.println("pending migrations: " + migrations.pending());

        // application of the pending migrations
        for (Migrations.Script script : migrations.apply(target)) {
            IO.println("migration applied: " + script);
        }

        // Hibernate checks that the database schema matches the entities (validate)
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("clients")
                .managedClass(Client.class)
                .jdbcUrl(URL)
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .schemaToolingAction(Action.VALIDATE)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
            IO.println("the database schema matches the entities");
            // the new column is usable
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session ->
                    session.persist(new Client("Dupont", "dupont@example.com", "01 23 45 67 89")));
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session
                    .createSelectionQuery("from Client", Client.class)
                    .getResultList()
                    .forEach(IO::println));
        } catch (PersistenceException e) {
            // the validation error is the cause of the exception
            Throwable cause = e.getCause() == null ? e : e.getCause();
            IO.println(cause.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + cause.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
  • line 16: You can specify, as an argument, the version up to which to apply the migrations; by default, all are applied;
  • lines 19–26: the status of the migrations, followed by their application;
  • lines 29–35: [SessionFactory] is created with the action [VALIDATE]: Hibernate verifies that the database schema matches the entity [Client]. If this is not the case, the creation of [SessionFactory] fails, resulting in [PersistenceException], caused by the validation error (lines 44–48);
  • lines 38–43: the new column is used.

docs.title: 11.9.5. Generate the scripts with Hibernate
docs.text:
The SQL scripts are written by hand. However, Hibernate can help write them: it can generate—without executing it—the script to create the schema, or, by comparing the entities to an existing database, the script to update it. This is what the [GenerateScript] class does:

package clients;

import java.io.StringWriter;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

// generation by Hibernate of the SQL script that creates (create) or updates (update) the database schema
public class GenerateScript {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // the action: create (by default) or update
        String action = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "create";
        StringWriter script = new StringWriter();
        // a SessionFactory that writes the script without executing it
        try (SessionFactory _ = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("clients")
                .managedClass(Client.class)
                .jdbcUrl(Main.URL)
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, action)
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
                .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
            // the script, without the 4-space indentation of its lines
            script.toString().strip().lines()
                    .map(line -> line.startsWith("    ") ? line.substring(4) : line)
                    .forEach(line -> IO.println(line.stripTrailing()));
        }
    }
}
  • line 13: the action, passed as an argument: [create] or [update];
  • line 16: [SessionFactory] is created solely to generate the script; the variable that holds it is never used. Java 22 allows it to be called [_] (anonymous variable);
  • Lines 20–23: The script generation properties, which we’ve already seen in the [model] module. This time, Hibernate connects to the database: for the [update] action, it needs to know the database schema.

The creation script, generated from the current version of the entity, is used to create a brand-new database all at once (for testing, for example):

> mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=clients.GenerateScript
create table clients (
    id integer not null auto_increment,
    phone varchar(20),
    name varchar(50) not null,
    email varchar(100) not null,
    primary key (id)
) engine=InnoDB;

With the first version of the entity (without a phone number), it would have generated—with the same column order—the script [V1__create_clients.sql].

docs.title: 11.9.6. Apply the migrations
docs.text:
Suppose the database does not yet exist. We apply only the first migration, passing version 1 as an argument:

> mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.args="1"
applied versions: []
pending migrations: [V1 (create clients), V2 (add phone)]
migration applied: V1 (create clients)
SchemaManagementException : Schema validation: missing column [phone] in table [clients]
  • Lines 2–3: No version is applied; two scripts are pending. The history table was created by the [appliedVersions] method, and the [hbclients] database by MySQL ([createDatabaseIfNotExist=true]);
  • line 4: the script [V1] is applied;
  • Line 5: Hibernate detects that the [phone] column of the entity does not exist in the table: this is normal, since the database is at version 1 and the entity is at version 2. With the version 1 entity, the validation would have succeeded.

The application is evolving: we’re adding the phone number to the entity. To write the script for version 2, we ask Hibernate to compare the entity to the database, which is still at version 1:

> mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=clients.GenerateScript -Dexec.args="update"
alter table clients
   add column phone varchar(20);

This is, apart from the formatting, the same as the script [V2__add_phone.sql]. We now apply all pending migrations:

> mvn compile exec:java
applied versions: [1]
pending migrations: [V2 (add phone)]
migration applied: V2 (add phone)
the database schema matches the entities
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> insert into clients (email, name, phone)
    SQL> values (?, ?, ?)
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = dupont@example.com
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = Dupont
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = 01 23 45 67 89
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
    SQL> select c1_0.id, c1_0.email, c1_0.name, c1_0.phone
    SQL> from clients c1_0
[1, Dupont, dupont@example.com, 01 23 45 67 89]
  • Lines 2–4: Version 1 is applied, Version 2 is pending, and it is applied;
  • line 5: validation succeeds;
  • lines 6–15: the new column is ready for use.

The history table now contains both versions:

> mysql -uroot -t hbclients -e "SELECT * FROM migration_history"
+---------+----------------+---------------------+
| version | description    | applied_on          |
+---------+----------------+---------------------+
|       1 | create clients | 2026-10-03 17:27:22 |
|       2 | add phone      | 2026-10-03 17:27:27 |
+---------+----------------+---------------------+

Running the program again will not apply any changes: both versions are listed in the history.

docs.title: 11.9.7. Flyway
docs.text:
Flyway is the most widely used migration tool in the Java world (Spring Boot runs it automatically when an application starts if it is present in the classpath). It works exactly according to the same principle as our executor, but is more comprehensive: [V<version>__<description>.sql] scripts are searched for by default in the [db/migration] folder of the classpath, the [flyway_schema_history] history table, and the application of pending scripts in version order. In particular, it adds a checksum for each script, which detects changes to a script that has already been applied; “repeatable” scripts ([R__description.sql], reapplied with each change, for views for example); migrations written in Java, a lock that prevents two instances of the application from migrating the database at the same time, and a Maven extension ([mvn flyway:migrate], [mvn flyway:info]).

To use it in the [clients] module, simply add the dependencies [org.flywaydb:flyway-core] and [org.flywaydb:flyway-mysql] (in their latest versions), keep the two scripts as-is—since they already follow its convention—and replace the use of the [Migrations] class with a single line: [Flyway.configure().dataSource(URL, "root", "").load().migrate();]

Liquibase, the other commonly used tool, describes schema changes in files XML, YAML, or SQL (the “changelogs”), and can generate the SQL specific to each DBMS. In both cases, Hibernate is configured with [validate] or [none], and no longer modifies the schema.

docs.title: 11.10. Hibernate and Virtual Threads
docs.text:
A database query is an I/O operation: while the server is processing the request, the waiting thread does nothing. Chapter 9 presented two ways to avoid wasting threads during these waits: asynchronous programming ([CompletableFuture]) and virtual threads (Java 21). Hibernate’s API, like the JDBC it uses, is blocking: [getResultList] does not yield control until the rows have been read. With virtual threads, this is no longer a drawback: a virtual thread blocked on I/O releases the system thread that was executing it, and thousands of them can be created. Therefore, we write ordinary blocking code, executed by virtual threads.

One rule must be followed: a session is not thread-safe. It must never be shared among multiple threads: each thread (each task) opens its own session with [SessionFactory], which is itself shared. Hibernate does not always detect simultaneous use of the same session; the resulting errors are unpredictable.

The [async] module enforces this rule:

package async;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import jakarta.persistence.QueryTimeoutException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.createSessionFactory()) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
            BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory);

            // 1 - two queries executed at the same time by two virtual threads, each with its own session
            IO.println("--- two queries in parallel");
            try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
                Future<List<Article>> lowPrices = executor.submit(() -> sessionFactory.fromSession(s -> s
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article where price < 200 order by price", Article.class)
                        .getResultList()));
                String hql = "select count(*) from Article where currentStock < minimumStock";
                Future<Long> outOfStock = executor.submit(() -> sessionFactory.fromSession(s -> s
                        .createSelectionQuery(hql, Long.class)
                        .getSingleResult()));
                // get() waits for the end of each task
                lowPrices.get().forEach(IO::println);
                IO.println(outOfStock.get() + " article(s) out of stock");
            }

            // 2 - a transaction executed by a virtual thread, followed by a processing of its result
            IO.println("--- CompletableFuture");
            try (ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
                CompletableFuture<Void> processing = CompletableFuture
                        .supplyAsync(() -> sessionFactory.fromTransaction(session -> {
                            Article bow = session
                                    .createSelectionQuery("from Article where name = 'bow'", Article.class)
                                    .getSingleResult();
                            bow.setPrice(BigDecimal.valueOf(550));
                            return bow;
                        }), executor)
                        .thenAccept(bow -> IO.println("new price of the bow: " + bow.getPrice()));
                processing.join();
            }

            // 3 - a stream: the entities are processed as they are read
            IO.println("--- getResultStream");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> {
                try (Stream<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article where price >= 300", Article.class)
                        .getResultStream()) {
                    articles.forEach(article -> IO.println("read: " + article.getName()));
                }
            });

            // 4 - a query that is too long is interrupted after the set timeout (in seconds)
            IO.println("--- timeout exceeded");
            try {
                sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session
                        .createNativeQuery("select sleep(5)", Integer.class)
                        .setTimeout(1)
                        .getSingleResult());
            } catch (QueryTimeoutException e) {
                IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> mvn compile exec:java
--- two queries in parallel
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.price<200
    SQL> order by a1_0.price
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.currentStock<a1_0.minimumStock
[2, pump, 10.00, 10, 2]
[4, arrows - set of 6, 100.00, 12, 20]
[6, diver's oxygen tanks, 120.00, 10, 5]
1 article(s) out of stock
--- CompletableFuture
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.name='bow'
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set currentStock=?, minimumStock=?, name=?, price=?
    SQL> where id=?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 4
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = 1
    SQL> -- parameter 3 = bow
    SQL> -- parameter 4 = 550
    SQL> -- parameter 5 = 3
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
new price of the bow: 550
--- getResultStream
    SQL> select a1_0.id, a1_0.currentStock, a1_0.minimumStock, a1_0.name, a1_0.price
    SQL> from articles a1_0
    SQL> where a1_0.price>=300
read: bike
read: bow
read: diving suit
--- timeout exceeded
    SQL> select sleep(5)
    SQL> -- failure: Statement cancelled due to timeout or client request
QueryTimeoutException : JDBC exception executing SQL [Statement cancelled due to timeout or client request] [select sleep(5)]

Comments:

  • Line 25: an executor that creates a virtual thread for each task (Chapter 9). The [try] instruction with resources waits for all tasks to finish before closing it;
  • Lines 26–32: Two tasks submitted to the executor. Each opens its own session ([fromSession]) and executes a query; both queries run simultaneously, using two connections from the pool. Their order in the log (lines 3–9) may therefore vary from one execution to another;
  • lines 34–35: [get()] waits for each task to complete and returns its result (lines 10–13);
  • lines 41–50: a [CompletableFuture] (Chapter 9) whose first step—a complete transaction—is executed by a virtual thread ([supplyAsync(..., executor)]), and the second step displays its result. The record returned by the transaction is detached (its session is closed): its fields can be read, but its associations cannot be loaded;
  • Lines 56–60: [getResultStream] returns a stream: entities are processed as they are read, without forming a list (lines 33–35). This is useful for processing a large number of rows. With MySQL, note that by default the driver reads all rows of the result before returning the first one; for truly progressive reading, you must instruct it to use a cursor (parameter [useCursorFetch=true] of URL and batch size set by [setFetchSize]);
  • Lines 66–69: a maximum execution time, in seconds, set by [setTimeout]. The query (a native SQL query, which we’ll discuss later) takes five seconds; after one second, the JDBC driver interrupts it, and Hibernate launches a [QueryTimeoutException] (lines 37–39). This is the equivalent, for a query, of canceling a task ([Future.cancel], Chapter 9), which would have no effect here: interrupting a thread blocked in the JDBC driver does not interrupt the query currently running on the server.

For applications that require a truly non-blocking API, there is Hibernate Reactive, a variant of Hibernate that relies on reactive drivers (those from Vert.x) rather than JDBC, and whose methods return [CompletionStage] or objects from the Mutiny library. Virtual threads eliminate this complexity in most cases: that is the approach taken in this course.

docs.title: 11.11.1. Transactions
docs.text:
Chapter 10 introduced transactions: a set of operations that either all succeed or all fail. With Hibernate:

  • every write occurs within a transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] or [rollback]. The methods [inTransaction] and [fromTransaction] of [SessionFactory] handle this for us: they commit the transaction if the lambda completes normally, and roll it back if it throws an exception, which is then rethrown;
  • all commands sent during the transaction (immediate commands via [INSERT], explicit synchronizations via [flush], and synchronization via [commit]) are either committed or rolled back together;
  • an error from DBMS is propagated as a Hibernate exception, derived from [JDBCException], which encapsulates the driver’s [SQLException]: [ConstraintViolationException] for a constraint violation (primary key, uniqueness, foreign key, [NOT NULL]), [SQLGrammarException] for an error in the order SQL, etc.

The [transactions] module illustrates the two ways to handle a transaction:

package transactions;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.createSessionFactory()) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
            BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory);

            // 1 - inTransaction: commit if everything succeeds, rollback in case of exception
            IO.println("--- two additions, the second of which violates the uniqueness of the name");
            try {
                sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                    session.persist(new Article("racket", BigDecimal.valueOf(80), 5, 2));
                    session.persist(new Article("bike", BigDecimal.valueOf(450), 3, 1));
                });
            } catch (ConstraintViolationException e) {
                IO.println("%s : constraint [%s] violated"
                        .formatted(e.getClass().getSimpleName(), e.getConstraintName()));
            }
            display(sessionFactory, "racket");

            // 2 - a transaction managed by the code: several writes, committed or rolled back together
            IO.println("--- transaction rolled back");
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                try {
                    // sale of two bikes: the UPDATE is sent by flush
                    Article bike = session
                            .createSelectionQuery("from Article where name = 'bike'", Article.class)
                            .getSingleResult();
                    bike.setCurrentStock(bike.getCurrentStock() - 2);
                    session.flush();
                    // adding an article whose name already exists: error
                    session.persist(new Article("pump", BigDecimal.valueOf(12), 5, 1));
                    // commit of the whole (it is not reached here)
                    transaction.commit();
                } catch (ConstraintViolationException e) {
                    IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getSQLException().getMessage());
                    // rollback of all the operations of the transaction
                    transaction.rollback();
                }
            }
            // the sale of the bikes has been rolled back
            display(sessionFactory, "bike");
        }
    }

    // display of an article read from the database, with a new session
    private static void display(SessionFactory sessionFactory, String name) {
        Article article = sessionFactory.fromSession(session -> session
                .createSelectionQuery("from Article where name = :name", Article.class)
                .setParameter("name", name)
                .getSingleResultOrNull());
        IO.println("article [%s] in the database: %s".formatted(name, article == null ? "missing" : article));
    }
}

Comments:

  • Lines 21–24: Two items are added to a transaction managed by [inTransaction]; the second item has the same name as an existing item. Both [INSERT] processes are executed immediately (lines 4–15); the second violates the uniqueness constraint on the [name] column: MySQL rejects it (line 16), [persist] launches a [ConstraintViolationException]; [inTransaction] rolls back the transaction (line 17) and rethrows the exception;
  • lines 25–28: the exception is caught; [getConstraintName] provides the name of the violated constraint (line 18). This demonstrates the value of having named the constraint;
  • line 29: the racket, which had been successfully inserted, is not in the database (line 23): rolling back the transaction deleted it;
  • lines 33–51: a transaction managed by the code. Two bicycles are sold, and the update is sent to DBMS via an explicit [flush] (lines 29–36); then an item with an existing name is added: the insertion fails (line 43);
  • line 45: validation is never reached;
  • Lines 46–50: In [catch], the transaction is rolled back (line 45 of the results). [getSQLException] reports the original exception from the JDBC driver, and its message is that of MySQL (line 44);
  • line 53: the sale of bicycles, although sent to DBMS by [flush], was canceled: the bicycle inventory is still 10 (line 50);
  • Lines 58–64: A method that re-reads a record with a new session to view the actual state of the database rather than the entities from the current session.

After an exception, a session should no longer be used: its persistence context may contain entities in a state that is inconsistent with the database. We roll back the transaction, close the session, and start over as needed with a new session. This is what [inTransaction] does, and what our code does when exiting the [try] block, which closes the session.

The transaction isolation level is that of the JDBC connection: [REPEATABLE_READ], the default value for MySQL, as shown in the first example. You can change this for the entire [SessionFactory] using the [jdbcTransactionIsolation] method in the configuration.

docs.title: 11.11.2. Optimistic Concurrency
docs.text:
Two users are reading the same item, which has a stock of 10. The first user sells one item and updates the stock to 9. The second user, who read the stock value before this update, sells three items and updates the stock to 7: the first user’s sale is lost. This is the problem of lost updates.

One solution would be to lock the row for the entire duration of each user’s operation (“pessimistic” concurrency): this blocks other users, sometimes for a long time. With Hibernate, optimistic concurrency is generally preferred: nothing is locked, but a check is performed at the time of saving to ensure that the row has not been modified since it was read. The standard way to do this is to add a version number to the entity—a field annotated as [@Version]. Hibernate increments this number each time the row is modified, and adds the condition “the version still has the value read” to the [WHERE] clause, along with the commands [UPDATE] and [DELETE]. If the command does not modify any rows, it means another user has already accessed the data: Hibernate executes a [OptimisticLockException].

The [concurrency] module uses its own database, [hbconcurrency], and its own entity, [Article], stripped down to the essentials:

// an article whose modifications are controlled by a version number
@Entity
@Table(name = "articles")
public class Article {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    private String name;

    private int currentStock;

    // the version number: incremented by Hibernate on each modification of the row
    @Version
    private int version;

    protected Article() {
    }

    public Article(String name, int currentStock) {
        this.name = name;
        this.currentStock = currentStock;
    }

    public int getCurrentStock() {
        return currentStock;
    }

    public void setCurrentStock(int currentStock) {
        this.currentStock = currentStock;
    }

    public int getVersion() {
        return version;
    }
}
  • lines 16–17: the version number, of the form [int] (you can also use [long], or a date in the form [Instant]). The application never modifies this itself.

The program simulates the two users with two sessions:

package concurrency;

import jakarta.persistence.OptimisticLockException;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import tools.SqlLog;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("concurrency")
                .managedClass(Article.class)
                .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbconcurrency?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with a single article, without a log
            SqlLog.withoutLog(() -> {
                sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
                sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);
                sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> session.persist(new Article("bike", 10)));
            });

            // two users, two sessions: each one reads the same article
            try (Session session1 = sessionFactory.openSession();
                 Session session2 = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                IO.println("--- the two users read the bike");
                Article bike1 = session1.find(Article.class, 1);
                Article bike2 = session2.find(Article.class, 1);

                // user 1 sells 1 bike
                IO.println("--- user 1 sells 1 bike");
                Transaction transaction1 = session1.beginTransaction();
                bike1.setCurrentStock(bike1.getCurrentStock() - 1);
                transaction1.commit();
                IO.println("stock saved by user 1: %d (version %d)"
                        .formatted(bike1.getCurrentStock(), bike1.getVersion()));

                // user 2 sells 3 bikes based on outdated data (stock = 10, version 0)
                IO.println("--- user 2 sells 3 bikes");
                Transaction transaction2 = session2.beginTransaction();
                bike2.setCurrentStock(bike2.getCurrentStock() - 3);
                try {
                    session2.flush();
                    transaction2.commit();
                } catch (OptimisticLockException e) {
                    IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
                    transaction2.rollback();
                }
            }

            // resolution: user 2 rereads the article, with a new session, and starts again
            IO.println("--- user 2 rereads the bike and starts again");
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                Article bike = session.find(Article.class, 1);
                IO.println("reread stock: %d (version %d)"
                        .formatted(bike.getCurrentStock(), bike.getVersion()));
                bike.setCurrentStock(bike.getCurrentStock() - 3);
                session.flush();
                IO.println("stock saved by user 2: %d (version %d)"
                        .formatted(bike.getCurrentStock(), bike.getVersion()));
            });
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 21–25: The table is recreated with a single item, the bicycle, version 0;
  • lines 31–32: Each user reads the bicycle in their own session. The [version] column is read along with the others (lines 3–10);
  • Lines 36–38: The order [UPDATE] from the first user (lines 13–20) writes the new version (1) and contains the condition [version=?] with the read version (0). The row is modified; the entity’s [version] field is set to 1 (line 22);
  • lines 44–48: the second user’s request contains the same condition, with the version they read, 0, whereas the version of the row in the database is now 1. No rows are modified, and Hibernate triggers a [OptimisticLockException] (line 33). We explicitly synchronize the session ([flush]) before the [commit] to obtain this exception as-is; if it were thrown during the [commit], it would be encapsulated within a [RollbackException];
  • Lines 57–65: The resolution depends on the application: abort, notify the user, or, as here, re-read the item using a new session (the session that received the exception must no longer be used), and repeat the operation. The restocked inventory is 9 in version 1 (line 41), and the sale of the three bicycles results in an inventory of 6 in version 2 (line 50).

Two variations:

  • Without a version column, Hibernate can check the old values of the columns themselves: with the annotations [@OptimisticLocking(type = OptimisticLockType.DIRTY)] and [@DynamicUpdate] on the entity, the [WHERE] clause of the [UPDATE] contains the value read from each modified column ([where id=? and currentStock=?]). This is useful for an existing database that cannot be modified;
  • Pessimistic concurrency remains possible when conflicts are frequent: [session.find(Article.class, 1, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)] reads the row with a [select ... for update] order, which locks it until the end of the transaction.

docs.title: 11.12. The native SQL
docs.text:
Hibernate generates the SQL from HQL or the API Criteria, but it is still possible to write the SQL for a query yourself, to use a feature specific to the DBMS or to optimize a complex query: this is referred to as a native query. The [rawsql] module lists the available methods:

package rawsql;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.createSessionFactory()) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
            BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                // 1 - a hand-written SQL query that returns entities
                IO.println("--- createNativeQuery: entities");
                BigDecimal minPrice = BigDecimal.valueOf(200);
                List<Article> expensive = session
                        .createNativeQuery("""
                                select * from articles
                                where price > :minPrice order by name""", Article.class)
                        .setParameter("minPrice", minPrice)
                        .getResultList();
                expensive.forEach(IO::println);

                // 2 - a value passed as a parameter: no SQL injection possible
                IO.println("--- SQL injection attempt with a parameter");
                String name = "x' or '1'='1";
                long nb = session
                        .createNativeQuery("select count(*) from articles where name = :name", Long.class)
                        .setParameter("name", name)
                        .getSingleResult();
                IO.println(nb + " article(s) found");
                // the same query built by concatenation: never do this
                IO.println("--- the same attempt with a concatenation");
                String sql = "select count(*) from articles where name = '" + name + "'";
                nb = session.createNativeQuery(sql, Long.class).getSingleResult();
                IO.println(nb + " article(s) found");

                // 3 - results that are not entities
                IO.println("--- createNativeQuery: values");
                List<String> names = session
                        .createNativeQuery("""
                                select name from articles
                                where currentStock < minimumStock""", String.class)
                        .getResultList();
                IO.println("out of stock: " + String.join(", ", names));
                BigDecimal value = session
                        .createNativeQuery("select sum(price * currentStock) from articles", BigDecimal.class)
                        .getSingleResult();
                IO.println("stock value: %.2f euros".formatted(value));

                // 4 - an update statement
                IO.println("--- createNativeMutationQuery");
                int nbRows = session.fromTransaction(transaction -> session
                        .createNativeMutationQuery("""
                                update articles set price = price * :coefficient
                                where name = :name""")
                        .setParameter("coefficient", new BigDecimal("0.9"))
                        .setParameter("name", "bow")
                        .executeUpdate());
                IO.println(nbRows + " row(s) modified");

                // 5 - the JDBC connection of the session, for ordinary JDBC code
                IO.println("--- doWork: the JDBC connection");
                session.doWork(connection -> {
                    String query = "select name, price from articles where name = 'bow'";
                    try (Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
                         ResultSet rows = statement.executeQuery(query)) {
                        while (rows.next()) {
                            IO.println("%s : %.2f euros"
                                    .formatted(rows.getString("name"), rows.getBigDecimal("price")));
                        }
                    }
                });
            }
        }
    }
}

    SQL> where price > ?
    SQL> order by name
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 200
[1, bike, 500.00, 10, 5]
[3, bow, 600.00, 4, 1]
[5, diving suit, 300.00, 8, 2]
--- SQL injection attempt with a parameter
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles
    SQL> where name = ?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = x' or '1'='1
0 article(s) found
--- the same attempt with a concatenation
    SQL> select count(*)
    SQL> from articles
    SQL> where name = 'x' or '1'='1'
6 article(s) found
--- createNativeQuery: values
    SQL> select name
    SQL> from articles
    SQL> where currentStock < minimumStock
out of stock: arrows - set of 6
    SQL> select sum(price * currentStock)
    SQL> from articles
stock value: 12300.00 euros
--- createNativeMutationQuery
    SQL> -- start of transaction
    SQL> update articles
    SQL> set price = price * ?
    SQL> where name = ?
    SQL> -- parameter 1 = 0.9
    SQL> -- parameter 2 = bow
    SQL> -- transaction committed (COMMIT)
1 row(s) modified
--- doWork: the JDBC connection
bow : 540.00 euros

Comments:

  • Lines 22–27: [createNativeQuery] executes a query (SQL) that returns rows from an entity's table, and the second parameter ([Article.class]) instructs Hibernate to materialize them as entities managed by the session. The column names in the result must match those in the model: [select *] is appropriate here. The query is passed as-is to DBMS (lines 3–6), except that the parameter named [:minPrice] becomes a parameter JDBC ([?]);
  • lines 32–36: an attempt at a SQL injection. The value of [name] is passed as a parameter: it is compared as-is to the [name] column, and no record matches (line 16);
  • lines 40–41: the same query constructed by concatenation. The value of [name] becomes the code SQL, the condition remains true (line 20), and the query counts the six items (line 21): this is a successful SQL injection. As in Chapter 10, a native query must contain only constant text, with values passed as parameters;
  • lines 46–54: queries that return single values ([String], [BigDecimal]): the second parameter of [createNativeQuery] is then the type of the value. For multiple columns, you can specify a record (its components receive the columns in order) or use [Object[].class];
  • lines 59–65: [createNativeMutationQuery] prepares an update statement, executed by [executeUpdate], which returns the number of rows modified. It runs within a transaction: the session’s [fromTransaction] method opens it, commits it, and returns the result of the lambda;
  • lines 70–79: [doWork] provides access to the session’s JDBC connection ([java.sql.Connection]) for standard JDBC code (Chapter 10): calling a stored procedure, using a driver feature... The cost of the bow has indeed been reduced by 10% (line 40).

A native query is not portable from one DBMS to another, and Hibernate cannot verify it before executing it: it is reserved for cases where HQL is not sufficient. HQL also covers a large part of SQL (joins of all kinds, subqueries, windowing functions, [union]...), and allows you to call a function from DBMS that it does not recognize.

docs.title: 11.13. Bulk updates, read-only mode, and batches
docs.text:
Tracking changes comes at a cost: to increase the price of 100 items, you must read all 100 items, modify them one by one, and the session synchronization will send 100 [UPDATE] commands. Hibernate offers several ways to efficiently process large numbers of rows. The [bulkupdate] module introduces them:

package bulkupdate;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.createSessionFactory()) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
            BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();

                // 1 - HQL update: a single UPDATE statement, no entity loaded into memory
                IO.println("--- restocking of the out-of-stock articles");
                int nbRows = session
                        .createMutationQuery("""
                                update Article set currentStock = minimumStock * 2
                                where currentStock < minimumStock""")
                        .executeUpdate();
                IO.println(nbRows + " article(s) modified");

                IO.println("--- 10 % increase of the prices below 150 euros");
                nbRows = session
                        .createMutationQuery("update Article set price = price * 1.1 where price < 150")
                        .executeUpdate();
                IO.println(nbRows + " article(s) modified");

                // 2 - HQL delete: a single DELETE statement
                IO.println("--- deletion of the articles over 550 euros");
                nbRows = session
                        .createMutationQuery("delete from Article where price > 550")
                        .executeUpdate();
                IO.println(nbRows + " article(s) deleted");
                transaction.commit();

                // 3 - read-only: the entities read are not watched
                IO.println("--- read-only");
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                List<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by id", Article.class)
                        .setReadOnly(true)
                        .getResultList();
                articles.forEach(IO::println);
                // the modification of a read-only entity is ignored
                articles.getFirst().setPrice(BigDecimal.ZERO);
                IO.println("session modified: " + session.isDirty());
                transaction.commit();

                // 4 - an HQL update statement does not modify the entities already loaded by the session
                IO.println("--- HQL update and loaded entities");
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                Article pump = session.find(Article.class, 2);
                session.createMutationQuery("update Article set price = 9.5 where id = :id")
                        .setParameter("id", pump.getId())
                        .executeUpdate();
                IO.println("price in memory: " + pump.getPrice());
                session.refresh(pump);
                IO.println("price after refresh: " + pump.getPrice());
                transaction.commit();
            }

            // 5 - a stateless session (StatelessSession) and statements sent in batches
            IO.println("--- StatelessSession and batches of 3 statements");
            sessionFactory.inStatelessTransaction(session -> {
                session.setJdbcBatchSize(3);
                List<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by id", Article.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (Article article : articles) {
                    article.setCurrentStock(article.getCurrentStock() + 1);
                    // each modification is requested explicitly: the entities are not watched
                    session.update(article);
                }
            });
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • Lines 22–26: A [update] command written as HQL, prepared by [createMutationQuery], and executed by [executeUpdate]. It becomes a single command SQL [UPDATE] (lines 4–6), executed by DBMS on all affected lines, without any entity being loaded into memory. The new value may depend on the line itself ([minimumStock * 2]). Such a command is executed within a transaction (line 18);
  • lines 30–32: a 10% increase in low prices. The constants for the query HQL ([1.1], [150]) are written directly into the text of the command SQL (lines 10–11);
  • lines 37–39: a [delete] HQL order removes the bow, the only item priced over 550 euros (lines 14–16);
  • Lines 46–49: a read-only read ([setReadOnly(true)]). The entities being read are managed by the session, but the session does not retain their original state or monitor them: this is faster and more memory-efficient for data that is read without being modified (display, calculations). The trade-off is that any modification to such an entity is ignored (line 52): the session has nothing to synchronize (line 29), and the [commit] command sends no instructions. It is also possible to set an entire session to read-only ([session.setDefaultReadOnly(true)]);
  • lines 59–65: a pitfall. A [update] HQL command operates directly on the database: it does not modify entities already loaded by the session. The pump managed by the session retains its old price (line 37) until it is read again with [session.refresh(pump)] (lines 38–42);
  • lines 71–81: a stateless session ([StatelessSession]), opened here with a transaction via [inStatelessTransaction]. It has no persistence context: no first-level cache, no change tracking, no lazy loading, no cascades. Each operation is explicitly requested ([insert], [update], [delete], [get]) and executed as is. This is the tool for bulk processing: importing a large file, recalculating all rows in a table;
  • line 72: the SQL commands will be sent to DBMS in batches (see Chapter 10) of three: the JDBC driver transmits three commands in a single exchange with the server. The log shows the first three [UPDATE] entries, followed by the execution of the batch (line 58), and concludes with the final batch of two commands (line 63). An application sets the batch size for all its sessions using the [hibernate.jdbc.batch_size] property (typically between 10 and 50). Note that inserts into a table whose key is generated by [IDENTITY] cannot be grouped into batches.

For bulk processing with a regular session, you must prevent its persistence context from accumulating entities: synchronize and flush the session regularly, for example every fifty records ([session.flush(); session.clear();]).

docs.title: 11.14.1. The [SessionFactory] in the container
docs.text:
The previous examples created their own sessions. In a layered application (Chapter 6), and in all Spring applications, the [SessionFactory] is an object in the dependency injection container, just like the layers that use it. To achieve this, the Spring Framework provides the following in its [spring-orm] library:

  • the [LocalSessionFactoryBean] class, which constructs the [SessionFactory] from a data source ([DataSource], Chapter 10) and a list of entities;
  • the [HibernateTransactionManager] class, a transaction manager that opens a Hibernate session for each transaction, associates it with the current thread, and closes it at the end of the transaction;
  • the [@Transactional] annotation (library [spring-tx]): when applied to a method, or to a class for all its public methods, it instructs Spring to execute the method within a transaction, which is committed if the method completes normally and rolled back if it throws an uncaught exception. These are known as declarative transactions.

Inside a transactional method, [sessionFactory.getCurrentSession()] returns the current transaction session. A [dao] layer can then be a singleton that receives the [SessionFactory] (thread-safe) and requests the current session from it in each method: the rule “one session per unit of work, never shared between threads” is effortlessly enforced.

docs.title: 11.14.2. The [injection] module
docs.text:
The [injection] module depends, in addition to the [articles] module, on Spring and HikariCP:

    <dependencies>
        <!-- the [Article] entity and the [hbarticles] database (Hibernate, MySQL and the SQL log included) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.hibernate</groupId>
            <artifactId>articles</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Spring: container, declarative transactions, Hibernate integration -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-context</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-orm</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- the HikariCP connection pool -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>com.zaxxer</groupId>
            <artifactId>HikariCP</artifactId>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

The Spring configuration is written in Java, using the annotations [@Configuration] and [@Bean] from Chapter 6:

package injection;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import java.util.Properties;
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.hibernate.HibernateTransactionManager;
import org.springframework.orm.jpa.hibernate.LocalSessionFactoryBean;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.EnableTransactionManagement;

// the Spring configuration: connection pool, SessionFactory, transaction manager, [dao] layer
@Configuration
@EnableTransactionManagement
public class Config {

    // the HikariCP connection pool (chapter 10)
    @Bean(destroyMethod = "close")
    public HikariDataSource dataSource() {
        HikariDataSource dataSource = new HikariDataSource();
        dataSource.setJdbcUrl(BaseArticles.URL);
        dataSource.setUsername(BaseArticles.USER);
        dataSource.setPassword(BaseArticles.PASSWORD);
        return dataSource;
    }

    // the SessionFactory, built by Spring with the connection pool
    @Bean
    public LocalSessionFactoryBean sessionFactory(DataSource dataSource) {
        LocalSessionFactoryBean factory = new LocalSessionFactoryBean();
        factory.setDataSource(dataSource);
        factory.setAnnotatedClasses(Article.class);
        Properties properties = new Properties();
        properties.put(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, "true");
        factory.setHibernateProperties(properties);
        return factory;
    }

    // the transaction manager: one Hibernate session per transaction
    @Bean
    public HibernateTransactionManager transactionManager(SessionFactory sessionFactory) {
        return new HibernateTransactionManager(sessionFactory);
    }

    // the [dao] layer: a singleton that receives the SessionFactory
    @Bean
    public ArticlesDao articlesDao(SessionFactory sessionFactory) {
        return new ArticlesDao(sessionFactory);
    }
}
  • Line 18: [@EnableTransactionManagement] enables the [@Transactional] annotation: Spring will replace every object with a method bearing this annotation with a proxy that opens and commits the transaction around the call;
  • lines 22–29: the HikariCP connection pool from Chapter 10. The [destroyMethod] attribute specifies the method to be called when the container is closed;
  • Lines 32–41: the [SessionFactory]. A [LocalSessionFactoryBean] is a factory for [SessionFactory]: Spring registers the object it creates in the container, and requesting this bean returns a [SessionFactory]. It receives the connection pool (which replaces Hibernate’s built-in pool), the entities, and the Hibernate properties;
  • lines 44–47: the transaction manager;
  • lines 50–53: the [dao] layer, which receives the [SessionFactory].

The [dao] layer:

package injection;

import articles.Article;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

// the [dao] layer: each public method runs in a transaction opened by Spring
@Transactional
public class ArticlesDao {

    // the SessionFactory, shared by all the threads
    private final SessionFactory sessionFactory;

    public ArticlesDao(SessionFactory sessionFactory) {
        this.sessionFactory = sessionFactory;
    }

    // do two requests for the current session, in the same transaction, return the same session?
    public boolean sameSession() {
        return sessionFactory.getCurrentSession() == sessionFactory.getCurrentSession();
    }

    // the session of the transaction
    public Session session() {
        return sessionFactory.getCurrentSession();
    }

    // the articles to restock; a read-only transaction
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<String> articlesOutOfStock() {
        String hql = "select name from Article where currentStock < minimumStock";
        return sessionFactory.getCurrentSession().createSelectionQuery(hql, String.class).getResultList();
    }

    // the article with the given name
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public Article article(String name) {
        return sessionFactory.getCurrentSession()
                .createSelectionQuery("from Article where name = :name", Article.class)
                .setParameter("name", name)
                .getSingleResult();
    }

    // the sale of a quantity of an article: an exception rolls back the transaction
    public void sell(String name, int quantity) {
        Article article = article(name);
        article.setCurrentStock(article.getCurrentStock() - quantity);
        if (article.getCurrentStock() < 0) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient stock for the article [" + name + "]");
        }
    }
}
  • line 10: all public methods of the class are transactional;
  • lines 21–23: During the same transaction, do two requests from the current session return the same session?
  • lines 26–28: the transaction’s session is returned to the caller (for the following experiment—this is not done in a real application);
  • lines 31–35: a read-only transaction ([readOnly = true]): Spring sets the session to read-only and does not synchronize it;
  • Lines 47–53: The sale of a quantity of an item. If the inventory becomes negative, the method throws a [IllegalStateException], an unhandled exception: Spring rolls back the transaction. The call to the [article] method (line 48) is an internal call within the object that does not go through the proxy: it executes within the [sell] transaction.

The main program:

package injection;

import articles.BaseArticles;
import org.hibernate.HibernateException;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.AnnotationConfigApplicationContext;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // the Spring container, configured by the [Config] class
        try (var context = new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(Config.class)) {
            // the [articles] table is recreated with its six articles
            SessionFactory sessionFactory = context.getBean(SessionFactory.class);
            BaseArticles.initialize(sessionFactory);
            ArticlesDao dao = context.getBean(ArticlesDao.class);

            // 1 - during a transaction, the current session is always the same
            IO.println("--- sessions and transactions");
            IO.println("one transaction: same session = " + dao.sameSession());
            // 2 - two transactions: two sessions, closed at the end of their transaction
            Session session1 = dao.session();
            Session session2 = dao.session();
            IO.println("two transactions: same session = %s, first session open = %s"
                    .formatted(session1 == session2, session1.isOpen()));
            // 3 - outside a transaction, there is no current session
            try {
                sessionFactory.getCurrentSession();
            } catch (HibernateException e) {
                IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
            }

            // 4 - transactional methods of the [dao] layer
            IO.println("--- articles out of stock");
            IO.println("out of stock: " + dao.articlesOutOfStock());
            IO.println("--- sale of 2 bikes");
            dao.sell("bike", 2);
            IO.println("--- sale of 50 pumps");
            try {
                dao.sell("pump", 50);
            } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
                IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
            }
            IO.println("--- state of the database");
            IO.println(dao.article("bike"));
            IO.println(dao.article("pump"));
        }
    }
}
