After installation, open a new terminal to verify that the [java] and [javac] commands are available and display the version of JDK:

> java --version
openjdk 25.0.4.1 2026-08-18
OpenJDK Runtime Environment (build 25.0.4.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM (build 25.0.4.1+1-1-24.04.4-Ubuntu, mixed mode, sharing)
> javac --version
javac 25.0.4.1

These results were obtained with the JDK package from Ubuntu. With Temurin, lines 2 and 3 list [Temurin-25], and the exact version depends on the installation date: patch updates are released quarterly. All JDK and 25.0.x versions are suitable for this document. Multiple JDK files can coexist on the same system: the first one found in the [PATH] directory responds to the [java] command.

docs.title: 2.1.2. Commands for the JDK
docs.text:
The JDK provides numerous commands. Here are the ones we will use:

CommandRole[java File.java]compiles in memory and executes a program written in a source file (Java 11; multiple files starting with Java 22)[javac -d classes File.java]compiles one or more source files and places the resulting [.class] files in the [classes] folder[java -cp classes ClassName]executes the [main] method of a compiled class, searched for in the class path ([-cp])[java -cp "lib/*" File.java]executes a source file that uses the libraries ([.jar] files) in the [lib] folder[jshell]Interactive interpreter: you type Java statements and see their results immediately[jar]creates or reads a [.jar] archive (a ZIP file of compiled classes)

The [jshell] interpreter (Java 9) is useful for testing a method or expression without writing a program:

> jshell
|  Welcome to JShell -- Version 25.0.4.1
|  For an introduction type: /help intro

jshell> 1 + 2
$1 ==> 3

jshell> var s = "Java " + 25
s ==> "Java 25"

jshell> s.length()
$3 ==> 7

jshell> /exit
|  Goodbye

docs.title: 2.2.1. Installation
docs.text:
A real Java application uses libraries that are not part of JDK: a database driver, a testing framework, Hibernate, Spring… These are distributed as [.jar] archives via a public repository, Maven Central (https://central.sonatype.com). A build tool like Maven reads the [pom.xml] file of a project to determine which libraries it needs, downloads them (along with the libraries on which they depend), and then compiles, tests, and packages the project. Another widely used tool, Gradle, performs the same function; this document uses Maven.

Maven can be downloaded from https://maven.apache.org/download.cgi as a ZIP archive ([apache-maven-3.9.x-bin.zip]). Unzip it into a folder, for example [C:\Program Files\apache-maven-3.9.11], and add its subfolder [bin] to [PATH] (Windows: “Edit system environment variables”). On Linux, Maven is available in the distribution repositories ([sudo apt install maven]). Verify the installation in a new terminal:

> mvn -v
Apache Maven 3.9.11 (3e54c93a704957b63ee3494413a2b544fd3d825b)
Maven home: /opt/maven
Java version: 25.0.4.1, vendor: Ubuntu, runtime: /usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
Default locale: en_US, platform encoding: UTF-8
OS name: "linux", version: "6.18.44-fc-v64", arch: "amd64", family: "unix"

Line 4 is important: it shows the JDK used by Maven, which is referenced by the variable [JAVA_HOME]. It must be a JDK 25. The IDE, IntelliJ, IDEA, and VS Code packages include their own Maven: these are sufficient if you do not use Maven from the command line.

The libraries downloaded by Maven are stored on the local machine in the local repository [%USERPROFILE%\.m2\repository] (Linux, macOS: [~/.m2/repository]). They are downloaded only once and are then used by all projects. Therefore, an Internet connection is required when building a project for the first time.

docs.title: 2.2.2. Maven Commands
docs.text:
The command [mvn] is followed by one or more phases of the build cycle, or by a plugin target; it is entered in the folder containing the file [pom.xml]:

CommandRole[mvn compile]compiles the source code of [src/main/java]; the classes are organized in [target/classes][mvn test]compiles and then runs the unit tests for [src/test/java] (Chapter 6)[mvn package]compiles, tests, and creates the project archive [.jar] in [target][mvn install]as [package], then copies the archive to the local repository, where other projects can use it (Chapter 6)[mvn clean]deletes the folder [target][mvn compile exec:java]compiles and then runs the project’s main class ([exec-maven-plugin] plugin)[mvn spring-boot:run]runs a Spring Boot application (Chapter 13)

The phases are sequential: running [package] also triggers [compile] and [test]. The [-q] (“quiet”) option suppresses Maven messages and displays only those from the executed program; the [-Dexec.args="a b"] option passes arguments to the program launched by [exec:java].

docs.title: 2.3.1. IntelliJ IDEA
docs.text:
IntelliJ IDEA, from the company JetBrains, is the most widely used Java editor. Its basic features, which are more than sufficient for this document, are free. It supports Maven projects: select “File / Open,” then choose the folder containing the [pom.xml] file; IntelliJ downloads the libraries, compiles the project, and allows you to run a class by clicking the green triangle in the margin next to its method [main] ([Ctrl-Shift-F10]), or run a test by clicking the same triangle next to the test method. Specify the JDK to use in “File / Project Structure / SDK.”

You can open the entire [java-oct-2026] examples folder at once (“File / Open”): IntelliJ detects all the Maven projects there and displays them in its “Maven” panel. One precaution is necessary at this point. The projects in Chapters 10 through 13 (versions 6 through 9 of the [Tax] application) use the modules [tax-dao], [tax-business], and [tax-ui] from version 5, which was written in Chapter 6. These are not public libraries: Maven can only find them in the local repository if they have been installed there. You must therefore start by installing version 5: in the “Maven” panel, expand [tax-v5] / "Lifecycle" and double-click on [install] (or type [mvn install] in the [06-architectures/TaxV5] folder), then click the "Sync All Maven Projects" button in the panel. Chapter 6 explains what this command does and what to do if IntelliJ still reports unresolved dependencies.

docs.title: 2.3.2. VS Code
docs.text:
VS Code is a free, cross-platform editor. To program in Java, you can install Microsoft’s Extension Pack for Java (go to the “Extensions” menu and search for “Extension Pack for Java”), which includes language support, a debugger, test execution, and Maven support. This provides:

  • syntax highlighting, code completion, and tooltip help;
  • error detection as you type;
  • code navigation (F12: go to definition);
  • execution and debugging (the “Run” and “Debug” links above each method [main] or F5);
  • running unit tests (the “Testing” view) and a “Maven” view of projects.

In VS Code, open the folder containing the programs (“File / Open Folder”), for example, the [java-oct-2026] folder with the examples from this document. The built-in terminal (“Terminal / New Terminal”) allows you to enter the commands [java] and [mvn] without leaving the editor.

docs.title: 2.3.3. Eclipse
docs.text:
A third option is the open-source Eclipse IDE (https://eclipseide.org), historically the first major Java IDE, which also imports Maven projects (“File / Import / Maven / Existing Maven Projects”).

In the rest of this document, operations are described using the commands [java], [javac], and [mvn], which produce the same results regardless of the editor.

docs.title: 2.4. A First Program: A Compact Source File
2.4.1. The program
docs.text:
Starting with Java 25, a Java program can be a simple file containing a single method [main], without a class declaration. This is called a “compact source file.” Let’s create the following file [Hello.java]:

// first Java program: a compact source file
void main() {
    IO.println("1st try with Java 25");
}

and run it:

> java Hello.java
1st try with Java 25

Comments:

  • line 1: a comment. Everything following [//] until the end of the line is ignored by the compiler;
  • line 2: the method [main], the program’s entry point. In a compact source file, it does not need to be declared in a class, nor does it need to be [public] and [static], nor does it need to receive the program’s arguments; we’ll see in Chapter 3 that the compiler wraps it in a class itself;
  • Line 3: the program’s only statement: it prints a line of text to the screen. The class [IO] (Java 25) provides simple methods for writing ([print], [println]) and reading ([readln]) from the keyboard;
  • the command [java Hello.java] compiles the program in memory—without creating a [.class] file—and then executes it. This ability to run a source file directly was introduced in Java 11.

The file name must be a valid Java identifier: [Hello.java] or [Basics01.java] are acceptable, but [basics-01.java] is rejected by the compiler ([bad file name]) because the file name becomes the name of the generated class. By convention, class names—and therefore file names—begin with a capital letter.

You can also compile the program with [javac], which produces a file named [.class], and then run this compiled file:

> javac -d classes Hello.java
> dir classes (list of files)
Hello.class
> java -cp classes Hello
1st try with Java 25

The file [Hello.class] contains the bytecode for the [Hello] class generated by the compiler. The command [java -cp classes Hello] instructs the virtual machine to execute the method [main] of the class [Hello], which is located in the [classes] folder.

Compact source files are suitable for small programs, and we will use them for most of the examples. When a program requires an external library, it can still be launched using the [java -cp "lib/*" Program.java] command if you have copied the [.jar] archives of the library (and those it depends on) into a [lib] folder. But gathering these archives by hand quickly becomes tedious, so we’ll write a Maven project.

On Windows, accented characters written by [IO.println] or [System.out.println] display correctly in the terminal: Java converts the text to the terminal’s encoding. The source files must be saved in UTF-8, the default encoding for VS Code and IntelliJ IDEA, and the one the compiler assumes starting with Java 18.

docs.title: 2.5.1. Project Structure
docs.text:
A Maven project is a folder containing a [pom.xml] file (“Project Object Model”) and source files organized according to a standard directory structure. The [FirstProgram] project in the [02-installation] folder is as follows:

FirstProgram/
├── pom.xml
└── src/
    └── main/
        └── java/
            └── first/
                └── Main.java
  • [src/main/java] contains the program's source files; [src/main/resources] contains the data or configuration files to be placed alongside the compiled classes; [src/test/java] contains the tests (Chapter 6);
  • Under [src/main/java], the folder structure mirrors that of the packages (Chapter 4): the class [first.Main] is located in the folder [first].

You can create this directory structure manually, or let IDE create it (IntelliJ: “File / New / Project,” select “Maven” as the build system). The [pom.xml] file is as follows:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <!-- the project coordinates -->
    <groupId>examples.installation</groupId>
    <artifactId>first-program</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>

    <properties>
        <!-- target Java version and source file encoding -->
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <!-- the compiler, with all warnings -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.15.0</version>
                <configuration>
                    <compilerArgs>
                        <arg>-Xlint:all</arg>
                    </compilerArgs>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
            <!-- mvn exec:java runs the main class -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.5.1</version>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>first.Main</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
  • Lines 8–10: the project’s coordinates, which uniquely identify it: the group ([groupId], often a reverse domain name such as [org.hibernate]), the project name ([artifactId]), and its version. These are also the identifiers that another project will use to reference this one if needed, similar to how a library from Maven Central is referenced (Chapter 6);
  • line 14: the code is compiled for Java 25;
  • line 15: the source files are written in UTF-8;
  • lines 21–30: the compilation plugin, with the option [-Xlint:all], which enables all compiler warnings;
  • lines 32–39: the [exec-maven-plugin] plugin, which allows the project’s main class—specified on line 37—to be executed using the [mvn exec:java] command.

This project does not use any libraries. A project that uses a library declares it in a [<dependencies>] section using its coordinates, as we will do starting in Chapter 5:

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>tools.jackson.core</groupId>
        <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
        <version>3.1.5</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

The file [Main.java] contains the program in its standard form, with a class [public] and a method [public static void main(String[] args)]:

package first;

// the main program of the [FirstProgram] project
public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("1st try with a Maven project / Java 25");
    }
}
  • line 1: the class belongs to the package [first]; its full name is [first.Main];
  • lines 4–9: the class [Main]. A source file contains at most one public class, which bears the name of the file;
  • lines 6–8: the method [main], in the form it has had since the first version of Java. We will compare the two forms in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 2.5.2. Compilation and Execution
docs.text:
The command [mvn compile], entered in the project folder, compiles the project: Maven downloads any required plugins as needed, then compiles the [src/main/java] files and places the resulting classes in the [target/classes] folder, preserving the package hierarchy ([target/classes/first/Main.class]). The [mvn compile exec:java] command compiles the project and then runs it; with the [-q] option, only the program’s output is displayed:

> mvn -q compile exec:java
1st try with a Maven project / Java 25

Once the project is compiled, you can also run the class directly using the command [java], specifying the location of the classes:

> java -cp target/classes first.Main
1st try with a Maven project / Java 25

The [target] folder can be safely deleted ([mvn clean]): it will be recreated during the next compilation. The command [mvn package] also produces the archive [target/first-program-1.0.jar], which can be executed using [java -cp target/first-program-1.0.jar first.Main]: this is the format in which a Java program is delivered.

docs.title: 2.6.1. The aggregator project
docs.text:
A Maven project can group together several other projects, called its modules. The [02-installation] folder contains a file named [pom.xml] that groups together its two projects:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- an "aggregator" project: it groups the projects of the folder to build them together -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>examples.installation</groupId>
    <artifactId>installation</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>
    <packaging>pom</packaging>

    <modules>
        <module>FirstProgram</module>
        <module>TwoHands</module>
    </modules>
</project>
  • Line 11: This project does not produce an archive [.jar]: It serves only to group other projects ([pom]);
  • Lines 13–16: the modules, identified by their folder names.

In the [02-installation] folder, the [mvn compile] command compiles both projects; a IDE command that opens this folder sees both projects at once. In Chapter 6, we’ll see that a parent project can also pass a common configuration (library versions, compiler options) to its modules.

docs.title: 2.6.2. A project with multiple main methods
docs.text:
A project can contain multiple classes, each with a [main] method: each is a possible entry point, and the class to be executed is chosen at runtime. The project [TwoHands] contains two classes. The [P1] class:

package twohands;

public class P1 {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("main of the class P1");
    }
}

and the class [P2], which is identical except for its name. The command [java] executes the class specified:

> java -cp target/classes twohands.P1
main of the class P1
> java -cp target/classes twohands.P2
main of the class P2

For the command [mvn exec:java], the project file [pom.xml] specifies the class to be executed:

            <!-- the class whose main method is run by mvn exec:java -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.5.1</version>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>twohands.P2</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
  • Line 7: The method [main] that is executed belongs to the class [twohands.P2] (the full class name, including the package).

Results:

> mvn -q compile exec:java
main of the class P2

You can choose a different class without modifying the [pom.xml] file: [mvn -q exec:java -Dexec.mainClass=twohands.P1].

docs.title: 2.7. Examples in the document
docs.text:
To run the examples in this document:

  • download the [java-oct-2026] folder (link at the beginning of the document);
  • open it in VS Code (“File / Open Folder”), or, for a given Maven project, open its folder in IntelliJ IDEA;
  • in a terminal located in a chapter’s folder, run a compact source file using [java Name.java], or a Maven project using [mvn -q compile exec:java] in the project folder (the text of each chapter provides the exact command).

Chapters 10 and 11 use a database named MySQL; the installation of MySQL along with [Laragon] is described in the appendix.

docs.title: 3. The Basics of the Java Language
3.1. Introduction
docs.text:
We’ll start by treating Java as a traditional programming language. We’ll cover classes in the next chapter. A program consists of two things:

  • data;
  • the instructions that manipulate them.

We generally strive to separate data from instructions:

All the examples in this chapter are compact source files: a single file named [.java], without a Maven project, which is run using the command [java Basics01.java]. The [java] launcher then compiles the file in memory and executes it, without producing a [.class] file. This capability was introduced in Chapter 2, “Setting Up the Development Environment.” The examples are located in the [03-basics] folder of the course code. They run using the French language and conventions (the “locale” fr-FR), just as they would on a French Windows machine. We will see that this only affects numbers and dates formatted with a specific format: the simple conversion of a floating-point number to a string always uses the decimal point.

docs.title: 3.2.1. The compact source file
docs.text:
The program [Basics01.java] is as follows:

// minimal program written as a compact source file (Java 25)
// no class declaration, no public and static keywords: just a main method
void main() {
    IO.println("Hello world!");
    // the historical form: the out field of the System class, then its println method
    System.out.println("Hello world!");
    // List (java.util package) can be used without import in a compact file
    List<String> words = List.of("Hello", "the", "world");
    IO.println(words);
}

Results:

> java Basics01.java
Hello world!
Hello world!
[Hello, the, world]

Comments:

  • The file contains no class declarations—only a method named [main]. This is a compact source file (Java 25). The compiler itself wraps the file’s contents in an implicitly declared class that bears the file’s name: [Basics01]. This feature was introduced as a preview in Java 21 through Java 24 before becoming final in Java 25;
  • Line 3: The method [main] is the program's entry point: it is this method that the launcher [java] executes. Starting with Java 25, it can be written simply as [void main()], without the keywords [public] and [static] and without any parameters. The body of the method is enclosed in curly braces;
  • line 4: the method [println] of the class [IO] (Java 25) writes a line to the screen;
  • Line 6: The legacy form of the same operation. [System] is a class, [out] is one of its fields, which represents standard output (the screen), and [println] is a method of this object. [IO.println(x)] is simply a shortcut for [System.out.println(x)]. We will use [IO.println] in compact files and [System.out.println] in regular classes, where it appears throughout the existing Java code;
  • line 8: [List] is a list of character strings; Lists will be covered in Chapter 5. [List] belongs to the [java.util] package: a package groups related classes, just as a folder groups files. The full name of the class is [java.util.List]. It can be used without an import statement because the file is a compact file (see below);
  • line 9: a list is displayed with its elements enclosed in square brackets;
  • each statement ends with a semicolon; lines beginning with // are comments, which are ignored by the compiler.

With two command-line arguments (placed after the file name):

> java Basics01.java a0 a1
Hello world!
Hello world!
[Hello, the, world]

The arguments are ignored because the method [void main()] has no parameters to receive them. To use them, declare it as [void main(String[] args)]: the string array [args] then contains the command-line arguments. We’ll come back to this in the “Main Program Arguments” section.

docs.title: 3.2.2. The classic form with a class and a main method
docs.text:
Up to Java 24, the same program had to be written as follows: [Basics02.java]:

// the classic form of the program (the only standard form up to Java 24)
import java.util.Arrays;

public class Basics02 {
    // the main method is the entry point of the program
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello world!");
        System.out.println("Number of arguments received: " + args.length);
        // Arrays (java.util package) must be imported in an ordinary class
        System.out.println("Arguments: " + Arrays.toString(args));
    }
}

Results:

> java Basics02.java a0 a1
Hello world!
Number of arguments received: 2
Arguments: [a0, a1]

Comments:

  • Line 2: The directive [import] imports the class [Arrays] from the package [java.util]. You can then write [Arrays] instead of [java.util.Arrays]. In a regular class, only the classes from the [java.lang] package ([System], [String], [Math], [Integer], [IO]...) can be used without importing;
  • line 4: In Java, all code belongs to a class. The class here is named [Basics02]. A class declared as [public] must be located in a file bearing that name: [Basics02.java];
  • line 6: the method [main] is the program’s entry point. It is [public] (accessible from outside the class, in particular via the launcher [java]), [static] (it executes without requiring the creation of an object of the class), returns no result ([void]), and receives command-line arguments in the array [args];
  • line 8: the number of elements in the array [args] is [args.length]. The + operator concatenates a string and a number here: the number is first converted to a string;
  • Line 10: The [Arrays.toString] method constructs a string from the elements of an array.

A file containing a regular class can also be executed directly by the launcher ([java Basics02.java]). You can also compile it first using the [javac] compiler, which produces a [Basics02.class] file containing the class’s intermediate code (“bytecode”), and then execute that class using the command [java] followed by the class name (without the extension). This is what Maven and development environments do behind the scenes:

> javac Basics02.java
> ls
Basics02.class  Basics02.java
> java Basics02 a0 a1
Hello world!
Number of arguments received: 2
Arguments: [a0, a1]

The two programs [Basics01.java] and [Basics02.java] are similar in nature. When it encounters a compact file, the compiler itself generates a [final] class bearing the file’s name, whose methods and fields are those written in the file. The compact file is therefore simply a shorthand version of the standard form. It is well-suited for the small programs in this chapter; the standard form becomes necessary as soon as a program contains multiple classes, which will be the case starting in Chapter 4.

Since Java 25, the [main] method can take four forms: [static void main(String[] args)], [static void main()], [void main(String[] args)], and [void main()]; if a class contains several of them, the launcher prefers the one with the parameter [String[]]. The last two forms are instance methods: the launcher first creates an object of the class, then calls its [main] method. The keyword [public] is no longer required.

docs.title: 3.2.3. Automatic import of the java.base module
docs.text:
The program [Basics01.java] uses the class [List] without the [import java.util.List;] directive. This is possible because the compiler automatically adds the following directive to every compact file (Java 25):

import module java.base;

The classes in the Java standard library are organized into packages, which are in turn grouped into modules. The [java.base] module is the core module: it contains the most commonly used packages. The directive [import module java.base;] imports all public classes from all packages exported by this module at once, which is equivalent, among other things, to the following directives:

import java.io.*;
import java.math.*;
import java.net.*;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.text.*;
import java.time.*;
import java.time.format.*;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.function.*;
import java.util.regex.*;
import java.util.stream.*;
...

In a compact file, you therefore have access—without having to write a single line of code—to lists and dictionaries ([java.util]), files ([java.io], [java.nio.file]), large numbers ([java.math]), dates ([java.time]), etc. A class from another module—such as the JDBC classes from the [java.sql] module—must always be explicitly imported. In a regular class, nothing is automatically imported from outside the [java.lang] package: you write one directive per class ([import java.util.Arrays;]), one directive per package ([import java.util.*;]), or, since Java 25, one directive per module ([import module java.base;]). The class [IO] is part of the package [java.lang]: it can be used anywhere.

docs.title: 3.3. Java Data
docs.text:
Java uses the following data types:

  • integers;
  • real numbers;
  • decimal numbers;
  • characters and character strings;
  • Booleans;
  • objects.

docs.title: 3.3.1. Predefined data types
3.3.2. Notation for Literal Data
3.3.3.1. Role of Declarations
docs.text: A program manipulates data characterized by a name and a type. This data is stored in memory. When the program is compiled, the compiler assigns each piece of data a memory location characterized by an address and a size. It does this based on the declarations made by the programmer. Furthermore, these declarations allow the compiler to detect programming errors. Thus, the operation [x = x * 2;] will be flagged as an error if [x] is a string.

docs.title: 3.3.3.2. Declaring Constants
docs.text:
In Java, a constant is a variable declared with the keyword [final]: it can be assigned a value only once. The syntax is as follows:

final type name = value;

A constant used throughout the program is declared outside of methods, as a class field [static final]. For example:

static final double VAT_RATE = 0.2;

Why declare constants?

  • The program is easier to read if the constant is given a meaningful name;
  • it is easier to modify the program if the “constant” needs to be changed. Thus, if the VAT rate changes to 0.25, the only modification needed will be to the statement that defines its value: [static final double VAT_RATE = 0.25;]. If 0.2 had been used explicitly in the program, numerous statements would need to be modified.

By convention, in Java, the name of a constant [static final] is written in uppercase letters, with words separated by the _ character: [VAT_RATE], [MAX_VALUE]. A local variable can also be declared as [final]; in this case, it retains a regular name. The word [const] is reserved in Java, but it is not used.

docs.title: 3.3.3.3. Variable Declaration
docs.text:
A variable is identified by a name and is associated with a data type. Java distinguishes between uppercase and lowercase letters: the variables [END] and [end] are different. By convention, a variable name begins with a lowercase letter, and each subsequent word begins with an uppercase letter: [priceExclTax], [nbChildren].

Variables can be initialized when they are declared. The syntax for declaring one or more variables is:

type variable1 = value1, variable2 = value2, ...;

where [type] is a predefined type or a type defined by the programmer. Initialization is optional; however, Java does not allow the use of a local variable that has not yet been assigned a value (error message [variable x might not have been initialized]).

Since Java 10, you can also omit the type of a local variable by using the keyword [var] instead of the type:

var variable1 = value1;

The term [var] does not mean that the variable has no specific type: it has the type of the value assigned to it, as determined by the compiler. Initialization is required here so that the compiler can infer the type. [var] can only be used for local variables (not for fields or method parameters). It is used when the type is obvious from the value, particularly when the variable name is long.

The program [Basics05.java] is as follows:

// constants and variables
// a class constant: static final, name in uppercase
static final double VAT_RATE = 0.2;

void main() {
    // a local constant: final
    final String currency = "euros";
    double priceExclTax = 100;
    IO.println("Price incl. tax: " + priceExclTax * (1 + VAT_RATE) + " " + currency);

    // an explicitly typed piece of data
    int i = 2;
    IO.println("Type of int i=2: " + typeName(i));
    // implicitly typed data with var (Java 10)
    var j = 3;
    IO.println("Type of var j=3: " + typeName(j));
    var today = LocalDateTime.now();
    IO.println("Type of var today: " + typeName(today));
    var x = 3.5;
    var y = 3.5F;
    var z = 10L;
    var name = "dupont";
    IO.println("x : " + typeName(x) + ", y : " + typeName(y));
    IO.println("z : " + typeName(z) + ", name : " + typeName(name));
    // several variables declared on the same line
    int a = 1, b, c = 3;
    b = a + c;
    IO.println("a=" + a + ", b=" + b + ", c=" + c);
}

// returns the short name and the full name of the class of the received object
String typeName(Object o) {
    return o.getClass().getSimpleName() + "," + o.getClass().getName();
}

Results:

> java Basics05.java
Price incl. tax: 120.0 euros
Type of int i=2: Integer,java.lang.Integer
Type of var j=3: Integer,java.lang.Integer
Type of var today: LocalDateTime,java.time.LocalDateTime
x : Double,java.lang.Double, y : Float,java.lang.Float
z : Long,java.lang.Long, name : String,java.lang.String
a=1, b=4, c=3

Comments:

  • line 3: a class constant. In a compact file, a variable declared outside of methods is a field of the implicit class;
  • line 7: a local constant;
  • line 9: the result is a [double], displayed with at least one decimal place: 120.0;
  • line 12: an explicitly typed value;
  • line 13: [getSimpleName()] (line 33) is the short name of the class; [getName()] is its full name. As in the previous program, [int] is wrapped in a [Integer] to be passed to [typeName];
  • Line 15: an implicitly typed value. Because 3 is of type [int], [j] will be of type [int]. The display shows [Integer] for the same reason as in line 13;
  • line 17: because [LocalDateTime.now()] (the current date and time) is of type [LocalDateTime], [today] will be of type [LocalDateTime];
  • lines 19–22: the inferred type depends on how the literal is written: 3.5 is a [double], 3.5F is a [float], and 10L is a [long];
  • Line 26: three variables declared on the same line; only [a] and [c] are initialized. [b] is assigned a value on the next line.

A variable implicitly typed as [var] cannot change its type afterward. Thus, after line 17, the statement [today = "today";] is rejected by the compiler:

error: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to LocalDateTime

docs.title: 3.3.4. Missing Values: null, wrapper classes, and Optional
docs.text:
A variable of a primitive type, such as [int], always contains a value. It is sometimes useful to be able to express the absence of a value: an unknown age, an empty field in a database. In such cases, we use the wrapper class: a variable of type [Integer] is a reference, which can be [null]—that is, “no object.”

Any variable of a reference type can, in fact, have the value [null]: in that case, it does not reference any object. Attempting to use a member of such a variable—for example, its method [length()]—causes a runtime error, a [NullPointerException]: this is the most common error in Java. Since Java 15, the error message specifies exactly which expression evaluated to [null]. The Java compiler does not distinguish between a reference that can evaluate to [null] and one that cannot; annotations such as those in the JSpecify project ([@Nullable], [@NonNull]), which are used by analysis tools, help address this shortcoming, but we will not be using them.

To indicate that a method may return nothing, Java 8 added the [Optional<T>] class: a [Optional<String>] object is a "box" that contains a string or is empty. It is created using [Optional.of(value)], [Optional.empty()], or [Optional.ofNullable(valueOrNull)]; it is queried using [isPresent()], [isEmpty()] (Java 11), [get()], [orElse(defaultValue)]... The classes [OptionalInt], [OptionalLong], and [OptionalDouble] serve the same purpose for primitive types.

We’ll encounter the value [null] right from the first examples, because the method [IO.readln()], which reads a line typed on the keyboard, returns [null] when there is nothing left to read (end of the input stream). The program [Basics06.java] is as follows:

// missing values: null, wrapper classes and Optional
void main() {
    // an int always holds a value; an Integer can be null
    Integer age = null;
    IO.println("age is null: " + (age == null));
    // automatic boxing (autoboxing): the int 23 becomes an Integer
    age = 23;
    IO.println("age=" + age);
    // automatic unboxing: the Integer becomes an int
    int n = age;
    IO.println("n=" + n);
    // unboxing an Integer that is null throws a NullPointerException
    Integer unknown = null;
    try {
        int m = unknown;
        IO.println("m=" + m);
    } catch (NullPointerException e) {
        IO.println("Unboxing null: " + e.getClass().getName());
    }

    // an object reference can be null: it then designates no object
    String firstName = null;
    IO.println("firstName is null: " + (firstName == null));
    // Optional (Java 8): a box that contains a value or is empty
    Optional<String> name = Optional.of("dupont");
    Optional<String> nickname = Optional.empty();
    IO.println("name present: " + name.isPresent() + ", name has " + name.get().length() + " characters");
    IO.println("nickname present: " + nickname.isPresent() + ", nickname: " + nickname.orElse("none"));

    // IO.readln (Java 25) returns null if the input stream is exhausted
    String line = IO.readln("Type a line: ");
    if (line == null) {
        IO.println();
        IO.println("No line: the input stream is closed");
    } else {
        IO.println("You typed [" + line + "]: " + line.length() + " character(s)");
    }
}

Results when typing from the keyboard:

> java Basics06.java
age is null: true
age=23
n=23
Unboxing null: java.lang.NullPointerException
firstName is null: true
name present: true, name has 6 characters
nickname present: false, nickname: none
Type a line: hello
You typed [hello]: 5 character(s)

Results when the user presses Ctrl-D (Ctrl-Z followed by Enter on Windows), which closes the input stream:

> java Basics06.java
age is null: true
age=23
n=23
Unboxing null: java.lang.NullPointerException
firstName is null: true
name present: true, name has 6 characters
nickname present: false, nickname: none
Type a line: 
No line: the input stream is closed

Comments:

  • line 4: [age] does not reference any object;
  • line 7: [int] 23 is automatically wrapped: the compiler generated [age = Integer.valueOf(23);] for us;
  • line 10: [Integer] is automatically unwrapped: the compiler wrote [int n = age.intValue();];
  • lines 13–19: Unpacking a *[Integer]* that is equal to [null] is equivalent to calling *[intValue()] on a null reference: a *[NullPointerException] is thrown. The trap is all the more insidious because no method call is visible on line 15. The [try / catch] structure, which intercepts the error, is presented later; here, the full class name of the exception is displayed;
  • line 22: a string that does not reference any object;
  • line 25: a [Optional] that contains the string "dupont". The [get()] method (line 27) returns its contents; when applied to an empty [Optional], it would throw a [NoSuchElementException] exception;
  • line 26: an empty [Optional];
  • line 28: [orElse] returns the contents of [Optional], or the replacement value passed as a parameter if it is empty;
  • line 31: [IO.readln(prompt)] (Java 25) displays the prompt without moving to the next line, then reads the line typed on the keyboard. It returns [null] if the input stream is closed;
  • line 32: the value [null] is checked;
  • line 36: In the branch [else], [line] is not equal to [null]: [line.length()] can be used safely.

docs.title: 3.3.5. Conversions Between Numbers and Strings
3.3.6. Data Arrays
docs.text:
A Java array is an object that allows data of the same type to be grouped under a single identifier. It is declared as follows:

Type[] array = new Type[n];

[n] is the number of data elements the array can contain. The syntax [array[i]] refers to data element number i, where i belongs to the interval [0, n-1]. Any reference to data item [array[i]] where i is not in the range [0, n-1] causes a [ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException] exception. Upon creation, each element of the array is assigned the default value for its type: 0 for numbers, [false] for Booleans, and [null] for reference types. An array can be initialized at the same time it is declared:

    int[] integers = new int[]{0, 10, 20, 30};

or, more simply, in a declaration:

    int[] values = {0, 10, 20, 30, 40};

Arrays have a field [length] (without parentheses) that represents the number of elements. An array cannot change size after it is created: for a collection that grows, a list is used (Chapter 5). The notation [int integers[]], inherited from the C language, is also encountered: it is accepted but not recommended.

Java does not have true two-dimensional arrays: an array with two indices is an array of arrays. The declaration

Type[][] array = new Type[n][m];

creates an array of [n] elements, each of which is a reference to an array of [m] elements: [n] rows and [m] columns. The syntax [array[i][j]] refers to element j in row i. [array.length] is the number of rows, and [array[i].length] is the number of elements in row i. The array can also be initialized at the same time it is declared:

    double[][] reals = {{0.5, 1.7}, {8.4, -6}};

Since each row is an independent array, the rows can have different lengths (this is referred to as a "staircase array"). The declaration

Type[][] array = new Type[n][];

creates an array of n elements, each of which is a one-dimensional array reference. These references are not initialized by the declaration above: they have the value [null].

Java does not provide indices counted from the end of the array or a notation for extracting a range of elements. The last element is written as [array[array.length - 1]], and the method [Arrays.copyOfRange(array, start, end)] returns a new array consisting of the elements with indices from [start] (inclusive) to [end] (exclusive). The [java.util.Arrays] class offers many other utility methods: [toString], [deepToString], [sort], [fill], [equals], [copyOf]... Lists, which are more flexible, have had the methods [getFirst()] and [getLast()] since Java 21.

The program [Basics08.java] combines these different arrays:

// arrays
void main() {
    // an initialized 1-dimensional array
    int[] integers = new int[]{0, 10, 20, 30};
    for (int i = 0; i < integers.length; i++) {
        IO.println("integers[" + i + "]=" + integers[i]);
    }

    // a 2-dimensional array: an array of arrays of the same length
    double[][] reals = {{0.5, 1.7}, {8.4, -6}};
    for (int i = 0; i < reals.length; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < reals[i].length; j++) {
            IO.println("reals[" + i + "][" + j + "]=" + reals[i][j]);
        }
    }
    IO.println("reals=" + Arrays.deepToString(reals));

    // an array of arrays of different lengths (jagged array)
    String[][] names = new String[3][];
    for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
        names[i] = new String[i + 1];
    }
    // initialization
    for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < names[i].length; j++) {
            names[i][j] = "name" + i + j;
        }
    }
    // display
    for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < names[i].length; j++) {
            IO.println("names[" + i + "][" + j + "]=" + names[i][j]);
        }
    }

    // an array created without initial values: elements at the default value of the type
    boolean[] flags = new boolean[3];
    String[] strings = new String[2];
    IO.println("flags[0]=" + flags[0] + ", strings[0] is null: " + (strings[0] == null));

    // the short form of initialization
    int[] values = {0, 10, 20, 30, 40};
    // Arrays.toString builds a string with the elements of the array
    IO.println("values=" + Arrays.toString(values));
    // the last and the second-to-last element
    IO.println("last=" + values[values.length - 1] + ", second-to-last=" + values[values.length - 2]);
    // part of the array: the elements at indices 1 and 2 (the end bound is excluded)
    int[] slice = Arrays.copyOfRange(values, 1, 3);
    IO.println("copyOfRange(values, 1, 3)=" + Arrays.toString(slice));
    int[] end = Arrays.copyOfRange(values, 2, values.length);
    IO.println("copyOfRange(values, 2, length)=" + Arrays.toString(end));
    // the slice is a copy: the original array is not modified
    slice[0] = 100;
    IO.println("slice[0]=" + slice[0] + ", values[1]=" + values[1]);
    // a list (chapter 5) offers getFirst and getLast (Java 21)
    List<String> friends = List.of("paul", "hélène", "jacques");
    IO.println("first friend=" + friends.getFirst() + ", last friend=" + friends.getLast());
}

Results:

> java Basics08.java
integers[0]=0
integers[1]=10
integers[2]=20
integers[3]=30
reals[0][0]=0.5
reals[0][1]=1.7
reals[1][0]=8.4
reals[1][1]=-6.0
reals=[[0.5, 1.7], [8.4, -6.0]]
names[0][0]=name00
names[1][0]=name10
names[1][1]=name11
names[2][0]=name20
names[2][1]=name21
names[2][2]=name22
flags[0]=false, strings[0] is null: true
values=[0, 10, 20, 30, 40]
last=40, second-to-last=30
copyOfRange(values, 1, 3)=[10, 20]
copyOfRange(values, 2, length)=[20, 30, 40]
slice[0]=100, values[1]=10
first friend=paul, last friend=jacques

Comments:

  • line 4: a one-dimensional array is initialized;
  • line 5: a loop [for] iterates over indices from 0 to [integers.length - 1]. The loop [for] is shown below;
  • line 10: a two-dimensional array (2 rows, 2 columns). The integer -6 is converted to a floating-point number -6.0;
  • lines 11–12: [reals.length] is the number of rows, and [reals[i].length] is the number of columns in row i;
  • Line 16: [Arrays.deepToString] displays an array of arrays;
  • line 19: an array [names] with 3 elements. Each element is a reference to an array of type [String[]], currently [null];
  • line 21: the 3 elements of the array [names] are initialized. [names[i]] now references an array of i+1 strings;
  • line 26: [names[i][j]] is the jth element of the array referenced by [names[i]]. The expression "name" + i + j is evaluated from left to right: "name" + i yields a string, to which j is concatenated;
  • lines 37–38: arrays created without initial values: their elements have the default value for their type;
  • line 42: the shorthand form of initialization;
  • line 44: the method [Arrays.toString] constructs a string using the array’s elements. Displaying the array directly ([IO.println(values)]) would result in text such as [I@6328d34a (the array’s type and a numeric code), rather than its contents;
  • line 46: the last and second-to-last elements;
  • line 48: the elements at indices 1 and 2;
  • line 50: the elements starting at index 2 through the end;
  • lines 53–54: [copyOfRange] creates a copy: modifying [slice] does not modify [values];
  • lines 56–57: a non-modifiable list created by [List.of], and its methods [getFirst()] and [getLast()] (Java 21).

docs.title: 3.4. Java’s Basic Statements
docs.text:
There are two types:

  • basic instructions executed by the computer;
  • instructions that control the flow of the program.

Basic instructions become clear when considering the structure of a microcomputer and its peripherals:

  • 1: reading information from the keyboard;
  • 2: processing information;
  • 3: writing information to the screen.

docs.title: 3.4.1. Writing to the Screen
docs.text:
There are various instructions for writing to the screen:

System.out.println(expression);
System.err.println(expression);
IO.println(expression);

where [expression] is any data that can be converted to a character string for display on the screen. All Java objects have a [toString()] method that is used to perform this conversion; values of primitive types are converted by [String.valueOf]. The [print] method does the same thing as [println] without wrapping to the next line, and the [printf(format, value1, ...)] method writes the result in a specific format.

The [System] class provides access to two write streams, its static fields [out] and [err], of type [PrintStream]:

  • [System.out.println()] writes to the stream [out], the standard output, which is usually associated with the screen;
  • [System.err.println()] writes to the [err] stream, the error output, which is also usually associated with the screen.

The [IO] class (Java 25) provides the methods [println] and [print], which write to [System.out]. The streams [out] and [err] can be redirected to files at runtime, as we will see shortly.

docs.title: 3.4.2. Reading Data Entered from the Keyboard
docs.text:
The data stream from the keyboard is identified by the field [System.in], of type [InputStream]. It is a stream of bytes, which is not very convenient to use directly. For a long time, to read a line of text, it was necessary to wrap it in other objects:

BufferedReader keyboard = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in));
String line = keyboard.readLine();

or use the [Scanner] class (Java 5). Starting with Java 25, the [IO] class provides a much simpler method, [readln], in two forms:

String line = IO.readln();
String line = IO.readln("prompt: ");

The line typed on the keyboard, without the end-of-line character, is stored in the variable [line] and can then be processed by the program. The second form first displays a prompt, without moving to the next line. As we have seen, [readln] returns [null] when the input stream is exhausted. The stream [System.in] can be redirected to a file, just like the streams [out] and [err]. Finally, note the class [Console], derived from [System.console()], whose method [readPassword] reads a password without displaying it.

docs.title: 3.4.3. Example of Input/Output
docs.text:
The program [Basics09.java] illustrates keyboard and screen input/output operations:

// keyboard / screen input-output
void main() {
    // writing to the System.out stream
    Object obj = new Object();
    System.out.println(obj);

    // writing to the System.err stream
    int i = 10;
    System.err.println("i=" + i);
    System.err.printf("i=%d%n", i);

    // reading a line typed on the keyboard, after displaying a prompt
    String line = IO.readln("Type a line: ");
    IO.println("line=" + line);
}

Results:

> java Basics09.java
java.lang.Object@32464a14
i=10
i=10
Type a line: here I am
line=here I am

Comments:

  • Line 4: [obj] is an object reference;
  • Line 5: [obj] is displayed on the screen. The method [obj.toString()] is called to retrieve the text to be displayed;
  • line 9: data is written to the stream [err];
  • line 10: the same thing, but with a format. The first parameter, "i=%d%n," is the display format; the other parameters are the values to be displayed: %d is replaced by the value of [i], and %n by the system's line-end character (\r\n on Windows, \n on Linux, and macOS);
  • line 13: a prompt is displayed without moving to the next line, then the line typed on the keyboard is read;
  • line 14: if [line] were equal to [null], the concatenation would produce the string "null".

In the results:

  • line 2: the output generated by line 5 of the code. The [toString()] method of the [Object] class returns the object’s full class name, followed by the @ character and a hexadecimal numeric code (its “hash code”), which may vary from one execution or machine to another. Classes generally override this method to display something more useful, as we will do in Chapter 4;
  • lines 3–4: The two writes to the [err] stream appear on the screen just like those for the [out] stream.

docs.title: 3.4.4. Input/Output Redirection
docs.text:
Windows, Linux, and macOS recognize three standard devices:

  • the standard input device, which by default refers to the keyboard and is numbered 0;
  • the standard output device, which by default refers to the screen and is numbered 1;
  • the standard error device, which by default refers to the screen and is numbered 2.

In Java, the write stream [System.out] writes to device 1, the write stream [System.err] writes to device 2, and the read stream [System.in] reads data from device 0.

When you run a program in a command window, you can specify which devices will be 0, 1, and 2 for the program being executed. After the program arguments, you can redirect the standard input and output devices to files:

RedirectionMeaning0<in.txt or <in.txtStandard input stream No. 0 is redirected to the file in.txt. In the program, the stream [System.in] will therefore read its data from the file in.txt1>out.txt or >out.txtredirects output #1 to the file out.txt. In the program, the stream [System.out] will therefore write its data to the file out.txt1>>out.txt or >>out.txtSame as above, but the written data is appended to the current contents of the out.txt file2>err.txtredirects output #2 to the file err.txt. In the program, the stream [System.err] will therefore write its data to the file err.txt2>>err.txtSame as above, but the written data is appended to the current contents of the file err.txt1>out.txt 2>err.txtDevices 1 and 2 are both redirected to files

Note that to redirect a program’s input/output streams to files, the program does not need to be modified: the operating system determines the nature of devices 0, 1, and 2. Consider the following program, [Basics10.java]:

// redirections of the input-output streams
void main() {
    // reading the System.in stream
    String data = IO.readln();
    // writing the System.out stream
    System.out.println("writing to the out stream: " + data);
    // writing the System.err stream
    System.err.println("writing to the err stream: " + data);
}

The redirects apply to the program launched by the command [java]. Here is a session in a Linux terminal (bash):

> echo test > in.txt
> cat in.txt
test
> java Basics10.java < in.txt > out.txt 2> err.txt
> cat out.txt
writing to the out stream: test
> cat err.txt
writing to the err stream: test
> java Basics10.java < in.txt 2> err.txt
writing to the out stream: test
> java Basics10.java < in.txt > out.txt
writing to the err stream: test

Comments:

  • line 1: we put the string "test" into the file in.txt;
  • line 2: the contents of the file in.txt are displayed for verification;
  • line 4: run the program. The stream [System.in] is redirected to the file in.txt, the stream [System.out] to the file out.txt, and the stream [System.err] to the file err.txt. The execution does not result in any output;
  • lines 5–6: The contents of the file out.txt show that the file in.txt was read and that writing to the stream [out] was redirected to out.txt;
  • lines 7–8: similar verification for the file err.txt;
  • lines 9–10: only the [err] stream is redirected: the screen displays only the write operation to the [out] stream;
  • lines 11–12: only the [out] stream is redirected: the screen displays only the write operation on the [err] stream.

It is clear that the streams [out] and [err] do not write to the same devices, since they could be redirected separately. The [err] stream is intended for error messages: this allows you to redirect a program’s output to a file while still seeing its error messages on the screen.

The operators >, >>, and 2> are written the same way in the Windows command prompt ([cmd]), in PowerShell, and in bash. The < operator is recognized by [cmd] and bash, but not by PowerShell, which reserves it for future use: in PowerShell, it is used to send a file to a program’s standard input via a pipe (|). The following commands, provided for illustrative purposes (they were not executed for this course), do on Windows what the bash session above does:

rem Windows command prompt (cmd)
echo test>in.txt
java Basics10.java <in.txt >out.txt 2>err.txt
type out.txt
type err.txt

# PowerShell
"test" > in.txt
Get-Content in.txt | java Basics10.java > out.txt 2> err.txt
Get-Content out.txt
Get-Content err.txt

docs.title: 3.4.5. Assigning the value of an expression to a variable
docs.text: Here we are interested in the operation [variable = expression;]. The expression can be arithmetic, relational, Boolean, string, etc.

docs.title: 3.4.5.1. Interpretation of the assignment operation
docs.text:
The operation [variable = expression;] is itself an expression that is evaluated as follows:

  • the right-hand side of the assignment is evaluated: the result is a value V;
  • the value V is assigned to the variable;
  • the value V is also the value of the assignment, this time viewed as an expression.

This is why the operation [V1 = V2 = expression] is valid. Since the = operator is evaluated from right to left, we get [V1 = (V2 = expression)]. The expression [V2 = expression] is evaluated and has the value V. Its evaluation caused V to be assigned to V2. The next = operator is then evaluated as [V1 = V]. The value of this expression is still V; its evaluation results in V being assigned to V1. Thus, the operation [V1 = V2 = expression] is an expression whose evaluation:

  • causes the value of [expression] to be assigned to the variables V1 and V2;
  • returns the value of [expression].

This can be generalized to an expression of the form [V1 = V2 = ... = Vn = expression].

docs.title: 3.4.5.2. Arithmetic Expressions
docs.text:
The operators used in arithmetic expressions are as follows:

OperatorRole+addition-subtraction*multiplication/division: the result is the exact quotient if at least one of the operands is a real number. If both operands are integers, the result is the integer quotient. Thus, 5/2 equals 2 and 5.0/2 equals 2.5%remainder of division (modulo), regardless of the nature of the operands. The remainder has the same sign as the dividend: -5 % 2 equals -1. The method [Math.floorMod(-5, 2)] returns the remainder in the mathematical sense, with the same sign as the divisor: 1

There are various mathematical functions. Here are a few:

FunctionRole[double sqrt(double x)]square root[double cos(double x)], [sin], [tan]cosine, sine, tangent (angle in radians)[double pow(double x, double y)]x to the power of y[double exp(double x)]exponential[double log(double x)], [log10]natural logarithm, decimal[abs(x)], [max(x, y)], [min(x, y)]absolute value, maximum, minimum (for the int, long, float, and double types)[double floor(double x)], [ceil]lower integer part, upper integer part[long round(double x)], [double rint(double x)]rounded to the nearest integer[clamp(value, min, max)]value mapped to the interval [min, max] (Java 21)[Math.PI], [Math.E]the constants π and e

All of these functions are static methods of a Java class named [Math] (package [java.lang]). When using them, you must prefix them with the name of the class in which they are defined. Thus, you would write:

    double x, y = 4;
    x = Math.sqrt(y);

The complete description of the [Math] class can be found in the Java online documentation, docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/lang/Math.html.

Real numbers of type [double] are encoded in binary: most decimal numbers, such as 0.1, have only an approximate value in this representation. This is unimportant for scientific calculations but unacceptable for monetary amounts. The [BigDecimal] class (in the [java.math] package), on the other hand, represents a decimal number exactly, with as many digits as necessary. Since Java does not allow operators to be redefined, calculations are performed using methods: [add], [subtract], [multiply], [divide], [compareTo]... A [BigDecimal] is immutable: an operation does not modify the object to which it is applied; instead, it returns a new object.

The program [Basics11.java] is as follows:

// arithmetic expressions
void main() {
    // integer division and real division
    IO.println("5 / 2 = " + 5 / 2 + ", 5.0 / 2 = " + 5.0 / 2 + ", 5 / 2.0 = " + 5 / 2.0);
    // remainder of the division (modulo)
    IO.println("5 % 2 = " + 5 % 2 + ", -5 % 2 = " + -5 % 2 + ", 5.5 % 2 = " + 5.5 % 2);
    IO.println("Math.floorMod(-5, 2) = " + Math.floorMod(-5, 2));
    // real division by zero: no error, infinity or NaN (Not a Number)
    double zero = 0;
    IO.println("1 / 0.0 = " + 1 / zero + ", 0 / 0.0 = " + 0 / zero);
    // integer division by zero: an exception
    int integerZero = 0;
    try {
        IO.println(1 / integerZero);
    } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
        IO.println("1 / 0 : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
    }

    // a few methods of the Math class
    double x, y = 4;
    x = Math.sqrt(y);
    IO.println("Math.sqrt(4) = " + x);
    IO.println("Math.pow(2, 10) = " + Math.pow(2, 10));
    IO.println("Math.abs(-3.5) = " + Math.abs(-3.5) + ", Math.max(3, 7) = " + Math.max(3, 7));
    IO.println("Math.PI = " + Math.PI + ", Math.cos(Math.PI) = " + Math.cos(Math.PI));
    IO.println("Math.exp(1) = " + Math.exp(1) + ", Math.log(Math.E) = " + Math.log(Math.E));
    IO.println("Math.floor(-2.5) = " + Math.floor(-2.5) + ", Math.ceil(-2.5) = " + Math.ceil(-2.5));
    // Math.round rounds to the nearest integer, halves upwards; it returns a long
    IO.println("Math.round(2.5) = " + Math.round(2.5) + ", Math.round(-2.5) = " + Math.round(-2.5));
    // Math.rint rounds halves to the nearest even number
    IO.println("Math.rint(2.5) = " + Math.rint(2.5) + ", Math.rint(3.5) = " + Math.rint(3.5));
    // Math.clamp (Java 21) brings a value back into an interval
    IO.println("Math.clamp(150, 0, 100) = " + Math.clamp(150, 0, 100));

    // priorities: * / % before + -
    IO.println("2 + 3 * 4 = " + (2 + 3 * 4) + ", (2 + 3) * 4 = " + (2 + 3) * 4);
    IO.println("10 - 4 - 3 = " + (10 - 4 - 3) + ", \"x\" + 1 + 2 = " + "x" + 1 + 2);

    // assignment is an expression: multiple assignment
    int v1, v2;
    v1 = v2 = 7 * 6;
    IO.println("v1=" + v1 + ", v2=" + v2);

    // double reals are binary approximations
    IO.println("0.1 + 0.2 = " + (0.1 + 0.2));
    // BigDecimal computes exactly in base 10
    BigDecimal a = new BigDecimal("0.1"), b = new BigDecimal("0.2");
    IO.println("BigDecimal : 0.1 + 0.2 = " + a.add(b));
    BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("19.99");
    BigDecimal total = price.multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(3));
    IO.println("3 x 19.99 = " + total + ", with VAT = " + total.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.2")));
    // rounding to 2 decimals, halves upwards (commercial rounding)
    IO.println("2.565 rounded = " + new BigDecimal("2.565").setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP));
    // a division that does not come out exact requires a precision
    IO.println("10 / 3 = " + BigDecimal.TEN.divide(BigDecimal.valueOf(3), MathContext.DECIMAL64));
}

Results:

> java Basics11.java
5 / 2 = 2, 5.0 / 2 = 2.5, 5 / 2.0 = 2.5
5 % 2 = 1, -5 % 2 = -1, 5.5 % 2 = 1.5
Math.floorMod(-5, 2) = 1
1 / 0.0 = Infinity, 0 / 0.0 = NaN
1 / 0 : ArithmeticException - / by zero
Math.sqrt(4) = 2.0
Math.pow(2, 10) = 1024.0
Math.abs(-3.5) = 3.5, Math.max(3, 7) = 7
Math.PI = 3.141592653589793, Math.cos(Math.PI) = -1.0
Math.exp(1) = 2.718281828459045, Math.log(Math.E) = 1.0
Math.floor(-2.5) = -3.0, Math.ceil(-2.5) = -2.0
Math.round(2.5) = 3, Math.round(-2.5) = -2
Math.rint(2.5) = 2.0, Math.rint(3.5) = 4.0
Math.clamp(150, 0, 100) = 100
2 + 3 * 4 = 14, (2 + 3) * 4 = 20
10 - 4 - 3 = 3, "x" + 1 + 2 = x12
v1=42, v2=42
0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
BigDecimal : 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3
3 x 19.99 = 59.97, with VAT = 71.964
2.565 rounded = 2.57
10 / 3 = 3.333333333333333

Comments:

  • line 4: the division of two integers is an integer division. In this concatenation, the divisions are performed before the + operators because the / operator has higher precedence (see below);
  • line 6: the remainder has the same sign as the dividend; the % operator also applies to real numbers;
  • line 7: [Math.floorMod] returns a remainder with the same sign as the divisor;
  • line 10: dividing a real number by zero does not cause an error; it returns infinity ([Infinity]) or the special value [NaN] (“Not a Number”) for 0/0;
  • lines 12–17: however, dividing an integer by zero throws a [ArithmeticException] exception;
  • Lines 20–21: The example above. [Math.sqrt] is converted to [double]: 2.0;
  • line 27: [floor] is rounded down, [ceil] is rounded up. To truncate a real number to zero, it is converted to an integer, as we will see later;
  • line 29: [Math.round] rounds to the nearest integer; a value exactly halfway between two integers is rounded up: 2.5 becomes 3 and -2.5 becomes -2. The result is a [long];
  • line 31: [Math.rint] rounds a value located halfway to the nearest even integer (“banker’s” rounding): 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4. The result is [double];
  • line 33: [Math.clamp] (Java 21) brings 150 back into the range [0, 100];
  • line 36: operator precedence, as shown below;
  • line 37: "x" + 1 + 2 is evaluated from left to right: "x" + 1 yields the string "x1," to which 2 is concatenated. To perform the addition first, you must write "x" + (1 + 2);
  • line 41: a multiple assignment;
  • line 45: 0.1 and 0.2 do not have exact binary representations: their sum is not exactly 0.3;
  • line 47: two [BigDecimal] objects created from strings. Do not write [new BigDecimal(0.1)]: the parameter would be [double] 0.1, whose exact value is 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625. [BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)], which uses the string "0.1", works, however;
  • line 48: the exact addition;
  • lines 49–51: [BigDecimal.valueOf(3)] converts an integer. A product has as many decimal places as the sum of its two factors: 59.97 × 1.2 = 71.964;
  • line 53: [setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)] rounds to two decimal places, with values halfway between two digits rounded away from zero: this is commercial rounding;
  • line 55: 10/3 has no finite decimal representation. The [divide] method therefore requires a precision, given here as [MathContext.DECIMAL64] (16 significant digits). Without it, the division would result in [ArithmeticException]: [Non-terminating decimal expansion; no exact representable decimal result.]

docs.title: 3.4.5.3. Order of Operations in Evaluating Arithmetic Expressions
docs.text:
The order of operator precedence when evaluating an arithmetic expression is as follows (from highest to lowest):

[functions], [( )], [*, /, %], [+, -]

Operators within the same block [ ] have the same priority. When priorities are equal, evaluation proceeds from left to right: 10 - 4 - 3 evaluates to (10 - 4) - 3 = 3.

docs.title: 3.4.5.4. Relational Expressions
docs.text:
The operators are as follows: <, <=, ==, !=, >, >=. Their precedence is:

  • >, >=, <, <=;
  • ==, !=.

The result of a relational expression is the Boolean [false] if the expression is false, and [true] otherwise.

    int x = 5;
    boolean end = x > 4;

Comparing Two Characters

Let C1 and C2 be two characters. They can be compared using the operators <, <=, ==, !=, >, >=. Their Unicode codes—which are numbers—are compared. According to the Unicode order, the following relationships hold:

space < .. < '0' < '1' < .. < '9' < .. < 'A' < 'B' < .. < 'Z' < .. < 'a' < 'b' < .. < 'z' < .. < 'é'

Comparison of Two Strings

They are compared character by character. The first inequality encountered between two characters results in an inequality of the same direction for the strings. Consider comparing the strings "Cart" and "Cat":

"Cart"    "Cat"
---------------------
'C'   =   'C'
'a'   =   'a'
'r'   <   't'

This last inequality allows us to conclude that "Cart" < "Cat." Consider comparing the strings "Cat" and "Catkin." They are equal until the string "Cat" is exhausted. In this case, the exhausted string is declared the "smaller" one. We therefore have the relation "Cat" < "Catkin."

Methods for Comparing Two Strings

Warning: this is a classic pitfall in Java. When applied to two strings—or to any two objects—the operators == and != compare references, not contents. [s1 == s2] is true if the two variables refer to the same object in memory, not if the two strings contain the same characters. To test whether two strings are equal, use the [equals] method of the [String] class, or [equalsIgnoreCase] to ignore case differences. The operators <, <=, >, and >= do not apply to strings: you must use the [compareTo] method (or [compareToIgnoreCase]). It returns an integer:

  • zero if the two strings are equal;
  • positive if string #1 is greater than string #2;
  • negative if string #1 is less than string #2.

[compareTo] compares Unicode codes character by character: the result is the difference between the codes of the first two different characters, or the difference in length if one of the strings is the beginning of the other. This is not dictionary order: since the code for 'é' (233) is greater than that for 'f' (102), "élan" comes after "face." To sort text intended for users, use the [Collator] object ([java.text] package), which applies the sorting rules for a specific language. [compareTo] remains the correct method for identifiers, keywords, and file names.

The [Basics12.java] program is as follows:

// relational expressions and string comparison
void main() {
    int x = 5;
    boolean end = x > 4;
    IO.println("x > 4 : " + end + ", x == 5 : " + (x == 5) + ", x != 5 : " + (x != 5));

    // comparing characters: their Unicode codes are compared
    IO.println("'a' < 'b' : " + ('a' < 'b') + ", 'Z' < 'a' : " + ('Z' < 'a')
            + ", '9' < 'A' : " + ('9' < 'A'));
    IO.println("codes: 'A'=" + (int) 'A' + ", 'a'=" + (int) 'a' + ", 'é'=" + (int) 'é');

    // comparing strings with equals and compareTo
    String string1 = "cat", string2 = "dog";
    int n = string1.compareTo(string2);
    boolean equal = string1.equals(string2);
    IO.println("n=" + n + ", equal=" + equal);
    IO.println("\"Cat\".compareTo(\"Catkin\") : " + "Cat".compareTo("Catkin"));

    // == compares the references, not the content of the strings
    String string3 = "ca".concat("t");
    IO.println("string3=" + string3 + ", string1 == string3 : " + (string1 == string3)
            + ", string1.equals(string3) : " + string1.equals(string3));

    // compareTo compares the Unicode codes, character by character
    IO.println("\"élan\".compareTo(\"face\") : " + "élan".compareTo("face"));
    IO.println("\"Cat\".compareTo(\"cat\") : " + "Cat".compareTo("cat"));
    // ignoring case (uppercase / lowercase)
    IO.println("\"Cat\".compareToIgnoreCase(\"cat\") : " + "Cat".compareToIgnoreCase("cat"));
    IO.println("\"Cat\".equals(\"cat\") : " + "Cat".equals("cat"));
    IO.println("\"Cat\".equalsIgnoreCase(\"cat\") : " + "Cat".equalsIgnoreCase("cat"));
    // a Collator compares according to the sorting rules of a language
    Collator collator = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRENCH);
    IO.println("collator.compare(\"élan\", \"face\") : " + collator.compare("élan", "face"));
    IO.println("collator.compare(\"Cat\", \"cat\") : " + collator.compare("Cat", "cat"));
}

Results:

> java Basics12.java
x > 4 : true, x == 5 : true, x != 5 : false
'a' < 'b' : true, 'Z' < 'a' : true, '9' < 'A' : true
codes: 'A'=65, 'a'=97, 'é'=233
n=-1, equal=false
"Cat".compareTo("Catkin") : -3
string3=cat, string1 == string3 : false, string1.equals(string3) : true
"élan".compareTo("face") : 131
"Cat".compareTo("cat") : -32
"Cat".compareToIgnoreCase("cat") : 0
"Cat".equals("cat") : false
"Cat".equalsIgnoreCase("cat") : true
collator.compare("élan", "face") : -1
collator.compare("Cat", "cat") : 1

Comments:

  • line 4: a relational expression;
  • lines 8–9: character comparison;
  • line 10: the [(int)] conversion of a character returns its Unicode code;
  • line 14: the variable [n] is assigned a negative integer since "cat" < "dog": the difference between the codes for 'c' (99) and 'd' (100);
  • line 15: the variable [equal] has the value [true] if the two strings are equal, [false] otherwise;
  • line 17: the string that runs out first is the shorter one; the result is the difference in lengths: 3 - 6. In a string literal, \" denotes a quotation mark;
  • line 20: the method [concat] constructs, at runtime, a new string object that contains "cat";
  • lines 21–22: [string1] and [string3] have the same content but refer to two different objects: == returns [false], [equals] returns [true]. The trap is all the more insidious because two identical string literals are stored only once in memory, so ["cat" == "cat"] is true: a test using == may seem to work during testing. We will always use [equals];
  • line 25: 233 - 102 = 131: for [compareTo], “élan” comes after “face”;
  • line 26: 'C' (67) - 'c' (99) = -32;
  • lines 28–30: ignoring case, “Cat” and “cat” are equal;
  • lines 32–34: a [Collator] for French: “élan” precedes “face,” and “Cat” follows “cat” (when the letters are the same, the lowercase letter comes before the uppercase one). The [compare] method returns a negative, zero, or positive integer, just like [compareTo].

docs.title: 3.4.5.5. Boolean Expressions
docs.text:
The operators that can be used are AND (&&), OR (||), and NOT (!). The result of a Boolean expression is a Boolean value. Operator precedence:

  • ! ;
  • && ;
  • ||.
    double x = 3.5;
    boolean valid = x > 2 && x < 4;

Relational operators take precedence over the && and || operators. These two operators evaluate their right-hand operand only if necessary: in [a && b], b is not evaluated if a is false; in [a || b], b is not evaluated if a is true. This is called “short-circuit evaluation.” Therefore, it is safe to write [text != null && text.length() > 0]. The & and | operators, when applied to two Booleans, perform the same calculation but always evaluate both operands.

docs.title: 3.4.5.6. Bitwise Operations
docs.text:
Let [i] and [j] be two integers:

OperationRolei << nShifts i n bits to the left. The incoming bits are zerosi >> nShift i n bits to the right. The sign bit is preservedi >>> nunsigned right shift: the incoming bits are zeros, even if i is negativei & jperforms a bit-by-bit logical AND of i and ji|jperforms the bit-by-bit logical OR of i and j~icomplements i to 1i ^ jperforms the EXCLUSIVE OR operation on i and j bit by bit

The program [Basics13.java] is as follows:

// bit manipulation
void main() {
    short i = 100, j = -13;
    // char is the only unsigned integer type of Java (16 bits)
    char k = 0xF123;
    IO.println(String.format("i=0x%04x, j=0x%04x, k=0x%04x", i, j, (int) k));
    IO.println(String.format("i<<4=0x%04x, i>>4=0x%04x, k>>4=0x%04x", i << 4, i >> 4, k >> 4));
    IO.println(String.format("i&j=0x%04x, i|j=0x%04x, i^j=0x%04x, ~i=0x%04x",
            (short) (i & j), (short) (i | j), (short) (i ^ j), (short) ~i));
    IO.println(String.format("j<<2=0x%04x, j>>2=0x%04x", (short) (j << 2), (short) (j >> 2)));
    // the same values in binary
    IO.println("i=" + binary(i, 16) + ", j=" + binary(j, 16) + ", i&j=" + binary(i & j, 16));
    // unsigned right shift >>>: the incoming bits are zeros
    int m = -16;
    IO.println("m=" + binary(m, 32) + ", m>>2=" + binary(m >> 2, 32) + ", m>>>2=" + binary(m >>> 2, 32));
}

// the n low-order bits of value, as a string of 0s and 1s
String binary(int value, int n) {
    StringBuilder bits = new StringBuilder();
    for (int rank = n - 1; rank >= 0; rank--) {
        bits.append((value >>> rank) & 1);
    }
    return bits.toString();
}

Results:

> java Basics13.java
i=0x0064, j=0xfff3, k=0xf123
i<<4=0x0640, i>>4=0x0006, k>>4=0x0f12
i&j=0x0060, i|j=0xfff7, i^j=0xff97, ~i=0xff9b
j<<2=0xffcc, j>>2=0xfffc
i=0000000001100100, j=1111111111110011, i&j=0000000001100000
m=11111111111111111111111111110000, m>>2=11111111111111111111111111111100, m>>>2=00111111111111111111111111111100

Comments:

  • Line 3: two integers [short];
  • line 5: the value 0xF123 (61731) does not fit into a [short], whose maximum is 32767. The type [char], a 16-bit unsigned integer, can hold it;
  • line 6: the %04x specifier displays a 4-digit hexadecimal (x) integer padded with zeros (04). When applied to a [short], it shows its 16 bits: -13 becomes fff3. The %x specifier does not accept a [char]: it is converted to [int];
  • line 7: operations on [short] or [char] are performed on [int]: the operands are first converted to [int] (this is called promotion), and the result is a [int];
  • line 9: the results are then converted back to [short] to display 4 hexadecimal digits. Without conversion, ~i would be displayed as 8 digits (ffffff9b);
  • line 12: The [binary] method (lines 19–25) displays the n least significant bits of an integer. We check the logical AND of i and j bit by bit;
  • line 15: the [>>] shift preserves the sign bit of m, which is negative; the [>>>] shift fills with zeros;
  • line 22: [(value >>> rank) & 1] moves bit #[rank] to position 0 and then separates it from the others. The class [StringBuilder], introduced in Chapter 5, constructs a string by successive additions.

docs.title: 3.4.5.7. Combination of Operators
docs.text: [a = a + b] can be written as [a += b]; [a = a - b] can be written as [a -= b]. The same applies to the operators /, %, *, <<, >>, >>>, &, |, ^. Thus, [a = a / 2;] can be written as [a /= 2;]. One small difference: the combined operator includes an implicit conversion to the variable’s type. If [s] is a [short], [s = s + 1;] is rejected (the result of the addition is a [int]), whereas [s += 1;] is accepted.

docs.title: 3.4.5.8. Increment and Decrement Operators
docs.text:
The notation [variable++] means [variable = variable + 1] or [variable += 1]. The notation [variable--] means [variable = variable - 1] or [variable -= 1]. When used in an expression, these operators have two forms:

  • [i++] (postfix): the value of the expression is the value of i before the increment;
  • [++i] (prefixed): the value of the expression is the value of i after the increment.

docs.title: 3.4.5.9. The ternary operator ?
docs.text:
The expression [expr_cond ? expr1 : expr2] is evaluated as follows:

  • The expression [expr_cond] is evaluated. It is a Boolean expression;
  • if it is true, the value of the expression is that of [expr1], and [expr2] is not evaluated;
  • if it is false, the opposite occurs: the value of the expression is that of [expr2], and [expr1] is not evaluated.

The operation [i = (j > 4 ? j + 1 : j - 1);] will assign the value j+1 to the variable i if j > 4, and j-1 otherwise. This is the same as writing [if (j > 4) i = j + 1; else i = j - 1;], but it is more concise.

docs.title: 3.4.5.10. Null values: no specialized operators
docs.text:
Unlike other languages such as C# or Kotlin, Java does not have dedicated operators for the value [null] (replacement value, conditional access to a member). Instead, we use:

  • the ternary operator, [a != null ? a : b], or the [Objects.requireNonNullElse(a, b)] method (Java 9), which returns a if it is not equal to [null], and b otherwise. It is used to assign a fallback value: [String name = Objects.requireNonNullElse(IO.readln(), "");];
  • a simple test, [if (a == null) a = b;], to assign a value to a variable only if it is equal to [null];
  • the class *[Optional] and its method *[map] to access a member only if the object exists: [Optional.ofNullable(text).map(String::length)] returns an empty [Optional] if [text] is equal to [null], and a [Optional] containing the length of the text otherwise.

The program [Basics14.java] combines these various operators:

// other operators
void main() {
    // boolean expressions
    double x = 3.5;
    boolean valid = x > 2 && x < 4;
    IO.println("valid=" + valid + ", !valid=" + !valid + ", valid || x > 10 : " + (valid || x > 10));

    // compound operators
    int a = 10;
    a += 5;
    IO.print("a += 5 : " + a);
    a *= 2;
    IO.print(", a *= 2 : " + a);
    a /= 4;
    IO.print(", a /= 4 : " + a);
    a %= 4;
    IO.print(", a %= 4 : " + a);
    a <<= 2;
    IO.println(", a <<= 2 : " + a);

    // increment and decrement
    int i = 5;
    int j = i++;    // j receives the old value of i, then i is incremented
    int k = ++i;    // i is incremented, then k receives the new value of i
    IO.println("i=" + i + ", j=" + j + ", k=" + k);
    i--;
    IO.println("i=" + i);

    // ternary operator
