    int n = 5;
    int p = n > 4 ? n + 1 : n - 1;
    String parity = n % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd";
    IO.println("p=" + p + ", " + n + " is " + parity);

    // replacement value if a reference is null
    String input = null;
    String name = Objects.requireNonNullElse(input, "unknown");
    Integer age = null;
    int displayedAge = age != null ? age : -1;
    IO.println("name=" + name + ", displayedAge=" + displayedAge);
    // assignment only if the variable is null
    String title = null;
    if (title == null) {
        title = "Untitled";
    }
    IO.println("title=" + title);
    // accessing a member only if the object is not null: Optional and map
    String text = null;
    Optional<Integer> length = Optional.ofNullable(text).map(String::length);
    IO.println("length=" + length.map(String::valueOf).orElse("null"));
    text = "hello";
    IO.println("length=" + Optional.ofNullable(text).map(String::length).orElse(-1));
}

Results:

> java Basics14.java
valid=true, !valid=false, valid || x > 10 : true
a += 5 : 15, a *= 2 : 30, a /= 4 : 7, a %= 4 : 3, a <<= 2 : 12
i=7, j=5, k=7
i=6
p=6, 5 is odd
name=unknown, displayedAge=-1
title=Untitled
length=null
length=5

Comments:

  • line 5: a Boolean expression;
  • lines 9–19: combined operators: 10+5=15, 15*2=30, 30/4=7 (integer division), 7%4=3, 3<<2=12;
  • line 23: [j] is assigned 5, then [i] is set to 6;
  • line 24: [i] changes to 7, then [k] receives 7;
  • lines 31–32: two ternary operators;
  • line 37: [input] equals [null]: [name] is assigned "unknown";
  • line 39: the ternary operator allows switching from a [Integer] to a [int] without risk of an exception: [age] is unpacked only if it is not equal to [null];
  • lines 43–45: the assignment occurs only if [title] equals [null];
  • line 49: [text] equals [null]: [Optional.ofNullable(text)] is empty, and [map] returns an empty [Optional] without calling [length()]. The notation [String::length] is a method reference: it refers to the method [length] of the class [String]. We will examine this in Chapter 7;
  • line 50: if [length] is empty, the string "null" is displayed;
  • line 52: [text] is "hello": [map] applies [length()], and the result is 5.

docs.title: 3.4.5.11. General Operator Precedence
docs.text:
The following table lists the operator precedence, from highest to lowest:

OperatorsAssociativity[x.y] [f(x)] [a[i]] [x++] [x--] [new]lr[+x] [-x] [!x] [~x] [++x] [--x] [(T)x] (type change)rl[*] [/] [%]lr[+] [-]lr[<<] [>>] [>>>]lr[<] [<=] [>] [>=] [instanceof]lr[==] [!=]lr[&]lr[^]lr[|]lr[&&]lr[||]lr[? :] (ternary)rl[=] [+=] [-=] etc., [->] (lambda)rl

lr indicates that, when operators have equal precedence, left-to-right precedence is observed: when an expression contains operators of the same precedence, the operator farthest to the left is evaluated first. rl indicates right-to-left precedence. When in doubt, don’t hesitate to use parentheses: they also make the expression more readable.

docs.title: 3.4.5.12. Type Casting
docs.text:
It is possible, within an expression, to temporarily change the representation of a value. This is called type casting. The syntax for changing the type of a value in an expression is as follows:

(type) value

The value then takes on the specified type. This results in a change in the value’s representation. We distinguish between:

  • "Widening" conversions, performed automatically by the compiler: [byte] to [short], [short] to [int], [char] to [int], [int] to [long], [long] to [float] or [double], [float] to [double]... They retain the order of magnitude of the value. Those that go from a [int] to a [float], or from a [long] to a [float] or a [double], may, however, lose precision: a [float] has only 7 significant digits, while a [double] has 15 to 16;
  • narrowing conversions, which can result in a loss of information and must be explicitly requested by the programmer using the notation (type): from a [double] to a [int] (the decimal part is lost), from a [long] to a [int] (the most significant bits are lost), etc.

An overflow in an integer calculation or a conversion between integers is never reported: the result is simply incorrect. Java does not have a keyword to request a check. When this risk exists, use the methods [addExact], [subtractExact], [multiplyExact], [incrementExact], [toIntExact]... from class [Math] (Java 8), which throw a [ArithmeticException] exception if the limit is exceeded.

The program [Basics15.java] is as follows:

// type changes
void main() {
    int i = 3, j = 4;
    float f1 = i / j;
    float f2 = (float) i / j;
    IO.println("f1=" + f1 + ", f2=" + f2);

    // implicit conversions (widening): without loss of information
    long l = i;
    double d = l;
    IO.println("l=" + l + ", d=" + d);

    // explicit conversions (casting): possible loss of information
    double real = 3.99;
    int truncated = (int) real;
    int rounded = (int) Math.round(real);
    IO.println("(int) 3.99=" + truncated + ", (int) Math.round(3.99)=" + rounded);
    long large = 3_000_000_000L;
    int overflowed = (int) large;
    IO.println("(int) 3000000000L=" + overflowed);
    // a real that is too large is brought back to the largest integer value
    IO.println("(int) 1e10=" + (int) 1e10 + ", (int) Double.NaN=" + (int) Double.NaN);

    // characters and integers
    char c = (char) 65;
    int code = 'é';
    IO.println("(char) 65=" + c + ", code of 'é'=" + code);

    // capacity overflow: silent
    int max = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
    int next = max + 1;
    IO.println("Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 = " + next);
    // the ...Exact methods of Math report the overflow with an exception
    try {
        int verified = Math.addExact(max, 1);
        IO.println("verified=" + verified);
    } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
        IO.println("Math.addExact(max, 1) : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
    }
    try {
        int conversion = Math.toIntExact(large);
        IO.println("conversion=" + conversion);
    } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
        IO.println("Math.toIntExact(large) : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

Results:

> java Basics15.java
f1=0.0, f2=0.75
l=3, d=3.0
(int) 3.99=3, (int) Math.round(3.99)=4
(int) 3000000000L=-1294967296
(int) 1e10=2147483647, (int) Double.NaN=0
(char) 65=A, code of 'é'=233
Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 = -2147483648
Math.addExact(max, 1) : ArithmeticException - integer overflow
Math.toIntExact(large) : ArithmeticException - integer overflow

Comments:

  • Line 4: [f1] will have the value 0.0. The division 3/4 is an integer division since both operands are of type [int]; its result, 0, is then converted to [float];
  • Line 5: [(float) i] is the value of [i] converted to [float]. We now have a division between a real number of type [float] and an integer of type [int]: the value of [j] is also transformed into [float], and then the two real numbers are divided. [f2] has a value of 0.75. In the operation [(float) i], [i] is a value encoded exactly over 4 bytes, while [(float) i] is the same value encoded approximately as a real number over 4 bytes. This transcoding occurs only during the calculation: the variable [i] always retains its type [int];
  • lines 9–10: upconversions;
  • line 15: converting a real number to an integer truncates the decimal part (toward zero);
  • Line 16: To round the number, we use [Math.round], which results in [long], and then convert it to [int];
  • line 18: the suffix L is essential: 3 billion exceeds the range of [int];
  • line 19: 3 billion does not fit into a [int]: only the least significant 32 bits are retained, and the result no longer makes sense;
  • line 22: a real number too large for a [int] is reduced to [Integer.MAX_VALUE]; the value [NaN] becomes 0;
  • lines 25–26: conversions between characters and Unicode codes; the second is implicit;
  • line 31: the capacity overflow goes unnoticed: the smallest value, [int], is obtained;
  • line 35: with [Math.addExact], the overflow triggers a [ArithmeticException] exception;
  • line 41: [Math.toIntExact] converts a [long] to [int] and also throws an exception if the value does not fit into a [int].

Even when the overflow occurs in an expression consisting solely of constants, such as [Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1], the compiler accepts it without a warning: it calculates the value itself, -2147483648.

docs.title: 3.5.1. Stop
docs.text:
The [exit] method of the [System] class allows you to stop program execution:

System.exit(int status);

[exit] terminates the current process and returns control to the calling process, typically the command interpreter. The value of [status], known as the return code, can be used by the command interpreter. By convention, 0 indicates that the program executed successfully, while any other value signals an error. On Windows, the return code is available in the [%ERRORLEVEL%] variable at the command prompt and in the [$LASTEXITCODE] variable within PowerShell; on Linux and macOS, in the [$?] variable in the shell. Thus, [System.exit(0);] will terminate the program’s execution with a return code of 0.

Without a call to [System.exit], a program terminates with a return code of 0 when its [main] method ends, possibly with a [return] statement. If it is terminated by an exception that no one has caught, it displays that exception and terminates with a return code of 1. In Java, the [main] method cannot return an integer: [System.exit] is the only way to specify the return code.

The program [Basics16.java] receives its return code as an argument:

// stopping the program with an exit code
void main(String[] args) {
    IO.println("Start of the program");
    // the exit code is passed as an argument (see the section on the program arguments)
    int code;
    try {
        // without argument, the empty string is converted, which fails
        code = Integer.parseInt(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "");
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        System.err.println("Syntax: java Basics16.java exit_code");
        System.exit(1);
        return;
    }
    IO.println("Stopping with the exit code " + code);
    System.exit(code);
    IO.println("This line is never executed");
}

Results in a bash terminal:

> java Basics16.java 3
Start of the program
Stopping with the exit code 3
> echo $?
3
> java Basics16.java
Start of the program
Syntax: java Basics16.java exit_code
> echo $?
1

Comments:

  • line 2: The [main] method receives the command-line arguments in the [args] array. The program’s arguments are described below;
  • line 8: if there is at least one argument, the first one is converted to an integer; otherwise, the empty string is converted, which fails. Thus, the absence of an argument and a non-numeric argument are handled by the same clause [catch];
  • line 11: the program terminates with a return code of 1;
  • line 12: this instruction will never be executed, but the compiler does not know that [System.exit] never returns control. Without it, the compiler would assume that line 14 could be reached with an uninitialized [code] variable and would reject the program: [error: variable code might not have been initialized];
  • line 15: exit with the return code passed as an argument. The following line is not executed;
  • Lines 4–5 and 9–10 of the results: The command [echo $?] displays the return code of the last program executed: 3, then 1.

docs.title: 3.5.2. Simple decision structure
docs.text:
if (condition) {
    actions_condition_true;
} else {
    actions_condition_false;
}

Notes:

  • The condition is enclosed in parentheses. It must be in the format [boolean]: unlike the C language, Java rejects [if (n)] when [n] is an integer;
  • Each action ends with a semicolon;
  • curly braces are not followed by a semicolon;
  • curly braces are required only if there is more than one action; however, they are often used even for a single action, for readability and to avoid errors when adding an action. In Java, it is customary to place the opening curly brace at the end of the line;
  • the clause [else] may be omitted;
  • there is no [then] keyword.

The algorithmic equivalent of this structure is the if...then...else structure:

if condition
    then actions_condition_true
    else actions_condition_false
endif

Example:

if (x > 0) { nx = nx + 1; sx = sx + x; } else dx = dx - x;

Choice structures can be nested. This sometimes leads to the problem illustrated by the program [Basics17.java]:

// simple choice structure if
void main() {
    int n = 5;
    // an else always relates to the nearest if
    if (n > 1)
        if (n > 6)
            IO.println(">6");
        else
            IO.println("<=6");

    // with braces, the else is attached to the first if
    int n2 = 0;
    if (n2 > 1) {
        if (n2 > 6) {
            IO.println(">6");
        }
    } else {
        IO.println("<=1");
    }

    // a sequence of choices: else if
    int grade = 13;
    String honours;
    if (grade < 10) {
        honours = "failed";
    } else if (grade < 12) {
        honours = "pass";
    } else if (grade < 14) {
        honours = "fairly good";
    } else {
        honours = "good";
    }
    IO.println("grade=" + grade + ", honours=" + honours);
}

Results:

> java Basics17.java
<=6
<=1
grade=13, honours=fairly good

Comments:

  • Lines 5–9: Which [if] does the [else] on line 8 refer to? The rule is that a [else] always refers to the nearest [if]: [if (n > 6)], line 6. The code indentation, which has no effect on the compiler, was chosen to illustrate this;
  • lines 13–19: here, we wanted to place a [else] next to [if (n2 > 1)], and not a [else] next to [if (n2 > 6)]. Because of the previous rule, we are forced to enclose [if (n2 > 1) { ... }] in curly braces;
  • Lines 24–32: A sequence of mutually exclusive choices is written using successive [else if] statements. The conditions are tested in order; the first one that evaluates to true determines the action to be executed. The compiler verifies that the variable [honours], declared without a value on line 23, is assigned a value in all branches before being used on line 33.

docs.title: 3.5.3.1. The switch statement
docs.text:
The historical syntax is as follows:

switch (expression) {
    case v1:
        actions1;
        break;
    case v2:
        actions2;
        break;
    ...
    default:
        actions_otherwise;
        break;
}

Notes:

  • The value of the control expression for [switch] can be an integer ([int], [short], [byte], [char], or their wrapper classes), a string (Java 7), an enum value, and, since Java 21, any object (see pattern filtering below). The types [long], [float], [double], and [boolean] are not accepted;
  • the control expression is enclosed in parentheses;
  • the clause [default] may be omitted;
  • the values vi are possible values of the expression. If the expression evaluates to vi, the actions following the clause [case vi] are executed. Starting with Java 14, a clause can list multiple values: [case "saturday", "sunday":];
  • The [break] statement exits the case structure. Note: If it is omitted, execution continues with the actions of the following [case] clause (“fall-through”). The compiler accepts this; with the [-Xlint:all] option, it issues only the [warning: [fallthrough] possible fall-through into case] warning. This omission is a common error, which the arrow form shown below prevents.

Example in algorithmics:

depending on the value of choice
    case 0
        end of the module
    case 1
        execute module M1
    case 2
        execute module M2
    otherwise
        error <- true
endcase

docs.title: 3.5.3.2. The arrow form and the switch expression
docs.text:
Java 14 introduced a second form of the clause, [case v1, v2 -> action], where the arrow is followed by a single statement or a block enclosed in curly braces. Only the action of the selected clause is executed: there is no need to write a [break], nor is there a chaining of one clause to the next.

Very often, a case structure is used solely to select a value. In this case, [switch] can be used as an expression (Java 14):

result = switch (expression) {
    case v1 -> value1;
    case v2, v3 -> value2;
    ...
    default -> value_otherwise;
};

The switch expression must be exhaustive: it must provide a value for all possible values of the control expression, which generally requires a [default] clause. When a clause requires multiple statements, a block is written, which returns its value using the [yield] statement.

Since Java 21, a [case] clause can contain a pattern instead of a constant. A type pattern, [case Integer i], is matched if the object being examined is of type [Integer]; the object is then available, with that type, in the variable [i]. A guard [when condition] adds a condition: [case Integer i when i > 0] is only selected for a positive integer. A clause [case null] processes the value [null], which would otherwise trigger a [NullPointerException]. The clauses are evaluated in order: the first one that matches is selected. The same filtering applies to the [instanceof] operator (Java 16): [if (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 3)].

Java 25 does not yet allow writing such patterns for primitive types ([case int i when i > 0]): this feature is available in a preview version, which we will not use. To classify a [int] with guards, we apply the [switch] to a [Integer].

The [Basics18.java] program is as follows:

// case structure: switch statement and switch expression
void main() {
    int choice = 2;
    boolean error = false;
    switch (choice) {
        case 0:
            return;
        case 1:
            m1();
            break;
        case 2:
            m2();
            break;
        default:
            error = true;
            break;
    }
    IO.println("error=" + error);

    // several values for the same case, expression of type String
    String day = "saturday";
    switch (day) {
        case "saturday", "sunday":
            IO.println(day + " : weekend");
            break;
        default:
            IO.println(day + " : week");
            break;
    }
    // the arrow form (Java 14): no break, no fall-through between cases
    switch (day) {
        case "saturday", "sunday" -> IO.println(day + " : weekend");
        default -> IO.println(day + " : week");
    }

    // switch expression (Java 14): it returns a value
    String dayType = switch (day) {
        case "saturday", "sunday" -> "weekend";
        case "monday", "tuesday", "wednesday", "thursday", "friday" -> "week";
        default -> "unknown day";
    };
    IO.println(day + " : " + dayType);
    // a block of statements returns its value with yield
    int nbHours = switch (day) {
        case "saturday" -> 4;
        case "sunday" -> 0;
        default -> {
            int hours = 7;
            yield hours + 1;
        }
    };
    IO.println(day + " : " + nbHours + " opening hour(s)");

    // pattern matching with when guards (Java 21)
    IO.println("-5 : " + classify(-5));
    IO.println("0 : " + classify(0));
    IO.println("7 : " + classify(7));
    IO.println("42 : " + classify(42));
    IO.println("1000 : " + classify(1000));
    // matching on the type of the object
    Object[] objects = {12, -3, "java", 2.5, null};
    for (Object o : objects) {
        IO.println(o + " : " + describe(o));
    }
}

// methods used above
void m1() {
    IO.println("M1");
}

void m2() {
    IO.println("M2");
}

String classify(Integer n) {
    return switch (n) {
        case Integer i when i < 0 -> "negative";
        case 0 -> "zero";
        case Integer i when i <= 10 -> "small";
        case Integer i when i < 100 -> "medium";
        default -> "large";
    };
}

String describe(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case null -> "no object";
        case Integer i when i > 0 -> "positive integer";
        case Integer i -> "negative or zero integer";
        case String s -> "string of " + s.length() + " characters";
        default -> "object of type " + o.getClass().getSimpleName();
    };
}

Results:

> java Basics18.java
M2
error=false
saturday : weekend
saturday : weekend
saturday : weekend
saturday : 4 opening hour(s)
-5 : negative
0 : zero
7 : small
42 : medium
1000 : large
12 : positive integer
-3 : negative or zero integer
java : string of 4 characters
2.5 : object of type Double
null : no object

Comments:

  • lines 5–17: the Java implementation of the algorithm above;
  • line 7: [return] terminates the method [main], and thus the program;
  • line 23: two values for the same actions. Before Java 14, we would have written two successive clauses, [case "saturday":] and [case "sunday":], with the first—which is empty—"falling" into the second;
  • lines 31–34: the same case structure with arrows; no more [break];
  • lines 37–41: a switch expression on a string. It ends with a semicolon, like any assignment statement. The clause *[default]* makes it exhaustive;
  • lines 44–51: a clause whose action is a block: the statement [yield] (line 49) evaluates the expression;
  • lines 76–84: the method [classify]. Its parameter [Integer] receives the integers -5, 0, 7… automatically wrapped (lines 55–59). The [when] guards classify the integer, and the constant 0 is included in the patterns. The [default] clause handles the remaining values, in this case integers greater than or equal to 100;
  • line 61: an array of objects of different types: the numbers 12, -3, and 2.5 are wrapped in [Integer] and [Double];
  • lines 86–94: the method [describe] selects based on the object’s type. On line 91, the variable [s] is of type [String]: its method [length()] can be called without conversion. The clause without a guard, [case Integer i] (line 90), must be placed after the clause with a guard (line 89), which it would otherwise hide: the compiler would reject the program;
  • Lines 68–74: two methods called by the first one, [switch].

docs.title: 3.5.4.1. Known number of repetitions
docs.text:
"for" structure

The syntax is as follows:

for (i = id; i <= if; i = i + ip) {
    actions;
}

Notes:

  • The three arguments of [for] are enclosed in parentheses and separated by semicolons;
  • Each action in [for] is terminated by a semicolon;
  • curly braces are only required if there is more than one action;
  • the curly brace is not followed by a semicolon.

The algorithmic equivalent is the structure for:

for i varying from id to if in steps of ip
    actions
endfor

which can be translated into a while structure:

i <- id
while i <= if
    actions
    i <- i + ip
endwhile

For-each structure

The syntax is as follows:

for (Type variable : collection) {
    instructions;
}

Notes:

  • [collection] is an array or an iterable collection of objects (that implements the [Iterable] interface). We will cover collections ([List], [Set], [Map]...) in Chapter 5;
  • [Type] is the type of the collection’s elements. For an array, this would be the type of the array’s elements. You can write [var] instead;
  • [variable] is a local variable for the loop that will successively take on all the values in the collection. Assigning it a different value within the loop does not modify the collection; you can declare it as [final] to prevent this.

docs.title: 3.5.4.2. Unknown number of iterations
docs.text:
While loop

while (condition) {
    actions;
}

The loop continues as long as the condition is true. The loop may never be executed. The notes are the same as for [for]. The corresponding algorithmic structure is the while structure:

while condition
    actions
endwhile

"Do While" Loop

The syntax is as follows:

do {
    instructions;
} while (condition);

The loop continues until the condition becomes false. Here, the loop is executed at least once. The corresponding algorithmic structure is the “repeat … until” structure:

repeat
    actions
until not condition

General loop structure (for)

The syntax is as follows:

for (start_instructions; condition; end_of_loop_instructions) {
    instructions;
}

The loop continues as long as the condition is true (evaluated before each iteration). The [start_instructions] statements are executed before entering the loop for the first time. The [end_of_loop_instructions] statements are executed after each iteration of the loop. The various instructions in [start_instructions] and [end_of_loop_instructions] are separated by commas. The corresponding algorithmic structure is as follows:

start_instructions
while condition
    actions
    end_of_loop_instructions
endwhile

docs.title: 3.5.4.3. Loop Control Statements
docs.text: InstructionRole[break]Exits the loop [for], [while], [do ... while][continue]advances to the next iteration of the loops [for], [while], [do ... while][break label]exits the loop preceded by the label [label:], even if the statement is inside a nested loop[continue label]advances to the next iteration of the loop preceded by the label [label:]

docs.title: 3.5.4.4. Examples
docs.text:
The program [Basics19.java] is as follows:

// repetition structures
void main() {
    // four ways to compute the sum of the first 10 integers
    int i, sum, n = 10;
    for (i = 1, sum = 0; i <= n; i = i + 1) {
        sum = sum + i;
    }
    IO.println("for (1) : sum=" + sum);

    for (i = 1, sum = 0; i <= n; sum = sum + i, i = i + 1) {
    }
    IO.println("for (2) : sum=" + sum);

    i = 1;
    sum = 0;
    while (i <= n) {
        sum += i;
        i++;
    }
    IO.println("while : sum=" + sum);

    i = 1;
    sum = 0;
    do {
        sum += i++;
    } while (i <= n);
    IO.println("do while : sum=" + sum);

    // the loop variable can be declared in the for: it only exists in the loop
    int product = 1;
    for (int k = 1; k <= 5; k++) {
        product *= k;
    }
    IO.println("5! = " + product);

    // for-each: iterating over all the elements of an array or a collection
    String[] friends = {"paul", "hélène", "jacques", "sylvie"};
    for (String name : friends) {
        IO.println(name);
    }

    // break and continue
    for (int k = 1; k <= 10; k++) {
        // even numbers are skipped
        if (k % 2 == 0) {
            continue;
        }
        // we stop after 7
        if (k > 7) {
            break;
        }
        IO.print(k + " ");
    }
    IO.println();

    // infinite loop exited with break: the first multiple of 7 greater than 50
    int multiple = 50;
    while (true) {
        multiple++;
        if (multiple % 7 == 0) {
            break;
        }
    }
    IO.println("first multiple of 7 greater than 50: " + multiple);

    // break with a label: we exit both loops at once
    int[][] grid = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, -5, 6}, {7, 8, 9}};
    search:
    for (int row = 0; row < grid.length; row++) {
        for (int column = 0; column < grid[row].length; column++) {
            if (grid[row][column] < 0) {
                IO.println("first negative at [" + row + "][" + column + "]");
                break search;
            }
        }
    }
}

Results:

> java Basics19.java
for (1) : sum=55
for (2) : sum=55
while : sum=55
do while : sum=55
5! = 120
paul
hélène
jacques
sylvie
1 3 5 7 
first multiple of 7 greater than 50: 56
first negative at [1][1]

Comments:

  • lines 3–27: four ways to calculate the sum of the first 10 integers;
  • lines 5–7: a standard [for];
  • lines 10–11: all the work is done in the loop-ending statements; the loop body is empty. Java also accepts the syntax [for (...);], without a body, but a semicolon mistakenly placed after a [for] is a classic error that is difficult to spot. An empty block { } expresses the same thing unambiguously;
  • line 25: [i++] returns the value of [i] before it is incremented: [i] is added to [sum], then [i] is incremented;
  • line 31: the most common form of [for]: the loop variable is declared in [for] and exists only within the loop;
  • lines 38–40: the for-each loop iterates through the elements of the array [friends];
  • lines 43–53: [continue] moves to the next iteration for even numbers; [break] terminates the loop as soon as [k] exceeds 7;
  • lines 58–63: an infinite loop [while (true)], which is exited via [break]. This form is convenient when the termination condition is calculated in the middle of the loop. We will use it for keyboard input;
  • lines 67–76: searching for the first negative number in a two-dimensional array. The label [search:] (line 68) names the outer loop; the statement [break search;] (line 73) exits both loops at once. A simple [break] would exit only the inner loop. Java does not have a [goto] statement (the keyword is reserved but unused): labels serve this purpose in this specific case.

docs.title: 3.6. Exception Handling
docs.text: Many Java methods are capable of throwing exceptions, i.e., errors. When a method is capable of throwing an exception, the programmer should handle it in order to create more error-tolerant programs: you should always avoid a sudden termination of an application.

docs.title: 3.6.1. The try/catch/finally Structure
docs.text:
Exception handling follows this pattern:

try {
    code likely to throw an exception
} catch (Exception e) {
    handle the exception e
}
next statement

If the code in the [try] block does not throw an exception, execution proceeds to the next statement; otherwise, execution proceeds to the body of the [catch] block, then to the next statement. Note the following points:

  • [e] is an object of type [Exception] or a derived type. There are many types of exceptions: [ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException], [NumberFormatException], [ArithmeticException], [IllegalArgumentException], [NullPointerException], [IOException], etc. By writing [catch (Exception e)], you indicate that you want to handle all types of exceptions. If the clause code [try] is likely to generate multiple types of exceptions, you may want to be more specific by handling the exception with multiple [catch] clauses:
try {
    code likely to throw the exceptions
} catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e1) {
    handle the exception e1
} catch (NumberFormatException e2) {
    handle the exception e2
}
next statement

The [catch] clauses are evaluated in order; the first one whose type matches the exception is executed. A clause that handles a specific exception type must therefore precede one that handles a more general type: the compiler rejects a clause that could never be reached;

  • a clause [finally] can be added to the clauses [try / catch]:
try {
    code likely to throw an exception
} catch (Exception e) {
    handle the exception e
} finally {
    code executed after try or catch
}
next statement

Whether or not an exception occurs, the code in the [finally] clause is always executed. This clause used to be used to close a file; we will see that there is now a simpler form, the [try] with resources;

  • in the [catch] clause, you may not want to use the exception object. However, you must give it a name: since Java 22, you can write [catch (NumberFormatException _)], where the _ character denotes an anonymous variable that will not be used;
  • The class [Exception] has a method, [getMessage()], that returns the message detailing the error that occurred. To display it, write:
} catch (Exception ex) {
    System.err.println("The following error occurred: " + ex.getMessage());
    ...
}
  • The [toString()] method of an exception returns the full name of its class followed by its message; its [printStackTrace()] method also displays the call stack—that is, the list of methods that were executing at the time of the error—along with the source file name and line number. This is the most useful information for the developer, but it is not intended for the user. In this course, we will most often display the name of the exception class—[ex.getClass().getName()] or [ex.getClass().getSimpleName()]—and its message.

docs.title: 3.6.2. A First Example
docs.text:
The program [Basics20.java] demonstrates an exception generated by using a nonexistent array element:

// an exception caused by an incorrect array index
void main() {
    int[] tab = {0, 1, 2, 3};
    // displaying the array with a for
    for (int i = 0; i < tab.length; i++) {
        IO.println("tab[" + i + "]=" + tab[i]);
    }
    // displaying the array with a for-each
    for (int elmt : tab) {
        IO.println(elmt);
    }
    // generating an exception
    try {
        tab[100] = 6;
    } catch (Exception e) {
        System.err.println("The following error occurred: "
                + e.getClass().getName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
        return;
    } finally {
        IO.println("finally ...");
    }
    IO.println("This line is not executed");
}

Results:

> java Basics20.java
tab[0]=0
tab[1]=1
tab[2]=2
tab[3]=3
0
1
2
3
The following error occurred: java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException - Index 100 out of bounds for length 4
finally ...

Comments:

  • line 14: this statement throws an exception because the array [tab] does not have an element with index 100;
  • line 15: the [catch (Exception e)] clause catches all exceptions;
  • Lines 16–17: The exception is of type [java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException], and its message indicates the incorrect index and the size of the array (line 10 of the results);
  • line 18: the program exits the [main] method, and thus the program;
  • lines 19–20: the [finally] clause was executed (line 11 of the results), even though the [catch] clause contained a [return] statement. Note that the [finally] clause is always executed;
  • line 22: because of [return], this line is not executed.

docs.title: 3.6.3. A Validated Input
docs.text:
Here is another example, [Basics21.java], where we handle the exception caused by converting a string that does not represent an integer to an integer:

// entering an age with handling of the conversion exception
void main() {
    // we ask for the name
    String name = Objects.requireNonNullElse(IO.readln("Name: "), "");
    // we ask for the age
    int age = 0;
    boolean ageOK = false;
    while (!ageOK) {
        // question, reading-checking the answer
        try {
            age = Integer.parseInt(IO.readln("age: "));
            ageOK = age >= 1;
        } catch (NumberFormatException _) {
            // ageOK remains false
        }
        if (!ageOK) {
            IO.println("Incorrect age, try again...");
        }
    }
    // final display
    IO.println("Your name is " + name + " and you are " + age + " year(s) old");
}

Results:

> java Basics21.java
Name: dupont
age: 23
Your name is dupont and you are 23 year(s) old

> java Basics21.java
Name: durand
age: x
Incorrect age, try again...
age: -4
Incorrect age, try again...
age: 99999999999
Incorrect age, try again...
age: 12
Your name is durand and you are 12 year(s) old

Comments:

  • line 4: if the input stream is closed, [IO.readln] returns [null]; [Objects.requireNonNullElse] replaces it with an empty string;
  • lines 8–19: the age input loop;
  • line 11: the line entered via the keyboard is converted to an integer by the [Integer.parseInt] method. This method throws a [NumberFormatException] exception if the conversion is not possible, including when the string is [null]. This is why the operation was placed within a [try / catch];
  • line 12: if we reach this line, it means the conversion was successful. However, we verify that the resulting integer is indeed greater than or equal to 1;
  • line 13: if a [NumberFormatException] exception is thrown, control flows to [catch], where nothing is done. Thus, the Boolean variable [ageOK], initialized to [false], remains at [false]. The exception variable, which is unused, is the anonymous variable _. Only the expected exception is caught: a [catch (Exception _)] clause would also mask errors that were not anticipated;
  • lines 16–18: An error message is displayed if the age is incorrect.

A number that is too large for a [int], such as 99999999999, also triggers a [NumberFormatException]: it is therefore handled like other incorrect inputs (second execution).

docs.title: 3.6.4. Multiple catch clauses and exception throws
docs.text:
The program itself can throw an exception using the [throw] statement:

throw new IllegalArgumentException("error message");

Execution of the current method stops, and the exception is propagated up through the calling methods until a [catch] clause handles it; if none does, the program terminates, displaying the exception and the call stack. In a [catch] clause, the [throw e;] statement rethrows the current exception—for example, after logging it.

Java does not have a filter for [catch] clauses: to handle an exception only in certain cases, you test the condition within the clause and rethrow the exception if necessary. To check a parameter that must not be [null], use the [Objects.requireNonNull(value, message)] method: it returns the value if it is not null, and otherwise throws a [NullPointerException] with the specified message.

The program [Basics22.java] illustrates these possibilities:

// several catch clauses, throwing exceptions
void main() {
    String[] inputs = {"12", "abc", "", "99999999999", "-3", "150"};
    for (String input : inputs) {
        try {
            int age = readAge(input);
            IO.println("[" + input + "] : age=" + age);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            // no filter on a catch clause: we test inside the clause
            if (input.isEmpty()) {
                IO.println("[" + input + "] : empty input");
            } else {
                IO.println("[" + input + "] : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
            }
        } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
            IO.println("[" + input + "] : " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }

    // Objects.requireNonNull throws a NullPointerException if the reference is null
    String[] names = {"dupont", null};
    for (String name : names) {
        try {
            String valid = Objects.requireNonNull(name, "the name is mandatory");
            IO.println("name=" + valid);
        } catch (NullPointerException e) {
            IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

// a method that throws exceptions
int readAge(String text) {
    // Integer.parseInt throws NumberFormatException
    int age = Integer.parseInt(text);
    // we throw an exception ourselves if the age is out of bounds
    if (age < 0 || age > 130) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("age out of bounds [0,130]: " + age);
    }
    return age;
}

Results:

> java Basics22.java
[12] : age=12
[abc] : NumberFormatException - For input string: "abc"
[] : empty input
[99999999999] : NumberFormatException - For input string: "99999999999"
[-3] : IllegalArgumentException - age out of bounds [0,130]: -3
[150] : IllegalArgumentException - age out of bounds [0,130]: 150
name=dupont
NullPointerException - the name is mandatory

Comments:

  • line 3: simulated entries, valid or invalid;
  • line 6: the [readAge] method (lines 33–41) can throw several types of exceptions;
  • line 8: the entries "abc", "", and "99999999999" trigger a [NumberFormatException];
  • lines 10–14: in the absence of a filter, the empty input is distinguished within the [catch] clause;
  • line 15: the exception thrown by [readAge] itself;
  • line 24: [Objects.requireNonNull] throws a [NullPointerException] if [name] equals [null]; its message is the one passed as the second parameter (line 9 of the results);
  • line 38: the [readAge] method throws an exception if the age is out of bounds.

The order of the [catch] clauses on lines 8 and 15 matters: the class [NumberFormatException] derives from the class [IllegalArgumentException] (a [NumberFormatException] is a special case of an incorrect argument). If the two clauses are reversed, the clause [IllegalArgumentException] also intercepts the [NumberFormatException] clauses, and the compiler rejects the clause that has become inaccessible:

Basics22.java:10: error: exception NumberFormatException has already been caught
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
          ^
1 error

docs.title: 3.6.5. Checked and Unchecked Exceptions
docs.text:
Here is an important feature of Java. Exceptions are objects whose classes form a hierarchy:

  • the root class is [Throwable];
  • the class [Error] and its subclasses indicate serious problems with the virtual machine ([OutOfMemoryError], [StackOverflowError]...), which a program does not normally attempt to catch;
  • the class [RuntimeException] and its derivatives ([NullPointerException], [ArithmeticException], [ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException], [IllegalArgumentException], [NumberFormatException]...) generally indicate programming errors or incorrect data;
  • the other classes derived from [Exception] ([IOException], [InterruptedException], [ParseException], [SQLException]...) report incidents caused by the program’s environment (missing file, network outage, database down) that a correct program must anticipate.

Exceptions in this latter category are called “checked exceptions”: the compiler verifies that a method capable of throwing one—either directly or by calling another method—either catches it using a [catch] clause or declares it in its signature with the keyword [throws]:

String readFile(String name) throws IOException { ... }

The responsibility is then passed on to the calling methods. Exceptions derived from [RuntimeException] and [Error] are called "unchecked": they can be caught, but the compiler does not require it, and there is no need to declare them. Many other languages, such as C# or Kotlin, have only unchecked exceptions.

The program [Basics23.java] illustrates these different cases:

// checked and unchecked exceptions
void main() {
    // 1 - readFile declares a checked exception (IOException): it must be caught
    try {
        String content = readFile("missing.txt");
        IO.println(content);
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("readFile : " + e.getClass().getName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
    }
    // 2 - same thing with InterruptedException, declared by waitFor
    try {
        waitFor(100);
        IO.println("wait of 100 ms finished");
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        IO.println("wait interrupted");
    }
    // 3 - an unchecked exception does not have to be declared nor caught
    try {
        IO.println("divide(1, 0) = " + divide(1, 0));
    } catch (ArithmeticException e) {
        IO.println("divide : " + e.getClass().getName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
    }
    // 4 - a checked exception wrapped in an unchecked exception
    try {
        IO.println(readConfiguration("absent.properties"));
    } catch (UncheckedIOException e) {
        IO.println(e.getMessage() + " ; cause : " + e.getCause().getClass().getSimpleName());
    }
    // 5 - the place of a few exceptions in the class hierarchy
    IO.println(ancestors(new NoSuchFileException("x")));
    IO.println(ancestors(new NumberFormatException()));
    IO.println(ancestors(new OutOfMemoryError()));
}

// Files.readString throws an IOException (checked): we declare it
String readFile(String name) throws IOException {
    return Files.readString(Path.of(name));
}

// Thread.sleep throws an InterruptedException (checked)
void waitFor(long milliseconds) throws InterruptedException {
    Thread.sleep(milliseconds);
}

// an ArithmeticException is unchecked: no throws clause
int divide(int a, int b) {
    return a / b;
}

// the IOException is caught then rethrown as an unchecked exception
String readConfiguration(String name) {
    try {
        return Files.readString(Path.of(name));
    } catch (IOException e) {
        throw new UncheckedIOException("unreadable configuration: " + name, e);
    }
}

// the chain of parent classes of the class of an object
String ancestors(Object o) {
    StringBuilder chain = new StringBuilder();
    for (Class<?> type = o.getClass(); type != null; type = type.getSuperclass()) {
        if (!chain.isEmpty()) {
            chain.append(" -> ");
        }
        chain.append(type.getSimpleName());
    }
    return chain.toString();
}

Results:

> java Basics23.java
readFile : java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException - missing.txt
wait of 100 ms finished
divide : java.lang.ArithmeticException - / by zero
unreadable configuration: absent.properties ; cause : NoSuchFileException
NoSuchFileException -> FileSystemException -> IOException -> Exception -> Throwable -> Object
NumberFormatException -> IllegalArgumentException -> RuntimeException -> Exception -> Throwable -> Object
OutOfMemoryError -> VirtualMachineError -> Error -> Throwable -> Object

Comments:

  • Lines 36–38: The [Files.readString] method (Chapter 5) reads the entire contents of a file; it can call a [IOException], which is checked. The [readFile] method does not intercept it: it must therefore declare it using [throws IOException];
  • lines 4–9: in turn, the [main] method, which calls [readFile], must handle the [IOException]. Since the file does not exist, the exception thrown is a [NoSuchFileException]—a class derived from [IOException]—whose message is the file name;
  • lines 41–43: [Thread.sleep] suspends the program for the duration specified in milliseconds; it may throw a (checked) [InterruptedException], which we will discuss in Chapter 8;
  • lines 11–16: The call to [waitFor] must therefore also be placed within a [try / catch];
  • lines 46–48: an integer division can trigger an unchecked [ArithmeticException]; no [throws] clause is required;
  • lines 18–22: The caller still catches the exception because it chooses to;
  • lines 51–57: a common technique when a method cannot or does not want to declare a checked exception: intercept it and throw an unchecked exception instead—in this case, a [UncheckedIOException] (Java 8)—passing the original exception as its cause;
  • line 27: [getCause()] rethrows the original exception;
  • lines 60–69: The method [ancestors] traverses the parent class chain of an object ([getSuperclass()]) up to the class [Object], the root of all classes;
  • lines 30–32: the hierarchy described above is reflected in the results (lines 6–8).

If the clause [throws IOException] is removed from line 36, the compiler rejects the program. It reports both the unhandled exception in [readFile] and the [catch] clause, which has become redundant in [main], since no called method declares [IOException] anymore:

Basics23.java:7: error: exception IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement
    } catch (IOException e) {
      ^
Basics23.java:37: error: unreported exception IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown
    return Files.readString(Path.of(name));
                           ^
2 errors

The [main] method itself can throw exceptions: [void main() throws IOException]. An uncaught exception then terminates the program, which displays the exception and the call stack and exits with a return code of 1. This is acceptable for a small test program, but not for a production application. Checked exceptions are sometimes considered too restrictive, and many recent libraries (Spring, Hibernate, which we’ll use later) use only unchecked exceptions. In this course, we catch a checked exception where we know how to handle it, and wrap it in an unchecked exception otherwise.

docs.title: 3.6.6. Resource Release: The try Block with Resources
docs.text:
A resource (an open file, a network connection, a database connection) must be closed after use, even if an error occurs while it is being used. Before Java 7, it was closed within a [finally] clause, which required several lines of complex code. Java 7 introduced the try-with-resources statement:

try (Type resource = ...) {
    use of the resource
}

The resource declared in parentheses is automatically closed (by calling its [close()] method) when the block ends, whether it terminates normally or due to an exception. The resource type must implement the [AutoCloseable] interface, which contains only the [close()] method; this is the case for all Java file, network, and database classes. Multiple resources can be declared, separated by semicolons: they are closed in the reverse order in which they were opened. Such a [try] may have [catch] and [finally] clauses, which are executed after the resources are closed.

Java 7 also introduced multi-catch: a single [catch] clause can handle multiple exception types separated by the | character: [catch (NumberFormatException | ArithmeticException e)]. The listed types must not be derived from one another.

The program [Basics24.java] is as follows:

// try-with-resources and multi-catch
void main() throws IOException {
    // 1 - a resource is closed automatically when leaving the try
    try (Resource r = open("R1")) {
        IO.println("using " + r.name());
    }
    // 2 - several resources: they are closed in the reverse order of their opening,
    // even if an exception occurs, and before the catch and finally clauses are executed
    try (Resource r2 = open("R2"); Resource r3 = open("R3")) {
        IO.println("using " + r2.name() + " and " + r3.name());
        throw new IllegalStateException("incident during use");
    } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
        IO.println("catch : " + e.getMessage());
    } finally {
        IO.println("finally");
    }
    // 3 - a BufferedReader is a resource; readLine throws an IOException (checked)
    try (BufferedReader reader = new BufferedReader(new StringReader("line 1\nline 2"))) {
        String line;
        while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null) {
            IO.println("read: " + line);
        }
    }
    // 4 - multi-catch (Java 7): the same handling for several exception types
    String[][] operations = {{"10", "2"}, {"10", "zero"}, {"10", "0"}};
    for (String[] operation : operations) {
        try {
            int a = Integer.parseInt(operation[0]);
            int b = Integer.parseInt(operation[1]);
            IO.println(a + " / " + b + " = " + a / b);
        } catch (NumberFormatException | ArithmeticException e) {
            IO.println(Arrays.toString(operation) + " : "
                    + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " - " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

// a resource: an object that implements the AutoCloseable interface (chapter 4)
record Resource(String name) implements AutoCloseable {
    @Override
    public void close() {
        IO.println("closing " + name);
    }
}

Resource open(String name) {
    IO.println("opening " + name);
    return new Resource(name);
}

Results:

> java Basics24.java
opening R1
using R1
closing R1
opening R2
opening R3
using R2 and R3
closing R3
closing R2
catch : incident during use
finally
read: line 1
read: line 2
10 / 2 = 5
[10, zero] : NumberFormatException - For input string: "zero"
[10, 0] : ArithmeticException - / by zero

Comments:

  • line 2: the [main] method declares the checked exception [IOException], which can be thrown by the [readLine] method on line 20 and which we do not catch;
  • Lines 39–44: A demonstration resource. This is a record (Chapter 4), a very simple class in which each object has a name; it implements the [AutoCloseable] interface by defining the [close()] method, which displays a message;
  • lines 46–49: the [open] method displays a message and creates a resource;
  • lines 4–6: the resource [r] is automatically closed at the end of the block (line 4 of the results);
  • lines 9–16: two resources. An exception is thrown while they are in use (line 11). The results (lines 5–11) show that R3 is closed before R2, and that both are closed before the execution of clauses [catch] and [finally];
  • line 18: a [BufferedReader] that reads a string here as if it were a file. We’ll use it in Chapter 5 to read actual files;
  • line 20: [readLine()] returns the next line, or [null] at the end of the text. The assignment takes place within the condition of [while]: the value of the expression [(line = reader.readLine())] is the assigned value;
  • Line 31: a multi-catch: the same action for a [NumberFormatException] (line 15 of the results) and for a [ArithmeticException] (line 16).

docs.title: 3.7. Example Application - V1
docs.text:
We aim to write a program to calculate a taxpayer’s tax liability. We’ll consider the simplified case of a taxpayer who has only a single salary to report. The figures are taken from the 2004 tax schedule for 2003 income and are used as-is: this is a programming exercise, not a calculation of current taxes. This application will serve as our guiding thread: we will revisit it in the following chapters, incorporating classes, files, a database, and then network functionality.

  • We calculate the number of shares for the employee: shares = nbChildren/2 + 1 if he is unmarried, nbChildren/2 + 2 if he is married, where nbChildren is the number of his children;
  • if he has at least three children, he receives an additional half-share;
  • his taxable income R is calculated as R = 0.72 * S, where S is his annual salary;
  • his family quotient is calculated as QF = R / shares;
  • his tax I is calculated using the following table:
thresholdcoeffRcoeffN49620083820.068291.0914,7530.1911,322.9223,8880.2832,668.3938,8680.3744,846.9847,9320.4266,883.6600.4819,505.54

Each row has 3 fields. To calculate tax I, we search for the first row where QF is less than or equal to the limit. For example, if QF = 5000, we will find the row:

8382    0.068    291.09

Tax I is then equal to 0.068 * R - 291.09 * shares, rounded to the nearest euro. If QF is such that the condition QF <= limit is never satisfied, the coefficients from the last line are used: I = 0.481 * R - 9505.54 * shares. The limit 0 in the last row is therefore never used.

The calculations involve amounts and decimal coefficients: we perform them using class [BigDecimal]. The corresponding Java program, [Tax1.java], is as follows:

// tax calculation - version 1
// 2004 tax scale (2003 income): this is an exercise, not the tax scale in force
void main() {
    // data arrays needed for the tax calculation
    BigDecimal[] limits = decimals("4962", "8382", "14753", "23888", "38868", "47932", "0");
    BigDecimal[] coeffR = decimals("0", "0.068", "0.191", "0.283", "0.374", "0.426", "0.481");
    BigDecimal[] coeffN = decimals("0", "291.09", "1322.92", "2668.39", "4846.98", "6883.66", "9505.54");

    // marital status
    String answer;
    while (true) {
        answer = read("Are you married (Y/N)? ").toLowerCase();
        if (answer.equals("y") || answer.equals("n")) {
            break;
        }
        System.err.println("Incorrect answer. Try again");
    }
    boolean married = answer.equals("y");

    // number of children
    int nbChildren;
    while (true) {
        try {
            nbChildren = Integer.parseInt(read("Number of children: "));
            if (nbChildren >= 0) {
                break;
            }
        } catch (NumberFormatException _) {
            // non-numeric input: we start again
        }
        System.err.println("Incorrect answer. Try again");
    }

    // annual salary
    int salary;
    while (true) {
        try {
            salary = Integer.parseInt(read("Annual salary: "));
            if (salary >= 0) {
                break;
            }
        } catch (NumberFormatException _) {
            // non-numeric input: we start again
        }
        System.err.println("Incorrect answer. Try again");
    }

    // number of shares
    BigDecimal shares = BigDecimal.valueOf(nbChildren).divide(BigDecimal.TWO)
            .add(BigDecimal.valueOf(married ? 2 : 1));
    if (nbChildren >= 3) {
        shares = shares.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));
    }

    // taxable income
    BigDecimal income = new BigDecimal("0.72").multiply(BigDecimal.valueOf(salary));

    // family quotient (the division may not come out exact: a precision is set)
    BigDecimal quotient = income.divide(shares, MathContext.DECIMAL128);

    // searching for the tax bracket: the first one such that quotient <= limit,
    // the last one if none fits
    int i = 0;
    while (i < limits.length - 1 && quotient.compareTo(limits[i]) > 0) {
        i++;
    }

    // the tax (truncated to the euro)
    int tax = coeffR[i].multiply(income).subtract(coeffN[i].multiply(shares)).intValue();

    // displaying the result
    IO.println("Tax to pay: " + tax + " euros");
}

// displays a prompt, reads a line and returns it without leading and trailing spaces
// (empty string if the input stream is exhausted)
String read(String prompt) {
    return Objects.requireNonNullElse(IO.readln(prompt), "").trim();
}

// converts strings into exact BigDecimal numbers
BigDecimal[] decimals(String... values) {
    BigDecimal[] numbers = new BigDecimal[values.length];
    for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
        numbers[i] = new BigDecimal(values[i]);
    }
    return numbers;
}

Comments:

  • Lines 5–7: The three arrays in [BigDecimal] are constructed by the method [decimals] (lines 82–88) from character strings: each value, such as 0.068, is thus exact. With a [double], 0.068 would be only a binary approximation. The [decimals] method accepts any number of parameters ([String... values]), which it receives in an array; this notation is explained in the section “Passing Parameters to a Function”;
  • lines 10–18: entering the marital status, in a loop [while (true)] that exits via [break] when the answer is correct;
  • line 12: the method [read] (lines 77–79) displays the prompt and reads the response; if the input stream is closed, the value [null] is replaced with an empty string. The method [trim()] removes leading and trailing spaces from the read string, and [toLowerCase()] converts it to lowercase. This allows both Y and y to be accepted;
  • line 13: strings are compared using [equals], never with ==;
  • line 16: error messages are written to the stream [System.err];
  • line 18: the Boolean variable [married] is assigned the value [true] or [false] from the expression [answer.equals("y")];
  • Lines 21–32: Enter the number of children. [Integer.parseInt] triggers a [NumberFormatException] if the input is not an integer: the program then proceeds to the [catch] clause (line 28), which does nothing, then displays the error message and restarts. If the conversion succeeds and the number is positive or zero, the loop is exited (line 26). The variable [nbChildren], declared without a value on line 21, always has a value when the loop is exited: the compiler checks this;
  • lines 35–46: same thing for the salary;
  • lines 49–50: the number of shares is calculated in [BigDecimal]. You cannot simply write [nbChildren / 2]: if nbChildren is 3, you would get 3/2, an integer division that would result in 1 rather than 1.5. [BigDecimal.valueOf(nbChildren)] converts the integer, [divide(BigDecimal.TWO)] divides it by two (the constant [TWO] has existed since Java 19), and [add] adds 2 or 1. The method calls are chained together: each one applies to the result of the previous one;
  • line 52: a [BigDecimal] is immutable: [add] does not modify [shares] but returns a new object, which must be assigned to the variable. Writing only [shares.add(new BigDecimal("0.5"));] would have no effect: this is a classic pitfall;
  • line 56: taxable income;
  • line 59: the family quotient. Dividing income by 1.5 or 3.5 shares generally does not result in a finite decimal representation: we set a precision, here [MathContext.DECIMAL128] (34 significant digits), which is more than sufficient;
  • lines 63–66: determining the tax bracket. The search stops at the first upper limit that is greater than or equal to the family quotient, and no later than the last bracket, thanks to the condition [i < limits.length - 1]. The operators < and > do not apply to [BigDecimal]: [quotient.compareTo(limits[i]) > 0] means “quotient > limits[i].” Two [BigDecimal] values are not compared with [equals], which takes the number of decimal places into account: 2.0 and 2.00 are not “equal” for [equals];
  • Line 69: The tax amount is rounded to the nearest euro using method [intValue()], which discards the decimal portion.

Here are some examples of the output:

> java Tax1.java
Are you married (Y/N)? y
Number of children: 2
Annual salary: 60000
Tax to pay: 4282 euros

> java Tax1.java
Are you married (Y/N)? yes
Incorrect answer. Try again
Are you married (Y/N)? y
Number of children: three
Incorrect answer. Try again
Number of children: 3
Annual salary: 60000 euros
Incorrect answer. Try again
Annual salary: 60000
Tax to pay: 2959 euros
> java Tax1.java
Are you married (Y/N)? n
Number of children: 0
Annual salary: 60000
Tax to pay: 11519 euros

For an annual salary of 60,000 euros, a married taxpayer with 2 children pays 4,282 euros; with 3 children, 2,959 euros; and a single person with no children pays 11,519 euros. In the second run, the input “60000 euros” is rejected: [Integer.parseInt] accepts only strings that represent an exact integer (leading and trailing spaces were removed by [trim()]).

docs.title: 3.8. Main Program Arguments
docs.text:
The main method [main] can accept an array of strings [String[]] as a parameter. This array contains the command-line arguments used to launch the application. Thus, if we launch program P with the command:

java P arg0 arg1 ... argn

and if the method [main] is declared as follows:

    public static void main(String[] args) {

we will have args[0]="arg0", args[1]="arg1", and so on. In a compact file, you can obtain the same array by declaring [void main(String[] args)]. With the source file launcher, the arguments for the program are placed after the file name; the options for the [java] command itself (such as [-cp] or [-D]) are placed before:

java Prog.java a0 a1 a2

Here is an example, [Basics25.java]:

// the command-line arguments in a compact source file
void main(String[] args) {
    IO.println("There are " + args.length + " argument(s)");
    for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) {
        IO.println("args[" + i + "]=" + args[i]);
    }
}

Results:

> java Basics25.java a0 a1 a2 a3
There are 4 argument(s)
args[0]=a0
args[1]=a1
args[2]=a2
args[3]=a3

An argument that contains spaces must be enclosed in quotation marks:

> java Basics25.java "jean dupont" 23
There are 2 argument(s)
args[0]=jean dupont
args[1]=23

The same program written using a class and a standard method:

// the command-line arguments with a classic main method
public class Basics26 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("There are " + args.length + " argument(s)");
        for (int i = 0; i < args.length; i++) {
            System.out.println("args[" + i + "]=" + args[i]);
        }
    }
}

Results:

> java Basics26.java a0 a1 a2 a3
There are 4 argument(s)
args[0]=a0
args[1]=a1
args[2]=a2
args[3]=a3

Comments:

  • line 2: a public class, in the file [Basics26.java];
  • line 3: the program's entry point, in its standard form;
  • lines 4–7: the rest is identical to [Basics25.java], with [System.out.println] replacing [IO.println].

An application organized into packages places its classes in folders that match the names of the packages (Chapter 4); this is also how Maven projects are organized, which we will begin using in Chapter 5. Finally, note that in Java, the method [main] does not return a value: the program’s exit code is set using [System.exit].

docs.title: 3.9. Enumerations
docs.text:
An enumeration is a data type whose value domain consists of a set of named constants. Consider a program that needs to handle exam grades. There are five possible grades: Pass, Fairly Good, Good, Very Good, and Excellent. We can then define an enumeration for these five constants:

enum Honours { PASS, FAIRLY_GOOD, GOOD, VERY_GOOD, EXCELLENT }

By convention, the names of the constants are written in uppercase. A variable can be declared to take its values from the enumeration:

    Honours myHonours = Honours.PASS;

You can compare a variable to the different possible values of the enumeration using the == operator:

    if (myHonours == Honours.PASS) {
        IO.println("Could do better");
    }

Unlike in other languages where an enumeration is simply a set of named integers, a Java enumeration is a class—derived from the [java.lang.Enum] class—whose only objects are the declared constants. Each constant is a unique object, created once and for all; this is why they can be compared using ==. Each constant knows its name ([name()], or [toString()]) and its ordinal number in the declaration ([ordinal()], starting from 0). The compiler adds two static methods to every enum:

  • [Honours.values()] returns the array of constants from the enumeration [Honours], in the order in which they were declared;
  • [Honours.valueOf(name)] returns the constant named [name], and throws a [IllegalArgumentException] if no constant has that name.

An enumeration cannot be converted to an integer, nor can an integer be converted to an enumeration: you must use [ordinal()] and [values()].

The program [Basics27.java] highlights what has just been written:

// enumerations
enum Honours { PASS, FAIRLY_GOOD, GOOD, VERY_GOOD, EXCELLENT }

void main() {
    // a variable that takes its values from the Honours enumeration
    Honours myHonours = Honours.PASS;
    // displaying the value of the variable
    IO.println("honours=" + myHonours);
    // test with a value of the enumeration
    if (myHonours == Honours.PASS) {
        IO.println("Could do better");
    }
    // list of the honours: name and ordinal number
    for (Honours m : Honours.values()) {
        IO.println(m + " = " + m.ordinal());
    }
    // ordinal number --> enumeration
    Honours m3 = Honours.values()[3];
    IO.println("Honours.values()[3] = " + m3);
    // string --> enumeration
    Honours m2 = Honours.valueOf("GOOD");
    IO.println("m2=" + m2 + ", m2 after PASS : " + (m2.compareTo(Honours.PASS) > 0));
    try {
        Honours.valueOf("Good");
    } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) {
        IO.println("valueOf(\"Good\") : " + e.getMessage());
    }
    // an enumeration in a switch expression: no default needed if all cases are handled
    String assessment = switch (myHonours) {
        case PASS, FAIRLY_GOOD -> "correct";
        case GOOD, VERY_GOOD -> "very correct";
        case EXCELLENT -> "remarkable";
    };
    IO.println("assessment: " + assessment);
    IO.println("type: " + Honours.class.getName());
    IO.println("parent class: " + Honours.class.getSuperclass().getName());
}

Results:

> java Basics27.java
honours=PASS
Could do better
PASS = 0
FAIRLY_GOOD = 1
GOOD = 2
VERY_GOOD = 3
EXCELLENT = 4
Honours.values()[3] = VERY_GOOD
m2=GOOD, m2 after PASS : true
valueOf("Good") : No enum constant Basics27.Honours.Good
assessment: correct
type: Basics27$Honours
parent class: java.lang.Enum

Comments:

  • line 2: the enumeration declaration. In a compact file, it is placed next to the methods; in a program organized into classes, it is declared—like a class (Chapter 4)—in its own file, [Honours.java];
  • line 6: a variable of type [Honours];
  • line 8: an enumeration constant is displayed by its name;
  • lines 14–16: the list of constants and their index numbers;
  • line 18: the conversion of an index number to a constant;
  • line 21: the conversion of a string to an enumeration constant;
  • line 22: the constants are compared with [compareTo] according to their order of declaration: GOOD comes after PASS;
  • lines 23–27: [valueOf] is case-sensitive: “Good” is not a constant name;
  • lines 29–33: Enumerations work well with switch statements. The clauses [case] use the constant names without prefixing them with [Honours]. Since all constants are covered, the expression is exhaustive without a [default] clause; if a constant is added to the enumeration later, the compiler will flag the switch expression as incomplete;
  • line 35: the full name of the enumeration is [Basics27$Honours]: in a compact file, the enumeration is a member type of the implicit class [Basics27], and the $ character separates the two names;
  • line 36: The parent class of any enumeration is [java.lang.Enum].

docs.title: 3.9.1. Enhanced Enumerations
docs.text:
Since an enumeration is a class, it can have fields, a constructor, and methods. Each constant is then created by calling the constructor with the parameters written in parentheses after its name. This is a widely used feature in Java that eliminates the need to manage arrays of values associated with constants separately.

To represent a set of options, such as file access permissions (read, write, execute), people used to combine powers of 2 with the | operator (bitwise OR). In Java, we use an enum and the [EnumSet] class—a set of constants within an enum—which is just as efficient as a bitwise combination (it is one, internally) but much more readable. The [EnumMap] class is similarly a dictionary whose keys are the constants of an enumeration.

The program [Basics28.java] is as follows:

// enriched enumerations: fields, constructor, methods; EnumSet and EnumMap
// each honour has a minimum grade and a label
enum Honour {
    PASS(10, "Pass"),
    FAIRLY_GOOD(12, "Fairly good"),
    GOOD(14, "Good"),
    VERY_GOOD(16, "Very good"),
    EXCELLENT(18, "Excellent");

    // the fields of each constant
    private final int minimumGrade;
    private final String label;

    // the constructor is called once for each constant
    Honour(int minimumGrade, String label) {
        this.minimumGrade = minimumGrade;
        this.label = label;
    }

    int getMinimumGrade() {
        return minimumGrade;
    }

    String getLabel() {
        return label;
    }

    // a static method: the honour matching a grade (empty if grade < 10)
    static Optional<Honour> forGrade(double grade) {
        Honour result = null;
        for (Honour m : values()) {
            if (grade >= m.minimumGrade) {
                result = m;
            }
        }
        return Optional.ofNullable(result);
    }
}

// access rights: a set of values will be represented by an EnumSet
enum Right { READ, WRITE, EXECUTE }

void main() {
    for (Honour m : Honour.values()) {
        IO.println(m + " : \"" + m.getLabel() + "\" from " + m.getMinimumGrade());
    }
    double[] grades = {8.5, 12, 15.5, 19};
    for (double grade : grades) {
        String label = Honour.forGrade(grade).map(Honour::getLabel).orElse("no honours");
        IO.println("grade " + grade + " : " + label);
    }

    // EnumSet: a set of values of an enumeration (replaces bit combinations)
    EnumSet<Right> rights = EnumSet.of(Right.READ, Right.WRITE);
    IO.println("rights=" + rights + ", read : " + rights.contains(Right.READ)
            + ", execute : " + rights.contains(Right.EXECUTE));
    rights.add(Right.EXECUTE);
    rights.remove(Right.WRITE);
    IO.println("rights=" + rights);
    IO.println("all=" + EnumSet.allOf(Right.class) + ", none=" + EnumSet.noneOf(Right.class)
            + ", complement of [READ]=" + EnumSet.complementOf(EnumSet.of(Right.READ)));
    IO.println("from FAIRLY_GOOD to VERY_GOOD : " + EnumSet.range(Honour.FAIRLY_GOOD, Honour.VERY_GOOD));

    // EnumMap: a dictionary whose keys are the values of an enumeration (chapter 5)
    EnumMap<Honour, Integer> headcounts = new EnumMap<>(Honour.class);
    headcounts.put(Honour.GOOD, 7);
    headcounts.put(Honour.PASS, 12);
    IO.println("headcounts=" + headcounts);
}

Results:

> java Basics28.java
PASS : "Pass" from 10
FAIRLY_GOOD : "Fairly good" from 12
GOOD : "Good" from 14
VERY_GOOD : "Very good" from 16
EXCELLENT : "Excellent" from 18
grade 8.5 : no honours
grade 12.0 : Fairly good
grade 15.5 : Good
grade 19.0 : Excellent
rights=[READ, WRITE], read : true, execute : false
rights=[READ, EXECUTE]
all=[READ, WRITE, EXECUTE], none=[], complement of [READ]=[WRITE, EXECUTE]
from FAIRLY_GOOD to VERY_GOOD : [FAIRLY_GOOD, GOOD, VERY_GOOD]
headcounts={PASS=12, GOOD=7}

Comments:

  • lines 4–8: the constants of the enumeration, each with its two parameters. The semicolon after the last constant is required when members follow it;
  • lines 11–12: the fields of each constant. They are [private] (accessible only within the enumeration) and [final] (set once and for all);
  • lines 15–18: the constructor, called once for each constant when the enumeration is first used. The keyword [this] refers to the object being constructed: [this.minimumGrade] is the field, and [minimumGrade] is the parameter. An enumeration’s constructor is implicitly private: you cannot create additional constants;
  • lines 20–26: two methods that return the values of the fields. The names [getMinimumGrade] and [getLabel] follow the Java getter and setter convention, as described in Chapter 4;
  • lines 29–37: a static method, which is called on the enum itself ([Honour.forGrade(grade)]). Since the constants are declared in ascending order by score, the last one to reach the minimum score is the correct one. The result is a [Optional], which is empty if the score is less than 10;
  • line 41: a simple enumeration for access rights;
  • lines 44–46: the list of entries with their fields;
  • line 49: [map(Honour::getLabel)] transforms [Optional<Honour>] into [Optional<String>] containing the label; [orElse] provides text when [Optional] is empty;
  • line 54: a set of two rights;
  • lines 55–56: the method [contains] checks whether a constant belongs to the set, just as one would check a bit;
  • lines 57–58: constants are added and removed;
  • lines 60–61: the set of all constants, the empty set, and the complement of a set;
  • line 62: the constants between two constants, in the order in which they were declared;
  • lines 65–68: a [EnumMap] associates a set of values with certain entries. Its keys are always traversed in the order in which the constants were declared: PASS appears before GOOD, even though it was added later. Dictionaries are discussed in Chapter 5.

docs.title: 3.10. Passing Parameters to a Function
docs.text:
In Java, functions are called methods: they always belong to a class, possibly the implicit class of a compact file. Here, we focus on how parameters are passed to a method. Consider the following method:

void changeInt(int a) {
    a = 30;
    IO.println("Formal parameter a=" + a);
}

In the method definition, on line 1, [a] is called a formal parameter. It is included solely for the purposes of defining the method [changeInt]. It could just as easily have been named [b]. Let’s now consider an instance of this method:

    int age = 20;
    changeInt(age);
    IO.println("Actual parameter age=" + age);

Here, in the statement on line 2, [age] is the actual parameter that will pass its value to the formal parameter [a]. We are interested in how a formal parameter retrieves the value of an actual parameter.

docs.title: 3.10.1. Pass-by-value: Java’s only parameter-passing mode
docs.text:
Java has only one mode of parameter passing: pass-by-value. The value of the actual parameter is copied into the corresponding formal parameter. These are two distinct entities: if the method modifies the formal parameter, the actual parameter remains unchanged.

When the parameter is of a reference type (an array, an object), the copied value is the reference: the formal parameter and the actual parameter then refer to the same object. The method can therefore modify this object, if it is modifiable, and the caller will see the change; however, it cannot cause the caller’s variable to refer to a different object.

Unlike other languages, Java does not support pass-by-reference, in which the formal parameter and the actual parameter would be one and the same variable: a method cannot modify a local variable of its caller, nor can it “return” results to the caller via its parameters. Instead, we use:

  • the method’s return value, which the caller assigns to its variable;
  • a record when the method needs to return multiple values;
  • an array or a mutable object passed as a parameter, into which the method places its results.

Furthermore, a parameter declared as [final] cannot be assigned a new value within the method: the compiler thus ensures that it retains the value passed by the caller.

The program [Basics29.java] illustrates these different cases:

// parameter passing: always by value
void main() {
    // 1 - passing by value: the actual parameter is not modified
    int age = 20;
    changeInt(age);
    IO.println("Actual parameter age=" + age);

    // 2 - to modify a variable of the caller: the method returns the new value
    int age2 = 20;
    age2 = changeInt2(age2);
    IO.println("Actual parameter age2=" + age2);

    // 3 - to return several values: a record
    Conversion c1 = convert("123");
    Conversion c2 = convert("12x");
    IO.println("c1=" + c1 + ", c2=" + c2);
    if (c1.succeeded()) {
        IO.println("value of c1: " + c1.value());
    }

    // 4 - a swap of values: the values are stored in an array
    int[] xy = {1, 2};
    swap(xy);
    IO.println("after swap: x=" + xy[0] + ", y=" + xy[1]);

    // 5 - an array passed by value: it is its reference that is copied
    int[] array = {1, 2, 3};
    modifyArray(array);
    IO.println("array=" + Arrays.toString(array));

    // 6 - a modifiable (mutable) object: the method modifies the referenced object
    StringBuilder message = new StringBuilder("Hello");
    complete(message);
    IO.println("message=" + message);

    // 7 - a final parameter cannot receive a new value in the method
    BigDecimal price = new BigDecimal("100");
    IO.println("InclTax(" + price + ")=" + inclTax(price));
}

// the result of a conversion: success and value obtained
record Conversion(boolean succeeded, int value) {}

void changeInt(int a) {
    a = 30;
    IO.println("Formal parameter a=" + a);
}

int changeInt2(int a2) {
    a2 = 30;
    IO.println("Formal parameter a2=" + a2);
    return a2;
}

Conversion convert(String text) {
    try {
        return new Conversion(true, Integer.parseInt(text));
    } catch (NumberFormatException _) {
        return new Conversion(false, 0);
    }
}

void swap(int[] t) {
    int temp = t[0];
    t[0] = t[1];
    t[1] = temp;
}

void modifyArray(int[] t) {
    // we modify the referenced array: the caller sees the modification
    t[0] = 100;
    // we make t point to another array: the caller does not see it
    t = new int[]{7, 8, 9};
    IO.println("in modifyArray: t=" + Arrays.toString(t));
}

void complete(StringBuilder text) {
    text.append(" everyone");
}

BigDecimal inclTax(final BigDecimal amount) {
    // amount = BigDecimal.ZERO; would be rejected: the parameter is final
    return amount.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.2"));
}

Results:

> java Basics29.java
Formal parameter a=30
Actual parameter age=20
Formal parameter a2=30
Actual parameter age2=30
c1=Conversion[succeeded=true, value=123], c2=Conversion[succeeded=false, value=0]
value of c1: 123
after swap: x=2, y=1
in modifyArray: t=[7, 8, 9]
array=[100, 2, 3]
message=Hello everyone
InclTax(100)=120.0

Comments:

  • lines 4–6: The value 20 of the actual parameter [age] was copied into the formal parameter [a] (line 44). This parameter was then modified (line 45). The actual parameter remained unchanged;
  • lines 9–11: The method [changeInt2] (lines 49–53) returns its new value, which the caller assigns to its own variable [age2];
  • line 42: a record (Java 16) declares, in a single line, a class whose objects contain two immutable values, [succeeded] and [value].
