<-- Redirection to http://localhost:27110/loop -->

HTTP/1.1 302 Temporary Redirect
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:40:37 GMT
Location: /loop

<-- Giving up: more than 3 redirections -->

Our client followed three redirects and then gave up (line 24). With the command [HEAD], no document was sent.

The web server log recorded all requests for the entries [A web client] and [A web client that handles redirects]:

> java Internet03.java
Web server started on http://localhost:27110
HEAD / HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /hello?name=Serge HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /unknown HTTP/1.1 -> 404
GET /old HTTP/1.1 -> 302
GET /old HTTP/1.1 -> 302
GET /hello?name=visitor HTTP/1.1 -> 200
GET /moved HTTP/1.1 -> 301
GET / HTTP/1.1 -> 200
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302
HEAD /loop HTTP/1.1 -> 302

For each redirection, it shows the request that triggered it, followed by the request to the new address (lines 7–8 and 9–10), and the four requests from the interrupted loop (lines 11–14).

Writing a client HTTP on TCP helps you understand the protocol, but a real client must handle many other things: TLS encryption, chunked transmission, compression, persistent connections, HTTP/2… The second part of this chapter introduces the Java class [HttpClient], which handles all of this for us.

docs.title: 12.7. Java Classes Specialized for a Protocol
docs.text:
In the previous examples, the HTTP protocol was handled using a TCP client: we had to construct the requests ourselves, parse the status lines and headers, and track redirects. We could have built a SMTP or POP client in the same way. There are classes specialized for these protocols: they understand the communication protocol between the client and the server and spare the developer from having to manage it. For HTTP, JDK provides the [HttpClient] class; for email, the Jakarta Mail library is used. We will now present them.

The programs in this second part, like those in the first, are compact source files in the [12-internet] folder, numbered sequentially ([Internet10] through [Internet19]). Those that require a library (Jackson for JSON, Jakarta Mail for email) are Maven projects, organized in a folder of the same name ([Internet10/], [Internet14/], [Internet19/]). The sample application at the end of the chapter is a separate Maven project, [TaxV8]. The ports used are in the form 272xx.

docs.title: 12.7.1. The classes URL and HttpURLConnection, now deprecated
docs.text:
Before Java 11, a Java program that wanted to use HTTP had two classes, which have been available since the earliest versions of Java:

  • the [URL] class, whose [openStream] method returned, in a single statement, a read stream for the document designated by URL;
  • the [HttpURLConnection] class, obtained via the [openConnection] method of [URL], which was more flexible: it allowed the user to choose the HTTP method ([GET], [HEAD], [POST]), add headers, and read the status code and response headers.

These classes still exist in Java 25, but they have not aged well: [HttpURLConnection] is entirely synchronous, supports only HTTP/1.1, is used via a sequence of calls with a fixed order (set the headers before writing the document, read the status code before the document…), and reports error codes via exceptions. As for the constructors of the [URL] class, which did not correctly parse all URL files, they have been declared obsolete since Java 20: you now create a [URI] object, then convert it if necessary using its [toURL] method. A small [Old.java] program containing the [var url = new URL("http://localhost:27210/");] statement generates the following compilation warning:

> javac -Xlint:all Old.java
Old.java:2: warning: [deprecation] URL(String) in URL has been deprecated
    var url = new URL("http://localhost:27210/");
              ^
1 warning

Java 11 introduced the [HttpClient] class (in the [java.net.http] package), designed from the outset for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, for both synchronous and asynchronous requests, and capable of reusing its connections and being used by multiple threads simultaneously. This is the one you should use today. We will not discuss [URL] and [HttpURLConnection] further, as the reader will still encounter them in legacy code.

docs.title: 12.7.2.1. A Test Web Server
docs.text:
To illustrate the capabilities of [HttpClient], we need a web server with more features than the one from Part 1 ([Internet03.java]): it must accept forms, exchange JSON, and be able to handle delays. So we’ll write a second test server, [Internet10], which is also based on the HTTP server from JDK. To exchange JSON, it uses the Jackson library (Chapter 5): it is therefore a Maven project. Again, it is not necessary to understand this program in detail; you just need to know what each URL responds with. The project has the usual Maven directory structure:

12-internet/Internet10/
  pom.xml
  src/main/java/internet/
    Internet10.java      the server
    Person.java          a person, exchanged in JSON format

The file [pom.xml] is as follows:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- a local test web server for the java.net.http.HttpClient clients -->
<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0"
         xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
         xsi:schemaLocation="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0 https://maven.apache.org/xsd/maven-4.0.0.xsd">
    <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

    <groupId>examples.internet</groupId>
    <artifactId>internet10</artifactId>
    <version>1.0</version>

    <properties>
        <maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>
        <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
    </properties>

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Jackson 3 for the exchanges in JSON format -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>tools.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>3.1.5</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

    <build>
        <plugins>
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
                <artifactId>maven-compiler-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.15.0</version>
                <configuration>
                    <parameters>true</parameters>
                    <compilerArgs>
                        <arg>-Xlint:all</arg>
                    </compilerArgs>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
            <!-- mvn exec:java executes the main class -->
            <plugin>
                <groupId>org.codehaus.mojo</groupId>
                <artifactId>exec-maven-plugin</artifactId>
                <version>3.5.1</version>
                <configuration>
                    <mainClass>internet.Internet10</mainClass>
                </configuration>
            </plugin>
        </plugins>
    </build>
</project>
  • lines 8–10: the project ID;
  • lines 12–15: the Java version and the encoding of the source files;
  • lines 19–23: the only dependency, Jackson 3;
  • lines 28–38: the compiler, with all warnings ([-Xlint:all]);
  • lines 40–47: the plugin that runs the main class using the command [mvn exec:java].

The type [Person] is a record:

package internet;

// a person, exchanged in JSON format
public record Person(int id, String name, int age) {
}

The class [Internet10] is as follows:

package internet;

import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpExchange;
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.InetAddress;
import java.net.InetSocketAddress;
import java.net.URLDecoder;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.TreeMap;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

// a local web server that will be the target of the java.net.http.HttpClient clients
// call: mvn exec:java [-Dexec.args="port"]   (port 27210 by default); stop with Ctrl-C
public class Internet10 {

    // the home page: an HTML document
    private static final String HOME = """
            <!DOCTYPE html>
            <html lang="en">
            <head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Test server</title></head>
            <body><h1>Welcome to the HttpClient test server</h1></body>
            </html>
            """;
    // the types of the documents sent
    private static final String TEXT = "text/plain; charset=utf-8";
    private static final String JSON = "application/json";
    // GET /api/persons/n: a person designated by their number
    private static final Pattern PERSON = Pattern.compile("GET /api/persons/(\\d+)");

    // a small "database" of persons, exchanged in JSON format, and its lock
    private final List<Person> persons = new ArrayList<>(List.of(
            new Person(1, "Dupont", 42), new Person(2, "Durand", 35)));
    private final Object lock = new Object();
    // the objects <-> JSON converter
    private final JsonMapper mapper = JsonMapper.builder().build();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        int port = args.length == 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 27210;
        var address = new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port);
        HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(address, 0);
        server.createContext("/", new Internet10()::process);
        // each request is processed by a virtual thread: a slow request does not block the others
        server.setExecutor(Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor());
        server.start();
        IO.println("Web server started on http://localhost:" + port);
    }

    // processing of a request, then console trace: the request, the client port and the status code
    private void process(HttpExchange exchange) {
        String start = "%s %s %s (client port %d)".formatted(exchange.getRequestMethod(),
                exchange.getRequestURI(), exchange.getProtocol(), exchange.getRemoteAddress().getPort());
        try (exchange) {
            respond(exchange);
            IO.println(start + " -> " + exchange.getResponseCode());
        } catch (IOException e) {
            // the connection was cut during the exchange
            IO.println(start + " -> error: " + e.getMessage());
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }

    // the response according to the method and the path of the URL
    private void respond(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        String route = exchange.getRequestMethod() + " " + exchange.getRequestURI().getPath();
        // the parameters of the URL
        Map<String, String> urlParameters = parameters(exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery());
        switch (route) {
            // the home page: an HTML document
            case "GET /", "HEAD /" -> send(exchange, 200, HOME, "text/html; charset=utf-8");
            // a text document built from a parameter of the URL
            case "GET /hello", "HEAD /hello" -> send(exchange, 200,
                    "Hello " + urlParameters.getOrDefault("name", "unknown") + "!", TEXT);
            // the HTTP headers received by the server (alphabetical order), sent back as text
            case "GET /headers", "HEAD /headers" -> send(exchange, 200,
                    new TreeMap<>(exchange.getRequestHeaders()).entrySet().stream()
                            .map(header -> header.getKey() + ": " + String.join(", ", header.getValue()))
                            .collect(Collectors.joining("\n")),
                    TEXT);
            // temporary redirection (302) to a relative address
            case "GET /old", "HEAD /old" -> redirect(exchange, "/hello?name=visitor");
            // a redirection that loops on itself
            case "GET /loop", "HEAD /loop" -> redirect(exchange, "/loop");
            // a server error (500 Internal Server Error)
            case "GET /error", "HEAD /error" -> exchange.sendResponseHeaders(500, -1);
            // a response that takes its time: the virtual thread is suspended during the wait
            case "GET /slow" -> {
                int seconds = Integer.parseInt(urlParameters.get("seconds"));
                Thread.sleep(seconds * 1000L);
                send(exchange, 200, "Response obtained after " + seconds + " s", TEXT);
            }
            // a form sent by POST: what was received is described
            case "POST /form" -> {
                Map<String, String> fields = parameters(readDocument(exchange));
                String type = exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Content-Type");
                String description = fields.entrySet().stream()
                        .map(field -> field.getKey() + "=[" + field.getValue() + "]")
                        .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
                send(exchange, 200, "Content-Type received: " + type + "\nFields received: " + description,
                        TEXT);
            }
            // any text sent by POST: it is sent back in upper case
            case "POST /text" -> send(exchange, 200,
                    "Content-Type received: " + exchange.getRequestHeaders().getFirst("Content-Type")
                            + "\nText received in upper case: " + readDocument(exchange).toUpperCase(),
                    TEXT);
            // the list of persons
            case "GET /api/persons" -> {
                synchronized (lock) {
                    send(exchange, 200, mapper.writeValueAsString(persons), JSON);
                }
            }
            // addition of a person: the server assigns them a number and responds 201 Created
            case "POST /api/persons" -> {
                Person newPerson = mapper.readValue(readDocument(exchange), Person.class);
                synchronized (lock) {
                    int id = persons.stream().mapToInt(Person::id).max().orElse(0) + 1;
                    Person created = new Person(id, newPerson.name(), newPerson.age());
                    persons.add(created);
                    exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Location", "/api/persons/" + id);
                    send(exchange, 201, mapper.writeValueAsString(created), JSON);
                }
            }
            default -> {
                // a person designated by their number, or 404 if they do not exist
                Matcher matcher = PERSON.matcher(route);
                if (matcher.matches()) {
                    int id = Integer.parseInt(matcher.group(1));
                    synchronized (lock) {
                        var person = persons.stream().filter(p -> p.id() == id).findFirst();
                        if (person.isPresent()) {
                            send(exchange, 200, mapper.writeValueAsString(person.get()), JSON);
                            return;
                        }
                    }
                }
                // any other URL gives the 404 Not Found response
                exchange.sendResponseHeaders(404, -1);
            }
        }
    }

    // sending a text document with its status code and its type; no document for HEAD
    private void send(HttpExchange exchange, int code, String text, String type) throws IOException {
        byte[] bytes = text.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", type);
        if (exchange.getRequestMethod().equals("HEAD")) {
            exchange.sendResponseHeaders(code, -1);
        } else {
            exchange.sendResponseHeaders(code, bytes.length);
            exchange.getResponseBody().write(bytes);
        }
    }

    // temporary redirection (302): Location header, without a document
    private void redirect(HttpExchange exchange, String address) throws IOException {
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Location", address);
        exchange.sendResponseHeaders(302, -1);
    }

    // the document sent by the client, decoded in UTF-8
    private String readDocument(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {
        return new String(exchange.getRequestBody().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
    }

    // the name1=value1&name2=value2 parameters of a URL or of a form, decoded
    private Map<String, String> parameters(String string) {
        Map<String, String> result = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        if (string != null && !string.isEmpty()) {
            for (String pair : string.split("&")) {
                String[] fields = pair.split("=", 2);
                result.put(URLDecoder.decode(fields[0], StandardCharsets.UTF_8),
                        fields.length == 2 ? URLDecoder.decode(fields[1], StandardCharsets.UTF_8) : "");
            }
        }
        return result;
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 23: In a Maven project, we write regular classes, with their package ([internet]) and imports, rather than compact source files;
  • lines 40–44: server data: a small “database” of people, the lock that protects it, and the Jackson object [JsonMapper] that converts objects to JSON and vice versa;
  • lines 50–52: all URL objects are passed to the [process] method of a [Internet10] instance. By default, the JDK server processes all requests in a single thread: a slow request would block all others. The [setExecutor] method provides it with a [ExecutorService] that executes each request in a virtual thread;
  • lines 58–70: Each request is displayed on the console along with the client’s port and the response’s status code. The client’s port will allow us to determine whether two requests used the same TCP connection;
  • line 74: the request’s “route,” consisting of its method and the path of the URL ([GET /hello], [POST /form]…), over which the [switch] from line 77 is performed;
  • line 79: the URL [/] returns a small document HTML;
  • line 81: the URL [/hello?name=xx] generates the text [Hello xx!];
  • Line 84: URL [/headers] returns the headers HTTP from the client’s request to the client as text, sorted alphabetically using a [TreeMap]. This will allow us to see what [HttpClient] sends;
  • lines 90–92: a temporary redirect to [/hello?name=visitor] and a redirect that loops back on itself, as in the server from the first part;
  • line 94: a 500 response (internal server error);
  • lines 96–100: URL [/slow?seconds=n] does not respond until n seconds have elapsed. The virtual thread processing the request is suspended during this time, without blocking any system threads;
  • lines 102–110: URL [/form] receives a form sent via the [POST] method and describes what it received;
  • lines 112–115: URL [/text] receives arbitrary text via [POST] and returns it in uppercase;
  • lines 117–148: the “database” of people, exchanged in JSON format. [GET /api/persons] returns the list of people, [GET /api/persons/n] returns person No. n (or a 404 response), [POST /api/persons] adds the person sent by the client, assigns them a number, and responds with status code 201 (Created) and a header [Location] containing the URL of the new person. Since multiple requests can be processed simultaneously by different threads, the list is protected by a lock ([synchronized], Chapter 8). [writeValueAsString] converts an object into a JSON document; [readValue] performs the reverse operation;
  • line 147: any other URL returns a 404 response.

The server is launched in a command window from the [Internet10] folder using [mvn compile exec:java] and remains running there throughout the tests in this section. The requests it received will be presented at the end of the section.

docs.title: 12.7.2.2. Uploading a document: send and BodyHandlers
docs.text:
Using [HttpClient] involves three types:

  • [HttpClient]: the client itself, created by [HttpClient.newHttpClient()] or, to configure it, by [HttpClient.newBuilder()...build()];
  • [HttpRequest]: a request, also constructed by a “constructor” ([builder]): [HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri)...build()]. Unless otherwise specified, this is a [GET] request;
  • [HttpResponse<T>]: the response, returned by the client’s [send(request, handler)] method. The second parameter, a [BodyHandler<T>], specifies what to do with the received document; the [BodyHandlers] class provides the common handlers:
HandlerThe document is returned asBodyHandlers.ofString()character string ([HttpResponse<String>]), decoded according to the character set specified by the header [Content-Type]BodyHandlers.ofByteArray()byte array (an image, for example)BodyHandlers.ofInputStream(), ofLines()byte stream, or stream ([Stream<String>]) of lines, to be read as the document arrives (e.g., a large file)BodyHandlers.ofFile(Path)file in which the document is savedBodyHandlers.discarding()none: the document is ignored

The [send] method is synchronous: it returns the response once its headers and—except for streams—its document have arrived. It triggers a [IOException] in the event of a communication problem, but not for an error status code: a 404 response is treated like any other response. We will look at its asynchronous version, [sendAsync], later.

The program [Internet11.java] is as follows:

import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers;

// first steps with java.net.http.HttpClient: downloading a document
// the [Internet10] test server must be started on port 27210

// the base address of the relative URLs that will be requested
final URI BASE = URI.create("http://localhost:27210/");

void main() throws IOException, InterruptedException {
    // an HTTP client, closed when leaving the try (HttpClient is AutoCloseable since Java 21)
    try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient()) {
        // 1 - a text document: GET request, document received as a string
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve("hello?name=Serge")).build();
        HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
        IO.println("Document received: " + response.body());

        // 2 - the HTTP headers sent by HttpClient, as the server received them
        IO.println("--- headers sent by default");
        request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve("headers")).build();
        IO.println(client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());

        // 3 - an HTTP/1.1 request, with added headers
        request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve("headers"))
                .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1)
                .header("User-Agent", "java-course-client/1.0")
                .header("Accept-Language", "en-US")
                .build();
        IO.println("--- headers of an HTTP/1.1 request with User-Agent and Accept-Language");
        IO.println(client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());

        // 4 - an HTML document, as an array of bytes
        request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve("/")).build();
        byte[] bytes = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofByteArray()).body();
        IO.println("--- the home page is " + bytes.length + " bytes long");

        // 5 - a document that does not exist: no exception, it is up to the program to test the status code
        request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve("unknown")).build();
        response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
        IO.println("--- status code: " + response.statusCode() + ", document: [" + response.body() + "]");
    }
}

Results (the [Internet10] server was launched in another window):

> java Internet11.java
Document received: Hello Serge!
--- headers sent by default
Connection: Upgrade, HTTP2-Settings
Host: localhost:27210
Http2-settings: AAEAAEAAAAIAAAAAAAMAAAAAAAQBAAAAAAUAAEAAAAYABgAA
Upgrade: h2c
User-agent: Java-http-client/25.0.4.1
--- headers of an HTTP/1.1 request with User-Agent and Accept-Language
Accept-language: en-US
Host: localhost:27210
User-agent: java-course-client/1.0
--- the home page is 163 bytes long
--- status code: 404, document: []

Comments:

  • Line 10: [HttpClient] does not have a base address for the relative URL references: we use the [resolve] method from the [URI] class, as seen in the web client from Part 1, which resolves a relative URL ([hello?name=Serge]) from the base URI to obtain [http://localhost:27210/hello?name=Serge]. The trailing slash in the base address is important: without it, the last segment of the path would be replaced by the relative URL;
  • line 14: client creation. Since Java 21, [HttpClient] implements [AutoCloseable]: its [close] method waits for ongoing requests to complete and then releases its resources (connections, threads);
  • Lines 16–18: Three instructions are sufficient to retrieve the document: build the request, send it, and read the response document ([body]). [HttpClient] built the request HTTP, established a connection, parsed the response, and decoded the document;
  • Lines 22–23: Lines 4–8 of the results show what [HttpClient] sends by default: the required [Host] header and a [User-Agent] header specifying the Java version. The headers [Connection: Upgrade, HTTP2-Settings], [Upgrade: h2c], and [HTTP2-Settings] are more surprising: by default, [HttpClient] prefers HTTP/2, and suggests that the server switch to HTTP/2 on the unencrypted connection ([h2c]). Our server, which only recognizes HTTP/1.1, ignored the proposal and responded with HTTP/1.1. With URL and [https], the version of HTTP is negotiated during the establishment of the TLS connection. It is also noted that the JDK server displays the received header names with a single uppercase letter ([User-agent]);
  • Lines 26–30: A more precisely constructed query: the version of HTTP (1.1, which removes the headers from the transition to HTTP/2) and two headers specific to this query. [HttpClient] does not have headers common to all requests: when needed, a method is written to construct the requests. Lines 10–12 of the results show that the headers were indeed received by the server;
  • lines 35–36: the document is retrieved as bytes. Note URL and [/]: a relative URL starting with a forward slash refers to the root of the site from the base address;
  • lines 40–42: a nonexistent document. No exception is thrown: the response has status code 404 ([statusCode]) and an empty document. It is up to the program to check the status code.

docs.title: 12.7.2.3. Request and response: HttpRequest and HttpResponse
docs.text:
Let’s take a closer look at the client and request configuration, as well as the response content:

MemberRoleHttpClient.newBuilder() .followRedirects(Redirect r) .connectTimeout(Duration d) .version(Version v) .executor(Executor e) .proxy(ProxySelector p) .build()Client configuration: redirect tracking ([Redirect.NEVER] by default, [Redirect.NORMAL] to track them, except for [https] to [http], [Redirect.ALWAYS]), maximum connection establishment timeout, preferred version of HTTP, threads used for asynchronous operations, proxy…HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI uri) .GET() .POST(BodyPublisher p) .method(String method, BodyPublisher p) .header(String name, String value) .timeout(Duration d) .version(Version v) .build()the request: method and document sent (for [POST] and [PUT]), headers, maximum response time ([HttpTimeoutException] beyond that), version of HTTPHttpResponse.statusCode(), version()the status code and version of the response (HTTP). There is no method for the message following the code (it no longer exists in HTTP/2)HttpResponse.headers()the response headers, a [HttpHeaders] object: [firstValue(name)] returns the first value of a header (a [Optional<String>]), [map()] all headers in the form of a dictionary: key → list of valuesHttpResponse.body()the document, in the format chosen by [BodyHandler]HttpResponse.uri(), request(), previousResponse()the URI of the response and the corresponding request: in the case of a redirect, this is the last request sent; [previousResponse] returns the previous response (the redirect)

Using these classes, we resume with the web client from Part 1 ([Internet08.java], [Internet09.java]), which was called with a URL and the method [GET] or [HEAD]. The program [Internet12.java] is as follows:

import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpConnectTimeoutException;
import java.net.http.HttpHeaders;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers;
import java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException;

// web client based on HttpClient: displays the status, the headers and the document received
// call: java Internet12.java URL GET|HEAD

final String SYNTAX = "Syntax: java Internet12.java URL GET|HEAD";

void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
    if (args.length != 2) {
        IO.println(SYNTAX);
        return;
    }
    // the URL must be an absolute http or https URL
    URI uri = parse(args[0]);
    if (uri == null) {
        IO.println("Incorrect URL [" + args[0] + "]: give a URL of the form "
                + "http://machine[:port]/document");
        return;
    }
    // the HTTP method
    String command = args[1].toUpperCase();
    if (!command.equals("GET") && !command.equals("HEAD")) {
        IO.println(SYNTAX);
        return;
    }

    // at most 4 requests per requested URL, so 3 redirections followed (5 requests by default)
    // this property is read when HttpClient is used for the first time
    System.setProperty("jdk.httpclient.redirects.retrylimit", "4");
    // the HTTP client: it follows the redirections, except from https to http; at most 5 s to connect
    try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
            .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NORMAL)
            .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))
            .build()) {
        // the request: method, URL, headers, response timeout
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(uri)
                .method(command, HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.noBody())
                .header("User-Agent", "java-course-client/1.0")
                .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
                .build();
        // it is sent and we wait for the response
        HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
        // the status line: URL of the last request, HTTP version, code
        IO.println("The server " + response.uri() + " responded: " + response.version() + " "
                + response.statusCode());
        // the headers of the response
        IO.println("--- headers");
        displayHeaders(response.headers());
        // the document, if the status code indicates a success (200-299)
        if (response.statusCode() / 100 == 2) {
            IO.println("--- document");
            IO.println(response.body());
        }
    } catch (HttpConnectTimeoutException e) {
        IO.println("The connection could not be established within the allotted time");
    } catch (HttpTimeoutException e) {
        IO.println("The server did not respond within the allotted time");
    } catch (ConnectException e) {
        IO.println("Unable to connect to the server " + uri.getAuthority());
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

// a correct absolute http or https URL, or null
URI parse(String url) {
    try {
        URI uri = new URI(url);
        return uri.isAbsolute() && uri.getHost() != null
                && (uri.getScheme().equals("http") || uri.getScheme().equals("https")) ? uri : null;
    } catch (URISyntaxException e) {
        return null;
    }
}

// displays a collection of headers: a name can have several values
void displayHeaders(HttpHeaders headers) {
    headers.map().forEach((name, values) -> IO.println(name + ": " + String.join(", ", values)));
}

Comments:

  • Line 20: As in [Internet08.java], the program verifies that URL is valid (lines 72–80). The schema [https] is accepted this time: [HttpClient] is capable of performing the TLS negotiation;
  • line 35: the number of redirects followed is not a client property but a Java system property, [jdk.httpclient.redirects.retrylimit], which limits the total number of requests sent for a requested URL (5 by default). This value is read once and for all when [HttpClient] is first used: it is set here programmatically before creating the client, but it could also be specified on the command line ([java -Djdk.httpclient.redirects.retrylimit=4 ...]);
  • lines 37–40: the client follows redirects (but not those that would switch from [https] to [http], which would result in the loss of encryption) and waits up to 5 seconds for a connection to be established;
  • lines 42–46: the request, with the requested method (no document to send: [noBody()]), a header [User-Agent], and a maximum response time of 10 seconds;
  • line 48: the request is sent; the response is available once its headers and body have been received;
  • Lines 50–51: the status line. [response.uri()] is the URL from the last request: in the event of a redirection, it differs from the requested URL. [version()] returns a constant from the [HttpClient.Version] enumeration;
  • line 54: the response headers, displayed by the [displayHeaders] method (lines 83–85). A header name can have multiple values: [map()] associates each name with its list of values;
  • lines 56–59: the document is displayed only if the status code indicates success (2xx family);
  • lines 60–68: errors. [HttpConnectTimeoutException] (connection not established within the time limit) is a type of [HttpTimeoutException] (response not received within the time limit), which is itself a type of [IOException]: the [catch], which belongs to the most specific class, must come first. A connection refusal results in a [ConnectException].

Let’s request the site’s root:

> java Internet12.java http://localhost:27210/ GET
The server http://localhost:27210/ responded: HTTP_1_1 200
--- headers
content-length: 163
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:42:17 GMT
--- document
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Test server</title></head>
<body><h1>Welcome to the HttpClient test server</h1></body>
</html>

We find the information we obtained by analyzing the response ourselves using the client TCP: the status line, the response headers [Content-Length], [Content-Type], and [Date], followed by the document. [HttpClient] lists the header names in lowercase: this is the format required by HTTP/2, and [HttpHeaders] performs case-insensitive searches anyway.

A URL that is subject to a redirect:

> java Internet12.java http://localhost:27210/old GET
The server http://localhost:27210/hello?name=visitor responded: HTTP_1_1 200
--- headers
content-length: 14
content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:42:18 GMT
--- document
Hello visitor!

The redirect was followed automatically: the response received is that of URL [/hello?name=visitor] (line 2). Let’s compare this with the first part: the client [Internet09.java] had to read the status line, extract the code, look up the header [Location], calculate the new URL, and repeat the process in a loop limited to three redirects. Here, all of this is handled by [HttpClient]. To handle the redirects yourself, simply do not call [followRedirects]: the 302 response is then returned as-is.

A nonexistent document:

> java Internet12.java http://localhost:27210/unknown GET
The server http://localhost:27210/unknown responded: HTTP_1_1 404
--- headers
content-length: 0
date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:42:18 GMT

The 404 code is included in the response, along with its headers; the document is not displayed. No exception was thrown: it is up to the program to decide what to do with an error response.

The URL [/loop], which redirects to itself:

> java Internet12.java http://localhost:27210/loop HEAD
The server http://localhost:27210/loop responded: HTTP_1_1 302
--- headers
date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:42:19 GMT
location: /loop

After four requests—that is, three redirects—[HttpClient] gives up and returns the last response received, a 302 response.

A server error:

> java Internet12.java http://localhost:27210/error HEAD
The server http://localhost:27210/error responded: HTTP_1_1 500
--- headers
date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:42:19 GMT

A port on which no server is listening:

> java Internet12.java http://localhost:27299/ GET
Unable to connect to the server localhost:27299

The connection was refused ([ConnectException]). Finally, a URL [https] addressed to our server, which only speaks HTTP in plain text:

> java Internet12.java https://localhost:27210/ GET
The connection could not be established within the allotted time

The client sent the first message of the negotiation, TLS; our server, which was expecting a request line (HTTP), did not understand it and did not respond. After 5 seconds, since the secure connection had not been established, the connection timeout expired. On a machine connected to the Internet, a request like URL or [https://dev.java/] would normally be served as HTTP/2 if the server allows it.

One final note on proxies: these are the machines that workstations on a corporate network often must go through to access the Web. By default, [HttpClient] uses the proxy specified by the virtual machine’s system properties [http.proxyHost], [http.proxyPort], [https.proxyHost], and [https.proxyPort] (and none if they are not defined). You can specify a different one using the [proxy] method of the client’s constructor: [HttpClient.newBuilder().proxy(ProxySelector.of(new InetSocketAddress("proxy.example.org", 3128)))].

docs.title: 12.7.2.4. Sending data to the server: GET and POST
docs.text:
A client can send information to the server in two ways:

  • using the [GET] method, the information is part of the URL: [/document?param1=value1&param2=value2];
  • Using the [POST] method, they form the document attached to the request, following the blank line that ends the headers. The [Content-Type] header specifies its format. For a HTML form, the document has the same format as the parameters section of a URL: [param1=value1&param2=value2], with the type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded].

In both cases, the values must be encoded: certain characters (the space, [&], [=], [?], accented letters, etc.) cannot appear as-is in a URL or in a form. To do this, we use the static method [URLEncoder.encode(value, charset)], which generates the form format; [URLDecoder.decode], used by our test servers, performs the reverse operation.

The document to be sent is provided to the request via a [BodyPublisher]; the [BodyPublishers] class provides the most common ones:

MethodDocument SentBodyPublishers.ofString(String text[, Charset charset])text, encoded in UTF-8 by default. The document type is specified by a [Content-Type] header added to the request: [text/plain], [application/json], [application/x-www-form-urlencoded]…BodyPublishers.ofByteArray(byte[] bytes), ofFile(Path path), ofInputStream(...)any bytes, a file, a streamBodyPublishers.noBody()no document

There is no class in JDK that constructs a form: you construct the [name=value&...] string yourself. The [Internet13.java] program is as follows:

import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest.BodyPublishers;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers;

import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8;

// sending data to the server: URL parameters (GET), form and text (POST)
// the [Internet10] test server must be started on port 27210

final URI BASE = URI.create("http://localhost:27210/");

void main() throws IOException, InterruptedException {
    try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).build()) {
        // 1 - GET: the parameters are part of the URL; they must be encoded in it
        String name = "Jean & Marie";
        String url = "hello?name=" + URLEncoder.encode(name, UTF_8);
        IO.println("--- GET " + url);
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve(url)).build();
        IO.println(client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());

        // 2 - POST of a form: the parameters form the document sent to the server
        List<Map.Entry<String, String>> fields = List.of(
                Map.entry("name", "Jean & Marie"),
                Map.entry("age", "42"),
                Map.entry("city", "Angers"));
        // the document: name=value&name=value..., names and values encoded
        String form = fields.stream()
                .map(field -> URLEncoder.encode(field.getKey(), UTF_8) + "="
                        + URLEncoder.encode(field.getValue(), UTF_8))
                .collect(Collectors.joining("&"));
        IO.println("--- POST form, document sent: " + form);
        request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve("form"))
                .header("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded")
                .POST(BodyPublishers.ofString(form))
                .build();
        HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
        IO.println(response.statusCode() + " : " + response.body());

        // 3 - POST of any text, with its type and its encoding
        IO.println("--- POST text");
        request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve("text"))
                .header("Content-Type", "text/plain; charset=utf-8")
                .POST(BodyPublishers.ofString("naïve café", UTF_8))
                .build();
        response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
        IO.println(response.statusCode() + " : " + response.body());
    }
}

Results:

> java Internet13.java
--- GET hello?name=Jean+%26+Marie
Hello Jean & Marie!
--- POST form, document sent: name=Jean+%26+Marie&age=42&city=Angers
200 : Content-Type received: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Fields received: name=[Jean & Marie], age=[42], city=[Angers]
--- POST text
200 : Content-Type received: text/plain; charset=utf-8
Text received in upper case: NAÏVE CAFÉ

Comments:

  • Lines 17–18: The value [Jean & Marie] is placed inside URL. Without encoding, the character [&] would be interpreted as the separator between two parameters, and the server would receive the parameter [name] with the value [Jean]. In line 2 of the results, we see that the space has become [+] and the character [&] has become [%26]: this is the hexadecimal code for the character, preceded by [%]. [URLEncoder] generates the form layout, where the space is encoded as [+]; in the path for a URL, [%20] would be required, but in the parameters section, servers accept both;
  • lines 24–27: the form fields, in the form of a list of (name, value) pairs created by [Map.entry]. A list preserves the order of the fields, which a [Map.of] dictionary would not do;
  • Lines 29–32: The document is constructed by the API stream: each pair becomes [name=value], with names and values encoded, and the pairs are joined by [&]. Line 4 of the results shows the format [name=value&name=value];
  • lines 34–37: the form is sent using the [POST] method to URL [/form], along with its type. The server indicates (lines 5–6 of the results) that it received a document of type [application/x-www-form-urlencoded] and that it extracted and decoded the three fields from it;
  • lines 43–46: text encoded in UTF-8, of type [text/plain]. The server returns it in uppercase (line 9 of the results): the accented characters were correctly transmitted and received.

Let’s review the difference between [GET] and [POST]: a browser displays the parameters of a [GET] request in its address bar, not those of a [POST] request; furthermore, a [GET] request should only be used to retrieve information, while a [POST] request is used to send information or modify the server’s state.

docs.title: 12.7.2.5. Exchanging Objects in JSON Format
docs.text:
Applications today exchange most of their data in the JSON format, described in Chapter 5. JDK does not have a JSON library: [HttpClient] transports JSON documents as character strings, and Jackson is used for conversion between objects and JSON:

  • On the sending side, [mapper.writeValueAsString(object)] generates the document JSON, which [BodyPublishers.ofString] sends with the header [Content-Type: application/json];
  • On the receiving end, [mapper.readValue(json, Type.class)] converts the received document JSON into an object. For a generic type such as [List<Person>], a [TypeReference] is used, which preserves the type parameter that Java removes during compilation.

The [Internet14] program is a Maven project, in which the [pom.xml] differs from that of the [Internet10] server only in the project name ([internet14]) and the main class ([internet.Internet14]). It contains the same record, [Person], as the server. The [Internet14] class is as follows:

package internet;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers;
import java.util.List;
import tools.jackson.core.type.TypeReference;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

// exchanging objects in JSON format with a web server
// the [Internet10] test server must be started on port 27210
public class Internet14 {

    private static final URI BASE = URI.create("http://localhost:27210/");
    // the Jackson objects <-> JSON converter
    private static final JsonMapper MAPPER = JsonMapper.builder().build();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).build()) {
            // 1 - the list of persons: the JSON document is transformed into a list of objects
            List<Person> persons = readJson(client, "api/persons", new TypeReference<List<Person>>() {
            });
            IO.println("--- list of persons");
            persons.forEach(IO::println);

            // 2 - a person
            Person durand = readJson(client, "api/persons/2", new TypeReference<Person>() {
            });
            IO.println("--- person no. 2: " + durand);

            // 3 - addition of a person: the object is sent in JSON format
            var martin = new Person(0, "Martin", 25);
            HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve("api/persons"))
                    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(MAPPER.writeValueAsString(martin)))
                    .build();
            HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
            IO.println("--- addition of " + martin);
            IO.println("Status: " + response.statusCode() + ", Location: "
                    + response.headers().firstValue("Location").orElse("?"));
            // the JSON document received, raw then as an object
            IO.println("JSON received: " + response.body());
            Person created = MAPPER.readValue(response.body(), Person.class);
            IO.println("Person created: " + created);

            // 4 - a person who does not exist
            try {
                readJson(client, "api/persons/99", new TypeReference<Person>() {
                });
            } catch (IOException e) {
                IO.println("--- person no. 99: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }

    // GET [path] and transformation of the JSON document received into an object of type T
    // throws an IOException if the status code does not indicate a success
    private static <T> T readJson(HttpClient client, String path, TypeReference<T> type)
            throws IOException, InterruptedException {
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve(path))
                .header("Accept", "application/json")
                .build();
        HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
        if (response.statusCode() / 100 != 2) {
            throw new IOException("GET " + response.uri() + " : status code " + response.statusCode());
        }
        return MAPPER.readValue(response.body(), type);
    }
}

Results (from the [Internet14] folder):

> mvn compile exec:java
--- list of persons
Person[id=1, name=Dupont, age=42]
Person[id=2, name=Durand, age=35]
--- person no. 2: Person[id=2, name=Durand, age=35]
--- addition of Person[id=0, name=Martin, age=25]
Status: 201, Location: /api/persons/3
JSON received: {"id":3,"name":"Martin","age":25}
Person created: Person[id=3, name=Martin, age=25]
--- person no. 99: IOException : GET http://localhost:27210/api/persons/99 : status code 404

Comments:

  • line 19: Jackson’s [JsonMapper] is created once and for all; it can be used by multiple threads at the same time;
  • Lines 61–71: The generic method [readJson] performs the equivalent of a method that “requests a URL and converts the received JSON document into an object”: it sends the [GET] request with the [Accept: application/json] header, checks the status code (line 67), and converts the document into an object of the requested type (line 70);
  • Lines 24–25: the list of people. The document JSON [[{"id":1,"name":"Dupont","age":42},...]] sent by the server is directly converted into a list of [Person] objects. The expression [new TypeReference<List<Person>>() {}] creates an instance of an anonymous class derived from [TypeReference]: this is the trick that allows Jackson to determine, at runtime, the type [List<Person>];
  • line 27: each person is displayed using the [toString] method generated for the record;
  • lines 30–31: a single person;
  • lines 35–40: the [martin] object is converted to JSON and sent to the server via [POST]. The server responds with status code 201 (Created) and the header [Location], which provides the URL for the new resource (line 7 of the results);
  • lines 45–46: the received JSON document, first in raw form and then converted to an object. The property names are those of the record’s components ([id], [name], [age]), formatted as “camelCase” according to web conventions;
  • Lines 50–55: a nonexistent person: [readJson] triggers a [IOException] for a 404 response.

We’ll revisit these techniques in the next chapter, where the tax calculation server will become a JSON web service.

docs.title: 12.7.2.6. Timeout, cancellation, and client reuse
docs.text:
The [Internet15.java] program illustrates four important points for using [HttpClient] in a real-world application: client reuse, timeouts, request cancellation, and asynchronous requests. The [sendAsync] method of [HttpClient] is the asynchronous version of [send]: it sends the request and immediately returns a [CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<T>>] (Chapter 9), which will be completed when the response arrives. The program is as follows:

import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers;
import java.net.http.HttpTimeoutException;

// timeout, cancellation and reuse of an HttpClient; asynchronous requests (sendAsync)
// the [Internet10] test server must be started on port 27210

final URI BASE = URI.create("http://localhost:27210/");

void main() throws IOException, InterruptedException {
    // 1 - a single HttpClient instance for the whole application
    try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_1_1).build()) {

        // 2 - successive requests: the same TCP connection is reused
        IO.println("--- three successive requests");
        for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
            IO.println(client.send(request("hello?name=trial" + i), BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
        }

        // 3 - a response obtained within the 2 s timeout, then a response that is too slow
        for (int seconds : List.of(1, 3)) {
            IO.println("--- response expected in " + seconds + " s");
            try {
                IO.println(client.send(request("slow?seconds=" + seconds), BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
            } catch (HttpTimeoutException e) {
                IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }

        // 4 - an asynchronous request cancelled by the program after half a second
        IO.println("--- cancellation after 0.5 s");
        CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<String>> future =
                client.sendAsync(request("slow?seconds=1"), BodyHandlers.ofString());
        CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS).execute(() -> future.cancel(true));
        try {
            IO.println(future.join().body());
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            IO.println("Request cancelled (" + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ")");
        }

        // 5 - four simultaneous asynchronous requests with the same client
        IO.println("--- four simultaneous requests of one second each");
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        List<CompletableFuture<String>> responses = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 4)
                .mapToObj(_ -> client.sendAsync(request("slow?seconds=1"), BodyHandlers.ofString())
                        .thenApply(HttpResponse::body))
                .toList();
        // we wait for the end of the four requests
        CompletableFuture.allOf(responses.toArray(CompletableFuture[]::new)).join();
        responses.forEach(response -> IO.println(response.join()));
        IO.println("Total duration: %.1f s".formatted((System.nanoTime() - start) / 1e9));
    }
}

// a GET request to a URL relative to BASE: at most 2 seconds to get the response
HttpRequest request(String url) {
    return HttpRequest.newBuilder(BASE.resolve(url)).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build();
}

Results:

> java Internet15.java
--- three successive requests
Hello trial1!
Hello trial2!
Hello trial3!
--- response expected in 1 s
Response obtained after 1 s
--- response expected in 3 s
HttpTimeoutException : request timed out
--- cancellation after 0.5 s
Request cancelled (CancellationException)
--- four simultaneous requests of one second each
Response obtained after 1 s
Response obtained after 1 s
Response obtained after 1 s
Response obtained after 1 s
Total duration: 1.0 s

Comments:

  • Line 14: A single instance of [HttpClient] is used by the entire program. This is the rule: a [HttpClient] object manages a pool of connections and reuses them from one query to the next; it is designed to be long-lived and can be used by multiple threads simultaneously. Creating a [HttpClient] for each request is a common mistake: each instance opens its own connections, which the system then keeps in reserve for some time after they are closed (TIME_WAIT state of TCP); a program that makes many requests will eventually exhaust the available ports. We created a client in each of the previous programs because they only made a few requests before terminating;
  • lines 58–60: each request must receive a response within 2 seconds at most;
  • lines 18–20: three consecutive requests. We’ll see in the server log that they used the same connection, TCP;
  • lines 23–30: a response that arrives in 1 second, followed by a response that would take 3 seconds; after 2 seconds, the request is abandoned and a [HttpTimeoutException] connection is established (line 9 of the results);
  • lines 34–41: a cancellation initiated by the program. The request is launched asynchronously by [sendAsync], which immediately returns a [CompletableFuture]. A deferred executor ([CompletableFuture.delayedExecutor]) is instructed to call its method [cancel] after half a second; in an interactive application, this would be the effect of a [Cancel] button. Starting with Java 16, canceling a [CompletableFuture] returned by [sendAsync] actually terminates the exchange with the server. [join] waits for the result; for a canceled request, it initiates a [CancellationException];
  • lines 46–49: four requests launched simultaneously on the same client: each [sendAsync] immediately returns its [CompletableFuture], which is transformed by [thenApply] into [CompletableFuture<String>], which will yield the document. The anonymous pattern [_] (Java 22) replaces the lambda parameter, which is not needed;
  • line 51: [CompletableFuture.allOf] (Chapter 9) returns a completed [CompletableFuture] when all four are complete; this is expected by [join]. Each request takes one second to process on the server; the entire operation took one second (line 17 of the results): the requests were processed in parallel, both by the client and by the server.

With virtual threads, the same level of parallelism can also be achieved without [sendAsync]: simply execute four calls to the synchronous method [send] in four virtual threads. Both approaches are valid; [sendAsync] is convenient when responses need to be chained to other asynchronous processes.
