  • lines 3–7: the five requests from [Internet11.java] arrived over the same connection (same client port): the client kept it open between requests;
  • lines 9–10: the redirected request from [Internet12.java] and the request to the new address, made automatically over the same connection;
  • lines 12–15: the initial request to [/loop] and the three redirects that followed before the connection was abandoned;
  • lines 17–19: the requests from [Internet13.java], on the same connection;
  • lines 20–23: requests for [Internet14];
  • lines 24–28: the successive requests from [Internet15.java] all used the same connection. The request that took too long (line 28) was abandoned by the client after 2 seconds: [HttpClient] then closed the connection. The server did not detect this: after 3 seconds, it wrote its response to a connection that the client had already closed, and the system does not report an error for such a write operation. This is why the log shows status code 200;
  • Line 29: The request canceled by the program must have opened a new connection, since the previous one had been closed. Again, the server responded without knowing that the response would not be read;
  • the last four lines: the four simultaneous requests used four different connections, opened specifically for this purpose. In HTTP/1.1, a connection carries only one request at a time; HTTP/2 would allow all of them to be sent through a single connection.

A program that remains running for a long time (a server, a system service) must take one final point into account: a [HttpClient] keeps its connections inactive for a certain period of time (30 seconds by default, adjustable via the system property [jdk.httpclient.keepalive.timeout]) before closing them. In Spring applications, you can also use the framework’s HTTP client, [RestClient] (built on top of [HttpClient] or another library), which adds automatic conversion of objects to JSON; The clients in the next chapter, on the other hand, will simply use [HttpClient] and Jackson, just like [Internet14].

docs.title: 12.7.3. Application: A proxy client for a web translation service
docs.text: We will now demonstrate how [HttpClient] enables the use of web resources, even when those resources were not intended for use by a program.

docs.title: 12.7.3.1. The application
docs.text:
In the 2000s, there were free translation websites on the Web. Users would type in a text, select a translation direction (“French to English,” etc.) from a drop-down list, click a button, and receive a HTML page containing the translation. You can write a [TranslationService] class that does the same thing programmatically: it constructs the URL for the request, queries the site, and extracts the translation from the received HTML page using a regular expression. A graphical interface or another program can then rely on this class; this is referred to as a “proxy” client: the [TranslationService] class acts as a substitute for the website and hides it from its user.

Since our test machine does not have Internet access, we replace the website with a small local site that mimics those from that era: it has the same form (a text box, an old-style drop-down list of translation directions) and displays the translation in the same location on its page. Its “translations” are done word-for-word using small dictionaries: it is the client’s technique that interests us, not the quality of the translation. The client is used by a console test program. The architecture is as follows:

docs.title: 12.7.3.2. The translation site
docs.text:
The program [Internet16.java] is as follows:

import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpExchange;
import com.sun.net.httpserver.HttpServer;

import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8;

// a small word-for-word "translation" website, which imitates a translation site of the 2000s
// call: java Internet16.java [port]   (port 27220 by default); stop with Ctrl-C

// a translation direction: its label and its dictionary
record Translator(String label, Map<String, String> words) {
}

// the translation directions: code -> translator (LinkedHashMap: the insertion order is kept)
final Map<String, Translator> translationDirections = new LinkedHashMap<>();
// a word, possibly followed by an apostrophe
final Pattern WORD = Pattern.compile("\\p{L}+'?");

void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
    int port = args.length == 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 27220;
    translationDirections.put("fe", new Translator("French to English", Map.of(
            "ce", "this", "chien", "dog", "est", "is", "perdu", "lost", "malade", "sick",
            "l'", "the ", "été", "summer", "sera", "will be", "chaud", "hot")));
    translationDirections.put("ef", new Translator("English to French", Map.of(
            "my", "mon", "tailor", "tailleur", "is", "est", "rich", "riche",
            "this", "ce", "dog", "chien", "lost", "perdu")));
    translationDirections.put("fs", new Translator("French to Spanish", Map.of(
            "ce", "este", "chien", "perro", "est", "está", "perdu", "perdido",
            "l'", "el ", "été", "verano", "sera", "será", "chaud", "caliente")));

    HttpServer server = HttpServer.create(new InetSocketAddress(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), port), 0);
    server.createContext("/translation", this::translate);
    server.start();
    IO.println("Translation service started on http://localhost:" + port + "/translation");
}

// the translation page: the form, followed by the translation if a text was provided
void translate(HttpExchange exchange) throws IOException {
    try (exchange) {
        Map<String, String> parameters = parameters(exchange.getRequestURI().getRawQuery());
        String direction = parameters.get("direction");
        String text = parameters.getOrDefault("text", "");
        var page = new StringBuilder("""
                <!DOCTYPE html>
                <html lang="en">
                <head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Translator of the Java course</title></head>
                <body>
                <h1>Translation of texts</h1>
                <form action="/translation" method="get">
                <textarea name="text" rows="4" cols="60"></textarea>
                <select name="direction">
                """);
        // the list of translation directions, written the old way: unclosed <option> tags
        translationDirections.forEach((code, translator) -> page.append("    <option value='").append(code)
                .append("'>").append(translator.label()).append('\n'));
        page.append("""
                </select>
                <input type="submit" value="Translate">
                </form>
                """);
        // the translation, if there is a text to translate
        if (!text.isBlank()) {
            Translator translator = direction == null ? null : translationDirections.get(direction);
            if (translator != null) {
                // word-for-word translation; an unknown word is left as is
                String translation = WORD.matcher(text.strip().toLowerCase())
                        .replaceAll(word -> Matcher.quoteReplacement(
                                translator.words().getOrDefault(word.group(), word.group())));
                page.append("<strong>Translated text: </strong><div class=\"txtTrans\">")
                        .append(encodeHtml(translation)).append("</div>\n");
            } else {
                page.append("<p>Unknown translation direction</p>\n");
            }
        }
        page.append("</body>\n</html>\n");
        byte[] bytes = page.toString().getBytes(UTF_8);
        exchange.getResponseHeaders().set("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=utf-8");
        exchange.sendResponseHeaders(200, bytes.length);
        exchange.getResponseBody().write(bytes);
        // console trace of the requests
        IO.println("%s %s -> %d".formatted(exchange.getRequestMethod(), exchange.getRequestURI(),
                exchange.getResponseCode()));
    }
}

// HTML encoding: the special characters and the non-ASCII characters become &#nnn; entities
String encodeHtml(String text) {
    var result = new StringBuilder();
    text.codePoints().forEach(c -> {
        if (c > 127 || c == '<' || c == '>' || c == '&' || c == '"' || c == '\'') {
            result.append("&#").append(c).append(';');
        } else {
            result.appendCodePoint(c);
        }
    });
    return result.toString();
}

// the name1=value1&name2=value2 parameters of the URL, decoded
Map<String, String> parameters(String query) {
    Map<String, String> result = new HashMap<>();
    if (query != null) {
        for (String pair : query.split("&")) {
            String[] fields = pair.split("=", 2);
            result.put(fields[0], fields.length == 2 ? URLDecoder.decode(fields[1], UTF_8) : "");
        }
    }
    return result;
}

Comments:

  • lines 10–11: a translation direction is a record consisting of a label and a dictionary;
  • lines 20–28: the three proposed translation directions, along with their codes ([fe] for French → English, [ef] for English → French, [fs] for French → Spanish), their labels, and their dictionaries. [Map.of] accepts at most ten (name, value) pairs; for more than that, use [Map.ofEntries];
  • line 31: the site’s single page, [/translation], may receive two parameters: the translation direction [direction] and the text [text] (lines 39–41);
  • lines 53–54: the drop-down list. As was common on websites of that era, the [<option>] tags are not closed: the HTML code on actual websites isn’t always very clean, and our client will have to work around this;
  • lines 65–67: the word-for-word translation. The regular expression [\p{L}+'?] (line 16) matches a word—that is, a sequence of letters ([\p{L}])—possibly followed by an apostrophe ([l'], [d']). We did not use [\w]: in Java, [\w] by default refers only to unaccented letters, digits, and the character [_], and [été] would not have been recognized as a word. The [replaceAll] method of [Matcher] (Java 9) replaces each word with the result of a function: its translation, or the word itself if it is unknown. [Matcher.quoteReplacement] protects the characters [$] and [\], which have a specific meaning in a replacement text;
  • Lines 68–69: The translation is enclosed in a [<div class="txtTrans">] tag, as was common on websites of that era. It is encoded using the [encodeHtml] method (lines 86–96): characters that have meaning in HTML ([<], [&]…) and non-ASCII characters are replaced by numeric entities [&#nnn;]. JDK has no encoding method HTML: web applications use those of their framework;
  • Line 71: An unknown translation direction results in a page with no translation.

Here is the page generated using [curl] to translate [l'été sera chaud] into Spanish; note the text encoding in URL:

> curl -s "http://localhost:27220/translation?direction=fs&text=l%27%C3%A9t%C3%A9%20sera%20chaud"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Translator of the Java course</title></head>
<body>
<h1>Translation of texts</h1>
<form action="/translation" method="get">
<textarea name="text" rows="4" cols="60"></textarea>
<select name="direction">
    <option value='fe'>French to English
    <option value='ef'>English to French
    <option value='fs'>French to Spanish
</select>
<input type="submit" value="Translate">
</form>
<strong>Translated text: </strong><div class="txtTrans">el verano será caliente</div>
</body>
</html>

To write the client, we need to:

  • know what the site expects: a [GET /translation?direction=code&text=encoded text] request. On a real website, we can find this by looking at the URL displayed by the browser after a translation, or the [action] attribute of the form;
  • know where, within the received pages, the information we need is located: the translation directions are in the [<option value='code'>label] tags of the drop-down list (lines 10–12 of the page above), and the translation is in the [<div class="txtTrans">] tag (line 16). You can find this by viewing the page’s source code in the browser.

Two regular expressions (Chapter 5) can be used to extract this information:

  • [<option[^>]*value='(\w+)'>([^<\r\n]+)]: a [<option] tag, followed by characters other than [>], [value='], the code (first group), [>], and then the label—that is, the characters that follow until the next [<] or the end of the line (second group);
  • [<div class="txtTrans">(.*?)</div>]: the translation is the text (first group) between the opening tag and the first [</div>] tag that follows. The quantifier [*?] is “lazy”: it takes as few characters as possible.

docs.title: 12.7.3.3. The TranslationService client
docs.text:
To keep things brief, we combine the [ITranslationService] interface, its implementation [TranslationService], the exception [TranslationException], and the test program into a single compact source file; in a real application, the interface and its implementation would form a separate library. The program [Internet17.java] is as follows:

import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse.BodyHandlers;

import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8;

// "proxy" client of a translation web service: the TranslationService class
// hides from the program the HTTP dialog and the parsing of the HTML pages of the translation site
// call: java Internet17.java [siteUrl]   (by default http://localhost:27220/)

// a translation trial
record Trial(String text, String direction) {
}

void main(String[] args) {
    URI siteUrl = URI.create(args.length == 1 ? args[0] : "http://localhost:27220/");
    try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build()) {
        // creation of the translation service: it queries the site to know the translated languages
        ITranslationService service = TranslationService.create(client, siteUrl);
        IO.println("Translation directions offered by the site:");
        service.translatedLanguages().forEach((code, label) -> IO.println("  " + code + " : " + label));
        // a few translations
        List<Trial> trials = List.of(
                new Trial("ce chien est perdu", "fe"),
                new Trial("l'été sera chaud", "fs"),
                new Trial("my tailor is rich", "ef"),
                new Trial("xx", "ef"),
                new Trial("", "fe"),
                new Trial("hello", "fx"));
        for (Trial trial : trials) {
            try {
                String translation = service.translate(trial.text(), trial.direction());
                IO.println("Translation [%s] of [%s] : [%s]".formatted(
                        service.translatedLanguages().get(trial.direction()), trial.text(), translation));
            } catch (TranslationException e) {
                IO.println("The following error with code " + e.getCode() + " occurred: "
                        + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    } catch (TranslationException e) {
        IO.println("The following error with code " + e.getCode() + " occurred: " + e.getMessage());
        // the possible cause: toString gives its class, followed by its message if there is one
        if (e.getCause() != null) {
            IO.println("Cause: " + e.getCause());
        }
    }
}

// --------------------------------------------------------------------
// the interface presented to the program
interface ITranslationService {

    // the translation directions: code -> label, for example fe -> French to English
    Map<String, String> translatedLanguages();

    // translation of a text in the direction given by its code
    String translate(String text, String direction);
}

// the exception specific to the translation service (unchecked), with an error code
// static: in a compact source file, a class without static would be an inner class
static class TranslationException extends RuntimeException {

    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    private final int code;

    TranslationException(String message, int code) {
        this(message, null, code);
    }

    TranslationException(String message, Throwable cause, int code) {
        super(message, cause);
        this.code = code;
    }

    int getCode() {
        return code;
    }
}

// the implementation: an HTTP client of the translation site
static class TranslationService implements ITranslationService {

    // the options <option value='fe'>French to English of the form
    private static final Pattern OPTION = Pattern.compile("<option[^>]*value='(\\w+)'>([^<\\r\\n]+)");
    // the translation: <div class="txtTrans">...</div>
    private static final Pattern TRANSLATION = Pattern.compile("<div class=\"txtTrans\">(.*?)</div>");
    // an HTML entity: á or ç
    private static final Pattern ENTITY = Pattern.compile("&(#\\d+|\\w+);");
    // the few named entities that can be decoded
    private static final Map<String, String> ENTITIES = Map.of(
            "amp", "&", "lt", "<", "gt", ">", "quot", "\"", "apos", "'", "ccedil", "ç", "eacute", "é");

    // the HTTP client and the address of the site, provided by the program
    private final HttpClient client;
    private final URI siteUrl;
    private final Map<String, String> translatedLanguages;

    // private constructor: the factory method create is used
    private TranslationService(HttpClient client, URI siteUrl, Map<String, String> languages) {
        this.client = client;
        this.siteUrl = siteUrl;
        this.translatedLanguages = languages;
    }

    @Override
    public Map<String, String> translatedLanguages() {
        return translatedLanguages;
    }

    // creation of the service: the translation directions are read from the form of the site
    static TranslationService create(HttpClient client, URI siteUrl) {
        String page;
        try {
            HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(siteUrl.resolve("translation"))
                    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build();
            page = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString()).body();
        } catch (IOException | InterruptedException e) {
            throw new TranslationException("The translation site is unreachable", e, 11);
        }
        Map<String, String> languages = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        Matcher option = OPTION.matcher(page);
        while (option.find()) {
            // the HTML entities (ç...) are decoded
            languages.put(option.group(1), decodeHtml(option.group(2).strip()));
        }
        if (languages.isEmpty()) {
            throw new TranslationException("The site gives no translation direction", 13);
        }
        return new TranslationService(client, siteUrl, Collections.unmodifiableMap(languages));
    }

    // translation
    @Override
    public String translate(String text, String direction) {
        // is the requested translation possible?
        if (!translatedLanguages.containsKey(direction)) {
            throw new TranslationException("The translation direction [" + direction + "] is not recognized", 10);
        }
        // the URL to request: the text must be encoded
        URI url = siteUrl.resolve("translation?direction=" + direction + "&text=" + URLEncoder.encode(text, UTF_8));
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(url).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build();
        Optional<String> translation;
        try {
            // the document is returned as a stream of lines, read as they arrive
            HttpResponse<Stream<String>> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofLines());
            if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
                throw new TranslationException("The site responded with code " + response.statusCode(), 11);
            }
            // the translation is looked for line after line, and we stop as soon as it is found
            try (Stream<String> lines = response.body()) {
                translation = lines.map(TRANSLATION::matcher)
                        .filter(Matcher::find)
                        .map(result -> decodeHtml(result.group(1).strip()))
                        .findFirst();
            }
        } catch (IOException | UncheckedIOException | InterruptedException e) {
            throw new TranslationException("Error encountered during the translation", e, 11);
        }
        // the page did not contain a translation
        return translation.orElseThrow(
                () -> new TranslationException("The server did not send back a translation", 12));
    }

    // decoding of the HTML entities of a text
    private static String decodeHtml(String text) {
        return ENTITY.matcher(text).replaceAll(entity -> {
            String name = entity.group(1);
            String character = name.startsWith("#")
                    ? Character.toString(Integer.parseInt(name.substring(1)))
                    : ENTITIES.getOrDefault(name, entity.group());
            return Matcher.quoteReplacement(character);
        });
    }
}

Let’s start with the interface and the exception:

  • lines 52–59: the interface exposed to the program. The method [translatedLanguages] returns the dictionary of accepted translation meanings for the site, consisting of entries of the form [fe] → [French to English]; the method [translate] translates the text [text] into the direction with code [direction]. It is synchronous: a program that wants to run multiple translations in parallel will execute them in virtual threads;
  • lines 63–82: the service-specific, unhandled exception with an error code, modeled after [TaxException] (Chapter 6). In a compact source file, all declarations are members of the implicit class: a class declared without the keyword [static] would be an internal class, whose instances can only be created from an instance of the implicit class. Interfaces and records, on the other hand, are always implicitly static;
  • lines 65–66: an exception is serializable; [-Xlint:all] therefore requires a version number, annotated as [@Serial] (Java 14).

The class [TranslationService]:

  • lines 88–95: the regular expressions presented above, compiled once and for all, and a third set for HTML entities, which can be numeric ([á]) or named ([ç]);
  • line 98: the service does not create its own [HttpClient]; it receives it from the program, which determines its configuration and lifetime;
  • line 103: the constructor is private. The service can only be created after querying the site; rather than performing this network operation in a constructor, we use a static construction method, [create];
  • lines 115–134: creation of the service. The list of translation directions is read directly from the website itself, which ensures that it is up to date:
    • Lines 118–120: The form page is requested without any parameters;
    • lines 121–123: A communication error is encapsulated in a [TranslationException] with code 11;
    • lines 125–129: Each [<option>] tag found by the regular expression provides a code (group 1) and a label (group 2). The [decodeHtml] method (lines 169–177) replaces the HTML entities with the characters they represent: the site’s labels contain none, but [Français] would become [Français];
    • line 133: the dictionary is made non-editable by [Collections.unmodifiableMap], which preserves the order of [LinkedHashMap];
  • lines 138–166: the translation:
    • lines 140–142: the system checks whether the requested translation direction exists;
    • line 144: the URL request is made, as the text is encoded;
    • line 149: the [BodyHandlers.ofLines()] handler returns the response as soon as its headers arrive; its document is a stream ([Stream<String>]) of lines, read as they arrive;
    • Lines 154–159: The translation is searched for line by line, and the process stops at the first match found: [findFirst] interrupts the stream, and the rest of the page is never read. The stream is closed upon the exit of the [try] with resources, which frees up the connection. The result is a [Optional<String>], which is empty if no line contains a translation;
    • lines 160–162: a communication error results in a code 11 exception. An error while reading the line stream is signaled by a [UncheckedIOException], since the methods of [Stream] cannot throw a checked exception;
    • lines 164–165: if the page has been read in its entirety without finding any translations, a code 12 exception is thrown.

The test program:

  • line 17: the website address can be passed as an argument;
  • line 18: the application’s HTTP client;
  • line 20: creation of the service. The program then interacts with the service only through its [ITranslationService] interface;
  • lines 24–30: a few test runs, including two error cases: an empty text string and an unknown translation direction. Each test run is a [Trial] record (lines 13–14).

Results, with the [Internet16.java] site having been launched in another window:

> java Internet17.java
Translation directions offered by the site:
  fe : French to English
  ef : English to French
  fs : French to Spanish
Translation [French to English] of [ce chien est perdu] : [this dog is lost]
Translation [French to Spanish] of [l'été sera chaud] : [el verano será caliente]
Translation [English to French] of [my tailor is rich] : [mon tailleur est riche]
Translation [English to French] of [xx] : [xx]
The following error with code 12 occurred: The server did not send back a translation
The following error with code 10 occurred: The translation direction [fx] is not recognized
  • lines 3–5: the translation directions were read from the website form;
  • line 9: an unknown word is rendered as-is;
  • line 10: for an empty text, the site returned its form without a translation;
  • Line 11: The translation [fx] was rejected by the service without querying the website.

If the website is unavailable:

> java Internet17.java http://localhost:27299/
The following error with code 11 occurred: The translation site is unreachable
Cause: java.net.ConnectException

On the website side, we find the request for [curl] seen above, followed by those sent by the client: the first for the form, the subsequent ones for the translations (the translation [fx], rejected by the service, did not result in any requests). [URLEncoder] encoded the spaces using [+], whereas URL, which was passed to [curl], encoded them using [%20]:

> java Internet16.java
Translation service started on http://localhost:27220/translation
GET /translation?direction=fs&text=l%27%C3%A9t%C3%A9%20sera%20chaud -> 200
GET /translation -> 200
GET /translation?direction=fe&text=ce+chien+est+perdu -> 200
GET /translation?direction=fs&text=l%27%C3%A9t%C3%A9+sera+chaud -> 200
GET /translation?direction=ef&text=my+tailor+is+rich -> 200
GET /translation?direction=ef&text=xx -> 200
GET /translation?direction=fe&text= -> 200

docs.title: 12.7.3.4. Conclusion
docs.text:
This application demonstrated that [HttpClient] allows us to leverage web resources. The technique is the same every time:

  • determine the URL to query. It is usually preconfigured;
  • query it;
  • find what we’re looking for in the server’s response using regular expressions.

This technique, now known as “web scraping,” is fragile: over time, the URL being queried or the page’s structure may change, and the regular expression that used to find the result may no longer work. It’s a good idea to store this information in a configuration file, but that isn’t always enough; moreover, the terms of use for many sites prohibit it. A robust analysis of a HTML page would, in fact, be better performed using a specialized library, such as jsoup, rather than regular expressions. We’ll see in the next chapter that there are more stable resources on the Web, designed for use by programs: web services. Current translation services, for example, all offer an interface of this type, which accepts and returns JSON.

docs.title: 12.7.4. A SMTP client with Jakarta Mail
docs.text:
A SMTP client is a client of a SMTP server—a mail-sending server—whose protocol we described in Part 1. JDK does not have a class for email. The de facto standard library is Jakarta Mail (formerly JavaMail), whose reference implementation is now called Eclipse Angus Mail. It encapsulates the requirements of an email client: the developer does not need to know the details of the SMTP protocol or those of the MIME message format. Its main classes are [Session] (the configuration), [MimeMessage] (a message), [InternetAddress] (an email address), [MimeMultipart] and [MimeBodyPart] (a multipart message, such as text and attachments), and [Transport], which sends the message. It can also read mail in POP3 and IMAP, and handles the authentication and encryption (TLS) required by real servers.

We cannot send email to a real SMTP server: our test machine does not have Internet access, and, as we mentioned, ISPs block port 25. The email will be sent to a small test server, written in Java and running on the local machine, which will display everything it receives and forward nothing. For real-world use, there are full-featured test servers, such as Mailpit or GreenMail (written in Java), which also provide an interface for viewing received messages.

docs.title: 12.7.4.1. A SMTP test server
docs.text:
Our SMTP server follows the structure of the echo server from Part 1: a loop that waits for clients, one virtual thread per client, and clean termination via Ctrl-C. The service provided to each client is the minimal SMTP dialog presented in Part 1. The [Internet18.java] program is as follows:

import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8;

// test SMTP server: it plays the minimal SMTP dialog and displays the messages received,
// without ever delivering them to their recipients
// call: java Internet18.java [port]   (port 27225 by default); stop with Ctrl-C

final Set<Socket> connections = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
volatile boolean stop = false;

void main(String[] args) {
    int port = args.length == 1 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : 27225;
    // the server only accepts the clients of the local machine (loopback address)
    try (var listener = new ServerSocket(port, 50, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress());
         var services = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
        stopOnCtrlC(listener);
        IO.println("Test SMTP server started on " + listener.getLocalSocketAddress());
        try {
            for (int clientNum = 0; ; clientNum++) {
                Socket client = listener.accept();
                connections.add(client);
                int number = clientNum;
                services.submit(() -> serve(client, number));
            }
        } catch (SocketException e) {
            if (!stop) {
                throw e;
            }
            IO.println("Server stop requested");
            for (Socket connection : connections) {
                connection.close();
            }
        }
    } catch (IOException e) {
        IO.println("The following error occurred on the server: " + e.getMessage());
    }
}

// Ctrl-C: closing of the listening service, then waiting for the end of the main program
void stopOnCtrlC(ServerSocket listener) {
    Thread main = Thread.currentThread();
    Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(new Thread(() -> {
        stop = true;
        try {
            listener.close();
            main.join();
        } catch (IOException | InterruptedException e) {
            // we stop anyway
        }
    }));
}

// the SMTP dialog with a client: C: lines received from the client, S: lines sent by the server
void serve(Socket client, int clientNum) {
    IO.println("--- start of the dialog with client " + clientNum + " ("
            + client.getRemoteSocketAddress() + ")");
    try (client;
         var reader = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(client.getInputStream(), UTF_8));
         var writer = new OutputStreamWriter(client.getOutputStream(), UTF_8)) {
        // sending of a response line, also displayed on the console; SMTP requires \r\n line endings
        Responder reply = response -> {
            IO.println("S: " + response);
            writer.write(response + "\r\n");
            writer.flush();
        };
        // the envelope of the current message: sender and recipients
        String sender = null;
        List<String> recipients = new ArrayList<>();
        // welcome message
        reply.send("220 smtp.test ESMTP test server of the Java course");
        String command;
        while ((command = reader.readLine()) != null) {
            IO.println("C: " + command);
            // the verb: the first four characters, regardless of case
            String verb = command.length() >= 4 ? command.substring(0, 4) : command;
            verb = verb.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);
            // what follows the ":" character in MAIL FROM:<address> and RCPT TO:<address>
            String address = command.substring(command.indexOf(':') + 1).strip();
            switch (verb) {
                case "EHLO" -> {
                    // response on several lines: 250-... then 250 ...
                    reply.send("250-smtp.test hello");
                    reply.send("250-SIZE 10485760");
                    reply.send("250 8BITMIME");
                }
                case "HELO" -> reply.send("250 smtp.test hello");
                case "MAIL" -> {
                    sender = address;
                    recipients.clear();
                    reply.send("250 2.1.0 Ok");
                }
                case "RCPT" -> {
                    recipients.add(address);
                    reply.send("250 2.1.5 Ok");
                }
                case "DATA" -> {
                    // the sender and the recipients are required first
                    if (sender == null || recipients.isEmpty()) {
                        reply.send("503 5.5.1 Give the sender and the recipients first");
                        continue;
                    }
                    reply.send("354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>");
                    // the message: all the lines up to a line reduced to a dot
                    int nbLines = 0;
                    String line;
                    while ((line = reader.readLine()) != null && !line.equals(".")) {
                        IO.println("C: " + line);
                        nbLines++;
                    }
                    // the client closed the connection before the end of the message
                    if (line == null) {
                        IO.println("[incomplete message: connection closed by the client]");
                        return;
                    }
                    IO.println("C: .");
                    IO.println("[message from %s to %s: %d lines]".formatted(sender,
                            String.join(", ", recipients), nbLines));
                    reply.send("250 2.0.0 Ok: message accepted");
                    sender = null;
                    recipients.clear();
                }
                case "RSET" -> {
                    sender = null;
                    recipients.clear();
                    reply.send("250 2.0.0 Ok");
                }
                case "NOOP" -> reply.send("250 2.0.0 Ok");
                case "QUIT" -> {
                    reply.send("221 2.0.0 Bye");
                    return;
                }
                default -> reply.send("502 5.5.2 Command not recognized");
            }
        }
    } catch (IOException e) {
        if (stop) {
            IO.println("Dialog with client " + clientNum + " interrupted by the server stop");
        } else {
            IO.println("The following error occurred with client " + clientNum + ": "
                    + e.getMessage());
        }
    } finally {
        connections.remove(client);
        IO.println("--- end of the dialog with client " + clientNum);
    }
}

// sending of a response line: a functional interface whose method can throw an IOException
interface Responder {
    void send(String response) throws IOException;
}

We’ll only comment on what’s new compared to the echo server:

  • line 13: the server listens only on the loopback address; only programs on the same machine can connect to it. The second parameter (50) is the size of the connection queue;
  • lines 60–64: a lambda that sends a response line to the client, terminated by \r\n as required by SMTP, and displays it on the console, preceded by [S:]. Lines received from the client are displayed preceded by [C:], as in the sample dialogs from Part 1. The functional interfaces of JDK ([Consumer<String>]…) do not allow checked exceptions: so we declare our own functional interface, [Responder] (lines 148–150), whose method can invoke a [IOException];
  • lines 66–67: the envelope of the current message: the sender specified by [MAIL FROM] and the recipients specified by [RCPT TO];
  • line 69: the greeting message: in SMTP, the server speaks first;
  • lines 74–75: the command verb consists of its first four characters ([EHLO], [MAIL], [RCPT]…), capitalized. [Locale.ROOT] makes the conversion independent of the machine’s language (in Turkish, the uppercase version of [i] is not [I]);
  • Lines 79–84: The response to [EHLO] consists of several lines. The server lists its capabilities here: the maximum message size ([SIZE]) and support for 8-bit encoded characters ([8BITMIME]);
  • lines 97–100: the command [DATA] is rejected if the sender or recipients have not been specified; [continue] proceeds to the next command;
  • lines 101–119: the message itself. The server prompts the client to send it (code 354), then reads and displays all lines up to a line reduced to a single dot, and acknowledges receipt (code 250). If the client closes the connection before the end of the message, the message is discarded (lines 110–113);
  • lines 127–130: the client has finished; the server responds and closes the connection, exiting the method (the [try] method with resources closes the socket);
  • line 131: any other command is rejected.

This server does not perform many checks and does not handle the [STARTTLS] and [AUTH] extensions: it is sufficient for observing what Jakarta Mail sends.

docs.title: 12.7.4.2. The SMTP client
docs.text:
The [Internet19] program prompts the user for the email’s details (sender, recipients, subject, attachments, body), then sends it to the SMTP server specified as an argument. This is a Maven project, in which [pom.xml] declares the following dependency:

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Jakarta Mail: the jakarta.mail API and its Eclipse Angus implementation -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.eclipse.angus</groupId>
            <artifactId>angus-mail</artifactId>
            <version>2.0.3</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>

The [angus-mail] dependency provides the implementation and, through transitive dependencies, the API, [jakarta.mail], and [jakarta.activation] libraries that it uses. The code uses only API, found in the [jakarta.mail] and [jakarta.mail.internet] packages. The [Internet19] class is as follows:

package internet;

import jakarta.mail.Message.RecipientType;
import jakarta.mail.MessagingException;
import jakarta.mail.Session;
import jakarta.mail.Transport;
import jakarta.mail.internet.AddressException;
import jakarta.mail.internet.InternetAddress;
import jakarta.mail.internet.MimeBodyPart;
import jakarta.mail.internet.MimeMessage;
import jakarta.mail.internet.MimeMultipart;
import java.io.File;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Properties;

// sending an email with Jakarta Mail
// call: mvn exec:java -Dexec.args="smtpServer port"
// the attachments are looked for in the current folder
public class Internet19 {

    private static final String SYNTAX = "Syntax: mvn exec:java -Dexec.args=\"smtpServer port\"";

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        if (args.length != 2 || !args[1].matches("\\d{1,5}")) {
            IO.println(SYNTAX);
            return;
        }
        String server = args[0];
        String port = args[1];

        // input of the elements of the mail
        String sender = input("Sender");
        String recipients = input("Recipients (separated by commas)");
        String copies = input("Copy to (Cc)");
        String blindCopies = input("Blind copy to (Bcc)");
        String subject = input("Subject");
        String attachments = input("Attachments (separated by commas)");
        // the text: several lines, ended by an empty line
        IO.println("Text of the message (ended by an empty line):");
        var text = new StringBuilder();
        String line;
        while ((line = IO.readln()) != null && !line.isEmpty()) {
            text.append(line).append('\n');
        }

        try {
            // the mail session: it contains the configuration of the SMTP client
            var properties = new Properties();
            properties.put("mail.smtp.host", server);
            properties.put("mail.smtp.port", port);
            Session session = Session.getInstance(properties);

            // the message
            var message = new MimeMessage(session);
            var from = new InternetAddress(sender, true);
            from.validate();
            message.setFrom(from);
            message.setRecipients(RecipientType.TO, addresses(recipients));
            message.setRecipients(RecipientType.CC, addresses(copies));
            message.setRecipients(RecipientType.BCC, addresses(blindCopies));
            message.setSubject(subject, "UTF-8");
            // a multipart message: first the text, in UTF-8 transported as is (8 bits)
            var textPart = new MimeBodyPart();
            textPart.setText(text.toString(), "UTF-8");
            textPart.setHeader("Content-Transfer-Encoding", "8bit");
            var content = new MimeMultipart(textPart);
            // then the attachments, designated by their path
            List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
            for (String file : attachments.split(",")) {
                if (!file.isBlank()) {
                    var part = new MimeBodyPart();
                    part.attachFile(new File(file.strip()));
                    content.addBodyPart(part);
                    names.add(part.getFileName());
                }
            }
            message.setContent(content);

            // the sending: Transport knows the SMTP protocol; the message knows the MIME format
            Transport.send(message);

            // summary of the sending
            IO.println("Sending successful...");
            IO.println("Subject: " + message.getSubject());
            IO.println("Recipients: " + list(message, RecipientType.TO));
            IO.println("Cc: " + list(message, RecipientType.CC));
            IO.println("Bcc: " + list(message, RecipientType.BCC));
            IO.println("Attachments: " + String.join(", ", names));
        } catch (MessagingException | IOException e) {
            IO.println("The following error occurred: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : "
                    + e.getMessage());
            if (e.getCause() != null) {
                IO.println("Cause: " + e.getCause());
            }
        }
    }

    // a list of addresses separated by commas; each address is checked
    private static InternetAddress[] addresses(String list) throws AddressException {
        InternetAddress[] addresses = InternetAddress.parse(list, true);
        for (InternetAddress address : addresses) {
            address.validate();
        }
        return addresses;
    }

    // the addresses of a category of recipients, separated by commas
    private static String list(MimeMessage message, RecipientType type) throws MessagingException {
        return InternetAddress.toString(message.getRecipients(type));
    }

    // input of a line on the keyboard
    private static String input(String label) {
        String line = IO.readln(label + " : ");
        return line == null ? "" : line.strip();
    }
}

Comments:

  • lines 34–46: entering the email elements using the [input] method (lines 115–118). The message text consists of several lines, ending with a blank line;
  • lines 50–53: the email session. Its configuration is a [Properties] object: here, the machine and port of the SMTP server. For a real server, we would add [mail.smtp.auth=true], [mail.smtp.starttls.enable=true] (encryption via [STARTTLS]), and provide the username and password to [Transport.send];
  • lines 56–63: the message:
    • lines 57–59: the sender, an object named [InternetAddress]. The second parameter of the constructor ([true]) requires a strict validation of the address, and [validate] additionally verifies that it is in the form [name@domain]; an incorrect address results in a [AddressException];
    • Lines 60–62: the recipients, those in the “Cc” (Carbon Copy) field, and those in the “Bcc” (Blind Carbon Copy) field. Recipients in the “Bcc” field receive the message, but the other recipients are not aware of this. The [addresses] method (lines 101–107) parses a comma-separated list of addresses using [InternetAddress.parse] and validates each one;
    • line 63: the subject, along with its character set;
  • lines 65–68: the message consists of several parts ([MimeMultipart]). The first part is the text, in UTF-8. The header [Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit] specifies that it should be transmitted as-is, in 8-bit format (the server indicated that it accepts this); without it, Jakarta Mail would choose its own encoding (quoted-printable or base64), which would make the text difficult to read when displayed by the server;
  • Lines 71–78: the attachments, identified by their file paths. A relative path is relative to the current directory; in our tests, the file [attachment.txt] is located in the [Internet19] directory, from which the program is launched. [attachFile] creates a section whose content will be read from the file at the time of sending;
  • line 82: sending the message using the static method [Transport.send], which connects to the server specified by the session, executes the dialog SMTP, and transmits the message in the format MIME;
  • lines 85–90: a summary of the transmission. [InternetAddress.toString] (line 111) concatenates a list of addresses into a single string;
  • lines 91–97: An invalid address triggers a [AddressException]; a sending error triggers another [MessagingException], the cause of which is displayed. A missing attachment is only detected at the time of sending: it triggers a [MessagingException], the cause of which is a [FileNotFoundException].

The SMTP test server is launched in a command window on port 27225. In another window, from the [Internet19] folder, a message is sent to two recipients, with one recipient in carbon copy, one in blind carbon copy, and an attachment:

> mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.args="localhost 27225"
Sender : alice@example.org
Recipients (separated by commas) : bob@example.com, carole@example.com
Copy to (Cc) : david@example.com
Blind copy to (Bcc) : eve@example.com
Subject : Meeting minutes
Attachments (separated by commas) : attachment.txt
Text of the message (ended by an empty line):
Hello,
here are the minutes of the summer meeting.
Best regards,
Alice

Sending successful...
Subject: Meeting minutes
Recipients: bob@example.com, carole@example.com
Cc: david@example.com
Bcc: eve@example.com
Attachments: attachment.txt

The file [attachment.txt] contains two lines of text. Here is what the server displayed:

> java Internet18.java
Test SMTP server started on localhost/127.0.0.1:27225
--- start of the dialog with client 0 (/127.0.0.1:47628)
S: 220 smtp.test ESMTP test server of the Java course
C: EHLO localhost
S: 250-smtp.test hello
S: 250-SIZE 10485760
S: 250 8BITMIME
C: MAIL FROM:<alice@example.org>
S: 250 2.1.0 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<bob@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<carole@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<david@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<eve@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 End data with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: Date: Sat, 3 Oct 2026 19:41:44 +0200 (CEST)
C: From: alice@example.org
C: To: bob@example.com, carole@example.com
C: Cc: david@example.com
C: Message-ID: <1094834071.1.1791049304833@localhost>
C: Subject: Meeting minutes
C: MIME-Version: 1.0
C: Content-Type: multipart/mixed; 
C:     boundary="----=_Part_0_1213415012.1791049304796"
C: 
C: ------=_Part_0_1213415012.1791049304796
C: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-8
C: Content-Transfer-Encoding: 8bit
C: 
C: Hello,
C: here are the minutes of the summer meeting.
C: Best regards,
C: Alice
C: 
C: ------=_Part_0_1213415012.1791049304796
C: Content-Type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii; name=attachment.txt
C: Content-Transfer-Encoding: 7bit
C: Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=attachment.txt
C: 
C: This is the attachment of the test mail.
C: It contains two lines.
C: 
C: ------=_Part_0_1213415012.1791049304796--
C: .
[message from <alice@example.org> to <bob@example.com>, <carole@example.com>, <david@example.com>, <eve@example.com>: 28 lines]
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: message accepted
C: QUIT
S: 221 2.0.0 Bye
--- end of the dialog with client 0
Server stop requested

Comments:

  • line 5: Jakarta Mail identifies itself with the local machine name, in this case [localhost];
  • Lines 9–18: the message envelope: the sender, followed by all recipients, including the blind carbon copy recipient ([eve@example.com]). The envelope determines to whom the message is delivered;
  • Lines 21–29: the message headers, which make up what the recipients will see: the date, the sender, the recipients [To] and [Cc], a unique message identifier ([Message-ID]), the subject… The blind carbon copy recipient is not listed here: this is how it remains hidden. The subject line contains only ASCII characters and is sent as-is; since headers can only contain ASCII characters, a subject containing an accented character would have been encoded according to RFC 2047: [=?UTF-8?Q?...?=] means “text UTF-8 encoded in quoted-printable,” with each non-ASCII byte written as [=XX] in hexadecimal ([=C3=A9] for the two bytes of [é]) and each space as [_];
  • Lines 28–29: The message is in the format MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, RFC 2045 and following): it consists of several parts ([multipart/mixed]), separated by a boundary line ([boundary]) chosen at random by Jakarta Mail. A header that is too long may be wrapped to the next line, provided that line begins with a space or a tab;
  • lines 31–39: the first part, the message body, in 8-bit UTF-8: it is readable as is;
  • lines 40–47: the second part, the attachment. Jakarta Mail recognized a text file ([text/plain]) containing only ASCII characters ([charset=us-ascii]) and transmitted it as-is ([7bit]); a text containing other characters would have been encoded in quoted-printable: this encoding leaves the ASCII characters readable and encodes the others, such as [è] ([=C3=A8]). A binary file (an image, for example) would have been encoded in Base64, which represents arbitrary bytes using 64 characters from the ASCII set. The header [Content-Disposition: attachment] indicates that this is an attachment and provides its name;
  • lines 48–49: the closing delimiter, followed by two dashes, then the line reduced to a single period that ends the message;
  • line 50: our server received a message for four recipients;
  • lines 52–53: Jakarta Mail ends the session;
  • line 55: the server was stopped with Ctrl-C after the tests.

An invalid address is rejected before any message is sent:

> mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.args="localhost 27225"
Sender : alice@example.org
Recipients (separated by commas) : bob.example.com
Copy to (Cc) : 
Blind copy to (Bcc) : 
Subject : test
Attachments (separated by commas) : 
Text of the message (ended by an empty line):
text

The following error occurred: AddressException : Missing final '@domain'

If the server SMTP is not available, a [MailConnectException]—a variant of [MessagingException]—is launched; this is caused by the [ConnectException] on the socket:

> mvn compile exec:java -Dexec.args="localhost 27299"
Sender : alice@example.org
Recipients (separated by commas) : bob@example.com
Copy to (Cc) : 
Blind copy to (Bcc) : 
Subject : test
Attachments (separated by commas) : 
Text of the message (ended by an empty line):
text

The following error occurred: MailConnectException : Couldn't connect to host, port: localhost, 27299; timeout -1
Cause: java.net.ConnectException: Connection refused

docs.title: 12.8. Asynchronous Network Programming: From NIO Channels to Virtual Threads
docs.text:
With the exception of the [sendAsync] requests from [HttpClient], the programs in this chapter use blocking network operations, executed by threads (virtual threads for servers). This is not the only way to do it, and the reader will encounter in existing code the two other models that Java offered prior to Java 21.

The first, introduced in Java 1.4, is the non-blocking I/O model from the [java.nio.channels] package. A [SocketChannel] set to non-blocking mode ([channel.configureBlocking(false)]) immediately yields control, regardless of whether there is data to read; a [Selector] object allows a single thread to monitor a large number of channels and be woken up when one of them is ready (a new connection to accept, data to read, space to write to). The program then runs in a single loop that, each time it is woken up, processes the ready channels. Data is read in blocks into byte buffers ([ByteBuffer]): it is up to the program to reconstruct the lines—since a line may be split between two blocks—and to keep track, for each client, of the current state of their session.

The second, introduced in Java 7 (NIO.2), is for asynchronous channels: [AsynchronousSocketChannel] and [AsynchronousServerSocketChannel]. Each operation is initiated with a callback object ([CompletionHandler]), whose method [completed] is executed by a thread from a pool at the end of the operation. A client connection is thus written as [channel.connect(address, null, handler)], and the handler’s method [completed] must initiate the next read, whose method [completed] will initiate the next one, and so on. The code is lengthy, and the dialog logic is scattered across several callback methods.

Both of these models are efficient: they allow a few threads to handle thousands of connections. But they are difficult to program and debug; they are primarily used through libraries such as Netty, on which many servers are based. Java 21’s virtual threads have rendered these techniques unnecessary for most applications: a virtual thread blocked on a network operation does not block any system threads, and the code reads in the order in which it executes, just like synchronous code. The generic client TCP from Part 1 ([Internet06.java]) is an example of this: a virtual thread reads from the keyboard while the main thread reads from the network, using simple calls to [readLine].

Keep in mind that asynchrony offers little benefit to a client with only one connection: its thread has nothing else to do but wait for the response. It is, however, essential for a server: a server that serves its clients using blocked platform threads ties up one system thread per client; with virtual threads or non-blocking channels, just a few system threads are sufficient to serve a large number of clients. This is what the server in the following example application does.

docs.title: 12.9. Sample Application, Version 8: Tax Calculation Server
12.9.1. The Architecture of the New Version
docs.text:
Let’s revisit the tax calculation application. In version 5 (Chapter 6), it consisted of three layers, each in its own Maven module: [dao] (tax brackets), [business] (the calculation), and [ui] (the console dialog), assembled by Spring’s dependency injection container; versions 6 and 7 replaced the [dao] layer with database access. We’ll start with version 5, which is simpler to run: the new version would work the same way with the [dao] layer from versions 6 and 7.

We will deploy this architecture across two machines:

  • A [server] machine hosts the [business] and [dao] layers from version 5. A layer named [server] is built to allow clients on the network to query the tax calculation service using a text-based protocol named TCP;
  • a machine [client] hosts the [ui] layer of version 5. A new [business] layer, which acts as a client to the server’s TCP layer, enables the server to query the tax calculation service.

The architecture is undergoing a major change: Version 5 was a single-user application; Version 8 is becoming a client-server application, and the server will be able to serve multiple clients simultaneously. However, we will write only two new classes, [TaxServer] and [TaxBusinessTcp], an options record, and two main programs: everything else is reused without modification.

The [TaxV8] project is a multi-module Maven project consisting of two modules that use the modules from version 5. These must have been installed in the local Maven repository using the [mvn install] command, executed in the [TaxV5] folder (Chapter 6):

  tax-server/
    pom.xml                       dependencies: tax-dao and tax-business (V5), Spring
    server.properties             configuration of the [dao] layer and of the server
    TaxData.txt                   the tax brackets
    src/main/java/tax/server/
      Main.java                   integration of the layers, launch of the server
      ServerOptions.java          the options of the server
      TaxServer.java              the [server] layer
  tax-client/
    pom.xml                       dependencies: tax-business and tax-ui (V5), Spring
    src/main/java/tax/client/
      TaxBusinessTcp.java         the [business] layer of the client: a TCP client
      Main.java                   integration of the layers, dialog

docs.title: 12.9.2. The Communication Protocol
docs.text:
Once the client is connected, the server sends it a welcome message, then accepts the following commands, one per line, case-insensitive:

CommandServer responsehelpa list of accepted commands, on four linestax married nbChildren annualSalarythe tax for a married person (married is [y]) or unmarried ([n]) with [nbChildren] children and an annual salary of [annualSalary] euros, for example, [4282] in response to [tax y 2 60000]; or an error message, on a linegoodbyethe message [Goodbye...]; the server then closes the connection

Any other command receives the response [Command not recognized. Use the help command.]

The file [pom.xml] from the module [tax-server] is as follows:
