    // the numbers are typed and displayed in the current culture (fr-FR: decimal comma, en-US: decimal point)
    private static final NumberFormat FORMAT = NumberFormat.getInstance();

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException {
        URI serviceUrl = URI.create(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "http://localhost:5110/");
        // the JSON converter; Jackson 3 ignores the unknown JSON properties (instance...)
        JsonMapper mapper = JsonMapper.builder().build();

        try (HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient()) {
            while (true) {
                // input of the operation and of the two numbers (decimal separator of the current culture)
                String input = IO.readln("Operation a b (e.g.: add 1.5 2), nothing to stop: ");
                String[] fields = input == null ? new String[0] : input.strip().split("\\s+");
                if (fields.length == 0 || fields[0].isEmpty()) {
                    break;
                }
                if (fields.length != 3) {
                    IO.println("Three elements are needed: operation a b");
                    continue;
                }
                // local check of the two numbers, before any call to the service
                String operation = fields[0];
                Double a = readNumber(fields[1]);
                if (a == null) {
                    IO.println("Incorrect number a...");
                }
                Double b = readNumber(fields[2]);
                if (b == null) {
                    IO.println("Incorrect number b...");
                }
                if (a == null || b == null) {
                    continue;
                }
                String calculation = operation + "(" + FORMAT.format(a) + " ; " + FORMAT.format(b) + ")";

                // 1 - GET request: in the URL, the numbers are written with a decimal point
                String url = URLEncoder.encode(operation, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) + "?a=" + a + "&b=" + b;
                try {
                    HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(serviceUrl.resolve(url)).GET().build();
                    HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
                    if (response.statusCode() == 200) {
                        CalculationResult result = mapper.readValue(response.body(), CalculationResult.class);
                        IO.println("[GET " + url + "] " + calculation
                                + " = " + FORMAT.format(result.result()));
                    } else {
                        // failure: the status code and the document received are displayed, as they are
                        IO.println("[GET " + url + "] error " + response.statusCode()
                                + " : " + response.body());
                    }
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    // the service is unreachable
                    IO.println("[GET " + url + "] error: " + e);
                }

                // 2 - POST request: the request is sent in JSON in the body of the request
                try {
                    String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(new CalculationRequest(operation, a, b));
                    HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(serviceUrl.resolve("calculation"))
                            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(json))
                            .build();
                    HttpResponse<String> response = client.send(request, BodyHandlers.ofString());
                    if (response.statusCode() == 200) {
                        // success: the body contains the result
                        CalculationResult result = mapper.readValue(response.body(), CalculationResult.class);
                        IO.println("[POST calculation] " + calculation + " = " + FORMAT.format(result.result()));
                    } else {
                        // failure: the body contains the description of the problem
                        Problem problem = mapper.readValue(response.body(), Problem.class);
                        IO.println("[POST calculation] error " + response.statusCode() + " : " + problem.title());
                        if (problem.detail() != null) {
                            IO.println("  " + problem.detail());
                        }
                        if (problem.errors() != null) {
                            problem.errors().forEach((parameter, messages) ->
                                    IO.println("  " + parameter + " : " + String.join(" ; ", messages)));
                        }
                    }
                } catch (IOException e) {
                    // the service is unreachable
                    IO.println("[POST calculation] error: " + e);
                }
            }
        }
    }

    // a number typed in the current culture, null if the input is not one
    private static Double readNumber(String text) {
        ParsePosition position = new ParsePosition(0);
        Number number = FORMAT.parse(text, position);
        // the input must have been read entirely: "2.5x" is refused
        return number == null || position.getIndex() != text.length() ? null : number.doubleValue();
    }
}

Comments:

  • Lines 20–29: the client’s DTO files. They are declared here again: a client does not share the server’s code, only the format of the exchanged JSON documents. Spring’s [ProblemDetail] class is part of the web framework; a simple record is sufficient for the client. Its components are object types ([String], [Integer], [Map]): a property missing from the document, such as [detail] or [errors], is set to [null];
  • line 32: numbers are entered and displayed in the system language format, in this case English: decimal point;
  • Line 37: From Jackson 3, unknown properties in the record (here, [instance]) are ignored by default during deserialization;
  • lines 51–63: The numbers are verified locally before any call to the service is made. A service must always verify its parameters (since it does not know who is calling it), but a client can avoid unnecessary network traffic;
  • line 64: the text describing the calculation, with the numbers in the system language format;
  • line 67: the URL for the GET request. Numbers must be written with a decimal point: concatenating a [Double] to a string uses its [toString] method, which is independent of the system language. The operation, entered by the user, is coded as [URLEncoder];
  • lines 69–70: the request GET;
  • lines 71–74: if successful (status code 200), the response JSON is deserialized into a [CalculationResult] object;
  • lines 75–79: if the request fails, the status code and the received document are displayed as-is;
  • lines 80–83: The exception [IOException] indicates a communication error, such as a service that cannot be reached;
  • lines 87–92: the POST request. The [CalculationRequest] object is serialized into JSON by [writeValueAsString]; the request receives the header [Content-Type], followed by its body: [BodyPublishers.ofString] sends a string, encoded as UTF-8;
  • lines 97–107: in case of failure, the body is a “Problem Details” document, deserialized into a [Problem] object, whose title, details, and validation errors are displayed. The [forEach] method of a [Map] receives a lambda with two parameters: the key and value of each element (Chapter 7);
  • lines 118–123: reading a number in the system language format. The [parse(String, ParsePosition)] method of [NumberFormat] reads the beginning of the string and indicates in the [ParsePosition] object where it stopped: if it did not stop at the end, the input contains extra characters ([2.5x]).

Results, with the service running:

> mvn -q compile exec:java
Operation a b (e.g.: add 1.5 2), nothing to stop: add 1.5 2
[GET add?a=1.5&b=2.0] add(1.5 ; 2) = 3.5
[POST calculation] add(1.5 ; 2) = 3.5
Operation a b (e.g.: add 1.5 2), nothing to stop: divide 1 0
[GET divide?a=1.0&b=0.0] error 400 : {"detail":"The number b must be non-zero for a division","instance":"/divide","status":400,"title":"Division by zero"}
[POST calculation] error 400 : Division by zero
  The number b must be non-zero for a division
Operation a b (e.g.: add 1.5 2), nothing to stop: power 2 3
[GET power?a=2.0&b=3.0] error 400 : {"instance":"/power","status":400,"title":"Incorrect parameters","errors":{"operation":["Unknown operation [power]: use add, subtract, multiply or divide"]}}
[POST calculation] error 400 : Incorrect parameters
  operation : Unknown operation [power]: use add, subtract, multiply or divide
Operation a b (e.g.: add 1.5 2), nothing to stop: multiply 2.5 x
Incorrect number b...
Operation a b (e.g.: add 1.5 2), nothing to stop:
  • line 3: the URL from the GET query: the numbers 1.5 and 2 entered there are written as 1.5 and 2.0;
  • Lines 6–8: The same error observed in both requests: the raw document for request GET, and its processing for request POST;
  • Lines 10–12: The service detected an unknown operation;
  • line 14: the incorrect number was detected by the client, which did not query the service.

docs.title: 13.4. Sample Application—Version 9: A Web Service for Calculating Taxes
docs.text: We’ll revisit the tax calculation application. In the previous chapter (version 8), we had created a server named TCP that could be queried remotely, using its own communication protocol. We’ll now turn it into a web service named REST.

docs.title: 13.4.1. The Architecture
docs.text:
The architecture of version 9 is as follows:

  • on the server side, the [WsTax] web service receives HTTP requests and has them processed by the [business] and [dao] layers from Version 5 (Chapter 6), which are reused as-is;
  • on the client side, the [ui] layer from version 5 is also reused as-is. It communicates with a new type of [business] layer, [TaxBusinessHttp], which implements the [ITaxBusiness] interface by querying the web service: it acts as a proxy for the service. The [ui] layer is unaware that the calculation is performed on another machine;
  • on both sides, the integration of the layers is handled by Spring’s dependency injection container, just as in version 5.

docs.title: 13.4.2. The web service
docs.text:
The service contract is as follows:

RequestResponse on successResponse in case of an errorGET /tax?married=y&children=2&salary=60000200: [{"tax":4282}]400: "Problem Details" documentPOST /tax with the body [{"married":true,"children":2,"salary":60000}]200: [{"tax":4282}]400: "Problem Details" document

The [WsTax] project depends on the [tax-dao] and [tax-business] modules from version 5. For Maven to find them, you must first install them in the machine’s local Maven repository (the [.m2/repository] folder in the user’s home directory) by typing [mvn install] in the [06-architectures/TaxV5] folder (Chapter 6). The dependencies of the [pom.xml] file from [WsTax] are then as follows (the rest of the file is the same as [WsHello], except for the project name: [examples.tax:ws-tax:9.0]):

    <dependencies>
        <!-- Spring MVC, the embedded Tomcat server and Jackson -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-webmvc</artifactId>
        </dependency>
        <!-- the [dao] and [business] layers of version 5, reused as they are -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-dao</artifactId>
            <version>5.0</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-business</artifactId>
            <version>5.0</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
  • Lines 7–17: the two modules from version 5, identified by their Maven coordinates. The [tax-dao] module also includes the [TaxBracket] and [TaxException] classes from the [entities] layer. These modules depend on Jackson 3.1.5, which the web starter already provides.

The [application.properties] configuration file is as follows:

# the name of the application
spring.application.name=WsTax
# the listening port of the Tomcat server
server.port=5120
# the errors detected by Spring MVC are reported in the "Problem Details" format (RFC 9457)
spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true
# no banner at startup
spring.main.banner-mode=off
# shorter log messages: time, level, thread, class, message
logging.pattern.console=%d{HH:mm:ss.SSS} %-5level [%thread] %logger{0} : %msg%n

# the [dao] layer: its implementation and its data file
dao.implementation=JsonTax
dao.file=TaxData.json
  • line 4: the service listens on port 5120;
  • Lines 13–14: the configuration for the [dao] layer, in the same format as in the [tax.properties] file from version 5: the implementation to use and its data file. These are not Spring Boot properties, but properties specific to our application: a [application.properties] file can contain as many as desired. Here we are using the files JSON and [TaxData.json], located in the project folder, which is the service’s runtime folder along with [mvn spring-boot:run].

The [dao] and [business] layers are integrated into the Spring container via a configuration class:

package tax.ws;

import tax.dao.FileTax;
import tax.dao.HardwiredTax;
import tax.dao.ITaxDao;
import tax.dao.JsonTax;
import tax.entities.TaxException;
import tax.business.ITaxBusiness;
import tax.business.TaxBusiness;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

// the integration of the [dao] and [business] layers of version 5 in the Spring container
@Configuration
public class TaxConfig {

    // the [dao] layer: its implementation and its file come from the configuration
    @Bean
    public ITaxDao dao(@Value("${dao.implementation:HardwiredTax}") String implementation,
            @Value("${dao.file:}") String file) {
        return switch (implementation) {
            case "HardwiredTax" -> new HardwiredTax();
            case "FileTax" -> new FileTax(file);
            case "JsonTax" -> new JsonTax(file);
            default -> throw new TaxException(
                    "Unknown implementation [" + implementation + "] of the [dao] layer");
        };
    }

    // the [business] layer: Spring passes it the [dao] layer
    @Bean
    public ITaxBusiness business(ITaxDao dao) {
        return new TaxBusiness(dao);
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 15: the annotation [@Configuration] (Chapter 6): the class defines beans. Spring finds it because it is located in the same package as the main class ([@ComponentScan]);
  • Lines 19–29: The annotated method [@Bean] creates the layer [dao]. Its parameters are provided by Spring: the annotation [@Value] injects the value of a configuration property into it. In [${dao.implementation:HardwiredTax}], the text following the character [:] is the default value, used if the property is missing. This method and the next one are the same as those in the [TaxConfig] class from Version 5 (Chapter 6), without the [@PropertySource] annotation: Spring Boot reads the [application.properties] file itself;
  • lines 32–35: the [business] layer. The [dao] parameter of the method receives the bean of type [ITaxDao]: Spring therefore creates the [dao] layer before the [business] layer.

These lines replace the layer integration that the main program performed in version 5: the Spring container is the same, but it is now Spring Boot that creates it and locates the configuration class on its own. The beans defined this way are singletons, created when the application starts up, before any requests are processed: if the data file is missing or incorrect, the service does not start, rather than responding to all requests with a 500 error. We’ll verify this later.

The web service is the [TaxController] controller:

package tax.ws;

import tax.business.ITaxBusiness;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.Map;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

// the tax calculation web service (version 9)
@RestController
public class TaxController {

    // the log of the class
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(TaxController.class);

    // the [business] layer, injected by Spring
    private final ITaxBusiness business;

    public TaxController(ITaxBusiness business) {
        this.business = business;
    }

    // GET /tax?married=y&children=2&salary=60000
    @GetMapping("/tax")
    public TaxResponse calculateGet(@RequestParam(required = false) String married,
            @RequestParam(required = false) String children, @RequestParam(required = false) String salary) {
        Boolean isMarried = switch (married == null ? "" : married.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT)) {
            case "y" -> true;
            case "n" -> false;
            default -> null;
        };
        return calculate(isMarried, readInteger(children), readInteger(salary));
    }

    // POST /tax with the JSON body {"married":true,"children":2,"salary":60000}
    @PostMapping("/tax")
    public TaxResponse calculatePost(@RequestBody TaxRequest request) {
        return calculate(request.married(), request.children(), request.salary());
    }

    // the processing common to the two HTTP methods: the tax, or an exception if the request is incorrect
    private TaxResponse calculate(Boolean married, Integer children, Integer salary) {
        // correct parameters: the calculation is requested from the [business] layer
        if (married != null && children != null && children >= 0 && salary != null && salary >= 0) {
            int tax = business.calculateTax(married, children, salary);
            log.info("Tax(married={}, children={}, salary={}) = {}", married, children, salary, tax);
            return new TaxResponse(tax);
        }
        // incorrect parameters: the list of errors
        Map<String, List<String>> errors = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        if (married == null) {
            errors.put("married",
                    List.of("Indicate whether the taxpayer is married: y/n (GET) or true/false (POST)"));
        }
        if (children == null || children < 0) {
            errors.put("children", List.of("The number of children must be a positive or zero integer"));
        }
        if (salary == null || salary < 0) {
            errors.put("salary", List.of("The salary must be a positive or zero integer"));
        }
        log.warn("Incorrect request: {}", String.join(", ", errors.keySet()));
        throw new BadRequestException(errors);
    }

    // an integer, null if it is missing or incorrect
    private static Integer readInteger(String text) {
        try {
            return text == null ? null : Integer.valueOf(text);
        } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
            return null;
        }
    }

    // an incorrect request gives a 400 response in the "Problem Details" format
    @ExceptionHandler
    public ProblemDetail badRequest(BadRequestException e) {
        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);
        problem.setTitle("Incorrect parameters");
        problem.setProperty("errors", e.getErrors());
        return problem;
    }

    // the calculation request (body of the POST request): the properties missing from the JSON are null
    public record TaxRequest(Boolean married, Integer children, Integer salary) {
    }

    // the response: the amount of the tax
    public record TaxResponse(int tax) {
    }
}

Comments:

  • Line 24: the class log. Spring Boot uses the API logging framework (Simple Logging Facade for Java), which is implemented here using Logback. [LoggerFactory.getLogger] generates a log entry whose category is the full name of the class;
  • Lines 27–31: The controller receives the [business] layer from its constructor. Spring, which creates the controller, passes it the bean of type [ITaxBusiness] defined by [TaxConfig]: this is constructor injection as described in Chapter 6. A field named [final] ensures that the layer will not change;
  • lines 34–43: the GET request. The three parameters of the query string are received as strings and converted: [y]/[n] to [married] (lines 37–41, an expression [switch] whose type is [Boolean]), integers for [children] and [salary] ([readInteger], lines 76–82), [null] in case of an error;
  • lines 46–49: the query POST: the body JSON is deserialized into an object [TaxRequest] (line 94), whose object-type components ([Boolean], [Integer]) are used to detect missing values. The same URL [/tax] is associated with two methods, depending on the HTTP method of the query;
  • lines 52–73: the processing common to both requests. It returns a response if successful and throws an exception if an error occurs. The type of its result, like that of the methods on lines 35 and 47, is therefore simply [TaxResponse]: reading their signatures shows what the service returns when everything goes well;
  • line 54: Are the three parameters correct? The comparisons [children >= 0] and [salary >= 0] unpack the [Integer] objects: they are evaluated only if these are not [null], thanks to the lazy evaluation of the [&&] operator;
  • line 55: the calculation is delegated to the [business] layer of version 5;
  • line 56: each calculation is logged at the [INFO] level. The message text is a template: each instance of [{}] is replaced by the corresponding argument, in order. Unlike concatenation, the message is constructed only if it needs to be displayed (depending on the log level), and logging tools can record each value separately;
  • lines 60–72: In the event of an error, the error list is constructed, a warning ([warn]) is logged, and a [BadRequestException] exception is thrown that carries this list;
  • lines 85–91: An annotated method [@ExceptionHandler] acts as an exception handler: Spring calls it when a controller method throws an exception of the type specified by its parameter, in this case [BadRequestException]. What it returns becomes the HTTP response: a [ProblemDetail], whose status code (400) becomes the response’s status code;
  • lines 94–99: the service’s DTO responses.

The [BadRequestException] exception is as follows:

package tax.ws;

import java.io.Serial;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

// the exception thrown by the controller when the calculation parameters are incorrect
public class BadRequestException extends RuntimeException {

    @Serial
    private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;

    // the error messages, parameter by parameter
    // (transient: a Map is not necessarily serializable)
    private final transient Map<String, List<String>> errors;

    public BadRequestException(Map<String, List<String>> errors) {
        super("Incorrect parameters: " + String.join(", ", errors.keySet()));
        this.errors = errors;
    }

    public Map<String, List<String>> getErrors() {
        return errors;
    }
}
  • line 8: an unchecked exception, which does not need to be declared by the methods that throw it;
  • lines 10–11: an exception is serializable (in the sense of Java binary serialization): the compiler requires, with the [-Xlint:all] option, that it declare a version number;
  • line 15: the list of errors. The keyword [transient] excludes this field from binary serialization, since the type [Map] is not necessarily serializable; without it, the compiler would issue a warning. This has no consequence here: our exceptions are never serialized.

The main class [WsTaxApplication] is identical to that of the other two services. The [src/main/resources/static] folder contains the web client, which is discussed in the following section.

The web service is stateless: the controller's methods do not retain any state from one request to the next. The controller and the layers [business] and [dao] are singletons, created once and for all, that exist for as long as the application runs; they are shared by all requests, which may be processed simultaneously by different threads of the Tomcat server (Chapter 8). This isn’t a problem here because these objects are never modified after they are created: the tax brackets are read once and for all, and the controller has only one [final] field. A controller should never store request-specific data in its fields. The singleton is the default scope for Spring beans; but there are others: [prototype] (one object per request to the container), [request] (one object per request HTTP), [session] (one object per session HTTP). Finally, note that the [spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true] property causes each request to be processed by a virtual thread (Java 21, Chapter 8) instead of a thread from the Tomcat pool: the service can then handle a very large number of concurrent requests that are waiting for I/O operations.

docs.title: 13.4.3. Running the Service
docs.text:
Let’s start with a configuration error. Command-line arguments in the form [--property=value] are part of the application configuration and override the values of [application.properties]. With [mvn spring-boot:run], these are passed via the [spring-boot.run.arguments] property. Let’s specify a nonexistent data file (the course has abbreviated the lines in this log—which are very long—to [...]):

> mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.arguments=--dao.file=missing.json
19:01:41.197 INFO  [main] WsTaxApplication : Starting WsTaxApplication using Java 25.0.4.1 with PID 22677 (...)
...
19:01:49.390 INFO  [main] TomcatWebServer : Tomcat initialized with port 5120 (http)
...
19:01:50.956 WARN  [main] AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext : Exception encountered during context initialization - cancelling refresh attempt: org.springframework.beans.factory.UnsatisfiedDependencyException: Error creating bean with name 'taxController' ... Error creating bean with name 'business' ... Error creating bean with name 'dao' ... Factory method 'dao' threw exception with message: Error while reading the file missing.json
19:01:50.991 INFO  [main] StandardService : Stopping service [Tomcat]
...
19:01:51.454 ERROR [main] LoggingFailureAnalysisReporter : 

***************************
APPLICATION FAILED TO START
***************************

Description:

The service cannot start: Error while reading the file missing.json (missing.json: The file [missing.json] does not exist)

Action:

Check the dao.implementation and dao.file properties of the configuration.
  • line 4: the Tomcat server was created, but it hasn’t opened its port yet;
  • line 6: bean creation failed. To create the controller, Spring had to create the [business] layer, and therefore the [dao] layer, whose constructor instantiated a [TaxException] (Chapter 6). The messages for our layers, like those for Spring, are in English;
  • line 7: the Tomcat server is stopped; the service did not accept any requests;
  • lines 9–21: the startup failure report. Its description (line 17) and the recommended action (line 21) are generated by a class we wrote for this purpose.

In fact, when startup fails, Spring Boot normally displays the exception and the entire call stack: dozens of lines, where the relevant message is hard to find. Spring Boot can also pass the exception to failure analyzers, which translate it into a readable report. It provides analyzers for the most common errors (port already in use, bean not found, etc.), and we can add our own:

package tax.ws;

import tax.entities.TaxException;
import org.springframework.boot.diagnostics.AbstractFailureAnalyzer;
import org.springframework.boot.diagnostics.FailureAnalysis;

// Spring Boot calls this analyzer if the startup fails because of a TaxException
// (missing or incorrect data file, unknown implementation)
public class TaxFailureAnalyzer extends AbstractFailureAnalyzer<TaxException> {

    @Override
    protected FailureAnalysis analyze(Throwable rootFailure, TaxException cause) {
        // the description of the error: the message of the exception and that of its cause
        String description = "The service cannot start: " + cause.getMessage()
                + (cause.getCause() == null ? "" : " (" + cause.getCause().getMessage() + ")");
        // what the user must do
        String action = "Check the dao.implementation and dao.file properties of the configuration.";
        return new FailureAnalysis(description, action, cause);
    }
}
  • Line 9: Spring Boot’s [AbstractFailureAnalyzer<T>] class searches for an exception of type [T]—in this case, [TaxException]—in the chain of causes leading to the exception that caused the startup to fail. If it finds one, it calls the [analyze] method;
  • line 12: the parameter [rootFailure] is the initial exception, and [cause] is the [TaxException] found in the chain;
  • lines 14–18: The report is a [FailureAnalysis] object consisting of a description, a recommended action, and the analyzed exception.

This analyzer is not a bean (it must function even if the container could not be created): Spring Boot searches for it in the [META-INF/spring.factories] files of the libraries and the application. Ours is located in [src/main/resources/META-INF]:

# the analyzer of the startup failures caused by a TaxException
org.springframework.boot.diagnostics.FailureAnalyzer=tax.ws.TaxFailureAnalyzer
  • line 2: the key is the name of the [FailureAnalyzer] interface, and the value is the name of our class (multiple classes would be separated by commas).

Now let’s start the service as usual, using [mvn spring-boot:run], and then query it with [curl]:

> curl -s -i "http://localhost:5120/tax?married=y&children=2&salary=60000"
HTTP/1.1 200 
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 12
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:04:03 GMT

{"tax":4282}

This is the expected test result: a married taxpayer with two children and an annual salary of 60,000 euros pays 4,282 euros in taxes (note that the tax schedule used—the 2004 schedule—is retained only for this fiscal year). With incorrect parameters:

> curl -s -i "http://localhost:5120/tax?married=x&children=-2"
HTTP/1.1 400 
Content-Type: application/problem+json
Transfer-Encoding: chunked
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:04:03 GMT
Connection: close

{"instance":"/tax","status":400,"title":"Incorrect parameters","errors":{"married":["Indicate whether the taxpayer is married: y/n (GET) or true/false (POST)"],"children":["The number of children must be a positive or zero integer"],"salary":["The salary must be a positive or zero integer"]}}

Then in POST, with a document JSON:

> curl -s -i -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"married":true,"children":2,"salary":60000}' http://localhost:5120/tax
HTTP/1.1 200 
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 12
Date: Sat, 03 Oct 2026 17:04:04 GMT

{"tax":4282}

The service log will be shown at the end of the chapter: it contains a record of all the requested calculations.

docs.title: 13.4.4. The console output: a new [business] layer
docs.text:
The Version 9 client uses the [ui] layer from Version 5 without modifying it: the [tax.ui.Dialog] class, whose static method [run(ITaxBusiness business)] interacts with the user and requests calculations from the [business] layer that is passed to it. Simply pass it a layer named [business] that queries the web service. The dependencies of the [ClientWsTax] project are as follows (the rest of the [pom.xml] file is the same as that of [ClientWsHello], except for the project name and the main class: [examples.tax:client-ws-tax:9.0], [tax.client.Main]):

    <dependencies>
        <!-- the interface of the [business] layer and the [ui] layer of version 5 -->
        <!-- (tax-ui also brings tax-dao and the Spring container) -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-business</artifactId>
            <version>5.0</version>
        </dependency>
        <dependency>
            <groupId>examples.tax</groupId>
            <artifactId>tax-ui</artifactId>
            <version>5.0</version>
        </dependency>
        <!-- Jackson for the JSON documents exchanged with the service -->
        <dependency>
            <groupId>tools.jackson.core</groupId>
            <artifactId>jackson-databind</artifactId>
            <version>3.1.5</version>
        </dependency>
    </dependencies>
  • Lines 4–13: Version 5 modules: [tax-business] for the [ITaxBusiness] interface, [tax-ui] for the [Dialog] class. A project may depend on a module that contains a main program: in this case, it uses the module’s public classes without executing the program itself. The module [tax-dao] is an indirect (or transitive) dependency: the client uses only the class [TaxException] from it. Similarly, [tax-ui] provides the Spring container ([spring-context]);
  • lines 15–19: Jackson, for the JSON documents. It is also provided by [tax-dao], but the client uses it directly: it is preferable to declare it.

The new [business] layer is the class [TaxBusinessHttp]:

package tax.client;

import tax.entities.TaxException;
import tax.business.ITaxBusiness;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import java.net.http.HttpRequest;
import java.net.http.HttpResponse;
import tools.jackson.databind.json.JsonMapper;

// the [business] layer on the client side: a proxy of the tax calculation web service
// it implements the same interface as the local [business] layer of version 5
public class TaxBusinessHttp implements ITaxBusiness {

    // the objects exchanged with the web service
    private record TaxRequest(boolean married, int children, int salary) {
    }

    private record TaxResponse(int tax) {
    }

    // the HTTP client, the URL of the POST /tax method, the JSON converter
    private final HttpClient client;
    private final URI taxUrl;
    private final JsonMapper mapper = JsonMapper.builder().build();

    public TaxBusinessHttp(HttpClient client, URI serviceUrl) {
        this.client = client;
        this.taxUrl = serviceUrl.resolve("tax");
    }

    @Override
    public int calculateTax(boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary) {
        // the POST /tax request, with the request in JSON in its body
        String json = mapper.writeValueAsString(new TaxRequest(married, nbChildren, salary));
        HttpRequest request = HttpRequest.newBuilder(taxUrl)
                .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
                .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(json))
                .build();
        HttpResponse<String> response;
        try {
            // synchronous sending: the method waits for the response
            response = client.send(request, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
        } catch (IOException e) {
            // the service is unreachable
            throw new TaxException("The web service " + taxUrl + " is unreachable", e);
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            // the thread was interrupted during the wait: this is signaled again
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
            throw new TaxException("The tax calculation was interrupted", e);
        }
        // did the service accept the request?
        if (response.statusCode() != 200) {
            throw new TaxException("The web service responded " + response.statusCode()
                    + " : " + response.body(), response.statusCode());
        }
        // the JSON response {"tax":4282}
        return mapper.readValue(response.body(), TaxResponse.class).tax();
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 14: the class implements the [ITaxBusiness] interface from version 5;
  • lines 17–21: the DTO variables are declared inside the class ([private]) because no one else uses them;
  • lines 28–31: the class receives, via its constructor, the client HTTP and the service’s URL, from which it calculates the URL for the [POST /tax] method;
  • lines 36–40: the request [POST tax], with the request serialized as JSON in its body;
  • line 44: the request is sent synchronously: the [send] method waits for the response, which is consistent with the [calculateTax] method of the interface, which is itself synchronous (it returns a [int]);
  • Lines 45–47: [send] triggers a [IOException] if the service is unreachable. This is a caught exception, which the [calculateTax] method of the interface does not declare: it is encapsulated within a [TaxException], the uncaught exception of the [Tax] application;
  • lines 48–52: the same applies to [InterruptedException], which is thrown if the thread is interrupted while waiting. Catching the exception clears the thread’s interruption flag: best practice (Chapter 8) is to reset it using [Thread.currentThread().interrupt()] so that the calling code knows the thread was interrupted;
  • lines 54–57: An error response is converted to [TaxException], whose code is the status code HTTP;
  • line 59: the response JSON [{"tax":4282}] is deserialized, and the tax amount is returned.

With a SOAP service, the [wsimport] tool used to generate a proxy, and a class similar to this one implemented [ITaxBusiness] by delegating the calculation to it: today, we write the few dozen lines of the proxy ourselves.

Since the [calculateTax] method of the [ITaxBusiness] interface is synchronous, we used the synchronous [send] method of [HttpClient]. This interface also offers an asynchronous method, [sendAsync], which immediately returns a [CompletableFuture<HttpResponse<T>>] (Chapter 9). To take advantage of this, we would need to make the interface asynchronous: [CompletableFuture<Integer> calculateTaxAsync(boolean married, int nbChildren, int salary)], which would require modifying the [ITaxBusiness] interface, its implementations, and the [ui] layer. We did not do this in order to keep the layers from version 5 intact. With virtual threads (Java 21), synchronous code has once again become the recommended way to write programs that involve a lot of I/O: a virtual thread blocked by [send] does not block any system threads.

The client’s main program integrates the layers:

package tax.client;

import tax.business.ITaxBusiness;
import tax.ui.Dialog;
import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.HttpClient;
import org.springframework.context.support.GenericApplicationContext;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        // the URL of the web service: the one passed as an argument, or the default one
        URI serviceUrl = URI.create(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "http://localhost:5120/");

        // the exit code of the program
        int code = 0;
        // integration of the layers: the [business] layer is now a client of the web service
        try (GenericApplicationContext context = new GenericApplicationContext()) {
            // the URL of the service and the HTTP client, which Spring will pass to the constructor of TaxBusinessHttp
            context.registerBean(URI.class, () -> serviceUrl);
            context.registerBean(HttpClient.class, HttpClient::newHttpClient);
            context.registerBean(TaxBusinessHttp.class);
            context.refresh();
            ITaxBusiness business = context.getBean(ITaxBusiness.class);

            // the dialog of version 5, without any modification
            try {
                Dialog.run(business);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                // the service is unreachable or refused the request
                Dialog.displayError(e);
                code = 1;
            }
        }
        if (code != 0) {
            System.exit(code);
        }
    }
}

Comments:

  • line 13: the service’s URL, passed as an argument or, by default, [http://localhost:5120/];
  • line 18: the Spring container, as in version 5. It is closed at the end of the [try] block;
  • Lines 20–22: three beans are registered: the service bean URL and the client bean HTTP, provided by lambdas (of type [Supplier]), followed by the class [TaxBusinessHttp]. To create this class, Spring examines its constructor and passes it the beans of types [HttpClient] and [URI];
  • line 23: the container creates the beans;
  • line 24: the container is asked for a bean of type [ITaxBusiness]; it returns the object [TaxBusinessHttp], which implements this interface. The rest of the program is unaware of the implementation;
  • line 28: the dialog from version 5, without any modifications;
  • lines 29–33: if the service cannot be reached, the exception is propagated from the [business] layer through the [ui] layer, which does not handle it: it is displayed using the [Dialog.displayError] method from version 5;
  • lines 35–37: in the event of an error, the program terminates with code 1 after closing the container.

Results, with the service running:

> mvn -q compile exec:java
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Tax=4282 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 3 60000
Tax=2959 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: n 0 60000
Tax=11519 euros
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y -2 60000
syntax: Married NbChildren Salary
Married: y for married, n for not married
NbChildren: number of children
Salary: annual salary in euros
Incorrect NbChildren argument: type a positive or zero integer
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop:

The tax calculation check values are displayed: 4,282, 2,959, and 11,519 euros. The incorrect entry on line 8 was detected by layer [ui], which did not call layer [business]: the service received only valid requests. If the service is stopped:

> mvn -q compile exec:java
Tax calculation parameters in the format: Married (y/n) NbChildren Salary, or nothing to stop: y 2 60000
Exception chain:
----------------------------------------
tax.entities.TaxException: The web service http://localhost:5120/tax is unreachable
----------------------------------------
java.net.ConnectException: null
----------------------------------------
java.net.ConnectException: null
----------------------------------------
java.nio.channels.ClosedChannelException: null
----------------------------------------

Our proxy’s [TaxException] encapsulates the [ConnectException] exception thrown by [send], which itself encapsulates the network layer exceptions (Chapter 12). None of them have a message: [getMessage()] returns [null].

docs.title: 13.5. A web client for the tax calculation service
docs.text:
A “traditional” web application generates its pages (HTML) on the server: each time a button is clicked, the form is sent to the server, which returns a new, complete page to the browser. Today, the browser most often queries a web service itself, in JavaScript, and updates only the part of the page that has changed. That’s what we’re going to do. The architecture is as follows:

  • 1: The browser requests the page [/]; the server [WsTax] sends it the static file [index.html];
  • 2: Each time the [Calculate] button is clicked, the JavaScript code on the page sends the [POST /tax] request to the web service and displays the received tax amount on the page without reloading it.

The web service has not been modified: it simply serves one additional file. Spring Boot automatically serves files placed in the [static] folder within the application’s resources ([src/main/resources/static]) as static files: HTML pages, images, scripts, style sheets, etc. The [static/index.html] file is also served for the URL [/]: this is the welcome page. A single server can thus host both a website and a web service. The [index.html] page is as follows:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <title>Calculate your tax</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: sans-serif; background: #ffffe0; margin: 2em; }
    td { padding: 4px 8px; white-space: nowrap; }
    .error { color: #cc2200; }
    #tax:not(:empty) { background: #99ccff; padding: 2px 8px; font-weight: bold; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h2>Calculate your tax</h2>
  <form id="form">
    <table>
      <tr>
        <td>Are you married</td>
        <td>
          <label><input type="radio" name="married" value="yes"> Yes</label>
          <label><input type="radio" name="married" value="no" checked> No</label>
        </td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>Number of children</td>
        <td><input type="text" id="children" size="3"></td>
        <td class="error" id="childrenError"></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>Annual salary</td>
        <td><input type="text" id="salary" size="8"></td>
        <td class="error" id="salaryError"></td>
      </tr>
      <tr>
        <td>Tax to pay</td>
        <td><span id="tax"></span></td>
      </tr>
    </table>
    <p class="error" id="message"></p>
    <p>
      <button type="submit">Calculate</button>
      <button type="button" id="clear">Clear</button>
    </p>
  </form>

  <script>
    // the elements of the page
    const form = document.getElementById("form");
    const children = document.getElementById("children");
    const salary = document.getElementById("salary");
    const tax = document.getElementById("tax");
    const childrenError = document.getElementById("childrenError");
    const salaryError = document.getElementById("salaryError");
    const message = document.getElementById("message");

    // an entered integer, or null if the input is not an integer
    function readInteger(text) {
      return /^\s*-?\d+\s*$/.test(text) ? parseInt(text, 10) : null;
    }

    // clears the result and the error messages
    function clearMessages() {
      tax.textContent = "";
      childrenError.textContent = "";
      salaryError.textContent = "";
      message.textContent = "";
    }

    // [Calculate] button: we query the web service, without reloading the page
    form.addEventListener("submit", async (event) => {
      event.preventDefault();
      clearMessages();
      // the request, in the format expected by POST /tax
      const request = {
        married: form.married.value === "yes",
        children: readInteger(children.value),
        salary: readInteger(salary.value)
      };
      try {
        const response = await fetch("tax", {
          method: "POST",
          headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
          body: JSON.stringify(request)
        });
        const body = await response.json();
        if (response.ok) {
          // 200: {"tax": 4282}
          tax.textContent = `${body.tax} euros`;
        } else {
          // 400: a "Problem Details" document with the errors per parameter
          const errors = body.errors ?? {};
          childrenError.textContent = errors.children?.join(" ") ?? "";
          salaryError.textContent = errors.salary?.join(" ") ?? "";
          message.textContent = body.title;
        }
      } catch (e) {
        // the service is unreachable
        message.textContent = `Error communicating with the service: ${e.message}`;
      }
    });

    // [Clear] button: reset of the form
    document.getElementById("clear").addEventListener("click", () => {
      children.value = "";
      salary.value = "";
      clearMessages();
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

Comments:

  • Lines 15–44: the form: two radio buttons for marital status, two input fields for the number of children and salary—each followed by a cell where an error message (if any) will be displayed—one field for taxes, a paragraph for a general message, and two buttons;
  • lines 46–108: the page’s code, JavaScript, executed by the browser. The course does not cover JavaScript; however, this code is close enough to Java to be read without difficulty;
  • line 57: an input that is not an integer results in [null]; it is up to the service to report the error;
  • line 70: the click handler for the [Calculate] button (submit form). This is an asynchronous function ([async]): like [CompletableFuture] (Chapter 9), it does not block the browser while waiting for a response;
  • line 71: we prevent the browser from submitting the form on its own, which would cause a new page to load;
  • lines 74–77: the request, a JavaScript object that has the format expected by [POST /tax];
  • lines 80–83: The browser’s [fetch] function sends the HTTP request: the method [POST], the header [Content-Type], and the body—the request serialized into JSON by [JSON.stringify]. The URL [tax] is relative to the page: the request is sent to the server that provided the page. [await] waits for the response without blocking the browser;
  • line 85: the body of the response is deserialized into an object;
  • lines 86–88: if successful (2xx code), the tax amount is displayed;
  • lines 91–94: if an error occurs, the document title “Problem Details” is displayed, along with error messages regarding the number of children and the salary, each next to its corresponding input field. The operator [?.] returns [undefined] if the object to its left does not exist, rather than causing an error; the operator [??] replaces a missing value with the value that follows it. Java has no direct equivalent for these operators: in Java, you use [null] tests or a [Optional];
  • Lines 103–106: The [Clear] button resets the form locally, without querying the service.

Now that the service is running, let’s request the URL [http://localhost:5120/] using a browser:

After entering a calculation and clicking the [Calculate] button:

If the input is incorrect, the error messages are those from the web service:

These screenshots were taken using the Chromium browser, controlled by a program via the Playwright library: this is how we automate testing of a web interface.

Here, the page and the service share the same origin (same protocol, same machine, same port: [http://localhost:5120]). If the page were served by another site, for example [http://localhost:5000], the browser would enforce the same-origin policy: it would only allow the code JavaScript to read the service’s response if the service authorizes it via the header [Access-Control-Allow-Origin]. For a request like ours (POST with a body of JSON), the browser would even request this authorization before sending the request, via a preliminary request using the OPTIONS method (preflight). This is the CORS mechanism (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing), which protects the user from malicious pages that might attempt to use services where the user is logged in without their knowledge. To allow other origins, a Spring controller can be annotated with [@CrossOrigin(origins = "http://localhost:5000")]; global configuration is also possible (the [addCorsMappings] method of the [WebMvcConfigurer] interface). Clients that are not browsers ([curl], our console clients) are not affected by CORS.

For richer web interfaces generated by the server, Spring MVC also provides controllers that return HTML pages built from templates (such as Thymeleaf), which are beyond the scope of this course.

docs.title: 13.6. A web service is independent of its client’s programming language
docs.text:
With a SOAP service, the client had to have a tool capable of reading the WSDL and generating the proxy, and differences in how standards were interpreted across platforms often caused interoperability issues. With a REST/JSON service, any language that has a HTTP client and a JSON library, that is, all current languages, can query the service without any special tools. We’ve already seen this with [curl], which isn’t written in Java, and with the browser-based JavaScript. Here is a client written for Node.js, the runtime environment for JavaScript outside the browser:

// a JavaScript (Node.js) client of the tax calculation web service
// call: node client-tax.mjs [service url]
const serviceUrl = process.argv[2] ?? "http://localhost:5120/";

// the requests to send: the last one is incorrect
const requests = [
  { married: true, children: 2, salary: 60000 },
  { married: false, children: 0, salary: 60000 },
  { married: true, children: -1, salary: 60000 },
];

for (const request of requests) {
  // POST /tax with the request in JSON
  const response = await fetch(new URL("tax", serviceUrl), {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(request),
  });
  const body = await response.json();
  if (response.ok) {
    console.log(`${JSON.stringify(request)} -> tax = ${body.tax} euros`);
  } else {
    console.log(`${JSON.stringify(request)} -> error ${response.status}: ${JSON.stringify(body.errors)}`);
  }
}
  • line 3: the service’s URL, passed as an argument or set by default;
  • lines 6–9: three calculation requests, the last of which is incorrect;
  • lines 14–17: the same [fetch] function as in the browser;
  • lines 20–23: display of the tax amount or errors.

Once the service is running:

> node client-tax.mjs
{"married":true,"children":2,"salary":60000} -> tax = 4282 euros
{"married":false,"children":0,"salary":60000} -> tax = 11519 euros
{"married":true,"children":-1,"salary":60000} -> error 400: {"children":["The number of children must be a positive or zero integer"]}

In Python, you would similarly use the [requests] or [httpx] module; in C#, the [HttpClient] class. Finally, here is the log for the [WsTax] service during all the tests in this chapter ([curl], console client, browser, Node.js client), until it was terminated with Ctrl-C (the course has abbreviated the paths on line 2 to [...]):

> mvn spring-boot:run
19:03:44.598 INFO  [main] WsTaxApplication : Starting WsTaxApplication using Java 25.0.4.1 with PID 25879 (... in .../13-web-services/WsTax)
19:03:44.621 INFO  [main] WsTaxApplication : No active profile set, falling back to 1 default profile: "default"
19:03:50.050 INFO  [main] TomcatWebServer : Tomcat initialized with port 5120 (http)
19:03:50.140 INFO  [main] StandardService : Starting service [Tomcat]
19:03:50.166 INFO  [main] StandardEngine : Starting Servlet engine: [Apache Tomcat/11.0.24]
19:03:50.314 INFO  [main] WebApplicationContextInitializer : Root WebApplicationContext: initialization completed in 4921 ms
19:03:51.065 INFO  [main] WelcomePageHandlerMapping : Adding welcome page: class path resource [static/index.html]
19:03:53.070 INFO  [main] TomcatWebServer : Tomcat started on port 5120 (http) with context path '/'
19:03:53.142 INFO  [main] WsTaxApplication : Started WsTaxApplication in 10.178 seconds (process running for 11.043)

docs.title: 13.7.1. Response Types and Error Handling
docs.text:
The [WsOperations] service returns [ResponseEntity<?>] objects: based on the signatures of its methods alone, it is unclear what responses they might produce, and the compiler does not perform any checks. The [WsTax] service returns the specific type of its response upon success, [TaxResponse], and signals errors via exceptions, which are converted into responses by a [@ExceptionHandler] handler. This is the most common approach with Spring: the method code handles only the normal case, and the tools (the OpenAPI document generator in particular) know the JSON response schema without being explicitly told. A unit test can also directly call a controller method and examine its result, without going through HTTP. [ResponseEntity<T>], with a specific type, remains useful when you need to select the status code or add headers, for example, for a 201 (Created) response accompanied by its [Location] header: [ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(client)].

A [@ExceptionHandler] handler placed in a controller handles only that controller’s exceptions. To handle exceptions from all controllers in an application, place the handlers in a class annotated with [@RestControllerAdvice]. Spring also provides the [ErrorResponseException] class, an exception that directly carries a [ProblemDetail] and produces the corresponding response without a handler, and the [ResponseEntityExceptionHandler] class, which can be extended to customize responses to errors detected by Spring MVC itself (unreadable JSON document, invalid document type, etc.).

docs.title: 13.7.2. A common prefix for routes
docs.text: When multiple routes share a prefix, it is specified once and for all using the [@RequestMapping] annotation placed on the controller class. For example, with [@RequestMapping("/api/operations")] on the class [OperationsController], the routes become [GET /api/operations/add?a=1&b=2] and [POST /api/operations/calculation], with no other changes. This is also a simple way to manage service versions ([/api/v1/...], [/api/v2/...]).

docs.title: 13.7.3. Interceptors and Validation
docs.text:
Our services validate their own parameters. Spring provides two mechanisms for moving this code out of the controllers:

  • interceptors: a class that implements the [HandlerInterceptor] interface, registered via the [addInterceptors] method of [WebMvcConfigurer], is executed before and after controller methods; it can examine the request and respond on its own, without calling the controller. They are used for logging, measuring response times, authentication, and more. Servlet filters ([jakarta.servlet.Filter]) serve the same purpose at a lower level;
  • validation: with the [spring-boot-starter-validation] starter (which provides Hibernate Validator, the reference implementation of the API Jakarta Validation), components of a DTO can be annotated with constraints: [record TaxRequest(@NotNull Boolean married, @NotNull @Min(0) Integer children, @NotNull @Min(0) Integer salary)]. A [@Valid @RequestBody TaxRequest request] parameter is then validated before the method is called, and an invalid request is rejected with a 400 “Problem Details” response, such as the ones we have constructed.

docs.title: 13.7.4. Hosting
docs.text:
Our services are run by [mvn spring-boot:run], which is suitable for development. In production:

  • the application is first packaged by [mvn package]: the Spring Boot plugin generates a single “executable” [.jar] file, which contains the application, its dependencies, and the Tomcat server. Simply copy it to the server and run it using [java -jar ws-tax-9.0.jar]; the configuration can be modified using command-line arguments ([--server.port=80]), environment variables, or a [application.properties] file placed alongside the [.jar] file;
  • Tomcat can be exposed directly to the Internet, but it is often placed behind a reverse proxy (nginx or Apache on Linux, IIS on Windows) that receives requests HTTPS, manages certificates, and distributes the load across multiple instances of the application;
  • The application can also be deployed as a container image (Docker), which the Spring Boot plugin can generate without a [Dockerfile] file: [mvn spring-boot:build-image]. The image then runs on any container platform, whether on your own server or with a hosting provider;
  • HTTPS is essential: the Spring Boot properties [server.ssl.*] configure the Tomcat server certificate when the server is exposed directly.

docs.title: 13.8. Conclusion
docs.text:
This chapter introduced the REST/JSON web services, the successors to the SOAP web services, written using Spring Boot and Spring MVC. We have seen:

  • that a web service maps URL and HTTP methods to Java methods using [@RestController] annotations, [@GetMapping] and [@PostMapping], and that the parameters for these methods are drawn from the route ([@PathVariable]), the query string ([@RequestParam]), the body (JSON, [@RequestBody]), or the Spring container (constructor injection);
  • that the results are sent as JSON by Jackson, and errors are reported via a status code and a “Problem Details” document ([ProblemDetail], [ResponseEntity], [@ExceptionHandler]);
  • that a Java client uses [java.net.http.HttpClient] and Jackson, and that a client written in any other language can do the same;
  • that the layered architecture delivered on its promises: Version 9 of the tax calculation reuses, without modification, the server-side layers [dao] and [business] from Version 5, as well as its client-side layer [ui]; All it took was writing the web service (about 100 lines) and a new implementation of the [ITaxBusiness] interface (about 60 lines).
